title: StateAct: Program State, before Pixels, for Long-Horizon Computer-Use Agents
summary: Computer-use agents are usually improved by strengthening perception: better models for reading a screenshot and choosing where to click. Yet a screenshot is only a lossy rendering of the underlying program state, e.g., the files, application backends, and DOM that hold the task data. Different states can produce the same pixels, while code can inspect and modify that state directly. StateAct is a code-first, multi-agent harness built around this distinction. Its main agent works directly with program state by using code, while a dedicated GUI subagent handles screenshot-and-click interaction on the few subgoals that need it, just 28 of 108 tasks and 1.1% of main-agent steps. The same direct access to program state also supports verification: an independent finish gate double-checks the saved result for structural failures, e.g., output that is missing, unsaved, or written to the wrong path. To stay on track over hundreds of steps, the main agent hands subgoals to fresh subagents, keeping its own context focused. On OSWorld 2.0, StateAct lifts Claude Opus 4.8 from 20.6% to 26.9% on binary success, and from 54.8% to 61.6% on partial success, at ~ 9x lower cost per task than the same model driven by screenshots alone; a code-only variant with no GUI subagent reaches only 45.9% partial, below that screenshot-based baseline's 54.8%. In general, grounding action, verification, and memory in state, what we call state-grounding, shifts the main bottleneck from perception toward reasoning: failures depend more on what the agent thinks than on what it sees.

AI.tldr: StateAct is a code-first, multi-agent system that grounds actions in program state rather than screenshots, using a main code-based agent with a dedicated GUI subagent for minimal visual interaction. It achieves 26.9% binary success (up from 20.6%) and 61.6% partial success (up from 54.8%) on OSWorld 2.0 at ~9x lower cost, demonstrating that state-grounding shifts the bottleneck from perception to reasoning.
AI.motivation: Screenshots are lossy renderings of actual program state; different states can produce identical pixels, making screenshot-based agents inherently limited. The authors aim to bypass this perception bottleneck by operating directly on program state through code.
AI.method: StateAct uses a code-first, multi-agent harness: a main agent works directly with program state via code, while a dedicated GUI subagent handles screenshot-and-click interaction only when needed (28/108 tasks, 1.1% of steps). An independent finish gate verifies structural correctness. Subgoals are delegated to fresh subagents to maintain context focus.
AI.result: On OSWorld 2.0, StateAct lifts Claude Opus 4.8 from 20.6% to 26.9% binary success and 54.8% to 61.6% partial success, at ~9x lower cost. A code-only variant (no GUI subagent) reaches only 45.9% partial success, below the screenshot-based baseline of 54.8%.
AI.conclusion: State-grounding (grounding action, verification, and memory in program state) shifts the main bottleneck from perception to reasoning: failures depend more on what the agent thinks than on what it sees.

title: The Best Programming Language for Tokenmaxxing: An Investigation of Coding Agent Behavior Across Programming Languages
summary:
Although coding agents are now very effective in a variety of programming languages, this paper first shows that the cost (in tokens) can very significantly by programming language. We evaluate five recent models on programming problems in Python, Java, Rust, and OCaml. We carefully control for problem difficulty, and show that there can be stark variation in token consumption that is consistent across models. To understand why, we analyze both the structure and content of agent trajectories. First, we re-execute every intermediate solution and abstract each trajectory as a sequence of test-outcome vectors, then label the work between successive solutions. This reveals agents repeatedly producing noncompiling solutions in unfamiliar languages and revising solutions that already pass. Second, we analyze trajectory text, finding that agents plan solutions in code comments, distrust the provided tests in favor of inputs they invent, and sidestep unfamiliar target languages by prototyping in Python.
  Our results show that by-language token efficiency is a metric that should be considered when benchmarking and developing multilingual agents, and, for the tokenmaxxer, a guide to the most expensive language to work in.

AI.tldr: This paper reveals that coding agents' token consumption varies significantly by programming language (Python, Java, Rust, OCaml), even controlling for problem difficulty. Through analyzing agent trajectories—both test-outcome sequences and textual content—the authors find patterns like noncompiling solutions in unfamiliar languages, unnecessary revision of passing solutions, planning in code comments, distrusting provided tests, and prototyping in Python to sidestep target languages. They argue token efficiency by language should be a benchmarking metric.
AI.motivation: To show that token cost varies significantly by programming language in coding agents, and to understand the behavioral reasons behind this variation.
AI.method: Evaluated five recent models on programming problems across Python, Java, Rust, and OCaml with controlled problem difficulty. Analyzed agent trajectories by (1) re-executing intermediate solutions and abstracting as test-outcome vector sequences, and (2) analyzing trajectory text content.
AI.result: Token consumption varies starkly by language consistently across models. Agents produce noncompiling solutions in unfamiliar languages, revise already-passing solutions, plan in code comments, distrust provided tests in favor of invented inputs, and prototype in Python to avoid unfamiliar target languages.
AI.conclusion: By-language token efficiency should be a standard metric for benchmarking multilingual coding agents, and the findings serve as a guide to which languages are most expensive to work with.

title: Do Coverage and Mutation Scores of LLM-Generated Test Suites Correlate with Their Effectiveness? (Replicability Study)
comment: 24 pages, 4 figures, 14 tables. Accepted at ISSTA 2026; to appear in Proceedings of the ACM on Software Engineering (PACMSE), Vol. 3, No. ISSTA, Article ISSTA002
summary:
Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have driven growing interest in using LLMs to automate test generation. Prior work commonly evaluates generated test suites using proxy metrics such as code coverage and mutation score. However, studies by Inozemtseva et al. and Papadakis et al. show that, for human-written tests, correlations among coverage, mutation, and real-bug detection can largely vanish once test suite size is controlled, raising concerns about the validity of evaluations based on proxy metrics. It also remains unclear whether these conclusions carry over to LLM-generated tests, given that prevailing LLM-based test-generation workflows differ substantially from traditional approaches.
  In this paper, we conduct a large-scale replication study of these two prior works using a wide range of test suites generated by a diverse set of LLMs, and re-examine the relationships among coverage, mutation, and real-bug detection effectiveness. Our findings diverge substantially from prior results. We show that the usefulness of coverage and mutation is highly context-dependent: in regression-style settings where the code provided to the LLM can be reasonably assumed bug-free, these metrics can provide meaningful signals when comparing across models; in another common scenario where the code-under-test may already be buggy and the goal is to expose the bug within the code-under-test, they no longer serve as reliable indicators. We also find little evidence that test suite size is a dominant confounder for correlations among coverage, mutation, and real-bug detection for LLM-generated tests. Based on these findings, we discuss how to interpret results from prior studies and provide actionable guidance for evaluating LLM-based test generation.

AI.tldr: This replication study re-examines whether code coverage and mutation score correlate with real-bug detection for LLM-generated tests. Unlike prior findings with human-written tests, the study shows that these proxy metrics are useful in regression-style (bug-free code) settings but unreliable when the code-under-test is buggy. Test suite size is not a major confounder for LLM-generated tests.
AI.motivation: To assess whether prior findings (that coverage/mutation correlations vanish after controlling for test suite size) hold for LLM-generated tests, given that LLM-based test generation workflows differ substantially from traditional human-written approaches.
AI.method: Large-scale replication study using test suites generated by diverse LLMs, re-examining relationships among coverage, mutation score, and real-bug detection effectiveness across different testing scenarios.
AI.result: Coverage and mutation usefulness is context-dependent: meaningful signals in regression-style (bug-free code) settings, but unreliable when code-under-test is buggy. Test suite size is not a dominant confounder for LLM-generated tests.
AI.conclusion: Provides actionable guidance for evaluating LLM-based test generation and discusses how to interpret prior study results in light of these new findings.

title: Evaluating and Mitigating the Misguidance Effect of Buggy Code in LLM-Generated Unit Tests
comment: 24 pages, 7 figures, 12 tables. Accepted at ISSTA 2026; to appear in Proceedings of the ACM on Software Engineering (PACMSE), Vol. 3, No. ISSTA, Article ISSTA113
summary: While Large Language Models (LLMs) show great promise for automating unit test generation, recent studies suggest that the quality of generated tests can be negatively impacted when models are prompted with buggy code. This paper presents a new metric to quantitatively measure the "misguidance effect," a phenomenon where buggy code steers LLMs toward generating tests that validate its erroneous behavior rather than expose it. Our analysis reveals that prompting LLMs with buggy code has a severe, twofold impact: it significantly increases "misguided tests" that assert incorrect behavior while simultaneously suppressing the generation of effective, bug-finding tests. We further corroborate this effect from a model-internal perspective, showing that buggy code skews LLMs' preference toward tests that assert the same erroneous behavior. To counter this, we introduce and validate a specification-based unit test generation paradigm that replaces the code under test in the prompt with an LLM-generated specification docstring. Our results show that this paradigm effectively reduces misguided tests while substantially increasing effective tests, improves multi-round, feedback-driven test generation pipelines, and remains applicable to both buggy and bug-free code. Overall, these results suggest that specification-based prompting is a promising strategy for mitigating misguidance from buggy code in LLM-generated unit tests.

AI.tldr: Buggy code misleads LLMs to generate incorrect unit tests; the paper proposes a specification-based prompting paradigm using docstrings to replace buggy code in prompts, effectively reducing misguided tests and increasing effective bug-finding tests.
AI.motivation: Recent studies show that LLM-generated unit test quality degrades when prompted with buggy code, but the phenomenon lacks quantitative measurement and systematic analysis.
AI.method: The authors introduce a metric to quantify the "misguidance effect," analyze its impact from both behavioral and model-internal perspectives, and propose a specification-based test generation paradigm that replaces buggy code with LLM-generated specification docstrings.
AI.result: Buggy code significantly increases misguided tests (asserting incorrect behavior) while suppressing bug-finding tests; specification-based prompting reduces misguided tests, increases effective tests, and improves multi-round feedback-driven pipelines for both buggy and bug-free code.
AI.conclusion: Specification-based prompting is a promising strategy to mitigate the misguidance effect from buggy code in LLM-generated unit tests.

title: URHead: A Unified UV-Space Representation for Joint Mesh-3DGS Optimization in Head Avatars
summary: We present URHead, a unified representation for high-fidelity and animatable head avatars that fundamentally redefines mesh-Gaussian integration. While mesh-based methods offer precise geometric control but lack photorealistic detail, and Gaussian-based approaches achieve photorealism but suffer from poor structural consistency, existing hybrid solutions fail to fully leverage their complementary strengths. Our key contribution is a UV-space unification where both representations share a common UV parameterization. Through joint optimization with adaptive gaussian sampling, our method automatically learns to disentangle and allocate appropriate roles to each component. URHead maintains full parametric controllability while preserving subject-specific details, and outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in reconstruction quality and animation consistency.

AI.tldr: URHead is a unified representation for animatable head avatars that combines mesh and Gaussian representations through a shared UV parameterization, achieving both geometric control and photorealistic detail with state-of-the-art performance.
AI.motivation: Existing methods either offer geometric control (mesh-based) but lack photorealism, or achieve photorealism (Gaussian-based) but suffer from structural inconsistency. Hybrid solutions fail to leverage complementary strengths of both representations.
AI.method: A UV-space unification where both mesh and Gaussian representations share a common UV parameterization, combined with joint optimization and adaptive Gaussian sampling to automatically disentangle and allocate roles to each component.
AI.result: Outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in reconstruction quality and animation consistency, while maintaining full parametric controllability and subject-specific details.
AI.conclusion: URHead effectively redefines mesh-Gaussian integration for head avatars, demonstrating that shared UV parameterization with joint optimization enables both precise geometric control and photorealistic rendering.

title: FedTaste: Topology-Aware Structural Transfer for Multimodal Federated Learning with Missing Modalities
summary: Multimodal Federated Learning is often challenged by arbitrary modality missingness and Non-IID data distributions, which lead to severe representation drift and hinder effective collaboration across clients. Existing methods typically rely on generative imputation, external auxiliary data, or isolated unimodal training to bridge modality gaps, often incurring substantial communication and computational costs as well as potential privacy risks. To address these limitations, we propose FedTaste, a parameter-efficient framework for topology-aware structural transfer in Multimodal Federated Learning with missing modalities. Instead of aligning fragile first-order features, FedTaste focuses on more stable group-level semantic relations. Specifically, FedTaste leverages frozen foundation models to extract a joint multimodal topology from full-modality clients, which is then consolidated by the server into a global structural blueprint. To adapt clients with missing modalities, we introduce Modality-Adaptive Structural Prompts together with spectral consistency regularization, enabling lightweight branch-specific adaptation that aligns local partial representations with the shared blueprint. In this way, FedTaste avoids explicit modality imputation while preserving shared semantic structure across clients. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FedTaste consistently achieves superior performance across multiple datasets and challenging Non-IID settings, while substantially reducing communication overhead compared with existing methods.

AI.tldr: FedTaste is a parameter-efficient federated learning framework that handles missing modalities by transferring topology-aware structural information (group-level semantic relations) rather than fragile first-order features, using frozen foundation models, Modality-Adaptive Structural Prompts, and spectral consistency regularization to align partial client representations with a global structural blueprint without requiring explicit imputation.
AI.motivation: Multimodal Federated Learning suffers from arbitrary modality missingness and Non-IID distributions, causing representation drift. Existing methods (generative imputation, external auxiliary data, isolated unimodal training) incur high communication/computation costs and privacy risks.
AI.method: FedTaste uses frozen foundation models to extract joint multimodal topology from full-modality clients, consolidated by the server into a global structural blueprint. It introduces Modality-Adaptive Structural Prompts with spectral consistency regularization for lightweight branch-specific adaptation, aligning local partial representations with the shared blueprint without explicit imputation.
AI.result: Consistently achieves superior performance across multiple datasets and challenging Non-IID settings, while substantially reducing communication overhead compared to existing methods.
AI.conclusion: FedTaste effectively addresses modality missingness in MFL by shifting focus from first-order feature alignment to stable group-level semantic relations, avoiding explicit imputation and its associated costs/risks while preserving shared semantic structure across clients.

title: Infinite Canons: Maximally Self-Similar Melodic Lines and Canons with Infinite Solutions
comment: 19 pages, 15 figures. Versions of this material were presented at the Joint Mathematics Meetings (2011), Nancarrow in the 21st Century (2012), and the joint AMS/SEM/SMT meeting (2012). A more developed treatment, with musical applications, an interactive program, and greater mathematical detail, is in preparation
summary: Infinite Canons is an ongoing series of canons with infinite solutions. More specifically, each canon is based on a melodic line that can be combined in any number of voices, at any tempo ratios (rational or irrational), and with each voice moving either forward or in retrograde inversion, while maintaining harmonic consistency. This paper describes the structure of these maximally self-similar melodic lines based on two different constructions: 1) a discrete prime-factorization approach yielding self-similarity under all rational ratios, and 2) a continuous logarithmic approach extending this to irrational ratios. In both cases the vertical interval between voices in a tempo ratio of $λ_i / λ_j$ is given by a homomorphism $φ(λ_i / λ_j)$, which is a constant independent of time. Furthermore, under these constructions retrograde inversion collapses to transposition, allowing for all manner of table canons. These structures are demonstrated with suggestive realizations of several different infinite canons. Future work includes a more complete mathematical treatment, musical applications, and an interactive program that allows users to explore an unlimited number of realizations of these pieces.

AI.tldr: The paper presents "Infinite Canons" - melodic lines that can be combined in any number of voices at any tempo ratios (rational or irrational) and in forward or retrograde inversion, using two constructions: a discrete prime-factorization approach (rational ratios) and a continuous logarithmic approach (irrational ratios). The vertical interval between voices is given by a time-independent homomorphism, and retrograde inversion collapses to transposition, enabling table canons.
AI.motivation: To create maximally self-similar melodic lines that can serve as canons with infinite solutions - any number of voices, any tempo ratios, and any direction (forward or retrograde inversion) while maintaining harmonic consistency.
AI.method: Two constructions: (1) discrete prime-factorization approach yielding self-similarity under all rational tempo ratios, and (2) continuous logarithmic approach extending self-similarity to irrational ratios. Both use a homomorphism φ(λᵢ/λⱼ) to determine vertical intervals between voices in a tempo ratio λᵢ/λⱼ, which is time-independent.
AI.result: The vertical interval between voices at tempo ratio λᵢ/λⱼ is given by a constant homomorphism independent of time. Under these constructions, retrograde inversion collapses to transposition, enabling all manner of table canons.
AI.conclusion: The constructions enable infinite canons with unlimited realizations. Future work includes a complete mathematical treatment, musical applications, and an interactive program for user exploration.

title: DINOv3-MIL: Per-Kidney Multi-Label Tumour and Cyst Detection from Foundation-Model Patch Tokens on KiTS23
comment: Accepted at MIUA 2026 (poster). To appear in Frontiers in Medical Technology
summary: Foundation vision models trained on natural images transfer to medical tasks without domain pre-training, but volumetric classification requires aggregating tens of thousands of patch tokens per study, and the aggregator constrains how the resulting model can be interpreted. We compare three aggregators on identical frozen DINOv3 ViT-H/16+ features for renal tumour/cyst detection on KiTS23 (966 kidneys; n=97 test): a CLS-token linear probe, gated attention multiple instance learning (MIL) over 55,296 patch tokens, and a prototype head following ProtoViT. Attention MIL achieves the highest AUROC for tumour (0.74, 95% CI 0.64-0.83) and cyst (0.80, 0.70-0.88), with attention enriched 7.5-9.8x over chance within annotated lesions. The prototype head does not transfer to cyst detection (AUROC 0.51), exposing an interpretability-performance trade-off at this token scale.

AI.tldr: Compares three aggregators (CLS linear probe, gated attention MIL, prototype head) on frozen DINOv3 ViT-H/16+ features for renal tumour/cyst detection in CT volumes, finding attention MIL achieves best performance (AUROC 0.74 tumour, 0.80 cyst) but prototype head fails on cyst detection (AUROC 0.51), revealing interpretability-performance trade-off at large token scale.
AI.motivation: Foundation vision models trained on natural images may transfer to medical tasks without domain pre-training, but volumetric classification requires aggregating many patch tokens per study, and the choice of aggregator affects model interpretability.
AI.method: Three aggregators compared on identical frozen DINOv3 ViT-H/16+ features: (1) CLS-token linear probe, (2) gated attention multiple instance learning (MIL) over 55,296 patch tokens, (3) prototype head following ProtoViT. Evaluated on KiTS23 (966 kidneys, n=97 test) for renal tumour/cyst detection.
AI.result: Attention MIL achieves highest AUROC for tumour (0.74, 95% CI 0.64-0.83) and cyst (0.80, 0.70-0.88), with attention enriched 7.5-9.8x over chance within annotated lesions. Prototype head fails on cyst detection (AUROC 0.51), exposing interpretability-performance trade-off at this token scale.
AI.conclusion: Attention MIL provides the best performance for volumetric medical classification with frozen ViT features, but interpretable aggregators like prototype heads may incur significant performance costs at large token scales, highlighting a trade-off between interpretability and accuracy.

title: Semalith v1.4: A Calibrated 184M Safety Classifier Achieving State-of-the-Art Prompt-Injection Detection at 44x Fewer Parameters than Llama-Guard-3-8B
summary:
Deploying large language models in financial-services and agentic settings requires safety classifiers that simultaneously handle prompt injection, regulatory compliance, and general harm, a combination no existing open guardrail addresses in a single inference pass.
  Semalith v1.4 is a 184M-parameter DeBERTa-v3-base classifier performing simultaneous three-axis safety classification including prompt injection, general harm, and financial-services regulatory compliance, in a single forward pass. Its 22-class head (BENIGN, nine prompt-injection sub-types, general-harm, eleven BFSI labels) is trained with a 4-class auxiliary super-category head under jointly weighted loss, on a 76,204-row corpus mined from 49 public sources with SHA-1 deduplication against every held-out evaluation set, with 21 of 22 benchmarks at zero contamination (max 0.22%).
  Against Llama-Guard-3-8B on 22 held-out benchmarks, Semalith v1.4 wins every prompt-injection evaluation (7/7) and 11 of 18 benchmarks overall at 44x fewer parameters, with FPR = 0.000 on 208 benign agentic prompts vs 0.063 for Llama-Guard-3-8B. On general-harm benchmarks (WildGuardMix, HEx-PHI, HarmBench), Llama-Guard-3 leads; this complementary split is documented in Section 4. Six measured weak spots are disclosed in Section 6.
  Deployment guidance: v1.3 is recommended for conversational moderation deployments (ToxicChat F1 0.624); v1.4 is recommended when BFSI label coverage or zero-FPR on benign agentic prompts is the priority.

AI.tldr: Semalith v1.4 is a 184M-parameter DeBERTa-v3 classifier that performs simultaneous three-axis safety classification (prompt injection, general harm, financial regulatory compliance) in a single pass, outperforming Llama-Guard-3-8B on prompt injection and agentic benign prompts while being 44x smaller, though weaker on general harm benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Financial-services and agentic LLM deployments require safety classifiers covering prompt injection, regulatory compliance, and general harm simultaneously—a capability no existing open guardrail provides in a single inference pass.
AI.method: A 184M-parameter DeBERTa-v3-base model with a 22-class classification head (BENIGN, 9 prompt-injection subtypes, general harm, 11 BFSI labels) and a 4-class auxiliary super-category head, trained with jointly weighted loss on a 76,204-row corpus from 49 public sources with SHA-1 deduplication against held-out sets.
AI.result: Semalith v1.4 wins all 7 prompt-injection evaluations and 11/18 benchmarks overall vs Llama-Guard-3-8B at 44x fewer parameters, with FPR=0.000 on 208 benign agentic prompts (vs 0.063 for Llama-Guard-3-8B). Llama-Guard-3 leads on general-harm benchmarks (WildGuardMix, HEx-PHI, HarmBench).
AI.conclusion: Semalith v1.4 is recommended for BFSI label coverage or zero-FPR on benign agentic prompts; v1.3 is recommended for conversational moderation. The complementary strengths between v1.4 and Llama-Guard-3 are documented for deployment decisions.

title: Concept-based Visual Counterfactual Explanations with Diffusion Models
comment: Accepted at the 4th World Conference on eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI 2026)
summary: Visual counterfactual explanations aim to answer "what minimal change to this image would flip the model's prediction?", and are increasingly important as vision models are deployed in safety-critical domains (e.g., medicine). Existing diffusion-based methods can produce realistic edits, but they rely on external classifiers that must work reliably on noisy images, which makes them fragile and hard to deploy for robust explanations. We introduce C-VCE, a new diffusion framework that builds the classifier directly into the generative model via a concept bottleneck layer, so that counterfactuals are guided by human-interpretable features (concepts) instead of a separate noise robust classifier that works with pixel-level edits. Our model lets users to toggle on/off semantic concepts during sampling, then minimally adjusts relevant image regions, while preserving the rest of the image, respecting feature correlations. To keep edits small and controlled, we add a simple probabilistic regularizer that balances "change the prediction" against "stay close to the original", plus a gradient-based mask that confines modifications to the most relevant regions. On benchmarks such as CelebA, C-VCE matches or improves flip rates while producing counterfactuals that are visually closer to the input and less distorted than baselines that depend on separate noisy-image classifiers. These properties make C-VCE a practical tool for vision systems where users need concrete "what-if" images without having to trust an additional, noise-robust classifier. More broadly, our results suggest that exposing and controlling an internal concept layer is a promising way to make powerful generative models easier to understand and safer to use.

AI.tldr: C-VCE is a diffusion-based framework for visual counterfactual explanations that integrates a concept bottleneck layer directly into the generative model, eliminating the need for external noise-robust classifiers. It enables semantic concept toggling, minimal region-specific edits, and a regularizer balancing prediction change with image fidelity, achieving better visual closeness and less distortion than baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion-based visual counterfactual methods rely on external classifiers that must work reliably on noisy images, making them fragile and hard to deploy for robust explanations.
AI.method: C-VCE builds the classifier directly into the generative model via a concept bottleneck layer, guides counterfactuals by human-interpretable features (concepts), allows concept toggling during sampling, uses a probabilistic regularizer to balance prediction change vs. original closeness, and applies a gradient-based mask to confine edits to relevant regions.
AI.result: On CelebA and other benchmarks, C-VCE matches or improves flip rates while producing counterfactuals that are visually closer to the input and less distorted than baselines relying on separate noisy-image classifiers.
AI.conclusion: Exposing and controlling an internal concept layer is a promising way to make powerful generative models easier to understand and safer to use, positioning C-VCE as a practical tool for vision systems requiring concrete "what-if" images without trusting an additional noise-robust classifier.

title: AssumptionMiner: Extracting, Tracing, and Revising Implicit Assumptions in LLM Code Generation
comment: 20 pages, 6 figures, 9 tables. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering. Replication package: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21535058
summary: Large language models (LLMs) generate code from natural-language prompts, yet real-world prompts rarely provide complete specifications. When prompts leave input formats, error handling, or design decisions unspecified, LLMs fill these gaps with implicit assumptions that shape the generated code's behavior and correctness. Because these assumptions remain hidden, generated code may satisfy tests while violating developer intent. We present AssumptionMiner, a framework that makes implicit assumptions a first-class artifact of LLM-based code generation. In addition to code, AssumptionMiner produces an explicit assumption layer, a structured representation of inferred constraints and design decisions that developers can inspect, confirm, or revise. An AST-based dependency graph enables targeted regeneration of only the code affected by a revised assumption. We also introduce a benchmark of 180 ambiguous programming tasks with 676 annotated assumptions, including a human-verified subset for evaluating code localization. We evaluate assumption extraction, code localization, and assumption-guided regeneration. Across open-source LLMs, a confidence-weighted ensemble achieves an F1 score of 0.816 for assumption extraction, improving on the strongest offline baseline by 3.6x. On the human-verified localization benchmark, AST-guided localization identifies more precise code regions than keyword-based and whole-file baselines. During assumption revision, targeted regeneration modifies less code than non-targeted alternatives while exposing challenges in handling cascading edits. These results demonstrate that making assumptions explicit improves the transparency and controllability of LLM-based code generation.

AI.tldr: AssumptionMiner makes implicit assumptions in LLM code generation explicit, enabling developers to inspect and revise them. It achieves 0.816 F1 for assumption extraction (3.6x improvement) and enables targeted code regeneration from revised assumptions.
AI.motivation: LLMs generate code from ambiguous natural-language prompts, filling unspecified details with hidden assumptions that can violate developer intent even when tests pass.
AI.method: AssumptionMiner generates an explicit assumption layer alongside code, uses AST-based dependency graphs for targeted regeneration upon assumption revision, and employs a confidence-weighted ensemble for extraction.
AI.result: 0.816 F1 for assumption extraction (3.6x over baseline), AST-guided localization outperforms keyword/whole-file baselines, and targeted regeneration modifies less code during revision.
AI.conclusion: Making implicit assumptions explicit improves transparency and controllability of LLM-based code generation.

title: Text-based Tactile Graphics Generation for the Visually Impaired
summary: Tactile graphics are a primary medium for blind and low-vision (BLV) individuals to access non-textual information. However, they are difficult to scale or personalize. While recent generative models have revolutionized visual content creation, they are optimized for screen-based visual realism and fail to satisfy the haptic perceptual and physical fabrication constraints required for touch. We present the first integrated generative system that produces fabrication-ready 2.5D tactile graphics directly from natural language prompts, jointly generating global base geometry, fine-grained tactile surface textures, and standard-compliant braille within a unified 3D-printable representation. Our approach introduces fabrication-aware techniques, including template-guided relief generation, a fast diffusion-based text-to-texture module for high-resolution tileable normal maps, and strict base flattening to ensure tactile readability and printability, while supporting both automatic generation and interactive texture control. Extensive evaluations, together with in-person user studies with BLV participants and blindfolded sighted participants using physically 3D-printed outputs, show that participants consistently prefer our results over baselines. By extending generative graphics beyond screens to touchable reliefs, our work broadens access to generative AI for the BLV community and beyond.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first integrated generative system for creating fabrication-ready 2.5D tactile graphics from natural language prompts, including global geometry, tactile textures, and braille, with fabrication-aware techniques ensuring printability. User studies with BLV and sighted participants show preference over baselines.
AI.motivation: Tactile graphics are essential for BLV individuals but difficult to scale or personalize. Existing generative models are optimized for visual realism on screens and fail to meet haptic perceptual and physical fabrication constraints required for touch.
AI.method: The system jointly generates global base geometry, fine-grained tactile surface textures, and standard-compliant braille within a unified 3D-printable representation. It uses fabrication-aware techniques: template-guided relief generation, a fast diffusion-based text-to-texture module for high-resolution tileable normal maps, and strict base flattening to ensure tactile readability and printability.
AI.result: In-person user studies with BLV participants and blindfolded sighted participants using physically 3D-printed outputs show that participants consistently prefer the system's results over baselines.
AI.conclusion: By extending generative graphics beyond screens to touchable reliefs, this work broadens access to generative AI for the BLV community and beyond.

title: Child-Oriented AIGC Video Risk Reviewing: A Benchmark and Knowledge-Supported Iterative Reasoning Framework
summary: The rapid growth of Artificial Intelligence-generated content (AIGC) is reshaping video production and circulation, exposing children to an increasing volume of AIGC videos. Unlike traditionally produced videos, AIGC videos often exhibit greater uncertainty in visual details, narrative coherence, and content expression, which may introduce developmentally inappropriate risks for children. However, existing video safety research is largely designed for general violation detection from an adult perspective and remains insufficient for identifying the fine-grained, implicit, and context-dependent risks that children may encounter when viewing AIGC videos. To address this gap, we study child-oriented AIGC video reviewing, making three contributions. First, we construct CAVSR, a benchmark of 605 real-world videos collected from multiple platforms, and develop a hierarchical risk taxonomy comprising 6 top-level categories and 26 fine-grained labels to support systematic evaluation of children's viewing risks. Second, we propose QVRS-E, a knowledge- and experience-augmented video reviewing framework that combines multi-agent collaboration with expert and experiential knowledge to support targeted evidence acquisition and fact-grounded reviewing decisions. Third, extensive experiments demonstrate that our method significantly enhances the reviewing of child-related risks integrated with vision-language models, and yields more robust review reports.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the gap in child-oriented AIGC video safety by constructing a benchmark (CAVSR) with 605 videos and a 6-category, 26-label risk taxonomy, and proposes QVRS-E, a knowledge- and experience-augmented multi-agent video reviewing framework that significantly improves risk detection for children compared to existing vision-language models.
AI.motivation: Existing video safety research is designed for general adult-oriented violation detection and fails to identify fine-grained, implicit, and context-dependent risks that children may face when viewing AIGC videos, which exhibit greater uncertainty in visual details, narrative coherence, and content expression.
AI.method: The authors construct CAVSR, a benchmark of 605 real-world AIGC videos with a hierarchical risk taxonomy (6 top-level categories, 26 fine-grained labels). They propose QVRS-E, a knowledge- and experience-augmented framework combining multi-agent collaboration with expert and experiential knowledge for targeted evidence acquisition and fact-grounded reviewing.
AI.result: Experiments show QVRS-E significantly enhances child-related risk reviewing when integrated with vision-language models, and produces more robust review reports compared to baselines.
AI.conclusion: The proposed benchmark and framework effectively address the unique challenges of child-oriented AIGC video safety, enabling systematic evaluation and more accurate detection of developmentally inappropriate risks.

title: Music-Source-Separation-Training (MSST): A Unified Framework for Training and Evaluating Music Demixing Models
summary: Music Source Separation (MSS), the task of recovering individual sound components (stems) from a polyphonic mixture, is central to applications ranging from karaoke and remixing to audio restoration and content production. The separation quality depends on engineering decisions across the entire pipeline: model choice, training data preparation and augmentation, loss function and metrics choice, training configuration, validation, and post-processing. This paper presents MSST (Music-Source-Separation-Training) - a universal open-source framework for MSS tasks, which unifies training, validation, and inference for a broad range of modern demixing model families under a single, configuration-driven interface. The framework supports various model architectures, data preprocessing and augmentations, multiple loss functions and evaluation metrics, which helps with fast iterations and ablation studies. Additionally, the framework supports a range of practical techniques that improve separation quality, such as sliding-window inference with cross-fading, test-time augmentation, model ensembling, and fine-tuning via Low-Rank Adaptation (LORA). Our ablation studies demonstrate improvements of MSS using the above techniques. By consolidating these components into a reproducible, YAML-configurable framework, MSST lowers the barrier to systematic experimentation and enables rapid iteration from idea to verifiable result.

AI.tldr: MSST is a universal open-source framework for Music Source Separation that unifies training, validation, and inference across multiple model architectures under a single YAML-configurable interface, supporting techniques like sliding-window inference, test-time augmentation, model ensembling, and LoRA fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: The quality of Music Source Separation depends on many engineering decisions across the entire pipeline, and existing tools lack a unified, reproducible framework for systematic experimentation and ablation studies.
AI.method: The framework supports multiple model architectures, data preprocessing/augmentations, loss functions, evaluation metrics, sliding-window inference with cross-fading, test-time augmentation, model ensembling, and LoRA fine-tuning, all configured via YAML files.
AI.result: Ablation studies demonstrate improvements in separation quality using the techniques integrated into MSST.
AI.conclusion: MSST lowers the barrier to systematic experimentation in MSS by consolidating components into a reproducible, configuration-driven framework, enabling rapid iteration from idea to verifiable result.

title: MegaSlide-DiT: Memory-Centric Adaptation and Deformable Local Attention for Efficient Video Diffusion
summary: High-resolution video diffusion models built on Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) deliver strong fidelity but quickly exhaust the memory budget of a single workstation. A 100 billion-plus parameter DiT easily requires over a terabyte of persistent state, while naive spatiotemporal self-attention grows quadratically in sequence length. These two walls -- parameter memory and activation memory -- prevent researchers from adapting massive generative models without large GPU clusters. We revisit this problem from a systems perspective and introduce MegaSlide-DiT, a prototype that demonstrates how a pre-trained 105B DiT can be adapted on a single H200 GPU with 1.5 TB of host RAM. Our key insight is that the GPU need not own the model state: all persistent weights, master weights and optimizer moments remain in host memory, while only transient shards are streamed to the GPU on demand. Simultaneously, we replace quadratic global attention with 3D Deformable Slide Attention (3D-DSA), a motion-adaptive local attention operator that reduces both memory and computational complexity to linear in the sequence length. We report detailed memory accounting, execution traces and evaluation results to substantiate our design. MegaSlide-DiT does not claim to train a 105B model from scratch on a single GPU, nor does it magically solve bandwidth limits; rather, it offers a pragmatic path for full-parameter adaptation of massive video diffusion models on high-end workstations.

AI.tldr: MegaSlide-DiT adapts a 105B-parameter video diffusion model on a single H200 GPU by offloading persistent state to host RAM and replacing quadratic self-attention with linear-complexity 3D deformable slide attention.
AI.motivation: High-resolution video DiTs exceed single-GPU memory due to both parameter memory (100B+ parameters, >1TB persistent state) and activation memory (quadratic spatiotemporal self-attention). Researchers cannot adapt massive generative models without large GPU clusters.
AI.method: (1) Host-memory offloading: persistent weights, master weights, and optimizer moments stay in host RAM; only transient shards are streamed to GPU on demand. (2) 3D Deformable Slide Attention (3D-DSA): a motion-adaptive local attention operator that reduces memory and compute to linear in sequence length, replacing quadratic global attention.
AI.result: Demonstrates full-parameter adaptation of a 105B DiT on a single H200 GPU with 1.5 TB host RAM; reports detailed memory accounting, execution traces, and evaluation results.
AI.conclusion: MegaSlide-DiT offers a pragmatic path for adapting massive video diffusion models on high-end workstations without requiring large GPU clusters, though it does not eliminate bandwidth limitations or enable full training from scratch.

title: CORVUS: Context Optimization and Reduction Via Underlying Synchronization for LLM Coding Agents
summary: LLM coding agents operate by constructing trajectories that accumulate reasoning, tool calls, and results to enable multi-step decision-making. However, the conventional append-only trajectory architecture found in practice tightly couples file-read actions with their observations, capturing snapshots that become permanently fixed in the chronological history. As files change through agent edits or concurrent human modifications, these snapshots become stale, causing reasoning errors and causing agents to redundantly re-read files, with each re-read appending yet another copy to the trajectory. To mitigate this, we propose CORVUS, a novel trajectory architecture that decouples file-read actions from their observations by maintaining a synchronized registry of relevant files and injecting only their current contents at each reasoning cycle. This structural change produces significantly lighter-weight trajectories that remain synchronized with the actual codebase state by construction, eliminating redundant file copies and stale snapshots that bloat conventional trajectories. We evaluated CORVUS on SWE- POLYBENCH_VERIFIED and SWE-BENCH PRO across four LLMs, achieving 9-50% reduction in average input tokens per task, 15-32% shorter final prompts, and up to 37% fewer reasoning cycles while maintaining comparable pass rates.

AI.tldr: CORVUS proposes a novel trajectory architecture for LLM coding agents that decouples file-read actions from observations via a synchronized file registry, eliminating stale snapshots and redundant file copies, achieving 9-50% token reduction and up to 37% fewer reasoning cycles while maintaining pass rates.
AI.motivation: Conventional append-only trajectory architectures in LLM coding agents tightly couple file-read actions with observations, causing stale snapshots as files change, leading to reasoning errors and redundant re-reads that bloat trajectories.
AI.method: CORVUS decouples file-read actions from observations by maintaining a synchronized registry of relevant files, injecting only their current contents at each reasoning cycle instead of appending stale snapshots to the chronological history.
AI.result: On SWE-POLYBENCH_VERIFIED and SWE-BENCH PRO across four LLMs, CORVUS achieved 9-50% reduction in average input tokens per task, 15-32% shorter final prompts, up to 37% fewer reasoning cycles, while maintaining comparable pass rates.
AI.conclusion: The structural change of decoupling file reads from observations produces lighter-weight trajectories that stay synchronized with the actual codebase state, eliminating redundant copies and stale snapshots that bloat conventional trajectories.

title: SeT-Diff: Towards Semantic Foundation Models for HPC Telemetry and Time-Series
summary: Data centers and their compute nodes require accurate and flexible digital twins capable of modeling the complex interplay of workloads, environmental parameters, and physical metrics. Current machine learning approaches for HPC and its telemetry typically rely on a static subset of anonymous, fixed-position sensor variables tailored to single tasks. Consequently, these models become obsolete when target tasks change or sensor metrics vary. We propose SeT-Diff, the first foundational model for compute node telemetry and time-series. Unlike rigid architectures, our diffusion-based approach conditions the generative process on each sensor's semantic description, decoupling the system dynamics from the structure of the dataset. Experiments on a real-world supercomputer dataset demonstrate a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 0.0470 on reconstruction tasks. SeT-Diff exhibits zero-shot permutation stability, maintaining accuracy with negligible degradation even when sensors are shuffled. A single pre-trained model effectively performs data imputation, forecasting, and virtual sensing - achieving a 0.033 MAE in thermal inference - making SeT-Diff an effective data-driven digital twin for HPC systems.

AI.tldr: SeT-Diff is the first foundational model for compute node telemetry that uses diffusion-based generation conditioned on semantic sensor descriptions, achieving 0.047 MAE on reconstruction, zero-shot permutation stability, and effective data imputation, forecasting, and virtual sensing for HPC digital twins.
AI.motivation: Current ML models for HPC telemetry rely on static, anonymous sensor variables tailored to single tasks, becoming obsolete when tasks or sensor metrics change. A more flexible and generalizable approach is needed for accurate digital twins.
AI.method: SeT-Diff uses a diffusion-based generative model that conditions the generation process on each sensor's semantic description, decoupling system dynamics from dataset structure and enabling flexible handling of varying sensor configurations.
AI.result: Achieves 0.0470 MAE on reconstruction tasks, demonstrates zero-shot permutation stability with negligible degradation under sensor shuffling, and attains 0.033 MAE in thermal inference for virtual sensing.
AI.conclusion: SeT-Diff serves as an effective data-driven digital twin for HPC systems, with a single pre-trained model capable of handling multiple tasks including data imputation, forecasting, and virtual sensing.

title: Metamorphic Testing for Clinical ML Models: A Framework Proposal and Pilot Study
comment: 4 pages, 1 figure, 4 tables. Accepted at the AIware 2026 arXiv Track
summary:
Machine learning models for clinical prediction tasks, such as in-hospital mortality and sepsis onset, routinely achieve high AUROC scores. However, AUROC measures ranking performance rather than clinical sensibility. A model may rank patients correctly overall while predicting a lower mortality risk when a patient's SOFA score worsens, contradicting established medical knowledge.
  This paper proposes applying metamorphic testing (MT) to clinical machine learning models to evaluate behavioral correctness without requiring ground-truth labels for individual predictions. We design a catalog of 12 candidate metamorphic relations (MRs) for three ICU prediction tasks using the MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV datasets, with each MR grounded in an authoritative clinical guideline. We further propose a five-layer validation strategy to ensure that MRs are clinically sound before deployment.
  As a feasibility study, we evaluate the approach on the UCI Heart Disease dataset. Although the three clinical models achieve strong predictive performance (AUROC = 0.849-0.900), they exhibit MT violation rates ranging from 27% to 87% across five pilot MRs. An injected-fault experiment further shows that a sign-negation error in a blood pressure feature remains undetected by AUROC but increases the MT violation rate by 31-67 percentage points. These findings suggest that metamorphic testing provides a valuable complement to conventional performance metrics for assessing the behavioral correctness of clinical prediction models.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes metamorphic testing (MT) to evaluate behavioral correctness of clinical ML models beyond AUROC. Using 12 clinically-grounded metamorphic relations across ICU prediction tasks, they found violation rates of 27-87% despite strong AUROC scores (0.849-0.900). An injected fault experiment showed that sign-negation errors go undetected by AUROC but increase MT violation rates by 31-67 percentage points.
AI.motivation: AUROC measures ranking performance, not clinical sensibility. Models can achieve high AUROC while making clinically contradictory predictions (e.g., predicting lower mortality risk when SOFA scores worsen), which undermines trust in clinical decision support systems.
AI.method: The authors design 12 metamorphic relations (MRs) grounded in clinical guidelines for three ICU prediction tasks using MIMIC-III/IV. They propose a five-layer validation strategy to ensure MRs are clinically sound. Experiments use the UCI Heart Disease dataset with three models (AUROC 0.849-0.900) and five pilot MRs, plus an injected-fault experiment.
AI.result: MT violation rates range from 27% to 87% across five pilot MRs despite strong AUROC scores. A sign-negation error in blood pressure remains undetected by AUROC but increases MT violation rate by 31-67 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Metamorphic testing provides a valuable complement to conventional performance metrics for assessing behavioral correctness of clinical prediction models, as it can detect clinically implausible behaviors that AUROC cannot.

title: Nova3D: Code-Native Generation of Programmable 3D Assets
summary: Current 3D generative models mostly produce a final surface: a visually strong but largely opaque mesh. Interactive 3D worlds need more than a surface. They need named parts, an assembly hierarchy, measurable constraints, local edit handles, and joints for articulation. We present Nova3D, a system that generates 3D assets as executable Blender source code; the compiled mesh, a binary glTF (GLB), is treated as the artifact, not the asset. Because the output is a program, semantic handles exist at generation time rather than being recovered afterward by segmentation or rigging. We evaluate on Nova3D-Bench, a frozen, spec-grounded benchmark of 54 items across six domains and three difficulty levels with text and image inputs, against eleven baselines in four families (mesh-native, part-structured, code-native, and CAD) plus a same-LLM ablation. Nova3D produces an executable program and a valid artifact for 54/54 items. Every asset exposes named parts organized in a parent-child assembly tree; no mesh-native, CAD, or segmentation baseline exposes either. It satisfies 51/52 prompt-stated numeric and count constraints (best baseline: 11/52), passes 14/18 blinded local edits with locality preserved in 18/18, and articulates 59 joints across 12 assets at 98.3% geometric validity, where every baseline exposes zero native joints. Its geometry is competitive: it wins the structured domains in a pairwise shape-quality tournament and is second only to the strongest mesh-native model, while conceding texture realism to baked-PBR systems. The central result is representational: code-native generation turns a generated 3D object from an opaque surface into a programmable asset that downstream systems can inspect, measure, edit, and animate.

AI.tldr: Nova3D generates 3D assets as executable Blender source code rather than opaque meshes, producing named parts, assembly hierarchies, constraints, edit handles, and joints. It achieves 54/54 success on Nova3D-Bench, far outperforming baselines on constraints (51/52 vs 11/52) and articulation (59 joints across 12 assets vs zero), while remaining competitive in geometry quality.
AI.motivation: Existing 3D generative models produce only opaque surface meshes, lacking the named parts, assembly hierarchy, constraints, edit handles, and articulation joints needed for interactive 3D worlds. These semantic handles must be recovered post-generation via segmentation or rigging, rather than being present at generation time.
AI.method: Nova3D generates 3D assets as executable Blender source code (Python scripts), treating the compiled mesh (GLB) as a render artifact rather than the asset itself. This programmatic representation enables named parts organized in parent-child assembly trees, measurable constraints, local edit handles, and joints for articulation to exist at generation time.
AI.result: On Nova3D-Bench (54 items across 6 domains, 3 difficulty levels), Nova3D produces executable programs and valid artifacts for 54/54 items. It satisfies 51/52 prompt-stated constraints (best baseline: 11/52), passes 14/18 blinded local edits with full locality preservation, and articulates 59 joints across 12 assets at 98.3% geometric validity, while all baselines expose zero native joints. Geometry is competitive—winning structured domains in pairwise shape-quality tournament, second only to the strongest mesh-native model.
AI.conclusion: Code-native generation transforms a 3D object from an opaque surface into a programmable asset that downstream systems can inspect, measure, edit, and animate. The central contribution is representational: semantic handles exist at generation time natively, rather than requiring post-hoc recovery.

title: CachedSearch: Training-Free Cached Exploration for Test-Time Search in Video Diffusion
summary: Test-time search lets small video diffusion models rival larger ones, but costs 2-10x more. All candidates are fully denoised, although most are discarded. Training-free caching makes each rollout 2-3x faster at near-lossless quality. Composition is safe only if lossy caching preserves verifier rankings. We present the first study of whether caching corrupts candidate ranking in video test-time search. On Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B with an adaptive caching wrapper (~2x per-candidate speedup), ImageReward scores seed-matched cached and full rollouts. Median per-prompt Spearman rank correlation is 0.905, with 72% top-1 agreement on the VBench suite. VBench-2.0 replicates this result on a harder suite. Recomputing the cached winner at full compute retains 90-94% of the full-search gain. Errors cluster among near-tied candidates, making corruption self-limiting. This finding leads to CachedSearch. It explores every candidate with aggressive caching, then re-generates only the winner at full compute. At N=8, it captures 94.7% of best-of-N's gain at 63% of the cost. Capture rises with width. At matched budget, it searches twice as wide for 38% more gain. The result holds from 1.3B-14B across six models and four families: Wan, LTX, CogVideoX, and Hunyuan. Wan2.1-14B matches the 1.3B model's fidelity. Mid-trajectory pruning multiplies the exploration saving to 3.11x at 88.6% capture. Ports to other model families require recalibrating a single parameter, showing that fidelity tracks architecture rather than parameter count. CachedSearch is training-free, verifier-agnostic, and orthogonal to the search algorithm, making it a plug-in multiplier for test-time scaling.

AI.tldr: CachedSearch accelerates test-time search in video diffusion models by using lossy caching for candidate exploration and re-generating only the winner at full compute, capturing ~95% of best-of-N's gain at 63% cost, with consistent results across six models and four families.
AI.motivation: Test-time search improves small video diffusion models but is computationally expensive (2-10x cost). All candidates are fully denoised even though most are discarded, creating a need for efficient exploration without compromising verifier rankings.
AI.method: CachedSearch: (1) aggressive caching for fast candidate exploration (~2x per-candidate speedup), (2) re-generate only the winner at full compute. Validated via Spearman rank correlation (median 0.905), top-1 agreement (72%), and gain retention (90-94%). Mid-trajectory pruning further improves saving to 3.11x.
AI.result: At N=8, captures 94.7% of best-of-N gain at 63% cost. At matched budget, searches twice as wide for 38% more gain. Consistent across 1.3B-14B, six models, four families (Wan, LTX, CogVideoX, Hunyuan). Errors cluster among near-tied candidates, making corruption self-limiting.
AI.conclusion: CachedSearch is training-free, verifier-agnostic, and orthogonal to the search algorithm, serving as a plug-in multiplier for test-time scaling. Fidelity tracks architecture rather than parameter count; ports require recalibrating a single parameter.

title: Improving Zero-Shot Phonetic Classification through Language-Agnostic Articulatory Features
summary: Recent Phonetic Foundation Models (PFMs) for Speech-to-IPA transcription rely on Grapheme-to-Phoneme (G2P) labels, but the phoneme labels are not necessarily phonetically faithful. To investigate this issue, we evaluate zero-shot phonetic classification on Chinese aspiration and Japanese moraic nasals. A PFM trained on G2P-labeled data excluding these two languages yields poor accuracy on both tasks, showing that multilingual coverage with discrete IPA tokens is not sufficient for unseen settings. To overcome this limitation, we propose a classification method based on continuous Articulatory Feature (AF) vectors extracted from each frame. This AF-based approach outperforms discrete token-based methods, particularly for rare phones. We further show that it is crucial to adopt the optimal temporal aggregation of AF vectors for the target distinction: single-frame classification is best for aspiration, while segmental classification substantially improves nasal classification.

AI.tldr: Phonetic Foundation Models (PFMs) trained on Grapheme-to-Phoneme (G2P) labels show poor zero-shot phonetic classification for unseen languages (Chinese aspiration, Japanese moraic nasals). A proposed method using continuous Articulatory Feature (AF) vectors with optimal temporal aggregation significantly outperforms discrete token-based approaches, especially for rare phones.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether PFMs trained on G2P labels provide phonetically faithful representations, and to address the limitation that multilingual IPA token coverage is insufficient for zero-shot phonetic classification in unseen languages.
AI.method: Evaluate zero-shot phonetic classification on Chinese aspiration and Japanese moraic nasals using a PFM trained on G2P-labeled data (excluding these languages). Propose a classification method using continuous Articulatory Feature (AF) vectors per frame, with optimal temporal aggregation strategies (single-frame for aspiration, segmental for nasal classification).
AI.result: The G2P-based PFM achieved poor accuracy on both unseen language tasks. The AF-based approach outperformed discrete token methods, particularly for rare phones, with best performance when using task-specific temporal aggregation.
AI.conclusion: Continuous AF vectors with appropriate temporal aggregation are more effective than discrete IPA tokens for zero-shot phonetic classification, and optimal aggregation strategy is distinction-dependent.

title: FogDrive: A Multi-Modal Synthetic Driving Dataset for Perception under Graded Fog
summary: Perception under adverse weather remains a critical bottleneck for reliable autonomous driving, yet existing benchmarks lack the systematic multi-modal alignments needed to evaluate robust sensor fusion. Real-world weather datasets suffer from uncontrolled collection and single-level, uncalibrated conditions, while synthetic alternatives either target camera-only restoration or lack the paired clean-and-foggy structure needed to benchmark "defog-then-detect" pipelines. We present FogDrive, a rigorously calibrated, multi-modal autonomous-driving dataset bridging data-centric engineering and robust machine learning. Built with the CARLA simulator, FogDrive contains 660 scenes (~133k fully annotated frames, 50:50 day/night) across four synchronized cameras (RGB, depth, semantic segmentation), a LiDAR and semantic-LiDAR pair, and front radar. Physically consistent fog is modeled independently on camera channels (Koschmieder model) and LiDAR channels (Beer-Lambert law) at three calibrated visibility densities (160m, 100m, 50m). Every scene ships in four matched variants (clean plus three graded fog levels) with cross-calibrated 2D and 3D bounding boxes. A semantic-segmentation-based quality audit over 8k images validates annotations at 95.1% precision and over 99% recall for vehicles within 40m. We establish baseline benchmarks with state-of-the-art architectures (TransFusion, BEVFusion, YOLOv8-m) across two paradigms: 3D multi-modal fusion and 2D image restoration. These yield critical data-centric insights: mixing multi-density fog during training tightens 3D bounding-box geometry without added data-scaling cost, while in 2D pipelines image-quality metrics (PSNR, SSIM) prove poor predictors of downstream detection performance. FogDrive will be fully open-sourced alongside our data-generation framework to accelerate robust, multi-modal research.

AI.tldr: FogDrive is a rigorously calibrated multi-modal autonomous driving dataset under foggy conditions, built with CARLA simulator. It contains 660 scenes (~133k frames) with synchronized cameras (RGB, depth, semantic segmentation), LiDAR, semantic-LiDAR, and radar, across four visibility levels (clean, 160m, 100m, 50m). It enables systematic evaluation of "defog-then-detect" pipelines and provides data-centric insights: mixing multi-density fog during training improves 3D detection geometry, while image-quality metrics (PSNR, SSIM) are poor predictors of downstream 2D detection performance.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks lack systematic multi-modal alignments needed to evaluate robust sensor fusion under adverse weather. Real-world datasets suffer uncontrolled collection and uncalibrated conditions; synthetic alternatives focus on camera-only restoration or lack paired clean-and-foggy structures needed for defog-then-detect pipelines.
AI.method: Built with CARLA simulator, FogDrive uses Koschmieder model for fog on camera channels and Beer-Lambert law for LiDAR channels. It provides four synchronized cameras, LiDAR plus semantic-LiDAR, front radar, and semantic segmentation. Dataset has 660 scenes across four visibility levels with cross-calibrated 2D/3D bounding boxes and a semantic-segmentation-based quality audit.
AI.result: The quality audit yields 95.1% precision and >99% recall for vehicles within 40m. Baseline benchmarks show mixing multi-density fog during training tightens 3D bounding-box geometry without added data-scaling cost. In 2D pipelines, PSNR and SSIM are poor predictors of downstream detection performance.
AI.conclusion: FogDrive provides a rigorous multi-modal foggy driving benchmark that reveals data-centric insights for robust perception. The dataset and generation framework will be fully open-sourced to accelerate multi-modal research under adverse weather.

title: CausalGate: Causal Importance Distillation for Transformer Module Pruning
summary: Existing adaptive inference methods for Large Language Models rely on observational heuristics, such as hidden-state similarity or activation magnitudes, to drop redundant modules. However, these correlation-based metrics often fail to capture subtle, non-linear structural computations vital for semantic accuracy. We introduce CausalGate, an intervention-guided framework for compute-efficient transformer inference. During a calibration phase, CausalGate isolates individual Attention and MLP sub-layers, zeros out their respective outputs, and measures the exact semantic damage via the Kullback-Leibler divergence of the final logit distribution. To eliminate runtime routing overhead, this structural importance hierarchy is distilled into a global set of static, lightweight scalar gates using an Exponential Moving Average smoothing objective paired with a differentiable pairwise ranking loss. Evaluated on TinyLlama-1.1B, Qwen2.5-3B, and Llama-3.1-8B across language modeling and commonsense reasoning benchmarks, CausalGate consistently outperforms prominent dynamic routing and layer-skipping baselines, translating theoretical compute savings into concrete hardware latency reductions with zero operational overhead.

AI.tldr: CausalGate uses causal intervention to measure the semantic importance of Attention/MLP sub-layers via KL divergence, then distills this into static scalar gates for compute-efficient LLM inference without runtime overhead.
AI.motivation: Existing adaptive inference methods for LLMs rely on observational heuristics (e.g., hidden-state similarity, activation magnitudes) that are correlation-based and fail to capture subtle, non-linear structural computations essential for semantic accuracy.
AI.method: During calibration, CausalGate isolates individual Attention/MLP sub-layers, zeros their outputs, and measures semantic damage via KL divergence of final logit distribution. This importance hierarchy is distilled into static lightweight scalar gates using EMA smoothing with differentiable pairwise ranking loss, eliminating runtime routing overhead.
AI.result: Evaluated on TinyLlama-1.1B, Qwen2.5-3B, and Llama-3.1-8B across language modeling and commonsense reasoning tasks; consistently outperforms dynamic routing and layer-skipping baselines with concrete hardware latency reductions and zero operational overhead.
AI.conclusion: Intervention-guided importance measurement (causal) is superior to correlation-based heuristics for identifying redundant modules; static distillation of importance scores enables efficient deployment without runtime routing cost.

title: QFoldAgent: An Autonomous Quantum Optimization Multi-Agent System for Protein Structure Prediction
summary: Hybrid quantum-classical protein structure prediction depends strongly on Hamiltonian penalty weights, yet existing lattice-based workflows typically fix these coefficients by hand and evaluate only very short fragments in simulation. We present QFoldAgent, a closed-loop multi-agent framework for 5-residue tetrahedral-lattice folding in which a design agent proposes sequence-conditioned penalties, a VQE-based quantum-classical pipeline optimizes the resulting Hamiltonian under Qiskit Aer noise, and a feedback agent uses energy-landscape diagnostics and MolProbity validation signals to refine penalties across cycles. Ground-truth metrics such as RMSD are never exposed to the agents and are used only for evaluation. We study the framework on two complementary datasets: 55 QDockBank-derived fragments with known structures and 100 coverage-optimized unseen sequences. On the QDockBank benchmark, QFoldAgent reduces median RMSD from 3.64 Å to 3.20 Å, with the largest gains on the hardest targets. On unseen sequences, the closed loop raises structural validity from 87.5% to 98.7%, recovers 87% of initially invalid cases, and the strongest controller improves cycle-3 energy on 87% of sequences while maintaining 96% Ramachandran-favored geometry. These results show that iterative agent control can systematically improve optimization behavior and reduce failure cases in a 5-residue quantum setting.

AI.tldr: QFoldAgent is a closed-loop multi-agent framework for 5-residue tetrahedral-lattice protein folding that uses a design agent, VQE-based quantum-classical optimization, and a feedback agent to iteratively refine Hamiltonian penalty weights without exposing ground-truth metrics. It reduces median RMSD from 3.64 Å to 3.20 Å on QDockBank benchmarks and improves structural validity from 87.5% to 98.7% on unseen sequences.
AI.motivation: Hybrid quantum-classical protein structure prediction relies heavily on manually fixed Hamiltonian penalty weights, and existing lattice-based workflows only evaluate very short fragments in simulation, lacking systematic penalty refinement.
AI.method: QFoldAgent uses three agents: (1) a design agent proposing sequence-conditioned penalty weights, (2) a VQE-based quantum-classical pipeline optimizing the Hamiltonian under Qiskit Aer noise, and (3) a feedback agent using energy-landscape diagnostics and MolProbity validation signals to refine penalties across closed-loop cycles. Tested on 55 QDockBank fragments and 100 unseen sequences.
AI.result: On QDockBank: median RMSD reduced from 3.64 Å to 3.20 Å. On unseen sequences: structural validity improved from 87.5% to 98.7%, 87% of initially invalid cases recovered, cycle-3 energy improved on 87% of sequences with 96% Ramachandran-favored geometry maintained.
AI.conclusion: Iterative agent control systematically improves optimization behavior and reduces failure cases in a 5-residue quantum protein folding setting, demonstrating the value of closed-loop penalty refinement.

title: Adversarial Test-Hardening for AI-Written Code: An Instrument Autopsy and a Pre-Registered Causal Estimate of the Critic Loop
comment: 26 pages. Two pre-registered experiments; protocols, all run receipts, and analysis code at https://github.com/Jott2121/crucible
summary: Large language models increasingly write both code and the tests meant to check it; coverage records what ran, not what was verified. We study an adversarial test-hardening loop under a mechanical oracle: a Tester model writes tests, mutation testing names surviving injected defects, and a Critic model writes tests to kill exactly those, with every verdict decided mechanically, so no model judges another's output. In Experiment 1, on five Python subjects (one same-lineage-loop cell could not be scored), the loop killed 105 mutants that one-shot generation missed and lost none, and the cross-lineage-Critic question returned a pre-declared null. The central finding was an autopsy: an earlier analysis reported a cross-lineage effect at p = 9.5e-66 that was an instrument artifact, an output cap silently truncating the verbose model, caught only by adversarial review of the completed analysis. Review then found a further confound, each arm resampling its own initial suite; Experiment 2 removes it. Under a pre-registered frozen-shared-round-0 design (five replicates on each of four subjects, seeds committed in advance), same-lineage Critic rounds killed 78% of the survivors the frozen initial suite left standing (mean incremental kill rate 0.783, 95% cluster-bootstrap interval [0.592, 0.935]), a within-replicate causal estimate; the cross-provider configuration showed a positive pilot difference (rate gap 0.178, 95% interval [0.039, 0.347]; magnitude dominated by a single replicate) at 5.5x lower arm cost. This compares two named model-provider-harness configurations, not an isolated lineage effect: part of the gap is one configuration's receipted operational failures, including truncation recurrences, now detected and scored rather than laundered. Cross-model comparisons can inherit the asymmetries of the harness that runs them. We release both protocols, all receipts, and the analysis code.

AI.tldr: This paper studies an adversarial test-hardening loop where a Tester model writes tests, mutation testing identifies surviving defects, and a Critic model writes tests to kill them—all judged mechanically. The loop killed 105 mutants one-shot missed. A previously reported cross-lineage effect (p=9.5e-66) was an artifact of output truncation, caught by adversarial review. A corrected pre-registered experiment showed same-lineage Critics killed 78% of survivors (mean 0.783, 95% CI [0.592, 0.935]), with cross-provider showing a small positive pilot difference (gap 0.178, 95% CI [0.039, 0.347]) at lower cost. The paper warns that cross-model comparisons inherit harness asymmetries.
AI.motivation: To study whether LLMs can improve test quality through an adversarial loop (write tests, find surviving mutants, write tests to kill them) under a mechanical oracle, and to test for cross-lineage effects—whether a Critic model from a different provider outperforms same-lineage Critic—while auditing for artifacts in earlier analyses.
AI.method: Adversarial test-hardening loop: Tester writes tests, mutation testing identifies surviving mutants, Critic writes tests to kill those mutants; all verdicts mechanical. Experiment 1: five Python subjects, one unscoreable; compared same-lineage vs cross-lineage Critic. Post-hoc adversarial review discovered output truncation artifact causing spurious cross-lineage effect. Experiment 2: pre-registered frozen-shared-round-0 design, four subjects, five replicates, seeds committed, comparing same-lineage Critic vs cross-provider Critic.
AI.result: Experiment 1: loop killed 105 mutants one-shot missed, lost none; cross-lineage effect was an output-cap artifact (p=9.5e-66 spurious). Experiment 2: same-lineage Critic mean incremental kill rate 0.783, 95% CI [0.592, 0.935]; cross-provider gap 0.178, 95% CI [0.039, 0.347], 5.5x lower cost, but magnitude dominated by one replicate. Part of gap explained by one configuration's operational failures (truncation recurrences) now detected.
AI.conclusion: The adversarial test-hardening loop improves test suites effectively. Previously reported cross-lineage effects were artifacts. Cross-model comparisons can inherit asymmetries from the harness running them. The paper releases protocols, receipts, and analysis code.

title: Design-Intent Compilation for Heterogeneous Fabrication
summary: Computational fabrication workflows increasingly require designers to specify spatially varying behavior, appearance, material composition, and process state. Yet most workflows force these intentions into printer-specific representations, such as material fractions, voxel labels, mesh partitions, or slicer settings. This coupling makes heterogeneous designs difficult to reuse because each backend requires a different realization of the same property. We present a compiler architecture for heterogeneous fabrication that treats design as a staged, typed lowering problem. A source design consists of implicit geometry and named, typed spatial attribute fields over a shared object domain. These attributes may encode measured data, visual appearance, target mechanical behavior, material recipes, process parameters, or other user-specified attributes. Translation models derive compiler-required realization attributes from source or intent attributes, and backend compilers emit machine-facing outputs such as voxel material stacks, process G-code, or configured slicer project files. This separates source modeling, attribute translation, and backend compilation, allowing a design to remain expressed in fabrication-agnostic terms while each toolchain determines how intent becomes executable instructions. We validate the method through fabricated objects and measurements across sampled volumetric data, CT-derived visual and mechanical models, Shore-hardness fields, and full-color fields, implemented via material jetting and material extrusion. These results show that one source design can be lowered into distinct material, process, and slicer representations without rewriting it in printer-specific terms. We provide the representation, translation framework, compiler interface, and workflows as an open-source Python package to accelerate research in heterogeneous computational fabrication.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a compiler architecture for heterogeneous fabrication that decouples source design (typed spatial attributes over implicit geometry) from backend-specific representations (material fractions, G-code, slicer settings) through staged lowering, enabling design reuse across different printers and processes without rewriting.
AI.motivation: Current computational fabrication workflows force designers to express heterogeneous intentions (varying behavior, appearance, material composition) in printer-specific representations, making designs difficult to reuse across different backends.
