However, these methods fail to identify suitable optimization targets and usually conduct incomprehensive single-level optimization.
  To address these challenges, we propose Optimo, a multi-level LLM-based code optimization approach built on a novel Mixture-of-Prompts (MoP) architecture. In the MoP architecture, Optimo identifies time-critical code structures as performance bottlenecks via differential profiling. These structures are then routed to some optimization strategies, akin to expert models in MoE, each tailored to optimize specific code patterns. Unlike traditional approaches that focus only on statement-level optimizations, Optimo operates at four levels of abstraction, ranging from coarse-grained algorithmic improvements to fine-grained optimizations in API usage. We evaluate Optimo on two code efficiency benchmarks, COFFE and Effibench. Our results demonstrate that Optimo achieves an up to 57.48% opt%, i.e., the percentage of optimized programs that are correct and at least 10% faster than the original programs, and an up to 3.97x speedup when optimizing human-written code, and it consistently outperforms the best baseline by up to 96.51% in terms of opt%. Furthermore, Optimo achieves an up to 42.42% opt% and an up to 13.51x speedup when optimizing LLM-generated code.

AI.tldr: Optimo is a multi-level LLM-based code optimization approach using a Mixture-of-Prompts (MoP) architecture that identifies performance bottlenecks via differential profiling and routes them to specialized optimization strategies across four abstraction levels, achieving up to 57.48% opt% and 3.97x speedup on human-written code, and up to 42.42% opt% and 13.51x speedup on LLM-generated code, consistently outperforming baselines by up to 96.51% in opt%.
AI.motivation: Runtime efficiency is critical for software quality. Traditional code optimization methods work on IRs during compilation for static languages but fail for dynamic languages. LLM-based approaches can optimize source code directly but fail to identify suitable optimization targets and conduct incomprehensive single-level optimization.
AI.method: Optimo uses a Mixture-of-Prompts (MoP) architecture with differential profiling to identify time-critical code structures as performance bottlenecks, then routes them to specialized optimization strategies at four levels of abstraction (algorithmic improvements, statement-level optimizations, etc.).
AI.result: Up to 57.48% opt% and 3.97x speedup on human-written code; up to 42.42% opt% and 13.51x speedup on LLM-generated code; outperforms best baseline by up to 96.51% in opt% on COFFE and Effibench benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Optimo effectively addresses the limitations of prior LLM-based code optimization by enabling multi-level, targeted optimization, significantly improving runtime efficiency for dynamic languages.

title: Hybrid Semantic and Spectral Ensemble for Robust Synthetic Image Source Attribution
comment: Peer-reviewed and accepted to the DLMMDD Challenge Workshop at the 35th International Conference on Artificial Neural Networks (ICANN 2026). 7 pages, 1 figures
summary: The rapid advancement of text-to-image (T2I) models has necessitated robust Synthetic Image Source Attribution (SIA) methodologies. A critical challenge in SIA is the distribution shift between pristine training images and real-world deployed images, which undergo unknown post-processing operations such as JPEG compression and blurring. In this work, proposed for the DLMMDD Challenge at ICANN 2026, we introduce a dual-branch ensemble framework fusing Semantic Deep Learning with Mathematical Forensic Feature Extraction. The semantic branch employs EfficientNet-B0 regularized with Exponential Moving Averaging (EMA) and Label Smoothing. The forensic branch extracts 126 mathematical features -- including SVD spectral profiles and Local Binary Patterns -- from high-pass noise residuals, compressed via Truncated SVD and classified with XGBoost. Evaluated on a dataset of 10 generators where 55% of the test set is degraded, our approach achieves a private leaderboard accuracy of 95.60%. Furthermore, the entire pipeline is highly computationally efficient, requiring no GPU acceleration and executing end-to-end on a standard CPU in under 6.5 hours, highlighting the practicality and scalability of mathematical forensics for real-world deployment.

AI.tldr: A dual-branch ensemble framework combining EfficientNet-B0 (with EMA and Label Smoothing) and XGBoost on 126 mathematical forensic features (SVD, LBP from high-pass residuals) achieves 95.60% accuracy on the DLMMDD Challenge dataset (ICANN 2026) for synthetic image attribution under distribution shift, running entirely on CPU in under 6.5 hours.
AI.motivation: The need for robust Synthetic Image Source Attribution (SIA) methods that can handle distribution shifts caused by unknown post-processing operations (e.g., JPEG compression, blurring) encountered in real-world deployed images, as opposed to pristine training conditions.
AI.method: A dual-branch ensemble: (1) Semantic branch using EfficientNet-B0 with EMA regularization and Label Smoothing; (2) Forensic branch extracting 126 mathematical features (SVD spectral profiles, Local Binary Patterns) from high-pass noise residuals, compressed via Truncated SVD, and classified with XGBoost.
AI.result: 95.60% private leaderboard accuracy on a dataset of 10 generators with 55% of the test set degraded; computationally efficient with no GPU required, end-to-end CPU execution under 6.5 hours.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework demonstrates that combining semantic deep learning with mathematical forensic features provides both high accuracy and practical scalability for real-world SIA under distribution shift, without relying on GPU acceleration.

title: Predicting the Outcome of rTMS Depression Therapy using EEG Signals and CNN
comment: Presented at 8th International Conference on Recent Trends in Image Processing & Pattern Recognition (RTIP2R)
summary: Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) is a non invasive therapy for Major Depressive Disorder (MDD). In this study, we generate images using two time frequency methods to represent EEG signals: Fourier-Bessel Series Expansion with Euclidean Distance (FBSE-ED) and Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT). We propose an efficient deep learning classifier to predict the outcome of rTMS depression therapy. In this study, we use a private rTMS databases to train a lightweight custom Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) using 10-fold cross validation strategy in order to avoid any bias in our results. The results show that the FBSE-ED representation achieves the highest classification accuracy of 93.60\%, outperforming traditional time-frequency technique (DWT). In addition, the proposed architecture with FBSE-ED image representation technique outperforms more complex EEG-Specific deep learning models (EEGNet, DeepConvNet, SleepEEGNet) by 3.62-10.72% and pretrained models (Xception, DenseNet201, and MobileNetV2) by 23.03-27.35%. For more experiments, we utilize another private rTMS database as test database to show the robustness of the proposed model. Our results suggest that integrating advanced signal decomposition with deep learning can facilitate early prediction of rTMS treatment response and support more targeted clinical decision-making. The proposed framework is interpretable, computationally efficient, and well-suited for deployment in real-world local psychiatric clinics.

AI.tldr: This study proposes a lightweight CNN classifier using FBSE-ED time-frequency image representations of EEG signals to predict rTMS treatment outcomes in MDD patients, achieving 93.60% accuracy and outperforming DWT-based methods, EEG-specific deep learning models, and pretrained models across private rTMS databases.
AI.motivation: To enable early prediction of rTMS treatment response in MDD patients using EEG signals, facilitating more targeted and efficient clinical decision-making in psychiatric settings.
AI.method: EEG signals are transformed into time-frequency images using FBSE-ED and DWT methods; a lightweight custom CNN is trained with 10-fold cross-validation on a private rTMS database; the model is further validated on a second private database for robustness.
AI.result: FBSE-ED achieved 93.60% classification accuracy, outperforming DWT; the proposed lightweight CNN outperformed EEG-specific models (EEGNet, DeepConvNet, SleepEEGNet) by 3.62-10.72% and pretrained models (Xception, DenseNet201, MobileNetV2) by 23.03-27.35%.
AI.conclusion: Integrating advanced signal decomposition (FBSE-ED) with lightweight deep learning enables accurate, interpretable, and computationally efficient early prediction of rTMS treatment response, suitable for deployment in real-world psychiatric clinics.

title: Keyword Matters: Unveiling the Energy Sensitivity of On-Device LLM Prompting
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed on mobile and embedded devices to improve privacy and reduce network latency. Yet on-device inference faces a fundamental constraint: high energy consumption on battery-powered, resource-limited hardware. While model compression and runtime acceleration have been widely studied, the effect of \emph{prompt design} on energy efficiency remains underexplored. This paper presents an empirical study of the relationship between prompt wording and energy consumption for on-device LLMs. Using real power measurements collected on a smartphone, we quantify how linguistic features, particularly imperative keywords and instruction structure, affect decoding length and total energy. Our results show consistent energy differences across verbs and tasks, indicating that prompt engineering is a lightweight lever for improving energy efficiency.

AI.tldr: This paper empirically studies how prompt wording affects energy consumption of on-device LLMs, finding that linguistic features like imperative verbs and instruction structure influence decoding length and total energy, suggesting prompt engineering as a lightweight energy-efficiency lever.
AI.motivation: On-device LLM inference faces high energy consumption on battery-powered hardware, but the effect of prompt design on energy efficiency remains underexplored compared to model compression and runtime acceleration.
AI.method: Empirical study using real power measurements collected on a smartphone, quantifying how linguistic features (imperative keywords and instruction structure) affect decoding length and total energy consumption.
AI.result: Consistent energy differences were observed across different verbs and tasks, demonstrating that prompt wording has a measurable impact on energy usage during on-device inference.
AI.conclusion: Prompt engineering can serve as a lightweight, complementary lever for improving energy efficiency of on-device LLMs, alongside traditional compression and acceleration techniques.

title: Semantic-Enhanced Automatic Refinement of Architecture Recovery Results Using LLMs
summary:
Understanding the architecture is crucial for effectively maintaining and managing large software systems. However, discrepancies often exist between the designed and implemented architectures, which can pose significant risks. To identify these discrepancies, architects need to extract the architecture from the system implementation, which is both time-consuming and error-prone. To simplify this procedure, many automatic architecture recovery techniques have been developed. Yet, their accuracy is often limited. Architects must still invest significant effort in refining recovery results to ensure they accurately reflect the implemented architecture.
  To reduce such manual effort, we introduce Semref, a framework that combines LLMs with dependency analysis to automatically refine architectures recovered by existing architecture recovery tools. By leveraging the LLM's semantic understanding capabilities and integrating structural dependencies, Semref enhances both the accuracy and the comprehension of recovered architectures. To evaluate Semref, we tested on 9 projects with published ground-truth architectures and 10 state-of-the-art architecture recovery tools. 5 commonly used metrics are adopted to evaluate the effectiveness of Semref. The results show that Semref improves accuracy across various metrics, with normalized gains ranges from 17.72\% to 43.35\%. Specifically, for MoJoFM and $a2a_{adj}$ metrics, Semref achieves relative improvements of 118.57\% and 100.41\%, respectively.

AI.tldr: Semref is a framework combining LLMs and dependency analysis to automatically refine architectures recovered by existing tools, improving accuracy by 17.72-43.35% across 9 projects and 10 recovery tools.
AI.motivation: Architects need to extract architectures from system implementations to identify discrepancies between designed and implemented architectures, but existing automatic recovery techniques have limited accuracy, requiring significant manual refinement effort.
AI.method: Semref combines Large Language Models (LLMs) with structural dependency analysis to automatically refine architectures recovered by existing recovery tools, leveraging LLM's semantic understanding and integrating structural dependencies.
AI.result: Tested on 9 projects with ground-truth architectures and 10 state-of-the-art recovery tools using 5 metrics. Normalized accuracy gains range from 17.72% to 43.35%, with MoJoFM and a2a_adj achieving 118.57% and 100.41% relative improvements respectively.
AI.conclusion: Semref effectively reduces manual effort in architecture recovery by significantly improving the accuracy of existing recovery tools through the synergistic combination of LLMs and dependency analysis.

title: GNM Head: A Generative aNthropometric Model of the human head
comment: The GNM is publicly available at: https://github.com/google/GNM
summary: Parametric models of the human head are essential tools traditionally used in computer vision and graphics for animation, rendering, and reconstruction. More recently, they serve as crucial conditioning signals within generative large vision models, allowing for tight spatial control of generated imagery. However, existing publicly available models are typically limited in anatomical scope, modeling only outer geometry while ignoring intra-oral and ocular structures, and frequently suffer from reduced geometric quality stemming from low-fidelity input datasets. In this report we introduce a new parametric model dubbed Generative aNthropometric Model (GNM), named as a homophone of the human genome. GNM encompasses the head, face, neck, eyeballs, teeth, and tongue, and it is built on an extensive database of high-resolution 3D scans combined with high-quality anatomy specific artist-made samples. This report details the data provenance, the model architecture including the specialized sub-models for the ocular and intra-oral structures, and shows its SotA performance on fitting target 3D face scans. To foster community innovation, the complete GNM framework is made publicly available.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces GNM (Generative aNthropometric Model), a new parametric human head model that includes outer geometry (face, head, neck) as well as intra-oral (teeth, tongue) and ocular (eyeballs) structures. Built from high-resolution 3D scans and artist-made samples, it achieves state-of-the-art fitting performance and is publicly released.
AI.motivation: Existing parametric head models are limited in anatomical scope (ignoring intra-oral and ocular structures) and suffer from reduced geometric quality due to low-fidelity input datasets, motivating the need for a more complete and high-quality model.
AI.method: GNM is built on an extensive database of high-resolution 3D scans combined with high-quality anatomy-specific artist-made samples. It features specialized sub-models for ocular structures (eyeballs) and intra-oral structures (teeth, tongue) alongside the outer head/face/neck geometry.
AI.result: GNM demonstrates state-of-the-art (SotA) performance on fitting target 3D face scans.
AI.conclusion: The complete GNM framework is made publicly available to foster community innovation, offering a more comprehensive and higher-quality parametric head model than previously available.

title: Visual Token Compression Enhances Robustness of MLLMs
comment: 20 pages, 16 figures. Accepted at ACM Multimedia 2026. Code: https://github.com/Eurek001/OOD-VTP
summary: In this paper, we show for the first time that visual token pruning enhances the robustness of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), mitigating vulnerabilities such as jailbreak attacks and hallucinations. Given that vision and language modalities cannot be perfectly aligned, the misaligned visual tokens might act as out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs, leading to unpredictable outputs and introducing potential vulnerabilities. Building on this insight, we aim to enhance model robustness against jailbreaks and hallucinations by reducing OOD visual tokens at robust-pruning layers, while also reducing inference cost as a side benefit. Specifically, we measure the distance between each visual token and the language feature space. Then, visual tokens with large distances are identified as OOD tokens, which can be iteratively pruned. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, we evaluate it on seven diverse popular benchmarks. Notably, our method yields an average improvement of 13.29\% in defending jailbreak attacks, consistently achieves competitive performance in mitigating hallucinations, and maintains strong results on general datasets like MME.

AI.tldr: First demonstration that visual token pruning improves MLLM robustness by removing misaligned (OOD) visual tokens, reducing jailbreak attacks and hallucinations while also lowering inference costs.
AI.motivation: Vision and language modalities cannot be perfectly aligned; misaligned visual tokens act as out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs, causing unpredictable outputs and vulnerabilities like jailbreak attacks and hallucinations.
AI.method: Measure distance between each visual token and the language feature space; identify tokens with large distances as OOD tokens; iteratively prune these OOD visual tokens at robust-pruning layers.
AI.result: Average 13.29% improvement in defending jailbreak attacks; competitive performance in mitigating hallucinations; strong results on general datasets like MME across seven benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Visual token pruning is an effective approach to enhance MLLM robustness against jailbreaks and hallucinations by removing OOD visual tokens, with the side benefit of reduced inference cost.

title: LC-SEPLM: long-range contact-supervised adaptation for sequence-only protein representation learning
summary: Protein language models learn transferable sequence representations. However, because they primarily model contextual dependencies along amino-acid sequences, their training objectives do not explicitly constrain the model to learn three-dimensional residue contacts formed after folding . Here, we introduce LC-SEPLM (Long-range Contact-supervised ESM Protein Language Model), which adapts ESM2 with LoRA and long-range residue-pair contact supervision while retaining sequence-only downstream inference. Pair-specific queries use cross-attention over the complete sequence to extract global sequence context associated with long-range spatial contacts. To expose the model to diverse structural information, we trained LC-SEPLM on 500,000 AlphaFold Swiss-Prot proteins. In downstream evaluation, LC-SEPLM improved all eight protein-level tasks relative to ESM2. The largest gain occurred in remote-homology recognition, where macro-F1 increased from 0.6122 to 0.6769 (+0.0647, or 6.47 percentage points). On the official ESM-S EC benchmark, LC-SEPLM also outperformed ESM-S with a maximum absolute gain of 0.1771. These results support residue-pair contact supervision as a bounded route for introducing structural information into protein sequence representations while preserving sequence-only inference.

AI.tldr: LC-SEPLM adapts ESM2 with LoRA and long-range contact supervision, training on 500K AlphaFold proteins. It improves all 8 protein-level tasks over ESM2, with the largest gain in remote-homology recognition (macro-F1 +6.47 pp) and outperforms ESM-S on the EC benchmark (up to +0.1771).
AI.motivation: Protein language models like ESM2 learn sequence representations but lack explicit supervision for three-dimensional residue contacts formed after folding. The authors aim to introduce structural information without sacrificing sequence-only inference.
AI.method: LC-SEPLM extends ESM2 with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) and long-range residue-pair contact supervision. Pair-specific queries use cross-attention over the full sequence to capture global context for spatial contacts. Training uses 500,000 AlphaFold-predicted Swiss-Prot proteins.
AI.result: LC-SEPLM improved all eight protein-level tasks over ESM2. Remote-homology recognition macro-F1 rose from 0.6122 to 0.6769 (+0.0647). On the ESM-S EC benchmark, LC-SEPLM outperformed ESM-S with a maximum absolute gain of 0.1771.
AI.conclusion: Residue-pair contact supervision is a bounded and effective approach for injecting structural knowledge into protein sequence representations while preserving purely sequence-based inference.

title: Execution-Grounded Security Testing for Coding Agents in Software Engineering Pipelines
summary: Coding agents are increasingly integrated into system operations, where their tool use can directly modify project artifacts, execution environments, and the underlying system. For example, if a coding agent inserts a hook into a system startup or configuration script, that change can persist after the interaction, be triggered later, and abuse delegated user or system privileges to modify the system. This makes security testing a system problem: the key question is not only what the agent says, but what it actually does to the surrounding environment. We present an execution-grounded red-team testing framework for probing this execution-layer security boundary using observable sandbox evidence, including tool invocations, runtime traces, and file-system diffs. Our framework embeds target unsafe operations into routine software engineering workloads, including unit testing, regression testing, crash reproduction, and validation, and uses an execution oracle to guide refinement when an initial probe is rejected or fails. Across multiple agent frameworks and model backbones, our red-team workload reformulation substantially increases verified unsafe execution, reaching 73.61% on code carriers and 53.93% on text carriers. These results show that coding agents in system operations remain insecure under task disguise: once risky intent is hidden inside plausible engineering tasks, the agent can be induced to carry out unsafe actions on the surrounding system. More broadly, coding agents in system operations still demand stronger security testing and safeguards.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an execution-grounded red-team testing framework for evaluating security vulnerabilities in coding agents used in system operations. By embedding unsafe operations into routine software engineering tasks, the framework shows that agents can be induced to execute harmful actions (e.g., modifying system scripts) at alarming rates (73.61% on code carriers, 53.93% on text carriers), revealing that current coding agents remain insecure under task disguise.
AI.motivation: Coding agents with tool-use capabilities in system operations can directly modify project artifacts and execution environments, creating persistent security risks beyond what the agent says. The key question is what the agent actually does to the surrounding environment, making security testing a system-level problem rather than just a conversational one.
AI.method: The authors propose an execution-grounded red-team testing framework that uses observable sandbox evidence (tool invocations, runtime traces, file-system diffs) to probe the execution-layer security boundary. Target unsafe operations are embedded into routine software engineering workloads (unit testing, regression testing, crash reproduction, validation). An execution oracle guides refinement when an initial probe is rejected or fails.
AI.result: Across multiple agent frameworks and model backbones, the red-team workload reformulation substantially increased verified unsafe execution, reaching 73.61% on code carriers and 53.93% on text carriers.
AI.conclusion: Coding agents in system operations remain insecure under task disguise—once risky intent is hidden inside plausible engineering tasks, agents can be induced to carry out unsafe actions on the surrounding system. The results demand stronger security testing and safeguards for coding agents in system operations.

title: The Influence of Fraudulent AI-Generated Responses on Software Engineering Surveys
summary: Background: Large Language Models (LLMs) introduce new concerns regarding fraudulent or AI assisted participation in software engineering surveys. Aims: This study investigates how suspicious or potentially AI assisted responses may affect the validity of software engineering survey findings. Method: We conducted a secondary analysis of four software engineering survey datasets using manual identification of suspicious responses, automated AI generated text detection, descriptive statistical analysis, and thematic analysis. We compared findings obtained from the original and manually cleaned datasets. Results: Quantitative findings generally remained stable after filtering suspicious responses, although some demographic and analytical variables showed moderate variation, affecting the interpretation of specific participant groups and contextual characteristics. In contrast, qualitative findings were more strongly influenced by changes in contextual framing, code prominence, and the nature of the evidence supporting interpretation, shaping how participants' experiences and study contexts were interpreted and characterized. Conclusions: AI assisted participation may influence software engineering survey findings differently depending on the type of analysis being conducted. The findings reinforce the importance of combining multiple validation procedures, particularly in studies relying on open ended responses.

AI.tldr: This study examines how suspicious or AI-assisted responses affect software engineering survey validity by analyzing four datasets with manual and automated detection. Quantitative results remained mostly stable, but qualitative findings were more impacted by contextual changes. The study emphasizes combining validation procedures, especially for open-ended responses.
AI.motivation: LLMs introduce new concerns about fraudulent or AI-assisted participation in software engineering surveys, potentially threatening the validity of findings derived from such data.
AI.method: Secondary analysis of four software engineering survey datasets using manual identification of suspicious responses, automated AI-generated text detection, descriptive statistical analysis, and thematic analysis, comparing original vs. manually cleaned datasets.
AI.result: Quantitative findings remained generally stable after filtering suspicious responses, though some demographic/analytical variables showed moderate variation. Qualitative findings were more strongly influenced, with changes in contextual framing, code prominence, and evidence interpretation.
AI.conclusion: AI-assisted participation affects survey findings differently by analysis type; combining multiple validation procedures is especially important for studies relying on open-ended responses.

title: Head Avatars with Dynamic Explicit Hair
summary: We present DynHair, a novel method for tracking and modeling dynamic hair for human head avatars. From video input, we reconstruct a dynamic head avatar with an explicit strand-based hair representation using structured 3D Gaussian Splatting. In contrast to the face region of human head avatars, which can be modeled with 3D Gaussians that are attached or generated with respect to some expressive 3D head model, hair is particularly challenging as it exhibits dynamic motion effects. Therefore, we present a novel method that models the dynamic deformations of the hair strands using a temporal network that is conditioned on angular velocity and acceleration of the head, as well as relative gravity. Specifically, an LSTM encodes the motion history and modulates per-point strand features via FiLM conditioning which further used by MLP to produce physically plausible displacements to canonical hairstyle. We jointly optimize this motion and appearance representation of the hair, with a 3DGS-based representation of the face-region, via differentiable Gaussian splatting with photometric, geometric, and physics-based supervision. As a result of our method, we retrieve hair tracking of the training video data and an animatable head avatar with controllable hair dynamics. In our experiments, we demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in terms of hair dynamics, temporal consistency, and generalization across subjects.

AI.tldr: DynHair reconstructs dynamic hair for head avatars from video using structured 3D Gaussian Splatting and a temporal network (LSTM + FiLM) conditioned on head motion to produce physically plausible hair strand displacements, achieving state-of-the-art dynamic hair tracking and animation.
AI.motivation: Modeling dynamic hair motion is challenging for head avatars because hair exhibits complex dynamic effects not captured by standard 3D head models; prior methods struggle to handle hair's non-rigid, temporal behavior.
AI.method: DynHair uses an explicit strand-based hair representation with structured 3D Gaussian Splatting. A temporal network (LSTM) encodes motion history conditioned on angular velocity, acceleration, and gravity; FiLM conditioning modulates per-point strand features, and an MLP produces physically plausible displacements from a canonical hairstyle. The hair model is jointly optimized with a 3DGS-based face representation under photometric, geometric, and physics-based supervision.
AI.result: State-of-the-art performance in hair dynamics, temporal consistency, and generalization across subjects from video input.
AI.conclusion: DynHair enables hair tracking from training video and animatable head avatars with controllable, physically plausible hair dynamics.

title: TOM-GS: Editable Video Representation via Temporal Opacity Modulation of Static 3D Gaussians
summary: While Implicit Neural Representations (INRs) and dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) achieve impressive results in video processing, they often fall short of producing representations that are easily editable. Recent methods address this by introducing complex spatial deformations or folded distributions, which constrain optimization and reduce flexibility for downstream editing. In this paper, we introduce TOM-GS, an editable video representation that forgoes complex deformations in favor of regular 3D Gaussians equipped with a continuous temporal opacity formulation. By assigning a learnable temporal mean and scale to the opacity of each Gaussian, our model enables static 3D spatial components to fade smoothly in and out of the scene. Grounded by robust, off-the-shelf pose estimation, our approach maintains a static spatial geometry that naturally supports a wide range of manual and physics-based edits. TOM-GS outperforms prior editable video representations in visual fidelity, while its reliance on standard 3D Gaussians ensures seamless compatibility with established 3D editing tools.

AI.tldr: TOM-GS introduces an editable video representation using regular 3D Gaussians with continuous temporal opacity, avoiding complex deformations while enabling smooth object fade-in/out and compatibility with standard 3D editing tools.
AI.motivation: Existing INRs and dynamic 3DGS methods achieve good video processing results but produce representations that are difficult to edit, often requiring complex spatial deformations or folded distributions that constrain optimization and reduce editing flexibility.
AI.method: TOM-GS uses regular 3D Gaussians with learnable temporal mean and scale for each Gaussian's opacity, enabling static spatial components to fade smoothly in/out over time, grounded by off-the-shelf pose estimation to maintain static spatial geometry.
AI.result: TOM-GS outperforms prior editable video representations in visual fidelity and ensures seamless compatibility with established 3D editing tools due to its reliance on standard 3D Gaussians.
AI.conclusion: By forgoing complex deformations in favor of a continuous temporal opacity formulation, TOM-GS achieves both high-quality video representation and natural support for manual and physics-based edits.

title: Multimodal Surface EMG Hand Gesture Recognition Using Query-Based Transformers for Prosthetic Control
summary: Hand gesture recognition via surface electromyography (sEMG) is fundamental to prosthetic control. In this field, deep learning approaches have become the gold standard. However, current architectures struggle to scale; model performance typically decreases as the number of hand movements increases. Performance degradation is tied to the increased statistical complexity of decoding expanded gesture sets and compounded by the limitations of state-of-the-art methods, which primarily rely on low-latency unimodal convolutional architectures. Convolutions operate locally, limiting model's ability to capture long-range sequential patterns. Unimodal setups cannot leverage complementary information from coordinated signals characterizing movement execution, such as inertial and eye-tracking data. These limitations motivate architectures that integrate local and global features across multimodal physiological sequences. To bridge this gap, this study introduces EMG-CrossFormer, an end-to-end hybrid convolutional-transformer for seamless multimodal integration. EMG-CrossFormer combines representations from an arbitrary number of unimodal encoders through cascaded cross-attention fusion layers, and decodes the fused representations using learnable gesture queries. EMG-CrossFormer was evaluated on four NinaPro datasets (DB2, DB3, DB7, and DB10) and benchmarked against six state-of-the-art models using an increasing number of modalities. Using only sEMG, EMG-CrossFormer achieved mean accuracies of 72.33%, 52.48%, 79.16%, and 73.49% on DB2, DB3, DB7, and DB10, respectively. Incorporating inertial signals improved performance to 90.66%, 80.40%, 92.79%, and 92.06%. These results show that joint local-global feature modeling improves sEMG-only decoding and that multimodal fusion substantially amplifies this benefit, underscoring the value of both design principles for complex hand gesture recognition.

AI.tldr: EMG-CrossFormer is a hybrid convolutional-transformer architecture for multimodal hand gesture recognition from sEMG, inertial, and eye-tracking data. It uses cascaded cross-attention fusion to combine representations from multiple unimodal encoders and decodes via learnable gesture queries. Evaluated on four NinaPro datasets, it outperforms six state-of-the-art models, achieving up to ~93% accuracy with multimodal input, demonstrating that joint local-global feature modeling and multimodal fusion significantly improve gesture decoding performance.
AI.motivation: Current deep learning architectures for sEMG-based hand gesture recognition struggle to scale with increasing number of gestures due to (1) reliance on low-latency unimodal convolutional architectures that cannot capture long-range sequential patterns, and (2) inability to leverage complementary information from coordinated signals (inertial, eye-tracking) that characterize movement execution.
AI.method: EMG-CrossFormer is an end-to-end hybrid convolutional-transformer architecture that combines representations from an arbitrary number of unimodal encoders via cascaded cross-attention fusion layers, and decodes fused representations using learnable gesture queries.
AI.result: Using only sEMG, mean accuracies of 72.33%, 52.48%, 79.16%, and 73.49% on DB2, DB3, DB7, and DB10. Incorporating inertial signals improved to 90.66%, 80.40%, 92.79%, and 92.06%.
AI.conclusion: Joint local-global feature modeling improves sEMG-only decoding; multimodal fusion substantially amplifies this benefit, validating both design principles for complex hand gesture recognition.

title: Reference Feature Atlases for Mechanistic Auditing of Language Models
summary:
Auditing a new language model usually means relearning and reinterpreting its internal features from scratch. We propose a reference feature atlas: a sparse feature library trained once on a reference panel and reused for new targets, which attach by fitting only a linear decoder. This yields two complementary views. The atlas channel reads the target on already interpreted panel features, providing a stable coordinate system across models. The residual channel learns features only from what the atlas fails to reconstruct, making "outside the reference panel" an explicit audit signal.
  We train leave-one-out atlases over five 7-9B instruction-tuned models and audit held-out Mistral and Qwen targets. On three controlled LoRA hidden objectives injected into both targets, the residual channel makes the planted mechanism perfectly controllable at runtime while matched controls stay unaffected and recovers the planted objective as the top-ranked latent across both targets; on Mistral, where the per-target SAE and pairwise crosscoder baselines are retrained for a head-to-head benchmark, both baselines fail to do so. On Qwen-2.5, the same channel additionally reveals a panel-relative political-framing cluster; steering it shifts the audited framing metrics while out-of-domain controls remain unchanged.

AI.tldr: Proposes a reusable "reference feature atlas" for auditing new language models by fitting only a linear decoder, avoiding retraining from scratch. The residual channel explicitly detects out-of-panel features and enables controllable runtime steering, outperforming per-target SAE and crosscoder baselines on detecting hidden objectives and political framing.
AI.motivation: Auditing a new language model typically requires relearning and reinterpreting its internal features from scratch, which is inefficient and non-scalable. The authors aim to create a reusable auditing framework that transfers across models.
AI.method: A sparse feature library (atlas) is trained once on a reference panel. New target models attach by fitting only a linear decoder, producing two views: (1) the atlas channel reads target activations onto already-interpreted panel features, and (2) the residual channel captures features the atlas fails to reconstruct, serving as an explicit out-of-panel audit signal.
AI.result: On leave-one-out atlases over five 7-9B instruction-tuned models, auditing held-out Mistral and Qwen targets: the residual channel makes planted hidden objectives perfectly controllable at runtime while matched controls remain unaffected, and recovers the planted objective as the top-ranked latent across both targets. Per-target SAE and pairwise crosscoder baselines fail on Mistral. On Qwen-2.5, the residual channel reveals a panel-relative political-framing cluster; steering shifts audited framing metrics without affecting out-of-domain controls.
AI.conclusion: The reference feature atlas provides a stable, reusable coordinate system for cross-model auditing, with the residual channel offering a principled way to detect and control features outside the reference panel, outperforming existing baselines.

title: RESTOR: Automated Test Oracle Generation for RESTful APIs via Reinforcement Learning
comment: Accepted to ISSTA 2026. 22 pages, 8 figures, 2 tables
summary: Modern REST API testing faces a critical challenge in defining reliable test oracles, particularly in agile industrial environments where formal specifications (e.g., OpenAPI) are frequently missing or outdated, and historical execution logs are unavailable for newly deployed endpoints. In this paper, we present Restor (Reinforcement Enhanced Single-Traffic Oracle generator for REST APIs), a framework that generates executable test assertions from a single observed request-response pair in a black-box setting. Unlike existing approaches that rely on rule-based templates or massive training logs, Restor utilizes a novel data augmentation pipeline to fine-tune a lightweight Large Language Model (LLM) via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). This training process enables the model to internalize testing "common sense" by optimizing a reward function that jointly encourages: (i) the selection of stable, semantically meaningful fields for validation and the avoidance of dynamic noise (e.g., timestamps or trace IDs); (ii) the generation of robust assertions that withstand logic variations. We evaluate Restor on an industrial dataset comprising over 2,300 API traces across 246 real-world services. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that Restor significantly outperforms prompt-engineered baselines and generalist models, achieving a superior $F_1$ score of 85.42% in key field identification and increasing the proportion of semantically accurate assertions. Furthermore, deployment in a production CI/CD workflow at ByteDance confirms its practical value: the system raised the adoption rate of automatically generated test cases from 74.1% to over 96%, substantially reducing manual Quality Assurance (QA) effort while ensuring high execution stability.

AI.tldr: Restor is a reinforcement learning-based framework that generates reliable test assertions for REST APIs from a single request-response pair using a fine-tuned lightweight LLM, achieving 85.42% F1 score and raising test case adoption from 74.1% to 96% in production at ByteDance.
AI.motivation: Modern REST API testing lacks reliable test oracles in agile industrial environments where formal specifications (e.g., OpenAPI) are often missing or outdated, and historical logs are unavailable for newly deployed endpoints.
AI.method: Restor fine-tunes a lightweight LLM via GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) with a data augmentation pipeline, using a reward function that jointly encourages stable field selection (avoiding dynamic noise like timestamps) and generation of robust assertions that withstand logic variations.
AI.result: On an industrial dataset of 2,300+ API traces across 246 services, Restor achieves 85.42% F1 score in key field identification. In production at ByteDance, it raised test case adoption rate from 74.1% to over 96%, substantially reducing manual QA effort.
AI.conclusion: Restor demonstrates that reinforcement learning fine-tuning of lightweight LLMs can effectively generate reliable test oracles from a single traffic observation, significantly outperforming prompt-engineered baselines and providing practical value in industrial CI/CD workflows.

title: MMOE: Modernizing Diffusion Transformers with Efficient Expert Design
summary: Modern large language models scale successfully by pairing capacity growth with efficiency, keeping per-token and deployment costs under control as capacity grows. AIGC Foundation Models (AFMs), especially diffusion-transformer backbones, have begun to adopt sparse experts, but recent efforts mostly enlarge total parameter counts and sparsity ratios without importing the efficiency mechanisms that made LLM scaling practical, so generation quality is seldom balanced against training and deployment cost. This raises a natural question: can the architectural principles behind efficient LLM scaling be adapted to AFMs in a more balanced way? We introduce ModernMOE (MMOE), a modernization of SiT-style diffusion transformers that systematically adapts routed experts, shared and lightweight experts, gate-residual routing, and attention-residual information reuse to AIGC generation. Rather than treating MoE as a single plug-in replacement, MMOE studies how different modern expert components affect convergence, efficiency, and generation quality when composed inside a diffusion transformer. Every experiment in this paper is trained on a single eight-GPU H100 node with batch size 256 for 400k steps, an accessible single-machine budget. Under matched training and sampling protocols and at this budget, MMOE reaches lower FID at every recorded checkpoint, that is, it converges faster per training step, than dense and intermediate sparse-expert baselines, and among the sparse variants it attains the best quality-cost balance. Routing analysis further shows stable expert specialization across depth, substantial use of lightweight routes, and modest step-to-step routing changes during denoising. These results suggest that AFMs can follow the balanced scaling path of LLMs by importing proven efficiency designs, rather than by simply increasing total parameters and sparsity ratios.

AI.tldr: ModernMOE (MMOE) adapts efficient LLM-style expert routing and residual mechanisms to diffusion transformers, achieving faster convergence and better FID scores under a fixed single-machine budget than dense and prior sparse baselines.
AI.motivation: AIGC Foundation Models (AFMs) have adopted sparse experts but mostly enlarged parameter counts without importing the efficiency mechanisms that made LLM scaling practical, raising the question of whether LLM architectural principles can be balanced into AFMs.
AI.method: MMOE systematically integrates routed experts, shared/lightweight experts, gate-residual routing, and attention-residual information reuse into SiT-style diffusion transformers, treating MoE as a composable system rather than a single plug-in.
AI.result: At matched training/sampling protocols and a fixed single-machine budget (8×H100, batch 256, 400k steps), MMOE achieves lower FID at every checkpoint, faster convergence per step, and the best quality-cost trade-off among sparse variants, with stable expert specialization and moderate routing dynamics during denoising.
AI.conclusion: AFMs can follow balanced scaling paths like LLMs by importing proven efficiency designs rather than simply increasing total parameters and sparsity ratios.

title: DAMamba-UNet3D: A Parameter-Efficient Mamba State Space U-Net with Dynamic Adaptive Scan for 3D Medical Image Segmentation
summary: We propose parameter-efficient SSM-based U-Net architectures for 3D medical image segmentation. Convolutional U-Nets afford O(n) local mixing per layer but lack explicit global context; transformers provide global reasoning at O(n^2) cost in sequence length $n$. State-space models (SSMs), such as Mamba, offer $O(n)$ global propagation per block. Yet, existing medical SSM segmenters rely on fixed scan patterns and large parameter budgets. Dynamic Adaptive Scan (DAS), which learns data-dependent reordering before selective scan, has not been applied to medical imaging or extended to 3D volumes. We propose DAMamba-UNet3D, a hybrid encoder-decoder that integrates tri-plane 3D-DAS blocks at encoder stages E2-E4 while retaining convolutions elsewhere (~5.3M parameters). On BraTS 2020 five-fold cross-validation, DAMamba-UNet3D achieves mean Dice 0.815+/-0.013 (full-volume per-case evaluation) at ~13x lower parameter cost than SegMamba (0.824+\-0.014, ~70M). At comparable scale, DAMamba-L (~70M), a wide DAS-native variant with encoder-only DAMamba and a convolutional bottleneck, reaches 0.829+\-0.012, surpassing retrained SegMamba by 0.5pt. Component ablations show that encoder-only DAS placement is critical as bottleneck and decoder SSM blocks lower Dice. Together, the results suggest that learned tri-plane DAS in a hybrid U-Net is competitive with, and under our large-scale design may improve upon, SegMamba's fixed Tri-orientated Mamba (ToM) scanning on BraTS 2020. Code: https://github.com/marafathussain/DAMamba-UNet3D.

AI.tldr: DAMamba-UNet3D is a parameter-efficient hybrid U-Net using learned tri-plane Dynamic Adaptive Scan (DAS) blocks for 3D medical image segmentation, achieving competitive Dice scores (0.815 at ~5.3M params, 0.829 at ~70M) on BraTS 2020 with ~13x fewer parameters than SegMamba.
AI.motivation: Existing medical SSM segmenters rely on fixed scan patterns and large parameter budgets. Dynamic Adaptive Scan (DAS), which learns data-dependent reordering, has not been applied to medical imaging or extended to 3D volumes.
AI.method: Proposes DAMamba-UNet3D: a hybrid encoder-decoder integrating tri-plane 3D-DAS blocks at encoder stages E2-E4 with convolutions elsewhere (~5.3M params). Also introduces DAMamba-L (~70M) with encoder-only DAMamba and convolutional bottleneck.
AI.result: On BraTS 2020 five-fold cross-validation: DAMamba-UNet3D achieves mean Dice 0.815±0.013 at ~13x lower parameter cost than SegMamba (0.824±0.014, ~70M). DAMamba-L reaches 0.829±0.012, surpassing retrained SegMamba by 0.5pt.
AI.conclusion: Learned tri-plane DAS in a hybrid U-Net is competitive with fixed Tri-orientated Mamba scanning; encoder-only DAS placement is critical, as SSM blocks in bottleneck and decoder degrade performance.

title: What Softmax Throws Away: Mass-Aware Attention for Evidence Accumulation
summary:
High task performance does not show whether a model retains prediction-relevant structural information in its internal representation. Temporal graph models, for example, can achieve high future-link AUC while basic graph statistics remain difficult to recover from the same representation. We identify one source of this gap in the weighted averaging used by standard attention: when an evidence pattern is repeated, the numerator and denominator grow at the same rate, so inputs with different amounts of accumulated evidence can produce the same aggregate.
  We propose Mass-Aware Attention (MAA), which generalizes standard L1 normalization to an Lp family. Under repetition, MAA makes the numerator and denominator scale at different rates, retaining the effective number of contributing inputs in the representation magnitude. It adds no supervision, parameters, hidden dimensions, or explicit count features, and recovers standard attention at p=1.
  Across four continuous-time dynamic graph models and three datasets, MAA improves future-link AUC in 11 of 12 model-dataset cells. Linear recovery from the same hidden representation increases by 4.49% on average, and preferential-attachment recovery improves in all 12 cells after family-wise correction. We also observe consistent evidence in marked temporal point processes, temporal knowledge graphs, retrieval-augmented generation, and spatio-temporal point processes. Information accessibility and task utility remain distinct: NLL improves in MTPP, ranking is largely preserved in TKG, additional information in RAG does not improve the diagnostic head, and downstream LayerNorm can erase the signal in STPP. These results position MAA as a general normalization principle for improving predictor-facing representation informativeness by controlling repetition invariance in standard attention.

AI.tldr: Mass-Aware Attention (MAA) generalizes standard L1 normalization in attention to an Lp family, making repeated evidence patterns scale differently in numerator and denominator to preserve structural information in representations. It improves representation informativeness and task performance across temporal graphs, MTPP, TKG, RAG, and STPP without adding parameters or supervision.
AI.motivation: High task performance (e.g., future-link AUC) does not guarantee that a model retains prediction-relevant structural information in its internal representation. Temporal graph models can achieve good task metrics while basic graph statistics remain hard to recover from the same representation, indicating a representational gap.
AI.method: Mass-Aware Attention (MAA) generalizes standard L1 normalization in attention to an Lp family, where under repetition of evidence patterns, the numerator and denominator scale at different rates, preserving the effective number of contributing inputs in the representation magnitude. It adds no supervision, parameters, hidden dimensions, or explicit count features, and recovers standard attention at p=1.
AI.result: Across four continuous-time dynamic graph models and three datasets, MAA improves future-link AUC in 11/12 model-dataset cells. Linear recovery from hidden representation increases by 4.49% on average; preferential-attachment recovery improves in all 12 cells after correction. Consistent evidence observed in MTPP, TKG, RAG, and STPP.
AI.conclusion: MAA serves as a general normalization principle for improving predictor-facing representation informativeness by controlling repetition invariance in standard attention. Information accessibility and task utility remain distinct phenomena.

title: SCAIR: Schema-Conditioned Agentic Iterative Reasoning for Enterprise Knowledge Graphs
summary: Knowledge Graph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation (KG-RAG) enables natural language interaction with structured enterprise knowledge, yet existing agentic approaches that perform well on public benchmarks often fail to generalize to real-world enterprise Knowledge Graphs (KGs), which are dense, schema-driven, and operationally constrained. To address these limitations, we propose SCAIR (Schema-Conditioned Agentic Iterative Reasoning), a training-free framework that integrates structured planning with controlled iterative reasoning by injecting schema-conditioned structural priors and enforcing schema-aware traversal during multi-hop reasoning. Experiments on an enterprise-oriented benchmark constructed from a real-world Configuration Management DataBase (CMDB) demonstrate that SCAIR substantially improves performance over existing KG-RAG methods. Crucially, our study highlights that reliable enterprise graph reasoning cannot rely on generic agentic designs; instead, it must explicitly incorporate the target domain's structural and operational constraints into the reasoning process. We demonstrate that by aligning agent design with business logic, substantial performance gains can be achieved without the need for costly model retraining.

AI.tldr: SCAIR is a training-free framework for KG-RAG that injects schema-conditioned structural priors and enforces schema-aware traversal for multi-hop reasoning, outperforming existing methods on an enterprise CMDB benchmark and showing that aligning agent design with business logic yields gains without retraining.
AI.motivation: Existing agentic KG-RAG methods perform well on public benchmarks but fail to generalize to real-world enterprise KGs due to their dense, schema-driven, and operationally constrained nature.
AI.method: SCAIR integrates structured planning with controlled iterative reasoning by injecting schema-conditioned structural priors and enforcing schema-aware traversal during multi-hop reasoning, in a training-free framework.
AI.result: SCAIR substantially improves performance over existing KG-RAG methods on an enterprise-oriented benchmark constructed from a real-world Configuration Management DataBase (CMDB).
AI.conclusion: Reliable enterprise graph reasoning cannot rely on generic agentic designs; it must explicitly incorporate the target domain's structural and operational constraints, and aligning agent design with business logic achieves gains without costly model retraining.

title: Industrial Practice of LLM-Based Test Case Carving and Assertion Generation (Experience Paper)
comment: 23 pages, 6 figures, Proceedings of the 35th ACM SIGSOFT International Symposium on Software Testing and Analysis (ISSTA 2026)
summary:
Enterprise regression testing for microservice systems is often constrained by incomplete or outdated documentation. In practice, QA engineers frequently rely on real execution traffic to reconstruct business scenarios; however, turning raw traffic into replayable regression tests with stable validation logic remains labor-intensive and error-prone.
  This paper presents NL2Test, an end-to-end approach and tool that generates executable API regression tests from (i) a natural-language scenario description and (ii) a traffic capture recorded while executing the scenario. NL2Test addresses two coupled tasks: test case carving, which extracts a minimal replayable request sequence and reconstructs data dependencies so that dynamic values are bound from their responses rather than hard-coded; and assertion generation, which produces assertions aligned with business intent while avoiding non-deterministic fields and hallucinated paths. To improve reliability, NL2Test uses LLMs for semantic interpretation and constrained code synthesis, and uses deterministic algorithms for request filtering, dependency confirmation via value consistency, and assertion-path validation.
  We evaluate NL2Test on 51 industrial regression scenarios extracted from a large consumer-facing Internet company. NL2Test achieves an exact-match rate of 82.4% (42/51), and produces a functionally usable draft in 98.0% (50/51) of scenarios when allowing minor post-edits. In a 9-month production deployment starting in March 2025, NL2Test generated 3,196 test cases with an overall code adoption rate of 85.4%. These results indicate that traffic-grounded generation with deterministic guardrails can substantially reduce manual effort while improving regression automation in complex microservice environments.

AI.tldr: NL2Test is an end-to-end tool that generates executable API regression tests for microservice systems from natural-language scenario descriptions and real traffic captures. It uses LLMs for semantic interpretation and deterministic algorithms for dependency resolution and assertion validation. Evaluated on 51 industrial scenarios, it achieves 82.4% exact-match, 98.0% functionally usable drafts, and 85.4% code adoption rate in a 9-month production deployment with 3,196 test cases.
AI.motivation: Enterprise regression testing for microservice systems suffers from incomplete/outdated documentation, and manually turning raw execution traffic into replayable regression tests with stable validation is labor-intensive and error-prone.
AI.method: NL2Test couples two tasks: (1) test case carving — extracting minimal replayable request sequences and reconstructing data dependencies using value consistency checks instead of hard-coding; (2) assertion generation — producing business-intent-aligned assertions while avoiding non-deterministic fields and hallucinated paths. It combines LLMs for semantic interpretation and constrained code synthesis with deterministic algorithms for request filtering, dependency confirmation, and assertion-path validation.
AI.result: On 51 industrial scenarios: 82.4% exact-match rate (42/51), 98.0% functionally usable drafts with minor edits (50/51). In 9-month production deployment (starting March 2025): 3,196 test cases generated with 85.4% code adoption rate.
AI.conclusion: Traffic-grounded test generation with deterministic guardrails substantially reduces manual effort and improves regression automation in complex microservice environments.

title: $γ$-Bridge: A Look-Parametric Diffusion Bridge
summary: Multiplicative Gamma noise is a signal-dependent degradation in coherent imaging; synthetic aperture radar (SAR) despeckling is its most prominent real-world instance. Existing diffusion denoisers parameterize their forward process by abstract signal-to-noise schedules rather than by the physical look number $L$, so different deployment scenarios typically require separately trained models, and transfer from synthetic Gamma training to real SAR remains challenging without clean ground truth. We introduce $γ$-Bridge, a look-parametric bridge whose schedule $L(t)$ connects the noisy observation at $L_{obs}$ to the clean limit through exact multiplicative Gamma marginals. Its closed-form Gamma--Lévy reverse posterior admits both stochastic and deterministic processes, while observation conditioning and a two-step consistency loss stabilize multi-step inference in the low-SNR single-look regime. Because bridge time directly represents $L$, one conditioned network can smart-start from any admissible input look and stop at a target look number. These two orthogonal controls enable zero-shot restoration over the full admissible grid after training only at $L_{obs} = 1$ on natural images with synthetic Gamma corruption. Combined with a homogeneous-patch look estimator, $γ$-Bridge processes data from six spaceborne and airborne SAR sensors without sensor-specific fine-tuning, achieving leading results on standard synthetic benchmarks while providing physically interpretable input and output controls absent from prior denoisers. Codes are released \href{https://github.com/Teriri1999/GammaBridge}{here}.

AI.tldr: γ-Bridge introduces a look-parametric diffusion bridge for SAR despeckling that uses the physical look number L as its schedule, enabling a single model to handle various noise levels and transfer from synthetic to real SAR data without fine-tuning, achieving state-of-the-art results across multiple sensors.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion denoisers for multiplicative Gamma noise (SAR despeckling) use abstract signal-to-noise schedules rather than the physical look number L, requiring separately trained models for different deployment scenarios and struggling with synthetic-to-real transfer due to lack of clean ground truth.
AI.method: γ-Bridge defines a bridge process with schedule L(t) that connects noisy observations at L_obs to clean limits via exact multiplicative Gamma marginals. It uses a closed-form Gamma-Lévy reverse posterior enabling both stochastic and deterministic sampling, observation conditioning, and a two-step consistency loss for stable low-SNR inference. Bridge time directly represents L, allowing one conditioned network to start from any input look and stop at a target look number.
AI.result: Zero-shot restoration over the full admissible grid after training only at L_obs=1 on natural images with synthetic Gamma corruption. Combined with a homogeneous-patch look estimator, it processes data from six spaceborne and airborne SAR sensors without sensor-specific fine-tuning, achieving leading results on standard synthetic benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: γ-Bridge provides physically interpretable input (initial look) and output (target look) controls absent from prior denoisers, enabling practical zero-shot generalization across diverse SAR sensors and noise regimes.

title: Optimizing Transformer Neural Network for Real-Time Outlier Detection on FPGAs
summary:
In this work, we explore how the inference time of a Transformer Neural Network can be efficiently optimized with applications to real-time anomaly detection in financial time series. The financial time series are price series such as asset prices. Unfortunately, the data is often with errors or outliers that make the downstream data processing tasks useless, unstable or even harmful. Moreover, the amount of financial time-series data has been significantly increasing. Hence, there is a need for better data-cleaning methods in terms of accuracy and in terms of processing speed.
  Transformers as a neural network architecture have achieved superior performances in many tasks such as Natural Language Processing and Computer Vision. Time series modelling and especially anomaly detection tasks can benefit from the features of transformers architecture in multiple ways, including the capacity to capture long-range dependencies and interactions.
  Increasingly powerful hardware, such as field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs), have seen increasing usage in recent years due to their reconfigurability and high performance. They can be efficiently utilized to speed up the computations of the Transformer architecture.
  We explore different Transformer architectures for time series modelling and how they can be efficiently implemented on an FPGA board (PYNQ-Z2). In particular, we examine the application of Transformers to detect anomalies in time series and we show how they can be efficiently implemented on an FPGA board to minimize latency.
  The code is available at https://github.com/thxi/icl_thesis

AI.tldr: This paper explores optimizing Transformer inference time on FPGAs for real-time anomaly detection in financial time series, implementing efficient architectures on a PYNQ-Z2 board to minimize latency.
AI.motivation: Financial time series data contains errors/outliers that make downstream processing unstable, and the volume of such data is growing, creating a need for better data-cleaning methods in both accuracy and processing speed.
AI.method: The authors explore different Transformer architectures for time series modeling and implement them efficiently on an FPGA board (PYNQ-Z2) to leverage hardware reconfigurability and high performance for low-latency inference.
AI.result: Demonstrates that Transformers can be efficiently implemented on FPGA hardware to minimize latency for real-time anomaly detection in financial time series.
AI.conclusion: FPGA-based implementation of Transformer architectures offers a viable path to achieving low-latency anomaly detection in financial time series, addressing both accuracy and speed requirements for real-time applications.

title: Schema-Aware Localisation (SAL): Live Schema Grounding and Hallucination Validation for Oracle NL2SQL
summary: Large language models can generate fluent SQL from natural language, but on real enterprise Oracle databases they frequently fail at execution time: columns and aliases are hallucinated and dialect-specific syntax is missed, leading to ORA-00904 invalid-identifier errors. In this setting, failures are primarily due to missing schema grounding: the model cannot know which tables and columns actually exist. This paper introduces Schema-Aware Localisation (SAL), a lightweight middleware layer for Oracle NL2SQL that requires no model retraining. SAL queries Oracle's USER_TAB_COLUMNS catalog to build a live schema map, selects a relevant table subset for each question (falling back to the full schema for multi-table queries), and injects this ground-truth context into the LLM prompt. Generated SQL is then checked by the Hallucination Index (Hidx), which validates every alias.column reference against the live catalog, automatically rewrites predictable prefix errors, and otherwise triggers a structured retry with itemised corrections. We evaluate SAL on 500 TPC-H natural language questions executed against a live Oracle Autonomous Database 23c instance using GPT-4o-mini. Without any schema grounding, execution-grounded truth (EGT; executes and matches the reference result set) is 2.2% (12/500). A hand-written static schema hint brings EGT to 62.0%. SAL, with no manual schema curation, achieves 62.6% EGT (96% simple, 95% medium, 40.7% complex) while reducing execution failures from 97.6% to 2.6%.

AI.tldr: SAL is a lightweight middleware that improves NL2SQL accuracy on Oracle databases from 2.2% to 62.6% execution-grounded truth by querying live schema catalogs, selecting relevant tables, and validating generated SQL against actual database objects without model retraining.
AI.motivation: Large language models generate fluent SQL from natural language but frequently fail on real enterprise Oracle databases due to missing schema grounding—hallucinating columns/aliases and missing dialect-specific syntax—leading to ORA-00904 invalid-identifier errors.
AI.method: SAL (Schema-Aware Localisation) queries Oracle's USER_TAB_COLUMNS catalog to build a live schema map, selects relevant table subsets per question (falling back to full schema for multi-table queries), injects ground-truth context into LLM prompts, and validates generated SQL using Hallucination Index (Hidx) which checks alias.column references, rewrites predictable prefix errors, and triggers structured retry with itemised corrections.
AI.result: On 500 TPC-H questions against Oracle Autonomous Database 23c with GPT-4o-mini: no grounding achieves 2.2% EGT; static schema hint achieves 62.0% EGT; SAL achieves 62.6% EGT (96% simple, 95% medium, 40.7% complex) while reducing execution failures from 97.6% to 2.6%.
AI.conclusion: SAL demonstrates that live schema grounding through a lightweight middleware layer can dramatically improve NL2SQL reliability on real Oracle databases without any model retraining, outperforming even hand-written static schema hints.

title: Four Years of GenAI: How Educators and Industry Adapted Their Assessment Strategies
summary: GenAI's ability to solve a wide range of software engineering tasks is reshaping the software industry, raising the question of what an entry-level software engineer looks like today. In this work, we investigate whether the core skills for entry-level engineers have changed with GenAI and how the assessment of those skills has changed. Through two surveys, we consider both the educational and hiring perspectives, drawing on responses from 56 educators and 24 hiring professionals across diverse geographic regions to identify gaps and misaligned expectations. We find that educators frame their GenAI policies primarily around academic integrity, whereas GenAI use in industry is near-universal, with organizational policy governing how it should be used rather than whether to use it. Policies on GenAI use during interviews are still emerging, and respondents are split on whether they prefer candidates who demonstrate GenAI skills. Both populations are moving toward GenAI-resistant assessments built on observable real-time interactions and higher-order tasks, and both agree on which skills matter most, rating critical evaluation of AI-generated output, responsible and effective use of GenAI tools, and the ability to learn and adapt independently highly. However, they disagree on graduate readiness in these skills: hiring professionals report larger gaps, with the disagreement concentrated on foundational, non-GenAI-specific skills.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether core skills for entry-level software engineers have changed with GenAI, surveying 56 educators and 24 hiring professionals. Findings reveal a gap: educators focus on academic integrity in GenAI policies while industry has near-universal adoption governed by organizational usage policies. Both groups agree on top skills (critical evaluation of AI output, responsible GenAI use, independent learning) but disagree on graduate readiness, with hiring professionals perceiving larger gaps, especially in foundational non-GenAI skills.
AI.motivation: GenAI's growing ability to solve software engineering tasks is reshaping the industry, raising the question of what an entry-level software engineer looks like today and whether core skills and their assessment have changed.
AI.method: Two surveys were conducted targeting educators (56 respondents) and hiring professionals (24 respondents) across diverse geographic regions to compare educational and hiring perspectives on GenAI's impact on entry-level software engineering skills and assessments.
AI.result: Educators focus GenAI policies on academic integrity; industry adoption is near-universal with policies on how to use it. Interview policies on GenAI are still emerging. Both groups value critical evaluation of AI output, responsible GenAI use, and independent learning. However, hiring professionals perceive larger skill gaps than educators, particularly in foundational non-GenAI skills.
AI.conclusion: There is a misalignment between educational and hiring perspectives on graduate readiness: educators and hiring professionals agree on important skills but disagree on the extent to which graduates possess them, especially foundational skills. Both are moving toward GenAI-resistant assessments based on real-time interactions and higher-order tasks.

title: An Interactive Vision Language Platform for Cognitive Remediation in Schizophrenia
summary: Cognitive remediation tasks often require patients to perform structured actions involving object manipulation and sequential reasoning. For patients diagnosed with schizophrenia, these tasks are crucial for addressing severe cognitive deficits. However, evaluating the correctness of these physical actions generally relies on manual observation by clinicians, which introduces subjectivity and limits the scalability of therapeutic interventions. In this paper, we propose an automated framework based on Vision-Language Models for action verification in cognitive remediation tasks tailored for schizophrenia rehabilitation. The proposed system relies on a camera-monitored tabletop environment composed of structured miniature scenes including roads, a roundabout, a park, and toy vehicles. Patients receive audio instructions describing goal-oriented spatial actions to perform by manipulating a toy vehicle. These interactive physical activities are specifically designed to stimulate targeted cognitive functions, such as sustained attention, motor coordination, spatial navigation, and cognitive flexibility. To verify the correctness of the performed actions without requiring continuous clinical oversight, the system analyzes the video feed tracking the patient's hand and toy movements. A fine-tuned Vision-Language Model interprets the recorded video sequences and generates semantic descriptions of the observed activities, enabling high-level verification of the executed actions with respect to the initial textual instructions. A dedicated dataset of 4634 tabletop cognitive remediation video scenarios was collected to evaluate the proposed approach. Experimental results demonstrate that our specialized framework effectively bridges low-level physical telemetry with high-level clinical feedback, presenting a scalable and objective solution for advanced cognitive rehabilitation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an automated Vision-Language Model framework for verifying patient actions in cognitive remediation tasks for schizophrenia rehabilitation, using a camera-monitored tabletop setup with toy vehicles and miniature scenes. A fine-tuned VLM analyzes video feeds to generate semantic descriptions of actions, enabling objective, scalable verification without continuous clinician oversight, validated on a dataset of 4634 video scenarios.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation of physical actions in cognitive remediation tasks for schizophrenia patients relies on manual clinician observation, which is subjective and limits scalability of therapeutic interventions.
AI.method: A camera-monitored tabletop environment with structured miniature scenes (roads, roundabout, park, toy vehicles) is used. Patients receive audio instructions for spatial actions. A fine-tuned Vision-Language Model analyzes video feeds of hand and toy movements to generate semantic descriptions for verifying action correctness against instructions.
AI.result: A dedicated dataset of 4634 tabletop cognitive remediation video scenarios was collected. Experimental results show the framework effectively bridges low-level physical telemetry with high-level clinical feedback.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework provides a scalable and objective solution for action verification in cognitive rehabilitation, reducing reliance on continuous clinical oversight.

title: FMOPF: Latent Flow Matching with Constraint-Aware Interaction Priors for AC Optimal Power Flow
summary: AC optimal power flow determines the minimum-cost generation dispatch under nonlinear power balance constraints and is solved thousands of times daily in electricity market operations. Learning a direct mapping from load conditions to OPF solutions can accelerate this computation, yet with deepening renewable penetration, a single optimal dispatch is no longer sufficient. Operators require a characterization of the distribution of feasible near-optimal solutions for risk quantification, sensitivity analysis, and multi-objective trade-off assessment. Supervised neural networks provide fast point predictions but cannot capture this conditional distribution. Diffusion-based generative models can sample diverse solutions in principle, yet existing methods operating in the raw state space exhibit degraded solution quality and fail to scale beyond medium-sized systems. We identify the root cause as the conflation of two distinct tasks within a single model. Compressing the high-dimensional OPF solution manifold is one task, and learning the conditional mapping from loads to that manifold is another. This paper presents FMOPF, a framework that resolves this conflation by decoupling compression from generation through latent flow matching and by explicitly modeling load-state coupling through a Constraint-Aware Interaction Prior Network. Experiments on four IEEE test systems demonstrate that FMOPF provides the most effective Newton-Raphson warm starts, achieves the lowest tail risk among generative methods, and is the first such method to scale to systems with several hundred buses while preserving full feasibility. Ablation studies confirm that the latent generation pipeline is a necessary condition for physical feasibility and that the interaction prior functions as a late-stage tail-risk controller.

AI.tldr: FMOPF decouples compression from generation using latent flow matching and a Constraint-Aware Interaction Prior Network to generate diverse, feasible near-optimal AC-OPF solutions, achieving superior warm starts, lowest tail risk, and scaling to several hundred buses.
AI.motivation: Existing neural methods for AC-OPF provide only point predictions, while diffusion models in raw state space degrade solution quality and fail to scale. The root cause is conflating two distinct tasks: compressing the high-dimensional OPF manifold and learning the conditional mapping from loads to that manifold.
AI.method: FMOPF decouples compression from generation via latent flow matching and models load-state coupling through a Constraint-Aware Interaction Prior Network, enabling diverse feasible near-optimal solution sampling conditioned on load scenarios.
AI.result: FMOPF provides the most effective Newton-Raphson warm starts, achieves the lowest tail risk among generative methods, and is the first generative method to scale to several-hundred-bus systems with full feasibility.
AI.conclusion: Latent generation is necessary for physical feasibility, and the interaction prior acts as a late-stage tail-risk controller. Decoupling compression from generation is key to scaling generative models for AC-OPF.

title: PhononBench-MP40: a spectrum-resolved benchmark dataset for phonon stability
summary: Imaginary phonon modes remain a practical bottleneck in computational materials screening because otherwise plausible structures can be locally dynamically unstable under a chosen workflow. Here we present PhononBench-MP40, a spectrum-resolved benchmark dataset of Materials Project-derived crystals for workflow-defined phonon stability. The dataset starts from 47,969 MP40 workflow tasks and provides 46,899 completed records with paired stability labels and local phonopy YAML spectra, including 16,683 Stable records and 30,216 completed-phonon unstable records. A further 1,067 relaxation failures are reported separately rather than merged into the completed phonon denominator.
