The release centers on the local YAML spectrum: the stability label, the lowest sampled frequency and any threshold-dependent relabeling are derived from that spectrum. The dataset is openly available through Science Data Bank at https://doi.org/10.57760/sciencedb.38735. A companion GitHub repository provides the calculation code and lightweight access utilities. PhononBench-MP40 provides an auditable reference for workflow-defined stability classification, minimum-frequency analysis, threshold studies and failure-aware triage, while keeping the reference workflow, data schema and interpretation boundaries explicit.

AI.tldr: PhononBench-MP40 is a benchmark dataset of 46,899 phonon stability records from Materials Project, with paired stability labels and local YAML spectra, including 16,683 stable and 30,216 unstable records, plus 1,067 relaxation failures, openly available for workflow-defined stability classification and threshold analysis.
AI.motivation: Imaginary phonon modes are a practical bottleneck in computational materials screening because plausible structures can exhibit local dynamic instability under a chosen workflow, yet no standardized benchmark exists for workflow-defined phonon stability.
AI.method: Constructed from 47,969 MP40 workflow tasks, yielding 46,899 completed records with paired stability labels and local phonopy YAML spectra. Stability labels and minimum-frequency analysis are derived from the spectrum. Records include 16,683 Stable and 30,216 unstable; 1,067 relaxation failures are reported separately.
AI.result: 46,899 completed records with spectrum-resolved stability labels; dataset openly released via Science Data Bank (doi:10.57760/sciencedb.38735) with companion GitHub repository for code and access utilities.
AI.conclusion: The dataset provides an auditable reference for workflow-defined stability classification, minimum-frequency analysis, threshold studies, and failure-aware triage, with explicit workflow, data schema, and interpretation boundaries.

title: Alternative UX Extensions and Their Trade-offs for Code Completion in Pharo
summary: Complishon is Pharo's context-aware code completion engine, built on AST analysis, lazy candidate generation, and filter-based candidate selection. Its existing design already provides strong semantic completion, but several practical limits remain. Strict prefix matching is sensitive to small typing errors, framework prefixes often force redundant input, large completion menus are difficult to scan, and prefix-only matching does not support common camel-case abbreviations. This paper presents four extensions that address these limits: typo tolerance, implicit prefix expansion, grouped completion entries, and camel-case matching. For each extension, we describe the implementation, discuss alternative designs, and explain the trade-offs involved. The main contribution of the paper is to show that these improvements can be integrated into Complishon while preserving its modular architecture and predictable behavior.

AI.tldr: This paper presents four extensions to Pharo's Complishon code completion engine to address practical limits: typo tolerance, implicit prefix expansion, grouped completion entries, and camel-case matching.
AI.motivation: Complishon's existing design has practical limits: strict prefix matching is sensitive to typing errors, framework prefixes force redundant input, large completion menus are hard to scan, and prefix-only matching does not support camel-case abbreviations.
AI.method: The authors implement four extensions (typo tolerance, implicit prefix expansion, grouped completion entries, camel-case matching) into Complishon, describing implementation details, discussing alternative designs, and explaining trade-offs.
AI.result: The four extensions address the identified practical limits while preserving Complishon's modular architecture and predictable behavior.
AI.conclusion: The improvements can be integrated into Complishon while preserving its modular architecture and predictable behavior.

title: A New Kind of Adversarial Example: Measuring the Human-Model Gap, and Its Relationship to OOD Detection
summary: Almost all adversarial attacks add an imperceptible perturbation to fool a model. We instead study the opposite: a large, clearly visible perturbation that causes the model to keep its original, correct prediction, even though a human would no longer recognize the image. Prior work showed such examples can be generated at scale but left three questions untested: whether humans really perform worse than the model, whether standard out-of-distribution (OOD) detection and calibration tools catch it, and whether existing defenses mitigate it. We answer all three on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet. (i) An independent recognizer proxy drops to ~49% on CIFAR-10 while the model stays at 100% -- a gap a small human pilot (N=5) corroborates directly and that is not explained by signal loss (a matched-magnitude Gaussian control degrades recognizability faster); a CLIP zero-shot proxy confirms the gap at ImageNet scale too. (ii) Confidence- and energy-based OOD detectors and calibration are structurally blind (0% detection, ECE ~= 0), while a feature-space Mahalanobis detector flags 100% -- but is evaded by an adaptive attacker at no cost to success. (iii) No classical defense, including adversarial training (45% robust accuracy), reduces attack success (correlation with large-epsilon_l resistance r ~= 0). A mechanistic analysis further shows the attack destroys low-level texture far faster than edge/shape structure.

AI.tldr: This paper studies "adversarial robustness" in the opposite direction: large, visible perturbations that preserve a model's correct prediction while making images unrecognizable to humans. The authors test three untested questions on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet: (i) human recognition drops to ~49% on CIFAR-10 while the model stays at 100%, confirmed by a human pilot and CLIP proxy; (ii) standard OOD detectors and calibration fail to detect the attack (0% detection, ECE~0), while a Mahalanobis detector works but can be evaded; (iii) no classical defense reduces attack success, including adversarial training. Mechanistically, the attack destroys low-level texture faster than edge/shape structure.
AI.motivation: To investigate three untested questions about large-perturbation adversarial examples that maintain model accuracy despite being clearly unrecognizable to humans: whether humans perform worse, whether OOD detection/calibration tools catch it, and whether existing defenses mitigate it.
AI.method: The authors generate large, visible perturbations that preserve model predictions, then evaluate (i) human recognition via an independent recognizer proxy, a small human pilot (N=5), and CLIP zero-shot proxy; (ii) OOD detection using confidence-based, energy-based, and Mahalanobis detectors, plus calibration via ECE; (iii) classical defenses including adversarial training; and provide a mechanistic analysis of texture vs. edge/shape degradation.
AI.result: Human proxy recognition drops to ~49% on CIFAR-10 while model stays at 100%; a Gaussian control degrades recognizability faster. Confidence/energy-based OOD detectors and calibration are blind (0% detection, ECE~0), but Mahalanobis detection works and is evadable. No classical defense (incl. adversarial training at 45% robust accuracy) reduces attack success. The attack destroys low-level texture faster than edge/shape structure.
AI.conclusion: Large, visible perturbations can fully preserve model predictions while making images unrecognizable to humans; standard OOD detection and calibration tools are structurally blind to this phenomenon, and no existing defense mitigates it, highlighting a fundamental blind spot in current robustness evaluation.

title: Too much evidence, too little time: From text to actionable recommendations through multi-objective evidence reasoning
summary: Evidence-based clinical decision making requires specialists to identify, evaluate and synthesize relevant scientific literature. However, PubMed searches for complex clinical cases often return hundreds of publications that cannot be reviewed manually under time constraints. This study proposes SCEPTER (Single-Case Evidence-driven PubMed-To-rEcommendation Reasoner), a framework for transforming clinical case descriptions into evidence-based recommendations. SCEPTER combines PubMed retrieval, PubMedBERT semantic ranking, large language model (LLM)-based claim extraction, evidence-level weighting, contradiction detection, consensus analysis and multi-objective Pareto claim selection. The framework generates structured evidence syntheses and grounded actionable recommendations. A Paper Q&A module further enables interactive exploration of selected publications. The proposed framework introduces multi-objective reasoning model that integrates literature support, contradiction analysis and interactive literature interrogation into a unified clinical decision-support pipeline. Evaluation on 150 case studies demonstrated that the framework reduced an average search space of 576 papers to 53 retained papers, 7 Pareto-optimal claims and 3 final recommendations, corresponding to an overall compression ratio of 192:1. Despite this reduction, the retained evidence maintained high diversity (entropy=0.901). The ablation study showed that Pareto-based selection increased evidence diversity and recommendation utility compared with conventional ranking approaches.

AI.tldr: SCEPTER is a framework that transforms clinical case descriptions into evidence-based recommendations by combining PubMed retrieval, semantic ranking, LLM-based claim extraction, and multi-objective Pareto selection, achieving a 192:1 compression ratio while maintaining high evidence diversity (entropy=0.901).
AI.motivation: Evidence-based clinical decision-making requires reviewing extensive scientific literature, but PubMed searches often return hundreds of publications that cannot be manually reviewed under time constraints, creating a need for automated evidence synthesis and recommendation.
AI.method: SCEPTER combines PubMed retrieval, PubMedBERT semantic ranking, LLM-based claim extraction, evidence-level weighting, contradiction detection, consensus analysis, and multi-objective Pareto claim selection, along with a Paper Q&A module for interactive exploration.
AI.result: Evaluation on 150 case studies showed reduction from 576 papers to 53 retained papers, 7 Pareto-optimal claims, and 3 final recommendations (192:1 compression ratio), with high evidence diversity (entropy=0.901). Pareto-based selection outperformed conventional ranking approaches.
AI.conclusion: SCEPTER introduces a multi-objective reasoning model that integrates literature support, contradiction analysis, and interactive literature interrogation into a unified clinical decision-support pipeline, effectively compressing evidence while maintaining diversity and utility.

title: Motivations and Barriers to Communicating Software Engineering Research: Insights from Early Career Researchers
summary: Science communication is increasingly becoming a part of modern research careers, involving researchers to disseminate knowledge, engage broader communities, and increase the societal impact of their work. Despite its growing importance, little is known about how early-career software engineering researchers perceive and navigate science communication in practice. In this paper, we investigate how PhD students in software engineering experience science communication. We conducted semi-structured interviews with 18 doctoral candidates from diverse international backgrounds. Using thematic analysis, we examine three interconnected dimensions: motivations, communication channels, and barriers. Our findings reveal a strong tension between aspiration and practice. Participants were highly motivated to engage in science communication due to opportunities for collaboration, professional recognition, broader impact, and advocacy for themselves and their research. However, translating these motivations into action was frequently constrained by social anxiety, uncertainty regarding appropriate audiences and communication venues, limited feedback mechanisms, insufficient institutional guidance, and challenges associated with navigating an increasingly fragmented communication landscape. Our findings highlight the need for tailored, balanced support systems that empower software engineering PhD students to engage in science communication effectively and confidently across diverse cultural and institutional environments. We outline practical implications that offer initial guidance for addressing these challenges in future work.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how PhD students in software engineering experience science communication, revealing a tension between high motivation (for collaboration, recognition, impact, advocacy) and practice constrained by social anxiety, uncertainty about audiences/venues, limited feedback, insufficient institutional guidance, and a fragmented communication landscape.
AI.motivation: Despite the growing importance of science communication in modern research careers, little is known about how early-career software engineering researchers perceive and navigate science communication in practice.
AI.method: Semi-structured interviews with 18 doctoral candidates from diverse international backgrounds, analyzed using thematic analysis across three dimensions: motivations, communication channels, and barriers.
AI.result: A strong tension between aspiration and practice was found: participants were highly motivated but faced constraints including social anxiety, uncertainty about audiences/venues, limited feedback, insufficient institutional guidance, and challenges from a fragmented communication landscape.
AI.conclusion: Tailored, balanced support systems are needed to empower software engineering PhD students to engage in science communication effectively and confidently across diverse cultural and institutional environments. Practical implications are outlined for future work.

title: Visual Information Extraction from Documents via Classification-Guided Large Vision-Language Models
summary: Visual information extraction (VIE) from visually rich documents remains challenging due to high layout variability and real-world impairments. Existing methods typically rely on sequential OCR pipelines or end-to-end models requiring extensive labeled data and layout-specific training, limiting their scalability.We propose a classification-guided large vision-language model (LVLM) framework for multi-type VIE that achieves high accuracy with minimal supervision. The approach decouples document-type classification from content extraction and employs in-context learning (ICL)-based dynamic prompt engineering to inject task-specific knowledge, enabling robust zero-shot inference across diverse layouts. From a theoretical perspective, the proposed method can be viewed as a form of conditional computation that reduces task uncertainty and improves information efficiency during prompt-based inference. Evaluated on a real-world bidding dataset with 16 certificate types, our zero-shot method (based on Qwen2.5-VL-7B) outperforms a strong supervised baseline by 18.35 percentage points in F1-score (86.43\% vs. 68.08\%) and 0.23 in normalized edit distance (0.90 vs. 0.67). Optional domain-specific fine-tuning further improves performance to 93.65\% F1 and 0.93 NED, demonstrating superior robustness against seals, watermarks, and low contrast. The framework offers an efficient, scalable solution for complex document understanding in office automation. Code is available at https://github.com/FairmeHIT/Multi-VIE, and fine-tuned models at https://huggingface.co/fairme/Qwen2.5-VL-7B-SFT.

AI.tldr: A classification-guided LVLM framework for visual information extraction uses decoupled document-type classification and ICL-based dynamic prompt engineering to achieve zero-shot VIE, outperforming supervised baselines by 18.35% F1 on a real-world bidding dataset.
AI.motivation: Existing VIE methods rely on sequential OCR pipelines or end-to-end models requiring extensive labeled data and layout-specific training, limiting scalability across diverse document layouts and real-world impairments.
AI.method: Proposes a framework that decouples document-type classification from content extraction, using classification-guided ICL-based dynamic prompt engineering to inject task-specific knowledge into a large vision-language model (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) for zero-shot inference.
AI.result: Zero-shot method achieves 86.43% F1 and 0.90 NED on a 16-type bidding dataset, surpassing supervised baseline by 18.35% F1; optional fine-tuning reaches 93.65% F1 and 0.93 NED with robustness to seals, watermarks, and low contrast.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides an efficient, scalable solution for complex document understanding in office automation with minimal supervision requirements.

title: Physically Verifiable Evidence and LLM-Based Reporting for Bearing Fault Diagnosis
summary: Trustworthy deployment of AI-based diagnosis in safety-critical mechanical systems hinges on validation: whether a prediction can be checked against physical reality before it is acted upon. Current intelligent fault diagnosers fail this standard in two ways. Their standard output, a class label with a softmax confidence score, is an internal statistic of the classifier, offering nothing checkable against independent physical knowledge; and the growing use of generative language models in maintenance reporting adds a second risk: hallucinated content entering reports on which decisions rest. Taking bearing fault diagnosis as the testbed, this work addresses both problems from the output side. The proposed Diagnostic Evidence Network (DENet) is an encoder-agnostic multi-task framework extending the output to a structured evidence record: the classification, a predicted characteristic frequency comparable against the theoretical value determined by bearing geometry and shaft speed, and a temporal localization of transient impulses inspectable on the raw waveform. Across four encoders and three public datasets, this evidence incurs no statistically significant accuracy cost, with a frequency error of about 6 Hz on 1,024-point segments where spectral estimation is structurally inapplicable. Centrally, the deviation between predicted and theoretical frequency constitutes a label-free, inference-time validation signal: it detects misclassifications with AUROC values of 0.970 and 0.871, and remains discriminative in the high-confidence regime where confidence-derived detectors are blind. Finally, a QLoRA-adapted language model is constrained to translate, but never generate, diagnostic content, reducing unsupported-claim rates from 10-12% to 2% and eliminating fabricated quantities.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes DENet, a multi-task framework that extends AI diagnosis outputs to include checkable physical evidence (characteristic frequencies and temporal localizations), enabling validation against known physics and reducing hallucination risks in language model-generated maintenance reports.
AI.motivation: Current intelligent fault diagnosers fail to provide outputs that can be validated against independent physical knowledge; they rely on softmax confidence scores (internal classifier statistics) and generative language models risk hallucinating content in maintenance reports, undermining trustworthiness in safety-critical mechanical systems.
AI.method: DENet is an encoder-agnostic multi-task framework that extends the output to a structured evidence record including: classification, predicted characteristic frequency comparable against theoretical values, and temporal localization of transient impulses. A QLoRA-adapted language model is constrained to translate (not generate) diagnostic content.
AI.result: No statistically significant accuracy cost across four encoders and three datasets; frequency error ~6 Hz on 1,024-point segments; misclassification detection via frequency deviation yields AUROC 0.970 and 0.871, effective even in high-confidence regimes where confidence-based detectors fail; unsupported-claim rates reduced from 10-12% to 2% with eliminated fabricated quantities.
AI.conclusion: DENet enables trustworthy AI diagnosis by providing physically checkable evidence outputs and constraining language models to translation-only roles, offering validation signals at inference time without requiring ground-truth labels.

title: Temporal Context Reinstatement Drives Episodic-Like Order Memory in Long-Context Language Models
summary: Human episodic memory supports the retrieval of experiences that unfold over extended timescales, yet the computational mechanisms underlying this ability remain debated due to the limited mechanistic accessibility in long-term memory experiments in humans. Long-context LLMs may offer promising ways to reveal plausible computational mechanisms that drive this type of retrieval. Here, we investigate whether and how LLMs capture the core behavioral signatures of episodic memory via a temporal order memory task. Using a new dataset of human behavior based on memory of a full-length novel, we show that models exhibit the same characteristic distance effect observed in humans on this task. We next apply long-context mechanistic interpretability analyses to uncover how models solve this task, and find that model performance relies on a one-dimensional temporal code that is reinstated during retrieval by a single time-reinstatement attention head. These findings support temporal context reinstatement as an important mechanism for episodic-like temporal-order memory in LLMs, offering new insights into how temporal aspects of long-term episodic memory may be instantiated in both artificial and biological systems.

AI.tldr: LLMs exhibit human-like temporal distance effects in episodic memory retrieval via a single attention head that reinstates a one-dimensional temporal code, supporting temporal context reinstatement as a key mechanism.
AI.motivation: Human episodic memory supports retrieval over extended timescales, but its computational mechanisms remain debated due to limited mechanistic accessibility in human experiments. Long-context LLMs may offer a way to reveal plausible computational mechanisms.
AI.method: Used a temporal order memory task with a new human behavior dataset based on memory of a full-length novel. Applied long-context mechanistic interpretability analyses to uncover how LLMs solve the task, comparing model performance to human behavioral signatures (distance effect).
AI.result: LLMs exhibit the same characteristic distance effect as humans. Model performance relies on a one-dimensional temporal code reinstated during retrieval by a single time-reinstatement attention head.
AI.conclusion: Temporal context reinstatement is an important mechanism for episodic-like temporal-order memory in LLMs, offering insights into how temporal aspects of long-term episodic memory may be instantiated in both artificial and biological systems.

title: Evaluating the Impact of Explainable AI on Trust in AI-Assisted Code Review
comment: 23 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables. To appear in Proceedings of the ACM on Software Engineering (PACMSE), Vol. 3, No. ISSTA, Article ISSTA093 (ISSTA 2026). Published under CC BY 4.0. Replication package: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21457282
summary:
Background: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to automate code review, but the reasoning behind their decisions remains hard to understand. Developers struggle to assess the validity of LLM-generated reviews, making it difficult to gauge how much trust to place in them. The role of Explainable AI (XAI) in code review and its impact on trust remain underexplored.
  Objective: We study the influence of XAI on developer trust in AI-assisted code reviews.
  Method: We conducted a within-subjects user study with 34 participants, comparing three LLM-based code review systems with varying levels of XAI support: Condition A (detailed explanation and review feedback), Condition B (review feedback only), and Condition C (no explanations). Participants reviewed real-world code change requests alongside the AI-generated reviews. We measured trust perceptions, agreement with the AI recommendation, the reasoning given for each decision, and the time taken.
  Results: The level of explanation significantly influences both trust and agreement with AI recommendations, but in different ways. Full explanations (A) yield the highest perceived trust (M = 3.99/5) but not the highest agreement, whereas moderate explanations (B) achieve the highest agreement (89.22%). This could suggest that more explanation prompts developers to question AI recommendations more frequently. No explanations (C) results in the lowest trust and agreement. Explanation level did not significantly affect review time. The most commonly cited reasons for decisions were code readability and correctness.
  Conclusion: Incorporating XAI into code review significantly changes trust perceptions and agreement with AI recommendations. These results inform the design and evaluation of trustworthy AI-based code review systems, as well as studies on the human factors of AI-assisted software development.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how different levels of XAI (Explainable AI) support in LLM-based code review systems influence developer trust and agreement with AI recommendations, finding that full explanations increase perceived trust but moderate explanations yield higher agreement, while no explanations result in the lowest trust and agreement.
AI.motivation: Developers struggle to assess the validity of LLM-generated code reviews, and the role of Explainable AI in code review and its impact on trust remain underexplored.
AI.method: A within-subjects user study with 34 participants comparing three LLM-based code review systems: Condition A (detailed explanation and review feedback), Condition B (review feedback only), and Condition C (no explanations). Participants reviewed real-world code change requests alongside AI-generated reviews, measuring trust, agreement, reasoning, and time.
AI.result: Full explanations (A) yield highest perceived trust (M=3.99/5) but not highest agreement; moderate explanations (B) achieve highest agreement (89.22%); no explanations (C) result in lowest trust and agreement. Explanation level did not significantly affect review time. Most common cited reasons were code readability and correctness.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating XAI into code review significantly changes trust perceptions and agreement with AI recommendations, informing the design of trustworthy AI-based code review systems and studies on human factors in AI-assisted software development.

title: Structural Preservation Governs Data Augmentation in Deep Learning-Based Laser Speckle Material Classification
comment: Copyright 2026 IEEE. This is the author's version of the work that has been Accepted for publication in the Proceedings of the 2026 IEEE 2025 Intelligent Methods, Systems, and Applications (IMSA). Final published version will be available on IEEE Xplore
summary: Data augmentation is routinely used to improve generalization in image classification, but the assumptions underlying standard policies are poorly matched to coherent imaging. Laser speckle patterns are not generic textures; they arise from coherent interference, and their discriminative content is carried by structured stochastic spatial and frequency statistics. This study examines how controlled augmentation perturbations influence speckle-based material classification on the SensiCut dataset. We train ResNet18 and EfficientNet-B0 under a parametric augmentation framework comprising rotation, Gaussian blur, independent Gaussian noise, spatially correlated speckle-aware noise, intensity jitter, and spatial masking, and evaluate test performance using macro F1-score averaged over three random seeds. Separate ordinary least squares models link augmentation parameters to performance for each architecture. Across both models, Gaussian blur exerts a strong negative effect (p < 0.001), indicating that low-pass filtering suppresses high-frequency structure that is informative for material discrimination. Independent pixel-wise noise is likewise harmful (p = 0.003 for EfficientNet-B0 and p = 0.001 for ResNet18), consistent with disruption of local spatial coherence. In contrast, spatially correlated perturbations yield significant positive coefficients (p = 0.004 for EfficientNet-B0 and p = 0.001 for ResNet18), showing that variability can improve robustness when it preserves speckle organization. The fitted models explain a substantial fraction of performance variation (R2 = 0.796 for EfficientNet-B0 and R2 = 0.879 for ResNet18). These results show that, in laser speckle imaging, augmentation effectiveness is determined primarily by structural preservation rather than perturbation magnitude. The findings motivate physics-aware augmentation design for coherent optical sensing.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how data augmentation affects laser speckle-based material classification, finding that spatially correlated noise improves robustness while Gaussian blur and independent noise harm performance, highlighting the need for physics-aware augmentation in coherent imaging.
AI.motivation: Standard data augmentation policies are designed for natural image classification and do not account for the coherent interference structure of laser speckle patterns, which carry discriminative information through structured stochastic spatial and frequency statistics rather than generic textures.
AI.method: ResNet18 and EfficientNet-B0 are trained on the SensiCut dataset under a parametric augmentation framework (rotation, Gaussian blur, independent Gaussian noise, speckle-aware correlated noise, intensity jitter, spatial masking). Test performance (macro F1-score) is evaluated and separate ordinary least squares regression models link augmentation parameters to performance for each architecture.
AI.result: Gaussian blur has strong negative effect (p<0.001), independent noise is harmful (p=0.003 for EfficientNet-B0, p=0.001 for ResNet18), spatially correlated perturbations yield significant positive coefficients (p=0.004 for EfficientNet-B0, p=0.001 for ResNet18). Models explain substantial variance (R²=0.796 for EfficientNet-B0, R²=0.879 for ResNet18).
AI.conclusion: In laser speckle imaging, augmentation effectiveness is driven by structural preservation rather than perturbation magnitude, motivating physics-aware augmentation design for coherent optical sensing.

title: LithoFormer: A Robust Framework for Stratigraphic Inference via Transformers
summary: Accurate geological characterization of subsurface reservoirs from well log data is essential to support projects such as carbon capture and storage (CCS), geothermal development, and extraction of natural resources. Existing automated techniques for geological characterization primarily use sliding-window classification, which limits their ability to understand broader geological contexts, often leading to misaligned formation layers. To overcome these limitations, we introduce LithoFormer, a robust framework for stratigraphic inference using a Seq2Seq transformer model that ingests entire multivariate well logs in a single pass. The framework utilizes a channel-independent PatchTST backbone enhanced with rotary positional embeddings (RoPE) to capture long-range geological dependencies across entire multivariate well logs. A decoupled multi-task head is employed to jointly predict geological zonation and precise boundary probabilities, while a geology-informed loss function enforces physical constraints such as the Law of Superposition. Validated and deployed on three real-world datasets, LithoFormer demonstrates a 90% reduction in median boundary error and eliminates stratigraphic order violations compared to traditional sliding-window baselines. It also achieves a 80% reduction in manual expert labor and eliminates stratigraphic inconsistencies, providing a scalable and reliable solution for large-scale subsurface modeling.

AI.tldr: LithoFormer is a Seq2Seq transformer framework that processes entire multivariate well logs in a single pass for geological stratigraphic inference, using a PatchTST backbone with rotary positional embeddings and a geology-informed loss function. It achieves 90% reduction in boundary error, eliminates stratigraphic order violations, and reduces manual expert labor by 80% across three real-world datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing sliding-window classification methods for geological characterization from well logs fail to capture broader geological contexts, leading to misaligned formation layers and stratigraphic inconsistencies.
AI.method: A Seq2Seq transformer model (LithoFormer) with a channel-independent PatchTST backbone, Rotary Positional Embeddings (RoPE) for long-range dependencies, a decoupled multi-task head for joint zonation and boundary prediction, and a geology-informed loss function enforcing the Law of Superposition.
AI.result: 90% reduction in median boundary error, elimination of stratigraphic order violations, 80% reduction in manual expert labor, and elimination of stratigraphic inconsistencies across three real-world datasets.
AI.conclusion: LithoFormer provides a scalable, reliable solution for large-scale subsurface modeling, significantly outperforming sliding-window baselines in accuracy and efficiency for applications like CCS, geothermal development, and resource extraction.

title: cMoLLM at Scale: Horizontal Scaling Laws for Mixture-of-LLMs
summary: Scaling large language models (LLMs) has driven their success, yet dense Transformers couple capacity and computation: every parameter is activated for every token, making training and inference costs grow linearly with model size-a critical bottleneck as models approach trillion-parameter regimes. We aim to scale capacity through MoE-style mixture throughout the LLM pipeline rather than only the FFN. Prior pipeline-level approaches include ParaScale, which introduces virtual tokens and parallel streams but incurs substantial overhead and suffers from homogenized routing and gradient collapse, and AltUp, which uses an auxiliary prediction branch but offers limited adaptivity and slow convergence. We establish that MoE-style mixture layers can be reformulated as variable-kernel dynamic convolutions, where each expert corresponds to a $1{\times}1$ convolutional kernel and routing implements input-conditioned kernel aggregation. Building on this equivalence, we introduce cMoLLM: a convolutionally gated mixture-of-LLMs that routes over end-to-end streams through fully differentiable dynamic convolution. In GPT-2-style models trained on FineWeb, cMoLLM improves language modeling perplexity and downstream GLUE and SQuAD accuracy under matched compute, with better stream utilization, more stable optimization, and favorable scaling compared to ParaScale- and AltUp-style baselines.

AI.tldr: cMoLLM reformulates MoE-style mixture layers as dynamic convolutions to scale LLM capacity efficiently, outperforming ParaScale and AltUp on perplexity, GLUE, and SQuAD with better stream utilization and stable optimization.
AI.motivation: Dense Transformers couple capacity with computation, causing linear cost scaling as models approach trillion-parameter regimes; prior pipeline-level MoE approaches (ParaScale, AltUp) suffer from overhead, homogenized routing, gradient collapse, limited adaptivity, and slow convergence.
AI.method: Establishes equivalence between MoE mixture layers and variable-kernel dynamic convolutions (each expert = 1×1 conv kernel, routing = input-conditioned kernel aggregation), then proposes cMoLLM: convolutionally gated mixture-of-LLMs with fully differentiable dynamic convolution over end-to-end streams.
AI.result: On GPT-2-style models trained on FineWeb, cMoLLM improves language modeling perplexity, GLUE score, and SQuAD accuracy under matched compute, with better stream utilization, more stable optimization, and favorable scaling compared to ParaScale and AltUp baselines.
AI.conclusion: The dynamic convolution formulation offers a principled and effective alternative for pipeline-level MoE in LLMs, addressing key limitations of prior approaches.

title: Verification-Conditioned Use: A Qualitative Study on How Generative AI Reshapes Learning, Autonomy, and Market Entry for Junior Software Developers
summary: Objective: to investigate how the use of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools affects the early stages of a career in software development, from the perspective of the newcomers themselves. Method: thirteen interns and junior developers were interviewed individually, by videoconference. Interviews were analyzed using the six phases of Braun and Clarke's thematic analysis, with inductive coding and a semantic approach. Results: sixteen themes emerged, organized around a central concept: verification-conditioned use. Across the study's four research questions (usage patterns, learning, autonomy, and market entry), the criterion that most often decides between AI and manual work is not deadline or task complexity, but the ability to check the result. Two themes expose tensions in newcomers' self-perception: the autonomy paradox (feeling more capable yet less in ownership of the result) and the first-person denial of dependence. Together, these findings point to a theoretical contribution, the formative paradox: the shallow learning that AI induces makes it harder to build the very critical-judgment competence that, according to participants, the market has begun to demand. Conclusion: what makes AI use sustainable, from participants' own point of view, is not the tool itself but the individual practice of reviewing before accepting, refusing to use AI without understanding it, asking the tool for explanations, and keeping deliberate practice outside of AI-assisted work.

AI.tldr: This study explores how generative AI affects early-career software developers through interviews with 13 interns and junior developers. The central finding is that newcomers' AI usage is primarily governed by whether they can verify the output (verification-conditioned use). Key tensions include the autonomy paradox (feeling more capable but less ownership) and first-person denial of dependence. These culminate in a theoretical contribution: the formative paradox—AI-induced shallow learning hinders the critical judgment that the market now demands.
AI.motivation: To understand how generative AI tools impact the early stages of a software development career from the perspective of newcomers themselves, filling a gap in empirical research on AI's effects on junior developer development.
AI.method: Semi-structured individual videoconference interviews with 13 interns and junior developers, analyzed using Braun and Clarke's six-phase thematic analysis with inductive coding and a semantic approach.
AI.result: Sixteen themes emerged around verification-conditioned use. The primary determinant of AI use is verifiability of output rather than deadlines or complexity. Two key tensions found: the autonomy paradox (increased capability but reduced ownership) and first-person denial of dependence. The formative paradox describes how AI-induced shallow learning undermines development of critical judgment competence.
AI.conclusion: Sustainable AI use depends not on the tool but on individual practices: reviewing before accepting, refusing to use AI without understanding, asking for explanations, and maintaining deliberate practice outside AI-assisted work.

title: PCA: Persistence-Aware Compression and Aggregation for Fast Video Large Language Models
summary: Despite advances in Video Large Language Models (VLLMs) that have displayed promising outcomes in video understanding, the redundancy in the long-duration frames remains a hindrance to efficient reasoning. This paper introduces a training-free $\mathbf{P}$ersistence-Aware $\mathbf{C}$ompression and $\mathbf{A}$ggregation (PCA) method designed to preserve high-fidelity raw visual information before the encoding stage. PCA can be built on arbitrary VLLMs and consists of two modules: 1) A Dynamic Downsampling (DD) module that adaptively removes redundant frames by analyzing frame-wise similarity. 2) A Persistence-Aware Motion Enhancement (PAME) module that enriches each selected keyframe by aggregating the temporal context of its neighbors, ensuring that essential information is preserved even after aggressive frame reduction. Our approach substantially reduces the computation of long-context modeling, while enhancing the performance of the baseline model. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PCA consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches in both efficiency and accuracy, achieving a speedup of 1.8$\times$ to 2.5$\times$ compared to the baseline VLLM. The code is open-sourced at https://github.com/Heisenberg10110/PCA.

AI.tldr: A training-free Persistence-Aware Compression and Aggregation (PCA) method for VLLMs that reduces video frame redundancy via dynamic downsampling and motion enhancement, achieving 1.8-2.5× speedup while improving accuracy.
AI.motivation: Long-duration video frames contain redundant information that hinders efficient reasoning in Video Large Language Models (VLLMs).
AI.method: PCA consists of two modules: 1) Dynamic Downsampling (DD) adaptively removes redundant frames by analyzing frame-wise similarity. 2) Persistence-Aware Motion Enhancement (PAME) enriches keyframes by aggregating temporal context from neighboring frames.
AI.result: Consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches in both efficiency and accuracy, achieving 1.8× to 2.5× speedup compared to the baseline VLLM.
AI.conclusion: Training-free PCA effectively preserves high-fidelity raw visual information before encoding, substantially reduces computation for long-context modeling, and enhances baseline model performance.

title: OrchNAS: Orchestrated Neural Architecture Search Service for Personalised Federated Edge Intelligence
summary: We propose OrchNAS, an energy-aware, personalised, federated edge intelligence framework that leverages a Neural Architecture Search Service to automatically design service-adaptive models for heterogeneous edge environments. The framework orchestrates the architecture search process on a server-side NAS service, enabling edge services to derive personalised architectures under device-level energy, computation, and memory constraints. We introduce an energy-aware global architecture search mechanism that learns a compact global representation across heterogeneous services. We develop an energy-efficient architecture selection mechanism that enables each service to derive a personalised subnet that satisfies its resource constraints via a progressive, greedy, energy-aware pruning strategy. We propose an energy-efficient personalised model optimisation scheme that updates service-adaptive parameters while preserving global representations, where a primal-dual optimisation mechanism enforces strict energy budgets during architecture adaptation. Experiments on real-world and benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

AI.tldr: OrchNAS is an energy-aware, personalized federated edge intelligence framework that uses a Neural Architecture Search Service to automatically design resource-constrained models for heterogeneous edge environments, employing energy-aware architecture search, progressive pruning, and primal-dual optimization to enforce energy budgets.
AI.motivation: To address the challenge of designing service-adaptive deep learning models for heterogeneous edge environments with diverse device-level energy, computation, and memory constraints.
AI.method: (1) Energy-aware global architecture search learning compact global representations across heterogeneous services; (2) Energy-efficient architecture selection via progressive, greedy, energy-aware pruning to derive personalized subnets under resource constraints; (3) Energy-efficient personalized model optimization with primal-dual optimization to enforce strict energy budgets during architecture adaptation.
AI.result: Effectiveness demonstrated on real-world and benchmark datasets.
AI.conclusion: OrchNAS effectively enables automated, personalized model design for heterogeneous edge devices while respecting energy and resource constraints through a server-side NAS service with energy-aware mechanisms.

title: HeraSys: Collaborative Serving of Multiple LLM Workflows via Fine-Grained End-to-End Optimization
summary: The proliferation of Large Language Models (LLMs) has shifted serving systems from processing isolated requests to orchestrating high-concurrency, multi-tenant agentic workflows. However, existing solutions typically prioritize intra-workflow optimization, largely neglecting the significant potential for inter-workflow optimization. In this paper, we propose HeraSys, an LLM serving system designed to optimize the end-to-end performance of concurrent workflows. Through fine-grained orchestration, HeraSys eliminates cross-workflow computational redundancy via structural node merging and reuse. Furthermore, HeraSys introduces a load-aware joint scheduling policy that dynamically manages execution order by evaluating both inter- and intra-query priorities. By integrating a resource skewing mechanism with adaptive batching and pipeline decomposition, HeraSys effectively mitigates tail latency while maintaining low average latency, thereby substantially improving system throughput. Extensive experiments demonstrate that HeraSys reduces P99 latency by up to 2.17$\times$ and increases serving throughput by up to 1.85$\times$ under strict latency guarantees.

AI.tldr: HeraSys is an LLM serving system that optimizes concurrent multi-tenant agentic workflows via cross-workflow structural node merging/reuse, load-aware joint scheduling, resource skewing, adaptive batching, and pipeline decomposition, achieving up to 2.17× P99 latency reduction and 1.85× throughput improvement.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM serving systems prioritize intra-workflow optimization but neglect inter-workflow optimization potential, leading to computational redundancy and suboptimal performance in high-concurrency, multi-tenant agentic workflow scenarios.
AI.method: HeraSys uses (1) fine-grained orchestration with structural node merging and reuse to eliminate cross-workflow redundancy, (2) a load-aware joint scheduling policy that evaluates both inter- and intra-query priorities, and (3) a resource skewing mechanism integrated with adaptive batching and pipeline decomposition to reduce tail latency.
AI.result: P99 latency reduced by up to 2.17×, serving throughput increased by up to 1.85× under strict latency guarantees.
AI.conclusion: Cross-workflow optimization significantly improves end-to-end performance of concurrent LLM-serving workflows, and HeraSys demonstrates effective tail latency mitigation and throughput gains.

title: Trustworthy Medical Segmentation: Uncertainty-Aware U-Net Evaluation Under Clinical Image Degradation
summary: Medical image segmentation models often report high benchmark accuracy under ideal imaging conditions, yet their failures under clinical degradation can be quiet: sensor noise, patient motion, low- resolution acquisition, and contrast variability may all alter model behavior without producing an obvious warning. We present a reproducible framework for evaluating uncertainty-aware segmentation under con- trolled clinical degradation. Our experiments use a synthetic multimodal brain tumor MRI cohort generated with a biophysical phantom simulator that follows the BraTS protocol. We train U-Net and Attention U-Net baselines for multi-class tumor sub-region segmentation and augment both models with Monte Carlo dropout to estimate per-voxel uncertainty. Across eight clinically motivated corruption types at five severity levels, we measure segmentation accuracy, calibration, failure detection, and selective prediction coverage. On clean data, Attention U-Net achieves a whole-tumor Dice of 0.990; under severe Gaussian noise, its performance falls to 0.089. Predictive uncertainty rises with degradation and tracks segmentation error (Pearson r = 0.53 under severity-3 Gaussian noise), allowing us to flag failures with an AUROC of 0.843. These results argue for uncertainty-aware inference as a practical safety layer in physician-in-the-loop radiology workflows. We release the code, trained models, and evaluation protocol to support direct reproduction.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a reproducible framework for evaluating uncertainty-aware medical image segmentation under eight types of clinical degradation. Using synthetic multimodal brain tumor MRI data, U-Net and Attention U-Net with Monte Carlo dropout are tested, showing that predictive uncertainty correlates with segmentation error (r=0.53) and can detect failures (AUROC=0.843), arguing for uncertainty-aware inference as a safety layer in clinical workflows.
AI.motivation: Medical image segmentation models often report high benchmark accuracy under ideal conditions but silently fail under clinical degradation (noise, motion, low resolution, contrast variability), without providing obvious warnings. This motivates the need for a systematic, reproducible evaluation of model robustness and uncertainty quantification under clinically realistic corruptions.
AI.method: A synthetic multimodal brain tumor MRI cohort is generated using a biophysical phantom simulator following the BraTS protocol. U-Net and Attention U-Net baselines are trained for multi-class tumor sub-region segmentation, augmented with Monte Carlo dropout for per-voxel uncertainty estimation. Models are evaluated across eight clinically motivated corruption types at five severity levels, measuring segmentation accuracy, calibration, failure detection, and selective prediction coverage.
AI.result: On clean data, Attention U-Net achieves 0.990 whole-tumor Dice; under severe Gaussian noise, performance drops to 0.089. Predictive uncertainty rises with degradation and tracks segmentation error (Pearson r=0.53 under severity-3 Gaussian noise), enabling failure flagging with AUROC of 0.843.
AI.conclusion: Uncertainty-aware inference serves as a practical safety layer in physician-in-the-loop radiology workflows, with code, trained models, and evaluation protocol released for direct reproduction.

title: SLA-Constrained Carbon-Aware Routing in Geo-Distributed Serverless Clouds
summary: Modern cloud deployments distribute applications across multiple geographic regions, yet standard routing mechanisms prioritize latency while ignoring the fluctuating carbon intensity of local power grids. Latency-driven routing incurs avoidable carbon emissions, particularly when cleaner regions are within acceptable latency bounds. The proposed model formulates the carbon-aware serverless routing problem as a constrained optimization over geo-distributed cloud regions and introduces an SLA-constrained carbon-aware routing policy that achieves optimal carbon reduction within the SLA-feasible region, evaluated using real carbon intensity measurements across 5 primary AWS deployments. Experimental results show that the proposed policy achieves up to 46.8% carbon reduction while maintaining zero SLA violations across all evaluated thresholds. The system reduces carbon by an average of 27.4% under mixed workloads, and the routing overhead is very low (less than 0.02% of total request latency). A scalability study across 12 AWS regions spanning 6 continents demonstrates that average carbon savings increase from 27.4% to 47.5% as routing flexibility expands under mixed workloads. The proposed work contributes to SDG 13 (Climate Action) and SDG 7 (Affordable and Clean Energy) by enabling low-carbon routing decisions. These results indicate that cloud systems can achieve significant carbon savings without compromising user experience.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an SLA-constrained carbon-aware routing policy for geo-distributed serverless cloud deployments that reduces carbon emissions by up to 46.8% (27.4% average) without violating SLAs, with negligible routing overhead (<0.02% of latency), validated across AWS regions.
AI.motivation: Standard latency-driven routing in multi-region cloud deployments ignores fluctuating carbon intensity of local power grids, causing avoidable carbon emissions even when cleaner regions are within acceptable latency bounds.
AI.method: Formulates carbon-aware serverless routing as a constrained optimization problem over geo-distributed cloud regions, and introduces an SLA-constrained carbon-aware routing policy that achieves optimal carbon reduction within the SLA-feasible region.
AI.result: Up to 46.8% carbon reduction with zero SLA violations; average 27.4% reduction under mixed workloads; routing overhead <0.02% of total latency; scalability study across 12 AWS regions shows savings increase from 27.4% to 47.5% with more routing flexibility.
AI.conclusion: Cloud systems can achieve significant carbon savings without compromising user experience, contributing to SDG 13 (Climate Action) and SDG 7 (Affordable and Clean Energy).

title: Multi-Objective Structured Pruning of LLMs for Latency and Model Size Optimization
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved widespread adoption because of their strong reasoning and query-response capabilities. However, deploying them in embedded and edge computing environments remains challenging because of strict latency, memory, and energy constraints. Their large parameter counts and computational demands hinder efficient execution on resource-constrained platforms. Although model pruning has emerged as a viable solution for reducing scale while preserving performance, jointly optimizing layers, attention heads, and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) dimensions remains highly complex. Exhaustively exploring this combined design space is computationally expensive and often leads to local optima or unstable configurations. To address these limitations, we propose a hardware-aware, multi-objective structured pruning framework. The proposed two-stage method explicitly targets latency and model size for efficient deployment on edge devices. In the coarse-grained stage, multi-objective depth pruning removes entire attention and MLP blocks to reduce computational load and memory usage. In the subsequent fine-grained stage, Parallel Bayesian Optimization (PBO) searches for the optimal layer-wise pruning ratios for pruning under latency constraints, while importance-based strategies rank the specific components to be pruned within each layer's allocated budget. Experimental results show that our approach reduces model complexity with minimal impact on commonsense reasoning tasks and zero-shot performance. Our method achieves a favorable trade-off among accuracy, latency, and model size, making it suitable for edge deployment. Across multiple LLMs at 37.5% and 50% pruning ratios, the proposed approach achieves better performance on commonsense reasoning tasks than existing methods while significantly reducing inference cost.

AI.tldr: A hardware-aware, multi-objective structured pruning framework for LLMs that combines coarse-grained depth pruning (removing entire attention/MLP blocks) with fine-grained Parallel Bayesian Optimization for layer-wise pruning ratios, achieving efficient edge deployment with favorable accuracy-latency-size trade-offs.
AI.motivation: LLMs are difficult to deploy on embedded/edge platforms due to strict latency, memory, and energy constraints caused by their large parameter counts and computational demands.
AI.method: A two-stage structured pruning framework: (1) coarse-grained multi-objective depth pruning removes entire attention and MLP blocks; (2) fine-grained stage uses Parallel Bayesian Optimization (PBO) to search optimal layer-wise pruning ratios under latency constraints, with importance-based strategies ranking specific components within each layer's budget.
AI.result: At 37.5% and 50% pruning ratios, the method achieves better performance on commonsense reasoning tasks than existing methods while significantly reducing inference cost.
AI.conclusion: The approach achieves a favorable trade-off among accuracy, latency, and model size, making LLMs suitable for edge deployment with minimal impact on commonsense reasoning and zero-shot performance.

title: CRAFT: Learn the Schema, Execute the Plan
summary: Enterprise coding agents translate natural-language analytical requests into executable code over proprietary APIs, schemas, and metric definitions. Yet the prevailing deployment pattern injecting exhaustive schema and tool documentation into each prompt increases inference overhead, complicates schema evolution, and undermines reliability in multi-turn analysis. We investigate whether stable schema knowledge and tool-use behavior can instead be acquired through post-training while preserving the consistency required for production-facing analytics. We present CRAFT, a two-stage post-training recipe for schema-grounded coding agents. First, schema-stripped PLAN supervised fine-tuning learns domain-structured plans and executable behaviors from validated trajectories without exhaustive prompt-time schema injection. Second, execution-shaped reinforcement learning aligns the policy for tool selection, code quality, plan-code consistency, and recovery from failed executions. Training trajectories are curated through a Tri-Gate filter combining execution validation, data-integrity checks, and LLM-judge reasoning audit. We evaluate CRAFT for planned rollout in advertising analytics, covering campaign performance analysis, metric drill-downs, entity-level performance analysis, and multi-turn analytical refinement. The enterprise evaluation environment incorporates beta APIs as the agent-facing tool surface and spans 25 schema-linked core entities and 30 agentic workflows. Relative to a schema-stuffed baseline, CRAFT improves composite Agent Score by +9.6 pp, consistency by +4.1 pp, and multi-turn coherence by +4.2 pp, while reducing input-token burden by approximately 9x and schema-discovery loops by up to 5x. We further report deployment tradeoffs, reward-shaping limitations, and training-infrastructure extensions required for multi-turn tool-use reinforcement learning in enterprise settings.

AI.tldr: CRAFT is a two-stage post-training recipe for schema-grounded enterprise coding agents that replaces exhaustive prompt-time schema injection with learned schema knowledge via PLAN supervised fine-tuning and execution-shaped reinforcement learning, achieving +9.6 pp Agent Score improvement while reducing input tokens by ~9x and schema-discovery loops by up to 5x in advertising analytics.
AI.motivation: Current deployment of enterprise coding agents injects exhaustive schema and tool documentation into each prompt, increasing inference overhead, complicating schema evolution, and undermining reliability in multi-turn analysis. The goal is to investigate whether stable schema knowledge and tool-use behavior can be acquired through post-training while preserving production-facing consistency.
AI.method: Two-stage post-training: (1) Schema-stripped PLAN supervised fine-tuning learns domain-structured plans and executable behaviors from validated trajectories without exhaustive schema injection. (2) Execution-shaped reinforcement learning aligns policy for tool selection, code quality, plan-code consistency, and recovery from failed executions. Training trajectories curated via Tri-Gate filter combining execution validation, data-integrity checks, and LLM-judge reasoning audit.
AI.result: In advertising analytics (25 schema-linked core entities, 30 agentic workflows), CRAFT improves composite Agent Score by +9.6 pp, consistency by +4.1 pp, and multi-turn coherence by +4.2 pp, while reducing input-token burden by ~9x and schema-discovery loops by up to 5x relative to a schema-stuffed baseline.
AI.conclusion: CRAFT demonstrates that stable schema knowledge and tool-use behavior can be effectively acquired through post-training, offering substantial efficiency gains and reliability improvements over schema-stuffed prompting. The paper also reports deployment tradeoffs, reward-shaping limitations, and training-infrastructure extensions required for multi-turn tool-use reinforcement learning in enterprise settings.

title: CrossSpine: Multi-scale Cross-sequence Attention with Anatomical Priors for Automated Pfirrmann Grading
summary: Automated grading of Lumbar Disc Degeneration is essential for the objective quantification of structural changes associated with low back pain. Observing that baseline models underperformed on our data, we propose a framework designed to overcome these limitations. First, we present the Cross-sequence Attention Spine (CrossSpine) framework, a novel architecture that employs a cross-sequence attention mechanism to adaptively fuse features from different MRI sequences at multiple spa- tial scales. Second, we contribute a meticulously curated dataset aimed at automated Pfirrmann grading. Finally, we introduce an IVD-aware classification technique that integrates anatomical disc-level information, enabling the model to learn level-specific degeneration priors. Our experi- ments demonstrate the superiority of this approach: CrossSpine achieved a relative improvement exceeding 125% in the Macro F1 score, while boosting the Mean AUPRC by 99% and the Mean AUROC by 36% com- pared to the baseline.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes CrossSpine, a cross-sequence attention framework for automated Pfirrmann grading of lumbar disc degeneration, along with a new dataset and IVD-aware classification, achieving over 125% improvement in Macro F1 score over baseline.
AI.motivation: Automated grading of Lumbar Disc Degeneration is needed for objective quantification of structural changes in low back pain, but baseline models underperform on real-world data.
AI.method: (1) CrossSpine: a cross-sequence attention mechanism for adaptive multi-scale feature fusion from different MRI sequences. (2) A meticulously curated dataset for automated Pfirrmann grading. (3) IVD-aware classification that integrates anatomical disc-level information to learn level-specific degeneration priors.
AI.result: CrossSpine achieved a relative improvement exceeding 125% in Macro F1 score, 99% boost in Mean AUPRC, and 36% boost in Mean AUROC compared to the baseline.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach significantly outperforms baseline models, demonstrating the effectiveness of cross-sequence attention fusion and disc-level priors for automated lumbar disc degeneration grading.

title: From Hybrid Mechanistic--Data-Driven Modeling Toward Neuro-Symbolic AI: What, Why, and How
summary:
Hybrid mechanistic/data-driven models, which combine first-principles with learned components, are increasingly used in process engineering and scientific machine learning. Common hybrid modeling designs are specified primarily through their architectures and training losses, which offers a limited basis for a shared semantic interface to compare or verify them across domains, with comparatively little attention paid to epistemic uncertainty in the mechanistic part.
  We bridge hybrid modeling and neuro-symbolic (NeSy) AI by reconstructing these designs as instances of NeSy interface. The resulting translation, Hybrid-to-NeSy (H2N), places mechanistic knowledge on the language side, learned modules on the belief side, and validity domains together with constraints on the logic side. For each design, H2N then yields an explicit NeSy inference functional and a logic-belief decomposition.
  From this decomposition we derive two metrics: structural violation rate (SVR), measuring whether the learned belief respects the mechanistic structure; and belief dispersion (BD), measuring how concentrated the learned plausibility is, serving as a hybrid model's epistemic uncertainty in its mechanistic part. We instantiate H2N on a case study of a structured hybrid model for binary classification under label noise and show that models with higher SVR and BD exhibit greater variability in held-out accuracy. Under structural distribution shift, H2N further quantifies a model's uncertainty during extrapolations, whereas test accuracy reveals the same shift only post hoc.

AI.tldr: This paper presents H2N, a framework that translates hybrid mechanistic/data-driven models into neuro-symbolic AI constructs, deriving two metrics (SVR and BD) to quantify epistemic uncertainty in the mechanistic part, validated on a binary classification case study.
AI.motivation: Current hybrid modeling designs are specified primarily through architectures and training losses, lacking a shared semantic interface for comparison and verification across domains, and paying insufficient attention to epistemic uncertainty in the mechanistic component.
AI.method: The authors bridge hybrid modeling and neuro-symbolic AI by reconstructing hybrid designs as NeSy interfaces (H2N), placing mechanistic knowledge on the language side, learned modules on the belief side, and validity domains/constraints on the logic side. They derive two metrics: Structural Violation Rate (SVR) and Belief Dispersion (BD).
AI.result: On a structured hybrid model for binary classification under label noise, models with higher SVR and BD show greater variability in held-out accuracy. Under structural distribution shift, H2N quantifies uncertainty during extrapolations before test accuracy reveals the shift.
AI.conclusion: H2N provides a principled NeSy-based framework for analyzing hybrid models, offering interpretable uncertainty metrics that can detect structural issues (distribution shift) earlier than traditional accuracy-based evaluation.

title: Source-Aware Reranking for Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Reliability Prior Approach
summary: Standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation pipelines rank retrieved documents by semantic similarity alone, without accounting for source provenance or credibility. This work evaluates a simple and interpretable modification to RAG retrieval ranking that incorporates domain-informed source reliability priors. Each document is assigned a prior lambda(s) based on its source type, and retrieval scores are reweighted using score(q, d) = sim(q, d) * lambda(s). The framework is evaluated against a similarity-only baseline on a 120-document health-domain corpus. In this controlled setting, source-aware reranking improves Precision@5 from 0.48 to 0.72 and reduces average adversarial document retrieval under the evaluated threat model, where low-credibility sources are identifiable via metadata. All experiments were executed on Rosie, the high-performance computing cluster at the Milwaukee School of Engineering, which provided the GPU-accelerated infrastructure necessary to run the full experimental pipeline reliably and reproducibly. These results suggest a potential mitigation strategy for source quality degradation in RAG pipelines, within the limits of the experimental setup described.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a simple modification to RAG retrieval ranking that incorporates source reliability priors by reweighting similarity scores with domain-informed source type weights (lambda), achieving significant improvements in Precision@5 (0.48→0.72) and reducing adversarial document retrieval in a health-domain corpus.
AI.motivation: Standard RAG pipelines rank documents solely by semantic similarity, ignoring source provenance and credibility, which makes them vulnerable to low-quality or adversarial sources.
AI.method: Each document receives a prior lambda(s) based on its source type; retrieval scores are reweighted as score(q,d) = sim(q,d) * lambda(s). Evaluated against a similarity-only baseline on a 120-document health-domain corpus.
AI.result: Source-aware reranking improved Precision@5 from 0.48 to 0.72 and reduced average adversarial document retrieval under the evaluated threat model where low-credibility sources are identifiable via metadata.
AI.conclusion: Source-aware reranking offers a potential mitigation strategy for source quality degradation in RAG pipelines, within the limits of the controlled experimental setup.

title: Open Your Model's Eyes: Video and Context-Aware Multimodal Backchannel Prediction
summary: Backchannels, which signal listener states like empathy and understanding, are fundamental to natural human interaction. However, current approaches rely solely on audio and text. This omits crucial visual cues, such as facial expressions and gestures, as well as broader conversational contexts, which are necessary for accurate prediction. In this paper, we introduce Context-Aware Multimodal Alignment for Backchannel Prediction (CAMA-BC), a novel framework that leverages visual information through Multi-Layer Multimodal Alignment (MMA). Our alignment process comprises two stages. First, Context Alignment (MMA-CA) utilizes unlabeled dialogues with videos to capture conversational contexts. Next, Backchannel Alignment (MMA-BA) fine-tunes the representations specifically for backchannel prediction. Experimental results show that CAMA-BC significantly outperforms both existing methods and simple multimodal baselines, with particular effectiveness in recognizing complex backchannels such as empathy.

AI.tldr: CAMA-BC is a framework for backchannel prediction that incorporates visual information (facial expressions, gestures) through a two-stage multimodal alignment process (Context Alignment and Backchannel Alignment), significantly outperforming existing audio/text-only methods, especially for complex backchannels like empathy.
AI.motivation: Current backchannel prediction methods rely solely on audio and text, omitting crucial visual cues (facial expressions, gestures) and broader conversational contexts needed for accurate prediction.
AI.method: CAMA-BC uses Multi-Layer Multimodal Alignment (MMA) with two stages: (1) Context Alignment (MMA-CA) using unlabeled dialogue videos to capture conversational contexts, and (2) Backchannel Alignment (MMA-BA) fine-tuning representations specifically for backchannel prediction.
AI.result: CAMA-BC significantly outperforms existing methods and simple multimodal baselines, with particular effectiveness in recognizing complex backchannels such as empathy.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating visual information through structured multimodal alignment improves backchannel prediction, especially for nuanced listener responses like empathy.

title: MEMENTO: Memory-Guided Memetic Code-as-Policy Evolution
summary: Long-horizon embodied tasks require policies that execute many dependent actions before task success can be observed. Representing policies as executable control pro- grams (code-as-policy) enables their decision logic to be inspected and revised after rollout evaluation. Revised programs can then be executed and compared by rollout performance, framing policy improvement as execution-guided program search. Evo- lutionary methods driven by large language models (LLMs) provide a natural mecha- nism for this search by generating variants and selecting high-performing candidates. However, existing approaches primarily select among independently generated vari- ants and lack a sequential local improvement phase. We introduce MEMENTO, a memory-guided single-elite memetic framework for code-as-policy evolution. ME- MENTO first evolves a rollout evaluator that maps policy rollouts to scalar fitness and structured feedback metrics. Fitness selects accepted candidates and the next elite, while feedback metrics condition policy proposals generated by memory-guided hill-climbing, macro-mutation, and crossover. We evaluate MEMENTO on two long- horizon embodied domains: Robosuite Franka Tower-of-Hanoi manipulation and AI2- THOR household interaction. MEMENTO outperforms Eureka and REvolve, adapted as code-as-policy evolutionary baselines, in task success and generalization to held- out Robosuite object configurations and unseen AI2-THOR scenes. Ablations show that zero-shot generation and unevolved evaluators fail to solve either domain, and that removing policy-search branches reduces performance. Finally, we deploy the best-evolved Robosuite policy on a physical Franka robot, demonstrating the feasibil- ity of sim-to-real transfer of the evolved code-as-policy. Code, prompts, and videos are available at: https://github.com/sygkounas/MEMENTO.

AI.tldr: MEMENTO is a memory-guided memetic framework for evolving robot control programs (code-as-policy) that outperforms baselines in long-horizon embodied tasks like Tower-of-Hanoi manipulation and household interaction, with successful sim-to-real transfer.
AI.motivation: Existing code-as-policy evolutionary methods lack a sequential local improvement phase, as they primarily select among independently generated variants without memory-guided refinement.
AI.method: MEMENTO evolves a rollout evaluator to map rollouts to scalar fitness and structured feedback metrics. It uses fitness for candidate selection and elite definition, while feedback metrics condition policy proposals via memory-guided hill-climbing, macro-mutation, and crossover in a single-elite memetic framework.
AI.result: MEMENTO outperforms Eureka and REvolve baselines on Robosuite Franka Tower-of-Hanoi and AI2-THOR domains in task success and generalization. Ablations confirm zero-shot generation and unevolved evaluators fail, and removing search branches degrades performance. The best policy was successfully deployed on a physical Franka robot.
AI.conclusion: Memory-guided sequential improvement is critical for effective code-as-policy evolution in long-horizon embodied tasks, and evolved policies can transfer from simulation to real robots.

title: The Scaffold Effect in Coding Agents: Harness Choice as a Hidden Variable in Coding-Agent Evaluation
comment: 7 pages, 2 figures, 6 tables. Preliminary work; under review at the 5th DL4C Workshop @ ICML 2026
summary: Public leaderboards for coding agents typically rank systems by model name and pass rate, while the surrounding harness (the scaffold that issues tools, manages context, and decides when to stop) is often under-specified. Model-to-model comparison is valid when the harness is fixed; when it varies, performance and efficiency conflate model and scaffold effects. We evaluate Qwen 3.6 Plus and MiniMax M2.5 across three open-source harnesses (Goose, OpenCode, OpenHands-SDK) on a stratified 50-task subset of Terminal-Bench Pro. Harness choice induces up to a 40x difference in tokens per solved task, while paired within-model pass-rate differences remain 0-8 percentage points (95% paired-task bootstrap CIs include zero except for the largest gap). Failure fingerprints replicate across models (REASON for Goose, VERIFY/MAX_TURNS for OpenHands-SDK, idle-loop/TIME for OpenCode), indicating harness-level biases that are largely model-independent. For human-centered coding-agent evaluation, model name alone is an incomplete comparison unit: harness-model pairs determine real-world cost, latency, and oversight burden; no-action turns are a per-task wait tax, not just a token tax. We therefore recommend selecting harness-model pairs by pass rate under token/latency budgets, and reporting token usage, latency, and full harness specifications alongside any model comparison. We release anonymized configs, raw trial logs, aggregated snapshots, and analysis scripts.

AI.tldr: Harness choice causes up to 40x token cost variation per solved task with minimal pass-rate differences (0-8pp), revealing that coding-agent evaluations should compare harness-model pairs rather than model names alone, and should report token/latency/harness specs alongside pass rates.
AI.motivation: Public coding-agent leaderboards rank by model name and pass rate but under-specify the harness (scaffold, tools, context management, stopping criteria). When harness varies, performance and efficiency conflate model and scaffold effects, making comparisons incomplete and potentially misleading for real-world deployment.
AI.method: Evaluated Qwen 3.6 Plus and MiniMax M2.5 across three open-source harnesses (Goose, OpenCode, OpenHands-SDK) on a stratified 50-task subset of Terminal-Bench Pro, measuring pass rates, token usage, latency, and failure patterns using paired-task bootstrap confidence intervals.
AI.result: Harness choice induces up to 40x difference in tokens per solved task; within-model pass-rate differences are 0-8 percentage points (95% CIs include zero except for the largest gap). Failure fingerprints (e.g., REASON for Goose, VERIFY/MAX_TURNS for OpenHands-SDK, idle-loop/TIME for OpenCode) replicate across models, revealing model-independent harness-level biases.
AI.conclusion: Model name alone is an incomplete comparison unit; harness-model pairs determine real-world cost, latency, and oversight burden. Recommend selecting harness-model pairs by pass rate under token/latency budgets, and reporting token usage, latency, and full harness specifications alongside model comparisons.

title: How Well Can AI Generate Backlogs from App Mockups?
comment: Accepted at the AIRE Workshop, IEEE 34th International Requirements Engineering Conference (RE) 2026
summary: Creating sprint backlogs requires considerable effort, as items such as epics, user stories, and tasks can be missed or inconsistently specified. We propose a multimodal approach to support backlog generation from visual app mockups, an artifact available at early project stages. We evaluate three prompting strategies on GPT-4o: a zero-shot baseline, Compositional Chain-of-Thought (CCoT) for vision-language reasoning, and a persona-driven prompt. We study seven app development projects across two countries and interview developers about the results. Overall, we observed that the baseline prompt favours recall over precision, whereas CCoT is more balanced, achieving average F1 scores of 52-66% for epics and user stories. Tasks were more challenging to generate accurately. Precision gains were most consistent when adding architectural context, particularly for backend tasks (precision gains up to 35%). Interviews with developers revealed that up to 26% of false positives were still considered useful, reflecting the creative and open-ended nature of backlog creation. To capture this, we propose a new measure called Revised Recall, which complements ground-truth evaluation with developer assessments. Our findings suggest that hybrid prompting with architectural context can assist backlog generation from early mockups, though results vary by item type and developer oversight remains necessary.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a multimodal approach using GPT-4o with different prompting strategies (zero-shot, Compositional Chain-of-Thought, persona-driven) to generate sprint backlogs from visual app mockups. CCoT achieves balanced F1 scores (52-66% for epics/user stories), while adding architectural context improves precision (up to 35% for backend tasks). Developers found up to 26% of false positives useful, leading to a proposed Revised Recall metric.
