AI.motivation: Creating sprint backlogs is labor-intensive and prone to errors (missed or inconsistently specified items). The authors aim to automate backlog generation from visual app mockups, which are available early in development, to reduce manual effort and improve consistency.
AI.method: Three prompting strategies (zero-shot baseline, Compositional Chain-of-Thought for vision-language reasoning, persona-driven prompt) are evaluated on GPT-4o across seven app development projects in two countries. Developers are interviewed to assess generated items, and a Revised Recall metric is proposed to incorporate developer judgments of false positives.
AI.result: CCoT achieves average F1 scores of 52-66% for epics and user stories; tasks are harder to generate accurately. Architectural context yields precision gains up to 35% for backend tasks. Up to 26% of false positives are deemed useful by developers. The baseline favors recall over precision, while CCoT is more balanced.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid prompting with architectural context can assist backlog generation from early mockups, but results vary by item type and developer oversight remains necessary. The Revised Recall metric better captures real-world utility of generated items.

title: Calibration-Free 3D Multi-Camera People Tracking for Indoor Environment
summary: Multi-Camera People Tracking (MCPT) traditionally relies on precise intrinsic and extrinsic camera calibration to project 2D detections into a unified 3D world coordinate system.However, manual calibration constitutes a major bottleneck in large-scale dataset generation from unconstrained video archives.  This work proposes a unified calibration-free 3D MCPT framework that infers geometric structure directly from visual data using deep foundation models.  The system integrates anchor-free detection (YOLOX), robust tracking (BoT-SORT), omni-scale appearance embedding (OsNet), pose estimation (HRNet via MMPose), and transformer-based geometric reconstruction using the Visual Geometry Grounded Transformer (VGGT). A pose-guided 3D lifting strategy projects head keypoints onto a reconstructed manifold, eliminating dependence on ground-plane homography. Global identity association is formulated as hierarchical agglomerative clustering under a joint appearance-geometry cost with strict velocity gating. Evaluation on the AI City Challenge 2024 demonstrates a HOTA score of 53.13% without access to ground-truth calibration matrices, establishing a strong baseline for purely vision-based 3D tracking.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a calibration-free 3D multi-camera people tracking framework that uses deep foundation models (VGGT, YOLOX, BoT-SORT, OsNet, HRNet) to infer geometric structure directly from visual data, eliminating the need for manual intrinsic/extrinsic camera calibration, achieving 53.13% HOTA on the AI City Challenge 2024.
AI.motivation: Manual camera calibration is a major bottleneck in large-scale dataset generation from unconstrained video archives, limiting the scalability of traditional MCPT systems.
AI.method: Proposes a unified calibration-free framework integrating anchor-free detection (YOLOX), robust tracking (BoT-SORT), omni-scale appearance embedding (OsNet), pose estimation (HRNet via MMPose), and transformer-based geometric reconstruction (VGGT). Uses pose-guided 3D lifting to project head keypoints onto a reconstructed manifold, avoiding ground-plane homography. Global identity association uses hierarchical agglomerative clustering with joint appearance-geometry cost and velocity gating.
AI.result: Achieves 53.13% HOTA score on the AI City Challenge 2024 without access to ground-truth calibration matrices.
AI.conclusion: Establishes a strong baseline for purely vision-based 3D multi-camera people tracking that eliminates the dependency on manual calibration, enabling scalable tracking from unconstrained video archives.

title: Frustratingly Simple Black-Box Adaptation of Language Models via Logit Bias
comment: 36 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables. Appendix included. Code available at https://github.com/Ofek-Israeli/logit_bias_lm_adaptation
summary: Many organizations aim to adapt language models for internal use, both to improve performance on domain-specific tasks and to address privacy concerns around sensitive data. However, such adaptation remains non-trivial: it often requires operationally challenging fine-tuning of open-source models or ad hoc prompt optimization. We study a minimal alternative based on a simple API-level control: allowing users to bias the model's logits with a user-defined vector. We develop a black-box method for learning a single context-independent logit-bias vector, added at every decoding step, without modifying model weights or requiring gradients. Starting from a KL-regularized reinforcement learning (RL) objective, we characterize when such a fixed logit-bias vector can approximate the optimal prefix-dependent correction and derive a closed-form inverse-propensity estimator from rollouts, rewards, and token probabilities. Empirically, this simple decoding-time intervention improves over base models on mathematical and reasoning benchmarks while using far fewer trainable parameters than conventional fine-tuning. Our results suggest that learned logit bias is a lightweight mechanism for adapting language models under minimal access requirements.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a lightweight method for adapting language models by learning a single logit-bias vector applied at every decoding step, without modifying model weights or requiring gradients. Using a KL-regularized RL objective, they derive a closed-form estimator for the bias vector and show it improves reasoning benchmarks while requiring far fewer parameters than fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Organizations need to adapt language models for domain-specific tasks and privacy concerns, but existing methods (fine-tuning open-source models or prompt optimization) are operationally challenging and non-trivial.
AI.method: The authors develop a black-box method to learn a single context-independent logit-bias vector added at every decoding step. They derive a closed-form inverse-propensity estimator from a KL-regularized RL objective, using rollouts, rewards, and token probabilities without requiring model weights or gradients.
AI.result: The learned logit-bias vector improves over base models on mathematical and reasoning benchmarks while using far fewer trainable parameters than conventional fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: Learned logit bias is a lightweight and effective mechanism for adapting language models under minimal access requirements, offering a practical alternative to fine-tuning or prompt engineering.

title: MM-ShiftKV: Decode-Aware Prefill-Stage KV Selection for Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: Key-Value (KV) caching is essential for efficient inference in multimodal large language models (MLLMs), yet its memory footprint grows linearly with context length and becomes a major bottleneck due to the large number of visual tokens. Recent prefill-stage KV selection methods estimate KV importance from prefilling statistics, implicitly assuming that prefilling-time queries are representative of those encountered during decoding. We show that this assumption breaks down in multimodal inference, where decoding-time queries exhibit substantially larger variance than prefilling-stage representations, leading to unstable KV importance estimation under tight cache budgets. As a result, small ranking errors can disproportionately discard semantically critical visual tokens and degrade grounding and reasoning performance. We propose MM-ShiftKV, a training-free, decode-aware and strictly prefill-only KV selection method. MM-ShiftKV approximates decoding-time query behavior during prefilling by constructing variance-expanded query proxies and estimates prompt KV importance based on their aggregated attention mass. Experiments on multimodal benchmarks demonstrate that MM-ShiftKV consistently outperforms existing methods under strict KV-cache budgets. Our code is available at https://github.com/zjuDBxAI/MM-ShiftKV.

AI.tldr: MM-ShiftKV is a training-free KV cache selection method for MLLMs that addresses the instability of prefilling-stage importance estimation during decoding by constructing variance-expanded query proxies, improving multimodal grounding and reasoning under tight cache budgets.
AI.motivation: Existing prefill-stage KV selection methods assume prefilling queries are representative of decoding queries, but this assumption fails in multimodal inference where decoding queries have much larger variance, causing unstable importance estimation and loss of critical visual tokens under tight budgets.
AI.method: MM-ShiftKV constructs variance-expanded query proxies during prefilling to approximate decoding-time query behavior, then estimates prompt KV importance based on aggregated attention mass of these proxies. It is training-free, decode-aware, and strictly prefill-only.
AI.result: MM-ShiftKV consistently outperforms existing methods on multimodal benchmarks under strict KV-cache budgets, with code available at the provided GitHub link.
AI.conclusion: Decode-aware KV selection via variance-expanded query proxies effectively mitigates the instability of importance estimation in multimodal inference, enabling better preservation of semantically critical visual tokens under tight cache constraints.

title: Evaluating Fuzz Testing for Reinforcement Learning Agents
summary: Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents are increasingly deployed in safety-critical domains such as robotics, autonomous driving, and drone control, where unexpected behaviors may lead to severe real-world consequences. Fuzz testing has recently emerged as a promising method for exploring the vast state spaces of RL agents and exposing crashes. Although numerous RL fuzzing methods have been proposed, existing studies often differ in evaluation settings, baselines, and metrics, making it difficult to draw reliable conclusions about their relative effectiveness and practical usefulness. To address this gap, we present the first comprehensive empirical study that systematically evaluates RL fuzzing methods from four complementary perspectives: effectiveness, diversity, efficiency, and practical utility. We benchmark five state-of-the-art methods alongside random testing under unified configurations across three environments of increasing complexity (MountainCar, BipedalWalker, and CARLA), and further assess the downstream usefulness of detected crashes for agent robustness improvement and safety monitoring. Our results reveal several key insights. For instance,throughput-oriented methods like MDPFuzz demonstrate superior effectiveness and efficiency in crash discovery, while methods explicitly designed to encourage exploration like SeqDivFuzz excel at uncovering diverse crash behaviors. We also show that fuzzing-generated crashes can meaningfully improve agent robustness and enable accurate safety monitoring with strong cross-method generalization. Beyond these empirical findings, we distill actionable guidance for both researchers and practitioners, highlighting the benefits of combining complementary fuzzing strategies and adopting multi-level diversity analysis to achieve more comprehensive and practical RL testing.

AI.tldr: First comprehensive empirical study benchmarking five state-of-the-art RL fuzzing methods across three environments, revealing that throughput-oriented methods (MDPFuzz) excel at crash discovery while exploration-focused methods (SeqDivFuzz) uncover diverse crashes, with practical utility demonstrated for robustness improvement and safety monitoring.
AI.motivation: RL agents are deployed in safety-critical domains, and existing RL fuzzing studies differ in evaluation settings, baselines, and metrics, making it difficult to draw reliable conclusions about their relative effectiveness and practical usefulness.
AI.method: Systematically evaluated five state-of-the-art RL fuzzing methods plus random testing under unified configurations across three environments (MountainCar, BipedalWalker, CARLA) from four perspectives: effectiveness, diversity, efficiency, and practical utility. Assessed downstream usefulness for robustness improvement and safety monitoring.
AI.result: Throughput-oriented methods (MDPFuzz) show superior effectiveness and efficiency in crash discovery; exploration-focused methods (SeqDivFuzz) excel at uncovering diverse crash behaviors; fuzzing-generated crashes can improve agent robustness and enable accurate safety monitoring with cross-method generalization.
AI.conclusion: Distill actionable guidance for researchers and practitioners, highlighting benefits of combining complementary fuzzing strategies and adopting multi-level diversity analysis for more comprehensive and practical RL testing.

title: Generative Augmentation for EEG Motor Imagery Classification: A Class-Conditional VAE with Cycle-Consistent Decoder Refinement
summary: We investigate whether a generative model can supply useful synthetic motor-imagery (MI) electroencephalography (EEG) trials that improve the accuracy of independent downstream classifiers. We train a class-conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) with an integrated latent classifier on the Zhou motor-imagery dataset, using the learned per-class prior as a generator: sampling the prior for a given label and decoding it into a synthetic, label-consistent signal. A constraint on the covariance matrix of the generated data encourages preservation of covariance structure, and the model is trained with a schedule that alternates ordinary VAE training with a decoder-focused phase that sharpens the generative pathway used for augmentation. We measure the effect of adding synthetic trials to the training set under two evaluation protocols -- within-user (pooled 60/20/20 split across subjects) and cross-user (leave-one-subject-out, LOSO) -- across four representative EEG classification pipelines: Common Spatial Patterns with Linear Discriminant Analysis (CSP+LDA), tangent-space features with a Support Vector Machine (TGSP+SVM), Minimum Distance to Riemannian Mean (MDM), and a neural network based on EEGNetv4 (henceforth EEGNet). Results are aggregated across independent augmentation draws, random seeds (within-user), or leave-one-subject-out folds (cross-user), with uncertainty reported as 95\% confidence intervals (Student's $t$-distribution) computed over per-seed/per-fold averages. We find that synthetic EEG from the CVAE is most credible as a source of class-structured, covariance-like data rather than as a substitute for real raw EEG: it can raise the point estimate for MDM, but the broader augmentation claim remains conservative -- observed gains are small and classifier-dependent.

AI.tldr: A class-conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) with latent classifier and covariance constraint is trained on motor-imagery EEG data to generate synthetic trials for data augmentation. Adding these synthetic trials yields small, classifier-dependent improvements (e.g., for MDM) but overall gains are conservative; synthetic EEG is more credible as class-structured covariance-like data than as a substitute for real raw EEG.
AI.motivation: To determine whether synthetic EEG trials generated by a generative model can improve the accuracy of downstream classifiers for motor-imagery brain-computer interfaces, addressing the chronic problem of limited training data in MI-BCI.
AI.method: A class-conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) with an integrated latent classifier is trained on the Zhou motor-imagery dataset. Training alternates between ordinary VAE training and a decoder-focused phase. Generation uses the learned per-class prior. A covariance-matrix constraint preserves covariance structure. Evaluation uses within-user (60/20/20) and cross-user (LOSO) protocols with CSP+LDA, TGSP+SVM, MDM, and EEGNet classifiers.
AI.result: Synthetic EEG from the CVAE provides small, classifier-dependent accuracy improvements. MDM shows the most notable improvement, but overall gains are conservative and do not consistently outperform baselines across all classifiers and protocols.
AI.conclusion: The CVAE-generated synthetic EEG is most useful as class-structured, covariance-like data rather than as a direct substitute for real raw EEG. Data augmentation with such synthetic trials yields limited benefits, suggesting that broader augmentation claims should be tempered.

title: Same Predictions, Different Reasons: The Effect of Quantization on Model Explanations
summary: Post-training quantization (PTQ) has become a practical solution for deploying deep learning models on resource-constrained edge devices by compressing high-precision floating-point weights into low-precision representations without requiring retraining. Past research has demonstrated that quantization largely preserves classification accuracy; however, whether it also preserves the model's internal reasoning remains an open question. This study presents a systematic evaluation on how static PTQ affects the interpretability / explainability of five widely used CNN architectures: VGG19, ResNet18, EfficientNet-B0, DenseNet161, and MobileNetV2 at INT8 and INT4 precision. We employ a dual interpretability framework that combines Grad-CAM for spatial attention analysis with LIME for input-level feature attribution, and systematically compare full-precision and quantized models on two binary classification datasets. Interpretability is evaluated using three complementary metrics: the Pearson correlation coefficient, structural similarity index, and top-20% IoU to capture distributional and structural variations in model explanations, supplemented by deletion/insertion faithfulness analysis. The results show that classification accuracy is not a reliable indicator of interpretability stability under reduced precision. DenseNet161 maintains strong feature consistency across both precision levels, whereas EfficientNet-B0, despite achieving competitive spatial attention and classification accuracy at INT8 precision, exhibits a substantial degradation in input-level feature attribution. These findings have direct implications for the trustworthy deployment of quantized models in applications with high interpretability requirements, demonstrating that architecture selection is as important as the quantization strategy.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates how post-training quantization (INT8/INT4) affects the interpretability of five CNN architectures, finding that classification accuracy is not a reliable indicator of interpretability stability, with DenseNet161 maintaining strong feature consistency while EfficientNet-B0 shows substantial degradation in input-level feature attribution despite competitive accuracy.
AI.motivation: While past research shows PTQ preserves classification accuracy, whether it preserves the model's internal reasoning remains an open question, motivating this systematic evaluation of interpretability under reduced precision.
AI.method: Systematic evaluation of static PTQ on VGG19, ResNet18, EfficientNet-B0, DenseNet161, and MobileNetV2 at INT8 and INT4 precision using a dual interpretability framework combining Grad-CAM (spatial attention) and LIME (input-level feature attribution), evaluated with Pearson correlation, SSIM, top-20% IoU, and deletion/insertion faithfulness analysis.
AI.result: Classification accuracy is not a reliable indicator of interpretability stability under reduced precision. DenseNet161 maintains strong feature consistency across both precision levels, while EfficientNet-B0 exhibits substantial degradation in input-level feature attribution at INT8 despite competitive spatial attention and accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Architecture selection is as important as the quantization strategy for trustworthy deployment of quantized models in applications with high interpretability requirements.

title: TriSP: Tri-Signal Structured Pruning for Large Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) achieve strong performance across diverse tasks but their deployment is constrained by the memory and compute cost of their parameters. Structured pruning addresses this by removing entire structures such as attention heads and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) neurons to produce smaller dense models that run efficiently on standard hardware. However, existing methods rely on either gradient-based importance estimation, which is memory-prohibitive, or activation-based statistical proxies, which do not directly measure the effect of removal on the loss. Furthermore, the interaction between the importance criterion and the post-pruning recovery strategy has not been systematically studied. We propose TriSP (Tri-Signal Structured Pruning), an importance metric that combines weight magnitude scaled by activation norm with first-order gradient sensitivity via a geometric mean, producing a channel-level score that captures both structural and loss-sensitivity signals. Combined with adaptive per-layer budget allocation and low-rank adaptation (LoRA) recovery, TriSP achieves the lowest perplexity and highest zero-shot accuracy across all tested configurations, reaching 6.80 WikiText-2 perplexity at 20% pruning on LLaMA-7B. Inference throughput improves by 82% at 50% pruning, while still maintaining competitive performance.

AI.tldr: TriSP is a structured pruning method for LLMs that combines weight magnitude, activation norm, and gradient sensitivity to efficiently prune attention heads and MLP neurons, achieving low perplexity and high throughput with LoRA-based recovery.
AI.motivation: Existing structured pruning methods rely on either memory-prohibitive gradient-based importance estimation or activation-based statistical proxies that do not directly measure loss impact; moreover, the interaction between importance metrics and post-pruning recovery strategies is understudied.
AI.method: TriSP (Tri-Signal Structured Pruning) computes a channel-level importance score via geometric mean of weight magnitude scaled by activation norm and first-order gradient sensitivity, combined with adaptive per-layer budget allocation and LoRA-based recovery.
AI.result: Achieves 6.80 WikiText-2 perplexity at 20% pruning on LLaMA-7B, and 82% inference throughput improvement at 50% pruning with competitive performance; outperforms existing methods across all tested configurations.
AI.conclusion: TriSP effectively balances pruning efficiency and model quality by integrating multiple importance signals and LoRA recovery, enabling efficient deployment of pruned LLMs on standard hardware.

title: Fast Fourier Convolutional GAN for 30 m Clear-Sky Land Surface Temperature Gap-Free Reconstruction
summary: Satellite-derived Land Surface Temperature (LST) provides spatially comprehensive data that ground stations cannot match. However, its utility is frequently limited by severe data gaps due to the presence of clouds. As LST is essential for understanding land-atmosphere interactions, numerous methods have been proposed to address this challenge. Yet, the development of a scalable and adaptable pipeline for generating gap-free LST datasets and reconstructing cloud-contaminated pixels remains challenging. Moreover, the reconstruction of extensive missing regions in fine-spatial-resolution observations is particularly difficult. To address this challenge, we propose a Multimodal Fast Fourier Convolutional GAN for reconstructing cloud-contaminated pixels in fine-resolution (30 m) Landsat imagery to generate gap-free clear-sky LST products. The method leverages Fast Fourier Convolution to enable a global receptive field across the image, and is guided by a stack of data consisting of satellite observations and Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) data. Across all LST quantiles, the interquartile range of scene-averaged RMSE (computed over reconstructed pixels) is consistently between 0.8 K and 1.8 K. The proposed approach enables the recovery of extensive missing regions, including scenes with more than 70% cloud-induced gaps, while relying on auxiliary data that are readily available at a near-global scale.

AI.tldr: Proposes a Multimodal Fast Fourier Convolutional GAN to reconstruct cloud-contaminated pixels in 30m Landsat LST imagery, using SAR and satellite data as auxiliary inputs, achieving RMSE of 0.8-1.8 K even with >70% cloud cover.
AI.motivation: LST from satellites has extensive data gaps due to clouds, limiting its utility; existing methods lack scalability and struggle with reconstructing large missing regions in fine-resolution imagery.
AI.method: A Multimodal Fast Fourier Convolutional GAN that uses Fast Fourier Convolution for global receptive field, guided by multi-modal inputs including satellite observations and Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) data.
AI.result: Interquartile range of scene-averaged RMSE across all LST quantiles is consistently between 0.8 K and 1.8 K; effective for scenes with >70% cloud-induced gaps.
AI.conclusion: The approach enables scalable recovery of extensive missing LST regions in fine-resolution Landsat imagery using globally available auxiliary data.

title: Spatial Prediction of Soil Microplastics and Organic Matter Using Graph Attention Networks
summary: Accurate estimation of soil microplastics and organic matter is essential to assess ecosystem health and support sustainable land use. This study presents a graph-based deep learning approach using Graph Attention Networks (GATs) to model spatial dependencies among 91 georeferenced soil samples. By incorporating spatial coordinates, soil properties, and land use data, a two-layer GAT architecture was developed to capture local interactions. The final model showed strong performance, achieving RMSEs of 625.06 ($R^2 = 0.87$) for microplastics and 0.43 ($R^2 = 0.91$) for organic matter. However, cross-validation results revealed limited generalization, probably due to the small sample size and sparse graph structure. These findings demonstrate the potential of GATs for spatial soil prediction and underscore the need for dense datasets and improved graph connectivity.

AI.tldr: This study applies Graph Attention Networks (GATs) to estimate soil microplastics and organic matter from 91 georeferenced samples. The model achieves high performance (R² = 0.87 for microplastics, 0.91 for organic matter) but shows limited generalization in cross-validation due to small sample size and sparse graph connectivity.
AI.motivation: Accurate estimation of soil microplastics and organic matter is essential for assessing ecosystem health and supporting sustainable land use, motivating the need for improved spatial prediction methods.
AI.method: A two-layer Graph Attention Network (GAT) architecture was developed incorporating spatial coordinates, soil properties, and land use data to model spatial dependencies among 91 georeferenced soil samples.
AI.result: The GAT model achieved RMSE of 625.06 (R² = 0.87) for microplastics and 0.43 (R² = 0.91) for organic matter, though cross-validation revealed limited generalization likely due to small sample size and sparse graph structure.
AI.conclusion: Graph Attention Networks show promise for spatial soil prediction, but future work requires denser datasets and improved graph connectivity to enhance model generalization capability.

title: ParBench: A Benchmark for Reliable Evaluation of LLM Parallel Code Translation
summary:
Modern compute-intensive software must migrate across a changing ecosystem of accelerators, programming APIs, compiler stacks, and portability layers, including CUDA, OpenMP, OpenCL, and OpenMP target offload. Large language models and autonomous coding agents are increasingly proposed for such migration, but the field lacks reliable ways to measure whether they preserve the low-level parallel semantics that make translations behaviorally valid, including thread indexing, synchronization, memory management, host-device coordination, and API-specific execution structure.
  We present ParBench, a kernel-centric benchmark framework for evaluating LLM-based parallel API translation under executable, reproducible conditions. ParBench fixes the surrounding build, run, and verification infrastructure through declarative benchmark specifications and asks models to translate only the computational kernels. It draws on multiple open-source HPC suites and covers representative cross-API translation directions among CUDA, OpenMP, OpenCL, and OpenMP target offload. To test whether success reflects robust translation rather than surface-form memorization, ParBench includes AST-driven, intended behavior-preserving, baseline-validated source augmentation. Evaluations on state-of-the-art open and proprietary LLMs show persistent barriers to reliable parallel code translation, including direction asymmetry, multi-file coordination, incomplete API adaptation, and uneven robustness to source-level perturbations. Code is available at https://github.com/Scientific-Computing-Lab/ParBench.

AI.tldr: ParBench is a kernel-centric benchmark framework for evaluating LLM-based parallel API translation across CUDA, OpenMP, OpenCL, and OpenMP target offload. It fixes infrastructure via declarative specs, includes AST-driven source augmentation to test robust translation, and reveals persistent barriers including direction asymmetry, multi-file coordination, incomplete API adaptation, and uneven robustness to perturbations.
AI.motivation: The field lacks reliable ways to measure whether LLM-based parallel code migrations preserve low-level parallel semantics (thread indexing, synchronization, memory management, host-device coordination, API-specific execution structure) that make translations behaviorally valid.
AI.method: ParBench fixes surrounding build/run/verification infrastructure via declarative benchmark specifications, asks models to translate only computational kernels, draws on multiple open-source HPC suites covering cross-API directions (CUDA, OpenMP, OpenCL, OpenMP target offload), and includes AST-driven, intended behavior-preserving, baseline-validated source augmentation to distinguish robust translation from surface-form memorization.
AI.result: Evaluations on state-of-the-art open and proprietary LLMs show persistent barriers: direction asymmetry, multi-file coordination issues, incomplete API adaptation, and uneven robustness to source-level perturbations.
AI.conclusion: Reliable parallel API translation by LLMs remains challenging; the ParBench framework systematically exposes these limitations and provides executable, reproducible conditions for evaluation.

title: Benchmarking the Domain Gap: Model Selection Instability Under Domain Shift in Video Capsule Endoscopy
summary: Video capsule endoscopy (VCE) classification is typically evaluated within a single dataset, yet clinical deployment demands robustness across acquisition sources, labeling policies, and patient populations. We examine this gap using Kvasir-Capsule, Capsule Vision 2024 (CV2024), and a shared-label subset of Galar. We fine-tune a suite of general-domain pretrained backbones on the official Kvasir-Capsule folds under a standardized protocol and evaluate the same checkpoints on two non-source targets within a documented shared-label decision space. We find that the predictive value of in-domain ranking is target-dependent: Kvasir-Capsule ranking aligns more closely with Galar than with CV2024, while the two non-source targets agree only weakly. Consequently, the strongest in-domain backbone leads on one target yet falls to mid-pack on the other, and no single evaluation target reliably predicts the others. A second CV2024-trained configuration set reproduces this target-dependent instability. We conclude that capsule endoscopy model selection should report cross-target ranking stability rather than peak single-dataset performance.

AI.tldr: VCE classification models show target-dependent ranking instability across datasets, where the best in-domain backbone may underperform on another target, and no single evaluation set reliably predicts performance on others.
AI.motivation: Clinical deployment of VCE classification models requires robustness across different acquisition sources, labeling policies, and patient populations, yet current evaluation is typically limited to single datasets, creating a gap between research and real-world applicability.
AI.method: Fine-tuned general-domain pretrained backbones on Kvasir-Capsule using standardized protocol, evaluated on two non-source targets (CV2024 and a Galar subset) within a shared-label decision space; additionally trained a CV2024-based configuration set for comparison.
AI.result: In-domain ranking is target-dependent; Kvasir-Capsule ranking aligns more with Galar than CV2024; non-source targets agree weakly; the best in-domain backbone leads on one target but is mid-pack on another; CV2024-trained set confirms instability.
AI.conclusion: Capsule endoscopy model selection should prioritize cross-target ranking stability over peak single-dataset performance.

title: Efficient Learning of Truncated Boolean Product Distributions: Influence to the Rescue
summary:
Learning the natural parameters $z \in \mathbb{R}^n$ of discrete distributions $μ_z$ from independent samples constrained to a subset $S \subseteq \{0,1\}^n$ is a foundational challenge in high-dimensional statistics. Existing methods for efficiently estimating truncated Boolean product distributions, notably the work of [Fotakis et al' COLT'20, Algorithmica '22], require either strong local connectivity assumptions on $S$ -- a property denoted fatness -- or stringent anti-concentration assumptions and necessitate the total mass of the truncation set to be a constant with respect to $n$. Moreover, the results in [Fotakis et al' COLT'20, Algorithmica '22] suffer from sample complexities that scale as $Ω(2^n)$ if the mass of $S$ is exponentially small in $n$.
  In this work, we circumvent these limitations by analyzing the geometry of $S$ under the measure $μ_z$. We refine the existing parameter estimation guarantees under the fatness assumption, improving the prior sample complexity to $O( \log n / ε^2)$ for $\ell_\infty$-recovery, matching the untruncated minimax rate. We further generalize fatness using the notion of influence utilized in the analysis of Boolean functions and provide sufficient conditions for efficient inference. Notably, unlike previous work, our method does not require sampling at arbitrary parameterizations of the model. Lastly, we establish a theoretical lower bound demonstrating the sample complexity exhibits an intrinsic exponential dependence on the width of the model and the minimum distance between elements in the set.

AI.tldr: This paper improves parameter estimation for truncated Boolean product distributions by refining sample complexity to O(log n / ε²) under fatness assumptions, generalizing the framework via influence, and proving fundamental lower bounds.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for estimating truncated Boolean product distributions suffer from limitations: they require strong local connectivity (fatness) or anti-concentration assumptions, rely on constant truncation mass relative to n, and have sample complexities scaling as Ω(2^n) when truncation mass is exponentially small. This paper aims to circumvent these limitations.
AI.method: The paper analyzes the geometry of the truncation set S under the measure μ_z, refines existing fatness-based guarantees, generalizes fatness via influence (a concept from Boolean function analysis), and provides sufficient conditions for efficient inference without requiring arbitrary parameter sampling.
AI.result: Improved sample complexity to O(log n / ε²) for ℓ∞-recovery, matching the untruncated minimax rate. A theoretical lower bound demonstrating exponential dependence on model width and minimum distance between elements in S.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach significantly improves upon prior work by removing restrictive assumptions, achieving minimax-optimal sample complexity under fatness, and extending efficient inference to broader settings via influence-based generalization.

title: Lexical discovery in unknown environments orchestrated by Large Language Models
summary: Populations of autonomous agents deployed in unknown environments (e.g. planetary or deep-sea exploration) must develop shared vocabularies to refer to entities that have no name in any human language. We propose the Neuro-Symbolic Lexical Discovery (NSLD) framework, in which a population of LLM-based agents plays a referential game over out-of-distribution visual referents, autonomously self-organising a shared alien lexicon. Each agent combines a frozen CLIP vision encoder with a private FAISS vector index and a text-only LLM. Crucially, discovered alien words are anchored to natural language via semantic proximity in the embedding space, enlarging the human vocabulary with new perceptually grounded words. Consensus is reached in simulations with populations of up to twenty agents and ten visual referents. Convergence dynamics are characterised through three analytical models achieving R^2 > 0.95, representing a first step towards pre-deployment planning in autonomous exploration missions.

AI.tldr: NSLD enables populations of LLM-based agents to autonomously develop shared alien vocabularies for novel visual referents via referential games, reaching consensus with R² > 0.95 convergence dynamics.
AI.motivation: Autonomous agents deployed in unknown environments (planetary/deep-sea exploration) need shared vocabularies for entities with no human-language names, but existing approaches lack mechanisms for emergent lexical consensus grounded in perception.
AI.method: NSLD combines frozen CLIP vision encoder, private FAISS vector index, and text-only LLM per agent. Agents play referential games over out-of-distribution visual referents, anchoring discovered alien words via semantic proximity in CLIP embedding space to natural language.
AI.result: Consensus achieved in simulations with up to 20 agents and 10 visual referents. Three analytical models characterize convergence dynamics with R² > 0.95.
AI.conclusion: First step towards pre-deployment planning for autonomous exploration missions where agents self-organize shared grounded lexicons without human intervention.

title: Cortex: Compact Behavior Cloning for Quake with Frozen Visual Features
comment: 13 pages, 2 figures, made with heavy assistance from LLM
summary: We study how far a deliberately simple behavioral-cloning policy can progress in a visually rich first-person game before adding reinforcement learning or explicit memory. Cortex is a compact Quake policy with 10.98 million trainable parameters in a six-layer transformer over a frozen DINOv3 encoder. It is trained on the Quake subset of the public Pixels2Play corpus: 6,849 recordings (about 474.7 hours), represented as 17.09 million cached decision frames with keyboard and mouse actions. One sampled training epoch uses 517,048 four-frame windows and takes 3.3 minutes of policy-head optimization on one RTX 5080, excluding one-time feature extraction. We evaluate two independent batches of 20 stochastic, 120-second episodes on Quake E1M1. Cortex does not complete the level, but every episode reaches the opening door, button room, and gate descent; 19 of 20 episodes in each batch record at least one kill. Under the same time-controlled harness, released P2P-150M and NitroGen checkpoints remain shallower in five matched-duration episodes each. These comparisons are limited by small reference samples and different native interfaces. Ablations show that denser visual tokens improve combat and survival, while longer optimization and naive action history improve offline metrics without consistently improving play. The remaining failures are consistent with covariate shift and motivate targeted corrective data. We release the policy implementation, checkpoint, and a representative rollout.

AI.tldr: Cortex, a simple behavioral-cloning policy with a 6-layer transformer and frozen DINOv3 encoder (10.98M params), is trained on the Quake subset of Pixels2Play (6,849 recordings, ~474.7 hours). It doesn't complete Quake E1M1 but consistently reaches early areas and gets kills. Compared favorably to P2P-150M and NitroGen in limited tests. Ablations show visual token density helps combat/survival; longer training helps offline metrics but not gameplay. Failures point to covariate shift, motivating targeted corrective data.
AI.motivation: To investigate how far a simple behavioral-cloning policy can progress in a visually rich first-person game (Quake) before adding reinforcement learning or explicit memory.
AI.method: A compact policy (Cortex) with 10.98M parameters: a six-layer transformer over a frozen DINOv3 encoder. Trained via behavioral cloning on the Quake subset of Pixels2Play (6,849 recordings, ~474.7 hours). One sampled training epoch uses 517,048 four-frame windows, optimized in 3.3 minutes on one RTX 5080 (excluding feature extraction). Evaluated on 2 batches of 20 stochastic 120-second episodes on Quake E1M1.
AI.result: Cortex does not complete the level but reaches the opening door, button room, and gate descent in every episode; 19/20 episodes per batch record at least one kill. Outperforms P2P-150M and NitroGen checkpoints in matched-duration episodes (limited by small reference samples and different native interfaces). Ablations: denser visual tokens improve combat and survival; longer optimization and naive action history improve offline metrics without consistently improving play.
AI.conclusion: Remaining failures are consistent with covariate shift, motivating targeted corrective data. Policy implementation, checkpoint, and a representative rollout are released.

title: Learning from the Descent Direction: Adaptive Gradient Descent under One-Sided Hölder Regularity
summary: We study adaptive gradient descent for continuously differentiable, possibly nonconvex objectives under one-sided Hölder regularity. Unlike classical Hölder- or Lipschitz-gradient assumptions, which control the full gradient variation, our condition bounds only the directional term appearing in the descent inequality. This can allow less conservative step sizes when large gradient changes are orthogonal to, or favorable along, the update direction. We propose an adaptive scalar-step method based on an estimate of positive one-sided Hölder curvature, combined with a simple sufficient-decrease safeguard. For nonconvex objectives on a convex region containing the accepted update segments, we prove an explicit best-iterate stationarity bound with a rate determined by the Hölder exponent. Unlike predetermined diminishing step-size schemes, the method adapts to the local descent geometry. We evaluate the approach on two full-batch benchmarks designed to separate directional curvature from full gradient variation. On a binary classification problem, the method achieves the lowest final cross-entropy, objective value, and gradient norm, together with the largest classification margin among the compared scalar gradient methods. On a nonconvex Hölder regression problem, it attains the lowest final objective gap and gradient norm. These results indicate that one-sided Hölder curvature is an effective adaptive step-size signal when full-gradient variation is inflated by directions that do not hinder descent.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an adaptive scalar-step gradient descent method that leverages one-sided Hölder curvature (which bounds only the directional term in the descent inequality rather than full gradient variation), enabling less conservative step sizes when large gradient changes are orthogonal or favorable to the update direction, with explicit best-iterate stationarity guarantees for nonconvex objectives and empirical improvements on full-batch benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Classical Lipschitz- or Hölder-gradient assumptions control the full gradient variation, which can be overly conservative for adaptive step-size selection when gradient changes are large but orthogonal to (or favorable along) the descent direction. The authors aim to exploit this directional asymmetry for more efficient adaptive step sizes.
AI.method: The method uses an adaptive scalar step size based on estimating the positive one-sided Hölder curvature, combined with a sufficient-decrease safeguard. The analysis assumes a convex region containing the accepted update segments and derives best-iterate stationarity bounds with rates determined by the Hölder exponent.
AI.result: On binary classification: lowest final cross-entropy, objective value, gradient norm, and largest classification margin among compared scalar gradient methods. On nonconvex Hölder regression: lowest final objective gap and gradient norm.
AI.conclusion: One-sided Hölder curvature is an effective signal for adaptive step-size selection, particularly when full-gradient variation is inflated by directions that do not hinder descent.

title: Structure Over Scale: Schema-Constrained Causal Graphs for RAG
summary: Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (GraphRAG) grounds answers in structured knowledge, but current systems extract entities and relationships exhaustively, producing graphs whose size and construction cost scale with corpus length rather than with the reasoning a query requires. We introduce HCG-RAG (Hierarchical Causal Graph RAG), which replaces open-ended extraction with schema-constrained causal graphs: an automated pipeline distills a corpus into a fixed, typed vocabulary of causal variables and materializes a compact two-tier graph over it. Our schema-constrained graphs match entity-relation baselines on answer quality at a fraction of the cost: 3-20x fewer nodes, 8x-135x fewer build-time LLM calls than the most LLM-intensive baseline (MS-GraphRAG), and graphs compact enough for a domain expert to audit, correct, and extend. On medical and clinical benchmarks, including a neurologist-validated epilepsy dataset, HCG-RAG matches or exceeds the best entity-relation systems. An ablation isolates the causal graph as a structured retrieval filter, contributing +6 percentage points (pp) over embedding-only retrieval. Across all domains with discoverable hierarchical causal structure, only methods imposing higher-level organization outperform flat entity-relation retrieval, indicating that what is placed in the graph matters more than how many nodes it contains.

AI.tldr: HCG-RAG replaces exhaustive entity-relation extraction with schema-constrained causal graphs, achieving 3-20x fewer nodes, 8-135x fewer LLM calls, and comparable or better answer quality on medical/clinical benchmarks while remaining auditable by domain experts.
AI.motivation: Current GraphRAG systems extract entities and relationships exhaustively, producing graphs whose size and construction cost scale with corpus length rather than with query-necessary reasoning, making them costly and uninterpretable.
AI.method: HCG-RAG uses an automated pipeline to distill a corpus into a fixed, typed vocabulary of causal variables and builds a compact two-tier hierarchical causal graph over it, replacing open-ended entity extraction with schema-constrained construction.
AI.result: 3-20x fewer nodes, 8-135x fewer build-time LLM calls vs MS-GraphRAG; matches or exceeds entity-relation baselines on medical/clinical benchmarks; causal graph contributes +6pp over embedding-only retrieval; ablations confirm hierarchical organization outperforms flat retrieval.
AI.conclusion: What is placed in the graph matters more than how many nodes it contains; only methods imposing higher-level organization outperform flat entity-relation retrieval across domains with discoverable hierarchical causal structure.

title: A Diagnostic Gap Framework for Evaluating Reconstruction Fidelity in Weakly Supervised Mammography
summary: Weakly supervised pipelines for medical imaging have become increasingly popular over the years. These systems often include multiple stages and components, such as reconstruction, generation, and localization, yet standard evaluation metrics provide limited insight into whether clinically relevant information is preserved across each stage. We present the diagnostic gap framework, a practical evaluation tool that measures decision preservation and explanation preservation as a function of measured reconstruction fidelity. To isolate the effect of reconstruction from localization, we evaluate on curated lesion ROI crops using a fidelity ladder of three class-conditional reconstructors---VQ-VAE-GAN, VAE-GAN, and diffusion (SDEdit)---spanning a twenty-fold range in perceptual distance (LPIPS 0.029--0.584). At autoencoder fidelity, both decision and explanation are preserved: AUC changes remain within $\pm$0.005 and attribution similarity (HiResCAM, Grad-CAM++) stays high. At diffusion fidelity, both collapse: pooled AUC drops by 0.253 and mass-pathology AUC falls below chance. The diagnostic gap is thus a measurable function of reconstruction fidelity rather than an intrinsic cost of reconstruction, and the framework provides an architecture-agnostic instrument for identifying when and where multi-stage pipelines lose diagnostic signal.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the diagnostic gap framework to evaluate whether clinically relevant information is preserved across stages of weakly supervised medical imaging pipelines, showing that diagnostic preservation (decision and explanation) is a function of reconstruction fidelity rather than an intrinsic cost of reconstruction.
AI.motivation: Standard evaluation metrics for multi-stage medical imaging pipelines provide limited insight into whether clinically relevant information is preserved across stages, motivating the need for a practical evaluation tool that measures diagnostic preservation.
AI.method: The diagnostic gap framework measures decision preservation (AUC changes) and explanation preservation (attribution similarity via HiResCAM, Grad-CAM++) as functions of reconstruction fidelity. Evaluations use curated lesion ROI crops with a fidelity ladder of three class-conditional reconstructors (VQ-VAE-GAN, VAE-GAN, SDEdit diffusion) spanning LPIPS 0.029–0.584.
AI.result: At autoencoder fidelity, decision (AUC ±0.005) and explanation are preserved. At diffusion fidelity, pooled AUC drops by 0.253 and mass-pathology AUC falls below chance, indicating diagnostic collapse.
AI.conclusion: The diagnostic gap is a measurable function of reconstruction fidelity, not an intrinsic cost of reconstruction; the framework provides an architecture-agnostic tool for identifying when multi-stage pipelines lose diagnostic signal.

title: Beyond Directed Acyclic Graphs: Causal Zeros and Causal Differential Equations
summary: Pearl's structural causal model (SCM) framework, built on directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) and the do-calculus, is the dominant formal language for causal reasoning. Yet it carries two structural restrictions: every relationship must be pre-specified as a directed causal edge, and feedback cycles are forbidden. This paper examines two classes of phenomena that strain these restrictions. First, symmetric physical and economic constraints, the ideal gas law being the canonical case, carry no intrinsic causal direction. Direction emerges only under intervention, and which variable is solved for must be specified as part of the intervention. We formalize such constraints as causal zeros within an Extended Causal Model by adding an activation operator, subject to local solvability and graph-admissibility conditions. Second, for the class of finite-propagation state-space systems considered here, we treat apparent instantaneous cycles as artifacts of suppressed time and ground both causal zeros and feedback in Causal Differential Equations (CDEs). In these, the transient regime is a time-unrolled acyclic causal process, and causal zeros arise as the defining functions of attracting equilibrium manifolds; periodic and chaotic attractors define further regimes of the same dynamics, treated through attractor-relative intervention. We give the extended do-calculus, identifiability conditions, counterfactual semantics, and open problems.

AI.tldr: This paper extends Pearl's SCM framework by introducing causal zeros (for symmetric constraints like the ideal gas law) and grounding cycles in causal differential equations, thus handling symmetric constraints and feedback loops via an extended do-calculus and attractor-relative interventions.
AI.motivation: Pearl's SCM framework requires pre-specified causal direction and forbids cycles, but real-world phenomena like symmetric physical laws (e.g., ideal gas law) lack intrinsic causal direction, and feedback cycles arise in state-space systems. This paper aims to extend the framework to accommodate these cases.
AI.method: The authors propose an Extended Causal Model with an activation operator to formalize causal zeros (symmetric constraints), subject to local solvability and graph-admissibility conditions. For cycles, they use Causal Differential Equations (CDEs) where transient dynamics are time-unrolled acyclic causal processes, and causal zeros emerge as attracting equilibrium manifolds. They develop an extended do-calculus, identifiability conditions, and counterfactual semantics.
AI.result: The paper provides formal definitions for causal zeros and CDE-based cycles, an extended do-calculus, identifiability conditions, and counterfactual semantics for the proposed extensions, along with a discussion of open problems.
AI.conclusion: The extended framework successfully incorporates symmetric constraints and feedback cycles that strain Pearl's original SCM, offering a principled way to handle direction emergence under intervention and attractor-relative causal inference for dynamical systems.

title: xMIx: High-Performance Serving-Time Platform for Mechanistic Interpretability Apps
summary:
Mechanistic interpretability (MI) has emerged as a powerful approach for analyzing and intervening in inference computations, with a growing number of applications such as jailbreak attempt detection, truthfulness evaluation, and hallucination detection. Unfortunately, MI deployment in production model-serving systems is currently not practical, as most existing MI frameworks introduce prohibitively high runtime overheads. The fundamental problem is that MI functions do not compose cleanly with served models: they fragment deployment, often force draining requests and rebuilding serving state, and conflict with critical performance optimizations such as continuous batching and CUDA-graph execution, essential for production deployments.
  We present xMIx, a serving-native framework for deploying MI applications in production inference serving environments. xMIx enables attaching MI functions to a predefined set of locations in the model runtime, interposing on activations within the layers and residual streams. xMIx supports conditional invocation of MI functions depending on the outputs in preceding model layers. Multiple MI applications can be deployed in a single model instance. xMIx compiles them all into the serving path but activates them dynamically at runtime only when necessary, with negligible performance cost, and without requiring a separate model instance or alternative execution stack.
  We integrate xMIx with the vLLM serving system and evaluate it across three major models and seven diverse MI applications. xMIx achieves performance comparable to native vLLM execution, incurring a slowdown of 1.3% mean inter-token latency (ITL), 1.2% for tail P99 ITL, 2.6% for mean time to first token (TTFT), and 1.6% for mean total token throughput (TTT).

AI.tldr: xMIx is a serving-native framework that integrates mechanistic interpretability functions into production inference systems with minimal overhead (~1-2% slowdown), enabling practical deployment of MI applications like jailbreak detection and truthfulness evaluation without requiring separate model instances or disrupting critical optimizations like continuous batching and CUDA-graph execution.
AI.motivation: Current mechanistic interpretability (MI) frameworks are impractical for production deployment because they introduce high runtime overhead, fragment deployment, force request draining, and conflict with performance optimizations like continuous batching and CUDA-graph execution.
AI.method: xMIx attaches MI functions to predefined locations in the model runtime, interposing on activations within layers and residual streams. It supports conditional invocation based on preceding layer outputs and compiles multiple MI applications into the serving path with dynamic runtime activation, all integrated with the vLLM serving system.
AI.result: Across three major models and seven MI applications, xMIx achieves performance comparable to native vLLM execution: 1.3% mean ITL slowdown, 1.2% P99 ITL, 2.6% mean TTFT, and 1.6% mean total token throughput degradation.
AI.conclusion: xMIx demonstrates that MI applications can be deployed in production serving environments with negligible performance overhead, eliminating the need for separate model instances or alternative execution stacks while supporting conditional invocation and multiple concurrent MI applications.

title: AI-generated Images Challenge Visual Trust in High-risk Scenarios
summary: Rapid advances in image generation are eroding the evidentiary value of visual content in settings where authenticity can affect public safety and personal reputation. Yet existing detection benchmarks rarely examine synthetic images in public- and individual-safety contexts, where misleading visual content may carry substantial risks. Here we introduce SafeIMG, a safety-oriented benchmark spanning 12 public- and individual-safety scenarios generated using GPT Image 2. Unlike benchmarks centred on generic imagery and image-level labels, SafeIMG evaluates not only whether detectors recognise synthetic images, but also whether their decisions reflect human-identified anomalies. To this end, SafeIMG provides human annotations that localise suspicious regions and explain local artefacts and higher-level commonsense or physical inconsistencies. We evaluate specialized synthetic-image detectors and vision-language models (VLMs), and find that neither provides reliable detection. The strongest VLM identifies only 49.5% of generated images, whereas the best specialised detector identifies 33.1%, compared with 81.7% accuracy for human evaluators. Model explanations cover only 29.8\% of human-annotated anomalies and predominantly capture local defects in text, faces and hands. Their coverage falls to 15.0% for commonsense conflicts and 12.0% for physical inconsistencies, while detection performance deteriorates further after dissemination-induced image degradation. These findings show that current detectors lack the accuracy, explanatory alignment and robustness needed to evaluate AI-generated images reliably across public- and individual-safety settings.

AI.tldr: SafeIMG benchmarks synthetic image detection across 12 public/individual safety scenarios, finding top VLMs (49.5%) and specialized detectors (33.1%) far below human accuracy (81.7%), with poor explanatory coverage of anomalies (29.8%) and severe performance drops under image degradation.
AI.motivation: Existing detection benchmarks focus on generic imagery and lack evaluation in safety-critical contexts (public/individual safety) where misleading synthetic content poses real risks; also, they only assess binary detection without examining whether model explanations align with human-identified anomalies.
AI.method: Introduced SafeIMG benchmark spanning 12 safety scenarios generated via GPT Image 2; includes human annotations localizing suspicious regions and explaining artefacts, commonsense conflicts, and physical inconsistencies; evaluated specialized synthetic-image detectors and VLMs.
AI.result: Best VLM: 49.5% detection; best specialized detector: 33.1%; humans: 81.7%. Model explanations cover only 29.8% of human-annotated anomalies (15.0% for commonsense conflicts, 12.0% for physical inconsistencies). Detection further degrades after dissemination-induced image degradation.
AI.conclusion: Current detectors lack the accuracy, explanatory alignment, and robustness required for reliable synthetic image detection in public/individual safety settings.

title: Hidden Boundary Motion in Transformer Optimization: Function-Space Orthogonalization of Affine Weight and Bias Updates
summary:
Weights and biases are normally optimized as separate parameter tensors, yet they do not represent separate functions when the input to an affine layer has nonzero mean. For an affine map $z=Wx+b$ with input mean $μ$, a weight update contains a sample-independent displacement $ΔWμ$ that is functionally indistinguishable from a bias update. We call this hidden contribution \emph{boundary motion} and decompose each update into a centered, sample-varying \emph{shape} component and a shared \emph{boundary} component. On a four-layer Transformer trained from scratch on IMDb, the bias-like term $g_bμ^	op$ has a median norm equal to 0.664 of the raw weight-gradient norm across affine layers and training checkpoints. More strikingly, the median ratio $
orm{ΔWμ}/
orm{Δb}$ is 134.7, while $
orm{ΔWμ}/
orm{Δb+ΔWμ}$ is 0.994. Thus, under AdamW, the observed boundary motion is almost entirely realized through the weight matrix rather than the explicit bias.
  We implement a diagnostic optimizer, Shape--Boundary Orthogonal AdamW (SBO-AdamW), that optimizes $g_W-g_bμ^	op$ and $g_b$ with independent Adam states and compensates the weight-induced boundary displacement. In a single-seed experiment, SBO-AdamW raises validation accuracy from 81.68\% to 85.81\% and validation-selected test accuracy from 78.73\% to 82.73\%, with the best validation checkpoint occurring at step 800 instead of step 3000. However, the moving-batch-center compensation produces severe bias-coordinate drift and strongly reduces boundary energy. The present evidence therefore supports hidden boundary motion as an important optimization mechanism, but it does not yet establish a final general-purpose optimizer. A stable centered-affine parameterization is identified as the required next step.

AI.tldr: Weight updates in affine layers contain a bias-like "boundary motion" component (ΔWμ) that is functionally equivalent to a bias update when input means are nonzero. This term dominates over explicit bias updates (median ratio 134.7). A diagnostic optimizer (SBO-AdamW) that separates shape and boundary components improves accuracy from 81.68% to 85.81% but causes bias-coordinate drift, indicating boundary motion is important but a centered-affine parameterization is needed.
AI.motivation: Weights and biases are optimized as separate tensors, but when input means are nonzero, a weight update contains a sample-independent displacement ΔWμ that is functionally indistinguishable from a bias update. This hidden "boundary motion" means the two parameters are not functionally independent, yet standard optimizers treat them separately.
AI.method: The authors decompose weight updates into a centered "shape" component and a shared "boundary" component. They measure the empirical impact of boundary motion on a 4-layer Transformer trained on IMDb. They implement SBO-AdamW, which orthogonalizes shape and boundary by optimizing g_W - g_b μ^T and g_b independently with separate Adam states, compensating the weight-induced boundary displacement.
AI.result: Median norm ratio of ΔWμ to raw weight-gradient norm = 0.664; norm(ΔWμ)/norm(Δb) = 134.7; norm(ΔWμ)/norm(Δb+ΔWμ) = 0.994. SBO-AdamW raises validation accuracy from 81.68% to 85.81% and test accuracy from 78.73% to 82.73%, with best checkpoint at step 800 vs 3000. However, it causes severe bias-coordinate drift and reduces boundary energy.
AI.conclusion: Boundary motion is an important optimization mechanism that is largely realized through the weight matrix rather than explicit bias under AdamW. However, the proposed SBO-AdamW is not yet a final general-purpose optimizer due to bias-coordinate drift. A stable centered-affine parameterization is required as the next step.

title: An Agentic Orchestration of Atomistic Simulations
summary: Atomistic simulations are central to materials design, but their execution involves complex, multi-step workflows that require significant human expertise. Here, we present an agent-based system embedded within the URSA (Universal Research and Scientific Agent) framework that automates the design, execution, and validation of atomistic simulations, demonstrated using the Large-scale Atomic/Molecular Massively Parallel Simulator (LAMMPS) tool. Our system autonomously selects interatomic potentials, constructs and runs simulations, and performs iterative error recovery within a closed-loop workflow. We evaluate the scientific reliability of the agent by benchmarking its outputs against LAVA, a high-throughput toolkit for LAMMPS and the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP) calculations. Our framework reduces manual intervention and trial-and-error, thereby improving the rigor, reproducibility, and scalability of atomistic modeling.

AI.tldr: An AI agent within the URSA framework automates LAMMPS atomistic simulations, autonomously selecting potentials, building/running simulations, and performing error recovery. Benchmarked against LAVA, it reduces manual effort and improves reproducibility.
AI.motivation: Atomistic simulation workflows are complex, multi-step, and require significant human expertise, creating bottlenecks in materials design due to manual trial-and-error and lack of automation.
AI.method: An agent-based system embedded in the URSA framework that autonomously selects interatomic potentials, constructs and runs LAMMPS simulations, and performs closed-loop iterative error recovery without human intervention.
AI.result: The agent's outputs were benchmarked against LAVA (a high-throughput LAMMPS/VASP toolkit), demonstrating scientific reliability and reduced need for manual intervention.
AI.conclusion: The framework improves rigor, reproducibility, and scalability of atomistic modeling by eliminating manual trial-and-error in simulation workflows.

title: Advancing All-Weather Building Damage Mapping to the Instance Level: Outcomes and Insights from the 2026 Bright Challenge
summary: Rapid post-disaster response requires timely, building-level information on whether structures remain intact, are damaged, or are destroyed. Post-event optical imagery, however, may be unavailable because of cloud, smoke, or darkness. The Bright Challenge evaluated all-weather building damage mapping from a submeter-resolution pre-event optical image and a post-event SAR image. Participants were required to detect and delineate each building and assign exactly one of three mutually exclusive damage labels. The challenge extended the globally distributed \textsc{Bright} dataset with instance-level annotations for about 291,000 buildings across 16 disaster events spanning seven disaster types. The final phase was evaluated exclusively on two 2025 events absent from training: a wildfire event in California and a hurricane in Jamaica. A total of 157 participants made 1,289 submissions, and 46 teams entered the final phase. The two winning solutions achieved test mAPs of 0.182 and 0.181, approximately 8.7 times the public baseline of 0.021, but remained far below the best in-domain holdout score of 0.513. Across teams ranked in both phases, performance declined sharply and the rank order changed substantially. The two leading solutions independently favored modality-specific encoding, staged or late optical--SAR fusion, and an optical-dominant separation of building localization from damage recognition. The winning method additionally used scene-aware threshold adjustment and pseudo-label adaptation. These results identify cross-event generalization and stable severity discrimination as the principal remaining challenges. All data, annotations, baseline code, and winning solutions are publicly available at https://github.com/ChenHongruixuan/BRIGHT.

AI.tldr: The Bright Challenge evaluated all-weather building damage mapping using pre-event optical and post-event SAR imagery across 291,000 buildings in 16 disaster events. Winning solutions achieved test mAPs of 0.182 and 0.181 (8.7x baseline of 0.021) but far below the in-domain score of 0.513. Key challenges remain cross-event generalization and stable severity discrimination.
AI.motivation: Rapid post-disaster response requires timely building-level damage information, but post-event optical imagery is often unavailable due to cloud, smoke, or darkness, motivating the need for all-weather damage mapping using SAR imagery.
AI.method: Participants used submeter-resolution pre-event optical imagery and post-event SAR image to detect and delineate each building and assign one of three mutually exclusive damage labels. The dataset included ~291,000 buildings across 16 disaster events (7 disaster types). Final evaluation was on two 2025 unseen events (California wildfire and Jamaica hurricane). Winning solutions used modality-specific encoding, staged/late optical-SAR fusion, and optical-dominant separation of localization from damage recognition.
AI.result: 157 participants made 1,289 submissions; 46 teams entered final phase. Winning solutions achieved test mAPs of 0.182 and 0.181 (~8.7x baseline of 0.021) but far below best in-domain holdout score of 0.513. Cross-team performance declined sharply and rank order changed substantially between phases.
AI.conclusion: Cross-event generalization and stable severity discrimination remain the principal challenges in all-weather building damage mapping from optical-SAR fusion.

title: Distribution-Specific Curvature Control with Finite-Sample Guarantees for Open-Weight Safety
summary: A short fine-tuning run can undo the safety guards of an open-weight model---retraining a refusal-trained assistant to aid weapons development or produce hate speech. Preventing such harmful fine-tuning while retaining benign adaptability remains difficult: the only prior method with an explicit curvature certificate, spectral deformation, inflates curvature globally and thereby obstructs benign adaptation along with harmful adaptation. We propose HarmAlign, which applies function-preserving spectral deformation along a estimated contrastive activation subspace. We derive finite-sample bounds for the estimated subspace energy and the resulting local harmful-distribution curvature lower bound. A stability--progress dichotomy for constant-step gradient descent turns the certified curvature into conditional convergence-rate control. Empirically, within a fixed-architecture, finite-budget first-order threat model, HarmAlign blocks direct fine-tuning and three data- or objective-adaptive attacks across a hazardous-knowledge relearning setting and a harmful-assistance fine-tuning setting, while the protected benign tasks remain trainable. The block persists across the tested first-order optimizer variants over every attack checkpoint, and under out-of-distribution harmful fine-tuning, and it extends to important cases in our threat model: accidental safety degradation and emergent misalignment.

AI.tldr: HarmAlign is a method that applies function-preserving spectral deformation along a contrastive activation subspace to protect open-weight models from harmful fine-tuning while preserving benign adaptability, with theoretical curvature guarantees and empirical effectiveness against multiple attack types.
AI.motivation: Open-weight models are vulnerable to safety guard removal via short fine-tuning runs (e.g., enabling weapons development or hate speech). Existing methods like spectral deformation inflate curvature globally, which obstructs both harmful and benign adaptation. There is a need for a method that selectively blocks harmful fine-tuning while retaining benign task trainability.
AI.method: HarmAlign applies function-preserving spectral deformation along a estimated contrastive activation subspace. It derives finite-sample bounds for subspace energy estimation and local harmful-distribution curvature lower bounds. A stability-progress dichotomy for constant-step gradient descent turns certified curvature into conditional convergence-rate control.
AI.result: Under a fixed-architecture, finite-budget first-order threat model, HarmAlign blocks direct fine-tuning and three data- or objective-adaptive attacks in both hazardous-knowledge relearning and harmful-assistance fine-tuning settings. Protected benign tasks remain trainable. The block persists across tested first-order optimizer variants, attack checkpoints, out-of-distribution harmful fine-tuning, accidental safety degradation, and emergent misalignment.
AI.conclusion: HarmAlign provides a principled defense against harmful fine-tuning with certified curvature guarantees, outperforming prior methods by preserving benign adaptability while maintaining robust safety protection across diverse attack scenarios.

title: HyCE-RAG: Hypergraph Chain-of-Evidence Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Explainable Multi-hop Question Answering
summary: Multi-hop question answering requires systems to retrieve evidence from multiple documents and connect scattered facts into a coherent reasoning process. Standard retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) mainly relies on semantic similarity between a query and text chunks, and therefore often fails to model structural relations among entities, facts, and evidence units. Graph-based RAG improves this by introducing graph-structured knowledge, but pairwise edges are still limited in representing higher-order associations involving multiple entities and contexts. We propose HyCE-RAG, a Hypergraph Chain-of-Evidence Retrieval-Augmented Generation framework for explainable multi-hop question answering. HyCE-RAG organizes entities, relations, and contextual evidence into hyperedges, builds a query-aware evidence hypergraph, and performs confidence propagation over entity--hyperedge incidence structures. It then uses confidence-guided evidence assembly to select, connect, and rank evidence paths before answer generation. The scoring process jointly considers semantic relevance, entity connectivity, evidence coverage, relation reliability, extraction confidence, and propagated confidence. By providing the language model with structured evidence chains rather than flat retrieved passages, HyCE-RAG supports more faithful and interpretable reasoning. Experiments on HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, MuSiQue, and two GraphRAG-Bench subsets show that HyCE-RAG consistently outperforms standard RAG and graph-based RAG baselines in answer accuracy, context relevance, and faithfulness. These results suggest that hypergraph-based evidence organization is a promising direction for post-retrieval reasoning in complex question answering.

AI.tldr: HyCE-RAG organizes evidence into hypergraphs for explainable multi-hop QA, outperforming standard RAG and graph-based RAG baselines on multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Standard RAG fails to model structural relations among entities for multi-hop QA; graph-based RAG is limited by pairwise edges in representing higher-order associations.
AI.method: HyCE-RAG organizes entities, relations, and evidence into hyperedges, builds a query-aware evidence hypergraph, performs confidence propagation, and uses confidence-guided evidence assembly to select and rank evidence paths.
AI.result: Consistently outperforms standard RAG and graph-based RAG baselines on HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, MuSiQue, and GraphRAG-Bench subsets in accuracy, context relevance, and faithfulness.
AI.conclusion: Hypergraph-based evidence organization is a promising direction for post-retrieval reasoning in complex question answering.

title: Post-Operative Glioma Segmentation via Loss Stabilization, Normalization and Subspace Attention
comment: Accepted for presentation at the International Conference on Artificial Neural Networks (ICANN 2026)
summary: Tracking residual tumor after surgery is essential for catching recurrence early, but automating post-operative glioma segmentation remains a difficult task. Although transformer-based architectures, such as SwinUNETR, achieved impressive results, few studies test how well they generalize across clinical protocols. In this paper, we conduct an ablation study on the MU-GLIOMA-POST and UCSF-ALPTDG datasets and show that the standard Generalized Dice Loss (GDL) is unstable under domain shift: the Whole Lesion (WL) Dice drops from 0.88 on the internal validation set to 0.73 on the external UCSF test set. To address this, we pair brain-masked percentile normalization with voxel-level contrastive learning. We also propose a Subspace-Aware Class Attention (SACA) module that re-calibrates the bottleneck features and raises Enhancing Tumor (ET) sensitivity by 8% (9.1% relative improvement) on internal validation. Ensembling these refinements with nnU-Net brings every stable configuration to a WL Dice of 0.94, and the SACA variant ensemble achieves the best boundary error (HD95) of 2.92 mm on MU-GLIOMA-POST.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses domain shift issues in automated post-operative glioma segmentation. Standard Generalized Dice Loss is unstable under domain shift (WL Dice drops from 0.88 to 0.73 across datasets). The authors propose brain-masked percentile normalization, voxel-level contrastive learning, and a Subspace-Aware Class Attention (SACA) module, achieving WL Dice of 0.94 and HD95 of 2.92 mm when ensembled with nnU-Net.
AI.motivation: Tracking residual tumor after surgery is critical for early recurrence detection, but automated post-operative glioma segmentation remains difficult, and existing transformer-based architectures like SwinUNETR generalize poorly across clinical protocols due to domain shift.
AI.method: Ablation study on MU-GLIOMA-POST and UCSF-ALPTDG datasets. Proposes brain-masked percentile normalization, voxel-level contrastive learning, and a Subspace-Aware Class Attention (SACA) module to re-calibrate bottleneck features. Ensemble with nnU-Net.
AI.result: Standard GDL yields WL Dice drop from 0.88 (internal) to 0.73 (external). Proposed refinements achieve WL Dice of 0.94 across stable configurations; SACA variant ensemble achieves HD95 of 2.92 mm on MU-GLIOMA-POST; ET sensitivity improved by 8% (9.1% relative) internally.
AI.conclusion: Pairing normalization and contrastive learning with the SACA module effectively mitigates domain shift in post-operative glioma segmentation. Ensembling with nnU-Net yields state-of-the-art performance.

title: Spectral-Aware Analytic Class-Incremental Learning for Long-Tailed Distributions
summary: Analytic Continual Learning (ACL) offers a computationally efficient alternative to gradient-based approaches. Recent ACL methods are based on Recursive Least Squares (RLS) and have achieved the state-of-the-art results compared to other alternatives. However, they falter significantly in Class-Incremental Learning scenarios characterized by Long-Tailed distributions.
