AI.motivation: To address two unexplored gaps in the intersection of MFGs and generative modeling: the interaction term is zero in many existing models, and MFG solvers have never been applied to generative modeling, while also unifying twelve prominent models under a single variational framework.
AI.method: An open-source PyTorch library (MFGLab) with a cost tuple API where twelve models are specified via four composable cost functions with shared training loop, log-Jacobian, and reverse-ODE sampler; plus DI-Flow, a novel cost using differentiable entropy for mode coverage, and learning-based MFG solvers for stochastic dynamics.
AI.result: Experiments on two 2-D benchmarks confirm the unified API is lossless relative to hand-coded implementations; learning-based MFG solvers substantially outperform neural training on stochastic-dynamics rows.
AI.conclusion: The MFG framework provides a unifying lens for generative modeling, MFGLab enables modular exploration of previously unexplored cost dimensions, and DI-Flow with differentiable entropy improves mode coverage.

title: CHS-SQL: A Text-to-SQL approach based on Confidence-Guided Heuristic Search Schema Linking process
summary: Recently, there have been several works in the Text-to-SQL domain that utilize Small Language Models (SLMs) for training. These approaches achieve performance close to that of large models in generating SQL, using only the computational power of a single NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU, while also ensuring data security. Most existing methods filter out redundant tables and columns during Schema Linking to improve Text-to-SQL accuracy. However, they do not consider the precision-recall trade-off when selecting the candidate schema subset. Our research found that both the precision and recall of Schema Linking directly affect the final SQL accuracy. Therefore, we propose a novel framework for efficiently fine-tuning SLMs on Text-to-SQL tasks, CHS-SQL, that not only balances precision and recall but also improves overall performance on Text-to-SQL tasks. Its main innovation lies in the Schema Linking phase, where a heuristic search combined with model internal confidence is employed to achieve an optimal precision-recall trade-off. This elaborated mechanism maximizes the precision of relevant schema candidates for the generated SQL queries while suppressing irrelevant noise. The same strategy is further applied during SQL generation to refine candidate queries while helping the SLM to avoid trapping in a local optimum. Our method achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) results on Text-to-SQL tasks via SLMs.

AI.tldr: CHS-SQL is a novel fine-tuning framework for Small Language Models on Text-to-SQL tasks that introduces a heuristic search combined with model internal confidence during Schema Linking to balance precision and recall, achieving SOTA results on SLMs.
AI.motivation: Existing Schema Linking methods filter redundant tables/columns but ignore the precision-recall trade-off when selecting candidate schema subsets, which directly impacts final SQL accuracy.
AI.method: CHS-SQL employs a heuristic search combined with model internal confidence during the Schema Linking phase to achieve an optimal precision-recall trade-off, maximizing relevant schema candidates while suppressing irrelevant noise. The same strategy is applied during SQL generation to refine candidates and avoid local optima.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) results on Text-to-SQL tasks using Small Language Models.
AI.conclusion: Balancing precision and recall in Schema Linking is critical for Text-to-SQL performance, and the proposed heuristic confidence-based approach effectively improves SLM-based SQL generation.

title: Small-Pollinator Detection in Cluttered Field Video
comment: 13 pages, 2 figures. Code, experiment notebooks, and implementation details: https://github.com/OnurOnal7/buzzspot-pollinator-detection
summary: Detecting pollinators in field video is challenging: targets are small, visually similar, and observed against cluttered vegetation under blur and occlusion. We present a systematic empirical study of small-pollinator detection under a practical single-GPU compute budget. Using the BuzzSpot challenge dataset, we compare YOLO and RF-DETR models across input resolutions and evaluate sliced inference, class-gated fusion, size-routed ensembling, and post-hoc temporal processing. RF-DETR Large at 1344-pixel resolution achieved our best hidden-test result, reaching 0.405 mAP50:95 and outperforming the 1120-pixel model (0.379) and the best single-model YOLO26m baseline (0.366). The strongest gains came from adopting RF-DETR and increasing its input resolution, indicating that detector choice and input resolution were more effective levers than added inference-time complexity; the resolution gain was strongest for small objects and the rarer bumblebee and moth classes. Sliced-inference fusion, size-routed ensembling, and warm-started 1536-pixel continuation did not surpass this result, while post-hoc temporal processing did not improve the leaked diagnostic evaluation. Error analysis identified bee-hoverfly discrimination as the clearest remaining bottleneck: neighboring frames rarely supplied correctly classified hoverfly evidence for post-hoc correction. These findings motivate learned feature-level temporal aggregation before the final classification decision.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically studies small-pollinator detection under a single-GPU budget, finding that RF-DETR Large at 1344px resolution achieves the best performance (0.405 mAP50:95), with detector choice and input resolution being more impactful than inference-time complexity, while bee-hoverfly discrimination remains the key bottleneck motivating temporal feature aggregation.
AI.motivation: Detecting small pollinators in field videos is challenging due to small target size, visual similarity, cluttered backgrounds, blur, and occlusion; the authors aim to identify the most effective practical strategies under a constrained single-GPU compute budget.
AI.method: Systematic empirical comparison of YOLO and RF-DETR models across multiple input resolutions, evaluating sliced inference, class-gated fusion, size-routed ensembling, post-hoc temporal processing, and warm-started 1536-pixel continuation on the BuzzSpot challenge dataset.
AI.result: RF-DETR Large at 1344px achieved best hidden-test result (0.405 mAP50:95), outperforming 1120px model (0.379) and best YOLO26m baseline (0.366). Resolution gains were strongest for small objects and rare classes. Sliced inference, ensembling, 1536px continuation, and temporal processing did not surpass this result.
AI.conclusion: Detector choice and input resolution are more important than added inference-time complexity; bee-hoverfly discrimination remains the key bottleneck, motivating learned feature-level temporal aggregation before final classification.

title: Multi-Agent Privacy Game in Federated Learning: A Unified Mean-Field View
summary: Federated learning enables collaborative model training across distributed clients without centralising their data, yet privacy remains a persistent concern because the shared model updates can leak information about local datasets. Existing privacy-preserving methods either inject calibrated noise into client updates, limiting their composition guarantees, or formulate client privacy choices as a multi-agent game whose Nash equilibrium becomes intractable as the number of clients grows. We bridge these two lines of work by formulating privacy-preserving federated learning as a mean-field privacy game: each client strategically chooses its own privacy budget while interacting with the population only through a single mean-field statistic. The mean-field limit yields a tractable equilibrium for arbitrarily many clients, accommodates heterogeneous client preferences, and inherits an exponentially decaying privacy guarantee through a log-Sobolev contraction. The framework recovers the entropic privacy baseline as the homogeneous special case and the multi-agent privacy game as the finite-population case. Experiments on quadratic regression, logistic regression, and MNIST demonstrate that the proposed framework attains the privacy-utility trade-off of the entropic baseline while delivering a personalized privacy guarantee that the homogeneous baseline cannot express.

AI.tldr: The paper bridges two privacy-preserving FL approaches (noise injection and multi-agent games) by formulating a mean-field privacy game where clients strategically choose privacy budgets based on a population statistic, yielding tractable equilibrium, heterogeneous privacy, and exponential privacy guarantees via log-Sobolev contraction.
AI.motivation: Existing privacy-preserving FL methods have limitations: calibrated noise injection restricts composition guarantees, while multi-agent privacy games become intractable with many clients. There is a need for a scalable, tractable approach that accommodates heterogeneous client privacy preferences.
AI.method: Formulate privacy-preserving FL as a mean-field privacy game where each client selects its own privacy budget, interacting with the population through a single mean-field statistic. Leverages the mean-field limit to achieve tractable equilibrium for arbitrarily many clients, and uses log-Sobolev contraction for exponential privacy decay.
AI.result: The framework recovers entropic privacy baseline as homogeneous special case and multi-agent privacy game as finite-population case. Experiments on quadratic regression, logistic regression, and MNIST show it matches the privacy-utility trade-off of the entropic baseline while providing personalized privacy guarantees.
AI.conclusion: The mean-field privacy game framework provides a tractable, scalable solution for heterogeneous privacy in FL, achieving the privacy-utility trade-off of prior methods while enabling client-specific privacy budgets that homogeneous baselines cannot express.

title: TokenMem: Faithful Knowledge Injection for Frozen LLMs
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enhances large language models (LLMs) with external knowledge, but suffers from knowledge conflicts: when retrieved information contradicts parametric memory, the shared self-attention pathway produces unpredictable outputs. We present TokenMem, a lightweight memory system that injects knowledge into frozen LLMs through a dedicated cross-attention channel, bypassing competition with parametric memory in the residual stream. TokenMem trains only a thin gating adapter ($\sim$3-7M parameters) via a two-phase curriculum: first learning general knowledge utilization, then strengthening faithful compliance under counterfactual knowledge. In controlled experiments on five models spanning three families (Qwen3-4B/8B/14B, LLaMA-3.1-8B, OLMo-3-7B), TokenMem achieves 69-70% Knowledge Compliance (KC) on counterfactual benchmarks, compared to 20-52% for vanilla RAG, a gap of up to 49 percentage points. Ablation studies show that the two-phase curriculum is critical: removing Phase 2 collapses KC to near-zero. Mechanistic analysis reveals that the gate adapter learns a conflict-aware, layer-specific injection strategy without explicit supervision.

AI.tldr: TokenMem is a lightweight memory system that injects external knowledge into frozen LLMs via a dedicated cross-attention channel and two-phase curriculum training, achieving 69-70% Knowledge Compliance on counterfactual benchmarks (vs 20-52% for vanilla RAG) by bypassing parametric memory competition in the residual stream.
AI.motivation: Standard RAG suffers from knowledge conflicts when retrieved information contradicts the LLM's parametric memory, as both compete through the shared self-attention pathway in the residual stream, leading to unpredictable outputs.
AI.method: TokenMem trains a thin gating adapter (~3-7M parameters) that injects knowledge into frozen LLMs via a dedicated cross-attention channel. Training follows a two-phase curriculum: Phase 1 learns general knowledge utilization, Phase 2 strengthens faithful compliance under counterfactual knowledge. The cross-attention channel bypasses the residual stream competition with parametric memory.
AI.result: On five models across three families (Qwen3-4B/8B/14B, LLaMA-3.1-8B, OLMo-3-7B), TokenMem achieves 69-70% Knowledge Compliance vs 20-52% for vanilla RAG (up to 49pp improvement). Removing Phase 2 collapses KC to near-zero. The gate adapter learns a conflict-aware, layer-specific injection strategy without explicit supervision.
AI.conclusion: TokenMem effectively resolves knowledge conflicts in RAG by decoupling external knowledge injection from parametric memory through a dedicated cross-attention channel and curriculum learning, enabling faithful compliance with counterfactual knowledge while keeping the base LLM frozen.

title: Controlling Embedding Spaces with Text-Conditioned Transformations
summary: Multimodal embedding spaces in models like CLIP enable powerful capabilities such as semantic similarity retrieval and cross-modal zero-shot classification. These embeddings compress high-level semantics into a single vector, which comes at the cost of primarily expressing a dominant semantics like main object while suppressing other important attributes such as camera angle or color tone. We propose a text-conditioned transformation of visual embeddings that makes such attributes explicitly accessible. Given a natural language description of an attribute category (e.g., "color" or "art style"), a network generates an affine transformation that emphasizes the specified attribute. Conditioning on text enables it to learn many attributes simultaneously, accessing them at inference time through an intuitive interface. The network is trained to align transformed embeddings with the frozen latent space, enabling retrieval using existing large-scale embeddings without any re-encoding. When applied to a full set, the same mechanism transforms the latent space for attribute disentanglement tasks such as multi-clustering. By operating directly in latent space, our method provides a unified and efficient framework for controlling embedding spaces, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance across both attribute-based retrieval and multi-attribute organization tasks with near-zero inference cost. Project page: https://joefioresi718.github.io/ControlEmbed_webpage/

AI.tldr: The paper proposes ControlEmbed, a text-conditioned transformation method that modifies CLIP visual embeddings to explicitly emphasize specific attributes (e.g., color, art style) without re-encoding images. It uses a network to generate affine transformations based on natural language attribute descriptions, enabling attribute-based retrieval and multi-attribute organization directly in latent space with near-zero inference cost.
AI.motivation: Multimodal embeddings like CLIP compress high-level semantics into a single vector, primarily expressing dominant semantics (e.g., main object) while suppressing other important attributes (e.g., camera angle, color tone). The authors aim to make such suppressed attributes explicitly accessible.
AI.method: A text-conditioned transformation network takes a natural language description of an attribute category (e.g., "color") and generates an affine transformation that emphasizes that specified attribute in visual embeddings. The network is trained to align transformed embeddings with the frozen latent space, enabling retrieval without re-encoding. The same mechanism can transform the entire latent space for attribute disentanglement tasks like multi-clustering.
AI.result: The method achieves state-of-the-art performance across both attribute-based retrieval and multi-attribute organization tasks with near-zero inference cost, operating directly in the latent space without requiring image re-encoding.
AI.conclusion: ControlEmbed provides a unified and efficient framework for controlling embedding spaces by operating directly in latent space, enabling attribute disentanglement and retrieval through an intuitive text-based interface while leveraging existing large-scale embeddings.

title: Online Policy Evaluation for MDPs with Dynamic UBSR Measures
summary: Developing efficient function-approximation methods for policy evaluation is a fundamental challenge in risk-aware reinforcement learning. Existing approaches either focus on restrictive classes of risk measures or rely on access to a simulator, limiting their applicability in fully online settings. In this work, we propose computationally efficient online learning algorithms for policy evaluation in Markov decision processes (MDPs) with dynamic utility-based shortfall risk (UBSR) measures under linear function approximation. Specifically, we introduce the UBSR-TD algorithm, establish conditions under which it converges almost surely, and develop several variants designed to accelerate convergence. Our formulation shows that existing policy evaluation algorithms for risk-neutral MDPs can be readily adapted to dynamic UBSR settings by incorporating a loss function into the temporal-difference error. Numerical experiments support our theoretical findings, and an application to a perishable inventory management problem with shelf-life uncertainty demonstrates the practical effectiveness of the proposed methods.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes computationally efficient online learning algorithms (UBSR-TD and variants) for policy evaluation in MDPs with dynamic utility-based shortfall risk measures under linear function approximation, showing convergence and effectiveness through theory and experiments including perishable inventory management.
AI.motivation: Existing risk-aware policy evaluation methods are limited to restrictive risk measure classes or require simulator access, hindering fully online applicability. The authors aim to develop online algorithms for dynamic utility-based shortfall risk that are computationally efficient and theoretically grounded.
AI.method: The authors propose UBSR-TD, a temporal-difference learning algorithm for dynamic UBSR under linear function approximation, establish almost sure convergence conditions, and develop accelerated variants. The key insight is adapting risk-neutral TD methods by incorporating a loss function into the TD error.
AI.result: Theoretical convergence conditions are established. Numerical experiments validate theoretical findings. A perishable inventory management application with shelf-life uncertainty demonstrates practical effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: Risk-neutral policy evaluation algorithms can be adapted to dynamic UBSR settings by incorporating a loss function into the TD error, enabling efficient online risk-aware RL.

title: Masked Distillation: Internalizing the Chain-of-Thought in Language Models
summary: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) produce long, explicit chains of intermediate steps before generating a final answer at inference time. These intermediate traces dominate latency, memory usage, and serving cost, even though the final answer correctness is not causally related to the trace correctness and the trace length is not a reliable indicator of the problem complexity. This raises a natural question: can the computation expressed in these intermediate tokens be internalized into the parameters of a language model, enabling it to produce answers directly (or with much shorter intermediate traces)? We introduce \textit{masked distillation}, a knowledge-distillation framework in which a student LLM is trained to predict only the solution tokens conditioned on the question, while a reasoning teacher provides feedback on the student's responses after conditioning on the question and its own CoT trace. We instantiate this framework in two settings: (i) a \textit{self-distillation} setting, in which the same model serves as the teacher in thinking mode and as the student in non-thinking mode, and (ii) a \textit{dual-model} setting, in which a larger reasoning teacher supervises a separate smaller non-thinking student over the solution tokens. By treating intermediate tokens as a scaffold which reasoning models use to fit over the solution tokens, We additionally vary the length of intermediate-token scaffolding the student is supervised on, interpolating between full internalization (the student emits only the solution) and no internalization (the student emits the full trace before the answer). We evaluate the framework through controlled experiments on two reasoning domains: GSM8K (grade-school arithmetic) and Countdown (a number-puzzle search task).

AI.tldr: The paper proposes masked distillation, a knowledge-distillation framework that internalizes the intermediate reasoning traces of Large Reasoning Models into student LLMs, allowing them to produce answers directly (or with shorter traces). Experiments on GSM8K and Countdown show that students can learn to skip or shorten intermediate reasoning steps while maintaining accuracy.
AI.motivation: LRMs produce long intermediate traces that dominate latency, memory, and serving cost, but trace correctness and length are not causally related to final answer correctness. The authors ask whether the computation expressed in these intermediate tokens can be internalized into model parameters to enable direct answer generation or much shorter traces.
AI.method: A masked distillation framework where a student LLM is trained to predict solution tokens conditioned on the question, while a reasoning teacher conditions on both question and its own CoT trace to provide feedback. Two settings: (i) self-distillation (same model as teacher in thinking mode and student in non-thinking mode), (ii) dual-model (larger reasoning teacher supervises smaller non-thinking student). Also varies intermediate-token scaffolding length to interpolate between full internalization (only solution) and no internalization (full trace).
AI.result: Evaluated on GSM8K (grade-school arithmetic) and Countdown (number-puzzle search task), showing that students can effectively learn to produce answers with reduced or eliminated intermediate traces while maintaining correctness.
AI.conclusion: The intermediate reasoning traces of LRMs can be successfully internalized into student model parameters via masked distillation, enabling more efficient inference by reducing or eliminating the need for explicit chain-of-thought tokens at test time.

title: Layering Virtual Try-On
summary: In the real world, fashion is about layering: adding a jacket over a shirt, or a sequence of adding and removing layers, rather than just a single-layer swap. This fundamental real-world task remains a challenge in existing Virtual Try-On (VTON) methods, which excel at single-layer replacement but are not designed to layer or de-layer an existing outfit. This paper proposes Layering Virtual Try-On (LVTON), a layering benchmark and method that preserves an existing outfit while enabling sequential layering. We find that current VTON paradigms are fundamentally ill-equipped for LVTON, as their reliance on cloth-agnostic representations and single-item datasets discards essential layering context. Our key insight is that the LVTON challenge must be disentangled into two distinct competencies: (1) General VTON Priors (e.g., deformation, identity preservation) and (2) Specific Layering Knowledge (e.g., layering order and occlusion reasoning). First, our model obtains general VTON priors by being trained on data produced by an automatic data generation pipeline that synthesizes samples from fashion videos via segmentation and inpainting. Second, the model is fine-tuned on a small, dedicated LVTON dataset to learn the layering logic. Our method achieves state-of-the-art results on our LVTON benchmark and demonstrates superior generalizability on traditional VTON benchmarks, setting new state-of-the-art results when fine-tuned and exhibiting zero-shot capabilities.

AI.tldr: LVTON proposes a virtual try-on method that handles sequential layering (adding/removing garments) rather than just single-layer swaps, using a two-stage training process: general VTON priors from synthetic data + fine-tuning on a small layering-specific dataset.
AI.motivation: Existing VTON methods only handle single-layer garment replacement and cannot address the real-world task of layering (e.g., adding a jacket over a shirt), which is a fundamental limitation.
AI.method: Disentangles LVTON into two competencies: (1) General VTON Priors learned from synthetic data generated via an automatic pipeline (segmentation + inpainting from fashion videos), and (2) Specific Layering Knowledge (layering order, occlusion reasoning) learned via fine-tuning on a small dedicated LVTON dataset.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art results on the LVTON benchmark, and demonstrates superior generalizability on traditional VTON benchmarks, including new SOTA when fine-tuned and zero-shot capabilities.
AI.conclusion: The proposed two-stage disentanglement approach effectively bridges the gap between single-layer VTON and the real-world layering scenario, with strong performance on both layering-specific and traditional benchmarks.

title: MixQuant: Adaptive Mixed-Precision Quantization for Large Language Models
summary: Mixed-precision quantization improves the accuracy of post-training quantization by allocating higher bitwidths to sensitive layers, but existing methods solve the allocation for a single fixed memory budget. In practice the budget varies across deployments and is unknown at calibration time. Adaptive quantization addresses this with one offline calibration that serves any budget, yet current methods score layer sensitivity in a manner that does not consider its dependency on quantization levels of other layers. We show that a layer's sensitivity depends strongly on the bitwidths of its upstream layers and that this dependence shifts the resulting preferred bit allocation. We propose MixQuant, a technique-agnostic adaptive framework that wraps any base quantizer. MixQuant marginalizes each layer's distortion over random quantized upstream configurations to obtain budget-agnostic scores, calibrates the quantizer's parameters on plans the allocator itself produces, and penalizes allocations that leave layers at the lowest bitwidths. A single greedy pass then serves any budget at deployment. Across Llama-3.2-3B, Llama-2-7B, and Mistral-7B under AWQ and GPTQ, MixQuant outperforms adaptive and mixed-precision baselines in every setting, improving average accuracy by up to 8 points and reducing perplexity from 12.43 to 10.70 at the tightest budget, while matching an ILP solver at negligible deployment cost.

AI.tldr: MixQuant is a technique-agnostic adaptive quantization framework that accounts for inter-layer sensitivity dependencies, enabling one-shot calibration to serve any memory budget at deployment, outperforming existing adaptive and mixed-precision methods across multiple LLMs.
AI.motivation: Existing mixed-precision and adaptive quantization methods ignore the dependency of a layer's sensitivity on the quantization levels of its upstream layers, and they require recalibration for each fixed memory budget, making them impractical for variable deployment scenarios.
AI.method: MixQuant wraps any base quantizer; it marginalizes each layer's distortion over random quantized upstream configurations to obtain budget-agnostic sensitivity scores, calibrates quantizer parameters on allocation plans the allocator itself generates, and penalizes allocations using the lowest bitwidths. A single greedy pass then serves any budget at deployment.
AI.result: Under AWQ and GPTQ on Llama-3.2-3B, Llama-2-7B, and Mistral-7B, MixQuant outperforms adaptive and mixed-precision baselines in every setting, improving average accuracy by up to 8 points, reducing perplexity from 12.43 to 10.70 at the tightest budget, and matching an ILP solver at negligible deployment cost.
AI.conclusion: Accounting for cross-layer sensitivity dependencies is crucial for effective adaptive quantization; MixQuant achieves budget-agnostic, high-quality allocation with a single offline calibration, making it practical for diverse deployment constraints.

title: VlogReward: Learning Multi-Dimensional Evaluation for Vlog Editing
summary: The rapid rise of vlogs as a personalized storytelling medium has created a demand for automated systems to evaluate and refine vlog editing plans. However, vlog assessment is highly subjective and remains challenging due to a lack of standardized criteria, dataset and benchmark, and effective reward models. To address these challenges, we define a comprehensive vlog evaluation framework guided by professional vlog creators and product managers, establishing a taxonomy of six key dimensions, i.e., Creativity, Consistency, Concept Design, Cinematography, Narration, and Pacing. Subsequently, we curate a large-scale dataset of 100k vlog edits and a dedicated benchmark, VRMBench, to evaluate the vlog rewarding capabilities of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). Finally, we present VlogReward, a robust vlog reward model that can provide both fine-grained multi-dimensional scores and actionable feedback for iterative refinement. Technically, we enhance the Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) framework by introducing an adjustable inter-group comparison reward, which mitigates the "direction blindness" issue of standard GRPO and enables the model to better distinguish varied-quality edits. VlogReward achieves state-of-the-art results that significantly outperform existing MLLMs, including GPT-5 and Gemini-3-Pro. We hope that our study can help vlog creators and foster automated vlog evaluation and refinement systems.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces VlogReward, a vlog reward model with a six-dimension evaluation framework (Creativity, Consistency, Concept Design, Cinematography, Narration, Pacing), a 100k dataset, VRMBench benchmark, and an enhanced GRPO with inter-group comparison reward that outperforms GPT-5 and Gemini-3-Pro.
AI.motivation: Vlog assessment is highly subjective, lacks standardized criteria, datasets, benchmarks, and effective reward models, creating a need for automated evaluation and refinement systems for vlog editing plans.
AI.method: (1) Defined a six-dimension vlog evaluation taxonomy guided by professionals; (2) Curated a 100k vlog edits dataset and VRMBench benchmark; (3) Developed VlogReward using an enhanced GRPO framework with adjustable inter-group comparison reward to address "direction blindness."
AI.result: VlogReward achieves state-of-the-art results, significantly outperforming existing MLLMs including GPT-5 and Gemini-3-Pro on the VRMBench benchmark.
AI.conclusion: This study provides a comprehensive framework, dataset, benchmark, and reward model that can help vlog creators and foster automated vlog evaluation and refinement systems.

title: HALLELUAI: A Hallucination-Aware AI System for Ultra-Realistic Image-to-Video Generation at Scale
summary: AI-generated video is increasingly used across marketing, product storytelling, and creative workflows, yet automated; high-precision quality control remains a major constraint to scaling production. We present HALLELUAI, an end-to-end system that moderates and regenerates image-to-video outputs to meet expert-level creative standards and deliver ultra-realistic videos with consistent end-user quality of experience (QoE) at scale. The system integrates a video moderation module that evaluates frame-level aesthetics, temporal motion fidelity, and fine-grained hallucination risks relative to the source image, with an agentic regeneration module that iteratively fixes failures through prompt refinement, controlled camera adjustments, targeted model or image switching, and structured retry strategies. The moderation logic is aligned with domain-specific creative guidelines and produces granular, machine-actionable feedback that directly drives regeneration. In human-in-the-loop evaluations with creative experts, HALLELUAI shows strong alignment and reliably outputs ultra-realistic, production-grade videos suitable for product and marketing placements at scale. This framework advances trustworthy AI generated video content by enforcing visual realism, brand safety, and strict input-image fidelity while enabling image-to-video generation at scale.

AI.tldr: HALLELUAI is an end-to-end system that moderates and regenerates image-to-video outputs to ensure expert-level creative standards, ultra-realism, and consistent QoE at scale, using modular evaluation and agentic refinement loops.
AI.motivation: AI-generated video is increasingly used in marketing and creative workflows, but the lack of automated, high-precision quality control prevents scaling production to meet expert-level creative standards.
AI.method: The system integrates a video moderation module (evaluating frame-level aesthetics, temporal motion fidelity, and hallucination risks relative to source image) with an agentic regeneration module that iteratively fixes failures via prompt refinement, camera adjustments, model/image switching, and structured retry strategies. Moderation produces granular, machine-actionable feedback to drive regeneration.
AI.result: In human-in-the-loop evaluations with creative experts, HALLELUAI shows strong alignment with expert standards and reliably outputs ultra-realistic, production-grade videos suitable for product and marketing placements at scale.
AI.conclusion: This framework advances trustworthy AI-generated video content by enforcing visual realism, brand safety, and strict input-image fidelity while enabling scalable image-to-video generation.

title: The Entropic Bound for Transformers: Why Static Rank Fails and Attention-Native Rank Recovers
comment: 11 pages, 1 figure, 5 tables. Code and reproduction scripts included as supplementary material
summary: Neural scaling laws describe how loss decreases as models, data, and compute grow, but they do not answer a prior question: for a fixed task, what is the minimum model capacity required to solve it? We study this through the Entropic Bound, a spectral notion of task-intrinsic capacity for Transformers. We first prove that, in a linear attention surrogate, the intrinsic rank $r^*$ of the token-mixing operator is a tight lower bound: any rank-deficient model incurs unavoidable excess risk, and the bound is achievable at $r^*$. We further show that gradient descent recovers this rank under standard low-rank implicit-bias assumptions, confirm all three properties empirically, and show $r^*$ is recoverable from data before training. We then ask whether this transfers to real attention. A naive transfer fails, and a controlled interpolation ladder localizes the cause precisely: it is not softmax and not a rank constraint, but the input-conditioned nature of attention's mixing operator, which a static weight kernel cannot summarize. Motivated by this, we introduce an attention-native intrinsic rank -- the minimum query-key kernel rank realizing the task within the attention class -- and show that under this definition the full Entropic Bound structure (deficiency, achievability, recovery) is restored for both linear and softmax attention, with the energy effective rank as the estimator robust to softmax distortion. Finally, we map the boundary of data-only predictability: $r^*$ is exactly recoverable for linear QK attention, even without the value map at scale, while softmax attention admits only partial pre-training recovery due to nonlinear inversion and kernel-value identifiability effects. Our results reframe the Entropic Bound from a post-hoc descriptor into an attention-native capacity measure with a precisely characterized predictability frontier.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that attention-based models have an intrinsic minimum capacity (rank) needed to solve a task, defined via the Entropic Bound. For linear attention, the intrinsic rank is a tight lower bound: deficiency causes unavoidable error, achievability is possible, and gradient descent recovers it. For softmax attention, a naive transfer fails due to the input-conditioned nature of the attention kernel, so the authors introduce an attention-native intrinsic rank that restores all properties, with the energy effective rank as a robust estimator. They map the predictability frontier: exact pre-training recovery is possible for linear QK attention but only partial for softmax due to nonlinear inversion and identifiability issues.
AI.motivation: Existing neural scaling laws describe how loss decreases with scale but do not answer a more fundamental question: for a fixed task, what is the minimum model capacity required to solve it? The authors aim to define and characterize such a task-intrinsic capacity measure for Transformers.
AI.method: The authors prove theoretical bounds for a linear attention surrogate, showing the intrinsic rank r* of the token-mixing operator is a tight lower bound. They empirically confirm deficiency, achievability, and recovery properties. They then diagnose why this fails for softmax attention (input-conditioned mixing) and propose an attention-native intrinsic rank based on the minimum query-key kernel rank. They use the energy effective rank as a robust estimator and analyze pre-training recoverability.
AI.result: For linear attention, r* is a tight lower bound with deficiency, achievability, and recovery via gradient descent. For softmax attention, the cause of failure is the input-conditioned nature of the mixing operator, not softmax itself or rank constraints. Under the attention-native intrinsic rank definition, all Entropic Bound properties are restored. The data-only predictability frontier shows exact recovery for linear QK attention but only partial recovery for softmax attention.
AI.conclusion: The Entropic Bound is reframed from a post-hoc descriptor into an attention-native capacity measure with a precisely characterized predictability frontier. This provides a principled way to determine the minimum model capacity required for a task before training.

title: Evolving from Lessons: Skill-Augmented Table Graph Reasoning for Operation-wise Table Question Answering
summary: Table Question Answering (TableQA) aims to reason over tables to answer user queries. Existing research treats all questions uniformly and evaluates solely through overall accuracy, obscuring a critical reality that LLMs excel at simple lookups yet struggle with complex operations like aggregation and arithmetic. To reveal this disparity, we introduce a novel \emph{Operation-wise TableQA} task with a fine-grained question taxonomy and release two datasets named WikiTQ-ow and TabFact-ow for evaluation. As for modeling bottlenecks, existing methods flatten tables into linearized texts, disrupting inherent structures and inducing the ``lost-in-the-middle'' issue, which poses a primary barrier to complex cross-row reasoning. Moreover, they typically reason from scratch, neglecting reusable patterns shared across similar operations. To address these limitations, we propose a Skill-augmented Table Graph Reasoning (SkillTGR) framework for self-evolving structured reasoning. Specifically, SkillTGR represents tables as attributed graphs with explicit row-column-cell structures, where LLMs plan and execute dynamic chains to retrieve evidence subgraphs for graph traversal reasoning. Based on this, SkillTGR builds a hierarchical SkillBank to distill reason trajectories into abstract skills under cognitive heuristics, then hybrid retrieves both successful and failed skills for contrastive augmented table graph reasoning, thereby enabling the continual self-evolution. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SkillTGR achieves superior performance with an average of 5.91\% overall and 6.03\% operation-wise improvement, also reducing 19.76\% token consumption and 27.64\% inference latency. Our codes and data will be released upon publication.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SkillTGR, a framework for Table Question Answering that uses graph-based table representation and a hierarchical SkillBank with contrastive retrieval to improve complex operation reasoning, achieving significant gains in accuracy, token efficiency, and inference speed.
AI.motivation: Existing TableQA research treats all questions uniformly and evaluates solely via overall accuracy, masking the reality that LLMs excel at simple lookups but struggle with complex operations (e.g., aggregation, arithmetic). Additionally, linearized table representations disrupt inherent structures causing "lost-in-the-middle" issues, and current methods reason from scratch without reusing patterns shared across similar operations.
AI.method: SkillTGR (Skill-augmented Table Graph Reasoning) represents tables as attributed graphs with explicit row-column-cell structures, where LLMs plan and execute dynamic chains to retrieve evidence subgraphs. It builds a hierarchical SkillBank to distill reasoning trajectories into abstract skills under cognitive heuristics, then hybrid retrieves both successful and failed skills for contrastive augmented table graph reasoning, enabling continual self-evolution.
AI.result: SkillTGR achieves 5.91% overall accuracy improvement and 6.03% operation-wise improvement, while reducing 19.76% token consumption and 27.64% inference latency.
AI.conclusion: SkillTGR demonstrates that structured graph reasoning with reusable skill patterns significantly outperforms existing linearized text approaches for TableQA, particularly on complex operations, while also being more efficient in both computation and inference.

title: mmSimPrior: Learning Simulation Priors for Data-Efficient Real-World Generalizable Radar-Based Human Motion Reconstruction
comment: 19 pages, 11 figures, including supplementary material. Project page: https://ch3ngguo.github.io/mmsimprior/
summary: Millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar offers privacy-preserving and lighting-robust sensing for human motion reconstruction, but learning models that generalize across real deployments require diverse paired radar-motion data that are costly to collect. Simulation provides scalable supervision, yet models trained on clean synthetic signals transfer poorly because of multipath, clutter, response statistics, and resolution degradation. We present mmSimPrior, a simulation-pretrained framework that factorizes transferable knowledge into signal, motion, and radar-to-motion mapping priors. A multi-modal signal encoder is pretrained with a physics-informed domain-randomization curriculum that emulates propagation- and acquisition-level variations, while a joint-temporal tokenizer learns a discrete prior over plausible human motion. A shared mapping prior supports classification over a learned motion codebook for constrained zero-shot reconstruction and continuous regression for flexible limited-data adaptation. We further construct a 4.2M-frame, 31K-sequence dataset suite and introduce a No-Overlap Setting that excludes repeated complete subject-environment-location-motion configurations across adaptation and test. Experiments on mmSimPrior-Real and RT-Pose demonstrate consistent gains: with only 24 paired real sequences, mmSimPrior-Reg reduces MPJPE by 24.7% to 39.0% over the strongest baseline across the three environments, while mmSimPrior-Cls reduces zero-shot MPJPE by 8.5% without finetuning.

AI.tldr: mmSimPrior is a simulation-pretrained framework for mmWave radar-based human motion reconstruction that factorizes transferable knowledge into signal, motion, and mapping priors. Using physics-informed domain randomization and a learned motion codebook, it achieves significant MPJPE reductions (24.7-39.0% with 24 real sequences, 8.5% zero-shot) across real environments.
AI.motivation: Paired radar-motion data is costly to collect for real-world deployments, and models trained on clean synthetic signals fail to transfer due to multipath, clutter, response statistics, and resolution degradation in real environments.
AI.method: (1) Multi-modal signal encoder pretrained with physics-informed domain-randomization curriculum simulating propagation/acquisition variations. (2) Joint-temporal tokenizer learning a discrete prior over human motion. (3) Shared mapping prior supporting both classification over a learned motion codebook (zero-shot) and continuous regression (limited-data adaptation). (4) A 4.2M-frame, 31K-sequence dataset suite with a No-Overlap Setting.
AI.result: With 24 paired real sequences, mmSimPrior-Reg reduces MPJPE by 24.7%-39.0% over the strongest baseline across three environments; mmSimPrior-Cls reduces zero-shot MPJPE by 8.5% without finetuning.
AI.conclusion: Factorizing sim-to-real transfer into signal, motion, and mapping priors, combined with physics-informed domain randomization and a discrete motion codebook, enables effective generalization from simulated mmWave radar data to real-world human motion reconstruction with minimal real data.

title: Through the Bottleneck: How Multi-head Latent Attention Separates Content from Position in Language Models
summary: Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA), introduced in DeepSeek-V2, compresses key-value pairs through a shared low-rank bottleneck (cKV), achieving 81% KV-cache reduction during inference. Despite its adoption in massive production models, no prior work has studied what information this bottleneck preserves or discards, nor how it reshapes internal transformer circuits. We present the first comprehensive mechanistic interpretability study of MLA, training a 114M-parameter transformer (pretrained on a web/code/math mixture, fine-tuned on TinyStories) and analyzing its representations through SVD, attention head taxonomy, linear probing, and a disruption-attribution analysis. Our key findings are: (1) the cKV bottleneck learns a pure content representation, preserving entity identity (98% retention) while discarding positional information, validating MLA's separation of content from position via RoPE; (2) induction heads co-locate at a single layer (Layer 12), unlike their distributed formation in standard MHA; (3) a single "semantic hub" layer (Layer 15) simultaneously exhibits the highest SVD effective rank and strongest disruption-attribution score; and (4) the bottleneck is globally over-provisioned, using only 46% of its capacity on average. These findings suggest MLA does not merely compress attention passively, but reshapes how the model organizes content, position, and circuit structure. We view this as an initial data point and detail scope limitations in Section 5.

AI.tldr: First mechanistic interpretability study of Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) showing the cKV bottleneck preserves content (98% entity retention) while discarding position, induction heads co-locate at a single layer, a semantic hub layer emerges, and the bottleneck is globally over-provisioned (only 46% capacity used).
AI.motivation: Despite MLA's widespread adoption in production models (e.g., DeepSeek-V2) achieving 81% KV-cache reduction, no prior work has studied what information the shared low-rank bottleneck preserves or discards, nor how it reshapes internal transformer circuits.
AI.method: Trained a 114M-parameter transformer (pretrained on web/code/math, fine-tuned on TinyStories) and analyzed via SVD, attention head taxonomy, linear probing, and disruption-attribution analysis.
AI.result: (1) cKV bottleneck preserves content (98% entity identity retention) and discards positional info; (2) induction heads co-locate at Layer 12 unlike distributed formation in MHA; (3) Layer 15 is a semantic hub with highest SVD rank and disruption-attribution score; (4) bottleneck uses only 46% of capacity on average.
AI.conclusion: MLA does not merely passively compress attention but actively reshapes how the model organizes content, position, and circuit structure; initial data point with scope limitations.

title: PRESTO: Prefix-Aligned Tree Drafting for Diffusion Speculative Decoding
summary: Diffusion Large Language Models (dLLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive (AR) LLMs, generating tokens in parallel. This makes them effective draft models for speculative decoding (SD), producing an entire block of draft tokens in a single forward pass. Yet existing diffusion-based drafting methods rely on linear drafting, even though dLLMs emit multiple candidate tokens across positions, inducing a large combinatorial space of decoding paths. Consequently, they limit acceptance length and decoding efficiency. To exploit this multi-candidate structure, we apply tree-based drafting to diffusion drafters, enabling exploration of diverse candidate paths. However, we find that naive tree drafting is suboptimal: diffusion marginals are prefix-blind, mismatching the prefix-based AR verification and yielding unreliable path ranking. We propose PRESTO, a principled framework that extends tree-based drafting to diffusion drafters while resolving the fundamental mismatch between diffusion draft confidence and prefix-based AR verification through PREfix-aligned Scoring and priority-based Tree search for diffusion speculative decOding. The key principles behind PRESTO are that (1) candidate ranking should align with the prefix-based nature of AR verification, and (2) tree construction should prioritize candidate paths with high verification potential to maximize acceptance length. Extensive experiments show that PRESTO achieves up to an average of $1.5\times$ end-to-end throughput speedup on the state-of-the-art dedicated diffusion drafter SD and an average of $1.12\times$ on self-speculative diffusion LLMs across diverse benchmarks.

AI.tldr: PRESTO is a tree-based speculative decoding framework for Diffusion Large Language Models that resolves the mismatch between prefix-blind diffusion marginals and prefix-based AR verification via prefix-aligned scoring and priority-based tree search, achieving up to 1.5× throughput speedup over existing diffusion drafting methods.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion-based speculative decoding methods rely on linear drafting, which fails to exploit the multi-candidate structure (multiple tokens across positions) emitted by dLLMs, limiting acceptance length and decoding efficiency.
AI.method: PRESTO extends tree-based drafting to diffusion drafters with two key principles: (1) PREfix-aligned Scoring to align candidate ranking with the prefix-based nature of AR verification, (2) priority-based Tree search to prioritize candidate paths with high verification potential, resolving the fundamental mismatch between diffusion draft confidence and prefix-based AR verification.
AI.result: Achieves up to 1.5× end-to-end throughput speedup on state-of-the-art dedicated diffusion drafter SD and 1.12× on self-speculative diffusion LLMs across diverse benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: PRESTO provides a principled framework that effectively exploits the multi-candidate structure in diffusion drafters for speculative decoding by aligning draft confidence with AR verification and optimizing tree construction, significantly improving decoding efficiency.

title: Breaking the Synthetic-Real Domain Shortcut for Training-Free Generative Replay-based Class Incremental Learning
summary: Class-incremental learning (CIL) requires models to continuously acquire new knowledge while avoiding catastrophic forgetting. While exemplar replay is effective, it raises concerns regarding privacy and storage. Thus, generative replay has emerged as a viable alternative, synthesizing old data using frozen pretrained text-to-image (T2I) models without any extra training. However, we observe that directly mixing synthetic old-class data with real new-class data during incremental training leads to significant performance degradation. This issue stems from a "domain shortcut", where models rely on domain-discriminative features instead of semantic class cues. To address this, we propose DREAM ($\underline{\mathbf{D}}$omain-$\underline{\mathbf{R}}$egularized $\underline{\mathbf{E}}$xemplar-free $\underline{\mathbf{A}}$lignment $\underline{\mathbf{M}}$odel), which uses a training-free generator to synthesize old-class data and eliminates domain shortcut via subspace rectification and orthogonal projection, while reinforcing semantic alignment through real-anchored prototype regularization. Extensive experiments on 4 datasets demonstrate that DREAM outperforms existing exemplar-free CIL methods and achieves state-of-the-art performance. Our source code is available at https://github.com/Light-ZhangTao/DREAM.

AI.tldr: DREAM proposes a domain-regularized exemplar-free class-incremental learning method that uses frozen pretrained T2I models for generative replay and addresses the "domain shortcut" problem (where models rely on domain-discriminative features when mixing synthetic old data with real new data) through subspace rectification, orthogonal projection, and real-anchored prototype regularization, achieving SOTA on multiple datasets.
AI.motivation: Exemplar replay in CIL raises privacy and storage concerns; generative replay using frozen pretrained T2I models offers an alternative, but directly mixing synthetic old-class data with real new-class data causes performance degradation due to a "domain shortcut" problem where models exploit domain-discriminative features rather than semantic class cues.
AI.method: DREAM uses a training-free frozen T2I generator for old-class data synthesis, then eliminates domain shortcut via (1) subspace rectification, (2) orthogonal projection, and (3) real-anchored prototype regularization for semantic alignment.
AI.result: Outperforms existing exemplar-free CIL methods and achieves state-of-the-art performance across 4 datasets.
AI.conclusion: Domain shortcut is a key obstacle in generative replay for CIL, and the proposed domain-regularized alignment effectively mitigates it without requiring extra generator training.

title: Self-Boosting Vision-Language Models with Noisy Student On-Policy Self-Distillation
summary: Post-training enables vision-language models (VLMs) to understand human instructions and perform various downstream tasks. Current post-training methods usually rely on human-annotated data, distillation from external models, reinforcement learning with human feedback, or verifiable answers. This limits their ability to improve without external supervision. To tackle this, we propose NOPD (Noisy Student On-Policy Self-Distillation), a simple yet effective self-distillation approach that improves VLMs without any external models or ground-truth answers. Our key insight is that prediction discrepancies between clean and corrupted inputs naturally induce a self-supervision signal. In NOPD, the model learns from corrupted inputs while using its own predictions under clean inputs as token-level supervision. We show the effectiveness of NOPD on five visual reasoning tasks; it can match and even outperform reinforcement learning approaches or distillation from external models. Notably, when trained with 2.1K samples from Geometry3K, NOPD improves Qwen2.5-VL-7B by 20 points on its validation set. It also shows generalization on out-of-distribution test sets and achieves 7.4 point gains on MathVista. Furthermore, we demonstrate that NOPD is a general approach to enhance VLMs, achieving improvements across three models on 12 benchmarks.

AI.tldr: Post-training VLMs via self-distillation from clean vs. corrupted input discrepancies (NOPD) improves performance without external supervision, matching/exceeding RL and distillation methods across 12 benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current post-training methods for VLMs rely on human annotations, external models, RLHF, or verifiable answers, limiting their ability to improve without external supervision.
AI.method: NOPD (Noisy Student On-Policy Self-Distillation): model learns from corrupted inputs while using its own clean-input predictions as token-level supervision, leveraging prediction discrepancies between clean and corrupted inputs as a self-supervision signal.
AI.result: Matches/surpasses RL and distillation methods on five visual reasoning tasks; +20 points on Geometry3K validation (2.1K samples, Qwen2.5-VL-7B); +7.4 points on MathVista; generalizes across 3 models and 12 benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: NOPD is a simple, effective, and general self-distillation approach that enhances VLMs without any external supervision, outperforming existing methods reliant on external models or ground-truth answers.

title: CallBench: A Benchmark for Dual-Goal Coordination in Phone Call Assistants
summary: Target-oriented dialogue systems have demonstrated strong capabilities in completing user goals through interactive conversations. However, existing studies are primarily designed for single, explicit goal completion, while phone call assistants face a proxy setting that requires coordinating the device owner's explicit preset goal with the caller's implicit and dynamic goal. We introduce \textsc{CallBench}, a Chinese benchmark for evaluating dual-goal coordination in phone call assistants. \textsc{CallBench} contains 50,000 complete multi-turn phone call dialogues across six scenarios: takeout, delivery, taxi, work, life, and harassment. It covers regular presets, emergent presets, and no-preset cases, and includes diverse relations between owner-side and caller-side goals, such as alignment, complementarity, irrelevance, and conflict. We further design a preset-aware turn-level evaluation protocol covering semantic understanding, context use, active guidance, response quality, preset compliance, dialogue rhythm, and safety. Experiments on representative dialogue methods show that existing approaches still struggle with this task, highlighting the need for phone call assistants that can make reliable turn-level decisions between two independent goals under proxy constraints.

AI.tldr: CallBench is a Chinese benchmark with 50,000 multi-turn phone call dialogues across six scenarios, designed to evaluate dual-goal coordination in phone call assistants where the assistant must balance the device owner's preset goals with the caller's implicit, dynamic goals under varying goal relations (alignment, complementarity, irrelevance, conflict).
AI.motivation: Existing target-oriented dialogue systems focus on single, explicit goal completion, but phone call assistants face a proxy setting requiring coordination between the device owner's preset goal and the caller's implicit, dynamic goal—a dual-goal coordination problem not addressed by current benchmarks.
AI.method: Constructed CallBench with 50,000 multi-turn dialogues across six scenarios (takeout, delivery, taxi, work, life, harassment), covering regular presets, emergent presets, and no-preset cases, with diverse owner-caller goal relations. Designed a preset-aware turn-level evaluation protocol covering semantic understanding, context use, active guidance, response quality, preset compliance, dialogue rhythm, and safety.
AI.result: Experiments on representative dialogue methods show existing approaches still struggle with dual-goal coordination under proxy constraints.
AI.conclusion: There is a need for phone call assistants that can make reliable turn-level decisions between two independent goals under proxy settings, as current methods are insufficient.

title: OmniMate: Open-Ended Real-Time Streaming Audio-Visual Generation for Interactive Avatars
summary: Recent advances in diffusion-based generative models have enabled real-time audio-driven avatar generation and unified audio-visual synthesis, providing a promising foundation for interactive avatar systems. However, extending these models to real-time interactive streaming remains challenging, as the generation horizon is unknown in advance and cross-modal identity consistency gradually degrades during long-term generation. To address these challenges, we propose OmniMate, a unified framework for open-ended real-time interactive audio-visual avatar generation. OmniMate jointly synthesizes visual content, speech, and audio effects in real time, enabling natural and immersive multi-turn interactions. To achieve adaptive response progression, we introduce a Generation Progress Controller (GPC) that explicitly models the generation progress of each streaming chunk, allowing the model to complete responses according to the desired progress and achieve seamless transitions between execution and listening states. To preserve long-term cross-modal identity consistency, we propose a Multi-Reference Conditioning Module (MRCM), which leverages multiple reference images and a reference speech segment to provide persistent visual and speaker identity cues throughout long-duration streaming interactions. Extensive experiments on an interaction-oriented adaptation of VerseBench demonstrate that OmniMate achieves high-quality, low-latency streaming generation while maintaining strong long-term audio-visual consistency. The results further show that OmniMate supports realistic, coherent, and responsive interactive avatar experiences over extended multi-turn conversations.

AI.tldr: OmniMate is a unified framework for real-time, open-ended interactive audio-visual avatar generation that addresses unknown generation horizons and cross-modal identity degradation through a Generation Progress Controller (GPC) for adaptive streaming chunk progression and a Multi-Reference Conditioning Module (MRCM) for long-term identity consistency.
AI.motivation: Extending diffusion-based generative models to real-time interactive streaming remains challenging because the generation horizon is unknown in advance and cross-modal identity consistency gradually degrades during long-term generation.
AI.method: OmniMate jointly synthesizes visual content, speech, and audio effects in real time. It introduces a Generation Progress Controller (GPC) to explicitly model generation progress of streaming chunks for adaptive response progression and seamless state transitions, and a Multi-Reference Conditioning Module (MRCM) leveraging multiple reference images and a reference speech segment to maintain long-term visual and speaker identity cues.
AI.result: Experiments on an interaction-oriented adaptation of VerseBench show OmniMate achieves high-quality, low-latency streaming generation with strong long-term audio-visual consistency, supporting realistic, coherent, and responsive multi-turn conversations.
AI.conclusion: OmniMate effectively addresses the key challenges of real-time interactive audio-visual avatar streaming, enabling natural multi-turn interactions with preserved identity consistency over extended durations.

title: Diffusion-Guided Search via Exponential Tilting (DiffTilt): An Application to Falsification of Safety-Critical Systems
summary:
Discovering rare safety-critical failures in autonomous and cyber-physical systems is a fundamental challenge in verification and validation. Existing falsification approaches rely on conditional sampling strategies that factor the joint distribution over environments and system executions, and therefore suffer from multiplicative rarity effects: the simultaneous scarcity of failure-inducing inputs and failure-inducing traces makes exhaustive search prohibitively expensive.
  This paper develops DiffTilt, a distributional framework that exponentially tilts a diffusion model-induced joint distribution over environments and executions. We show that diffusion-guided sampling admits an exact interpretation as importance sampling in the joint space, where guidance scores induce a KL-optimal reallocation of probability mass towards failure-relevant behaviors. We further show that tilting provably amplifies failure probability and strictly outperforms conditional sampling, which is limited by multiplicative rarity. In this framework, the joint generative model serves as a reusable prior over scenarios and need not faithfully represent the system under test. Expensive system simulations are instead limited to learning a scoring function that characterizes scenario quality, enabling their selective and adaptive use.
  We study DiffTilt on ARCH-COMP benchmarks, and we propose an additional tractor-trailer benchmark showing the behavior of several approaches when scenario generation is guided by a well-defined specification rather than a reward. The proposed method achieves competitive or improved falsification performance compared to state-of-the-art approaches, with larger gains when specification definition is not limited to STL formulas.

AI.tldr: DiffTilt is a distributional framework that uses diffusion model-induced exponential tilting to jointly sample environments and executions for falsification, achieving provable failure probability amplification and outperforming conditional sampling that suffers from multiplicative rarity effects.
AI.motivation: Existing falsification methods rely on conditional sampling that factors the joint distribution over environments and executions, suffering from multiplicative rarity effects—simultaneous scarcity of both failure-inducing inputs and traces makes exhaustive search prohibitively expensive.
AI.method: DiffTilt exponentially tilts a diffusion model-induced joint distribution over environments and executions; uses diffusion-guided sampling as importance sampling in joint space with guidance scores inducing KL-optimal probability mass reallocation; uses joint generative model as a reusable prior with system simulations limited to learning a scoring function.
AI.result: Achieves competitive or improved falsification performance on ARCH-COMP benchmarks and a new tractor-trailer benchmark compared to state-of-the-art approaches, with larger gains when specification definition is not limited to STL formulas.
AI.conclusion: Exponential tilting via diffusion models provably amplifies failure probability and strictly outperforms conditional sampling limited by multiplicative rarity; the framework enables selective and adaptive use of expensive system simulations.

title: Answering Path Queries under Linear and Guarded Existential Rules
summary: Ontology-mediated query answering is concerned with the problem of answering queries over knowledge bases consisting of a database instance and an ontology. While most work in the area focuses on conjunctive queries (CQs), navigational queries have gained increasing attention. In this paper, we investigate the complexity of answering two-way (conjunctive) regular path queries ((C)RPQs) over knowledge bases whose ontology is given by a set of guarded existential rules. We first consider the subclass of linear existential rules and show that (C)RPQ answering is NL-complete in data complexity, which matches the data complexity of answering RPQs over plain graph databases (i.e., without an ontology). In combined complexity, both tasks are ExpTime-complete in the general case, but RPQ and CRPQ answering drop to PTime-complete and PSpace-complete respectively if there is a bound on predicate arity. For guarded rules, we provide a non-trivial reduction to the linear case, which allows us to show that the complexity of (C)RPQ answering is the same as for CQs, namely 2ExpTime-complete in combined complexity (ExpTime-complete in the bounded-arity case) and PTime-complete in data complexity.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the complexity of answering two-way (conjunctive) regular path queries over knowledge bases with guarded existential rules, showing NL-complete data complexity for linear rules (matching plain graph databases) and various combined complexity results (ExpTime-complete for general linear, PTime/PSpace for bounded-arity; 2ExpTime-complete for guarded rules, matching CQ complexity).
AI.motivation: To bridge the gap between conjunctive queries and navigational queries in ontology-mediated query answering by investigating the complexity of (C)RPQ answering under guarded existential rules.
AI.method: The paper analyzes two subclasses of guarded existential rules: (1) linear existential rules, with direct complexity analysis, and (2) general guarded rules, via a non-trivial reduction to the linear case.
AI.result: For linear rules: data complexity is NL-complete (both RPQ and CRPQ); combined complexity is ExpTime-complete generally, dropping to PTime-complete (RPQ) and PSpace-complete (CRPQ) under bounded predicate arity. For guarded rules: data complexity is PTime-complete; combined complexity is 2ExpTime-complete (ExpTime-complete under bounded arity), matching CQ complexity.
AI.conclusion: (C)RPQ answering under guarded existential rules has the same complexity as CQ answering for guarded rules, while for linear rules the data complexity matches plain graph databases without ontologies.

title: When Less Is More: A Controlled Benchmark of Lightweight CNNs for Satellite Land-Cover Segmentation on DeepGlobe
summary: High-resolution satellite imagery is the backbone of good land-cover classification, and without that, environmental monitoring, urban planning, and sustainable resource management all fall short. Deep learning architectures perform well in semantic segmentation, but the efficiency-accuracy trade-off across classical convolutional encoders is not well quantified under controlled, reproducible conditions. This study compares five architectures VGG16, MobileNetV2, InceptionV3, AlexNet, and CNN on the DeepGlobe Land Cover Classification dataset using three progressively optimized iterations to isolate regularisation, transfer learning, and architectural depth. To ensure performance differentials reflect architectural properties, all experiments used identical preprocessing, hyperparameter, and training protocols without data augmentation or class-imbalance correction. At 24.98 MB, MobileNetV2_v1 had the highest overall accuracy (0.7906) and mean Intersection over Union (0.4625), outperforming deeper alternatives like InceptionV3_v2 (125.17 MB, accuracy 0.7610) and VGG16_v2 (71.13 MB, accuracy 0.7653). Class-wise analysis showed strength in urban, agricultural, and water categories, but rangeland-barren confusion showed that architectural optimization alone cannot optimize spectrally similar minority classes. Strong spatial generalization and crisp boundary delineation were confirmed on held-out test imagery, validating operational applicability. These results show that lightweight, transfer-learned models can match or outperform deeper models in resource-constrained remote-sensing environments, enabling scalable land-cover mapping.

AI.tldr: This study compares five deep learning architectures (VGG16, MobileNetV2, InceptionV3, AlexNet, CNN) for satellite image land-cover classification on the DeepGlobe dataset. MobileNetV2_v1 achieved the best accuracy (0.7906) and mIoU (0.4625) at only 24.98 MB, outperforming larger models like InceptionV3 and VGG16, demonstrating that lightweight transfer-learned models are viable for resource-constrained remote sensing.
AI.motivation: High-resolution satellite imagery is critical for land-cover classification, which underpins environmental monitoring, urban planning, and sustainable resource management. However, the efficiency-accuracy trade-off across classical convolutional encoders has not been well quantified under controlled, reproducible conditions.
AI.method: Five architectures (VGG16, MobileNetV2, InceptionV3, AlexNet, CNN) were compared on the DeepGlobe Land Cover Classification dataset using three progressively optimized iterations per architecture. All experiments used identical preprocessing, hyperparameters, and training protocols without data augmentation or class-imbalance correction to isolate the effects of regularization, transfer learning, and architectural depth.
AI.result: MobileNetV2_v1 achieved the highest overall accuracy (0.7906) and mean IoU (0.4625) at only 24.98 MB, outperforming larger alternatives like InceptionV3_v2 (125.17 MB, 0.7610) and VGG16_v2 (71.13 MB, 0.7653). Class-wise analysis showed strength in urban, agricultural, and water categories, but rangeland-barren confusion persisted for spectrally similar minority classes.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight, transfer-learned models can match or outperform deeper models in resource-constrained remote-sensing environments, enabling scalable land-cover mapping. However, architectural optimization alone cannot resolve confusion in spectrally similar minority classes.

title: Foundation Models and Fine-Tuning: Toward a New Generation of Models for Time Series Forecasting
summary: Inspired by recent breakthroughs in large language models for natural language processing, foundation models have emerged as a promising paradigm for zero-shot time series forecasting, enabling accurate predictions on datasets never seen during pre-training. Ranging from tens to hundreds of millions of parameters, these models are pre-trained on vast and diverse collections of time series, learning generalizable representations that support both point and probabilistic forecasting. This approach alleviates the need for dataset-specific model design and manual tuning, offering a unified solution across forecasting problems. In this work, we review the main architectures, pre-training strategies, and optimization methods underpinning these models. We further investigate post-pre-training fine-tuning of selected foundation models to enhance their performance on specific datasets. Our empirical results demonstrate that this step consistently improves forecasting accuracy over the zero-shot baseline.

AI.tldr: This paper reviews foundation models for zero-shot time series forecasting, including architectures, pre-training strategies, and optimization methods, and shows that fine-tuning improves accuracy over zero-shot baselines.
AI.motivation: To leverage large-scale pre-trained foundation models for zero-shot time series forecasting, eliminating the need for dataset-specific model design and manual tuning while maintaining strong predictive performance.
AI.method: Reviews main architectures, pre-training strategies, and optimization methods of foundation models for time series; conducts post-pre-training fine-tuning of selected models to improve dataset-specific performance.
AI.result: Fine-tuning foundation models consistently improves forecasting accuracy over zero-shot baselines across datasets.
AI.conclusion: Foundation models offer a unified solution for time series forecasting, and fine-tuning provides a reliable performance boost beyond zero-shot capabilities.

title: Fast Cross-Scenario Adaptation of CSI Models via Channel Conditional Parameter Generation
summary: Deep learning has shown strong potential for massive multiple-input multiple-output (Massive MIMO) physical-layer tasks, including channel state information (CSI) feedback and channel estimation. However, environmental heterogeneity can severely degrade CSI models in unseen scenarios, while conventional adaptation requires target-domain data and substantial computation. This paper proposes Channel Conditional Parameter Generation (CCPG), an end-to-end pipeline for rapid deployment of CSI models in dynamic wireless environments. CCPG identifies scene-sensitive adaptation bottlenecks through component-freezing experiments and generates only lightweight LoRA weights instead of full model parameters. It compresses high-dimensional channel features into compact latent conditions using cascaded SVD and a Perceiver Resampler. An energy-based canonicalization mechanism mitigates permutation and sign ambiguities in LoRA weights, while a diffusion-based generator incorporates structural information and an asymmetric size-aware loss for topology-aware parameter generation. Experiments on DeepMIMO and WAIR-D for CSI feedback and channel estimation show that CCPG adapts to new scenarios in about 3 seconds with a single forward pass, without target-scenario training or fine-tuning, and achieves cross-domain recovery performance comparable to costly online adaptation. These results demonstrate that CCPG enables efficient deployment of CSI models in large-scale dynamic wireless scenarios for intelligent 6G communications.

AI.tldr: CCPG proposes an end-to-end pipeline that uses lightweight LoRA weights generated via a diffusion model conditioned on compressed channel features to rapidly deploy CSI feedback and estimation models in new wireless scenarios, achieving cross-domain adaptation in ~3 seconds without target-domain training.
AI.motivation: Environmental heterogeneity degrades CSI models in unseen scenarios, and conventional domain adaptation requires target-domain data and substantial computation, making deployment in dynamic wireless environments inefficient.
AI.method: CCPG identifies scene-sensitive bottlenecks via component-freezing, generates only LoRA weights (not full parameters), compresses channel features using cascaded SVD + Perceiver Resampler, applies energy-based canonicalization to resolve permutation/sign ambiguities, and uses a diffusion-based generator with asymmetric size-aware loss for topology-aware parameter generation.
AI.result: On DeepMIMO and WAIR-D benchmarks for CSI feedback and channel estimation, CCPG adapts to new scenarios in ~3 seconds with a single forward pass, achieving cross-domain recovery performance comparable to costly online adaptation methods.
AI.conclusion: CCPG enables efficient deployment of CSI models in large-scale dynamic wireless scenarios for intelligent 6G communications by eliminating the need for target-scenario training or fine-tuning.

title: Structured Redundancy Modeling for Efficient Visual Token Pruning in High-Resolution MLLMs
summary: Recent high-resolution Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) generate thousands of visual tokens per input, leading to a visual token explosion that introduces severe latency bottlenecks. While token pruning mitigates this issue, state-of-the-art subset-optimization methods typically rely on iterative subset construction to jointly capture visual diversity and instruction relevance. As visual token counts scale, this sequential dependency introduces significant selection overhead, severely limiting the translation of theoretical FLOPs reductions into actual wall-clock speedups. To address this limitation, we propose Single-Forward Pruner (SFPruner), a structural reformulation of visual token pruning that embeds redundancy control directly into the scoring space, bypassing the need for iterative combinatorial optimization. Our non-iterative framework achieves redundancy-aware importance selection in a single forward pass through two complementary mechanisms. First, to attenuate redundancy at the covariance level, we introduce a semantics-guided ridge leverage scheme. By integrating instruction relevance and visual saliency, this mechanism suppresses dominant covariance directions and mitigates representation bias. Second, ranking-based directional masking resolves residual overlap through asymmetric similarity competition, where higher-scoring tokens explicitly suppress redundant lower-scoring alternatives via parallel tensor operations. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that our approach maintains stable selection costs, reducing the token selection process by up to 110 ms, from 112.4 ms to just 2.5 ms at 512 tokens in Qwen2.5-VL. This structural efficiency successfully translates theoretical token reductions into tangible inference speedups while preserving highly competitive performance against state-of-the-art techniques under aggressive compression.
