summary: As constrained learning becomes increasingly common, models are trained under explicit feasibility requirements to enforce fairness, safety, robustness, regulariza- tion, and physics or logic constraints. Understanding how training samples in- fluence the model solution (e.g., learned parameters) is crucial for interpretability and robustness. The classical influence function (IF) estimates sample contribu- tions via local sensitivity analysis, measuring how the solution changes when a specific training sample is perturbed or removed. However, IF becomes unreli- able in constrained settings: data perturbations can reshape both the objective and the feasible region, leading to estimates that violate feasibility. In response, we propose the Directional Influence Function (DIF), a novel estimator that explicitly incorporates these constraints into influence estimation. DIF formulates the opti- mality conditions of constrained learning as a variational inequality (VI) and ana- lyzes how perturbing training data affects this VI. We validate DIF on constrained linear regression and demonstrate that it recovers leave-one-out retraining results, whereas IF and penalty-based IF exhibit significant bias. We further apply DIF to fairness-constrained CNNs, where DIF accurately predicts test loss changes under data removal and aligns closely with actual retraining. Our results establish DIF as an efficient and reliable tool for data attribution in constrained learning.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Directional Influence Function (DIF) for estimating sample contributions in constrained learning settings, where classical influence functions fail because data perturbations can violate feasibility constraints. DIF formulates constrained learning as a variational inequality and accurately recovers leave-one-out retraining results in constrained linear regression and fairness-constrained CNNs.
AI.motivation: Classical influence functions become unreliable in constrained learning settings because data perturbations can reshape both the objective and the feasible region, leading to estimates that violate feasibility constraints.
AI.method: The authors propose the Directional Influence Function (DIF), which formulates the optimality conditions of constrained learning as a variational inequality (VI) and analyzes how perturbing training data affects this VI to estimate sample contributions.
AI.result: DIF recovers leave-one-out retraining results in constrained linear regression (where IF and penalty-based IF exhibit significant bias), and accurately predicts test loss changes under data removal for fairness-constrained CNNs, closely aligning with actual retraining.
AI.conclusion: DIF is established as an efficient and reliable tool for data attribution in constrained learning, overcoming the feasibility violation issues of classical influence functions.

title: AIR-BENCH Live: An Evolving Safety Benchmark for Foundation Models
summary: Foundation-model safety benchmarks capture the AI risks of their time of publication: as models improve and governments pass new AI-safety legislation, their risk taxonomies become incomprehensive and their attack prompts become ineffective. We present AIR-BENCH Live, a self-evolving successor to AIR-BENCH 2024. An automated update pipeline monitors government regulation and classifies new policies against the current four-tier risk taxonomy, either matching them to existing categories or proposing new granular categories. Then, a multi-agent, persona-driven prompt generation algorithm generates realistic, multilingual prompts with minimal human review, leaving room for improvement with modern jail breaking techniques. This algorithm is used to overhaul legacy prompts and generate prompts for new categories. In our current version, the pipeline has expanded the benchmark from 314 to 335 granular risks, with the 21 new categories drawing from 31 truly novel policy clauses across seven jurisdictions. Evaluating 14 recent models, we find a wide safety spread (from 0.17 to 0.89 among the models judged on their own behavior), that the modernized prompts are on average 0.06 points harder than the 2024 set, with the largest drops concentrated among the most compliant models, and that most models are modestly less safe on non-English prompts. By continuously absorbing new regulation and regenerating prompts, AIR-BENCH Live is designed to evolve alongside a fast-moving field.

AI.tldr: AIR-BENCH Live is a self-evolving AI safety benchmark that automatically monitors government regulations, updates risk taxonomies, and generates realistic multilingual prompts to keep pace with evolving AI risks, outperforming static benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Static safety benchmarks become outdated as AI models improve and new regulations emerge; existing risk taxonomies become incomprehensive and attack prompts become ineffective over time.
AI.method: An automated pipeline that (1) monitors government regulation and classifies policies against a four-tier risk taxonomy, (2) uses a multi-agent, persona-driven prompt generation algorithm to produce realistic multilingual prompts with minimal human review, and (3) continuously evolves the benchmark by expanding granular risk categories and overhauling legacy prompts.
AI.result: Benchmark expanded from 314 to 335 granular risks (21 new categories from 31 novel policy clauses across 7 jurisdictions). Evaluation of 14 models showed a wide safety spread (0.17-0.89), modernized prompts are 0.06 points harder than 2024 set, most models are modestly less safe on non-English prompts.
AI.conclusion: AIR-BENCH Live demonstrates a viable approach for a continuously evolving safety benchmark that adapts to regulatory and model advancements, addressing the fundamental limitation of static benchmarks in a fast-moving field.

title: Omni-Prune: Query-Aware Unified Token Pruning for Efficient Omnimodal Large Language Models
summary: Omnimodal large language models (OmniLLMs) are rapidly extending multimodal reasoning to cover synchronized audio and video. However, the resulting audio-video token sequences are long, leading to high prefill latency and GPU memory usage at inference time. Existing token pruning methods, designed mainly for vision-only inputs, miss both the cross-modal links between audio and video and the user query that decides which content matters. To bridge this gap, we present Omni-Prune, a training-free, query-aware audio-visual token pruning framework that jointly removes redundancy from both modalities while keeping task-relevant cross-modal evidence. Specifically, Omni-Prune first splits the token sequence into adaptive time windows placed at audio saliency peaks, then scores audio and video tokens on a single scale that combines encoder attention with text-query relevance, and pairs related audio-video tokens so that they are kept together. Within each window, a final K-medoids step then selects a few representative tokens, adding diverse cues that score-based selection alone would miss. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Omni-Prune outperforms established baseline methods, delivering up to 3.25x prefill speedup and 1.3x memory reduction while retaining over 99% of full-model performance.

AI.tldr: Omni-Prune is a training-free, query-aware audio-visual token pruning framework that reduces prefill latency and GPU memory for OmniLLMs by jointly pruning redundant audio-video tokens while retaining cross-modal task-relevant evidence, achieving up to 3.25x speedup and 1.3x memory reduction with over 99% performance retention.
AI.motivation: OmniLLMs face high prefill latency and GPU memory usage due to long audio-video token sequences at inference time. Existing token pruning methods are designed for vision-only inputs and ignore cross-modal links between audio and video as well as user query relevance.
AI.method: Omni-Prune is a training-free, query-aware audio-visual token pruning framework that: (1) splits token sequences into adaptive time windows aligned with audio saliency peaks; (2) scores audio and video tokens on a unified scale combining encoder attention with text-query relevance; (3) pairs related audio-video tokens to keep them together; (4) applies K-medoids within each window to select representative tokens adding diverse cues beyond score-based selection.
AI.result: Omni-Prune outperforms baseline methods, delivering up to 3.25x prefill speedup and 1.3x memory reduction while retaining over 99% of full-model performance.
AI.conclusion: Joint, query-aware, cross-modal token pruning effectively reduces inference overhead for OmniLLMs without significant performance degradation, addressing limitations of vision-only pruning methods.

title: When Can Depth Replace Precision? A Resource Theory of Quantized Neural Computation
comment: 141 pages, 26 figures, 15 tables. Includes complete proofs and documents the QReplace decision-support and Lean 4 verification companions. To be submitted to the Journal of Machine Learning Research
summary: When can additional low-bit residual computation replace missing numerical precision for a fixed input-output map? We model a quantized residual system over a fixed horizon as a pure schedule selecting fields from a declared low-bit operation library, and use relaxed controls to characterize its infinite-depth limit. The distance from the target to the closed relaxed reachable set is the exact structural floor: no increase in depth can remove it for that library. Pure schedules approach the relaxed class at rate $O(D^{-1})$ under bounded-variation time dependence and $O(D^{-\vartheta}+D^{-1})$ under Holder dependence of exponent $\vartheta$. Execution arithmetic can reverse this conclusion: full-state write-back introduces a $Dρ_z$ penalty and can freeze residual updates, whereas increment error feedback replaces this growth by a bounded carry term and obeys an exact common-lattice conservation law. A fixed-teacher converse makes this rate sharp: for coherent depth-$L$ first-order high-precision comparators, accuracy matching requires $D=Θ(L)$. Learned codebooks add a metadata resource, while state-dependent routing introduces hybrid event conditions. Verified primal and dual bounds yield feasible, impossible, or unresolved decisions before training. Companion software implements the workflow, and Lean 4 machine-checks the exact discrete core. Depth replaces precision only relative to a declared library, horizon, execution semantics, and routing model.

AI.tldr: This paper theoretically characterizes when low-bit residual computation can replace numerical precision in quantized neural networks, showing that depth-precision trade-offs depend on library, horizon, execution semantics, and routing model, with formal bounds verified via Lean 4.
AI.motivation: To formally understand the conditions under which increasing depth (more residual computations) can compensate for reduced numerical precision in quantized networks, and to identify fundamental limitations that no amount of depth can overcome.
AI.method: Models quantized residual systems as pure schedules over a fixed-horizon low-bit operation library; uses relaxed controls to characterize infinite-depth limits; derives convergence rates under bounded-variation and Hölder time dependence; analyzes execution semantics (full-state write-back vs. increment error feedback); proves a fixed-teacher converse establishing sharp depth-precision scaling.
AI.result: Distance to the relaxed reachable set is the exact structural floor (no depth increase can remove it). Pure schedules converge at O(D^{-1}) or O(D^{-ϑ}+D^{-1}) rates. Full-state write-back incurs a Dρ_z penalty, while increment error feedback yields bounded carry and a common-lattice conservation law. Accuracy matching for coherent depth-L high-precision comparators requires D=Θ(L).
AI.conclusion: Depth can replace precision only conditionally—dependent on the declared library, time horizon, execution semantics (write-back vs. incremental feedback), and routing model. The framework provides verifiable feasibility bounds before training, with machine-checked proofs in Lean 4.

title: How LLM Task-Adaptation Reshapes Alignment: A Multi-dimensional Study of Behavioral and Representational Drift
summary: Post-training is a key mechanism for adapting large language models to downstream tasks. While prior work suggests that task adaptation can alter a model's pre-existing alignment, especially its safety behavior, its broader effects across alignment domains remain poorly understood. We address this gap through a systematic evaluation of representative task-adaptation methods, including supervised fine-tuning (SFT), KL-regularized SFT, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) across 15 alignment aspects spanning six key domains: safety, factuality, stance stability, social harm, controllability, and instructability. Our results reveal that post-training does not reshape alignment uniformly. RLVR improves task performance while inducing comparatively small, but non-zero, metric-specific shifts, while SFT leads to substantially larger alignment drift across domains. KL regularization mitigates this effect: stronger reference-model anchoring reduces alignment drift from the baseline, although KL-SFT still falls short of RLVR in preserving alignment. Representation-level analysis further supports this pattern, with shifts in alignment-relevant representations tracking behavioral drift. Together, these results show that task adaptation is not merely a capability-improving step, but an alignment intervention in its own right, motivating multi-dimensional alignment evaluation as a standard component of post-training pipelines.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically evaluates how post-training methods (SFT, KL-regularized SFT, RLVR) affect 15 alignment aspects across six domains, finding that RLVR preserves alignment best while SFT causes significant drift, and KL regularization mitigates but does not fully close this gap.
AI.motivation: Prior work suggests task adaptation can alter a model's pre-existing alignment (especially safety), but broader effects across alignment domains remain poorly understood. The authors aim to fill this gap through systematic evaluation.
AI.method: Systematic evaluation of SFT, KL-regularized SFT, and RLVR across 15 alignment aspects spanning six domains (safety, factuality, stance stability, social harm, controllability, instructability), including representation-level analysis.
AI.result: RLVR improves task performance with small, non-zero metric-specific shifts; SFT causes substantially larger alignment drift; KL regularization mitigates drift but still falls short of RLVR; representation shifts track behavioral drift.
AI.conclusion: Task adaptation is not merely a capability-improving step but an alignment intervention, motivating multi-dimensional alignment evaluation as a standard component of post-training pipelines.

title: Multi-Modal Object Re-Identification with Prompt-S6 and Semantic-Aware Knowledge Guidance
comment: Accepted by IEEE TIP 2026. The version of record may differ slightly
summary: Multi-modal object Re-Identification (ReID) aims to retrieve specific objects by integrating complementary information from multiple modalities. However, existing multi-modal ReID methods do not effectively address background interference suppression or achieve tri-modal alignment, instead focusing on pairwise feature fusion. Moreover, many current aggregation approaches suffer from high computational complexity. To address these limitations, we propose PRISM, a novel multi-modal ReID framework built upon Prompt-S6 (PS6) and semantic-aware knowledge guidance. PS6 maintains the linear complexity and strong sequence modeling capability of Mamba while enabling efficient cross-modal interaction. Leveraging these advantages, we design two key components: Semantic-Driven Token Pruning (SDTP) and Progressive Fusion Network (PFN). Parsing semantic priors from the segmentation foundation models, the SDTP then leverages these priors and applies dynamic token pruning to suppress background noise and refine feature representations. The PFN progressively aggregates multi-modal features to achieve tri-modal alignment and fully exploit modality complementarity. With the proposed modules, PRISM generates more robust multi-modal representations under complex scenarios. Extensive experiments on four multi-modal object ReID benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our approach. The source code is available at https://github.com/zw-absin/PRISM.

AI.tldr: PRISM is a multi-modal object ReID framework using Prompt-S6 (based on Mamba) for efficient cross-modal interaction, Semantic-Driven Token Pruning (SDTP) for background suppression, and Progressive Fusion Network (PFN) for tri-modal alignment, achieving robust performance with linear complexity.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-modal ReID methods fail to effectively suppress background interference, achieve tri-modal alignment (instead only doing pairwise fusion), and suffer from high computational complexity.
AI.method: PRISM introduces Prompt-S6 (PS6) built upon Mamba for linear complexity and strong sequence modeling; Semantic-Driven Token Pruning (SDTP) leverages semantic priors from segmentation foundation models to dynamically prune tokens and suppress background noise; Progressive Fusion Network (PFN) progressively aggregates multi-modal features for tri-modal alignment.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on four multi-modal object ReID benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of PRISM.
AI.conclusion: PRISM generates more robust multi-modal representations under complex scenarios by addressing background interference and achieving efficient tri-modal alignment.

title: A Statistical Difference between Single-Layer Learning and Hierarchical Learning in Wide Neural Networks
summary:
Hierarchical neural networks are widely used in artificial intelligence, yet their mathematical properties remain incompletely understood. In the infinite-width limit, two different theoretical frameworks have been proposed. One reduces deep learning to kernel regression with a fixed kernel by assuming that the parameters remain close to their initialization, whereas the other allows the parameters to move away from their initialization, requiring the kernel itself to be optimized.
  In this paper, we study a three-layer neural network with a finite but large number of hidden units. We show that training the input-to-hidden weights yields a smaller generalization error than keeping them fixed. Furthermore, the latter setting exhibits singularities in the parameter space, whereas the former does not. These findings indicate that singularities play an essential role even in wide neural networks.

AI.tldr: This paper studies three-layer neural networks with finite but large hidden units, showing that training input-to-hidden weights yields better generalization than keeping them fixed, and that fixed-weight settings exhibit singularities while trained ones do not, highlighting the role of singularities in wide neural networks.
AI.motivation: To resolve inconsistencies between two theoretical frameworks for infinite-width neural networks (kernel regression with fixed kernel vs. optimized kernel) by studying a finite-width three-layer network, and to understand the role of singularities in wide networks.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of a three-layer neural network with a finite but large number of hidden units, comparing settings where input-to-hidden weights are trained versus kept fixed, and examining the presence of singularities in the parameter space.
AI.result: Training input-to-hidden weights yields smaller generalization error than keeping them fixed. Fixed-weight settings exhibit singularities in parameter space, while trained settings do not.
AI.conclusion: Singularities play an essential role even in wide neural networks, suggesting that the kernel optimization framework may be more appropriate than the fixed-kernel regression framework for understanding deep learning.

title: DOSA: A Tree-Guided, Self-Regressive Framework for Long Document Structure Analysis
summary: In visually-rich documents, information is encoded not only in individual page objects such as tables, headers, and text blocks, but also in the structural relations among them, making document structure analysis fundamental to information retrieval and document understanding. However, accurately inferring such relations remains challenging in multi-page documents with long-range dependencies and heterogeneous layouts. To address this, we propose a tree-guided and self-regressive framework, termed DOcument Structure Analyzer (DOSA), for inferring relations among page objects and reconstructing document-level semantic trees. DOSA processes documents chunk-by-chunk, fusing visual, textual, and layout features for each page object and predicting hierarchical and ordering relations. The predicted relations are used to incrementally construct a semantic tree, which is then leveraged as structural context to guide inference on subsequent chunks. Experimental results on five benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of DOSA, with improvements of up to 4 F1 points and 19 TEDS points on DocHieNet, the most challenging multi-page hierarchy benchmark.

AI.motivation: Document structure analysis is fundamental to information retrieval and document understanding, but accurately inferring structural relations among page objects remains challenging in multi-page documents with long-range dependencies and heterogeneous layouts.
AI.method: Proposes DOSA (DOcument Structure Analyzer), a tree-guided and self-regressive framework that processes documents chunk-by-chunk, fusing visual, textual, and layout features for each page object, predicting hierarchical and ordering relations, and incrementally constructing a semantic tree that serves as structural context for subsequent chunks.
AI.result: Achieves improvements of up to 4 F1 points and 19 TEDS points on DocHieNet, the most challenging multi-page hierarchy benchmark, with effectiveness demonstrated across five benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The tree-guided, self-regressive chunk-by-chunk processing approach effectively addresses long-range dependencies and heterogeneous layouts in multi-page document structure analysis.

title: Robust 6-DoF Object Pose Tracking with Built-In Recovery under Occlusions and Rapid Object Motions
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures. Accepted for publication in IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L)
summary: Real-time 6-DoF object pose tracking is essential for many robotics applications, and several approaches exist. Yet even today's approaches remain unreliable under temporary full occlusions and rapid object motions. Once tracking is lost, most methods struggle to detect the failure and recover automatically, often requiring manual re-initialization. In this paper, we address the problem of robust model-based 6-DoF tracking of unseen objects from RGB-D data, especially in scenarios with occlusion and fast motion. We propose a novel method that combines efficient learning-based keypoint matching with optimization-based alignment and introduces a novel failure detection and recovery module. Our system monitors pose reliability, detects tracking divergence or occlusions, and performs a global re-detection and pose estimation step that robustly verifies recovery candidates before resuming tracking. Our evaluation on standard tracking benchmarks and on a new dataset of occluded and fast-moving scenes shows that our method matches state-of-the-art accuracy on easy tracking sequences, maintains high tracking speed at 57.6 frames per second, and provides the most robust tracking performance under challenging conditions. Thus, we believe that our approach is a relevant step forward in robust 6-DoF object tracking from RGB-D data.

AI.tldr: A novel RGB-D 6-DoF object tracking method combining learning-based keypoint matching with optimization-based alignment and a failure detection/recovery module, achieving robust tracking under occlusion and fast motion at 57.6 FPS.
AI.motivation: Existing 6-DoF tracking methods remain unreliable under temporary full occlusions and rapid object motions, and most fail to detect tracking loss and recover automatically without manual re-initialization.
AI.method: The method combines efficient learning-based keypoint matching with optimization-based alignment, and introduces a failure detection and recovery module that monitors pose reliability, detects tracking divergence or occlusions, and performs global re-detection with robust verification of recovery candidates.
AI.result: Matches state-of-the-art accuracy on easy tracking sequences, maintains high tracking speed at 57.6 FPS, and provides the most robust tracking performance under challenging conditions (occlusion, fast motion).
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach is a relevant step forward in robust 6-DoF object tracking from RGB-D data, addressing the critical failure detection and recovery gap.

title: Transfer Learning Architectures for Scalable Multi-Fidelity Bayesian Optimization
summary: Self-driving laboratories increasingly rely on multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization (MFBO) to balance cheap, approximate evaluations against scarce, expensive ones, with a predictive surrogate at its core. Gaussian processes (GPs) are the default choice, but they scale poorly as data accumulate and assume a smooth landscape that molecular and materials search spaces routinely violate. Transfer learning offers an alternative suited to this regime: it learns a representation from abundant cheap data and adapts it to sparse expensive data. Despite its use in property prediction, transfer learning has not been tested as the engine of a closed-loop optimization. Here we benchmark eleven transfer-learning surrogates against four GP methods under an identical selection rule, fidelity budget, and model size, across nine tasks spanning synthetic functions to real chemistry and materials problems. GPs win on smooth, low-dimensional functions but perform worst on molecular and materials problems, where transfer-learning surrogates reach substantially better solutions using far less computation. Because acquisition policy is held fixed across surrogates, this advantage is attributable to the surrogate itself. Uncertainty-driven exploration is not reliably beneficial, and calibration does not predict optimization performance, so greedy exploitation of the transfer-learned mean is the more robust default. Transfer learning is therefore the surrogate of choice for molecular and materials MFBO.

AI.tldr: This paper benchmarks transfer-learning surrogates against Gaussian processes for multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization in self-driving laboratories, finding that transfer learning outperforms GPs on molecular and materials problems with lower computational cost, and that greedy exploitation of the transfer-learned mean is more robust than uncertainty-driven exploration.
AI.motivation: Gaussian processes (GPs) are the default surrogate for multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization (MFBO) but scale poorly and assume smooth landscapes that molecular/materials search spaces violate. Transfer learning offers an alternative suited to abundant cheap data and sparse expensive data, but has not been tested as the engine of closed-loop optimization.
AI.method: Benchmarked 11 transfer-learning surrogates against 4 GP methods under identical selection rule, fidelity budget, and model size across 9 tasks (synthetic functions to real chemistry/materials problems). Acquisition policy was held fixed, isolating surrogate model performance.
AI.result: GPs win on smooth, low-dimensional functions but perform worst on molecular and materials problems. Transfer-learning surrogates reach substantially better solutions with far less computation. Uncertainty-driven exploration is not reliably beneficial, and calibration does not predict optimization performance.
AI.conclusion: Transfer learning is the surrogate of choice for molecular and materials MFBO, with greedy exploitation of the transfer-learned mean being the more robust default strategy.

title: A Vocabulary for Multi-Agent Automated Research Systems
summary:
We introduce a vocabulary for automated research systems built from one or more agents to make their design choices easier to describe and compare. The vocabulary specifies 1) who the agents are, 2) what operations are available in the system, 3) who may invoke them, 4) how agents communicate, 5) what information is visible within and across runs, 6) how the next action is chosen, 7) how a run begins, and 8) how outputs are evaluated. A trajectory records one run from the input task to the returned artifact. Because agents, operations, and initialization may be stochastic, repeated runs on the same task induce a distribution over trajectories rather than a single behavior.
  Our vocabulary turns structural design questions, such as when agents should communicate, gain or lose a capability, or carry information across runs, into testable choices. It also makes the evaluator a component of the system, since reported gains depend on how closely the proxy score matches true quality. That separation also splits the vague complaint that these systems lack taste into two failures with different solutions. Generative taste is the rate at which a system proposes novel trajectories before any score is observed, and evaluative taste is the gap between the proxy score and the quality it should match. We instantiate the vocabulary on recent autoresearch systems to illustrate that it covers designs that differ widely in structure.

AI.tldr: A vocabulary is introduced to describe and compare automated research systems built from agents, covering 8 design dimensions (agents, operations, invocation, communication, visibility, action selection, initialization, evaluation). The framework distinguishes between generative taste (proposing novel trajectories) and evaluative taste (proxy score accuracy), and is instantiated on recent autoresearch systems.
AI.motivation: Existing automated research systems lack a common vocabulary to describe and compare their design choices, making it difficult to systematically analyze structural variations, communication patterns, and evaluation methodologies across different architectures.
AI.method: The authors propose a structured vocabulary with 8 dimensions (agents, operations, invocation, communication, visibility, action selection, initialization, evaluation), define trajectories as stochastic runs, and separate generative from evaluative taste. The framework is instantiated on existing autoresearch systems for validation.
AI.result: The vocabulary turns structural design questions into testable hypotheses, makes the evaluator a distinct system component, and splits the vague "lack of taste" criticism into two concrete failures: generative taste (proposal rate of novel trajectories) and evaluative taste (proxy score accuracy gap).
AI.conclusion: This vocabulary enables systematic comparison and testing of design choices in multi-agent automated research systems, with clear operational definitions of taste that separate generation quality from evaluation quality.

title: VIPER: Visual In-Context Physics Reasoning for Physically Plausible Video Generation
summary: Modern video generation models can synthesize visually compelling and temporally coherent clips, yet controlling their physical behavior remains difficult with standard text and image conditions. The core challenge is a conditioning bottleneck: material response, contact interaction, deformation, and motion trajectory are continuous and relational physical cues that are hard to specify exhaustively in language but can be demonstrated naturally by video. We propose VIPER, a Visual In-Context Physics Reasoning framework for reference-guided image-to-video generation. Given a target image, a brief target prompt, and a reference video, VIPER treats the reference as a dense visual demonstration of the desired physical process rather than an appearance template. It uses a Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) to extract reference-derived physical cues and guide a pretrained image-to-video generator through a hierarchical training strategy, enabling physical behavior transfer while preserving the visual prior of the base generator. To support this setting, we construct VIPER-19K, a curated dataset with material, trajectory, and physical-impact annotations, together with filtered reference-target pairs. Experiments on an unseen validation set show that VIPER achieves stronger reference-video physical similarity and higher human preference than representative video generation and video-as-prompt baselines, while maintaining competitive general video quality. Qualitative results further demonstrate that VIPER can transfer reference-derived physical behavior to new target scenes without requiring carefully engineered prompts.

AI.tldr: VIPER is a Visual In-Context Physics Reasoning framework that uses reference videos as dense physical demonstrations to guide image-to-video generation, enabling transfer of physical behaviors (material response, contact, deformation, motion) to new target scenes without requiring exhaustive text prompts.
AI.motivation: Standard text and image conditions struggle to specify continuous, relational physical cues (material response, contact, deformation, motion trajectory) for video generation. This conditioning bottleneck is addressed by using reference videos as natural demonstrations of physical processes.
AI.method: VIPER uses a Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) to extract physical cues from a reference video, then guides a pretrained image-to-video generator via a hierarchical training strategy. It uses VIPER-19K, a curated dataset with material, trajectory, and physical-impact annotations and filtered reference-target pairs.
AI.result: On an unseen validation set, VIPER achieves stronger reference-video physical similarity and higher human preference than video generation and video-as-prompt baselines, while maintaining competitive general video quality. It transfers physical behavior without carefully engineered prompts.
AI.conclusion: VIPER demonstrates that reference videos can effectively serve as dense visual demonstrations for transferring physical behaviors to new target scenes, overcoming the conditioning bottleneck of text/image-only video generation controls.

title: Blood Pressure Estimation from PPG: A Comparative Study of Direct and ECG-Mediated Deep Learning Pipelines
summary:
Continuous cuffless blood pressure (BP) monitoring is essential for connected health systems and wearable devices, enabling early detection, longitudinal tracking, and personalized management of cardiovascular disease. Many prior approaches attempt to estimate BP indirectly by reconstructing electrocardiography (ECG) from photoplethysmography (PPG), assuming ECG provides a stronger physiological link to BP. However, ECG sensing is less accessible in wearable settings and may introduce unnecessary complexity.
  In this work, we first perform a large-scale physiological correlation analysis on the MIMIC-III waveform database, revealing that PPG exhibits substantially stronger coupling with arterial blood pressure (ABP) ($|r|=0.247$, $p<0.001$) than ECG does ($r=0.018$, $p=0.187$), challenging the assumption that ECG provides a superior intermediate representation. Motivated by this insight, we conduct a systematic comparison between direct PPG-to-BP prediction and ECG-mediated pipelines using multiple state-of-the-art deep learning models.
  Across 1.74M segments from 3,127 patients, direct PPG-to-BP prediction achieves British Hypertension Society Grade A performance ($\mathrm{MAE}_{\mathrm{SBP}} = 4.82 mmHg$, $\mathrm{MAE}_{\mathrm{DBP}} = 4.31 mmHg$), outperforming all ECG-mediated approaches, which achieve only Grade B accuracy.
  Our findings suggest that accurate continuous BP monitoring can be achieved directly from wearable PPG signals, enabling simpler, more efficient pipelines for real-world connected health systems.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that direct PPG-to-BP prediction outperforms ECG-mediated approaches for continuous blood pressure monitoring, based on large-scale analysis of MIMIC-III data (1.74M segments, 3,127 patients). PPG exhibits stronger correlation with BP than ECG, and direct prediction achieves BHS Grade A accuracy (MAE_SBP=4.82 mmHg, MAE_DBP=4.31 mmHg), while ECG-mediated methods only reach Grade B.
AI.motivation: To challenge the prevailing assumption that ECG provides a superior intermediate representation for BP estimation, and to investigate whether direct PPG-to-BP prediction can achieve comparable or better accuracy, enabling simpler wearable-based continuous BP monitoring without the complexity of ECG sensing.
AI.method: Large-scale physiological correlation analysis on MIMIC-III comparing PPG-ABP vs ECG-ABP coupling; systematic comparison between direct PPG-to-BP prediction and ECG-mediated pipelines using multiple state-of-the-art deep learning models across 1.74M segments from 3,127 patients.
AI.result: PPG shows significantly stronger coupling with ABP (|r|=0.247, p<0.001) than ECG (r=0.018, p=0.187). Direct PPG-to-BP achieves BHS Grade A (MAE_SBP=4.82 mmHg, MAE_DBP=4.31 mmHg), outperforming all ECG-mediated approaches which only reach Grade B.
AI.conclusion: Accurate continuous BP monitoring can be achieved directly from wearable PPG signals without ECG mediation, enabling simpler and more efficient pipelines for connected health systems.

title: Imprompt: A Language Framework for Prompt Programming
summary: With the unprecedented success of Language Models (LMs), the science of Prompt Engineering has evolved the powerful idea of Prompt Programming, where prompts are treated as a programmable control surface for describing complex tasks and leveraging LM capabilities. However, existing prompt programming frameworks suffer from various complexities and inelegances, which make them hard to utilize in practice for effectively describing tasks. We propose Imprompt, a new language framework for the study and practice of prompt programming. We undertake a foundational investigation of prompt programming, and contend that prompt programs must contain only the task descriptions and must be decoupled from lower-level 'execution' details. We further develop this position by illustrating structured prompting as a combination of prompt programming and prompt program 'compilation'. We exemplify this view by formally defining two compilers for Imprompt programs. We then explore the idea of typing for prompt programs and draw a correspondence between type checking and constrained decoding. Finally, we implement our compilers and type checkers and evaluate them on a variety of case studies. We believe our work contributes programming-language foundations toward the emerging area of prompt programming.

AI.tldr: Imprompt is a new language framework for prompt programming that decouples task descriptions from execution details, introduces structured prompting with compilers, and connects type checking with constrained decoding.
AI.motivation: Existing prompt programming frameworks suffer from complexities and inelegances that make them hard to use for effectively describing tasks.
AI.method: Imprompt proposes that prompt programs should contain only task descriptions decoupled from execution details, introduces structured prompting as a combination of prompt programming and prompt program compilation, formally defines two compilers, and explores typing with a correspondence to constrained decoding.
AI.result: Implemented compilers and type checkers were evaluated on various case studies.
AI.conclusion: The work contributes programming-language foundations for the emerging area of prompt programming.

title: PlanCraft: Sketch, Refine, and Furnish for Architect-Inspired Progressive 3D Residential Scene Generation
summary: Two structural insights have been overlooked in automated residential floor plan generation. First, design is inherently progressive. Architects begin with rough strokes and refine them over time, whereas existing methods typically require their conditioning representation to be fully specified before generation, a fundamental mismatch with how design actually works. Second, the 2D floor plan is not an optional intermediate but an irreplaceable spatial contract. Once room boundaries, doors, and windows are fixed, furnishing reduces from open-ended spatial reasoning to bounded constraint satisfaction. Bypassing this contract, as existing 3D systems do by delegating layout to language models, yields overlapping rooms and implausible proportions; directly calling general-purpose language models likewise produces geometrically invalid layouts. Guided by these insights, we present PlanCraft. SketchPlan supplies the missing training signal by replaying the architect's drawing process on 80K real floor plans, producing partial sketches at every completeness level. PlanCraft-Diff progressively sharpens an incomplete sketch into a geometrically precise, vectorizable floor plan through a coarse-to-fine strategy. With the spatial contract established, PlanCraft-Agent then furnishes the scene within well-defined room boundaries. Experiments show that PlanCraft achieves a 61.1\% lower FID than the best existing 2D method and surpasses existing 3D systems by 15 points in expert-rated spatial rationality, with a sketch at only 25\% completion already outperforming all fully specified baselines.

AI.tldr: PlanCraft introduces a progressive floor plan generation framework that first generates 2D spatial contracts (room boundaries, doors, windows) via a diffusion model from partial sketches, then furnishes within those fixed boundaries, achieving state-of-the-art geometric validity and spatial rationality.
AI.motivation: Existing methods either require fully specified conditioning before generation (mismatch with progressive design) or bypass the 2D spatial contract by delegating layout to language models, yielding overlapping rooms and implausible proportions.
AI.method: Three components: (1) SketchPlan — replays architect drawing process on 80K real floor plans to produce partial sketches at all completeness levels; (2) PlanCraft-Diff — coarse-to-fine diffusion that progressively sharpens an incomplete sketch into a precise vectorizable floor plan; (3) PlanCraft-Agent — furnishes the scene within the fixed room boundaries established by the spatial contract.
AI.result: 61.1% lower FID than best existing 2D method; surpasses existing 3D systems by 15 points in expert-rated spatial rationality; a sketch at only 25% completion already outperforms all fully specified baselines.
AI.conclusion: The 2D floor plan is an irreplaceable spatial contract; progressive generation from partial sketches yields superior geometric validity and rationality compared to both fully-specified 2D methods and 3D layout-from-language approaches.

title: Harmonized Interpretable ECG Waveform Features for Robust Cross-Dataset Clinical Prediction
comment: Full version of the work presented as a 2-page paper at the 39th IEEE International Symposium on Computer-Based Medical Systems (CBMS 2026)
summary: Electrocardiograms (ECGs) are widely used for cardiovascular risk prediction, yet models often fail to transfer across hospitals because of protocol, population, and measurement differences. We benchmark cross-dataset generalization on three tasks - heart failure classification, 30-day all-cause mortality, and 30-day mortality among sinus-rhythm ECGs - using two large cohorts (MIMIC-IV and the Alberta Cohort). To reduce vendor-specific measurement mismatch, we build a harmonized, interpretable feature representation computed directly from raw waveforms: FeatureDB morphology/heart-rate-variability summaries plus compact time-frequency descriptors (autoregressive and wavelet features). We train XGBoost models on this unified feature space and evaluate with patient-disjoint internal and bidirectional external testing. We pre-specify two hypotheses: (H1) external AUROC retains at least 90% of source-site internal AUROC under transfer, and (H2) internal AUROC of the harmonized feature set stays within 10% of dataset-native machine-measurement models. Across tasks, internal AUROC is 0.79-0.82 and cross-dataset AUROC is 0.74-0.78, with larger and direction-dependent AUPRC shifts under transfer. As an exploratory benchmark, an end-to-end ConvNeXt model trained directly on raw ECG waveforms with age and sex achieves higher internal AUROC, while the harmonized representation remains competitive in relative cross-dataset transfer stability. These findings show that a consistent waveform-derived feature interface preserves performance, supports realistic external validation, and provides a transparent alternative for cross-site clinical prediction.

AI.tldr: This paper benchmarks cross-dataset ECG generalization using a harmonized feature representation (FeatureDB) derived from raw waveforms, demonstrating that XGBoost models on this unified feature space retain 90%+ internal AUROC under external transfer (0.79-0.82 internal, 0.74-0.78 cross-dataset), competitive with end-to-end deep learning (ConvNeXt) while offering interpretability and transparency for cross-site clinical prediction.
AI.motivation: ECG-based cardiovascular risk prediction models often fail to transfer across hospitals due to protocol, population, and measurement differences, motivating the need for a harmonized, interpretable feature representation that supports realistic external validation.
AI.method: Built a harmonized feature representation (FeatureDB) from raw waveforms using morphology/HRV summaries and time-frequency descriptors (autoregressive + wavelet features). Trained XGBoost models on this unified feature space with patient-disjoint internal and bidirectional external testing across MIMIC-IV and Alberta Cohort on three tasks.
AI.result: Internal AUROC 0.79-0.82; cross-dataset AUROC 0.74-0.78; external AUROC retained ≥90% of source-site internal AUROC; harmonized feature set stayed within 10% of native machine-measurement models. ConvNeXt achieved higher internal AUROC but harmonized representation showed competitive transfer stability.
AI.conclusion: A consistent waveform-derived feature interface preserves performance, supports realistic external validation, and provides a transparent alternative for cross-site clinical prediction.

title: Co-Harness: Co-Evolving Harnesses and Model Weights for LLM Agents
summary: Post-training agents for automated AI research requires optimizing not only model parameters, but also the runtime harness that shapes how research trajectories are generated, evaluated, and learned from. Existing pipelines typically train models under a fixed harness, including prompts, tools, skills, middleware, and memory, while leaving the data-generating process outside the optimization objective. This creates a mismatch between model updates and the static scaffolding that determines trajectory quality. We introduce Co-Harness, a framework that jointly optimizes the agent harness and model parameters during post-training. Co-Harness alternates between harness optimization and model optimization. An LLM-based HarnessCritic analyzes failed trajectories, identifies harness-level failure modes, and proposes validated local updates. The model is then fine-tuned on high-quality trajectories generated by the improved harness, distilling effective scaffolding into model parameters. A 200+ hour autonomous case study further shows that Co-Harness can recover from system crashes, improve inference efficiency, and discover ensemble strategies without human intervention. These results suggest that joint harness and model optimization is an effective way to improve agents beyond fixed-harness post-training.

AI.tldr: Co-Harness jointly optimizes an agent's runtime harness (prompts, tools, memory, etc.) and its model parameters during post-training, using an LLM-based critic to identify harness failures and suggest improvements, leading to better research trajectories and autonomous recovery capabilities.
AI.motivation: Existing post-training pipelines optimize only model parameters under a fixed harness, creating a mismatch between model updates and the static scaffolding that determines trajectory quality, since the data-generating process is left outside the optimization objective.
AI.method: Co-Harness alternates between harness optimization (using a HarnessCritic LLM to analyze failed trajectories, identify failure modes, and propose validated local updates) and model optimization (fine-tuning on high-quality trajectories generated by the improved harness to distill effective scaffolding into model parameters).
AI.result: A 200+ hour autonomous case study showed Co-Harness can recover from system crashes, improve inference efficiency, and discover ensemble strategies without human intervention, outperforming fixed-harness post-training.
AI.conclusion: Joint optimization of harness and model parameters is an effective approach for improving agents beyond what fixed-harness post-training can achieve.

title: To Erase, or Not to Erase: Robust Training-Free Concept Erasure with Preservation aware Adaptive Ranked Subspace Expansion
summary: Concept erasure techniques (CETs) edit text-to-image diffusion models to erase undesired targets such as NSFW content or copyrighted styles, while preserving model utility on benign concepts. Current CETs face a trade-off between erasure robustness and utility: stronger edits erase the target more reliably but degrade utility on non-target concepts, and vice versa. This stems from how existing methods define what to erase and what to preserve. Many CETs rely on static concept banks specified manually, generated by LLMs, or selected by CLIP image-text similarity. Such banks do not model how prompts steer the model during denoising, leaving it vulnerable to triggers that reintroduce the target while suppressing nearby benign concepts. We present Preservation-aware Adaptive Ranked Subspace Expansion (PARSE), a training-free framework for robust concept erasure in latent diffusion models. Given a target, PARSE queries the diffusion model with classifier-free guidance to dynamically discover target-inducing erase concepts and nearby retain concepts in the model vocabulary. It then edits the cross-attention value space with a preservation-aware projection that removes target directions while leaving retain directions intact. For triggers beyond this vocabulary-indexed space, PARSE iteratively searches for re-emergence triggers by textual inversion and adaptively expands the erased subspace only when a new trigger direction does not conflict with retain semantics. We also introduce the Balanced Erasure Utility Score (BEUS), which combines robustness (ASR under multiple attacks) and utility preservation (FID) via bounded monotone transforms and harmonic mean aggregation. Experiments on NSFW, artistic style, and object erasure, with a large-scale robustness-utility analysis over many CET baselines, show that PARSE erases multiple concepts robustly without sacrificing post-edit utility.

AI.tldr: PARSE is a training-free framework for robust concept erasure in diffusion models that dynamically discovers target-inducing and retain concepts via classifier-free guidance, edits cross-attention value space adaptively, and introduces BEUS for balanced evaluation.
AI.motivation: Current CETs face a trade-off between erasure robustness and utility preservation because they rely on static concept banks that fail to model how prompts steer the model during denoising, leaving vulnerability to triggers that reintroduce the target while suppressing benign concepts.
AI.method: PARSE queries the diffusion model with classifier-free guidance to dynamically discover target-inducing erase concepts and nearby retain concepts; edits cross-attention value space with a preservation-aware projection; iteratively searches for re-emergence triggers via textual inversion and adaptively expands the erased subspace only when no conflict with retain semantics.
AI.result: Experiments on NSFW, artistic style, and object erasure with large-scale robustness-utility analysis show PARSE erases multiple concepts robustly without sacrificing post-edit utility.
AI.conclusion: PARSE effectively resolves the robustness-utility trade-off in concept erasure by dynamically discovering concepts and adaptively expanding the erased subspace, achieving robust erasure while preserving utility.

title: Short-Term Pain for Long-Term Gain: Adaptive Experiment with Post-Commitment Reward Shift
comment: A one-page abstract appeared in ACM EC'26
summary:
Decision-makers in learning environments face a dilemma when their short-term optimal actions may not favor their long-term benefits the most. To understand the fundamental tradeoff behind the dilemma, we study adaptive experimentation with post-commitment reward shifts. During an experiment phase, the decision-maker may adaptively test multiple options; during a subsequent commitment phase, the decision-maker must commit to a single option, whose reward may differ from its pre-commitment reward. We propose the Reserved Arm Eliminations for Commitment (RAEC) algorithm, which reserves a predetermined portion of the experiment phase to identify the best post-shift option while using the remaining rounds to minimize short-run regret. We establish regret upper bounds for RAEC across all parameter regimes and matching minimax lower bounds, providing a tight characterization of the cost of balancing short-term performance and long-term commitment.
  We also study two extensions. With prior structural knowledge linking pre- and post-shift rewards, we show that correctly identifying the ranking-changing component of the shift is more important than estimating its absolute magnitude. For settings with concave commitment rewards and portfolio choice, we develop the Reserved Online Stochastic Convex Optimization for Commitment (ROSCOC) algorithm, which directly converts its reserved exploration history into a commitment portfolio and achieves tight regret bound. Finally, we also conduct numerical experiments which confirm that our proposed algorithms achieve the desired regret predicted by our theory, and also outperform other baseline algorithms.

AI.tldr: This paper studies adaptive experimentation with post-commitment reward shifts, where a decision-maker tests options in an experiment phase then commits to one option with potentially different rewards. The proposed RAEC algorithm reserves part of the experiment phase to identify the best post-shift option while minimizing short-run regret, achieving tight regret bounds and matching minimax lower bounds. Extensions include using prior structural knowledge about reward shifts and the ROSCOC algorithm for concave commitment rewards and portfolio choice.
AI.motivation: To understand the fundamental tradeoff between short-term optimal actions and long-term benefits in learning environments where decision-makers face a dilemma: actions that are optimal in the short run may not maximize long-term rewards, especially when post-commitment rewards differ from pre-commitment rewards.
AI.method: The paper introduces the Reserved Arm Eliminations for Commitment (RAEC) algorithm, which reserves a predetermined portion of the experiment phase to identify the best post-shift option and uses remaining rounds to minimize short-run regret. For extensions, it develops the Reserved Online Stochastic Convex Optimization for Commitment (ROSCOC) algorithm for settings with concave commitment rewards and portfolio choice.
AI.result: Established regret upper bounds for RAEC across all parameter regimes and matching minimax lower bounds, providing a tight characterization of the cost of balancing short-term performance and long-term commitment. Numerical experiments confirm the algorithms achieve the desired regret and outperform baseline algorithms.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a tight theoretical characterization of the exploration-commitment tradeoff, showing that correctly identifying ranking-changing components of reward shifts is more important than estimating absolute magnitudes, and that the proposed algorithms achieve optimal regret bounds.

title: Beyond Sequential Interaction: Benchmarking Parallel Execution and Coordination for GUI Agents
summary: Graphical user interface (GUI) agents are systems powered by large multimodal models (LMMs). They perceive screen state and execute user instructions through GUI actions such as clicking, typing, and scrolling on desktops and mobile devices. However, current agents scale poorly to long-horizon tasks: actions incur costly LMM inferences, and performance degrades as context grows. Humans divide such workloads among collaborators who complete sub-tasks in parallel. Yet parallel coordination among GUI agents has received little attention. To close this gap, we introduce ParaGUIBench, to our knowledge, the first benchmark dedicated to parallel execution and coordination of multiple GUI agents on separate desktop instances. It consists of three components: a multi-device Docker infrastructure with a shared file system; a dataset of 233 tasks spanning six task categories; and an evaluation system with efficiency metrics, including step reduction ratio and token cost. We further introduce ParaGUI, a planner-worker agent that decomposes GUI tasks and dispatches sub-tasks to concurrent workers on separate desktop instances. On ParaGUIBench, ParaGUI reaches a 46.4% success rate, outperforming the strongest serial baseline (Claude Sonnet 4.6) by 12.9 points while using roughly half the steps and less than half the tokens. These results show that parallel execution can improve both success rate and efficiency on decomposable, long-horizon GUI tasks, pointing to a direction worth further study.

AI.tldr: ParaGUIBench is a benchmark for parallel GUI agent coordination, and ParaGUI is a planner-worker agent that decomposes tasks for concurrent execution, achieving 46.4% success rate—12.9 points higher than serial baselines—while using half the steps and tokens.
AI.motivation: Current GUI agents scale poorly to long-horizon tasks due to costly LMM inferences and performance degradation with growing context. Parallel coordination among GUI agents has received little attention, despite humans naturally dividing workloads among collaborators.
AI.method: The authors introduce ParaGUIBench, a benchmark with three components: (1) a multi-device Docker infrastructure with a shared file system, (2) a dataset of 233 tasks across six categories, and (3) an evaluation system with efficiency metrics (step reduction ratio, token cost). They also propose ParaGUI, a planner-worker agent that decomposes GUI tasks and dispatches sub-tasks to concurrent workers on separate desktop instances.
AI.result: ParaGUI achieves a 46.4% success rate on ParaGUIBench, outperforming the strongest serial baseline (Claude Sonnet 4.6) by 12.9 points, while using roughly half the steps and less than half the tokens.
AI.conclusion: Parallel execution can improve both success rate and efficiency on decomposable, long-horizon GUI tasks, pointing to a promising direction for further study in GUI agent coordination.

title: Token-Region Guided Cross-Attention Fusion for Multimodal Affect Interpretation
summary: Automated analysis of multimodal content on social networks has become a critical task for understanding public sentiment and information diffusion in the digital age. However, classifying internet memes remains computationally challenging due to the intricate interplay between visual cues and embedded, often stylized, text, particularly in low-resource languages like Bengali Language. This paper addresses the detection of political intent in Bengali memes by introducing Multimodal Cross-Attention Fusion framework. We first leverage a Vision-Language Model to extract high-fidelity OCR text from noisy meme images. Subsequently, we encode visual and textual features and synthesize them through a cross-modal multi-head attention mechanism that aligns semantic tokens with visual regions. We also investigate the integration of a domain-specific political lexicon as a knowledge prior. Experimental evaluation on the PoliMemeDecode1 dataset shows that our attention-based fusion significantly outperforms unimodal baselines and standard concatenation methods, achieving a state-of-the-art Macro-F1 of approximately 0.94. Interpretability analyzes further confirm that the model effectively learns to ground textual semantics in visual evidence.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a Multimodal Cross-Attention Fusion framework for detecting political intent in Bengali memes, using a Vision-Language Model for OCR, cross-modal multi-head attention for feature fusion, and a domain-specific political lexicon as knowledge prior, achieving state-of-the-art Macro-F1 of ~0.94 on the PoliMemeDecode1 dataset.
AI.motivation: Classifying internet memes is computationally challenging due to complex interplay between visual cues and embedded text, especially in low-resource languages like Bengali. Automated analysis of multimodal social media content is critical for understanding public sentiment and information diffusion.
AI.method: Proposes Multimodal Cross-Attention Fusion framework: (1) uses Vision-Language Model for high-fidelity OCR from noisy meme images; (2) encodes visual and textual features; (3) synthesizes them via cross-modal multi-head attention aligning semantic tokens with visual regions; (4) integrates domain-specific political lexicon as knowledge prior.
AI.result: Evaluated on PoliMemeDecode1 dataset, attention-based fusion significantly outperforms unimodal baselines and standard concatenation methods, achieving state-of-the-art Macro-F1 of approximately 0.94.
AI.conclusion: The model effectively learns to ground textual semantics in visual evidence, as confirmed by interpretability analyses. The cross-modal attention mechanism is key to improved performance over simpler fusion strategies.

title: PerturbPFN: Probing the Limits of Synthetic Priors in Drug Perturbation Modelling
comment: 19 pages. Accepted at the 2nd ICML Workshop on Foundation Models for Structured Data (FMSD 2026), Seoul, South Korea
summary: Predicting cellular responses to unseen chemical perturbations is challenging due to unknown targets and mechanisms, high-dimensional expression responses, and limited experimental coverage of the large small-molecule design space. We propose PerturbPFN, a PFN-style amortized model for unknown-target perturbation prediction under a hierarchical synthetic structural prior. Instead of directly regressing high-dimensional expression responses, PerturbPFN infers a latent system graph, sparse atomic intervention targets, and intervention strengths, then propagates their effects through an SCM decoder. The model is trained entirely on prior-predictive synthetic episodes generated from biologically motivated graph and expression simulators, enabling structured in-context learning without test-time gradient updates. We evaluate PerturbPFN on both real single-cell perturbation data and synthetic benchmarks, covering effect prediction, target identification, and regulatory structure discovery. Our results show that PerturbPFN offers a complementary trade-off to specialized baselines, achieving competitive perturbation prediction with low inference cost while exposing interpretable intermediate estimates of targets, strengths, and system structure.

AI.tldr: PerturbPFN is a Prior-data Fitted Network that uses a hierarchical synthetic structural prior and structural causal model decoder to predict cellular responses to unseen chemical perturbations, achieving competitive performance with low inference cost and interpretable intermediate estimates of targets, strengths, and system structure.
AI.motivation: Predicting cellular responses to unseen chemical perturbations is challenging due to unknown targets, high-dimensional expression data, and limited experimental coverage of the small-molecule design space.
AI.method: PerturbPFN employs a PFN-style amortized model trained on prior-predictive synthetic episodes from biologically motivated simulators. It infers a latent system graph, sparse atomic intervention targets, and intervention strengths, then propagates effects through a structural causal model (SCM) decoder, enabling structured in-context learning without test-time gradient updates.
AI.result: PerturbPFN achieves competitive perturbation prediction with low inference cost on both real single-cell perturbation data and synthetic benchmarks, while providing interpretable intermediate estimates of targets, strengths, and regulatory structure.
AI.conclusion: PerturbPFN offers a complementary trade-off to specialized baselines, combining strong predictive performance with interpretability and computational efficiency for perturbation effect prediction, target identification, and regulatory structure discovery.

title: LazyMem: Retrieve Broadly, Construct Selectively for Efficient Long-Term Agent Memory
summary: Long-term memory lets LLM agents reuse past interactions, but raw dialogue histories are verbose and information-sparse. Retrieving broadly improves evidence coverage yet overwhelms downstream reasoning with noise; compressing at write time reduces noise but irreversibly discards details the future query may need. We introduce LazyMem, which sidesteps this dilemma by deferring all memory construction to query time. A lightweight 4B model processes the retrieved candidate pool in overlapping parallel windows, selectively retaining and compressing only query-relevant content. The model is trained through supervised fine-tuning followed by group-based reinforcement learning with a format-gated composite reward that combines a rule-based action signal measuring selection accuracy with an LLM-judged quality signal measuring source faithfulness and query utility. On the LongMemEval benchmark, LazyMem-4B achieves an LLM-judge accuracy of 0.85 with only 213 memory tokens, 68.7$\times$ fewer than retrieval-only, and generalizes to LoCoMo (0.68) without target-domain training, while reducing mean latency over the prior query-time baseline. The 32B variant reaches 0.93, surpassing oracle-context references on aggregation-heavy question types. The code associated with this work is publicly available at https://github.com/allacnobug/LazyMem.

AI.tldr: LazyMem defers memory construction to query time, using a lightweight 4B model with parallel window processing and reinforcement learning to selectively compress only query-relevant content from retrieved candidates, achieving high accuracy with minimal memory tokens (68.7× fewer than retrieval-only) on LongMemEval.
AI.motivation: Raw dialogue histories are verbose and information-sparse; retrieval improves coverage but introduces noise, while write-time compression discards potentially useful details. LazyMem sidesteps this dilemma by deferring all memory construction to query time.
AI.method: A lightweight 4B model processes the retrieved candidate pool in overlapping parallel windows, selectively retaining and compressing only query-relevant content. Trained with supervised fine-tuning + group-based reinforcement learning using a format-gated composite reward (rule-based action signal for selection accuracy + LLM-judged quality signal for faithfulness and query utility).
AI.result: LazyMem-4B achieves LLM-judge accuracy of 0.85 with only 213 memory tokens (68.7× fewer than retrieval-only); generalizes to LoCoMo (0.68) without target-domain training; reduces mean latency over prior query-time baseline; 32B variant reaches 0.93, surpassing oracle-context references on aggregation-heavy question types.
AI.conclusion: Query-time memory construction with selective compression is an effective strategy for LLM agents, balancing accuracy, memory efficiency, and latency while generalizing across domains.

title: MemVLN: Episodic and Procedural Memory for Vision-and-Language Navigation
summary: Vision-and-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments (VLN-CE) requires agents to maintain long-horizon visual history for trajectory consistency while executing actions with low latency. Existing video-based VLN approaches typically struggle to satisfy both demands simultaneously. To address these challenges, we propose MemVLN, a novel VLN framework that achieves state-of-the-art performance with real-time inference efficiency (14 FPS). MemVLN utilizes a visual encoder to process continuous observations and a Large Language Model (LLM) to interpret instructions and generate actions. Central to our approach is an Episodic Memory management that applies pyramidal resolutions. This mechanism concentrates computation on immediate percepts while retaining compressed long-term history. Complementing to this design, we introduce Procedural Memory for fast action with a compact vocabulary of atomic mid-level actions to bypass auto-regressive decoding latency. Experiments on VLN-CE show that MemVLN-4B surpasses the baseline Qwen3-VL-4B architecture by 5.8\% SR in R2R and 9.7\% SR in RxR, while achieving a 7$\times$ speedup in inference latency.

AI.tldr: MemVLN is a Vision-and-Language Navigation framework for continuous environments that achieves state-of-the-art performance with real-time inference (14 FPS). It uses Episodic Memory with pyramidal resolutions to balance immediate perception and compressed long-term history, and Procedural Memory with atomic mid-level actions to bypass auto-regressive decoding latency. MemVLN-4B outperforms the baseline by 5.8% SR (R2R) and 9.7% SR (RxR) with 7× speedup.
AI.motivation: Existing video-based VLN approaches struggle to simultaneously satisfy long-horizon visual history for trajectory consistency and low-latency action execution.
AI.method: MemVLN combines a visual encoder for continuous observations with an LLM for instruction interpretation and action generation. It introduces Episodic Memory management using pyramidal resolutions (high resolution for immediate percepts, compressed long-term history) and Procedural Memory with a compact vocabulary of atomic mid-level actions to eliminate auto-regressive decoding latency.
AI.result: MemVLN-4B surpasses Qwen3-VL-4B by 5.8% SR on R2R and 9.7% SR on RxR, while achieving 14 FPS real-time inference and a 7× speedup in latency.
AI.conclusion: The proposed dual-memory architecture (Episodic + Procedural Memory) effectively addresses the trade-off between visual history retention and low-latency action execution in VLN-CE, enabling state-of-the-art performance with real-time efficiency.

title: Local Regularization Does Not Characterize Multiclass PAC Learnability
summary: Local regularization assigns each hypothesis a test-point-dependent score and predicts with a minimum-score hypothesis consistent with the sample. Asilis et al. asked whether this principle characterizes multiclass PAC learnability. We give a negative answer. There is a countable class of Daniely--Shalev-Shwartz dimension at most two with realizable PAC sample complexity \[ O\!\left(\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\log\frac{1}δ\right), \] that no local regularizer learns. Hypotheses are edges of complete graphs and instances are tournaments. At a test tournament, the scores fix an edge ranking while the training sample independently removes competitors. Cyclic triangles force enough inversions that surviving competitors produce constant population error at arbitrarily large sample sizes.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that local regularization does not characterize multiclass PAC learnability, by constructing a countable class with low DS dimension and efficient PAC sample complexity that no local regularizer can learn, using tournaments and cyclic triangles to force constant error.
AI.motivation: To determine whether local regularization, which assigns test-point-dependent scores to hypotheses and predicts with the minimum-score consistent hypothesis, characterizes multiclass PAC learnability—a question posed by Asilis et al.
AI.method: Constructs a counterexample: a countable class of hypotheses (edges of complete graphs) over instances (tournaments) with Daniely–Shalev-Shwartz dimension at most two and realizable PAC sample complexity O((1/ε) log(1/δ)). Shows that no local regularizer can learn this class because cyclic triangles force enough inversions in the edge ranking that surviving competitors produce constant population error at arbitrarily large sample sizes.
AI.result: Local regularization does not characterize multiclass PAC learnability; the constructed class is PAC learnable but not learnable by any local regularizer.
AI.conclusion: Local regularization is not a universal characterization of multiclass PAC learnability, refuting the conjecture raised by Asilis et al.

title: HiLLTS: Zero-Shot Hierarchical LLM-Guided Traffic Signal Control for Sustainable Transportation
summary: Urban traffic congestion significantly increases fuel consumption, greenhouse gas emissions, and commuter delays, resulting in substantial economic losses and environmental harm in modern cities. Traditional traffic signal control strategies such as fixed-time scheduling, actuated control, and reinforcement learning (RL)-based methods, offer different degrees of adaptability; however, RL-based methods can require extensive retraining, careful reward design, and substantial simulation data when transferred across networks or demand regimes. To address these challenges, we propose HiLLTS, an LLM-guided traffic signal control framework that employs a hierarchical three-layer architecture consisting of a central coordination agent, a district layer and multiple cluster-level intersection agents. Experimental results demonstrate consistent improvements in both congestion and environmental performance. Compared with the strongest non-LLM baseline in each scenario, HiLLTS reduces average waiting time by 36.73% under the low-congestion scenario and 14.71% under the high-congestion scenario, while reducing average CO2 emissions by 7.87% and 8.57%, respectively. Larger gains are observed against weaker baselines: under low congestion, HiLLTS achieves reductions of up to 18.00% in emissions and 62.07% in waiting time relative to Fixed-Time control; under high congestion, reductions of up to 28.89% in emissions and 40.36% in waiting time are observed relative to Max Pressure. The ablation study further validates the contribution of LLM-guided coordination over rule-based control

AI.tldr: HiLLTS is a hierarchical LLM-guided traffic signal control framework using a three-layer architecture (central coordinator, district layer, cluster-level intersection agents) that reduces average waiting time by 14.71-36.73% and CO2 emissions by 7.87-8.57% compared to non-LLM baselines, addressing retraining and transferability issues of RL-based methods.
AI.motivation: Traditional traffic signal control methods (fixed-time, actuated, RL-based) have limitations: RL methods require extensive retraining, careful reward design, and substantial simulation data when transferred across networks or demand regimes, motivating the need for a more adaptable and transferable approach.
AI.method: HiLLTS employs a hierarchical three-layer architecture consisting of a central coordination agent, a district layer, and multiple cluster-level intersection agents, guided by an LLM for adaptive traffic signal control.
AI.result: HiLLTS reduces average waiting time by 36.73% (low congestion) and 14.71% (high congestion) vs. strongest non-LLM baseline; reduces CO2 by 7.87% and 8.57% respectively. Larger gains vs. weaker baselines: up to 62.07% waiting time and 18.00% emissions reduction under low congestion, and up to 40.36% waiting time and 28.89% emissions under high congestion.
AI.conclusion: HiLLTS demonstrates consistent improvements in congestion and environmental performance across scenarios, with ablation studies validating the contribution of LLM-guided coordination over rule-based control.

title: MOJITO: Modal Joint Learning for Unified End-to-End Autonomous Driving
summary: End-to-end autonomous driving systems commonly follow a cascaded two-stage pipeline where a perception stage compresses multi-modal sensor inputs into a compact context and a downstream planner predicts trajectories conditioned on this context. We argue that this one-way perception-to-planning interface forces sensor inputs into a compact representation, losing the fine-grained details critical for planning. Moreover, by constraining the planner to this compressed context, it is difficult to leverage the rich representations offered by modern vision foundation models. To address these issues, we propose MOJITO, a unified sensor-to-action framework for end-to-end autonomous driving built on modal joint learning. MOJITO removes the cascaded interface and instead performs block-wise Modal Joint Attention that simultaneously updates action, image, and LiDAR features, allowing the planner to directly access multi-modal features during action generation. MOJITO achieves 88.9 PDMS on the NAVSIM v1 dataset and 88.4 EPDMS on the more challenging NAVSIM v2 dataset, setting a new state-of-the-art. Extensive experiments further demonstrate strong scalability, instruction following, and diverse trajectory generation. Code and models are available at https://github.com/mumucc01/MOJITO.

AI.tldr: MOJITO replaces the traditional cascaded perception-to-planning pipeline in autonomous driving with a unified sensor-to-action framework that uses block-wise Modal Joint Attention, allowing the planner to directly access rich multi-modal features. It achieves state-of-the-art performance with 88.9 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 88.4 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2.
AI.motivation: Current end-to-end autonomous driving systems use a cascaded two-stage pipeline where perception compresses multi-modal sensor data into a compact context for the planner, losing fine-grained details critical for planning and preventing the use of rich representations from vision foundation models.
AI.method: MOJITO removes the cascaded perception-to-planning interface and introduces block-wise Modal Joint Attention that simultaneously updates action, image, and LiDAR features, enabling the planner to directly access multi-modal features during action generation.
AI.result: 88.9 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 88.4 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 (new state-of-the-art), with strong scalability, instruction following, and diverse trajectory generation demonstrated in extensive experiments.
AI.conclusion: The unified sensor-to-action framework with modal joint learning effectively addresses information loss in cascaded pipelines and sets new state-of-the-art results for end-to-end autonomous driving.

title: Generalization bounds and sample complexity for remaining useful life prediction from complete degradation trajectories
comment: This manuscript has been accepted for publication in Measurement Science and Technology. The final Version of Record is available at https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6501/ae7109/meta
