summary: Data-driven remaining useful life (RUL) prediction requires complete degradation trajectories for training, yet such run-to-failure data are scarce and expensive. Practitioners currently lack principled guidance on how many failure examples suffice for a given model and accuracy target. This paper develops a sample complexity framework for RUL prediction comprising seven main results organised around three themes. First, we establish fundamental learning rates: a distribution-free generalization bound shows that the uniform deviation of the mean squared error decreases as $O(B^{2}\sqrt{p/n})$, where $p$ is the model complexity and $n$ the number of trajectories, and a minimax lower bound proves that the $Θ(p/n)$ rate is unimprovable.} \rev{Second, we quantify how domain knowledge accelerates learning: incorporating degradation physics reduces data requirements by up to two orders of magnitude for deep networks, a Bernstein-type analysis achieves the minimax-optimal $O(p/n)$ rate under high signal-to-noise conditions, and closed-form penalties reveal when an incorrectly assumed physics model hurts rather than helps. Third, we characterise the impact of data quality: fleet variability induces an irreducible bias$-$variance tradeoff, while right-censored observations suffer an efficiency loss that depends critically on the degradation class.} Closed-form expressions are provided for exponential, power-law, and stretched-exponential degradation. \rev{Cross-domain validation against published turbofan, battery, and bearing benchmarks confirms the theoretical predictions within a factor of 2$-$3 on average. The results yield practical guidelines for planning data collection, selecting model complexity, and evaluating physics model assumptions in prognostics applications.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a sample complexity framework for RUL prediction, establishing generalization bounds ($O(B^2\sqrt{p/n})$), minimax lower bounds ($\Theta(p/n)$), and showing that physics-informed domain knowledge reduces data needs by up to two orders of magnitude. It also characterizes the impact of fleet variability and right-censoring on prediction performance, validated across turbofan, battery, and bearing benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Practitioners lack principled guidance on how many failure trajectories are sufficient for a given RUL prediction model and accuracy target, as run-to-failure data are scarce and expensive.
AI.method: The paper derives distribution-free generalization bounds, minimax lower bounds, Bernstein-type analyses for physics-informed learning, and closed-form penalties for model misspecification, all organized around three themes: fundamental learning rates, domain knowledge acceleration, and data quality impact.
AI.result: Generalization error decays as $O(B^2\sqrt{p/n})$ with an unimprovable minimax rate of $\Theta(p/n)$; physics knowledge reduces data needs by up to 100x; fleet variability creates an irreducible bias-variance tradeoff; censoring efficiency loss depends on degradation class. Cross-domain validation confirms predictions within a factor of 2–3.
AI.conclusion: The framework yields practical guidelines for data collection planning, model complexity selection, and evaluation of physics model assumptions in prognostics.

title: Risk Governance for Generative AI Mental Health Support: A Multi-Turn Safety Architecture
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for emotional support despite lacking mechanisms to safely govern evolving mental health risk. Existing safety approaches primarily detect risk but rarely shape how models respond as conversational risk unfolds. We developed a model-agnostic safety governance architecture that combines contextual risk detection, reasoning-based verification, and protocol-guided response generation for multi-turn mental health interactions. Synthetic conversations grounded in real-world mental health narratives were used to evaluate the architecture's performance, tested with GPT-5-chat and Qwen3.5-27B, achieving high risk detection performance (specificity: 0.85 (95\%CI: 0.78;0.91), sensitivity: 0.92 (95\%CI: 0.88;0.95)) and increasing clinician-preferred escalation responses by 25.6--59.2pp while preserving rapport and connection. Performance remained stable across conversation length and generalized across both proprietary and open-source models. These findings demonstrate that clinically-grounded safety governance can extend beyond risk detection to improve how LLMs manage evolving mental health risk, providing a scalable framework for safer deployment across models.

AI.tldr: A model-agnostic safety governance architecture combining contextual risk detection, reasoning-based verification, and protocol-guided response generation was developed for LLMs in mental health interactions, achieving high risk detection (specificity 0.85, sensitivity 0.92) and increasing clinician-preferred escalation responses by 25.6–59.2 percentage points while maintaining rapport.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used for emotional support but lack mechanisms to safely govern evolving mental health risks. Existing safety approaches mainly detect risk but do not shape how models respond as conversational risk unfolds.
AI.method: Developed a model-agnostic safety governance architecture with three components: contextual risk detection, reasoning-based verification, and protocol-guided response generation. Evaluated using synthetic conversations grounded in real-world mental health narratives, tested with GPT-5-chat and Qwen3.5-27B.
AI.result: High risk detection performance (specificity: 0.85, sensitivity: 0.92), clinician-preferred escalation responses increased by 25.6–59.2 percentage points while preserving rapport. Performance stable across conversation length and generalized across proprietary and open-source models.
AI.conclusion: Clinically-grounded safety governance can extend beyond risk detection to improve how LLMs manage evolving mental health risk, providing a scalable framework for safer deployment across models.

title: Real-Time Human-Centric World Modeling for Upper-Body Human-Object Interaction
summary: We present a real-time human-centric world model for upper-body interactive generation, aiming to synthesize coherent local world dynamics centered on a person, where coordinated body, hand, and facial motions evolve jointly with controllable human-object discrete interaction. To this end, we adopt a continuous-discrete joint control scheme with two complementary components: a continuous human state and a discrete interaction state. For continuous human-state control, we introduce a unified implicit representation based on multi-scale motion encoding, in which motion latents from the upper body, hands, and face are fused into a shared latent space. This multi-scale design improves expressiveness across different spatial scales, captures fine-grained human dynamics more effectively, and enables direct control without explicit retargeting. For discrete object interaction-state control, we represent object contact using a small set of language-encoded discrete interaction states, where text serves as an explicit interaction-state command, such as \emph{no contact} or \emph{grasp}, rather than an open-ended generation prompt, and we further construct a dedicated rendering pipeline for human-object interaction data to supervise such discrete interaction states. By combining continuous implicit human-state control with discrete interaction-state control, our model enables precise modeling of how a person moves and interacts with the local environment, including controllable changes to nearby scene states. Finally, we distill the model for efficient streaming real-time inference, achieving 25 FPS on two H100 GPUs. Experiments demonstrate improved fine-grained motion fidelity, more realistic hand-object coordination, and effective real-time interaction, establishing a practical step beyond motion reproduction toward real-time human-centric world modeling.

AI.tldr: A real-time human-centric world model for upper-body interactive generation that combines continuous implicit human-state control (unified multi-scale motion encoding for body, hands, face) with discrete interaction-state control (language-encoded object contact states like "grasp") to synthesize coherent local world dynamics with controllable human-object interactions, achieving 25 FPS on two H100 GPUs.
AI.motivation: To move beyond motion reproduction toward real-time human-centric world modeling that can generate coordinated upper-body, hand, and facial motions jointly with controllable discrete human-object interactions in dynamic local environments.
AI.method: A continuous-discrete joint control scheme: (1) Continuous human-state control via unified implicit representation with multi-scale motion encoding fusing upper body, hand, and face motion latents; (2) Discrete interaction-state control using language-encoded discrete states (e.g., "no contact", "grasp") with a dedicated rendering pipeline for human-object interaction supervision; (3) Model distillation for streaming real-time inference.
AI.result: Achieves 25 FPS on two H100 GPUs; demonstrates improved fine-grained motion fidelity, more realistic hand-object coordination, and effective real-time interaction.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach establishes a practical step beyond motion reproduction toward real-time human-centric world modeling, enabling controllable generation of how a person moves and interacts with the local environment.

title: Extending Fourier Neural Operators for Modeling Parameterized and Coupled PDEs
summary: Parameterized and coupled partial differential equations (PDEs) are central to modeling phenomena in science and engineering, yet neural operator methods that address both aspects remain limited. We extend Fourier neural operators (FNOs) with minimal architectural modifications along two directions. For parameterized dynamics, we propose a hypernetwork-based modulation that conditions the operator on physical parameters. For coupled systems, we conduct a systematic exploration of architectural choices, examining how operator components can be adapted to balance shared structure with cross-variable interactions while retaining the efficiency of standard FNOs. Evaluations on benchmark PDEs, including the one-dimensional capacitively coupled plasma equations and the Gray-Scott system, show that our methods achieve up to 55-72% lower errors than strong baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of principled modulation and systematic design exploration.

AI.tldr: This paper extends Fourier neural operators (FNOs) to handle parameterized PDEs via hypernetwork-based modulation and coupled PDEs via systematic architectural exploration, achieving 55-72% error reduction on benchmark problems.
AI.motivation: Parameterized and coupled PDEs are fundamental in science and engineering, but existing neural operator methods have limited support for handling both aspects simultaneously.
AI.method: (1) A hypernetwork-based modulation that conditions FNOs on physical parameters for parameterized dynamics. (2) Systematic exploration of architectural choices to adapt operator components for coupled systems, balancing shared structure with cross-variable interactions while maintaining FNO efficiency.
AI.result: Achieves 55-72% lower errors than strong baselines on benchmarks including 1D capacitively coupled plasma equations and the Gray-Scott system.
AI.conclusion: Principled modulation and systematic design exploration are effective for extending FNOs to parameterized and coupled PDEs with minimal architectural changes.

title: Bayesian Repetition Penalty: A Principled Adjacent-Conditional Framework for Reversing Attention Collapse in Autoregressive Language Models
summary: Attention collapse in autoregressive language models -- manifested as repetitive token loops where the model becomes trapped in self-reinforcing attractors -- is a persistent pathology that existing decoding-time heuristics fail to address at its root cause. We present a principled framework that penalises or compensates anomalous confidence arising from collapsed generation patterns, by comparing a token's observed frequency against its corpus prior through an adjacent-conditional probability construction. The resulting self-normalising penalty ratio $R=f(m,n,p)/f(np,n,p)$ requires no ad hoc standardisation and admits a closed-form logit offset with zero approximation error. The correction is isolated from the loss gradient and accumulated into a frozen output-layer bias via exponential moving average, enabling deployment as a repair mechanism for models that have already collapsed without requiring intrusive modifications to standard training pipelines. Experimental validation on a 1.5B-parameter model demonstrates that the frozen-bias mechanism can rescue a model already trapped in a collapsed attractor, reducing 2-gram repetition from 0.073 to near 0 while preserving generation quality.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a principled framework to address attention collapse in autoregressive language models (manifested as repetitive token loops) by penalizing anomalous confidence via a self-normalizing penalty ratio based on adjacent-conditional probability. The correction is applied as a frozen output-layer bias via EMA, requiring no training modifications, and successfully rescues a collapsed 1.5B-parameter model, reducing 2-gram repetition from 0.073 to near 0 without quality loss.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive language models suffer from attention collapse, causing repetitive token loops that existing decoding-time heuristics cannot fundamentally address. A principled, root-cause solution is needed.
AI.method: A self-normalizing penalty ratio R = f(m,n,p)/f(np,n,p) is derived from adjacent-conditional probability, comparing observed token frequency against corpus prior. The correction is isolated from the loss gradient and accumulated as a frozen output-layer bias via exponential moving average, requiring no training pipeline modifications.
AI.result: On a 1.5B-parameter model, the frozen-bias mechanism reduced 2-gram repetition from 0.073 to near 0 while preserving generation quality.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework effectively rescues already-collapsed models without intrusive training modifications, offering a deployable repair mechanism for attention collapse in autoregressive LMs.

title: ATCNet-CIAM for Multi-Session Motor Imagery EEG Signal Classification
comment: This manuscript has been accepted for publication in the International Conference on Intelligence Systems and Robotics for Sustainable Development (ISRSD) 2026
summary: Motor imagery (MI)-based electroencephalography is widely used in non-invasive brain--computer interfaces (BCIs), but robust decoding remains challenging due to inter-subject variability and cross-session non-stationarity. This work proposes ATCNet-CIAM, an enhanced attention temporal convolutional network that integrates a lightweight channel-integrated attention module (CIAM) into the ATCNet framework to improve channel-spatial feature representation for MI decoding. The proposed model is evaluated on BCI Competition IV-2a, BCI Competition IV-2b, and the multi-day WBCIC-MI dataset under standard, within-session, and cross-session protocols. Experimental results show that ATCNet-CIAM achieves 86.32% accuracy on BCI IV-2a and 87.96% on BCI IV-2b under the standard protocol, while reaching 89.46% and 83.64% in the within-session WBCIC-MI on 2C and 3C, respectively. The proposed framework consistently improves classification stability and robustness under session-varying conditions, and ablation study confirms the complementary contribution of the proposed architectural components.

AI.tldr: This work proposes ATCNet-CIAM, an enhanced attention temporal convolutional network with a lightweight channel-integrated attention module (CIAM) for improved motor imagery EEG decoding, achieving 86.32% on BCI IV-2a and 87.96% on BCI IV-2b with robust cross-session performance.
AI.motivation: MI-based EEG decoding remains challenging due to inter-subject variability and cross-session non-stationarity, motivating the need for improved channel-spatial feature representation.
AI.method: Integrates a lightweight channel-integrated attention module (CIAM) into the ATCNet framework to enhance channel-spatial feature representation for MI decoding.
AI.result: 86.32% accuracy on BCI IV-2a, 87.96% on BCI IV-2b under standard protocol; 89.46% (2C) and 83.64% (3C) on within-session WBCIC-MI.
AI.conclusion: ATCNet-CIAM consistently improves classification stability and robustness under session-varying conditions; ablation study confirms complementary contributions of the architectural components.

title: Learning to Optimize: Joint Routing and Flow Allocation on Sparse Non-Euclidean Networks
summary: We study an integrated pickup-and-delivery problem on sparse, non-Euclidean networks that jointly optimizes cyclic routing, cargo flow allocation, and cross-cycle service. The tight coupling of these operational constraints creates a complex discrete-continuous decision space with highly restricted feasible regions. To overcome these computational challenges, we propose Double-Channel Graph Attention (DCGA), an end-to-end reinforcement learning framework. DCGA isolates network reachability and demand-service logic into separate graph channels and constructs valid routes using a simulator-coupled, constraint-informed decoder. Experiments on LinerLib benchmarks demonstrate that DCGA achieves seconds-level inference and delivers state-of-the-art solution quality on instances beyond a specific scale, with its advantage over existing baselines widening significantly as problem size increases. Supported by extensive stability and ablation analyses, our results demonstrate that this structure-aware learning approach provides an effective, low-latency engine for realistic routing-and-flow optimization.

AI.tldr: Proposes Double-Channel Graph Attention (DCGA), an end-to-end RL framework for joint optimization of cyclic routing, cargo flow allocation, and cross-cycle service on sparse, non-Euclidean networks, achieving state-of-the-art solution quality with seconds-level inference on large-scale instances.
AI.motivation: The tight coupling of cyclic routing, cargo flow allocation, and cross-cycle service creates a complex discrete-continuous decision space with highly restricted feasible regions, making traditional optimization computationally prohibitive.
AI.method: DCGA uses a dual-channel graph attention mechanism that separates network reachability and demand-service logic into distinct channels, coupled with a simulator-informed constraint-aware decoder to construct valid routes within an end-to-end RL framework.
AI.result: Achieves seconds-level inference and state-of-the-art solution quality on LinerLib benchmarks beyond a specific scale, with advantages widening as problem size increases; supported by stability and ablation analyses.
AI.conclusion: The structure-aware learning approach (DCGA) provides an effective, low-latency engine for realistic routing-and-flow optimization problems.

title: PANOPTICON: A PII-Based Assemblage of Naturalistic Output Tokens for Investigating Privacy Leakage Within LLM Context Window
comment: 9 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Submitted to IEEE CARS 2026
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are capable of generalizing human language for the completion of never-before-seen tasks, leading to widespread deployment. While this automation provides clear utility, completing these tasks often requires the insertion of Personally Identifiable Information (PII), strings of information that uniquely identify some individual, raising privacy concerns. However, ethics has prevented the curation of a public, authentic dataset of PII. Without an appropriate dataset, it is difficult to quantify privacy risks. Thus, we introduce the PANOPTICON pipeline and dataset. The dataset, generated by Meta's Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct model, contains 67, 718 prompts, intended for the models context window, containing PII spans derived from 9,674 publicly available synthetic user profiles. We measure lexical diversity and S-BERT diversity of the created dataset to evaluate realism. Finally, we present a case study showcasing the utility of PANOPTICON data for understanding Prompt Inversion Attacks (PIAs). PANOPTICON thus emerges as the first benchmark dataset for studying PIAs over private corpora, providing a foundation for future LLM privacy research.

AI.tldr: PANOPTICON is the first benchmark dataset of 67,718 prompts containing synthetic PII, generated by Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, designed to study Prompt Inversion Attacks and privacy risks in LLMs.
AI.motivation: Ethical constraints prevent curation of public authentic PII datasets, making it difficult to quantify privacy risks when LLMs insert PII during task completion.
AI.method: Used Meta's Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct to generate 67,718 prompts with PII spans from 9,674 synthetic user profiles, measured via lexical diversity and S-BERT diversity.
AI.result: Created a dataset with measurable lexical and semantic diversity, validated through realism metrics and a case study on Prompt Inversion Attacks.
AI.conclusion: PANOPTICON is the first benchmark dataset for studying PIAs over private corpora, establishing a foundation for future LLM privacy research.

title: Geometry Meets Semantics: Fractional Gradient Stabilization for Semantic-Driven Bounding Box Optimization in Visual Detection Tasks
summary: Bounding boxes are fundamental for object localization in visual detection tasks. Among them, oriented bounding boxes are widely used in visual detection tasks, which provide a more precise directional representation. Generally, IoU-based losses are widely adopted to optimize box regression. However, we observed that IoU-driven box optimization suffers from two key issues: (1) it relies solely on geometric properties while ignoring semantic cues; (2) orientation optimization suffers from unstable gradients, causing oscillations in orientation convergence. In this paper, we propose a Fractional Semantic IoU loss to achieve unified semantic-geometric learning with gradient stabilization. First, we design a semantic similarity metric to guide IoU optimization, building a Semantic IoU loss (SIoU loss) with an adaptive gradient gating mechanism. Then, we revisit the gradient instability issue in oriented box optimization and extend the SIoU loss to a fractional-order formulation to build the \textbf{Fr}actional \textbf{S}emantic \textbf{IoU} \textbf{loss} (FrSIoU loss). The FrSIoU loss accumulates historical IoU states to regularize abnormal gradients during bounding box optimization process. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach achieves stable performance gains across different bounding box formulations and diverse visual detection tasks. The code will be available on GitHub.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Fractional Semantic IoU (FrSIoU) loss that combines semantic similarity metrics with fractional-order gradient regularization to improve oriented bounding box regression in visual detection tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing IoU-based losses for oriented bounding box regression suffer from two issues: (1) relying solely on geometric properties while ignoring semantic cues, and (2) unstable gradients during orientation optimization causing oscillations in convergence.
AI.method: The method first designs a semantic similarity metric to guide IoU optimization, building a Semantic IoU (SIoU) loss with an adaptive gradient gating mechanism. Then it extends SIoU to a fractional-order formulation (FrSIoU loss) that accumulates historical IoU states to regularize abnormal gradients during box optimization.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate stable performance gains across different bounding box formulations and diverse visual detection tasks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed FrSIoU loss effectively unifies semantic-geometric learning with gradient stabilization, achieving consistent improvements over existing IoU-based losses for oriented object detection.

title: Sparse Gaussian-Mixture-Model Q-Functions via Hadamard Overparametrization for Online Reinforcement Learning
comment: This work has been submitted to the Elsevier for possible publication
summary: This paper develops an online, off-policy policy-iteration framework for reinforcement learning (RL), based on sparse Gaussian-mixture-model Q-functions (S-GMM-QFs). The framework reconciles streaming, non-stationary data with the Riemannian structure of the parameter space while handling distributional mismatch through experience replay. S-GMM-QFs are introduced via Hadamard overparametrization, enabling interpretable sparsification through smooth regularization that facilitates Riemannian-based optimization. Overparametrization allows the framework to adaptively identify meaningful components from a large initial pool, yielding sparse models where interpretability emerges naturally from geometry: each component's parameters (means and covariances) explicitly encode its geometric role in the ambient state-action space. These geometric roles are learned through online gradient descent on a smooth objective over a (Cartesian-product) Riemannian manifold. Numerical tests demonstrate that S-GMM-QFs match or exceed deep RL methods while using substantially fewer parameters and achieving faster improvement per observed transition. Notably, parameter efficiency and interpretability combine to maintain strong generalization in low-parameter regimes where sparsified deep RL approaches degrade.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an online, off-policy RL framework using sparse Gaussian-mixture-model Q-functions (S-GMM-QFs) with Hadamard overparametrization, Riemannian optimization, and experience replay. It achieves interpretable sparsification, matches/exceeds deep RL methods with fewer parameters, and maintains strong generalization where sparsified deep RL degrades.
AI.motivation: To develop an RL framework that reconciles streaming non-stationary data with Riemannian structure of the parameter space, while providing interpretability and parameter efficiency through sparse Gaussian mixture models, addressing limitations of black-box deep RL approaches.
AI.method: An online, off-policy policy-iteration framework using Sparse Gaussian-Mixture-Model Q-functions (S-GMM-QFs) with Hadamard overparametrization for interpretable sparsification via smooth regularization, Riemannian-based optimization on a Cartesian-product manifold, and experience replay to handle distributional mismatch.
AI.result: S-GMM-QFs match or exceed deep RL methods with substantially fewer parameters, achieve faster improvement per observed transition, and maintain strong generalization in low-parameter regimes where sparsified deep RL approaches degrade.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework successfully combines parameter efficiency, interpretability (via geometric roles of components), and strong generalization, offering a principled alternative to deep RL methods that is particularly effective in low-parameter regimes.

title: Test-Time Coverage: Test-Conditioned Data Curation for Deployment-Aware Learning
summary: Deployed AI systems are often trained from broad candidate data pools, necessitating data curation towards the deployment test distribution. However, standard data curation methods score training-side criteria rather than directly optimizing deployment match. We introduce TTCov (Test-Time Coverage), a data-level test-conditioned curation method that uses test-side information before training instead of updating model weights at inference. TTCov decomposes deployment-conditioned curation into coverage and distribution. To represent coverage, it builds a task Atlas, a collection of LLM-based atomic propositions (APs) describing deployment-relevant concepts, seeded from open task knowledge and expanded with unmatched APs extracted from unlabeled deployment samples. To represent distribution, it instantiates the matched deployment APs with their frequencies, yielding a Knowledge Atlas (K-Atlas) that operationalizes the deployment distribution as a curation target. TTCov then selects a budgeted training set whose deployment APs distribution approximates this target. We apply TTCov towards autonomous driving (AD), keeping adaptation off the inference path while selecting data with greater deployment-relevant coverage, closer K-Atlas matching, and stronger downstream end-to-end driving performance than data-curation baselines, including seamless adaptability to novel domains via city-to-city expansion.

AI.tldr: TTCov is a test-time data curation method that selects training data to match the deployment distribution by building a Knowledge Atlas of atomic propositions, without requiring model weight updates at inference. Applied to autonomous driving, it outperforms standard curation baselines in coverage, distribution matching, and driving performance.
AI.motivation: Deployed AI systems are trained from broad candidate data pools, but standard data curation methods score training-side criteria rather than directly optimizing deployment match.
AI.method: TTCov decomposes deployment-conditioned curation into coverage and distribution. It builds a task Atlas (collection of LLM-based atomic propositions describing deployment-relevant concepts), expands it with unmatched APs from unlabeled deployment samples, then creates a Knowledge Atlas by instantiating matched deployment APs with frequencies. It selects a budgeted training set whose deployment AP distribution approximates this target.
AI.result: In autonomous driving, TTCov selects data with greater deployment-relevant coverage, closer K-Atlas matching, and stronger downstream end-to-end driving performance than data-curation baselines. It shows seamless adaptability to novel domains via city-to-city expansion.
AI.conclusion: TTCov effectively uses test-side information before training to curate data that matches the deployment distribution, keeping adaptation off the inference path, and demonstrates strong performance in autonomous driving applications.

title: GaitFace: A Multimodal Dataset for Long-Range Person Identification
summary: Efficient border control is becoming a significant global challenge, mainly due to severe congestion and extended passenger waiting times. To mitigate these bottlenecks and facilitate passenger flow, biometric technologies are increasingly deployed to streamline identity verification and enhance crossing efficiency. Technical limitations frequently impede biometric identification, particularly in long-range surveillance, where systems must deal with adverse atmospheric conditions and degraded image quality. While high-quality frameworks like BRIAR exist, they are frequently restricted to specific government agencies. This paper introduces GaitFace, a new public dataset that contains face and gait data captured at long distances. To ensure that the research reflects authentic border scenarios, we use Pre-Enrollment data, where a traveler registers via a mobile device, and "In-the-Wild" captures, which records individuals at a distance across multiple viewing angles and different cameras. Benchmarking SOTA face and gait models reveals that current architectures fail under low-resolution and elevated viewpoints despite success with optical assistance. GaitFace exposes these critical vulnerabilities, providing a rigorous public benchmark to drive more robust, unconstrained biometric research.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces GaitFace, a new public dataset combining face and gait data captured at long distances using Pre-Enrollment and In-the-Wild recordings, to benchmark biometric models and expose their vulnerabilities under low-resolution and elevated viewpoints in real-world border scenarios.
AI.motivation: Border control faces severe congestion and long waiting times; biometric technologies are used to streamline identity verification but suffer from technical limitations in long-range surveillance (adverse atmospheric conditions, degraded image quality). Existing high-quality frameworks like BRIAR are restricted to specific government agencies, lacking public benchmarks for unconstrained biometric research.
AI.method: GaitFace dataset is constructed using two data types: Pre-Enrollment data (traveler registration via mobile device) and "In-the-Wild" captures (long-distance recordings across multiple viewing angles and cameras). SOTA face and gait models are benchmarked on this dataset.
AI.result: Current SOTA face and gait architectures fail under low-resolution and elevated viewpoint conditions, despite success with optical assistance. GaitFace exposes these critical vulnerabilities.
AI.conclusion: GaitFace provides a rigorous public benchmark that drives more robust, unconstrained biometric research for real-world border control scenarios.

title: A Multi-stage Constrained Optimization Framework for Data-driven Problems
summary: Variational autoencoders (VAEs) transform high-dimensional, often noisy data into a compact latent representation, making downstream optimization more tractable. Three challenges persist in VAE-based constrained optimization: (i) sampling effectively within the latent space, (ii) identifying the active decision variables that actually influence the objective and constraints, and (iii) enforcing constraints without destabilizing training. We propose a Multi-stage Constrained Optimization Framework (MCOF). First, an entropy-constrained VAE (EC-VAE) coupled with a feature selector embeds objective and constraint information into a designated subset of latent variables, so that optimization proceeds over a low-dimensional subspace while the remaining coordinates supply solution diversity. Second, a Uniform Transformation (UT) module applies a per-dimension probability integral transform, replacing the irregular aggregate posterior with a uniform distribution over a bounded box and mitigating posterior collapse and Gaussian mixture bias. Third, a constraint-priority filter method (CPFM) solves the resulting surrogate problem by alternating violation-reduction and objective-reduction steps under a filter acceptance test, returning solutions that are feasible for the learned surrogate to a specified tolerance without requiring multiplier estimation. Finally, unselected latent coordinates are resampled to generate diverse decodings of a single optimized solution. We validate MCOF on a synthetic problem, where we ablate each stage and recover the analytic optimum, and on a ZINC250k drug design task, where the generated molecules satisfy the imposed constraints and are entirely novel relative to the training set.

AI.tldr: MCOF is a multi-stage framework for VAE-based constrained optimization that combines an entropy-constrained VAE with feature selection (EC-VAE), a uniform transformation (UT) to regularize the latent space, and a constraint-priority filter method (CPFM) for surrogate optimization, validated on synthetic and drug design tasks.
AI.motivation: To address three key challenges in VAE-based constrained optimization: ineffective latent space sampling, difficulty identifying active decision variables, and unstable constraint enforcement during training.
AI.method: (1) EC-VAE with feature selector embeds objective/constraint information into a low-dimensional latent subspace; (2) UT module applies per-dimension probability integral transform to regularize the aggregate posterior into a uniform distribution; (3) CPFM alternates violation-reduction and objective-reduction steps under a filter acceptance test to find feasible solutions without multiplier estimation; (4) unselected latent coordinates are resampled for diverse decoding.
AI.result: On a synthetic problem, MCOF recovers the analytic optimum with all stages ablated. On ZINC250k drug design, generated molecules satisfy imposed constraints and are entirely novel relative to the training set.
AI.conclusion: MCOF effectively addresses VAE constrained optimization challenges by structured latent space partitioning, posterior regularization, and filter-based constraint handling, yielding feasible and novel solutions.

title: Similarity All The Way Up: Multilingual Generalization in LLMs Relies on Language-Level Similarity Structures
summary: As Large Language Models (LLMs) grow more capable across diverse tasks, their (in)ability to generalize remains difficult to quantify and poorly understood beyond limited domains. In particular, LLMs are known to struggle generalizing multilingually, to languages outside of English, and that are poorly attested in their training data. To understand why this may be, and what enables some models to perform better than others, we turn to a long history of work across the cognitive sciences, arguing that successful generalization derives from appropriate representations in similarity space. We look at how well LLMs' representations capture the hierarchical similarity structure between distinct languages. Strikingly, we show LLMs' latent representations largely recover the hierarchical structure of the Indo-European language family tree -- grouping languages that are members of the same subfamily closely together in representation space. Furthermore, we show that the degree to which models reflect the similarity structure of languages correlates with their performance on XNLI, a multilingual natural language inference benchmark. This extends classic work on similarity-driven generalization at scale, showing how models that represent similar languages similarly generalize better from one language to another.

AI.tldr: LLMs recover the hierarchical structure of the Indo-European language family tree in their representations, and the degree to which they reflect this similarity structure correlates with better multilingual generalization performance on XNLI.
AI.motivation: To understand why LLMs struggle with multilingual generalization, particularly to low-resource and non-English languages, and to identify what enables some models to generalize better than others.
AI.method: The authors draw on cognitive science theories of similarity-driven generalization to analyze LLMs' latent representations, examining whether these representations recover the hierarchical similarity structure of the Indo-European language family tree, and correlating this with XNLI benchmark performance.
AI.result: LLMs' latent representations largely recover the hierarchical structure of the Indo-European language family tree, with languages from the same subfamily clustered closely together. The degree of this structural recovery correlates with performance on the XNLI benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Models that represent similar languages similarly generalize better across languages, extending classic similarity-driven generalization principles to LLMs at scale.

title: D3O: Dynamic Distribution Distillation for Ordinal Regression
summary: Ordinal regression is widely used in scenarios where labels are discrete yet inherently ordered. In practice, however, ordinal labels are often obtained by discretizing underlying continuous semantics through subjective human judgment, resulting in ambiguous boundaries and annotation noise. Such uncertainty challenges existing methods that rely on fixed supervision targets, which may reinforce biased ordering under subjective annotations. To address this limitation, we propose D3O, a dynamic distribution distillation framework that replaces static supervision with training-driven evolution of ordinal label distributions via self-distillation. Specifically, we introduce a contrastive ordinal-aware label enhancement module that leverages vision-language alignment to recover refined label distributions capturing both inter-class ambiguity and instance-level uncertainty. Furthermore, we design a CDF-based cross-layer interaction distillation mechanism to propagate cumulative ordinal structure across network hierarchy, ensuring consistent ordinal geometry in intermediate representations. Extensive experiments on four general ordinal regression tasks demonstrate that our proposed D3O consistently outperforms existing approaches, particularly under severe class imbalance and noisy supervision. These results highlight the effectiveness of dynamic supervision in learning robust ordinal representations beyond fixed targets. The code will be publicly available.

AI.tldr: D3O is a dynamic distribution distillation framework for ordinal regression that replaces static supervision with self-distillation-driven evolution of ordinal label distributions, incorporating contrastive ordinal-aware label enhancement via vision-language alignment and CDF-based cross-layer interaction distillation, consistently outperforming existing methods on four general ordinal regression tasks.
AI.motivation: Ordinal labels obtained by discretizing continuous semantics through subjective human judgment suffer from ambiguous boundaries and annotation noise, which existing static supervision methods fail to handle as they may reinforce biased ordering under subjective annotations.
AI.method: (1) A dynamic distribution distillation (D3O) framework that replaces static supervision with training-driven evolution of ordinal label distributions via self-distillation. (2) A contrastive ordinal-aware label enhancement module leveraging vision-language alignment to recover refined label distributions capturing inter-class ambiguity and instance-level uncertainty. (3) A CDF-based cross-layer interaction distillation mechanism to propagate cumulative ordinal structure across network hierarchy for consistent ordinal geometry in intermediate representations.
AI.result: Consistently outperforms existing approaches on four general ordinal regression tasks, particularly under severe class imbalance and noisy supervision.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic supervision is effective for learning robust ordinal representations beyond fixed targets, and D3O demonstrates strong performance in handling ambiguous boundaries and annotation noise in ordinal regression.

title: Charging Phase Health Indicators for Battery State-of-Health Estimation: A Systematic Comparison of CC, CV, and Combined Approaches under Cross-Battery Validation
comment: This paper has been published in Eksploatacja i Niezawodnosc. Please cite the published version
summary: Accurate State-of-Health estimation is essential for safe battery operation and cost-effective maintenance. Although numerous health indicators have been derived from constant-current (CC) and constant-voltage (CV) charging phases, their effectiveness under realistic cross-battery validation remains insufficiently studied. This work addresses this gap through a systematic comparison of CC-only, CV-only, and combined indicator sets using rigorous Leave-One-Battery-Out (LOBO) validation on the NASA battery aging dataset. Four CV-phase indicators and CC phase duration are evaluated individually and in combination. Results show that the combined CC+CV approach achieves the best performance (R2 = 0.874), confirming that CC and CV phases capture complementary degradation information. Moreover, a 119% performance gap is observed between standard 5-fold cross-validation and LOBO validation, indicating that conventional evaluation overestimates practical accuracy. Based on these findings, practical guidelines are provided for indicator selection under data and computational constraints.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically compares CC-only, CV-only, and combined CC+CV health indicators for battery State-of-Health estimation using Leave-One-Battery-Out (LOBO) validation. The combined approach achieves best performance (R²=0.874), revealing complementary degradation information. A 119% performance gap exists between standard 5-fold cross-validation and LOBO, showing conventional methods overestimate real-world accuracy.
AI.motivation: Despite many health indicators derived from CC and CV charging phases, their effectiveness under realistic cross-battery validation (LOBO) remains insufficiently studied, leading to potential overestimation of practical performance.
AI.method: Systematic comparison of CC-only, CV-only, and combined indicator sets using Leave-One-Battery-Out (LOBO) validation on NASA battery aging dataset. Four CV-phase indicators and CC phase duration are evaluated individually and in combination.
AI.result: Combined CC+CV approach achieves best performance (R²=0.874). A 119% performance gap exists between standard 5-fold cross-validation and LOBO validation.
AI.conclusion: CC and CV phases capture complementary degradation information; conventional cross-validation significantly overestimates practical accuracy; practical guidelines for indicator selection under data/computational constraints are provided.

title: RoleMix: Unifying Sequential and Non-Sequential Features via Semantic Tokenization for Post-Click Conversion Rate Prediction
summary: Post-click conversion rate (PCVR) prediction is central to industrial recommendation, but remains challenged by the structural mismatch between sparse, unordered multi-field features and long, domain-specific behavior histories. Existing models often process these signals through separate pathways and fuse them late, weakening semantic roles and limiting cross-signal refinement. We propose RoleMix, a unified interaction architecture that represents sequential and non-sequential evidence through a shared, role-preserving token interface. Non-sequential fields are converted into explicit semantic tokens that preserve user, item, pairwise, dense, contextual, and cross-feature roles, while long behavior domains are compressed into item- and context-aware sequence-query tokens through two-stage hierarchical window attention. The resulting global, semantic, and sequence-query tokens are jointly refined by stacked UniMixing-Lite blocks for PCVR prediction. On the large-scale KDD Cup 2026 Tencent UniRec Challenge, RoleMix achieves 83.648% online AUC, outperforming the official industrial baseline by 1.953%. Ablation studies show that semantic tokenization yields the largest isolated gain, highlighting a key principle for large-scale PCVR modeling: preserving field semantics at the token-interface level is as important as scaling the interaction backbone.

AI.tldr: RoleMix unifies sparse multi-field features and long behavioral histories into a shared token interface with role-preserving semantics, achieving 83.648% AUC on the KDD Cup 2026 Tencent UniRec Challenge, outperforming the industrial baseline by 1.953%.
AI.motivation: Post-click conversion rate (PCVR) prediction suffers from a structural mismatch between sparse, unordered multi-field features and long, domain-specific behavioral histories. Existing models process these signals through separate pathways and fuse them late, weakening semantic roles and limiting cross-signal refinement.
AI.method: RoleMix converts non-sequential fields into explicit semantic tokens preserving user, item, pairwise, dense, contextual, and cross-feature roles, and compresses long behavior domains into item- and context-aware sequence-query tokens via two-stage hierarchical window attention. All tokens are jointly refined by stacked UniMixing-Lite blocks.
AI.result: Achieved 83.648% online AUC on the KDD Cup 2026 Tencent UniRec Challenge, outperforming the official industrial baseline by 1.953%. Ablation studies show semantic tokenization yields the largest isolated gain.
AI.conclusion: Preserving field semantics at the token-interface level is as important as scaling the interaction backbone for large-scale PCVR modeling.

title: Neuromorphic Object Detection: An In-Depth Study and Future Directions
comment: Accepted by Proceedings of the IEEE
summary: Conventional frame-based cameras face significant challenges in detecting objects under high-speed motion blur or in low-light environments. Neuromorphic cameras provide asynchronous visual streams with high temporal resolution and a wide dynamic range, offering a promising solution for object detection under challenging conditions. Despite the development of numerous models and the emergence of various applications in neuromorphic object detection, there is still a lack of deep understanding and standardized benchmarks to assess progress and address key challenges. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive survey and benchmark of existing neuromorphic object detection algorithms. Specifically, we first present a problem description, review the available datasets, and revisit the evaluation metrics. We then explore existing neuromorphic object detection approaches from various perspectives, including event representation, temporal modeling, multimodal fusion, asynchronous processing, low-latency processing, and energy-efficient computing. Furthermore, we evaluate a wide range of representative neuromorphic object detection models and offer detailed analyses of the comparative results. Finally, we discuss unresolved issues in neuromorphic object detection and propose potential future research directions. We hope this survey and benchmark will be a valuable resource for researchers and provide guidance for future advancements in neuromorphic object detection.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a comprehensive survey and benchmark of neuromorphic object detection algorithms, covering event representation, temporal modeling, multimodal fusion, asynchronous/low-latency/energy-efficient processing, with evaluations of representative models and discussions of future directions.
AI.motivation: Despite the promise of neuromorphic cameras for object detection under challenging conditions (high-speed motion blur, low-light), there is a lack of deep understanding and standardized benchmarks to assess progress and address key challenges in this field.
AI.method: The paper conducts a comprehensive survey and benchmark: (1) presents problem description, reviews datasets, and revisits evaluation metrics; (2) explores existing approaches from perspectives of event representation, temporal modeling, multimodal fusion, asynchronous processing, low-latency processing, and energy-efficient computing; (3) evaluates representative models with detailed comparative analysis.
AI.result: A wide range of representative neuromorphic object detection models are evaluated with detailed analyses of comparative results, establishing a standardized benchmark for the field.
AI.conclusion: The survey identifies unresolved issues in neuromorphic object detection and proposes potential future research directions, serving as a valuable resource for researchers in the field.

title: An adaptive multi-fuzzy logic model for diagnosing transformer faults using dynamic weight optimization
comment: This paper has been published in e-Prime - Advances in Electrical Engineering, Electronics and Energy. Please cite the published version
summary: Dissolved gas analysis (DGA) is crucial for diagnosing early power transformer failures. Traditional DGA interpretation methods like Duval Triangle, IEC ratio, Roger ratio, Doernenburg ratio and Key Gas are inconsistent and vary in accuracy, especially for multiple fault conditions. We propose an Adaptive Multi-Fuzzy Logic (AMFL) model integrating multiple DGA methods with fuzzy logic and a dynamic weight adjustment mechanism. Unlike existing approaches with fixed weights, this system iteratively evaluates each method's diagnostic performance, identifies multiple fault types, and adjusts weights based on fault prediction accuracy. A feedback-based optimization recalibrates weights after each cycle to ensure optimal solution convergence. The model, implemented in MATLAB/Simulink, is validated against DGA datasets with known error conditions. Results show the AMFL model significantly improves diagnostic accuracy, especially in complex error scenarios, and enhances adaptability to new datasets. Comparative analysis demonstrates the proposed method outperforms traditional fixed weight multi-fuzzy systems in accuracy, consistency, and reliability of error detection. This work provides a robust, flexible diagnostic tool for transformer condition monitoring and supports more accurate asset management decisions.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an Adaptive Multi-Fuzzy Logic (AMFL) model that integrates multiple DGA interpretation methods with fuzzy logic and a dynamic weight adjustment mechanism, outperforming traditional fixed-weight multi-fuzzy systems in diagnostic accuracy, consistency, and reliability for transformer fault detection.
AI.motivation: Traditional DGA interpretation methods (Duval Triangle, IEC ratio, Roger ratio, Doernenburg ratio, Key Gas) are inconsistent and vary in accuracy, particularly for multiple fault conditions, necessitating a more robust diagnostic approach.
AI.method: An Adaptive Multi-Fuzzy Logic (AMFL) model integrating multiple DGA methods with fuzzy logic and a dynamic weight adjustment mechanism, featuring feedback-based optimization that iteratively evaluates diagnostic performance and recalibrates weights after each cycle to ensure convergence.
AI.result: The AMFL model significantly improves diagnostic accuracy, especially in complex error scenarios, and enhances adaptability to new datasets. It outperforms traditional fixed-weight multi-fuzzy systems in accuracy, consistency, and reliability of error detection.
AI.conclusion: The proposed AMFL model provides a robust, flexible diagnostic tool for transformer condition monitoring, supporting more accurate asset management decisions through adaptive weight adjustments and feedback-based optimization.

title: MPR-CiteG: Enhancing RAG with Multi-Portfolio Retrieval and Citation-Grounded Generation
comment: 12 pages, 1 figure, 7 tables. The 1st International Workshop on Retrieval-Driven Generative AI & ScienceON AI Challenge 2025@CIKM
summary: This paper presents the MPR-CiteG framework, which achieved second place in the ScienceON AI Challenge by addressing two fundamental challenges in generative AI: inefficient retrieval and the absence of source verification. We propose a dual-component system, termed MPR-CiteG, in which the Multi-Portfolio Retriever (MPR) efficiently retrieves diverse and relevant information, while the Citation-Grounded Generation (CiteG) module ensures that every generated output remains factually consistent and explicitly attributed to its source. MPR-CiteG represents a significant step toward building more trustworthy and accurate LLMs that are not only capable of generating information but also of grounding their responses in reliable evidence, thereby mitigating common issues like model hallucination. Extensive experiments on the challenge dataset validate the effectiveness and reliability of our approach. Our code is available at https://github.com/2noweyh/MPR-citeG.

AI.tldr: MPR-CiteG is a dual-component system (Multi-Portfolio Retriever + Citation-Grounded Generation) that placed second in the ScienceON AI Challenge, addressing inefficient retrieval and lack of source verification in generative AI by ensuring factual consistency and explicit source attribution.
AI.motivation: To address two fundamental challenges in generative AI: inefficient retrieval of diverse and relevant information, and the absence of source verification leading to model hallucination.
AI.method: A dual-component system: (1) Multi-Portfolio Retriever (MPR) for efficient retrieval of diverse and relevant information, and (2) Citation-Grounded Generation (CiteG) module that ensures factual consistency and explicit source attribution for every generated output.
AI.result: Achieved second place in the ScienceON AI Challenge; extensive experiments on the challenge dataset validated the effectiveness and reliability of the approach.
AI.conclusion: MPR-CiteG represents a significant step toward building more trustworthy and accurate LLMs that ground responses in reliable evidence, mitigating issues like model hallucination.

title: SketchMamba: A Lightweight State-Space Model for Joint Progressive Sketch Classification and Stroke Auto-Completion
summary: Existing vector-sketch models treat recognition and generation as separate tasks, leaving a gap for streaming interfaces that must understand a drawing as it is being made. We present SketchMamba, a single causal sequence model that continuously classifies a sketch from any partial prefix while simultaneously generating its continuation. We achieve this by applying a dense per-step classification loss to a selective state-space backbone. Evaluated on a 58-class subset of the Quick, Draw! dataset, SketchMamba yields 94.93% final-step accuracy and a progressive-accuracy Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.706, crossing 90% of its final accuracy by the time 70% of the strokes are drawn. In a matched-budget comparison, the 1.55 million-parameter backbone ties a causal Transformer while outperforming recurrent and convolutional baselines. Ablations confirm that the dense supervision regime, rather than the architecture alone, drives the early-prediction capability. The results demonstrate that a single causal hidden state can unify progressive recognition and autoregressive generation without auxiliary encoders or task-specific branching.

AI.tldr: SketchMamba is a single causal sequence model that unifies progressive sketch recognition and autoregressive generation using a selective state-space backbone with dense per-step classification loss, achieving 94.93% accuracy and early prediction capabilities on a Quick, Draw! subset.
AI.motivation: Existing vector-sketch models treat recognition and generation as separate tasks, leaving a gap for streaming interfaces that must understand a drawing as it is being made.
AI.method: A single causal sequence model (SketchMamba) using a selective state-space backbone, trained with dense per-step classification loss to simultaneously classify partial sketch prefixes and generate continuations.
AI.result: 94.93% final-step accuracy, progressive-accuracy AUC of 0.706, crosses 90% accuracy by 70% strokes drawn; 1.55M parameters ties causal Transformer, outperforms RNN/CNN baselines.
AI.conclusion: A single causal hidden state can unify progressive recognition and autoregressive generation without auxiliary encoders or task-specific branching.

title: Learning Sampling Parameters for Diffusion Models
summary: Text-to-image diffusion models expose many inference-time sampling parameters, including prompts, negative prompts, classifier-free guidance scales, and noise schedules. These parameters are typically manually chosen once and then held fixed across prompts and denoising timesteps, even though different prompts and stages of generation can benefit from different parameter values. We introduce LeSAMP, a framework for learning prompt-conditioned, timestep-varying sampling parameters. We formulate parameter selection as a reinforcement learning problem: Given a user prompt, a large language model is trained to emit schedules for the chosen sampling parameters. We optimize our model using rewards from human preference models and VLM-as-a-judge. We evaluate our model on Flux.1 [dev] and Stable Diffusion 3.5, and find that compared to baselines, LeSAMP has a win rate of up to 68.12% using human preference scores and 73.37% using VLM-as-a-judge. These gains are validated in a user study where we achieve win rates of up to 59.46% over previous baselines. Our results suggest that learned sampling-parameter policies provide a complementary approach to existing post-training methods for improving diffusion model outputs.

AI.tldr: LeSAMP learns prompt-conditioned, timestep-varying sampling parameters (e.g., guidance scale, noise schedule) for text-to-image diffusion models using reinforcement learning with human preference and VLM-based rewards, achieving up to 68-73% win rates over fixed-parameter baselines.
AI.motivation: Current diffusion models use fixed sampling parameters across all prompts and timesteps, even though different prompts and generation stages benefit from different parameter values. This paper aims to learn adaptive, prompt-conditioned, timestep-varying parameter schedules.
AI.method: Formulates parameter selection as an RL problem: a large language model is trained to emit schedules for sampling parameters (prompts, negative prompts, CFG scales, noise schedules) conditioned on a user prompt. The model is optimized using rewards from human preference models and VLM-as-a-judge.
AI.result: On Flux.1 [dev] and SD 3.5, LeSAMP achieves up to 68.12% win rate via human preference scores and 73.37% via VLM-as-a-judge. A user study confirms a 59.46% win rate over previous baselines.
AI.conclusion: Learned sampling-parameter policies offer a complementary approach to existing post-training methods for improving diffusion model outputs.

title: SEGRA: Structured Experience-Guided Graph Reasoning Agent for Gremlin Based Question Answering
summary: Enterprise IT support knowledge graphs capture rich relationships among cases, users, devices, symptoms, taxonomic categories, root causes, and historical resolutions. Yet querying them in Gremlin requires knowledge of graph schemas, traversal semantics, edge directionality, and property-graph-specific constraints, making them difficult for non-expert operators to use. We introduce SEGRA, an experience-guided agent for enterprise text-to-Gremlin question answering. SEGRA integrates intent routing, schema- and taxonomy-grounded query generation, multi-shot decomposition, execution-aware verification, and a curriculum-bootstrapped skill library that reuses verified query patterns. On an enterprise IT support benchmark, SEGRA achieves a $7.0\times$ higher mean judge score than backbone-only chain-of-thought prompting. Its skill library further reduces LLM calls by $20\%$ and dollar cost by $18\%$ relative to SEGRA without skills, while preserving answer quality. These results show that schema-grounded agent design and reusable execution experience improve both accuracy and efficiency for enterprise graph QA.

AI.tldr: SEGRA is an experience-guided agent for enterprise text-to-Gremlin QA that integrates intent routing, schema-grounded query generation, multi-shot decomposition, execution-aware verification, and a curriculum-bootstrapped skill library. It achieves 7.0× higher mean judge score than chain-of-thought prompting and reduces LLM calls by 20% and cost by 18% while maintaining answer quality.
AI.motivation: Enterprise IT support knowledge graphs are difficult for non-expert operators to query using Gremlin due to complex graph schemas, traversal semantics, edge directionality, and property-graph constraints.
AI.method: SEGRA combines intent routing, schema- and taxonomy-grounded query generation, multi-shot decomposition, execution-aware verification, and a curriculum-bootstrapped skill library that reuses verified query patterns.
AI.result: SEGRA achieves a 7.0× higher mean judge score than backbone-only chain-of-thought prompting on an enterprise IT support benchmark. The skill library reduces LLM calls by 20% and dollar cost by 18% relative to SEGRA without skills, with preserved answer quality.
AI.conclusion: Schema-grounded agent design and reusable execution experience improve both accuracy and efficiency for enterprise graph QA.

title: JarvisHub: An Open Harness for Canvas-Native Multimodal Creative Agents
comment: 15 pages, 9 figures. Project page: https://www.jarvishub.site/ Code github: https://github.com/LYL1015/JarvisHub
summary: Creative AI is moving from single-step asset generation toward long-horizon multimodal production. Although recent generative models can synthesize high-quality images, videos, audio clips, UI elements, storyboards, slides, and other creative assets, real-world creative work requires more than isolated prompt-output interactions. It involves references, drafts, alternatives, edits, failed attempts, version relations, tool actions, evaluation signals, and human feedback, which together form an evolving project state. Existing prompt-based, chat-based, and node-based generation systems only partially support this state, as they often discard intermediate context, rely on linear conversations, or require manually specified workflows. Recent commercial systems indicate a shift toward agent-assisted creative production, but their closed architectures make it difficult to study how agents represent context, choose tools, revise artifacts, recover from failures, and maintain consistency over time. To address this gap, we introduce JarvisHub, a canvas-native creative agent harness for long-horizon multimodal creation. JarvisHub treats an editable canvas as the user workspace, the agent's external memory, action space, and shared project state, representing multimodal artifacts, dependencies, versions, and feedback as typed canvas nodes and links. Through a three-layer architecture of canvas state, protocol bridge, and agent runtime, JarvisHub enables agents to act within an inspectable and editable creative state. This design moves creative agents beyond isolated tool use toward sustained, human-steerable creative automation, where agents can progressively plan, generate, revise, and organize multimodal projects while users remain able to inspect, guide, and intervene throughout the process.

AI.tldr: JarvisHub is a canvas-native creative agent system that enables long-horizon multimodal production by treating an editable canvas as the workspace, external memory, action space, and shared project state, supporting sustained human-steerable creative automation beyond single-step generation.
AI.motivation: Existing generative AI systems (prompt-based, chat-based, node-based) only partially support the evolving, stateful nature of real-world creative work, which involves references, drafts, edits, versions, feedback, and failures. Current commercial agent-assisted systems are closed, making it difficult to study how agents represent context, choose tools, revise artifacts, and maintain consistency.
AI.method: JarvisHub employs a three-layer architecture: (1) canvas state layer representing multimodal artifacts, dependencies, versions, and feedback as typed nodes and links; (2) protocol bridge layer; and (3) agent runtime layer. The canvas serves as user workspace, agent's external memory, action space, and shared project state.
AI.result: The system enables agents to progressively plan, generate, revise, and organize multimodal projects within an inspectable and editable creative state, allowing users to inspect, guide, and intervene throughout the process.
AI.conclusion: JarvisHub moves creative agents beyond isolated tool use toward sustained, human-steerable creative automation, addressing the gap in studying how agents represent context and maintain consistency over long-horizon multimodal creation.

title: Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Discovering Periodic Orbits in the Gravitational Three-Body Problem
summary: Locating periodic solutions of chaotic dynamical systems normally requires an initial guess close enough to the target orbit for numerical continuation or gradient-based search to converge. We show that Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) trained on sparse, noisy observations \emph{without} initial conditions recover periodic orbits of the gravitational three-body problem, including orbit families absent from the training data. The method rests on a second-order ODE formulation, fixed-frequency Fourier features, percentile-based adaptive refinement, and a trainable scaling parameter, each validated on forward problems. Across two 100-seed ensembles, $23$--$25\%$ of runs converge to families not present in the training data. We then ask what determines which family emerges. Two $χ^2$ tests give a consistent answer: changing the training data source significantly shifts the distribution of recovered families ($p < 0.001$, Cramér's $V = 0.339$), whereas switching between the two initialization distributions tested does not ($p = 0.620$, $V = 0.094$). The random seed selects which family a given run recovers; the \emph{distribution} the weights are drawn from does not shift the aggregate frequencies, but the training data does. The evidence is empirical: we do not characterize the loss landscape analytically, and PINNs remain slower than conventional integrators on well-posed initial-value problems. What the experiments establish is that the recovered orbits are verifiable rather than merely plausible: the identified ones refine to genuine periodic solutions, a network trained on Lagrange data recovers the figure-eight choreography (Li--Liao class I.A.1, matched to seven significant digits in $T^*$), and one trained on figure-eight data recovers a Broucke--Hadjidemetriou--Hénon orbit closing to $δ_T < 10^{-9}$.

AI.tldr: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) trained on sparse, noisy observations without initial conditions can recover periodic orbits of the gravitational three-body problem, including orbit families absent from training data. The method uses second-order ODE formulation, fixed-frequency Fourier features, percentile-based adaptive refinement, and a trainable scaling parameter. Across ensembles, 23-25% of runs converge to families not in training data. The training data source significantly shifts recovered family distributions (p<0.001), while weight initialization distribution does not (p=0.620). Recovered orbits are verifiable: e.g., network trained on Lagrange data recovers figure-eight choreography to seven significant digits.
AI.motivation: Locating periodic solutions of chaotic dynamical systems normally requires initial guesses close to target orbits for convergence. The authors aim to remove this requirement by using PINNs trained on sparse, noisy observations without initial conditions.
AI.method: PINNs with second-order ODE formulation, fixed-frequency Fourier features, percentile-based adaptive refinement, and a trainable scaling parameter. Two 100-seed ensembles with χ² tests to determine factors affecting which orbit family emerges.
AI.result: 23-25% of runs converge to families not in training data. Training data source significantly shifts distribution (p<0.001, V=0.339), initialization distribution does not (p=0.620, V=0.094). Recovered orbits refine to genuine solutions with high precision.
AI.conclusion: PINNs can discover verifiable periodic orbits of the three-body problem without initial conditions. The recovered families are determined by training data rather than weight initialization. While slower than conventional integrators for well-posed problems, the method enables discovery of orbits not present in training data.

title: Spatial Reasoning in LLM Game Agents: Impact of Causal Context and Multi-Step Planning
summary: LLM-based game agents often perform poorly on more complex tasks. This work examines whether these failures are linked to limited spatial reasoning and evaluates whether causal prompt augmentation and multi-step planning can improve win-rates while managing response latency. Using the open-source Qwen3 model family, we conduct experiments across varying model scales, reasoning modes, and planning horizons. We further introduce a focused GVGAI benchmark consisting of three custom games with five difficulty levels to isolate spatial navigation. The evaluation follows two paradigms: an initial ``positioning experiment'' to test an agent's ability to find its exact coordinates, and a study of game-play success. Our results show that while larger models with an enabled thinking mode identify their positions more accurately, overall performance in coordinate matching remains limited for smaller models. Win rates decrease as game levels and layout complexity increase, validating the benchmark's difficulty scaling. Integrating causal context into the prompts tends to improve the agents' success rates, particularly for bigger models. While enabling thinking mode and longer planning horizons significantly improve performance, multi-step planning further reduces mean per-step response times, offering a practical trade-off between reasoning depth and execution speed.

AI.tldr: This study investigates spatial reasoning limitations in LLM-based game agents using Qwen3 models, introduces a GVGAI benchmark with three custom games and five difficulty levels, and finds that causal prompt augmentation, thinking mode, and multi-step planning improve win rates while managing response latency, though smaller models struggle with coordinate matching.
AI.motivation: To examine whether poor performance of LLM-based game agents on complex tasks is linked to limited spatial reasoning, and to evaluate whether causal prompt augmentation and multi-step planning can improve win-rates while managing response latency.
AI.method: Using the Qwen3 model family across varying scales, reasoning modes, and planning horizons, with a focused GVGAI benchmark of three custom games at five difficulty levels. Evaluated via a positioning experiment (coordinate matching) and a game-play success study.
AI.result: Larger models with thinking mode identify positions more accurately, but smaller models struggle with coordinate matching. Win rates decrease with increasing level/layout complexity. Causal prompt augmentation improves success rates, especially for larger models. Thinking mode and longer planning horizons improve performance; multi-step planning reduces mean per-step response times.
AI.conclusion: Causal context augmentation and multi-step planning offer practical trade-offs between reasoning depth and execution speed for LLM-based game agents, though spatial reasoning remains a bottleneck for smaller models.

title: Weakly Supervised Instance-Level Gleason Pattern Estimation Using Primary and Secondary Labels
summary: In prostate cancer histopathology, the Gleason Score is determined by the most frequent (Primary) and second most frequent (Secondary) Gleason patterns within a whole-slide image. Although these slide-level labels are routinely available in clinical practice, instance-level Gleason annotations are rarely provided, making patch-level learning challenging. We propose a Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) framework that estimates instance-level Gleason patterns from slide-level Primary and Secondary labels. The proposed method formulates instance-level learning according to the clinical definition of the Gleason Score by aggregating instance predictions into class counts and explicitly modeling the Primary pattern, Secondary pattern, and their dominance. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed formulation enables effective instance-level learning and outperforms existing MIL approaches on the SICAP-MIL dataset.

AI.tldr: A MIL framework that estimates instance-level Gleason patterns from slide-level Primary and Secondary labels by modeling class counts and pattern dominance, outperforming existing methods on the SICAP-MIL dataset.
AI.motivation: To enable patch-level learning for Gleason scoring in prostate cancer histopathology when only slide-level Primary and Secondary pattern labels are available, not instance-level annotations.
AI.method: A Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) framework that aggregates instance predictions into class counts and explicitly models the Primary pattern, Secondary pattern, and their dominance using the clinical definition of Gleason Score.
AI.result: The proposed method enables effective instance-level learning and outperforms existing MIL approaches on the SICAP-MIL dataset.
AI.conclusion: Formulating instance-level learning according to clinical Gleason Score definition with class count aggregation and dominance modeling is effective for MIL-based Gleason pattern estimation.

title: Impute On-Demand: Adaptive Correlated Time Series Imputation for Changing Environments
comment: 15 pages, 9 figures. Accepted for publication in IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering (IEEE TKDE)
summary: Internet of Things (IoT) applications generate vast amounts of Correlated Time Series (CTS) data that often contain missing values and require imputation. Existing methods emphasize accuracy but often lack adaptability to changing IoT environments: they are vulnerable to sensor failures, cannot selectively impute only incomplete sensors, and use static architectures that do not adapt to resource availability. To address these limitations, we propose AdaCTSi, an adaptive CTS imputer for changing environments. AdaCTSi combines a One-shot Temporal Convolutional Network with a Learned Time-Sensor Index Table to extract and decouple complex spatio-temporal features into sensor-wise embeddings, enabling adaptation to varying sensor subsets. Sparse Spatial Attention efficiently extracts dynamic spatial correlations, while Correlation-Weighted Sensor Selection selects informative sensors to provide sufficient spatial context. Experiments with twelve baseline methods, three adaptability scenarios, and five benchmark datasets covering traffic, air quality, and trajectory data show that AdaCTSi reduces MAE by an average of 33.1% relative to the strongest baseline on each dataset. A single trained model supports sensor-subset and resource-adaptive inference, and its modest memory footprint enables deployment on commodity computing devices, including MCUs.

AI.tldr: AdaCTSi is an adaptive imputation method for Correlated Time Series IoT data that combines One-shot TCN with Learned Time-Sensor Index Table, Sparse Spatial Attention, and Correlation-Weighted Sensor Selection to handle missing values in dynamic environments, achieving 33.1% average MAE reduction over baselines with subset and resource-adaptive inference on commodity devices.
AI.motivation: Existing CTS imputation methods prioritize accuracy but lack adaptability to changing IoT environments: they are vulnerable to sensor failures, cannot selectively impute incomplete sensors, and use static architectures that do not adapt to resource availability.
AI.method: AdaCTSi combines (1) a One-shot Temporal Convolutional Network with a Learned Time-Sensor Index Table to extract and decouple spatio-temporal features into sensor-wise embeddings, (2) Sparse Spatial Attention for dynamic spatial correlations, and (3) Correlation-Weighted Sensor Selection for informative sensor selection.
AI.result: Evaluated against twelve baselines across three adaptability scenarios and five benchmark datasets (traffic, air quality, trajectory), AdaCTSi reduces MAE by 33.1% on average relative to the strongest baseline per dataset. A single model supports sensor-subset and resource-adaptive inference with a modest memory footprint deployable on commodity devices including MCUs.
AI.conclusion: AdaCTSi effectively addresses the adaptability limitations of existing CTS imputation methods, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy while enabling flexible, resource-aware deployment on edge devices.

title: Commitment To Cooperation With Self-Negotiated Contracts
summary: As AI agents operate with increasing autonomy in a multi-agent world, they will need to learn to cooperate with other agents and with humans to generate mutual benefits. However, cooperation is a challenge because the costs of cooperation are often incurred early on, but the benefits are only realized later, creating an incentive to defect.
