  Once modeling is no longer the bottleneck, trusting AI to reason over large, complex networks no longer makes sense. Our position therefore cuts against the prevailing race to put autonomous AI agents in charge end-to-end. We instead confine AI to translation and rely on a solver for reliable long-horizon reasoning, building a reusable formal model of general network behavior that can then be specialized to specific tasks, e.g., root-cause analysis (RCA). We build TypoNet that constructs and validates a symbolic model of an emulated production-scale WAN from the network's own artifacts. Our preliminary evaluation shows TypoNet helps in two ways. On its own, TypoNet answers operational questions (e.g., reachability verification and change-impact analysis) faster, more cheaply, and more reliably than an LLM. As a tool for an AI agent, TypoNet boosts fault localization at lower cost. The result makes the case for AI that builds verifiable network models and relies on a solver for reliable long-horizon reasoning.

AI.tldr: TypoNet uses LLMs to translate network artifacts into formal logic models, then relies on solvers for reliable reasoning, achieving faster and more accurate network operations than autonomous AI agents.
AI.motivation: Writing formal network models by hand requires rare expertise and is hard to maintain as networks change frequently. Virtually no production network has a formal model despite its benefits for reachability verification, outage localization, and change-impact analysis.
AI.method: TypoNet uses LLMs to translate network artifacts (configurations, topology, routing state) into formal logic rules, then validates the model and uses a solver for reliable long-horizon reasoning. AI is confined to translation only, not end-to-end autonomous reasoning.
AI.result: TypoNet answers operational questions (reachability verification, change-impact analysis) faster, more cheaply, and more reliably than an LLM alone. As a tool for AI agents, it boosts fault localization at lower cost.
AI.conclusion: AI should be used to build verifiable network models rather than being trusted as autonomous end-to-end agents. The combination of LLM-based translation + solver-based reasoning is more effective than pure autonomous AI approaches for network operations.

title: DP-IVON-Gradsq: Differentially Private Squared-Gradient Improved Variational Online Newton
comment: Accepted at the 2nd Workshop on Machine Unlearning and Privacy Preservation (WIPE-OUT 2), held in conjunction with ECML PKDD 2026
summary: Differential privacy provides formal privacy guarantees for training neural networks on sensitive data, while Bayesian deep learning offers a principled framework for uncertainty-aware prediction. Combining these two objectives remains challenging, as privacy noise can interact with the stochasticity introduced by Bayesian posterior sampling. In this work, we investigate differentially private variational Bayesian learning through the Improved Variational Online Newton (IVON) optimizer. We introduce DP-IVON-Gradsq, a private variant of IVON. The proposed method constructs its curvature estimate from the privatized gradient using a noise-corrected squared-gradient estimator, reducing the direct interaction between posterior-sampling noise and privacy noise while preserving the Adam-like computational efficiency of IVON. We evaluate DP-IVON-Gradsq on CIFAR-10 against the standard private optimizers DP-SGD and DP-Adam over a range of privacy budgets. The results show that DP-IVON-Gradsq is competitive under weak-to-moderate privacy constraints, i.e., large-to-moderate values of $\varepsilon$, while degrading under strong privacy. Code is available at https://github.com/NourJamoussi/DP-IVON-Gradsq.git.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes DP-IVON-Gradsq, a differentially private variant of the IVON optimizer for variational Bayesian learning. It uses a noise-corrected squared-gradient estimator to reduce interaction between posterior-sampling noise and privacy noise. Experiments on CIFAR-10 show competitiveness under weak-to-moderate privacy budgets but performance degradation under strong privacy.
AI.motivation: Combining differential privacy with Bayesian deep learning is challenging because privacy noise interacts with the stochasticity from Bayesian posterior sampling. Existing methods do not address this interaction effectively.
AI.method: The method (DP-IVON-Gradsq) privatizes the IVON optimizer by constructing curvature estimates from privatized gradients using a noise-corrected squared-gradient estimator. This reduces interference between posterior-sampling noise and privacy noise while maintaining Adam-like efficiency.
AI.result: On CIFAR-10, DP-IVON-Gradsq is competitive with DP-SGD and DP-Adam under weak-to-moderate privacy (large-to-moderate ε values) but degrades under strong privacy (small ε).
AI.conclusion: DP-IVON-Gradsq offers a promising approach for differentially private Bayesian deep learning under relaxed privacy constraints, but strong privacy regimes remain challenging and require further research.

title: Share No More Than the Request Requires: Federated Disclosure for Perspective-Aware AI
summary: Modern AI systems bring societal risks such as mass surveillance, extreme concentrations of power, and loss of user autonomy---calling into question a model where third-parties collect and control massive amounts of user data. Users require a sovereign system to securely own, govern, and disclose their context while remaining compliant across regulated domains with strict provenance, interpretability, and policy adherence. Perspective-aware AI approaches this by transforming a user's aggregated personal data into a structured identity model called a \emph{Chronicle}: a temporal knowledge graph that represents and grows with the user. Chronicles support the secure disclosure of context across federated networks. A Chronicle holder may expose a queryable, authorized view that a third-party agent may consult without centralizing anyone's data. This paper explores the problem of minimum-necessary disclosure across domain boundaries: when a requester's agent queries a Chronicle, how can the system constrain its response to release only what the requester's relationship, stated purpose, and specific task require? We propose \textbf{Provenance Preserving Chronicles} (PPC), a federated protocol that compiles each holder's Chronicle into a compact \emph{authorized evidence subgraph} governed by one rule: \emph{share no more than the request requires}. Holders keep local sovereignty; an access controller projects relationship-aware views over domain-expert ontologies; and a two-phase flow returns provenance-linked text first, releasing raw artifacts only after explicit holder approval. We frame the problem, map gaps in blockchain, P2P, and holder-sovereign designs, define the core constructs, and sketch the protocol with an explicit threat model.

AI.tldr: Provenance Preserving Chronicles (PPC) is a federated protocol enabling users to securely control and disclose minimal-necessary personal data across domains via temporal knowledge graphs called Chronicles, governed by the principle of sharing no more than the request requires.
AI.motivation: Modern AI systems pose societal risks (mass surveillance, power concentration, loss of autonomy) by allowing third parties to collect and control massive amounts of user data, necessitating a sovereign system where users own, govern, and selectively disclose their data while remaining compliant with regulations.
AI.method: The paper proposes PPC, a federated protocol where each user's personal data is structured as a Chronicle (temporal knowledge graph). An access controller projects relationship-aware views over domain-expert ontologies, and a two-phase flow first returns provenance-linked text, releasing raw artifacts only after explicit holder approval, enforcing the rule of minimum-necessary disclosure.
AI.result: The paper frames the problem, maps gaps in existing blockchain, P2P, and holder-sovereign designs, defines core constructs (Chronicle, authorized evidence subgraph), and sketches the protocol with an explicit threat model.
AI.conclusion: PPC enables secure, minimum-necessary data disclosure across domain boundaries while maintaining holder sovereignty, provenance, interpretability, and policy adherence, addressing limitations of current centralized and decentralized data-sharing approaches.

title: Parameter-Efficient Adaptation of SAM3 for Prompt-Driven Surgical Concept Segmentation
comment: Accepted by The 2nd MICCAI Workshop on Efficient Medical AI
summary: Efficient surgical segmentation empowers clinical diagnosis, intraoperative monitoring, and downstream robotic pipelines for reconstruction and simulation. Although prompt-driven foundation models like Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM3) achieve strong segmentation performance on natural images, surgical data exhibits domain gaps against its pre-training data, resulting in degraded segmentation accuracy. Furthermore, existing medical SAM methods require full-parameter fine-tuning, incurring heavy computational consumption and low efficiency. To address these limitations, this work proposes a parameter-efficient Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adaptation of SAM3 for surgical concept segmentation. We inject low-rank adapters into the prompt encoder, detector and tracker while fully freezing the vision backbone, which only optimizes 0.98% of the total model parameters and supports training on a single consumer GPU. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms zero-shot SAM3 and other mainstream baselines, and the generated segmentation results can be directly deployed to support downstream robotic surgical scene reconstruction and physical simulation pipelines.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a parameter-efficient Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) of SAM3 for surgical concept segmentation, freezing the vision backbone and only optimizing 0.98% of parameters via adapters in the prompt encoder, detector, and tracker. The method outperforms zero-shot SAM3 and baselines, enabling downstream robotic reconstruction and simulation on a single consumer GPU.
AI.motivation: Surgical data exhibits domain gaps against SAM3's pre-training data, causing degraded segmentation accuracy, while existing medical SAM methods require full-parameter fine-tuning with heavy computational cost and low efficiency.
AI.method: Inject low-rank adapters into SAM3's prompt encoder, detector, and tracker while freezing the vision backbone; only 0.98% of total parameters are optimized, enabling training on a single consumer GPU.
AI.result: Consistently outperforms zero-shot SAM3 and other mainstream baselines on surgical concept segmentation; generated results support downstream robotic scene reconstruction and physical simulation.
AI.conclusion: Parameter-efficient LoRA adaptation of SAM3 is effective for surgical segmentation, bridging domain gaps with minimal computational overhead while enabling practical downstream robotic applications.

title: Breaking the Total Variance Barrier: Sharp Sample Complexity for Linear Heteroscedastic Bandits with Fixed Action Set
summary: Recent years have witnessed increasing interests in tackling heteroscedastic noise in bandits and reinforcement learning. In these works, the cumulative variance of the noise $Λ= \sum_{t=1}^T σ_t^2$, where $σ_t^2$ is the variance of the noise at round $t$, is used to characterize the statistical complexity of the problem, yielding \emph{simple regret} bounds of order $\tilde{\cal{O}}(d \sqrt{Λ/ T^2})$ for $d$-dimensional linear bandits with heteroscedastic noise. However, with a closer look, $Λ$ remains the same order even if the noise is close to zero at half of the rounds, which indicates that the $Λ$-dependence is not optimal. In this paper, we revisit the stochastic linear bandit problem with heteroscedastic noise, where the action set is prefixed throughout the learning process. We propose a novel variance-adaptive algorithm \texttt{VAEE} (Variance-Aware Exploration with Elimination) for large action set, which actively explores actions that maximizes the information gain among a candidate set of actions that are not eliminated. With the active-exploration strategy, we show that \texttt{VAEE} achieves a \emph{simple regret} with a nearly \emph{harmonic-mean} dependent rate. For finitely many actions, we propose a variance-aware variant of G-optimal design based exploration, which achieves a simple regret with sharper dependence on $d$. We also establish a nearly matching lower bound for the fixed action set setting indicating that \emph{harmonic-mean} dependent rate is unavoidable. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that breaks the $\sqrtΛ$ barrier for stochastic linear bandits with heteroscedastic noise.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes variance-aware algorithms (VAEE) for stochastic linear bandits with heteroscedastic noise that achieve simple regret bounds with a nearly harmonic-mean dependent rate, breaking the previous $\sqrt{\Lambda}$ barrier for the first time.
AI.motivation: Existing works on heteroscedastic noise in bandits use cumulative variance $\Lambda$ to characterize complexity, but this dependence is suboptimal because $\Lambda$ remains large even when noise is near zero in half the rounds. The paper aims to break the $\sqrt{\Lambda}$ barrier.
AI.method: Proposes VAEE (Variance-Aware Exploration with Elimination) for large action sets, which actively explores actions maximizing information gain among a candidate set not eliminated. For finite actions, proposes a variance-aware variant of G-optimal design based exploration.
AI.result: Achieves simple regret with a nearly harmonic-mean dependent rate, breaking the $\sqrt{\Lambda}$ barrier. Establishes a nearly matching lower bound showing harmonic-mean dependent rate is unavoidable for fixed action sets.
AI.conclusion: This is the first work that breaks the $\sqrt{\Lambda}$ barrier for stochastic linear bandits with heteroscedastic noise, with a nearly matching lower bound confirming optimality.

title: ConsistencyGate: Preventing Memory Contamination in LLM Agents via Self-Consistency Admission Control
comment: 24 pages, 2 figures, 6 tables, 1 algorithm; includes appendices
summary: LLM agents that operate over many turns accumulate facts in an external memory store and reuse them as premises for downstream reasoning. A hallucinated fact written at one step therefore persists as a false premise for every subsequent step, a failure mode we call memory contamination. Existing memory management addresses retrieval and capacity but not write-time correctness; this admission problem cannot be solved by utility- or recency-based criteria, and uncontrolled contamination compounds across long trajectories. We propose ConsistencyGate, a write-time admission gate that, before committing a candidate fact m extracted from context c, queries the LLM K times for a soft support score and admits m only when the average exceeds a threshold. The mechanism is model-agnostic, requires no fine-tuning, and reduces to a single forward pass in a log-probability variant for latency-sensitive deployments. To measure the effect on natural data, we construct two real-conversation benchmarks (LoCoMo-Contam and MSC-Contam) by planting controlled single-detail corruptions in long-term conversations from LoCoMo and MSC, and complement them with a structured synthetic corpus (MemContam) that isolates a near-oracle upper bound. Across four LLM backbones, ConsistencyGate reduces contamination on every benchmark relative to a write-everything baseline, with the cost concentrated on facts that are stated only implicitly in the source context. We release all three benchmarks together with the gate implementation.

AI.tldr: ConsistencyGate is a write-time admission mechanism that prevents memory contamination in LLM agents by verifying candidate facts through repeated LLM queries before storing them, reducing false premises across long trajectories without requiring fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: LLM agents operating over multiple turns accumulate facts in external memory, but hallucinated facts persist as false premises for subsequent reasoning steps (memory contamination). Existing memory management focuses on retrieval and capacity but not write-time correctness, and uncontrolled contamination compounds across long trajectories.
AI.method: ConsistencyGate: a write-time admission gate that, before committing a candidate fact m extracted from context c, queries the LLM K times for a soft support score and admits m only when the average exceeds a threshold. The mechanism is model-agnostic, requires no fine-tuning, and has a log-probability variant for latency-sensitive deployments. Three benchmarks (LoCoMo-Contam, MSC-Contam, MemContam) were constructed to evaluate the approach.
AI.result: Across four LLM backbones, ConsistencyGate reduces contamination on every benchmark relative to a write-everything baseline, with the cost concentrated on facts stated only implicitly in the source context.
AI.conclusion: ConsistencyGate effectively addresses memory contamination at write time, reducing false premises across long trajectories without sacrificing efficiency or requiring model modifications.

title: DAP-Pose: Deep Temporal Alignment and Physics-aware Cross-modal Sensor Fusion for Robust Pose Estimation
summary: Robust and accurate pose estimation with multi-modal sensors is fundamental for autonomous vehicles and mobile robotic systems in complex environments. In this paper, we propose DAP-Pose, a unified end-to-end model for robust multi-modal pose estimation. DAP-Pose introduces a Bi-level Cross-modal Fusion (BCF) module that captures complementary semantic and geometric motion cues from visual, inertial, and GNSS measurements. To handle temporal offsets, we designed a Deep Temporal Alignment (DTA) module that explicitly aligns asynchronous streams in latent space, enabling coherent motion modeling without strict hardware synchronization. Furthermore, we incorporate physics-aware constraints via manifold geometry and GNSS-guided absolute metric scale, enforcing motion consistency and mitigating drift. Experiments upon the public KITTI benchmark dataset were conducted to evaluate the performance of DAP-Pose against existing methods. DAP-Pose achieved the state-of-the-art performance, with the lowest average translation error ($t_{rel}$) of 1.31% and rotation error ($r_{rel}$) of 0.46$^{\circ}$. Furthermore, it accurately estimates poses and maintains robust performance under severe artificially injected temporal misalignment.

AI.tldr: DAP-Pose is a unified end-to-end model for multi-modal pose estimation that uses Bi-level Cross-modal Fusion (BCF) to combine visual, inertial, and GNSS data, a Deep Temporal Alignment (DTA) module to handle asynchronous sensor streams, and physics-aware constraints for motion consistency. It achieves state-of-the-art results on KITTI (1.31% translation error, 0.46° rotation error) and remains robust under severe temporal misalignment.
AI.motivation: Robust and accurate multi-modal pose estimation is critical for autonomous vehicles and mobile robots, but existing methods struggle with sensor synchronization issues and effective cross-modal fusion of complementary semantic and geometric motion cues from visual, inertial, and GNSS measurements.
AI.method: DAP-Pose introduces three key components: (1) a Bi-level Cross-modal Fusion (BCF) module that captures complementary semantic and geometric motion cues from visual, inertial, and GNSS data; (2) a Deep Temporal Alignment (DTA) module that explicitly aligns asynchronous sensor streams in latent space without requiring strict hardware synchronization; and (3) physics-aware constraints via manifold geometry and GNSS-guided absolute metric scale to enforce motion consistency and mitigate drift.
AI.result: On the KITTI benchmark, DAP-Pose achieves state-of-the-art performance with the lowest average translation error (t_rel) of 1.31% and rotation error (r_rel) of 0.46°. It also maintains robust performance under severe artificially injected temporal misalignment.
AI.conclusion: DAP-Pose provides a robust, accurate, and temporally resilient unified framework for multi-modal pose estimation, effectively addressing sensor fusion, alignment, and drift challenges in complex environments.

title: Extreme Volatility Warning under Label Scarcity via Multi-Source Anomaly Fusion
summary: Early warning of extreme market volatility is central to financial risk management, but actionable events are rare, nonstationary, and often triggered by exogenous information shocks. In our CSI~300 setting, only $\sim$80 positive samples are observed across 791 training days, making heavily supervised multi-source models unstable. We first analyze a 100K-parameter hierarchical text-signal fusion model (HTSF) and find that added parameterization hurts in this low-label regime. Motivated by this failure, we propose \textbf{AAMSF} (Anomaly-Augmented Multi-Signal Fusion), a semisupervised framework that combines Isolation Forest anomaly scores over market indicators, GDELT events, Chinese financial news, and English media with lightweight Ridge score fusion. We further introduce \textbf{T-AAMSF}, a temporal extension for multi-day anomaly accumulation. On CSI~300 (2018--2023), AAMSF achieves test AUC-ROC \textbf{0.680}, outperforming the strongest unsupervised baseline (0.630) and neural baseline (0.588), while T-AAMSF improves PR-AUC to 0.291. Ablations reveal strong source asymmetry: GDELT and domestic financial news provide complementary risk signals, whereas English media consistently reduces performance, and learned weighting is unreliable under validation noise. These results suggest an empirical design principle for label-scarce financial risk warning: robust anomaly geometry and source reliability can matter more than supervised representation capacity.

AI.tldr: AAMSF and T-AAMSF are semisupervised frameworks that use Isolation Forest anomaly scores and lightweight Ridge fusion across multiple signals (market data, GDELT events, Chinese/Euro news) to predict extreme market volatility in a low-label regime (only ~80 positive samples in 791 days), achieving AUC-ROC 0.680 and PR-AUC 0.291 on CSI 300, outperforming neural baselines. Key findings include source asymmetry (English media hurts performance) and that robust anomaly geometry matters more than supervised capacity.
AI.motivation: Extreme market volatility events are rare, nonstationary, and triggered by exogenous shocks. In the CSI 300 setting, only ~80 positive samples exist across 791 days, making heavily supervised multi-source models unstable and prompting the need for a semisupervised approach.
AI.method: Proposes AAMSF (Anomaly-Augmented Multi-Signal Fusion), a semisupervised framework combining Isolation Forest anomaly scores over market indicators, GDELT events, Chinese financial news, and English media with lightweight Ridge score fusion. Also introduces T-AAMSF for temporal multi-day anomaly accumulation.
AI.result: AAMSF achieves test AUC-ROC 0.680 on CSI 300 (2018-2023), outperforming the strongest unsupervised baseline (0.630) and neural baseline (0.588). T-AAMSF improves PR-AUC to 0.291. Ablations show GDELT and domestic financial news complement each other, while English media consistently reduces performance.
AI.conclusion: For label-scarce financial risk warning, robust anomaly geometry and source reliability can matter more than supervised representation capacity. Learned weighting is unreliable under validation noise.

title: Reason Popper-ly: Patching In-Context Reasoning with Inductive Logic Programming
comment: Accepted at the 20th Conference on Neurosymbolic Learning and Reasoning
summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting enables large language models (LLMs) to tackle multi-step reasoning tasks, yet the generated intermediate steps are not guaranteed to be logically sound. We present Reason Popper-ly, a neurosymbolic framework that uses inductive logic programming (ILP) to learn relation composition rules from reasoning traces and deploys them as an online verifier for step-level correction. Given an LLM-generated trace, the method checks each inferred step against the learned rule table, diagnoses the violation type, rewrites incorrect steps with symbolically derived repairs, and regenerates the remaining suffix so that the model can produce its final answer conditioned on a verified trace. We evaluate on CLUTRR, a multi-hop kinship reasoning benchmark, using five language models over reasoning chains of 2 to 10 hops. Across all models, Reason Popper-ly consistently improves terminal accuracy over standard CoT, with gains of up to 48 percentage points for small models and 15 points for frontier models on the longest chains. Compared with a fully exogenous symbolic pipeline, our method performs better on harder instances by preserving the model's successful grounding while correcting only verifiable reasoning failures. In addition, step-level ILP verification yields a fine-grained error taxonomy that provides diagnostic insight beyond final-answer accuracy.

AI.tldr: Reason Popper-ly is a neurosymbolic framework that uses inductive logic programming to learn relation composition rules from LLM reasoning traces and applies them as an online verifier to detect and correct logically unsound steps, improving multi-step reasoning accuracy by up to 48 percentage points on the CLUTRR benchmark.
AI.motivation: Chain-of-thought prompting enables multi-step reasoning in LLMs, but the generated intermediate steps are not guaranteed to be logically sound, motivating the need for a verification mechanism that can detect and correct reasoning errors at the step level.
AI.method: The framework uses ILP to learn relation composition rules from reasoning traces, then deploys these rules as an online verifier: for each LLM-generated step, it checks against the learned rule table, diagnoses violation types, rewrites incorrect steps with symbolically derived repairs, and regenerates the remaining suffix conditioned on the verified trace.
AI.result: On CLUTRR (2-10 hop kinship reasoning), across five LLMs, the method consistently improves accuracy over standard CoT, with gains of up to 48 percentage points for small models and 15 points for frontier models on the longest chains. It also outperforms fully exogenous symbolic pipelines on harder instances.
AI.conclusion: Step-level ILP verification provides both accuracy gains and fine-grained error taxonomy for diagnostic insight beyond final-answer accuracy, showing that preserving the model's successful grounding while correcting verifiable reasoning failures is an effective strategy.

title: RoadVGGT: Road-Structure-Aware Feed-Forward Road Surface Reconstruction
summary: Large-scale road surface reconstruction supports high-definition mapping, autonomous-driving perception, annotation, and simulation. Existing road-specialized optimization methods can produce high-quality road representations, but they typically require per-scene training and scene-dependent coverage design around the driving trajectory, limiting scalable reconstruction over newly collected roads. To address these limitations, we introduce RoadVGGT, a road-structure-aware feed-forward framework that reconstructs compact Gaussian road surfaces without test-time per-scene optimization. RoadVGGT uses a geometric foundation model to exploit multi-view images together with provided pose and depth observations, and predicts dense pixel-aligned Gaussian attributes through a learned Gaussian head. To make these dense predictions usable for large road surfaces, we align them into a consistent metric world coordinate system and fuse redundant Gaussians on the road-aligned XY plane through confidence-weighted grid fusion. Category-aware grouping and road--sidewalk junction protection further control fusion around vulnerable road structures. The resulting representation supports RGB and semantic bird's-eye-view maps, elevation estimation, and novel view synthesis. RoadVGGT eliminates the need for per-scene optimization in prior methods, reconstructs complete road surfaces with a compact Gaussian representation, and improves image quality, semantic mapping, and elevation accuracy. Extensive experiments demonstrate the potential of geometric foundation models for scalable feed-forward road surface reconstruction.

AI.tldr: RoadVGGT is a feed-forward framework for large-scale road surface reconstruction that eliminates per-scene optimization by using a geometric foundation model and confidence-weighted grid fusion to produce compact Gaussian representations supporting RGB/semantic BEV maps, elevation estimation, and novel view synthesis.
AI.motivation: Existing road-specialized optimization methods require per-scene training and scene-dependent coverage design around the driving trajectory, which limits scalable reconstruction over newly collected roads.
AI.method: RoadVGGT uses a geometric foundation model to exploit multi-view images with pose and depth observations, predicts dense pixel-aligned Gaussian attributes through a learned Gaussian head, aligns predictions into a consistent metric world coordinate system, and fuses redundant Gaussians on the road-aligned XY plane via confidence-weighted grid fusion with category-aware grouping and road-sidewalk junction protection.
AI.result: Eliminates per-scene optimization, reconstructs complete road surfaces with compact Gaussian representation, and improves image quality, semantic mapping, and elevation accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates the potential of geometric foundation models for scalable feed-forward road surface reconstruction.

title: The Intruder Threshold: A Spectral Law for LoRA Fine-Tuning
summary: LoRA fine-tuning can create intruder dimensions: new leading singular vectors of the updated weight matrix $W+BA$ that are nearly orthogonal to all pretrained singular vectors and that drive catastrophic forgetting. Since their discovery, no theory has predicted, layer by layer on measured spectra, when they appear. We derive a per-layer critical update strength $s^\ast=\barθ/(γσ_1(BA))$, computed from the measured spectrum of $W$ alone through the rectangular spiked-deformation transform, together with an exact secular-equation characterization of the updated spectrum, with no fitted parameters. In a pre-specified study spanning four dense Transformer families, a state-space model, a mixture-of-experts model, and an encoder-decoder (18 adapters, 9{,}840 layer scans), the law localizes the empirical threshold within a factor of two on $82\%$ of layers, separates intruder-bearing from intruder-free layers at deployment with a mean AUC of $0.89$, holds unchanged on six third-party adapters, and predicts where WikiText-2 perplexity begins to degrade; a combination of the two pre-specified edge evaluations reaches $98\%$ and is confirmed out-of-bag on the external adapters ($0.997$). Full fine-tuning disperses its update far below the threshold of every layer, which resolves the asymmetry between LoRA and full fine-tuning. Norm-matched interventions confirm that threshold-crossing layers, rather than update magnitude, carry the forgetting, and a spike-budget rule derived from the thresholds, requiring one SVD and no validation sweeps, reduces forgetting by $62\%$ on the most fragile model at no task cost.

AI.tldr: This paper derives a per-layer critical update strength threshold that predicts when intruder dimensions (causing catastrophic forgetting) appear during LoRA fine-tuning, validated across 18 adapters and 9,840 layer scans with high accuracy.
AI.motivation: LoRA fine-tuning creates intruder dimensions—new singular vectors orthogonal to pretrained ones—that drive catastrophic forgetting, but no theory has predicted layer-by-layer when they appear.
AI.method: The authors derive a per-layer critical update strength s* using the rectangular spiked-deformation transform and a secular-equation characterization of the updated weight spectrum, with no fitted parameters. They validate across 4 dense Transformer families, a state-space model, a mixture-of-experts model, and an encoder-decoder (18 adapters, 9,840 layer scans).
AI.result: The law localizes the empirical threshold within a factor of two on 82% of layers, separates intruder-bearing from intruder-free layers with mean AUC 0.89, holds on six third-party adapters, and predicts perplexity degradation. Combined edge evaluations reach 98% (0.997 out-of-bag). Full fine-tuning stays below threshold in all layers. Norm-matched interventions confirm threshold-crossing layers carry forgetting. A spike-budget rule reduces forgetting by 62% on the most fragile model at no task cost.
AI.conclusion: The derived threshold theory successfully predicts intruder dimension emergence during LoRA fine-tuning, resolves the asymmetry between LoRA and full fine-tuning, and provides a practical spike-budget rule to mitigate catastrophic forgetting without validation sweeps.

title: Stress-testing large language model agents in a robotic chemistry laboratory
summary: AI is evaluated through knowledge, reasoning and plan generation, yet scientific agency requires reliable physical action and adaptation to evidence. Here, we use a robotic chemistry laboratory as a physical-world testbed to make scientific agency measurable. Its 45 modular workstations exposed as machine-readable skills enabled 4,608 trials. Only 3.3% of trials produced expert-assessed executable workflows under laboratory constraints; even the best system achieved 28.1%. Long-horizon planning remained a challenge: only three executable workflows exceeded 30 operations, although the longest contained 44. Across five rounds, experimental feedback prompted local adjustments but no workflow-level replanning or analytical-method redesign. By making physical executability and evidence-driven replanning measurable, our study provides an evidence-based assessment of deployment readiness and a diagnostic framework to guide closed-loop improvements towards physically grounded autonomous research.

AI.tldr: Only 3.3% of 4,608 trials in a robotic chemistry lab produced expert-assessed executable workflows; the best system achieved 28.1%. While experimental feedback enabled local adjustments, no workflow-level replanning or analytical-method redesign occurred, highlighting the gap between AI reasoning and reliable physical scientific agency.
AI.motivation: To bridge the evaluation gap between AI's knowledge/reasoning capabilities and the requirements of physical scientific agency, using a robotic chemistry laboratory as a testbed to make scientific agency measurable.
AI.method: A robotic chemistry lab with 45 modular workstations (exposed as machine-readable skills) was used to conduct 4,608 trials. Expert assessment evaluated workflow executability under laboratory constraints across five rounds with experimental feedback.
AI.result: Only 3.3% of trials produced executable workflows; best system achieved 28.1%. Only three executable workflows exceeded 30 operations (longest: 44). Feedback prompted local adjustments but no workflow-level replanning or analytical-method redesign.
AI.conclusion: The study provides an evidence-based assessment of AI deployment readiness in physical science and a diagnostic framework for guiding closed-loop improvements toward physically grounded autonomous research.

title: PathScale-R1: Cross-scale Reasoning for Pathological Image Analysis
summary: Pathological diagnosis is inherently multi-scale, requiring the integration of global tissue architecture at low magnification with cellular morphology at higher magnification. However, existing pathology benchmarks and vision-language models (VLMs) are still largely developed under single-scale settings, limiting their ability to learn clinically meaningful multi-magnification reasoning. Moreover, naively constructed visual question answering (VQA) tasks may be susceptible to text-only or superficial visual shortcuts, leading to unreliable assessments of visual understanding. To address these limitations, we introduce a benchmark and training framework for shortcut-resistant cross-scale pathology reasoning. We design an Adversarial Text-only Screening strategy for semantic reasoning questions and a Structure-controlled Distractor Sampling strategy for visual grounding questions, encouraging models to rely on cross-scale visual evidence. Based on this pipeline, we construct PathScale-VQA, a high-quality cross-scale pathology VQA benchmark with 10,373 multiple-choice questions grounded in 1,368 diagnostic paths across multiple magnification levels. Building on the semantic reasoning set, PathScale-R1 is optimized through Difficulty-driven Reasoning Distillation supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning with a Scale-aware Reasoning Structure reward, which encourages the use of evidence across magnifications. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance of PathScale-R1 on cross-scale reasoning tasks and effective transfer to conventional single-scale pathology VQA. Our code is available at https://github.com/iMVR-PL/PathScale-R1.

AI.tldr: PathScale-VQA is a cross-scale pathology VQA benchmark with 10,373 questions across 1,368 diagnostic paths, and PathScale-R1 is a model optimized via difficulty-driven reasoning distillation and reinforcement learning with scale-aware rewards, achieving SOTA on cross-scale and single-scale pathology VQA tasks. The framework uses adversarial text-only screening and structure-controlled distractor sampling to prevent shortcut learning.
AI.motivation: Existing pathology benchmarks and VLMs are developed under single-scale settings, lacking the ability to learn multi-magnification reasoning; also, naive VQA tasks suffer from text-only or superficial visual shortcuts, making assessments of visual understanding unreliable.
AI.method: 1) Adversarial Text-only Screening for semantic reasoning; 2) Structure-controlled Distractor Sampling for visual grounding; 3) PathScale-VQA benchmark construction (10,373 questions, 1,368 diagnostic paths); 4) PathScale-R1 optimized via Difficulty-driven Reasoning Distillation SFT + RL with Scale-aware Reasoning Structure reward.
AI.result: PathScale-R1 achieves state-of-the-art performance on cross-scale reasoning tasks and shows effective transfer to conventional single-scale pathology VQA.
AI.conclusion: The proposed shortcut-resistant benchmark and training framework effectively enables cross-scale reasoning in pathology VLMs, setting a new SOTA while mitigating shortcut learning issues.

title: Outcome-Confounded Local Supervision in On-Policy Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own trajectories while a teacher supplies dense token-level likelihoods at student-visited prefixes. These likelihoods are often read locally: agreement appears safe to imitate, whereas disagreement appears to identify an error. We show that both readings are confounded by the outcome of the completed trajectory. We introduce an outcome-resolved diagnostic that crosses pointwise teacher-student divergence with final-answer correctness, separating safe imitation, productive divergence, harmful divergence, and agreement-on-failure. In an eight-seed mathematical-reasoning study with a Qwen3-8B student and Qwen3-32B teacher, agreement-on-failure constitutes 67.84% of pooled response-token mass; with a Qwen2.5-7B/32B pair it remains 67.68%. The result persists across threshold, sequence-level, format, and truncation audits. Even on prompts that the Qwen3 teacher solves in all four independent attempts, student accuracy rises to 86.91% but agreement-on-failure remains 14.76%. We then run three matched training probes that use the available signals to imitate, mask, or contrast whole trajectories; none consistently reduces agreement-on-failure. The result points to a localization limitation: local divergence paired with a trajectory-level outcome does not identify where a failed trajectory became unrecoverable. Addressing this limitation requires additional positional information, such as process labels, teacher continuations from student prefixes, or token-level alignment across rollouts. Our contribution is therefore diagnostic rather than a new training method.

AI.tldr: On-policy distillation's local teacher-student divergence is confounded by trajectory outcomes; a diagnostic reveals that "agreement-on-failure" dominates token mass (~68%) and persists across models, audits, and training probes, indicating that local divergence + outcome cannot localize where a trajectory became unrecoverable.
AI.motivation: To reveal that conventional readings of local teacher-student agreement/disagreement in on-policy distillation are confounded by final-answer correctness, and to diagnose the prevalence and persistence of "agreement-on-failure" (teacher and student agree but the final answer is wrong).
AI.method: Introduces an outcome-resolved diagnostic crossing pointwise teacher-student divergence with final-answer correctness (safe imitation, productive divergence, harmful divergence, agreement-on-failure). Tests on Qwen3-8B/Qwen3-32B and Qwen2.5-7B/32B pairs with mathematical reasoning tasks, including threshold, sequence-level, format, and truncation audits, plus three training probes (imitate, mask, contrast).
AI.result: Agreement-on-failure constitutes ~67.68–67.84% of pooled response-token mass across both model pairs. Even on prompts the teacher solves in all four attempts, agreement-on-failure is 14.76%. None of the three training probes consistently reduces this phenomenon.
AI.conclusion: Local divergence paired with trajectory-level outcome cannot identify where a failed trajectory became unrecoverable; addressing this requires additional positional information (process labels, teacher continuations, token-level alignment). The contribution is diagnostic rather than a new training method.

title: SymStep: Symbolic Step Verification for Logical Reasoning
summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting can fail severely on constraint-dense logical reasoning tasks, where unverified errors accumulate silently across steps. We introduce SymStep: an LLM makes one atomic claim at a time (DEDUCE: Alice, pet, Cat), then a lightweight constraint propagator checks the claim for consistency with prior accepted deductions, rejects contradictions, and cascades implied facts automatically. SymStep+G additionally provides MRV guidance after each accepted step, directing the LLM toward the most constrained unresolved variable. On a 35-puzzle retained subset of ZebraLogicBench, a benchmark of 1,000 Einstein-style logic puzzles, Direct and CoT both achieve 0%, while SymStep+G reaches 97%. On AR-LSAT analytical reasoning problems, SymStep achieves 100% vs. CoT's 87%. On LGP-14, SymStep+G achieves 100% vs. 0% for CoT and Logic-LM, the strongest prior symbolic+LLM baseline we compare against. Ablation studies reveal that MRV guidance is a key mechanism for reducing directionless cycling, while consistency checking provides a safety net against explicit contradictions. Across six benchmarks spanning five task domains, SymStep variants match or exceed every baseline on constraint-dense and arithmetic tasks. Experiments on AQUA-RAT algebra confirm the advantage is constraint-density-specific.

AI.tldr: SymStep is a hybrid LLM-symbolic method for constraint-dense logical reasoning, where an LLM makes atomic claims one at a time and a lightweight constraint propagator checks consistency, cascades implied facts, and optionally provides MRV guidance. It achieves near-perfect accuracy on multiple benchmarks where standard CoT and Direct prompting fail completely (e.g., 0%→97% on ZebraLogicBench, 0%→100% on LGP-14).
AI.motivation: Chain-of-thought prompting fails severely on constraint-dense logical reasoning tasks because errors accumulate silently across steps without verification, leading to catastrophic failure (0% accuracy on multiple benchmarks).
AI.method: SymStep operates in two alternating phases: (1) the LLM makes a single atomic DEDUCE claim (e.g., "Alice, pet, Cat"), and (2) a lightweight constraint propagator checks consistency against prior accepted deductions, rejects contradictions, and cascades implied facts. The variant SymStep+G additionally provides MRV (Minimum Remaining Values) guidance after each accepted step, directing the LLM toward the most constrained unresolved variable.
AI.result: SymStep+G achieves 97% on ZebraLogicBench (vs. 0% for Direct and CoT), 100% on AR-LSAT (vs. 87% for CoT), and 100% on LGP-14 (vs. 0% for CoT and Logic-LM). Ablations show MRV guidance reduces directionless cycling and consistency checking prevents explicit contradictions. Advantage is confirmed to be constraint-density-specific via AQUA-RAT experiments.
AI.conclusion: SymStep variants match or exceed all baselines on constraint-dense and arithmetic tasks across six benchmarks spanning five domains, demonstrating that interleaving atomic LLM deductions with symbolic constraint propagation is highly effective for logical reasoning problems where pure LLM approaches fail.

title: Source-Free Controlled Adaptation of Teachers for Continual Test-Time Adaptation
summary: In many real-world scenarios, encountering continual shifts in domain during inference is very common. Consequently, continual test-time adaptation (CTTA) techniques leveraging a teacher-student framework have gained prominence, allowing models to adapt continuously even after deployment. In such a framework, a weight-averaged mean teacher is used to produce pseudo-labels from test data for self-training. The mean teacher gets updated as an exponential moving average of the student parameters using a high value of momentum that is kept fixed even if different distributions of test data are encountered. To combat the resulting drift of the model, we propose a novel controlled teacher adaptation methodology that dynamically sets a proper momentum value depending on the quality of the incoming data. Additionally, we estimate class prototypes from the source pretrained model to help align the target data as they come in. Importantly, our method does not require access to source data or its statistics at any stage of the pipeline, making it truly source-free. We perform extensive experiments on benchmark datasets to demonstrate that our approach outperforms different state-of-the-art adaptation frameworks, many of which require access to source data.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a controlled teacher adaptation method for continual test-time adaptation (CTTA) that dynamically adjusts the momentum value in a teacher-student framework based on data quality, and uses class prototypes from a source pretrained model for alignment, without requiring any source data access. It outperforms SOTA methods on benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Real-world systems face continual domain shifts during inference, and existing CTTA methods use a fixed high momentum value for the mean teacher update, which leads to model drift when encountering varying test distributions.
AI.method: The method (1) dynamically sets the momentum value for the exponential moving average of the mean teacher based on the quality of incoming test data, and (2) estimates class prototypes from the source pretrained model to align target data, all without accessing source data or its statistics.
AI.result: The proposed approach outperforms various state-of-the-art adaptation frameworks, including those requiring access to source data, on benchmark datasets.
AI.conclusion: Controlled teacher adaptation with dynamic momentum and source-free class prototype alignment effectively mitigates model drift in CTTA, achieving superior performance without reliance on source data.

title: Structure over Depth: A Single-Block Spatio-Temporal Transformer for Multi-Entity Reasoning
summary: Modeling multi-entity temporal data requires capturing dependencies across entities, time, and their interactions. Transformer-based approaches perform well but often rely on deep stacks of layers to learn these heterogeneous dependencies implicitly, increasing computational cost. We revisit this problem from a structural perspective and decompose multi-entity temporal dynamics into three interaction types: spatial interactions among entities, temporal interactions across time, and cross interactions coupling the two domains. We propose a structured spatio-temporal transformer block that explicitly models all three within a single stage. It uses parallel spatial and temporal self-attention, followed by bidirectional cross-attention, and combines the outputs through learnable gated fusion. By directly encoding these complementary views, the model reduces the need for deep stacking. We evaluate the approach on video-based group activity recognition, skeleton-based human interaction analysis, and wearable sensor-based activity recognition. Despite its simplicity, the single structured Transformer block matches or outperforms deeper architectures with only 1.76M parameters. The results suggest that depth in prior models partly compensates for implicit and entangled interaction modeling, whereas explicit factorization offers a more efficient and transparent alternative. More broadly, this work supports a structure-first design principle: expressive multi-entity temporal reasoning can emerge by exposing interaction structure rather than relying on depth.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a structured spatio-temporal Transformer block that explicitly decomposes multi-entity temporal dynamics into spatial, temporal, and cross interactions, using parallel self-attention and bidirectional cross-attention with gated fusion. With only 1.76M parameters, a single block matches or outperforms deeper architectures across three activity recognition tasks, supporting a structure-first design principle.
AI.motivation: Existing Transformer-based models for multi-entity temporal data rely on deep stacks of layers to implicitly learn heterogeneous dependencies across entities and time, which increases computational cost and lacks transparency. The motivation is to design a more efficient and explicit alternative by decomposing these dynamics into structured interaction types.
AI.method: The method introduces a structured spatio-temporal Transformer block with three components: (1) parallel spatial self-attention (entity-level dependencies) and temporal self-attention (time-level dependencies), (2) bidirectional cross-attention coupling the spatial and temporal domains, and (3) learnable gated fusion to combine the complementary outputs. This single block explicitly models all three interaction types (spatial, temporal, cross) in one stage.
AI.result: Evaluated on video-based group activity recognition, skeleton-based human interaction analysis, and wearable sensor-based activity recognition. The single structured block with only 1.76M parameters matches or outperforms deeper architectures, demonstrating that explicit factorization is more efficient and transparent than depth-based implicit learning.
AI.conclusion: Depth in prior models partly compensates for implicit and entangled interaction modeling. Explicitly exposing interaction structure (structure-first design) enables expressive multi-entity temporal reasoning without relying on depth, offering a more efficient and transparent alternative.

title: Consistent Evidence, Robust Recognition: Faithful Attribution Regularization under Geometric Transformations
summary: Attribution methods are widely used to characterize the evidence underlying model predictions, yet their potential to improve model behavior remains underexplored. Attribution inconsistency under label-preserving geometric transformations may indicate transformation-sensitive evidence reliance, motivating attribution regularization. However, such supervision is valid only when attribution faithfully reflects the evidence driving predictions. Existing self-supervised methods typically align gradient-based maps such as Grad-CAM, whose limited faithfulness means that attribution consistency need not imply consistency of the underlying decision process, leaving transformation robustness unresolved. We propose an annotation-free attribution regularization framework based on submodular search over image regions. By measuring how candidate subsets affect model outputs, the search extracts compact, class-discriminative evidence as search-derived supervision. We further introduce a submodular ranking loss with path-consistency and termination-alignment terms that respectively align spatially corresponding candidate rankings along paired search trajectories and encourage the transformed trajectory to satisfy the stopping criterion at the target terminal step. The loss provides a differentiable surrogate for regularizing both final attributions and the otherwise discrete evidence-selection process. Experiments on ImageNet-100 show that our method substantially improves attribution stability, Insertion, and Deletion on ViT-B/16 with only a 0.28-point accuracy drop, with similar gains on ViT-L/16. On ImageNet-1K, it improves transformed-input accuracy on ResNet-50 and ConvNeXt-B while limiting the clean-accuracy drop to 0.30 points, demonstrating more consistent evidence reliance with minimal performance loss. Code will be released soon.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an annotation-free attribution regularization framework using submodular search over image regions to improve transformation robustness of model predictions, without requiring ground-truth labels for the regularization.
AI.motivation: Existing attribution methods are not effectively used to improve model behavior. Self-supervised attribution regularization methods rely on gradient-based maps like Grad-CAM which have limited faithfulness, so attribution consistency doesn't guarantee consistency of the underlying decision process, leaving transformation robustness unresolved.
AI.method: The framework uses submodular search over image regions to extract compact, class-discriminative evidence as search-derived supervision. A submodular ranking loss is introduced with path-consistency and termination-alignment terms: path-consistency aligns spatially corresponding candidate rankings along paired search trajectories, and termination-alignment encourages the transformed trajectory to satisfy the stopping criterion at the target terminal step. This provides a differentiable surrogate for regularizing final attributions and the discrete evidence-selection process.
AI.result: On ImageNet-100, the method substantially improves attribution stability, Insertion, and Deletion on ViT-B/16 with only a 0.28-point accuracy drop, with similar gains on ViT-L/16. On ImageNet-1K, it improves transformed-input accuracy on ResNet-50 and ConvNeXt-B while limiting clean-accuracy drop to 0.30 points.
AI.conclusion: The method demonstrates more consistent evidence reliance with minimal performance loss, effectively improving transformation robustness through attribution regularization without requiring annotations.

title: Soft-Constrained Optimization of Latent Space in Variational Autoencoders
summary: The usefulness of a variational autoencoder (VAE) depends on two properties of its latent space that are hard to obtain together: high encoding capacity in the individual latent variables, and a low-dimensional, disentangled organization of those variables. Weakening the Kullback-Leibler regularization raises capacity but degrades disentanglement, while strengthening it prunes latent variables away entirely. We formulate VAE training as a soft-constrained optimization problem that addresses both. First, we impose an entropy-based constraint (EC) on individual latent variables, showing that the entropy of a latent code upper-bounds the mutual information it carries about the generative factors of the data. Second, we propose a weight-filter method that exploits the slack of the soft constraint to prune low-entropy dimensions during downstream training. On dSprites, the EC raises the aggregate latent-variable activation score by 43-62% over a vanilla VAE, attains the highest FactorVAE score among the \b{eta} \b{eta}-VAE variants (0.891 vs 0.847), and lowers reconstruction error by up to 38%. On MNIST, the weight filter reduces the latent dimensionality supplied to a downstream classifier from ten to two while holding accuracy above 90%, converging in 37% fewer epochs than the same procedure without the EC. We also find that low-entropy discrete factors tend to merge into a single latent variable, whereas high-entropy continuous factors are distributed across several.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the trade-off between encoding capacity and disentanglement in VAEs by introducing an entropy-based constraint (EC) on latent variables and a weight-filter pruning method, achieving better disentanglement, lower reconstruction error, and efficient latent dimensionality reduction.
AI.motivation: VAEs struggle to simultaneously achieve high encoding capacity in individual latent variables and a low-dimensional, disentangled organization; weakening KL regularization raises capacity but harms disentanglement, while strengthening it prunes latent variables entirely.
AI.method: Formulates VAE training as a soft-constrained optimization problem: (1) imposes an entropy-based constraint (EC) on individual latent variables, using the entropy of a latent code as an upper bound on mutual information with generative factors; (2) proposes a weight-filter method that exploits slack in the soft constraint to prune low-entropy dimensions during downstream training.
AI.result: On dSprites: aggregate latent-variable activation score improved by 43-62% over vanilla VAE; highest FactorVAE score among β-VAE variants (0.891 vs 0.847); reconstruction error reduced by up to 38%. On MNIST: weight filter reduced latent dimensionality from 10 to 2 while maintaining >90% accuracy, converging 37% fewer epochs than without EC.
AI.conclusion: Low-entropy discrete factors tend to merge into a single latent variable, while high-entropy continuous factors are distributed across several; the proposed methods effectively balance capacity and disentanglement.

title: Compiler-Grounded Hierarchical Diagnosis for LLM-Based Triton Kernel Optimization
summary:
Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled automated kernel generation and optimization, but most existing approaches rely on surface signals such as compilation feedback and profiling metrics. These signals reveal that a kernel is slow, but not why the backend compiler fails to realize a profitable optimization, especially on emerging accelerators such as NPUs. We therefore formulate kernel optimization as a progressive cross-layer diagnosis problem that links runtime symptoms to IR structure and compiler behavior before rewriting source. Based on this insight, we present our system, a compiler-grounded and hierarchical optimization framework for Triton kernels. the system escalates from lightweight pattern triage and profiling diagnosis to IR attribution and compiler-grounded analysis only when deeper evidence is needed, then proposes evidence-backed source-level rewrites.
  We implement the system on Triton for Ascend NPUs and evaluate it on 37 successfully converted entries from a standardized NPUKernelBench-derived Ascend 950 benchmark. Across these entries, the system attains a geometric-mean speedup of 4.35$\times$ and a median speedup of 2.73$\times$ from the initial to optimized Triton kernel; 22/37 exceed 2$\times$ and 13/37 exceed 5$\times$. The complete distribution ranges from near-baseline entries to large wins, motivating transparent reporting of the current system's scope and limitations.

AI.tldr: A compiler-grounded, hierarchical optimization framework for Triton kernels that diagnoses performance bottlenecks by linking runtime symptoms to IR structure and compiler behavior, achieving 4.35× geometric-mean speedup on Ascend NPUs.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based kernel optimization approaches rely on surface signals (compilation feedback, profiling metrics) that reveal a kernel is slow but not why the backend compiler fails to realize profitable optimizations, especially on emerging accelerators like NPUs.
AI.method: Formulates kernel optimization as a progressive cross-layer diagnosis problem, escalating from lightweight pattern triage and profiling diagnosis to IR attribution and compiler-grounded analysis, then proposes evidence-backed source-level rewrites.
AI.result: On 37 entries from an Ascend NPU benchmark, achieves 4.35× geometric-mean speedup, 2.73× median speedup, with 22/37 exceeding 2× and 13/37 exceeding 5× speedup.
AI.conclusion: Compiler-grounded hierarchical diagnosis is effective for kernel optimization on NPUs; the wide speedup distribution motivates transparent reporting of system scope and limitations.

title: STEER: Steerable Dyadic Head Avatars
summary: Facial movement and expression are central to face-to-face communication, conveying turn-taking, attention, agreement, and engagement alongside speech. While speech-driven facial animation has made strong progress in lip synchronization and audio-conditioned motion generation, most methods treat conversational behavior as an emergent byproduct of audio, or expose only coarse sequence-level affect control. As a result, key non-verbal channels such as gaze contact and aversion, rhythmic head motion, and emotion remain difficult to explicitly control. We present STEER, a controllable 3D dyadic motion prior for reactive conversational head avatars. STEER factorizes conversational behavior into explicit controls for gaze, head rhythm, and emotion, allowing users to steer how an avatar listens, reacts, and engages with a conversation partner. Since temporally aligned annotations for these behaviors are not available in public dyadic corpora, we introduce a tracking and annotation pipeline that recovers behavioral pseudo-labels from in-the-wild dyadic video. A causal flow-matching transformer then learns partner-aware target motion conditioned on audio, partner motion, emotion and the proposed behavioral controls. We further embed STEER in a photorealistic avatar pipeline by extending a Universal Gaussian Head-Avatar Prior with a learned mapping from tracked parametric motion into its avatar-driving space. This enables controllable animation of high-fidelity Gaussian head avatars without re-training the underlying avatar model. STEER outperforms recent dyadic motion baselines on motion quality, dynamics, and diversity, remains competitive on partner coupling, and enables gaze, head-rhythm, and emotion edits together with an interactive live deployment. We make our code and dataset annotations available at our webpage.

AI.tldr: STEER is a controllable 3D dyadic motion prior for reactive conversational head avatars that explicitly factorizes conversational behavior into gaze, head rhythm, and emotion controls, enabling users to steer avatar listening and reacting. It uses a tracking/annotation pipeline for pseudo-labels from in-the-wild video, a causal flow-matching transformer for partner-aware motion generation, and integrates with a Gaussian head-avatar prior for high-fidelity animation without retraining.
AI.motivation: Existing speech-driven facial animation methods treat conversational behavior as an emergent byproduct of audio or offer only coarse sequence-level affect control, making it difficult to explicitly control key non-verbal channels such as gaze contact/aversion, rhythmic head motion, and emotion in dyadic interactions.
AI.method: (1) A tracking and annotation pipeline that recovers behavioral pseudo-labels from in-the-wild dyadic video; (2) A causal flow-matching transformer that learns partner-aware target motion conditioned on audio, partner motion, emotion, and behavioral controls; (3) Integration with a Universal Gaussian Head-Avatar Prior via a learned mapping from tracked parametric motion to avatar-driving space for controllable high-fidelity animation without retraining.
AI.result: STEER outperforms recent dyadic motion baselines on motion quality, dynamics, and diversity, remains competitive on partner coupling, and enables gaze, head-rhythm, and emotion edits with interactive live deployment.
AI.conclusion: Explicit factorization of non-verbal conversational behaviors (gaze, head rhythm, emotion) into controllable priors is feasible and achieves superior motion quality while enabling fine-grained editing and interactive avatar control, without sacrificing partner coupling performance.

title: On the post-hoc Evaluation of PDE Discovery: A Multifaceted Challenge of Scientific Advancement
summary: Partial differential equation (PDE) discovery aims to identify from data the governing law of a physical system. Constituting a cornerstone of scientific advancement, it has become during the past decade a major line of research in the rapidly evolving field of Physics-informed Machine Learning (PiML). Among the remaining open problems to address in this domain, the post-hoc evaluation of discovered PDEs raises the particular difficulty of being multifaceted. Indeed, it requires jointly considering predictive accuracy, physical consistency, interpretability, and out-of-distribution generalization capacity. Given that some of these properties are conflicting, it is worth noting that the wide range of existing evaluation metrics only partially address the overall problem, potentially leading to overly interpreted conclusions about the validity of a presumed new physical theory. From an abundant literature spanning machine learning, numerical analysis, information theory or symbolic regression, we propose, to our knowledge, the first taxonomy of PDE evaluation metrics, and discuss their advantages and limitations in depth. Based on the observation that evaluation is often achieved on a case-by-case basis and that a universally accepted methodology remains elusive, we further provide recommendations with the aim of promoting standardized and reliable practices, before sketching promising future lines of research in this field. We argue that this paper is intended both for ML experts who design new PDE discovery algorithms and for users of these methods aiming, in real applications, to discover and validate well-founded scientific laws.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first taxonomy of evaluation metrics for PDE discovery, analyzing their advantages and limitations across multiple dimensions (predictive accuracy, physical consistency, interpretability, OOD generalization), and provides recommendations for standardized evaluation practices in Physics-informed Machine Learning.
AI.motivation: The post-hoc evaluation of discovered PDEs is inherently multifaceted and involves conflicting properties (accuracy, physical consistency, interpretability, generalization). Existing metrics only partially address the problem, leading to potentially misleading conclusions about discovered physical laws.
AI.method: The authors conduct a literature review spanning machine learning, numerical analysis, information theory, and symbolic regression to systematically categorize PDE evaluation metrics into a taxonomy. They analyze the pros and cons of each metric class and provide recommendations for standardized evaluation.
AI.result: The first taxonomy of PDE evaluation metrics is proposed, along with an in-depth discussion of their limitations in jointly addressing predictive accuracy, physical consistency, interpretability, and out-of-distribution generalization. The paper identifies that evaluation is often case-by-case with no universally accepted methodology.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides actionable recommendations for standardized and reliable PDE evaluation practices and outlines future research directions, aiming to serve both ML algorithm designers and domain scientists who apply PDE discovery.

title: SQBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Task Delivery by Language-Model Agents in Production-Oriented Workflows
comment: 17 pages, 8 figures. Code and aggregate results: https://github.com/shaqiu-ai/SQBench
summary: Existing evaluations of large language models cover knowledge, reasoning, coding, and tool use, but they rarely treat a verifiable deliverable produced within a constrained workflow as the unit of evaluation. We introduce SQBench, a benchmark for evaluating production-oriented task delivery by language-model agents. SQBench v1.0 contains 220 standardized tasks organized into L1 atomic capabilities, L2 composite skills, and L3 business scenarios. Each task requires an agent to process input assets, use available tools, and produce an explicitly specified deliverable. The evaluation first computes functional Completion and then derives Risk Penalty and Performance from independently evidenced triggers in a 10D Risk Matrix. A Strict Pass requires Completion = 1 and Risk Penalty = 0. We evaluate 27 model configurations under a common protocol, with one run per configuration-task pair. The highest prespecified Weighted Pass@1 is 60.5%. Mean Strict Pass@1 on L3 is 18.5%, and every configuration performs worse on L3 than on both L1 and L2, indicating that delivery under domain constraints is a shared weakness within the current task set. Of 2,348 results with Completion = 1, 113 (4.8%) fail the Strict Pass criterion because of risks such as unverifiable citations, inappropriate resource use, or format violations. These results show that functional completion alone does not fully characterize delivery quality and that risk determinations should be reported separately.

AI.tldr: SQBench is a benchmark with 220 tasks evaluating LLM agents on production-oriented deliverable generation. It uses a 10D Risk Matrix alongside functional Completion. On 27 model configs, highest Weighted Pass@1 is 60.5%, mean Strict Pass@1 on L3 is 18.5%, and 4.8% of functionally complete outputs fail due to risk issues.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM evaluations rarely treat verifiable deliverables within constrained workflows as the unit of evaluation; SQBench fills this gap by assessing production-oriented task delivery.
AI.method: 220 tasks across L1 (atomic), L2 (composite), and L3 (business scenarios). Evaluation computes functional Completion, then derives Risk Penalty and Performance from a 10D Risk Matrix. Strict Pass requires Completion=1 and Risk Penalty=0. 27 model configs evaluated under a common protocol with one run per pair.
AI.result: Highest prespecified Weighted Pass@1 is 60.5%. Mean Strict Pass@1 on L3 is 18.5%, lower than L1 and L2 across all configs. Of 2,348 functionally complete results, 113 (4.8%) fail Strict Pass due to unverifiable citations, inappropriate resource use, or format violations.
AI.conclusion: Functional completion alone does not fully characterize delivery quality; risk determinations should be reported separately. Delivery under domain constraints is a shared weakness among current models.

title: OmniCache: Multidimensional Hierarchical Feature Caching For Diffusion Models
summary: High-resolution image and video diffusion models, including SD3, FLUX, and recent video diffusion transformers, have substantially improved generative quality but remain expensive at inference time because they repeatedly evaluate attention-heavy denoisers over many sampling steps. We address this inefficiency by exploiting redundancy in intermediate diffusion features rather than changing model weights or retraining. We identify four complementary redundancy sources in image and video generation: intra-frame, inter-frame, motion, and denoising-step redundancy. Based on this analysis, we propose OmniCache, a unified hierarchical caching framework that performs multidimensional feature reuse through Token Cache, Frame Cache, Block Cache, and Layered Cache. Unlike token-merging baselines that average matched features, OmniCache uses similarity matching to select cacheable features, skips redundant computation, and restores positionally consistent cached activations, preserving feature order and spatial-temporal structure. The resulting framework reuses spatial features in temporal layers and temporal features in spatial layers, while Layered Cache captures cross-step redundancy at the model-layer level. Across SD3, SVD-XT, and Latte, OmniCache reduces inference latency by up to 35%, 25%, and 28%, respectively, while maintaining visual fidelity and motion coherence in a training-free setting.

AI.tldr: OmniCache is a training-free hierarchical caching framework that exploits four types of redundancy (intra-frame, inter-frame, motion, denoising-step) in diffusion models to reuse intermediate features, reducing inference latency by up to 35% on SD3, 25% on SVD-XT, and 28% on Latte while maintaining visual quality.
AI.motivation: High-resolution image/video diffusion models (SD3, FLUX, video diffusion transformers) achieve high generative quality but suffer from expensive inference due to repeated evaluation of attention-heavy denoisers across many sampling steps.
AI.method: OmniCache is a unified hierarchical caching framework with four components: Token Cache (intra-frame), Frame Cache (inter-frame), Block Cache (motion), and Layered Cache (denoising-step). It uses similarity matching to select cacheable features, skips redundant computation, and restores positionally consistent cached activations, preserving feature order and spatial-temporal structure.
AI.result: On SD3, SVD-XT, and Latte, OmniCache reduces inference latency by up to 35%, 25%, and 28% respectively, while maintaining visual fidelity and motion coherence in a training-free setting.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting multidimensional redundancy via hierarchical caching is an effective training-free approach to accelerate diffusion model inference without sacrificing generation quality.

title: WISERouter: LLM Routing with Workload Budget Constraint
summary: Large language models (LLMs) achieve impressive performance across multiple domains, but using the most capable model for every query is prohibitive at scale. LLM routing exploits diversity in model capability and cost by assigning each query to a suitable model to balance utility and budget. Current methods have two limitations: (i) they either use heuristics that do not always enforce the budget constraint or impose a fixed per-query budget that cannot adapt across the workload and leads to suboptimal performance; (ii) they require supervised learning on a dense dataset with statistics for every query-model pair, which is expensive to collect. To address these challenges, we formulate LLM routing as a constrained contextual multi-armed bandit problem and introduce WISERouter (WR for short), a framework that supports offline learning from historical interactions as well as online learning with exploration. We further prove that WR-Online achieves a sublinear regret bound of $O(\sqrt{T})$ over a time horizon $T$. Empirical results on RouterBench and SWE-Bench demonstrate that (i) WR-Offline surpasses existing baselines in performance under a fixed budget and adheres more closely to budget constraints, and (ii) WR-Online achieves comparable performance to the baselines, while using substantially less exploration data.

AI.tldr: WISERouter (WR) is a framework for LLM routing that formulates the problem as a constrained contextual multi-armed bandit, supporting both offline learning from historical data and online learning with exploration, achieving sublinear regret and outperforming baselines on RouterBench and SWE-Bench under budget constraints.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM routing methods either use heuristics that fail to enforce budget constraints or require expensive dense supervised datasets with query-model pair statistics, making them impractical at scale.
AI.method: Formulates LLM routing as a constrained contextual multi-armed bandit problem. Proposes WISERouter (WR) with two variants: WR-Offline for offline learning from historical interactions, and WR-Online for online learning with exploration. Provides theoretical regret bound analysis for WR-Online.
AI.result: WR-Offline surpasses existing baselines in performance under fixed budget while adhering more closely to budget constraints. WR-Online achieves comparable performance to baselines using substantially less exploration data. WR-Online has a sublinear regret bound of O(√T).
AI.conclusion: The proposed WISERouter framework effectively addresses the limitations of prior LLM routing methods by balancing utility and budget without requiring expensive dense datasets, and is validated on RouterBench and SWE-Bench.

title: AgentOmnia: Scaling Agentic Models for Full-Scenario Applications
summary: Large language model agents have advanced rapidly, yet progress remains fragmented across domains, capabilities, task difficulty, and interaction settings. We frame this as full-scenario agentic scaling and present AgentOmnia, a framework coordinating task-space definition, data synthesis, post-training, evaluation, and improvement across To-Consumer (ToC), To-Business (ToB), and To-Employee (ToE) applications. An extensible Domain x Capability x Atomic Difficulty taxonomy aligns these stages and enables fine-grained diagnosis with OmniaBench. AgentOmnia combines bidirectional environment-task synthesis with tool-dependency, program-structured, and solver-based pipelines, constructing 5,018 stateful environments with 255,375 tools and 52,361 tasks. Programs, solvers, and verifiers provide correctness signals, while supervised fine-tuning, online agentic reinforcement learning, and a rollback curriculum support post-training. Evaluation failures translate into Product Requirement Documents (PRDs) for targeted self-evolution. Starting from Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507, AgentOmnia raises the pass rate on the OmniaBench challenging subset from 9.16% to 37.11% and the macro-average across OmniaBench, $τ^2$-Bench, DeepPlanning, and VitaBench from 22.86% to 41.69%. Under a unified protocol,it leads the evaluated agentic post-trained baselines on OmniaBench and retains the highest four-benchmark macro-average. It also surpasses Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking-2507 on all four benchmarks and exceeds Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on the macro-average. Gains span three application splits, ten capability dimensions, eight atomic-difficulty factors, and 76 of 90 level-1 domains, indicating broad rather than category-specific improvement. A one-round study provides initial evidence for PRD-guided self-evolution, motivating validation at larger scales and in industrial settings.

AI.tldr: AgentOmnia is a unified framework for full-scenario agentic scaling that coordinates task-space definition, data synthesis, post-training, evaluation, and self-evolution across ToC, ToB, and ToE applications. Starting from Qwen3-30B-A3B, it raises challenging pass rate from 9.16% to 37.11% and macro-average across four benchmarks from 22.86% to 41.69%, surpassing much larger models.
AI.motivation: Progress in large language model agents remains fragmented across domains, capabilities, task difficulty, and interaction settings, lacking a unified framework to coordinate development across the full spectrum of real-world applications (ToC, ToB, ToE).
