AI.method: AgentOmnia uses a Domain x Capability x Atomic Difficulty taxonomy to align task-space definition, data synthesis, post-training, evaluation, and improvement. It combines bidirectional environment-task synthesis with three pipeline types (tool-dependency, program-structured, solver-based), constructing 5,018 environments with 255,375 tools and 52,361 tasks. Post-training employs SFT, online agentic RL, and rollback curriculum. Evaluation failures are translated into PRDs for self-evolution.
AI.result: Pass rate on OmniaBench challenging subset rises from 9.16% to 37.11%; macro-average across OmniaBench, τ²-Bench, DeepPlanning, and VitaBench from 22.86% to 41.69%. Surpasses Qwen3-235B-A22B on all four benchmarks and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on macro-average. Gains span 3 application splits, 10 capabilities, 8 difficulty factors, and 76/90 level-1 domains.
AI.conclusion: AgentOmnia demonstrates broad rather than category-specific improvement through its unified framework. A one-round study provides initial evidence for PRD-guided self-evolution, motivating further validation at larger scales and in industrial settings.

title: A Comparison of Data Augmentation Methods for Training Deep Neural Networks on Synthetic Aperture Sonar
comment: This paper was originally published in the proceedings of the International Conference on Underwater Acoustics 2026
summary: In this work we study Automatic Target Recognition (ATR) for Synthetic Aperture Sonar (SAS) data with a focus on deep neural networks (DNNs). The main challenge in training DNNs for SAS ATR arises from the limited quantity of labeled target examples, which arises due to the significant costs and time required to collect real-world SAS data. One successful general strategy for mitigating the problem of limited training data is augmentation, which generates additional synthetic training data by introducing realistic variations to available real-world data. Prior research has investigated a variety of augmentation strategies for SAS ATR, including conventional image augmentations (e.g., contrast changes, cropping) as well as physics-based augmentations, which are motivated the specific physics of SAS data. Building on prior work, we systematically compare many of these existing augmentation strategies for training DNNs for SAS ATR. We also investigate the impact of augmentation when combined with modern DNN architectures such as transformers. The results indicate that augmentation can improve target recognition accuracy, although benefits vary, and not all augmentations are beneficial.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically compares various augmentation strategies (conventional and physics-based) for training deep neural networks on limited Synthetic Aperture Sonar data for Automatic Target Recognition, finding that augmentation improves accuracy but benefits vary across strategies and architectures like transformers.
AI.motivation: Limited labeled SAS target examples due to high data collection costs hinder DNN training; augmentation is a promising mitigation strategy that needs systematic comparison.
AI.method: Systematically compare conventional image augmentations and physics-based augmentations for training DNNs (including transformer architectures) on SAS ATR tasks.
AI.result: Augmentation improves target recognition accuracy, but not all augmentations are equally beneficial; benefits vary across strategies and architectures.
AI.conclusion: Augmentation is effective for SAS ATR with limited data, but careful selection of augmentation strategies is necessary as some may not be beneficial.

title: Long-Tailed Medical Image Classification
summary: In this paper, we examine the difficulties of using standard techniques for medical image classification due to long-tailed distributions (wherein rarer conditions have very few samples) resulting in bias towards diagnosing common diseases and away from rarer diseases. We then discuss and implement deep learning models with techniques such as augmentation to minimize error, especially from rarer diseases. We evaluate various different models with AP, F1 score, AUROC, and loss (all on the validation set). We conclude with the promising results from our best model, and potential applications in the healthcare space.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the challenge of long-tailed distributions in medical image classification, where rare diseases have few samples, leading to bias towards common diseases. The authors implement deep learning models with augmentation techniques to minimize errors, especially for rare diseases, and evaluate using AP, F1, AUROC, and loss metrics. Their best model shows promising results for healthcare applications.
AI.motivation: Standard medical image classification techniques struggle with long-tailed distributions, where rare conditions have limited samples, causing models to be biased toward diagnosing common diseases while underperforming on rare diseases.
AI.method: Deep learning models with augmentation techniques were implemented to mitigate errors from rare disease samples. Models were evaluated using Average Precision (AP), F1 score, AUROC, and loss on the validation set.
AI.result: The best model achieved promising results, demonstrating improved performance on rare disease classification as measured by AP, F1, AUROC, and loss.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach with augmentation techniques shows promise for addressing long-tail issues in medical image classification, with potential applications in healthcare for improving diagnosis of rare diseases.

title: Scale Weight Decay and Train Better
summary: The discovery of scaling laws has motivated training neural networks on ever increasing quantities of data. This is typically done with a constant decoupled weight decay which causes the network weights to shrink steadily over the course of training. Taking inspiration from the Robbins--Monro conditions, we propose to scale weight decay by the fraction of the peak learning rate $η/η_{\max}$. We prove that this scaled weight decay preserves the asymptotic stationarity guarantees of the corresponding unregularized methods for both stochastic gradient descent and the non-Euclidean spectral optimizer Muon, thereby avoiding the additional asymptotic bias introduced by constant decoupled weight decay. This retains the stability benefits of weight decay without changing the asymptotic optimization target. Using a steady-state analysis, we explain why under standard weight decay the weight norm shrinks steadily as training proceeds, whereas under scaled weight decay it settles to a roughly constant value. When applied to the training of mixture-of-experts models, Muon with scaled weight decay (Muon-SW) consistently outpaces Muon with identical hyperparameters, reaching the same validation loss $\mathbf{30\%}$ faster at our largest scale across models from $72 - 930$ million parameters trained at $\sim 600$ tokens per active parameter. If this trend continues to hold, the method promises to substantially accelerate the pre-training of frontier models while requiring only a few lines of code to implement.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes scaling weight decay by the fraction of the peak learning rate (η/η_max), inspired by Robbins-Monro conditions, which preserves asymptotic stationarity guarantees and avoids bias introduced by constant decoupled weight decay. Applied to Muon optimizer for mixture-of-experts models, it achieves 30% faster convergence to the same validation loss across 72M-930M parameter models.
AI.motivation: Standard constant decoupled weight decay causes network weights to shrink steadily over training, introducing asymptotic bias and deviating from the unregularized optimization target. The authors aim to eliminate this bias while retaining weight decay's stability benefits.
AI.method: Scale weight decay by the fraction of the peak learning rate η/η_max, satisfying Robbins-Monro conditions. The authors provide theoretical proofs of asymptotic stationarity for both SGD and the non-Euclidean spectral optimizer Muon, and use steady-state analysis to explain weight norm behavior.
AI.result: Muon with scaled weight decay (Muon-SW) reaches the same validation loss 30% faster than Muon with identical hyperparameters across models from 72M to 930M parameters trained at ~600 tokens per active parameter.
AI.conclusion: Scaled weight decay preserves asymptotic guarantees of unregularized methods, avoids bias, and substantially accelerates pre-training of mixture-of-experts models with minimal implementation overhead.

title: An Ontology for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
summary: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) approximate quantum-mechanical energies and forces---conventionally computed by density functional theory (DFT) or wave-function methods---at a fraction of the cost. The field encompasses a growing ecosystem of algorithms, training datasets, hyperparameters, and target materials, yet the metadata needed to systematically compare, reproduce, and build upon MLIP studies remains scattered across papers, scripts, and ad-hoc file formats. We present the MLIPs ontology, an OWL 2 DL ontology that captures the concepts needed to describe MLIP methods, their hyperparameters, training datasets with DFT provenance, and published benchmarks. The ontology is organized into three modules---Method, Training Data, and Benchmark---and connects existing ontologies in materials science (MDO, CMSO/ASMO) and machine learning (ML-Schema), complementing dataset-side schemas such as Croissant. It declares 27 formal axioms enforcing data completeness and consistency, including property chains that link trained models to their methods and training data. We demonstrate the ontology through a running example based on Moment Tensor Potentials and evaluate it through competency-question execution on a 20-paper seeded knowledge graph, OWL reasoning, and comparison with existing ontologies.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the MLIPs ontology, an OWL 2 DL ontology for systematically describing machine learning interatomic potentials, including their methods, hyperparameters, training datasets, and benchmarks, with formal axioms and modular design to improve reproducibility and comparability.
AI.motivation: Metadata needed to systematically compare, reproduce, and build upon MLIP studies is scattered across papers, scripts, and ad-hoc file formats, hindering progress in the field.
AI.method: The authors developed the MLIPs ontology as an OWL 2 DL ontology organized into three modules (Method, Training Data, Benchmark), integrating existing ontologies (MDO, CMSO/ASMO, ML-Schema), and declaring 27 formal axioms including property chains to enforce data completeness and consistency.
AI.result: Demonstrated through a Moment Tensor Potentials running example and evaluated via competency-question execution on a 20-paper seeded knowledge graph, OWL reasoning, and comparison with existing ontologies.
AI.conclusion: The MLIPs ontology provides a structured, formal framework for describing MLIP studies, enabling systematic comparison, reproducibility, and building upon prior work.

title: Embeddings based Anomaly Detection for Cleaning Global Crop Type Reference Datasets
summary:
High quality reference data remain a critical bottleneck for crop-type mapping at any spatial and temporal scale. Operational systems such as WorldCereal aggregate labels from heterogeneous sources such as parcel registers, national databases, field surveys, and map-derived products, each with their own biases, coverage gaps and unknown label noise. Simple global rules are inadequate, since crop phenology and observation conditions vary strongly across regions and seasons.
  In this study, we focus on a single, operationally relevant question: whether embeddings produced through geospatial foundation models are a viable basis for cleaning the reference data. We propose a practical, locality-aware, embedding-based anomaly (EBA) detection framework that operates on the embeddings of a pretrained Earth-observation encoder. We score each labelled sample against other samples of the same crop in the same area using a pretrained embedding, flag the ones that stand out, and test whether removing or down-weighting them before training yields a better model.
  We establish that the flagged points are genuinely mislabelled or misplaced in two independent ways: against synthetic ground truth, the detector concentrates injected label errors 2.5-5x above chance in its flagged set (detection AUROC up to 0.84); and on real data, a model-independent test shows that removing or confidence-weighting the flagged held-out points raises measured accuracy in trained models, for both crop type and land cover. Acting on the flags then improves the WorldCereal crop-type model across five macro-regions, evaluated on a fixed held-out split under three views. We find conservative cleaning helps while over-cleaning hurts.
  The EBA detector approach is designed to be reproducible and extensible, and can serve as a template for cleaning large, noisy Earth observation reference datasets beyond crop mapping.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an embedding-based anomaly (EBA) detection framework that leverages pretrained geospatial foundation models to clean noisy reference data for crop-type mapping. By flagging samples that are anomalous in embedding space compared to same-class samples in the same region, and then removing or down-weighting them before training, the method improves WorldCereal crop-type model accuracy across five macro-regions, with flagged points showing 2.5-5x concentration of synthetic label errors and detection AUROC up to 0.84.
AI.motivation: High-quality reference data for crop-type mapping remain scarce and noisy, as operational systems like WorldCereal aggregate labels from heterogeneous sources (parcel registers, field surveys, map-derived products) with unknown biases and label noise. Simple global rules fail due to varying crop phenology and observation conditions across regions and seasons.
AI.method: A locality-aware, embedding-based anomaly (EBA) detection framework that uses embeddings from a pretrained Earth-observation encoder. Each labeled sample is scored against other samples of the same crop in the same area using the pretrained embedding; samples that stand out are flagged. The framework then tests whether removing or down-weighting these flagged samples before training improves the model.
AI.result: Flagged points concentrate injected label errors 2.5-5x above chance (detection AUROC up to 0.84). On real data, removing or confidence-weighting flagged held-out points raises measured accuracy in trained models for both crop type and land cover. The WorldCereal crop-type model improved across five macro-regions, though conservative cleaning helps while over-cleaning hurts.
AI.conclusion: The EBA detector approach is reproducible and extensible, and can serve as a template for cleaning large, noisy Earth observation reference datasets beyond crop mapping.

title: SCTA: An Agentic Framework for Stable and Interpretable Target Gene Discovery from Single-Cell RNA Sequencing
comment: 10 pages, 4 figures. To appear in the ACM SIGKDD Workshop on Data Mining in Bioinformatics (BioKDD 2026)
summary: Identifying therapeutic target genes from single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data remains a fundamental challenge in translational biology. Unlike bulk assays, scRNA-seq captures heterogeneous cellular states and rare subpopulations, but this same heterogeneity makes target discovery highly sensitive to analytical choices throughout the pipeline, including preprocessing, cell population selection, differential expression analysis, and downstream biological interpretation. As a result, existing workflows and general-purpose analysis agents often produce unstable or difficult-to-interpret target hypotheses, limiting their reliability for disease-focused discovery. We present SCTA (Single-Cell Target Agent), a decision-centric agentic framework for stable and interpretable target gene discovery from scRNA-seq data. Rather than treating analysis as a single general-purpose reasoning task, SCTA decomposes target discovery into specialized agents aligned with key decision points in the single-cell pipeline and constrains downstream reasoning with structured biological evidence. In a representative ablation study on hereditary chronic pancreatitis, we demonstrate that SCTA's full evidence integration yields the most stable target selection across independent runs among the tested configurations, while recovering biologically coherent, disease-relevant mechanisms validated in prior studies. These results suggest that decision-aware agent orchestration tailored to the structure of single-cell analysis can improve the robustness, interpretability, and practical utility of target discovery in precision medicine.

AI.tldr: SCTA is a decision-centric agentic framework that decomposes target gene discovery from scRNA-seq data into specialized agents aligned with key analytical decision points, improving stability and interpretability over general-purpose approaches.
AI.motivation: Identifying therapeutic target genes from scRNA-seq data is challenging due to cellular heterogeneity and high sensitivity to analytical choices across the pipeline, leading to unstable or difficult-to-interpret target hypotheses in existing workflows and general-purpose analysis agents.
AI.method: SCTA decomposes target discovery into specialized agents aligned with key decision points in the single-cell pipeline (preprocessing, cell population selection, differential expression, biological interpretation) and constrains downstream reasoning with structured biological evidence, rather than treating analysis as a single general-purpose reasoning task.
AI.result: In an ablation study on hereditary chronic pancreatitis, SCTA with full evidence integration achieved the most stable target selection across independent runs among tested configurations, and recovered biologically coherent, disease-relevant mechanisms validated in prior studies.
AI.conclusion: Decision-aware agent orchestration tailored to the structure of single-cell analysis can improve the robustness, interpretability, and practical utility of target gene discovery in precision medicine.

title: Characterisation of Density-based FM generation methods in the context of Information Fusion
summary: Fuzzy Integral (FI) based aggregation provides a powerful mechanism for nuanced aggregation, for example, in ensemble approaches or decision-level fusion more generally. The main challenge of this approach is the appropriate parametrization of the Fuzzy Measure (FM), which captures the worths of the individual components--and their combinations--which are being fused. Here, widely used approaches including the Sugeno-$λ$ and Decomposable FMs, parametrize the FM by extrapolating from the densities, i.e. the weights associated with individual sources, while respecting the FM's monotonicity constraint. This paper articulates that this information is, in general, insufficient to uniquely identify a discrete FM; but shows how an interval-valued FM can indeed be determined uniquely. We proceed to show how the incorporation of additional information beyond the above, such as the choice of a specific FI and a dataset, then allows for obtaining even more specific interval-valued FMs. In practice, establishing the quality of an empirically determined FM is not trivial. To help address this, we show how the likelihood with which a resulting interval FM encompasses the `ideal', i.e. the commonly intangible, best, or ground-truth numeric FM, can be determined, producing a confidence interval at a given confidence level. Finally, based on a series of experiments, we demonstrate empirically that the Choquet FI output based on this FM can also be regarded as the confidence interval for the `ideal' information fusion result, providing a novel means to characterize FI fusion outcomes a priori and charting a pathway for future research.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that density information alone is insufficient to uniquely determine a discrete Fuzzy Measure (FM) for Fuzzy Integral (FI) aggregation, but can produce a unique interval-valued FM. Additional information (FI choice, dataset) refines the interval, and a confidence interval for the "ideal" FM can be derived. Experiments demonstrate the Choquet FI output can be interpreted as a confidence interval for ideal fusion results.
AI.motivation: The main challenge in Fuzzy Integral-based aggregation is properly parameterizing the Fuzzy Measure, which captures the importance of individual sources and their combinations. Existing approaches (e.g., Sugeno-λ, Decomposable FMs) extrapolate from source densities while respecting monotonicity, but it was unclear whether this information is sufficient to uniquely determine the FM.
AI.method: The paper first proves that density information alone is insufficient for unique FM identification but is sufficient for a unique interval-valued FM. Then it shows how additional information (specific FI choice, dataset) yields more specific interval-valued FMs. A statistical method is developed to determine the likelihood that the interval FM contains the "ideal" (ground truth) numeric FM, producing confidence intervals at a given confidence level.
AI.result: A unique interval-valued FM can be determined from densities alone, and incorporating extra information refines the interval. The confidence interval for encompassing the ideal FM is established. Experiments show that the Choquet FI output based on this interval FM corresponds to a confidence interval for the ideal fusion result.
AI.conclusion: Density information alone yields an interval-valued FM rather than a unique numeric one, but this interval can be statistically characterized. The Choquet FI output from such an FM can be interpreted as a confidence interval for ideal fusion, providing a novel framework for characterizing FI fusion outcomes a priori and guiding future research.

title: SimBEV2X: A Large-Scale Dataset and Data Generation Tool for Multi-Task Vehicle-to-Everything Cooperative Perception
summary: Cooperative perception through vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communication can overcome the inherent physical limitations of individual autonomous vehicles, such as occlusions and limited sensor range. However, the development of robust V2X algorithms, particularly those relying on unified spatial representations like bird's-eye view (BEV) representation, is hampered by the lack of large-scale, multi-modal, multi-task datasets. Moreover, collecting and annotating a large set of synchronized, real-world multi-agent data is prohibitively expensive. This has resulted in a landscape where existing V2X datasets are notably limited in both size and scope. To overcome this, we introduce SimBEV2X, an advanced synthetic data generation tool built on the CARLA simulator. SimBEV2X automatically creates randomized driving scenarios to collect multi-modal sensor data alongside various types of ground truth including 3D bounding boxes with unique track IDs, HD map information, BEV segmentation maps, and semantic occupancy voxel grids from both vehicles and RSUs. We also present the SimBEV2X dataset, the largest V2X perception dataset to date. The dataset comprises 258 scenes, each involving up to 8 connected vehicles and up to 4 RSUs across a variety of road networks. The SimBEV2X dataset is an order of magnitude larger than existing V2X datasets and contains 102,200 frames, 588,520 lidar point clouds, more than 3 million images, over 27 million bounding boxes, and a comprehensive set of other annotations. Finally, we establish a strong baseline on the SimBEV2X dataset using CoopDet3D and propose CoBEVFusion, a novel architecture that combines CoopDet3D with fused axial attention (FAX) for context-aware multi-agent feature aggregation, resulting in superior performance. SimBEV2X, the SimBEV2X dataset, and CoBEVFusion are available at https://simbev2x.org and https://github.com/GoodarzMehr/SimBEV2X.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces SimBEV2X, a synthetic data generation tool and the largest V2X perception dataset to date (258 scenes, 102K frames, 3M+ images, 27M+ bounding boxes) built on CARLA, along with a novel CoBEVFusion architecture using fused axial attention for context-aware multi-agent feature aggregation.
AI.motivation: The development of robust V2X cooperative perception algorithms (especially BEV-based) is limited by the lack of large-scale, multi-modal, multi-task datasets, as real-world multi-agent data collection and annotation is prohibitively expensive.
AI.method: SimBEV2X is built on CARLA to automatically generate randomized driving scenarios with multi-modal sensor data and diverse ground truth annotations. CoBEVFusion combines CoopDet3D with fused axial attention (FAX) for context-aware multi-agent feature aggregation.
AI.result: The SimBEV2X dataset is an order of magnitude larger than existing V2X datasets: 258 scenes, up to 8 connected vehicles and 4 RSUs, 102,200 frames, 588,520 LiDAR point clouds, over 3 million images, and over 27 million bounding boxes.
AI.conclusion: SimBEV2X, the accompanying dataset, and CoBEVFusion provide a comprehensive framework and strong baseline for advancing V2X cooperative perception research.

title: DriveDNA: A Large-Scale Multimodal Naturalistic Driving Dataset and Benchmark for Driving Style Identification
summary: Driving style captures stable, driver-specific patterns in how a vehicle is driven. In naturalistic data, however, this signal is hard to isolate because drivers are observed in different vehicles, on different roads, and under different conditions, so models may mistake vehicle- or situation-specific regularities for driver-specific style. We introduce DriveDNA, a large-scale naturalistic dataset and benchmark for personalized driving-style modeling, comprising 4,121 drives from 465 drivers across 115 vehicle models and totaling 975 hours of human-controlled driving at 10 Hz with forward video, collected from community drivers in everyday use. DriveDNA defines driving style as a consistent, driver-specific behavioral pattern in how a vehicle moves under similar conditions. The benchmark evaluates this signal through three core tasks: few-shot driver re-identification, personalized behavior prediction, and condition-matched comparison, and provides behavioral annotations plus 276,248 rule-generated maneuver events across six classes with large-scale human auditing. We evaluate baselines spanning classical descriptors, supervised and self-supervised time-series encoders, multimodal fusion, probabilistic prediction, and zero-shot foundation models under a fixed multi-seed protocol. Learned representations substantially outperform classical descriptors on unseen drivers (AUROC .935 vs. .707) and retain driver-specific information under matched driving conditions, while descriptor performance approaches chance. Video-only models achieve comparable re-identification accuracy but exhibit severe route leakage, showing that strong recognition may arise from contextual shortcuts rather than driving behavior. These findings show that reliable driving-style evaluation must assess both the behavioral value of learned representations and their robustness to vehicle, drive, and condition confounds.

AI.tldr: DriveDNA is a large-scale naturalistic driving dataset (4,121 drives, 465 drivers, 115 vehicle models, 975 hours) with a benchmark for personalized driving-style modeling. It defines driving style as driver-specific behavioral patterns under similar conditions, evaluates through three tasks (few-shot re-identification, behavior prediction, condition-matched comparison), and finds that learned representations outperform classical descriptors (AUROC .935 vs .707) while video-only models suffer from route leakage, emphasizing the need to assess behavioral value and robustness to confounds.
AI.motivation: Driving style signals are hard to isolate in naturalistic data because drivers are observed across different vehicles, roads, and conditions, causing models to mistakenly attribute vehicle- or situation-specific regularities to driver-specific style. There is a lack of large-scale benchmarks designed to disentangle these confounds.
AI.method: The paper introduces DriveDNA, a dataset of 4,121 drives from 465 drivers across 115 vehicle models (975 hours, 10 Hz, with forward video). Three core tasks are defined: few-shot driver re-identification, personalized behavior prediction, and condition-matched comparison. Behavioral annotations and 276,248 rule-generated maneuver events across six classes (with human auditing) are provided. Baselines include classical descriptors, supervised/self-supervised time-series encoders, multimodal fusion, probabilistic prediction, and zero-shot foundation models under a fixed multi-seed protocol.
AI.result: Learned representations substantially outperform classical descriptors on unseen drivers (AUROC .935 vs .707) and retain driver-specific information under matched driving conditions, while descriptor performance approaches chance. Video-only models achieve comparable re-identification accuracy but exhibit severe route leakage, indicating that strong recognition may arise from contextual shortcuts rather than driving behavior.
AI.conclusion: Reliable driving-style evaluation must assess both the behavioral value of learned representations and their robustness to vehicle, drive, and condition confounds.

title: CAPT: A Multi-task Continuous Autoregressive Transformer enabling Cross-dataset and Cross-species Transfer for Calcium Population Dynamics
summary: Large-scale calcium imaging has created an opportunity to build foundation-style models for neural population dynamics, but a central question remains unresolved: \textbf{whether a model pretrained on one collection of recordings can generalize to new datasets, experimental paradigms, and even species.} Existing approaches are often designed for specific tasks and evaluated on a single dataset, making it unclear whether their learned representations are reusable for new calcium trace datasets. To tackle this gap, we present \textbf{CAPT}, a \textbf{C}ontinuous \textbf{A}utoregressive \textbf{P}opulation \textbf{T}ransformer for calcium population dynamics. CAPT models continuous calcium traces directly through a continuous patch tokenization strategy and is trained autoregressively, enabling end-to-end pretraining and adaptation to diverse downstream tasks. We first pretrain CAPT on a large-scale mouse calcium imaging dataset and evaluate its transferability across independent mouse, larval zebrafish, and \textit{C. elegans} datasets collected by different laboratories. In these transfer settings, the pretrained backbone is frozen and only adaptation modules are updated. Across neural population forecasting and behavior decoding tasks, CAPT consistently outperforms specialized and general-purpose baselines. Alongside predictive performance, multimodal analyses using NeuroPAL annotations in \textit{C. elegans} datasets show that CAPT embeddings form a shared functional space across datasets and capture anatomical cell-identity-related structure. These results suggest that the continuous autoregressive modeling opens up possibilities for a simple route towards general-purpose neural foundation models for calcium imaging, which can generalize across datasets, experimental paradigms, and species.

AI.tldr: CAPT is a Continuous Autoregressive Population Transformer for calcium imaging that, after pretraining on mouse data, generalizes to multiple species (mice, zebrafish, C. elegans) across different labs, outperforming baselines in forecasting and behavior decoding while learning shared functional embeddings.
AI.motivation: A central question in calcium imaging foundation models is whether pretraining on one collection of recordings can generalize to new datasets, paradigms, and species. Existing approaches are task-specific and evaluated on single datasets, leaving reusability unclear.
AI.method: CAPT models continuous calcium traces via continuous patch tokenization and autoregressive training. It is pretrained on large-scale mouse data, then transferred to other species with a frozen backbone and updated adaptation modules.
AI.result: CAPT consistently outperforms specialized and general-purpose baselines across neural population forecasting and behavior decoding tasks in mice, zebrafish, and C. elegans. Multimodal analyses show CAPT embeddings form a shared functional space and capture anatomical cell-identity structure.
AI.conclusion: Continuous autoregressive modeling offers a simple route toward general-purpose neural foundation models for calcium imaging that generalize across datasets, experimental paradigms, and species.

title: Gaze-to-text Generation: Beyond Categorical Decoding of Human Attention
comment: To appear in European Conference on Computer Vision (ECCV) 2026
summary: We introduce a novel learning problem: decoding gaze into natural language descriptions of human goals across diverse visual tasks. Unlike prior work, which frames gaze decoding as a discriminative task over predefined categories, we formulate it as a generative learning problem: training a model to produce free-form descriptions that capture the rich nuances and open-ended nature of human intentions beyond fixed labels. To this end, we introduce Gazette, the first gaze-to-text decoding framework. Based on multimodal large language models (MLLMs), Gazette learns to decode gaze scanpaths into natural language for goals that may extend beyond categorical labels and require articulation in natural language. To help Gazette filter out individual differences in gaze behavior and learn the goal-specific spatiotemporal dynamics crucial for generating accurate natural language goal descriptions, we propose a novel strategy that leverages the encyclopedic knowledge and reasoning abilities of a large language model to synthesize natural language explanations of goal-directed attentional behavior called think-aloud transcripts. Instruction tuning on these synthetic narratives allows Gazette to achieve state-of-the-art performance in gaze decoding across multiple tasks, demonstrating its generalizability and versatility, thereby enabling gaze to serve as a powerful, non-intrusive cue for inferring human goals and intentions in diverse scenarios.

AI.tldr: Introduces Gazette, the first gaze-to-text decoding framework using multimodal large language models to generate free-form natural language descriptions of human goals from gaze scanpaths, outperforming prior discriminative approaches.
AI.motivation: Existing gaze decoding methods are limited to discriminative classification over predefined categories, failing to capture the rich, open-ended nature of human intentions. The authors aim to formulate gaze decoding as a generative problem that produces free-form natural language descriptions.
AI.method: (1) Gazette, a multimodal large language model (MLLM)-based framework for decoding gaze scanpaths into natural language. (2) A novel strategy using LLMs to synthesize think-aloud transcripts—natural language explanations of goal-directed attentional behavior—for instruction tuning to filter individual gaze differences and learn goal-specific spatiotemporal dynamics.
AI.result: State-of-the-art performance across multiple gaze decoding tasks, demonstrating generalizability and versatility.
AI.conclusion: Gazette establishes gaze as a powerful, non-intrusive cue for inferring human goals in diverse scenarios, moving beyond categorical labels to open-ended goal description generation.

title: Latent-LoRA: Compact Latent-Space Adapters with Gradient-Free Routing for Continual Learning
summary: Large language models generalize well to individual tasks but lack an inherent mechanism for learning them sequentially, leading to catastrophic forgetting. To mitigate this, LoRA-based continual learning methods allocate a separate low-rank adapter per task, yet existing approaches either require task identity at inference or sum all adapters indiscriminately, letting irrelevant branches distort the output. Recent gating-based solutions route inputs to the correct adapter but introduce trainable parameters that themselves need protection against forgetting. In this work, we observe that pooled token embeddings from a frozen LLM embedding layer already separate task distributions throughout the learning sequence. A Gaussian mixture model fitted on these embeddings, without any gradient-based training, is sufficient for task-agnostic adapter selection at test time. This eliminates the need for a learned gating module. On the adapter side, constraining each task's parameters to the principal subspace of the pretrained weights via SVD yields a compact latent-space parameterization. Within this subspace, orthogonal regularization directly controls inter-task interference. The resulting system, Latent-LoRA, is replay-free, requires no trainable routing component, and uses substantially fewer parameters per task. Experiments across five model scales and two established continual learning benchmarks show state-of-the-art performance with near-zero forgetting.

AI.tldr: Latent-LoRA is a replay-free continual learning method that uses a Gaussian mixture model on frozen LLM embeddings for task-agnostic adapter selection and SVD-based subspace constraints with orthogonal regularization to prevent inter-task interference, achieving state-of-the-art performance with near-zero forgetting.
AI.motivation: Large language models suffer from catastrophic forgetting when learning tasks sequentially, and existing LoRA-based continual learning methods either require task identity at inference, sum all adapters indiscriminately causing output distortion, or introduce trainable gating modules that themselves need protection against forgetting.
AI.method: (1) Uses pooled token embeddings from a frozen LLM embedding layer to separate task distributions; (2) Fits a Gaussian mixture model on these embeddings for task-agnostic adapter selection at test time without gradient-based training; (3) Constrains each task's LoRA parameters to the principal subspace of pretrained weights via SVD; (4) Applies orthogonal regularization within this subspace to control inter-task interference.
AI.result: Experiments across five model scales and two established continual learning benchmarks show state-of-the-art performance with near-zero forgetting.
AI.conclusion: The proposed Latent-LoRA eliminates the need for a learned gating module, requires no replay buffer, and uses substantially fewer parameters per task while achieving superior continual learning performance.

title: SeekJudge: A Practical Reward Framework for Reinforcement Learning in Computer-Use Agents
summary: Deciding whether a trajectory actually fulfills its instruction governs how we measure computer-use agents on long-horizon graphical-user-interface tasks and how we train them with reinforcement learning. This judgment has long relied on rule-based evaluation, which struggles to align with human intention and goes stale when an app updates or its online content drifts. Existing model-based judges attempt to address these problems but still leave a performance gap to the rule-based evaluation. We propose the \textbf{SeekJudge} framework, in which four role-specialized agents, a Condense, a Ground, a Seek and an Analyze agent, reach a verdict through a Seek--Analyze loop over the trajectory. A seed-calibrated distillation pipeline trains one specialized $9$B model to serve as the shared backbone for all four agents. Measured by downstream success rate on held-out RL test goals, SeekJudge is the first practical model-based reward to match or surpass native rule-based supervision in online RL. Beyond accuracy, SeekJudge provides step-level judgments, runs far cheaper than a closed-source large model, and keeps a small per-call context that scales to much longer trajectories. We further contribute a general architectural improvement to the reward server that speeds up judging in RL. Together these make model-based reward a practical drop-in for rule-based supervision in CUA reinforcement learning.

AI.tldr: SeekJudge is a model-based framework using four specialized agents (Condense, Ground, Seek, Analyze) with a shared 9B backbone to judge whether GUI trajectories fulfill instructions, achieving the first model-based reward that matches or surpasses rule-based supervision in online RL.
AI.motivation: Rule-based trajectory evaluation struggles to align with human intention and becomes stale with app updates or content drift, while existing model-based judges still underperform compared to rule-based evaluation.
AI.method: A framework with four role-specialized agents (Condense, Ground, Seek, Analyze) operating via a Seek-Analyze loop, trained through a seed-calibrated distillation pipeline with a shared 9B backbone model, plus a general architectural improvement to the reward server for faster RL judging.
AI.result: SeekJudge is the first practical model-based reward to match or surpass native rule-based supervision in online RL on held-out test goals, while providing step-level judgments, lower cost than closed-source LLMs, and small per-call context scaling to longer trajectories.
AI.conclusion: Model-based reward can now serve as a practical drop-in replacement for rule-based supervision in computer-use agent reinforcement learning.

title: What Can I Edit? Open-Ended Strategy Discovery and the Emotion Editability Landscape
summary: Emotional image editing requires more than applying affective filters or modifying predefined visual factors: an effective edit must identify what a particular image can afford for a target emotion. Existing affective image manipulation methods, including recent agentic variants, largely operate within bounded strategy spaces based on predefined factor taxonomies, knowledge libraries, or conventional editing templates, and therefore often miss image-specific, context-grounded strategies. We introduce EmoScope, a multi-agent framework that reframes the task from "how should I edit?" to "what can I edit?" EmoScope first discovers an image-specific editable space through emotion-conditioned affordance reasoning, then uses a semantic hierarchy of anchors, variables, and context to balance content consistency and emotional expressiveness before executing and verifying the edit. Because its plans are expressed as image-specific affordances rather than retrieved templates, EmoScope also exposes the editing strategy as an interactive surface for user refinement at the plan level. In a large-scale human evaluation covering all eight Mikels emotion categories, with 4,693 valid responses across 1,824 pairwise questions, participants preferred EmoScope over two competitive baselines by 88.1% on average. Attribution analysis further shows that EmoScope selects target-emotion-adaptive strategies rather than applying a uniform template. The same affordance-level plan also supports lightweight user refinement in an interactive pilot. Finally, we show that classifier-based metrics exhibit emotion-conditional blind spots toward non-stereotypical, context-grounded edits, and present a relative content-emotion preference-affinity landscape showing that EmoScope's advantage varies systematically across image-emotion combinations.

AI.tldr: EmoScope is a multi-agent framework for emotional image editing that discovers image-specific, emotion-conditioned affordances rather than relying on predefined templates or taxonomies. It reframes editing from "how should I edit?" to "what can I edit?" and outperforms baselines by 88.1% in human evaluation across 8 emotion categories.
AI.motivation: Existing affective image manipulation methods operate within bounded strategy spaces (predefined factor taxonomies, knowledge libraries, or templates), missing image-specific, context-grounded strategies for emotional editing.
AI.method: EmoScope uses a multi-agent framework that first discovers an image-specific editable space through emotion-conditioned affordance reasoning, then employs a semantic hierarchy of anchors, variables, and context to balance content consistency and emotional expressiveness before executing and verifying the edit.
AI.result: In a large-scale human evaluation (4,693 responses across 1,824 pairwise questions, all 8 Mikels emotion categories), participants preferred EmoScope over competitive baselines by 88.1% on average. EmoScope selects target-emotion-adaptive strategies rather than uniform templates. Classifier-based metrics show emotion-conditional blind spots toward non-stereotypical edits.
AI.conclusion: EmoScope effectively discovers image-specific affordances for emotional editing, outperforms template-based approaches, exposes editing strategies as interactive surfaces for user refinement, and reveals limitations of classifier-based evaluation metrics for non-stereotypical emotional edits.

title: Covariance Last-Layer Ensembles: Function-Space Diversity for Efficient Uncertainty Quantification
summary: A Last-Layer Ensemble (LLE), $K$ linear units on one shared frozen feature map, is an efficient single-pass approach to the disagreement-based epistemic uncertainty for out-of-distribution (OOD) detection. Its weakness is that members share the backbone gradient and can converge toward the same function, collapsing the inter-member diversity the signal depends on. Whether last-layer diversity can be restored, and what mitigates the collapse, is an open question. The weight-orthonormality defining Orthonormal Certificates (OC), the weight-orthonormal special case of the LLE, is only an indirect correction; it decorrelates the weights of the members, not their predictions. Here, we instead target the collapse directly in function space, with a Covariance Last-Layer Ensemble (cov-LLE) that places a direct covariance penalty on member activations. Cov-LLE restores the function-space diversity that weight-orthonormality cannot, and at matched $K$ recovers much of the diversity and calibration of a deep ensemble at $1\times$ backbone cost (in-distribution prediction variance $0.05\!\to\!9.3$ vs.\ $22.1$ ($\times10^{-3}$), and ECE $0.135\!\to\!0.090$ vs.\ $0.035$, for a $K\times$-cost deep ensemble), at no cost to accuracy. Viewing OC as a last-layer ensemble also organizes detectors into a two-axis taxonomy (by how their units are trained and how their outputs are scored) and exposes the OC score as a magnitude, motivating a scale-invariant, label-free direction score that repairs its near-OOD failure, adding $+0.16$ to $+0.18$ ROC AUC on every backbone.

AI.tldr: A covariance-penalized last-layer ensemble (cov-LLE) directly enforces function-space diversity among ensemble members, overcoming the diversity collapse problem of standard last-layer ensembles. It matches deep ensemble quality at single-backbone cost and improves OOD detection with a scale-invariant scoring method.
AI.motivation: Standard Last-Layer Ensembles (LLE) suffer from diversity collapse because members share backbone gradients and converge toward similar functions, undermining disagreement-based epistemic uncertainty for OOD detection. Existing remedies like weight-orthonormality (OC) decorrelate weights but not predictions, failing to restore true functional diversity.
AI.method: Cov-LLE adds a direct covariance penalty on member activations to enforce prediction diversity in function space. The paper also reorganizes OOD detectors into a two-axis taxonomy (training unit type vs. scoring method), identifies the OC score as a magnitude-based metric, and proposes a scale-invariant, label-free direction score to fix near-OOD failures.
AI.result: At matched K, cov-LLE recovers much of deep ensemble's diversity and calibration at 1× backbone cost (ID prediction variance 0.05→9.3 vs. deep ensemble's 22.1 (×10⁻³), ECE 0.135→0.090 vs. 0.035), with no accuracy loss. The proposed direction score adds +0.16 to +0.18 ROC AUC across all backbones for near-OOD detection.
AI.conclusion: Direct covariance-based diversity regularization in function space effectively restores ensemble diversity that weight-orthonormality cannot. The proposed cov-LLE and taxonomy provide both practical performance gains and theoretical organization of OOD detection methods.

title: TopoFE: topology-aware LLM-guided Automated Feature Engineering
summary: Automatic feature engineering (AutoFE) for tabular learning can be naturally formulated as a program synthesis problem, where the objective is to discover predictive feature transformations from an exponentially large search space. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have expanded the expressiveness of AutoFE by enabling feature program generation beyond predefined operator libraries. However, existing LLM-based approaches remain fundamentally limited by stateless generation and homogeneous search: feature proposals are produced from static prompts without accumulating search experience, while single-population exploration quickly converges to dominant transformation patterns and rarely discovers complementary feature compositions across transformation families. We propose TOPOFE, a topology-aware multi-island evolutionary framework for LLM-guided feature engineering. TOPOFE combines family-specialized exploration, adaptive prompt memory, and topology-guided knowledge transfer to efficiently discover diverse and compositional feature programs. Experiments on 29 public tabular datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art AutoFE methods across classification and regression tasks. Beyond predictive performance, TOPOFE discovers more diverse and transferable feature programs that generalize across multiple downstream predictors and LLM backbones.

AI.tldr: TOPOFE is a topology-aware multi-island evolutionary framework that improves LLM-guided automatic feature engineering by enabling family-specialized exploration, adaptive prompt memory, and topology-guided knowledge transfer, achieving state-of-the-art results on 29 tabular datasets with more diverse and transferable feature programs.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based AutoFE methods are limited by stateless generation (static prompts without accumulating search experience) and homogeneous search (single-population exploration quickly converges to dominant patterns, failing to discover complementary feature compositions across transformation families).
AI.method: TOPOFE proposes a topology-aware multi-island evolutionary framework combining: (1) family-specialized exploration that partitions feature programs into transformation families, (2) adaptive prompt memory that accumulates search experience, and (3) topology-guided knowledge transfer that enables complementary feature compositions across families.
AI.result: Consistent improvements over state-of-the-art AutoFE methods across 29 public tabular datasets for both classification and regression tasks, with more diverse and transferable feature programs generalizing across multiple downstream predictors and LLM backbones.
AI.conclusion: TOPOFE demonstrates that incorporating evolutionary search structure (multi-island topology) with LLM guidance effectively overcomes the stateless and homogeneous limitations of prior LLM-based AutoFE, producing superior predictive performance and more diverse, transferable feature transformations.

title: DDVT: Dynamic Dual-level Vision Transformer Fusion Network for Answer Grounding in Visual Question Answering
summary: Answer grounding in visual question answering aims to locate the region from a given natural language question associated with the visual content of an image, which has garnered significant attention due to its practical applications. In this paper, we introduce the Dynamic Dual-level Vision Transformer Fusion Network (DDVT) for answer grounding in visual question answering. Specifically, we propose a question-guided dynamic regional-level module (QGDR) that combines complementary image context through ROI Align and text content, enabling precise localization of text-related visual content. Moreover, we present a cross-modal multi-scale aggregation module (CMA) that enhances feature fusion between pixel-level and region-level features, facilitating the effective localization of visual content associated with grounded answers. Furthermore, we fuse the located visual content with text features to locate the region and provide answers to questions posed about the image. Experimental results demonstrate that our DDVT outperforms state-of-the-art methods on several widely-used benchmarks.

AI.tldr: DDVT is a Dynamic Dual-level Vision Transformer Fusion Network for answer grounding in VQA that uses a question-guided dynamic regional module (QGDR) for precise localization and a cross-modal multi-scale aggregation module (CMA) for enhanced feature fusion, outperforming SOTA on benchmarks.
AI.motivation: To improve answer grounding in VQA by accurately locating image regions corresponding to natural language questions and their answers, addressing the need for precise visual-textual alignment.
AI.method: Proposes DDVT with two key modules: (1) QGDR - question-guided dynamic regional-level module combining ROI Align-derived image context with text content for precise localization; (2) CMA - cross-modal multi-scale aggregation module fusing pixel-level and region-level features. Fuses located visual content with text features for answer grounding.
AI.result: DDVT outperforms state-of-the-art methods on several widely-used benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed dual-level fusion approach effectively enhances answer grounding performance in VQA tasks.

title: Controllable Diversity in Normalization-Based Implicit Ensembles via Softmax-Temperature Modulation
summary: Deep ensembles provide the most reliable uncertainty estimates in deep learning, but their cost grows linearly with the number of members. Implicit ensembles lower this cost by sharing a single backbone across members. Member diversity is a primary determinant of ensemble quality, yet no implicit ensemble can shape it during training; existing methods fix it at initialisation or build it into the architecture. We introduce $σ$N-Ens, a normalisation-based implicit ensemble that treats each member as a task in a multi-task architecture and modulates the shared backbone through sigmoid-bounded scalers. We also introduce a softmax-temperature regulariser, which shapes the equilibrium level of sharing between members and traces the accuracy-calibration frontier. Because only normalisation layers are replicated, the mechanism can wrap convolutional and transformer backbones alike, also allowing pretrained models to be adapted through a short fine-tune. We frame the epistemic uncertainty such an ensemble expresses as modulation uncertainty, and explain why its calibration holds under input corruption, and why its out-of-distribution detection is weaker. Our method is evaluated across ResNets and transformers on CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet and SST-2. $σ$N-Ens matches or outperforms deep ensembles at a fraction of their parameter cost, scales with ensemble size where partitioning methods collapse, and maintains calibration under distribution shift.

AI.tldr: σN-Ens is a normalization-based implicit ensemble that treats members as tasks in a multi-task architecture, using sigmoid-bounded scalers and softmax-temperature regularization to shape member diversity, matching deep ensemble performance at lower cost across ResNets and transformers.
AI.motivation: Deep ensembles provide the best uncertainty estimates but incur linear cost with member count. Implicit ensembles reduce cost via shared backbones but cannot shape member diversity during training—diversity is fixed at initialization or built into architecture. The paper aims to enable trainable member diversity in implicit ensembles.
AI.method: σN-Ens: (1) Normalization-based implicit ensemble replicating only normalization layers (wrapping conv/transformer backbones). (2) Each member treated as a task in multi-task architecture, modulated by sigmoid-bounded scalers on the shared backbone. (3) Softmax-temperature regularizer that shapes the equilibrium of sharing between members and traces the accuracy-calibration frontier. (4) Can adapt pretrained models via short fine-tuning.
AI.result: Matches or outperforms deep ensembles at fraction of parameter cost on CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet, SST-2 across ResNets and transformers. Scales with ensemble size where partitioning methods collapse. Maintains calibration under distribution shift.
AI.conclusion: σN-Ens frames epistemic uncertainty as "modulation uncertainty," explains why calibration holds under input corruption and why OOD detection is weaker. Provides an efficient, scalable alternative to deep ensembles with trainable diversity.

title: RareLens: Towards End-to-End Rare Disease Care via Aligning Divergent Large Language Model Reasoning
summary: Rare diseases collectively affect an estimated 3.5% to 5.9% of the population, yet more than 70% of patients are misdiagnosed and many endure years of evaluation before a diagnosis is reached, because early presentations are nonspecific and relevant expertise is scarce and unevenly distributed. Artificial intelligence could provide support, but existing systems address isolated stages of care, overwhelmingly diagnosis. They typically depend on the results of downstream investigations, and they treat the variability between models as noise to be eliminated. Here we present RareLens, a system that supports clinical decision-making across the entire rare disease trajectory by exploiting this variability. When heterogeneous large language models evaluate the same case, they generate divergent but complementary reasoning, which RareLens aligns and calibrates into a single convergent, actionable decision at each stage. Four coordinated modules perform primary-visit risk screening, diagnosis, treatment planning and prognosis. Developed and evaluated on RareBench, a real-world dataset of 157,525 cases spanning all 33 Orphanet categories and more than 7,000 conditions, RareLens outperformed every frontier model tested, including GPT-5, DeepSeek-R1, Claude-3.7-Sonnet and Gemini-2.5-Pro, at each stage. It achieved an area under the curve of 0.917 for screening and top-1 accuracies of 65.5% and 89.8% for diagnosis and treatment. In an external study spanning 1,287 cases and 23 physicians, autonomous RareLens and physicians assisted by RareLens both substantially outperformed unaided physicians. These findings indicate that aligning divergent model reasoning, rather than scaling a single model, offers a generalizable strategy for high-uncertainty clinical decision-making.

AI.tldr: RareLens is a multi-module AI system that leverages divergent reasoning from heterogeneous LLMs to support clinical decision-making across the entire rare disease trajectory (screening, diagnosis, treatment, prognosis), outperforming frontier models and unaided physicians on a large real-world dataset.
AI.motivation: Rare diseases affect 3.5-5.9% of the population but >70% of patients are misdiagnosed due to nonspecific early presentations and scarce expertise. Existing AI systems address only isolated stages (mostly diagnosis), depend on downstream investigation results, and treat model variability as noise rather than a resource.
AI.method: RareLens uses four coordinated modules (risk screening, diagnosis, treatment planning, prognosis) that exploit divergent reasoning from heterogeneous LLMs. Instead of eliminating variability, the system aligns and calibrates diverse model outputs into a single convergent, actionable decision at each stage.
AI.result: On RareBench (157,525 cases, 33 Orphanet categories, >7,000 conditions), RareLens outperformed GPT-5, DeepSeek-R1, Claude-3.7-Sonnet, and Gemini-2.5-Pro at all stages. AUC for screening: 0.917; top-1 accuracy: 65.5% (diagnosis), 89.8% (treatment). In an external study (1,287 cases, 23 physicians), autonomous RareLens and physician+RareLens both outperformed unaided physicians.
AI.conclusion: Aligning divergent model reasoning (rather than scaling a single model) offers a generalizable strategy for high-uncertainty clinical decision-making in rare diseases.

title: DuoAD: Leveraging [CLS] Dual Characteristics for Training-Free Few-Shot Anomaly Detection
summary: Vision foundation models have enabled strong training-free anomaly detection (AD). However, most existing approaches rely primarily on independent local patch features, leaving the global contextual information encoded by Vision Transformers (ViTs) underexploited. In this work, we identify the dual characteristics of the ViT [CLS] token: its embedding provides anomaly-invariant global semantic representation, while its attention maps implicitly highlight spatially abnormal regions. Building on this observation, we propose a fully automated AD framework leveraging global context to remove manual tunings. Our framework introduces (1) an automatic augmentation selection strategy driven by [CLS]-level semantic consistency, and (2) an attention-guided feature reweighting mechanism that dynamically adjusts patch contributions according to [CLS] attention saliency. By integrating these components over multi-level features, our method achieves stable anomaly scoring and precise localization without training or parameter tuning. Under the one-shot setting, it achieves Image-AUC scores of 97.7%, 93.2%, and 84.5% on MVTec-AD, VisA, and Real-IAD. Using a single fixed configuration across categories, backbones, and datasets, the method establishes a new state-of-the-art for plug-and-play, training-free anomaly detection while maintaining strong robustness and practical scalability.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies dual properties of the ViT [CLS] token (invariant global semantics from embeddings + implicit anomaly localization from attention maps) and proposes a training-free AD framework with automatic augmentation selection and attention-guided feature reweighting, achieving SOTA one-shot AD results on MVTec-AD (97.7%), VisA (93.2%), and Real-IAD (84.5%) without tuning.
AI.motivation: Existing training-free AD methods over-rely on independent local patch features, underutilizing the global contextual information encoded by ViTs, particularly the [CLS] token.
AI.method: (1) Automatic augmentation selection driven by [CLS]-level semantic consistency; (2) Attention-guided feature reweighting that adjusts patch contributions based on [CLS] attention saliency; integrated over multi-level features for stable anomaly scoring and localization.
AI.result: One-shot Image-AUC: 97.7% on MVTec-AD, 93.2% on VisA, 84.5% on Real-IAD. Single fixed configuration works across categories, backbones, and datasets.
AI.conclusion: The method establishes a new SOTA for plug-and-play, training-free AD with strong robustness and practical scalability, fully automated without manual tuning.

title: XMix: Combating Extremely Noisy Labels via Local Smoothness in Self-Supervised Feature Space
summary: Supervised deep learning models rely on large, accurately labeled datasets, yet noisy annotations are often unavoidable and can severely degrade performance under high noise levels. Recent state-of-the-art methods tackle this by using sample selection strategies that exploit the memorization effect to filter out clean data for semi-supervised learning. However, these methods struggle with extreme noise, class imbalance, and require careful tuning or prior noise knowledge. To address these limitations, we propose XMix, a novel framework that leverages local smoothness in the self-supervised feature space to systematically enhance all stages of the sample selection process, without dependence on potentially corrupted labels. First, XMix estimates the noise rate using maximum likelihood among self-supervised feature neighbors. Second, these neighbors then help identify additional clean samples and ensure balanced selection across classes during sample selection. Finally, in the semi-supervised learning phase, XMix uses neighboring samples to generate more reliable pseudo-labels. Our empirical results show that XMix substantially outperforms existing methods in extremely noisy environments and maintains superior performance in standard LNL benchmarks.

AI.tldr: XMix proposes leveraging local smoothness in self-supervised feature space to improve sample selection for learning with noisy labels, outperforming existing methods especially under extreme noise.
AI.motivation: Supervised deep learning suffers from noisy labels, and existing sample selection methods struggle with extreme noise, class imbalance, and require careful tuning or prior noise knowledge. The goal is to address these limitations without relying on corrupted labels.
AI.method: XMix enhances sample selection via three stages using self-supervised feature space: (1) noise rate estimation via maximum likelihood among feature neighbors, (2) identifying additional clean samples and ensuring class-balanced selection, (3) generating more reliable pseudo-labels from neighboring samples during semi-supervised learning.
AI.result: XMix substantially outperforms existing methods in extremely noisy environments and maintains superior performance in standard LNL benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging self-supervised feature space local smoothness provides a robust, label-free way to enhance sample selection across all stages, making the method effective under extreme noise and class imbalance without requiring careful tuning.

title: Ordered Network Analysis of Epistemic Emotions during Collaborative Problem Solving
summary: Investigating how affective states such as confusion and frustration persist and transition during co-situated collaborative problem solving (CPS) is important for understanding the dynamics of epistemic emotions. However, the accurate identification of affective states remain challenging as there is no gold-standard truth in this space. Here, we analyze affective states collected through retrospective cued-recall during an in-person CPS task. Using ordered network analysis (ONA), we examine (1) the overall ordered structure of affective states and how this structure differs across self-caught and probe-caught reporting methods, and (2) what aspects of this ordered structure are emphasized differently in slower and faster groups. We find that ONA reveals differences in persistence and transition patterns that are not apparent from descriptive summaries alone. In particular, we observe a stable epistemic core linking curiosity, optimism, and confusion, with different reporting methods emphasizing different connections among states. An analysis between faster and slower groups show that roles of confusion and disengagement also shift significantly during collaboration, particularly in their relationship to conflict. We interpret our findings in the context of collaboration and discuss their implications in developing AI systems that support CPS.

AI.tldr: This paper uses ordered network analysis (ONA) on retrospective cued-recall affective state data from a collaborative problem-solving task, revealing distinct persistence and transition patterns of epistemic emotions (especially curiosity, optimism, confusion) that differ across self-caught vs. probe-caught reporting methods and between faster vs. slower groups, with implications for AI-supported CPS systems.
AI.motivation: Understanding how affective states like confusion and frustration persist and transition during co-situated CPS is important for understanding epistemic emotion dynamics, yet accurate identification of these states remains challenging without a ground truth.
AI.method: Collected retrospective cued-recall affective state data during in-person CPS tasks and applied ordered network analysis (ONA) to examine overall ordered structures, compare self-caught vs. probe-caught reporting methods, and analyze differences between slower and faster groups.
AI.result: ONA revealed differences in persistence and transition patterns not apparent in descriptive summaries. A stable epistemic core linking curiosity, optimism, and confusion emerged, with different reporting methods emphasizing different connections. Faster vs. slower group analysis showed significant shifts in the roles of confusion and disengagement, particularly in relation to conflict.
AI.conclusion: The findings are interpreted in the context of collaboration, with implications for developing AI systems that support CPS.

title: Manifold-Constrained Noise Optimization for Diverse Diffusion Sampling
summary: Few-step distilled diffusion models generate high-quality images quickly, but often lose per-prompt diversity, producing near-identical samples across random seeds. Optimizing the initial noise at inference time offers an appealing way to recover this diversity, yet existing methods directly update the initial noise in an unconstrained Euclidean space, ignoring both the geometry of the Gaussian prior and the model's sensitivity to noise frequencies. They therefore introduce auxiliary quality-control objectives to maintain generation fidelity, adding compute and weighting hyperparameters while still requiring conservative updates to prevent degradation. In this work, we propose MoNO, a training-free method that performs Manifold-constrained Noise Optimization on a low-dimensional, quality-stabilizing noise manifold. MoNO sequentially optimizes each new initial noise so that its predicted visual feature complements previous generations, while Riemannian updates on an affine low-frequency sphere preserve prior likelihood and fix unstable high-frequency components by construction. This enables large geodesic steps, removes the need for auxiliary quality-control objectives, and converges in far fewer iterations than prior noise-optimization methods. Experiments with multiple distilled text-to-image diffusion models show that MoNO consistently improves per-prompt diversity while maintaining image quality.

AI.tldr: MoNO is a training-free method that optimizes initial noise on a low-dimensional manifold for few-step distilled diffusion models, improving per-prompt diversity without quality-control objectives by using Riemannian updates on an affine low-frequency sphere.
AI.motivation: Few-step distilled diffusion models produce high-quality images quickly but lack per-prompt diversity, generating near-identical samples across random seeds. Existing noise optimization methods operate in unconstrained Euclidean space, ignoring the Gaussian prior geometry and frequency sensitivity, requiring auxiliary quality-control objectives.
AI.method: MoNO performs Manifold-constrained Noise Optimization on a low-dimensional, quality-stabilizing noise manifold. It sequentially optimizes initial noise so predicted visual features complement previous generations, using Riemannian updates on an affine low-frequency sphere to preserve prior likelihood and stabilize high-frequency components.
AI.result: Enables large geodesic steps, eliminates need for auxiliary quality-control objectives, converges in far fewer iterations than prior methods. Experiments with multiple distilled text-to-image models show consistent improvement in per-prompt diversity while maintaining image quality.
AI.conclusion: MoNO effectively recovers diversity in few-step distilled diffusion models by respecting the geometric structure of the noise prior and frequency sensitivity, achieving training-free diversity enhancement without quality degradation.

title: A Coulomb Particle Model for Learning Kernel Attention in Transformers
comment: Workshop on High-dimensional Learning Dynamics (HiLD), ICML 2026
summary: Randomized features provide a scalable approximation to kernel machines, but their performance depends strongly on the choice of feature distribution. We propose a particle-based method that learns this distribution by optimizing kernel-target alignment while regularizing particles with a Riesz/Coulomb repulsive potential. The resulting Hamiltonian yields diverse, task-adaptive random features and admits a mean-field description through a McKean--Vlasov equation. We instantiate the method in linearized Transformer attention by learning positive random-feature maps in a first alignment phase, then freezing the kernel and training the remaining network parameters with cross-entropy. Experiments on synthetic classification and sentence-level benchmarks show that learned kernelized attention can improve accuracy, calibration, and robustness for several feature maps while preserving linear-attention inference complexity.

AI.tldr: A particle-based method learns optimized random feature distributions for kernel approximation using Riesz/Coulomb repulsive regularization, applied to linearized Transformer attention, improving accuracy, calibration, and robustness while maintaining linear complexity.
AI.motivation: Randomized features for kernel machines are sensitive to the choice of feature distribution; existing methods lack an adaptive, principled way to learn this distribution for better task performance.
AI.method: Particle-based optimization with kernel-target alignment regularized by Riesz/Coulomb repulsive potential, governed by a McKean-Vlasov mean-field equation; applied in a two-phase procedure: first learn positive random-feature maps for linearized attention, then freeze kernel and train remaining parameters with cross-entropy.
AI.result: Improved accuracy, calibration, and robustness on synthetic classification and sentence-level benchmarks for several feature maps, while preserving linear-attention inference complexity.
AI.conclusion: Learning task-adaptive random feature distributions via repulsive particle dynamics enhances kernel approximation quality and downstream Transformer performance without sacrificing computational efficiency.

title: ESF-Bench: Benchmarking Challenging Slot-Filling Scenarios for Real-World Enterprise Applications
summary: The rapid rise of large language models (LLMs) has driven transformative adoption across enterprises. However, deploying these models in real-world settings presents unique challenges due to complex system constraints and unexpected user behaviors. Among these applications, slot filling is essential for converting unstructured input into structured, actionable data. In this work, we introduce ESF-Bench, a challenging Enterprise Slot Filling benchmark consisting of 810 multi-turn samples and 6530 slots over 8 unique domains. Curated using a taxonomy of the 57 most challenging slot-filling scenarios observed during real-world enterprise deployments, ESF-Bench exposes notable limitations in current state-of-the-art LLMs, with GPT-OSS-120b low successfully extracting slots for only 20.7% of benchmark samples. To support continued research in this area, we publicly release the benchmark dataset, taxonomy, and accompanying evaluation code on GitHub.

AI.tldr: ESF-Bench is a new Enterprise Slot Filling benchmark with 810 multi-turn samples and 6530 slots across 8 domains, designed to test LLMs on 57 challenging real-world scenarios. Current SOTA LLMs (e.g., GPT-OSS-120b) achieve only 20.7% success rate, highlighting significant limitations.
AI.motivation: LLMs face unique challenges in real-world enterprise deployments due to complex system constraints and unexpected user behaviors; slot filling is critical for converting unstructured input to structured data, yet existing benchmarks fail to capture the difficulty of enterprise scenarios.
AI.method: The authors constructed ESF-Bench using a taxonomy of 57 challenging slot-filling scenarios observed in real-world enterprise deployments, resulting in 810 multi-turn samples and 6530 slots across 8 domains. They evaluated current SOTA LLMs against this benchmark.
AI.result: GPT-OSS-120b successfully extracted slots for only 20.7% of benchmark samples, demonstrating notable limitations in current state-of-the-art LLMs for enterprise slot filling.
AI.conclusion: ESF-Bench exposes significant gaps in LLM performance for enterprise slot filling. The benchmark, taxonomy, and evaluation code are publicly released to support continued research in this area.

title: TimePLE: Rethinking Temporal Representation for Video Temporal Grounding
summary: Video temporal grounding (VTG) aims to localize the continuous video interval described by a natural-language query. However, current VLM-based methods typically produce this interval indirectly through two endpoint outputs, represented either as discrete timestamp tokens or continuous boundary coordinates. These formulations differ in how endpoints are encoded, but not in what is predicted: the event interval remains a derived object, while interval validity, duration, and interval-level similarity are handled only implicitly. We propose TimePLE, which reformulates VTG from endpoint prediction to interval-native grounding by predicting a single joint distribution over valid temporal intervals. TimePLE maps each interval to a point in a canonical position-duration square, where every support point corresponds to a valid span and neighboring points represent geometrically similar intervals. Given a video and query, the VLM generates a single latent <|TIMESPAN|> token whose hidden state is decoded into a joint interval distribution, refined through duration-aware coordinate correction, and converted into continuous boundaries. The same interval representation is used to encode input temporal anchors, aligning video-side temporal evidence with output-side span prediction. To reliably align the latent span representation with complete event intervals, we curate 90K-scale grounded samples and human-verify 3K-scale benchmark annotations. Experiments across four VTG benchmarks show that TimePLE consistently outperforms endpoint prediction baselines, achieving an average mIoU of 58.9, with clear gains on short-duration and medium-duration events.

AI.tldr: TimePLE reformulates video temporal grounding from endpoint prediction to interval-native grounding by predicting a single joint distribution over valid temporal intervals in a canonical position-duration square, achieving 58.9 average mIoU across four benchmarks with gains on short/medium-duration events.
AI.motivation: Current VLM-based VTG methods predict intervals indirectly via two endpoints (discrete tokens or continuous coordinates), treating the interval as a derived object while interval validity, duration, and interval-level similarity are handled only implicitly.
AI.method: TimePLE maps each interval to a point in a canonical position-duration square, uses a single latent <|TIMESPAN|> token decoded into a joint interval distribution, applies duration-aware coordinate correction, and encodes input temporal anchors using the same interval representation. 90K-scale grounded samples and 3K-scale human-verified annotations are curated for training/evaluation.
AI.result: Outperforms endpoint prediction baselines across four VTG benchmarks with average mIoU of 58.9, showing clear gains on short-duration and medium-duration events.
AI.conclusion: Predicting a joint interval distribution directly (interval-native grounding) is more effective than traditional endpoint prediction for video temporal grounding.
