title: Flash-CNNCap: Capacitance Extraction via Image Mapping
summary: We present Flash-CNNCap, a CNN-based capacitance extractor that reformulates full-matrix capacitance prediction as image-to-image regression over spatial contribution maps. Prior scalar CNN-based extractors require $O(n^2)$ forward passes to recover all pairwise capacitances in a window with $n$ conductors. Flash-CNNCap replaces the scalar target with dense contribution maps: a total-capacitance model and a master-conditioned coupling model each predict a spatial map that is reduced to conductor-level values through mask aggregation, cutting full-matrix reconstruction to $O(n)$ passes. The resulting totals and symmetrized pairwise couplings define the corresponding Maxwell-style capacitance matrix under the standard off-diagonal sign convention. The maps are learned from conductor-level labels without per-pixel supervision. An ablation study over 13 model configurations selects a U-Net that matches ResNet baselines on total capacitance (1.5-3.1% MARE) and achieves the strongest coupling accuracy (3.0-4.6% MARE) across all evaluated CapBench subsets, with a $17.5\times$ full-matrix speedup on windows containing 134 conductors on average. A deployed pipeline reads Design Exchange Format (DEF) geometry and writes Standard Parasitic Exchange Format (SPEF) output, processing 1,024 windows in 51.23 seconds with a $4.4\times$ speedup over OpenRCX on the same benchmark. Code and trained models are available at https://github.com/THU-numbda/flash-cnncap.

AI.tldr: Flash-CNNCap is a CNN-based capacitance extractor that reformulates full-matrix capacitance prediction as image-to-image regression over spatial contribution maps, achieving O(n) full-matrix reconstruction speed (vs. O(n²) for prior scalar CNNs) with 17.5× speedup on windows averaging 134 conductors and 4.4× throughput gain over OpenRCX.
AI.motivation: Prior scalar CNN-based capacitance extractors require O(n²) forward passes to recover all pairwise capacitances in a window with n conductors, creating a computational bottleneck for dense full-matrix extraction.
AI.method: Replaces scalar targets with dense spatial contribution maps using two models: a total-capacitance model and a master-conditioned coupling model. Each predicts a spatial map reduced to conductor-level values via mask aggregation, cutting full-matrix reconstruction to O(n) passes. A U-Net architecture is selected via ablation study over 13 configurations.
AI.result: U-Net matches ResNet baselines on total capacitance (1.5-3.1% MARE) and achieves strongest coupling accuracy (3.0-4.6% MARE) across all CapBench subsets, with 17.5× full-matrix speedup on 134-conductor windows. Deployed pipeline processes 1,024 windows in 51.23s with 4.4× speedup over OpenRCX.
AI.conclusion: Flash-CNNCap demonstrates that reformulating capacitance extraction as image-to-image regression over contribution maps yields significant speedups without sacrificing accuracy, enabling practical CNN-based full-matrix extraction.

title: Confidently Wrong: Exception Chain Collapse in Frontier LLM Rule Evaluation
comment: 43 pages, 9 figures. Working paper v3.13.0. Benchmark data, rule encodings and per-case result artefacts: https://github.com/Aethis-ai/confidently-wrong-benchmark
summary: We document a failure class in frontier large language models -- exception chain collapse -- observed in eligibility evaluation under nested conditional rules of the form "A is required UNLESS B applies, UNLESS C overrides B". The failure reproduces at first observation, but its empirical surface is unstable: between March and April 2026 several failure cells closed silently under the same model alias, with no version bump (GPT-5.4 on construction insurance moved from 96.6% to 100%, same prompt and harness). For regulated workflows, frontier-model accuracy is a moving compliance boundary that shifts without notice. We present the Aethis Eligibility Module, a neuro-symbolic architecture in which LLMs author rules from authoritative sources and an SMT-based layer executes them deterministically, consistent with the authored specification regardless of model drift, reasoning-effort defaults, or prompt format. Three evidence bases: (i) a controlled benchmark of 225 scenarios across four regulatory domains documents the pattern and, in replication, the drift that partially closed it; (ii) a 20-scenario adversarial extension on construction insurance, where the engine scores 20/20, as does one of four frontier configurations (GPT-5.4 at low reasoning effort), while the other three, including Anthropic's strongest model at evaluation time, fail the same coverage-gap edge case; (iii) external validation on nine peer-reviewed LegalBench tasks, 949 held-out cases, where the engine is significantly more accurate than all three frontier models (combined McNemar's p <= 0.003), with margins up to +41 points on the curated multi-prong tasks against the Anthropic models. The contribution is to relocate uncertainty from the inference boundary, where it is silent, to the specification boundary, where it is deliberate and audited. All scenarios, rule encodings, and results are public and reproducible.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies "exception chain collapse" in frontier LLMs for eligibility tasks with nested conditional rules, shows the failure is unstable (can disappear without notice across model versions), and proposes a neuro-symbolic architecture (Aethis Eligibility Module) where LLMs author rules but an SMT solver executes them deterministically, outperforming frontier models on benchmarks and LegalBench tasks.
AI.motivation: Frontier LLMs exhibit silent, unstable failures in regulated eligibility workflows with nested conditional rules ("A is required UNLESS B applies, UNLESS C overrides B"), creating a moving compliance boundary that shifts without version bumps or alerts—a serious risk for domains like insurance and legal reasoning.
AI.method: The Aethis Eligibility Module is a neuro-symbolic architecture where LLMs author formal rules from authoritative sources, and an SMT (Satisfiability Modulo Theories) solver executes those rules deterministically, decoupling specification from inference. The paper evaluates across three evidence bases: (i) a 225-scenario controlled benchmark across four regulatory domains; (ii) a 20-scenario adversarial extension on construction insurance; (iii) external validation on nine LegalBench tasks (949 held-out cases).
AI.result: The failure pattern was documented and replicated; between March and April 2026, some failure cells closed silently under the same model alias (GPT-5.4 on construction insurance went from 96.6% to 100%). On the adversarial benchmark, Aethis scored 20/20, matching only GPT-5.4 at low reasoning effort while three other frontier configurations failed. On LegalBench, the engine was significantly more accurate than all three frontier models (combined McNemar's p ≤ 0.003), with margins up to +41 points on curated multi-prong tasks against Anthropic models.
AI.conclusion: The contribution relocates uncertainty from the inference boundary (where it is silent and unannounced) to the specification boundary (where it is deliberate, auditable, and subject to human review). All scenarios, rule encodings, and results are public and reproducible.

title: RODR: Riemannian Orthogonally Decoupled Regularization for Disentangled Manifold Representation
summary: Point cloud denoising is essentially a geometric recovery task that aims to reconstruct the intrinsic structure of a smooth 2D Riemannian manifold embedded in R^3 from noisy, discrete ambient-space samples. Despite the remarkable progress of modern manifold-aware encoders and generative transport models in geometric representation learning, a fundamental objective-geometry mismatch remains underexplored. Theoretically, we identified that this mismatched coupling leads to geometric gradient interference, where conflicting optimization objectives result in structural degradation and point clustering. We introduce Riemannian Orthogonally Decoupled Regularization (RODR) to reformulate the optimization trajectory by disentangling the normal (fitting) and tangential (distribution) components. Guided by a vector-attention and entropy-aware adaptive strategy, RODR effectively preserves high-fidelity geometric details while maintaining sampling uniformity. Experiments demonstrate that RODR reaches performance comparable to state-of-the-art baselines and suggests improved distribution regularity and reduced local aggregation effectively. Our work establishes a generic and interpretable framework for disentangled geometric optimization in point cloud processing.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies an objective-geometry mismatch in point cloud denoising that causes geometric gradient interference, leading to structural degradation and point clustering. The authors propose Riemannian Orthogonally Decoupled Regularization (RODR) to disentangle normal (fitting) and tangential (distribution) components using vector-attention and entropy-aware adaptive strategy, achieving state-of-the-art performance with improved distribution regularity and reduced local aggregation.
AI.motivation: Point cloud denoising suffers from an underexplored objective-geometry mismatch, where conflicting optimization objectives cause geometric gradient interference, resulting in structural degradation and point clustering.
AI.method: RODR (Riemannian Orthogonally Decoupled Regularization) reformulates the optimization trajectory by disentangling normal (fitting) and tangential (distribution) components, guided by a vector-attention and entropy-aware adaptive strategy.
AI.result: The method achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art baselines with improved distribution regularity and reduced local aggregation.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a generic and interpretable framework for disentangled geometric optimization in point cloud processing, effectively preserving high-fidelity geometric details while maintaining sampling uniformity.

title: Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Predicting Nitrous Oxide Flux
summary: Nitrous oxide (N$_2$O) is the dominant ozone-depleting substance emitted in the 21st century, and the third largest contributor to anthropogenic greenhouse gases due to its high potency and long atmospheric lifetime, with more than 70% of N$_2$O emissions occurring as a result of agricultural processes. Current approaches to predicting N$_2$O flux emissions include process-based models such as DayCent and Cycles, as well as classical AI models, but the application of Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) to predicting N$_2$O flux emissions is largely underexplored. Our paper draws upon the mechanistic equations that underlie the DayCent family of process-based models to construct a rigorously derived, literature-traceable physics residual. We then build and train an MLP-based PINN on a multi-site agricultural dataset spanning four geographically distinct US agricultural sites. Across all tested values of the physics loss weighting hyperparameter $λ$, our PINN consistently and substantially outperformed uncalibrated Cycles simulation (R$^2=0.01$), with our MLP baseline achieving mean R$^2=0.411$ across ten random seeds. Physics constraints consistently degrade model performance in holdout validation, with marginal degradation at low $λ$ and significant degradation at high $λ$, but consistently improve model performance and reduce performance variability in leave-one-site-out validation. This suggests that physics constraints sacrifice in-distribution accuracy for out-of-distribution robustness, anchoring the model toward biogeochemically plausible behavior on unfamiliar soil conditions --- though cross-site generalization remains challenging, with negative R$^2$ across all seeds and $λ$ values on our geographically distinct held-out site.

AI.tldr: This paper explores the use of Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) for predicting N₂O flux emissions from agricultural soils. The authors construct a physics residual based on mechanistic equations from DayCent process-based models and train an MLP-based PINN on multi-site agricultural data. While physics constraints hurt in-distribution accuracy, they improve out-of-distribution robustness (leave-one-site-out), though cross-site generalization remains poor with negative R² on held-out sites.
AI.motivation: N₂O is a major ozone-depleting substance and greenhouse gas, with over 70% of emissions from agriculture. Existing approaches (process-based models like DayCent, Cycles, and classical AI) have limitations, and PINNs remain largely unexplored for this task. The authors aim to leverage mechanistic knowledge to improve N₂O flux prediction.
AI.method: The authors derive a physics residual from mechanistic equations underlying DayCent process-based models, build an MLP-based PINN, and train it on a multi-site agricultural dataset from four US sites. They compare PINN performance against an uncalibrated Cycles simulation and an MLP baseline across varying physics loss weighting hyperparameter λ, using both holdout validation and leave-one-site-out validation.
AI.result: The PINN consistently outperformed uncalibrated Cycles (R²=0.01), with the MLP baseline achieving mean R²=0.411. Physics constraints degraded holdout validation performance (marginal at low λ, significant at high λ) but improved performance and reduced variability in leave-one-site-out validation. However, cross-site generalization remained challenging, with negative R² across all seeds and λ values on the geographically distinct held-out site.
AI.conclusion: Physics constraints in PINNs sacrifice in-distribution accuracy for out-of-distribution robustness, anchoring predictions toward biogeochemically plausible behavior on unfamiliar soil conditions. However, cross-site generalization remains a significant challenge, suggesting that further research is needed to improve transferability of these models across geographically distinct agricultural sites.

title: Key-Interval A*: Accelerating Grid Pathfinding via Structural Abstraction
summary: Existing exact methods for 4-connected grid pathfinding reduce online search, but often either retain fine-grained search states or require substantial preprocessing. This paper presents Key-Interval A* (KIA*), an optimal pathfinding algorithm that uses lightweight preprocessing to construct and search over a compact interval-level abstraction of free space. KIA* represents free space using intervals: maximal contiguous runs of traversable cells. It extracts key intervals that capture structural boundary changes and connects them through contiguous non-key regions. KIA* then performs A*-style search on the resulting key-interval graph and constructively reconstructs grid paths from interval chains, without cell-level local search. We prove the completeness and optimality of KIA* on 4-connected grids. Experiments on standard benchmarks show that KIA* preserves exact shortest-path lengths and achieves the fastest runtime on seven of eight benchmark groups, with the largest gains on structured and game maps.

AI.tldr: KIA* is an optimal pathfinding algorithm for 4-connected grids that uses lightweight preprocessing to create a compact interval-level abstraction, enabling fast search and path reconstruction without cell-level operations.
AI.motivation: Existing exact pathfinding methods for 4-connected grids either retain fine-grained search states (causing slow online search) or require substantial preprocessing overhead. The authors aim to find a middle ground with lightweight preprocessing that still significantly accelerates online search.
AI.method: KIA* represents free space as intervals (maximal contiguous traversable cell runs), extracts key intervals at structural boundaries, builds a key-interval graph connecting them through non-key regions, performs A*-style search on this graph, and reconstructs grid paths from interval chains without cell-level local search.
AI.result: KIA* preserves exact shortest-path lengths and achieves the fastest runtime on seven of eight benchmark groups, with the largest gains on structured and game maps.
AI.conclusion: KIA* is proven complete and optimal for 4-connected grids, and empirically outperforms existing methods on most benchmarks, particularly benefiting structured and game-like environments.

title: Development of Vision-Language Model-based GNSS Spoofing Detection for Autonomous Vehicle Navigation
summary: Autonomous vehicles (AVs) depend on Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) for localization and navigation, making them vulnerable to spoofing attacks that can covertly redirect vehicles or induce unsafe maneuvers. In this paper, we develop the first Vision-Language Model (VLM)-based framework for GNSS spoofing detection for autonomous vehicles by fusing front-camera visual data with in-vehicle sensor readings (e.g., speed, acceleration, yaw rate) against GNSS-derived maneuvers. Our approach introduces a three-stage fine-tuning process that first grounds visual cues, and then calibrates sensor data within a shared semantic space to detect discrepancies between predicted and GNSS-derived maneuvers across three attack scenarios. We also generated an independent real-world dataset by driving an instrumented vehicle on public roads in Tuscaloosa, Alabama, equipped with time-synchronized GNSS, IMU, and camera logs to validate cross-regional generalization of our fine-tuned model on unseen data from training data. On this dataset, we then generated intelligent spoofing attacks, including trajectory mirroring with road-network snapping for wrong-turn attacks, position freezing for overshoot scenarios, and drift generation for stop attacks. On this validation dataset, the zero-shot VLMs baseline F1-score ranges from 23% to 32%, whereas our fine-tuned model achieves an F1-score ranging from 94% to 95%. Results show that our VLM-based approach correctly classified every wrong-turn and stop attacks, and attains 88%-93% accuracy for overshoot attacks. Furthermore, we introduce an adaptive inference policy that reduces VLM invocations to 14% (~86% computational reduction) and yields 65ms-73ms per 4s window. These results point to a practical, on-road layer of defense that complements signal-level integrity checks with the use of VLMs.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a VLM-based GNSS spoofing detection framework for autonomous vehicles by fusing camera and in-vehicle sensor data. Through three-stage fine-tuning, the model achieves 94-95% F1-score on real-world datasets (vs. 23-32% for zero-shot VLMs), with an adaptive inference policy reducing computational cost by ~86%.
AI.motivation: Autonomous vehicles rely on GNSS for localization, making them vulnerable to spoofing attacks that can covertly redirect vehicles or induce unsafe maneuvers, necessitating a robust detection mechanism.
AI.method: A three-stage VLM fine-tuning process that first grounds visual cues from front cameras, then calibrates in-vehicle sensor data (speed, acceleration, yaw rate) within a shared semantic space to detect discrepancies between predicted and GNSS-derived maneuvers across three attack scenarios (trajectory mirroring, position freezing, drift generation). An adaptive inference policy reduces computational overhead.
AI.result: Fine-tuned model achieves 94-95% F1-score (vs. 23-32% for zero-shot baselines), correctly classifies all wrong-turn and stop attacks, attains 88-93% accuracy for overshoot attacks, reduces VLM invocations to 14% (~86% reduction), and yields 65-73ms per 4s window.
AI.conclusion: The VLM-based approach provides a practical, on-road layer of defense against GNSS spoofing that complements signal-level integrity checks, validated on real-world data with cross-regional generalization.

title: ADVERSARIAL: And-Inverter Graph-Assisted Hardware Trojan Detection At Scale
comment: 9 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables. Accepted for publication at the IEEE/ACM International Conference on Computer-Aided Design (ICCAD 2026)
summary: Modern System-on-Chip (SoCs) often contain hundreds of millions to tens of billions of gates, making existing Hardware Trojan (HT) detection methods impractical due to their immense scale. The proposed approach incorporates symbolically enabled learning by modeling flattened gate-level netlists as Boolean networks represented as And-Inverter Graphs (AIGs), where all internal nodes are 2-input AND gates and inversions reside on the edges. Each directed connection is expressed as a triple within a Knowledge Graph Embedding (KGE) framework, producing compact, constant-size per-node representations that retain multi-hop structural context. The AIG's bounded fan-in and uniform semantics ensure training and inference complexity scale linearly with edge count, addressing major scalability bottlenecks in HT detection. Symbolically enabled learning across deep datapaths enables the model to differentiate circuit structures from rare and functionally inconsistent connections that signify potential Trojan triggers and payloads. Experiments on large-scale SoC benchmarks demonstrate clear geometric separation between Trojan and benign nodes and practical scalability.

AI.tldr: A symbolic knowledge-graph embedding approach using And-Inverter Graphs (AIGs) for scalable Hardware Trojan detection in large-scale SoCs, achieving linear complexity and clear geometric separation between Trojan and benign nodes.
AI.motivation: Existing HT detection methods are impractical for modern SoCs containing hundreds of millions to tens of billions of gates due to scalability limitations.
AI.method: Models flattened gate-level netlists as Boolean networks (And-Inverter Graphs) and encodes directed connections as triples within a Knowledge Graph Embedding framework, producing compact per-node representations. Leverages AIG's bounded fan-in and uniform semantics for linear scaling with edge count.
AI.result: Demonstrates linear scaling complexity, clear geometric separation between Trojan and benign nodes, and practical scalability on large-scale SoC benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The symbolically enabled learning approach effectively addresses scalability bottlenecks in HT detection while differentiating circuit structures from rare, functionally inconsistent connections indicative of Trojans.

title: Inference-Time Consensus for Mitigating Hidden Behaviors from LLM Fine-Tuning
summary: Recent work shows that fine-tuning language models on even a small amount of poisoned data can install targeted misbehavior, and ostensibly benign data can transmit hidden preferences that generalize broadly. Standard defenses, such as data filtering, mixing in harmless data, and regularization, attenuate these effects but do not eliminate them. We instead pursue robustness through redundancy: collecting multiple datasets from different sources and only learning what is common between them. Thus, if only a subset of sources are malicious, the misbehavior will be blocked. In order to implement this defense strategy, we fine-tune a separate reference model on each source's dataset and aggregate their next-token distributions at decoding time. We introduce two consensus decoders: a token-wise minimum, which caps each token at the lowest probability any source assigns, and a base-relative variant, which reverts to the base probability on any token the sources move in opposing directions. We further relax exact agreement to tolerate partial support across sources and different surface expressions of the same intention. Across controlled poisoning tasks, subliminal learning, and emergent misalignment, consensus decoding suppresses source-specific misbehavior while preserving shared desirable behavior, including cases where union training and weight averaging retain the unwanted behavior.

AI.tldr: Consensus decoding across multiple data sources can suppress source-specific misbehavior (poisoning, subliminal learning, emergent misalignment) while preserving shared desirable behavior, outperforming standard defenses like data filtering, mixing, and regularization.
AI.motivation: Standard defenses (data filtering, mixing harmless data, regularization) attenuate but fail to eliminate targeted misbehavior from poisoned or biased data during fine-tuning. A more robust approach is needed.
AI.method: The authors fine-tune a separate reference model on each source's dataset, then aggregate their next-token distributions at decoding time using two consensus decoders: (1) token-wise minimum (caps each token at the lowest probability any source assigns) and (2) base-relative variant (reverts to base probability on tokens where sources disagree). They also relax exact agreement to tolerate partial support and different surface expressions.
AI.result: Across controlled poisoning, subliminal learning, and emergent misalignment tasks, consensus decoding suppresses source-specific misbehavior while preserving shared desirable behavior. Union training and weight averaging retain unwanted behavior in some cases, while consensus decoding does not.
AI.conclusion: Robustness through redundancy—collecting multiple datasets from different sources and learning only what is common—effectively blocks malicious behavior from a subset of sources, providing stronger defense than existing methods.

title: Color Fundus Photography Analysis: Co-evolution of Data, Preprocessing, and Modeling toward Multimodal AI
summary: Color Fundus Photography (CFP) is a primary non-invasive imaging modality for large-scale screening of ophthalmic and systemic diseases. Existing surveys mainly summarize task-specific algorithms, datasets, or preprocessing techniques independently, lacking a unified perspective on their co-evolution with modern artificial intelligence. This review provides an integrated overview of CFP AI through the interplay of dataset evolution, preprocessing paradigms, and modeling frameworks. We show that CFP datasets have evolved from small single-center collections with task-specific labels to large multi-center resources featuring multimodal pairings and longitudinal clinical records. Preprocessing has progressed from conventional image enhancement to neural data-engineering pipelines, hardware-aware token optimization, and self-supervised imputation for incomplete electronic health records (EHRs). Meanwhile, modeling has advanced from convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to vision foundation models, state space models (SSMs), and multimodal expert architectures. At the multimodal frontier, CFP is increasingly integrated with EHRs and longitudinal patient information, enabling more comprehensive clinical reasoning beyond isolated image analysis. We conclude that future progress depends on the collaborative optimization of datasets, preprocessing, and multimodal modeling, providing a roadmap toward robust clinical deployment, improved cross-domain generalization, and resource-efficient edge intelligence.

AI.tldr: This review provides an integrated overview of Color Fundus Photography (CFP) AI, covering the co-evolution of datasets (from small single-center to large multi-center multimodal collections), preprocessing (from conventional enhancement to neural pipelines and self-supervised EHR imputation), and modeling (from CNNs to foundation models, SSMs, and multimodal architectures), with a future roadmap emphasizing collaborative optimization for clinical deployment and edge intelligence.
AI.motivation: Existing surveys on CFP AI focus on isolated aspects (task-specific algorithms, datasets, or preprocessing), lacking a unified perspective on how these components co-evolve with modern AI. This review aims to provide an integrated overview to fill that gap.
AI.method: The review systematically examines CFP AI through three intertwined dimensions: (1) dataset evolution (small single-center → large multi-center with multimodal/longitudinal data), (2) preprocessing paradigms (conventional image enhancement → neural data-engineering, token optimization, self-supervised EHR imputation), and (3) modeling frameworks (CNNs → vision foundation models, SSMs, multimodal expert architectures).
AI.result: CFP datasets have grown in scale and complexity; preprocessing has shifted toward neural and data-centric approaches; modeling has progressed to foundation models and multimodal architectures integrating EHRs and longitudinal data. The multimodal frontier enables more comprehensive clinical reasoning beyond isolated image analysis.
AI.conclusion: Future progress requires collaborative optimization of datasets, preprocessing, and multimodal modeling, providing a roadmap for robust clinical deployment, improved cross-domain generalization, and resource-efficient edge intelligence.

title: WorldDiT: A Unified Diffusion Architecture for World and Action Modeling
summary: Many recent robot policies pursue stronger control by using large pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) as the action backbone. We introduce WorldDiT, a unified diffusion transformer architecture that couples action generation with visual world modeling and achieves strong performance without a large pretrained VLM action backbone. During training, a single diffusion transformer generates continuous action chunks and predicts normalized RGB patch targets from future camera frames. Across four LIBERO simulation suites, WorldDiT lies on the reported Pareto frontier for total model parameters and mean success among methods reporting all four suites. These results provide a strong sub-billion-parameter baseline for future scaling studies.

AI.tldr: WorldDiT is a unified diffusion transformer that couples action generation with visual world modeling, achieving strong robotic control performance without relying on large pretrained VLMs. It sets a sub-billion-parameter baseline on LIBERO benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current robot policies heavily depend on large pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) as the action backbone; the authors aim to achieve strong control without such expensive large models.
AI.method: A unified diffusion transformer (WorldDiT) that jointly generates continuous action chunks and predicts normalized RGB patch targets from future camera frames during training.
AI.result: On four LIBERO simulation suites, WorldDiT lies on the reported Pareto frontier for total model parameters and mean success rate among methods reporting all four suites.
AI.conclusion: WorldDiT provides a strong sub-billion-parameter baseline for future scaling studies, showing that coupling action generation with world modeling can rival VLM-backed approaches.

title: NeurGO: Learning to Generate Elite Candidates for Meta-Black-Box Expensive Optimization
summary: Expensive black-box optimization is ubiquitous in science and engineering, where function evaluations are costly and the evaluation budget is limited. Traditional evolutionary algorithms and Meta-BlackBox Optimization (MetaBBO) approaches typically consume most evaluations on candidate selection, often wasting precious budget on inferior solutions. Although surrogate-assisted evolution and Bayesian optimization aim to reduce evaluations through surrogate models, constructing an accurate global model from limited data remains challenging, and model bias can easily trap the search in local optima. To overcome these limitations, we propose NeurGO, a generative MetaBBO framework that directly synthesizes elite candidates from historical population states. Specifically, we employ an attention-based encoder to capture the population-level search trend and condition a decoder on this representation to generate high-quality candidates, avoiding the expensive evaluation of large offspring pools. We then design a quality-diversity loss to maintain solution quality and population diversity throughout the search. Through extensive benchmarking on CEC 2008 and the COCO BBOB test suites, our method achieves better optimization performance under the same evaluation budget and exhibits faster convergence.

AI.tldr: NeurGO is a generative MetaBBO framework that uses an attention-based encoder to capture population-level search trends and a decoder to directly synthesize elite candidates, avoiding costly evaluations of inferior solutions. It employs quality-diversity loss to balance solution quality and population diversity, achieving better optimization performance and faster convergence on CEC 2008 and COCO BBOB benchmarks under limited evaluation budgets.
AI.motivation: Traditional evolutionary algorithms and MetaBBO methods waste evaluations on inferior solutions during candidate selection, while surrogate-assisted approaches struggle with accurate global modeling from limited data and are prone to local optima due to model bias.
AI.method: NeurGO uses an attention-based encoder to capture population-level search trends, then conditions a decoder on this representation to directly generate high-quality candidates. A quality-diversity loss is designed to maintain both solution quality and population diversity throughout the search.
AI.result: On CEC 2008 and COCO BBOB benchmarks, NeurGO achieves better optimization performance under the same evaluation budget and exhibits faster convergence compared to baselines.
AI.conclusion: Directly generating elite candidates from historical population states via a generative MetaBBO framework is an effective alternative to traditional evaluation-heavy selection, overcoming limitations of both evolutionary algorithms and surrogate-assisted optimization.

title: Mutual Modality Trust with Lightweight Reconstruction Regularization for Fine-grained Tire Pattern Recognition
summary: Visual tire recognition serves as a core supporting technique for vehicle safety monitoring, autonomous driving perception and automated automotive maintenance. Existing fine-grained tire recognition techniques suffer from three prominent limitations. They tend to depend on only one visual source, lack the capacity to jointly model spatial and frequency cues for minute tread texture extraction, and suffer severe overfitting given limited annotated tire imagery. This paper proposes a lightweight fine-grained tire pattern recognition method incorporating dual-branch independent inference and enhanced feature fusion to boost recognition performance. The framework employs two task-specialized branches dedicated to tire surface and tread indentation, respectively, to extract modality-specific discriminative features. Each branch conducts independent prediction, while cross-branch feature fusion exploits Mutual Modality Trust (M$^2$T) to realize complementary feature enhancement across two modalities. Besides, a frequency-domain hierarchical guidance module is devised, which leverages bandpass filters to decompose feature maps into high- and low-frequency components and enables fine-grained cross-layer feature modulation. Furthermore, a Lightweight Reconstruction Regularization (LR$^2$) is introduced to retain abundant intrinsic information within feature embeddings, substantially improving feature stability and recognition robustness under limited labeled training data. In addition, we establish a surface-indentation multi-source dataset namely MTire299 for fine-grained tire tread recognition, which covers 299 categories with a total of 14795 paired image samples. Extensive experiments conducted on two public tire datasets validate the superiority and efficacy of the proposed algorithm.

AI.tldr: A lightweight fine-grained tire pattern recognition method using dual-branch independent inference, Mutual Modality Trust (M²T) cross-branch fusion, frequency-domain hierarchical guidance via bandpass filters, and Lightweight Reconstruction Regularization (LR²) to overcome limited data, single-source dependency, and inadequate spatial-frequency modeling. A new 299-category dataset MTire299 is also introduced.
AI.motivation: Existing fine-grained tire recognition methods suffer from: (1) reliance on only one visual source, (2) inability to jointly model spatial and frequency cues for minute tread texture, and (3) severe overfitting due to limited annotated tire imagery.
AI.method: (1) Dual-branch architecture with task-specialized branches for tire surface and tread indentation; (2) Mutual Modality Trust (M²T) for cross-branch feature fusion; (3) Frequency-domain hierarchical guidance module using bandpass filters to decompose features into high/low-frequency components for cross-layer modulation; (4) Lightweight Reconstruction Regularization (LR²) to retain intrinsic information under limited labeled data; (5) MTire299 dataset with 299 categories and 14,795 paired samples.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on two public tire datasets validate the superiority and efficacy of the proposed algorithm over existing methods.
AI.conclusion: The proposed lightweight dual-branch framework with M²T fusion, frequency-guided modulation, and LR² regularization effectively addresses key limitations in fine-grained tire recognition, achieving robust performance even with limited training data.

title: Greedy dynamical meta-learning
summary: Gradient descent scales well to large models, but becomes unstable over long time horizons. Gradient-free optimizers can scale to arbitrary timespans, but are hobbled by high dimensions. Since learning occurs in large models over long timescales, neither of these approaches is likely to produce traits which can accelerate the learning process. Instead, we propose a meta-learning algorithm in which the agent learns to modify its own weights and biases. Our algorithm consists of an inner loop, wherein the agent performs some high-dimensional optimization upon itself, and an outer loop, wherein we perform some low-dimensional optimization upon the inner loop. Since the outer loop handles very few parameters, standard zeroth-order methods may be used.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a meta-learning algorithm where an agent modifies its own weights through an inner (high-dimensional) and outer (low-dimensional) loop, using zeroth-order methods for the outer loop to combine scalability with stability.
AI.motivation: Gradient descent becomes unstable over long time horizons for large models, while gradient-free methods scale to long timespans but fail in high dimensions. Neither approach alone can produce accelerating traits for learning in large models over long timescales.
AI.method: A meta-learning algorithm with two loops: an inner loop where the agent performs high-dimensional optimization on itself (modifying its own weights and biases), and an outer loop where low-dimensional optimization is performed on the inner loop using standard zeroth-order methods.
AI.result: The outer loop handles very few parameters, making zeroth-order methods feasible. This combines the strengths of gradient-based (high-dimensional scalability) and gradient-free (long-timespan stability) approaches.
AI.conclusion: The proposed bi-level meta-learning framework can potentially produce learning traits that accelerate the learning process by leveraging the complementary strengths of both optimization paradigms.

title: Separating Capability from Permission: A Governance Framework for Agentic AI Autonomy Levels
summary: As AI systems increasingly exhibit agentic behavior, discussions of autonomy often conflate what systems are technically capable of doing with what they should be permitted to do in practice. This paper introduces a governance framework that explicitly separates Allowed Autonomy Levels (AAL), which define the degree of autonomy an AI agent is authorized to exercise given risk, oversight, and accountability considerations, from Autonomous Capability Levels (ACL), which characterize an agent's inherent technical abilities. We present a structured set of autonomy levels spanning reactive execution, decision support, supervised action, goal-directed autonomy, and delegated operational authority, and describe how control, reversibility, and accountability change as autonomy increases. To operationalize this framework, we propose a risk-aware decision process for assigning allowed autonomy, analyze how risk and accountability evolve across autonomy levels, and demonstrate its application through a deployed enterprise data engineering agent, illustrating how a system assessed at a high capability level can be deliberately constrained to a lower allowed autonomy based on risk, reversibility, and organizational readiness. By distinguishing authorization from capability, this work provides practical guidance for the design, deployment, and governance of Agentic AI systems.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a governance framework that separates Allowed Autonomy Levels (AAL) from Autonomous Capability Levels (ACL) for AI agents, providing a risk-aware decision process to constrain technically capable systems to authorized autonomy levels based on risk, reversibility, and organizational readiness, demonstrated via a deployed enterprise data engineering agent.
AI.motivation: Discussions of AI autonomy often conflate technical capability with permissible authorization, leading to governance gaps.
AI.method: Proposes a structured framework distinguishing Allowed Autonomy Levels (AAL) from Autonomous Capability Levels (ACL), with levels spanning reactive execution to delegated operational authority, and a risk-aware decision process for assigning allowed autonomy.
AI.result: Demonstrates via a deployed enterprise data engineering agent that a system with high ACL can be deliberately constrained to a lower AAL based on risk, reversibility, and organizational readiness.
AI.conclusion: Distinguishing authorization from capability provides practical guidance for the design, deployment, and governance of Agentic AI systems.

title: Multimodal Semantic-Probabilistic Objectness for Open World Object Detection
summary: Open-world object detection (OWOD) requires a detector to recognize known categories, discover unnamed objects from unseen categories, and incrementally learn newly annotated classes. PROB improves unknown discovery by modeling class-agnostic probabilistic objectness in the decoder-query space. However, visual objectness alone cannot determine whether an object-like query corresponds to a hard known instance, an unseen-category object, or background clutter, resulting in an ambiguous known-unknown decision boundary. We propose MSPO, a lightweight semantic calibration framework that augments PROB with task-aware known-category language priors while preserving its detector architecture and incremental learning protocol. For each currently known category, MSPO constructs an extended text description covering category attributes, visual appearance, typical scenes, and functional usage, and encodes it using a frozen CLIP text encoder. Decoder query features are projected into the same semantic space to estimate their support from the current known-category semantics. This semantic evidence is fused with PROB's visual objectness to calibrate known and unknown predictions without turning OWOD into open-vocabulary classification. Importantly, MSPO never uses future-category names, and all unseen categories remain unnamed during evaluation. Experiments on M-OWODB and S-OWODB show that MSPO improves the strong PROB baseline on the main aggregate metrics while retaining competitive unknown recall. It also improves early unknown-confusion metrics and raises PASCAL VOC final mAP by up to 2.7 points. These results demonstrate that known-category language semantics provide an effective calibration signal for probabilistic objectness under the standard OWOD setting.

AI.tldr: MSPO enhances the OWOD detector PROB by fusing visual objectness with frozen CLIP-based semantic priors from known categories, improving known-unknown calibration without requiring future-category names or altering the incremental learning protocol.
AI.motivation: PROB's class-agnostic visual objectness alone cannot reliably distinguish hard known instances, unseen-category objects, and background clutter, leading to ambiguous known-unknown decision boundaries in open-world object detection.
AI.method: MSPO constructs extended text descriptions (attributes, appearance, scenes, functions) for each known category, encodes them via a frozen CLIP text encoder, projects decoder query features into the same semantic space, and fuses the resulting semantic support scores with PROB's visual objectness to calibrate known vs. unknown predictions.
AI.result: On M-OWODB and S-OWODB, MSPO improves PROB's aggregate metrics, retains competitive unknown recall, improves early unknown-confusion metrics, and raises PASCAL VOC final mAP by up to 2.7 points.
AI.conclusion: Known-category language semantics provide an effective calibration signal for probabilistic objectness under the standard OWOD setting, without requiring future-category names or transitioning to open-vocabulary classification.

title: DECAF: De-Clustering for Adaptive Representational Unlearning
summary: Machine unlearning, which aims to remove the influence of specific training data from a trained model, is a key requirement for privacy, accountability, and adaptive deployment. We argue that many unlearning methods are vulnerable to a simple clustering attack, which can recover class structure in an unsupervised manner, limiting their suitability for continual deployment where removal requests must be handled reliably on demand. To address this, we propose DECAF (DE-Clustering for Adaptive Forgetting), a post-hoc method that operates only on the forget set and is designed to break the cluster. DECAF combines input noise, confidence suppression, and entropy-based output diversification to disrupt the residual feature-space structure associated with forgotten data. On CIFAR-10 with ResNet-18, DECAF attains 0.10% forget-class accuracy, 79.4% retain accuracy, and an AUS of 0.88, surpassing all other baselines. In cluster-based analysis, it attains performance comparable to that of unlearning methods that use the full training set, while being significantly more efficient. Code: https://github.com/ale256/representation_unlearning.

AI.tldr: DECAF is a post-hoc unlearning method that breaks feature-space clusters via input noise, confidence suppression, and entropy-based output diversification, achieving strong forgetting (0.10% forget-class accuracy) and retain accuracy (79.4%) on CIFAR-10 ResNet-18 without requiring full training set access.
AI.motivation: Many unlearning methods are vulnerable to a simple clustering attack that can recover class structure in an unsupervised manner, limiting their suitability for continual deployment where removal requests must be handled reliably on demand.
AI.method: DECAF (DE-Clustering for Adaptive Forgetting) is a post-hoc method operating only on the forget set. It combines input noise, confidence suppression, and entropy-based output diversification to disrupt residual feature-space structure associated with forgotten data.
AI.result: On CIFAR-10 with ResNet-18, DECAF achieves 0.10% forget-class accuracy, 79.4% retain accuracy, and AUS of 0.88, surpassing all baselines. Cluster analysis shows performance comparable to full-training-set methods but with significantly higher efficiency.
AI.conclusion: DECAF effectively addresses the clustering vulnerability in unlearning by breaking feature-space structure using only the forget set, offering a more reliable and efficient solution for continual deployment scenarios.

title: Do LLMs Know Their Vulnerable Scenarios?
summary: Safety-aligned large language models are trained to refuse harmful requests, yet embedding the same requests in particular scenarios can bypass their safeguards. Existing red-teaming methods empirically identify effective scenarios through observed attack outcomes, but why particular scenarios weaken refusal remains mechanistically unclear. Meanwhile, mechanistic interpretability studies have characterized both refusal directions and jailbreak-associated features, without explaining the relationship between the two representations. In this work, we show that scenario-wrapped prompts activate internal scenario directions whose causal steering consistently reduces refusal scores. Building on this finding, we propose \textsc{Concept2Scenario}, a concept-based attribution framework for vulnerable scenario discovery. It instantiates a broad concept space with a sparse autoencoder, attributes refusal suppression to individual concepts, translates the identified concepts into interpretable natural-language scenarios, and identifies synergistic scenario combinations through interaction attribution. Across three open-source models, two safety benchmarks, and six black-box jailbreak methods, the discovered scenarios serve as reusable priors that improve average attack success rates by up to $18.2$ percentage points. They also transfer to GPT-5, Claude-Haiku-4.5, and Gemini-3-Flash, suggesting that some scenario-level refusal vulnerabilities are shared across model families. Moreover, the identified combinations outperform their individual constituents and enable iterative attacks to succeed in fewer turns.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies that scenario-wrapped prompts activate internal "scenario directions" in LLMs that causally suppress refusal behavior. The authors propose Concept2Scenario, a concept-based attribution framework using sparse autoencoders to discover vulnerable scenarios, which transfer across model families and improve jailbreak attack success rates by up to 18.2 percentage points.
AI.motivation: Existing red-teaming methods empirically identify effective jailbreak scenarios but lack mechanistic understanding of why certain scenarios weaken refusal. Meanwhile, mechanistic interpretability has characterized refusal directions and jailbreak features without explaining their relationship.
AI.method: Proposes Concept2Scenario: instantiates a broad concept space via sparse autoencoder, attributes refusal suppression to individual concepts, translates concepts into interpretable natural-language scenarios, and identifies synergistic scenario combinations through interaction attribution.
AI.result: Discovered scenarios improve average attack success rates by up to 18.2 percentage points across three open-source models, two safety benchmarks, and six black-box jailbreak methods. Scenarios transfer to GPT-5, Claude-Haiku-4.5, and Gemini-3-Flash. Identified combinations outperform individual constituents and require fewer attack turns.
AI.conclusion: Scenario-level refusal vulnerabilities are shared across model families; the discovered scenarios serve as reusable priors for more effective and efficient jailbreak attacks, bridging mechanistic understanding with practical red-teaming.

title: Effective Receptive Field Ordering Matters for Infrared Small Target Detection
summary: In this work, we investigate a previously unexplored architectural dimension for infrared small target detection: the organization of effective receptive fields (ERFs) during feature refinement. Unlike existing approaches that primarily improve individual feature operators, we argue that ERF organization constitutes an architectural dimension independent of receptive field design itself, and formulate deep feature transformation as a progressive residual correction process, from which a theoretical framework for ERF scheduling is established. Specifically, we reveal that ERF refinement is governed by two fundamental properties: scale-frequency correspondence, which aligns different ERF scales with distinct residual frequency characteristics, and nonlinear non-commutativity, which makes different ERF orderings produce fundamentally different refinement trajectories. Together, these properties show that ERF organization, rather than ERF scale alone, governs refinement dynamics. Guided by these principles, we propose Receptive Field Ordering Network (RFONet), which realizes hierarchical ERF scheduling through a multigrid-inspired V-cycle strategy using only standard $3\times3$ convolutions. RFONet achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks with only 1.16M parameters and over 157 FPS inference speed. Beyond empirical performance, our theoretical analysis provides theoretical guarantees for stable residual refinement under perturbations, frequency shifts, and partial occlusions, which are consistently reflected in superior noise robustness and cross-dataset generalization. Finally, our framework reformulates ERF organization as a task-dependent optimization objective, providing a principled foundation for future adaptive receptive field scheduling.

AI.tldr: RFONet proposes a novel framework for infrared small target detection by organizing effective receptive fields (ERFs) as a progressive residual correction process, governed by scale-frequency correspondence and nonlinear non-commutativity, achieving state-of-the-art performance with only 1.16M parameters using standard 3×3 convolutions via a multigrid-inspired V-cycle strategy.
AI.motivation: To explore ERF organization as an independent architectural dimension for infrared small target detection, moving beyond improving individual feature operators to understanding how ERF scheduling governs refinement dynamics.
AI.method: Formulates deep feature transformation as progressive residual correction; establishes theoretical framework with scale-frequency correspondence and nonlinear non-commutativity; proposes RFONet using multigrid-inspired V-cycle ERF scheduling with only standard 3×3 convolutions.
AI.result: State-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks with 1.16M parameters and 157+ FPS; superior noise robustness and cross-dataset generalization; theoretical guarantees for stable refinement under perturbations, frequency shifts, and partial occlusions.
AI.conclusion: ERF organization is a task-dependent optimization objective that governs refinement dynamics beyond ERF scale alone, providing a principled foundation for future adaptive receptive field scheduling.

title: Variational Boosting for Physics-Informed Neural Networks
summary:
Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) solve differential equations by minimizing the residual of a nonlinear operator over a neural parameterization of the solution. However, monolithic PINNs often suffer from ill-conditioning, spectral bias, and optimization instability.
  We introduce a variational boosting framework in which solutions are constructed additively in function space. Each stage trains a weak learner whose converged correction satisfies a local orthogonality condition, equivalent to a projected functional gradient descent step onto the tangent space of the network's function manifold. Because each correction network is deliberately small, the restricted minimization admits full Newton or conjugate gradient updates, which are typically infeasible in large PINNs. The resulting method separates global nonlinear refinement into a sequence of well-conditioned subproblems while preserving the full variational structure of the operator.
  This framework provides a geometric interpretation of multi-stage PINNs as projected functional gradient descent and enables stable second-order optimization for nonlinear differential equations.

AI.tldr: Introduces a variational boosting framework for PINNs that builds solutions additively via small weak learners, enabling stable second-order optimization and mitigating ill-conditioning, spectral bias, and optimization instability.
AI.motivation: Monolithic PINNs suffer from ill-conditioning, spectral bias, and optimization instability, limiting their practical effectiveness.
AI.method: A variational boosting framework that constructs solutions additively in function space, where each stage trains a small weak learner whose converged correction satisfies a local orthogonality condition, equivalent to projected functional gradient descent onto the tangent space of the network's function manifold. Small network size allows full Newton or conjugate gradient updates.
AI.result: Separates global nonlinear refinement into well-conditioned subproblems while preserving the full variational structure; enables stable second-order optimization for nonlinear differential equations.
AI.conclusion: Multi-stage PINNs can be interpreted as projected functional gradient descent, and the boosting framework allows stable second-order optimization that is typically infeasible in large monolithic PINNs.

title: Delegation Intelligence in Deep Search: A Controllable Framework for Disentangled Capability Diagnosis
summary: Deep search is becoming a core capability of modern agent systems, yet it is typically evaluated solely based on end-to-end answer accuracy. This coupled evaluation paradigm entangles retrieval quality, long-context comprehension, evidence verification, and tool-use decisions, making it difficult to determine whether a model truly knows when and how to delegate information seeking to search. To this end: (1) We formalize this meta-capability as Delegation Intelligence in deep search and decompose it into complementary dimensions-Search Decision-Making (recognizing information insufficiency and deciding whether, when, and how to search) and Information Synthesis and Verification (aggregating evidence from multiple sources, judging source reliability, and synthesizing information under noisy, potentially adversarial conditions). (2) To enable disentangled and reproducible measurement, we develop a controllable synthesis pipeline built on document-grounded reverse engineering. This yields a general recipe for constructing controlled deep-search evaluations rather than a single fixed dataset. (3) As a concrete instantiation, we construct DelegSearchBench, together with a disentangled evaluation protocol that isolates each capability dimension by varying document composition and tool access. (4) Across representative models, we demonstrate that deep-search competence cannot be adequately characterized by final-answer accuracy alone...

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Delegation Intelligence as a core meta-capability for deep search, decomposing it into Search Decision-Making and Information Synthesis and Verification. It proposes a controllable synthesis pipeline and DelegSearchBench for disentangled evaluation, showing that final-answer accuracy alone is insufficient to characterize deep-search competence.
AI.motivation: Current deep search evaluation relies solely on end-to-end answer accuracy, which entangles retrieval, comprehension, verification, and tool-use decisions, making it impossible to isolate whether a model truly knows when and how to delegate information seeking to search.
AI.method: (1) Formalizes Delegation Intelligence with two complementary dimensions: Search Decision-Making and Information Synthesis and Verification. (2) Develops a controllable synthesis pipeline based on document-grounded reverse engineering. (3) Constructs DelegSearchBench with a disentangled evaluation protocol that isolates each capability by varying document composition and tool access.
AI.result: Across representative models, deep-search competence cannot be adequately characterized by final-answer accuracy alone, demonstrating the need for disentangled evaluation.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework and benchmark enable more granular, reproducible assessment of deep-search capabilities, revealing limitations masked by conventional end-to-end metrics.

title: Low-light Image Enhancement via Multi-scale Attention combined with Fourier Transform
summary: Low-light image enhancement (LLIE) aims to improve image quality and clarity in diverse and demanding low-illumination environments. However, existing deep learning-based LLIE methods struggle to accurately capture real-world illumination and restore texture details, largely because their algorithmic strengths remain underutilized. To address these issues, we present a supervised frequency domain deep learning network for LLIE, named multi-scale attention combined with the Fourier transform (MSFT) which adopts a U-shaped, one-stage architecture that infuses guidance from low-light images into the network by channeling it through multi-scale attention. We further fuse the amplitude information from priori channels with that of the low-light image in MSFT's self-created module, and carry out multi-scale guidance along with the network. Subsequently, to better enhance the faint feature, such as fine content and textures, and to better fuse global context confidence in the decoding stage, we separately introduce a multi-shape synergistic attention and a lightweight network that effectively integrate information in high-dimensional space to embed into the superlative feature space channel containing rich texture information. Extensive experiments conducted on LOL, SID, SMID, and SDSD datasets demonstrate that MSFT significantly outperforms state-of-the-art competitors. For example, compared with Retinexformer, our method achieves a peak signal-to-noise ratio of up to 41.76 decibels on the SDSD-outdoor dataset with an increase of 11.92 decibels and a structural similarity index of 0.988 with a 13.80% improvement.

AI.tldr: MSFT is a supervised frequency-domain deep learning network for low-light image enhancement that uses multi-scale attention combined with Fourier transform in a U-shaped architecture, achieving significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods (e.g., 41.76 dB PSNR on SDSD-outdoor, 11.92 dB improvement over Retinexformer).
AI.motivation: Existing deep learning-based LLIE methods struggle to accurately capture real-world illumination and restore texture details because their algorithmic strengths remain underutilized.
AI.method: A U-shaped one-stage architecture (MSFT) that: (1) channels low-light image guidance through multi-scale attention; (2) fuses amplitude information from priori channels with low-light image amplitude via a self-created module; (3) introduces multi-shape synergistic attention and a lightweight network for fine texture enhancement and global context fusion in the decoding stage.
AI.result: Outperforms state-of-the-art competitors on LOL, SID, SMID, and SDSD datasets. On SDSD-outdoor, achieves 41.76 dB PSNR (11.92 dB improvement over Retinexformer) and 0.988 SSIM (13.80% improvement).
AI.conclusion: MSFT effectively addresses LLIE by combining Fourier domain processing with multi-scale attention, significantly improving illumination capture and texture restoration.

title: Joint Flow Matching for Generator-Consistent Classification
summary: We introduce Joint Flow Matching (JFM), a training framework for continuous normalising flows over multiple variables. Standard flow matching transports variables from noise to data simultaneously, offering no natural mechanism for forward and reverse conditional inference from a shared joint model. JFM resolves this by assigning opposite roles to each variable at the temporal endpoints. We prove that JFM produces a consistent joint distribution where that forward or reverse integration are conditionals of the same joint. We explore this consistency in the context of joint classification and generation as the basis for interpretability in discriminative-generative models. We validate JFM on conditional datasets producing competitive accuracy with inherently well-calibrated confidence scores without post-hoc calibration, and classifier-consistent image generation.

AI.tldr: Joint Flow Matching (JFM) is a training framework for continuous normalising flows that enables consistent forward and reverse conditional inference from a shared joint model, achieving competitive classification accuracy with well-calibrated confidence and classifier-consistent image generation.
AI.motivation: Standard flow matching transports variables from noise to data simultaneously but lacks a natural mechanism for forward and reverse conditional inference from a shared joint model. JFM resolves this by assigning opposite roles to each variable at the temporal endpoints.
AI.method: JFM assigns opposite roles to each variable at the temporal endpoints of the flow, proving that forward and reverse integration yield conditionals of the same consistent joint distribution.
AI.result: Competitive classification accuracy with inherently well-calibrated confidence scores without post-hoc calibration, and classifier-consistent image generation.
AI.conclusion: JFM provides a principled framework for joint discriminative-generative modeling with provable consistency, enabling interpretability and well-calibrated uncertainty without additional calibration steps.

title: ObsDriveBench: Benchmarking Multimodal Understanding under Adverse Weather with Observability Awareness
summary: Autonomous driving under adverse weather remains a critical challenge, yet existing vision-language benchmarks mainly evaluate under standard conditions, synthetic corruptions, or single modality. As a result, it remains unclear how vision-language models behave under real-world adverse weather with multi-modal inputs. We argue that a key difficulty lies in degraded environmental observability: under fog, rain, snow, and low illumination, multi-modal observations become unreliable and cross-modally inconsistent, posing challenges to scene understanding, and subsequent decision-making. To study this, we introduce \textbf{ObsDriveBench}, a real-world multi-modal benchmark for adverse-weather autonomous driving. Our benchmark is designed with three capability dimensions: \textbf{observability awareness}, \textbf{spatial reliability}, and \textbf{risk-aware decision-making}, enabling fine-grained diagnosis of model behavior under degraded observations. We construct the benchmark through observability meta-annotation, scene description, and capability oriented multiple-choice tasks over synchronized camera, LiDAR, and radar inputs, forming a benchmark with over 14k training and 13k test questions. Experiments reveal consistent performance degradation of existing vision-language models. We further introduce \textbf{ObsDrive} model with normal-weather supervised fine-tuning and adverse-weather reinforcement learning, improving robustness across all three capabilities. The dataset and evaluation code will be released at \href{https://github.com/russellyq/ObsDriveBench}{\texttt{ObsDriveBench}}.

AI.tldr: ObsDriveBench is a real-world multi-modal benchmark for evaluating vision-language models under adverse weather conditions (fog, rain, snow, low illumination). It tests three capabilities: observability awareness, spatial reliability, and risk-aware decision-making using synchronized camera, LiDAR, and radar data (14k train/13k test). The authors also propose ObsDrive, a model with normal-weather SFT and adverse-weather RL that improves robustness across all three dimensions.
AI.motivation: Existing vision-language benchmarks for autonomous driving mainly evaluate under standard conditions, synthetic corruptions, or single modality, leaving a gap in understanding how VLMs behave under real-world adverse weather with multi-modal inputs where environmental observability is degraded and cross-modal inconsistencies arise.
AI.method: The authors construct ObsDriveBench via observability meta-annotation, scene description, and capability-oriented multiple-choice tasks over synchronized camera, LiDAR, and radar inputs. They also propose the ObsDrive model using normal-weather supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by adverse-weather reinforcement learning (RL).
AI.result: Existing vision-language models show consistent performance degradation under adverse weather. The proposed ObsDrive model improves robustness across all three capability dimensions (observability awareness, spatial reliability, risk-aware decision-making).
AI.conclusion: Degraded environmental observability is a key difficulty for multi-modal autonomous driving under adverse weather, and both the benchmark (ObsDriveBench) and the trained model (ObsDrive) provide valuable resources for studying and improving VLM robustness in such conditions.

title: Structural Loss Metrics for Tensor Approximation via Matrix Low-Rank Approximation
summary: Matricized low-rank approximation via SVD is a standard surrogate for tensor decompositions, but entry-wise reconstruction error fails to capture multiway geometric degradation. Under an orthogonal Tucker model, we characterize this degradation using two metrics: cross-mode Direction Loss, measuring geometric subspace deviation from rank truncation and noise rotation, and Interaction Loss, quantifying multilinear interaction distortion in the core tensor. We prove that squared relative reconstruction error orthogonally decomposes into interaction loss and out-of-subspace energy, and derive a Wedin-type bound establishing the stability of a plug-in Direction Loss estimator. Experiments on synthetic and hyperspectral datasets demonstrate that nearly identical reconstruction errors can yield markedly different structural-loss profiles; hyperspectral patches with comparable reconstruction errors exhibit up to a 4.6-fold difference in Direction Loss, correlating with severe visual blurring.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces two new metrics—Direction Loss and Interaction Loss—to characterize geometric degradation in Tucker tensor decompositions beyond standard reconstruction error, proving theoretical properties and showing these metrics can reveal structural differences invisible to reconstruction error alone.
AI.motivation: Standard entry-wise reconstruction error (e.g., via SVD-based low-rank approximation) fails to capture multiway geometric degradation in tensor decompositions, motivating the need for metrics that reflect subspace and multilinear structure distortion.
AI.method: Under an orthogonal Tucker model, the authors propose two metrics: (1) Cross-mode Direction Loss, measuring geometric subspace deviation from rank truncation and noise rotation; (2) Interaction Loss, quantifying multilinear interaction distortion in the core tensor. They prove that squared relative reconstruction error decomposes orthogonally into Interaction Loss and out-of-subspace energy, and derive a Wedin-type bound for a plug-in Direction Loss estimator.
AI.result: Experiments on synthetic and hyperspectral datasets show that nearly identical reconstruction errors can yield markedly different structural-loss profiles. Hyperspectral patches with comparable reconstruction errors exhibited up to a 4.6-fold difference in Direction Loss, correlating with severe visual blurring.
AI.conclusion: Direction Loss and Interaction Loss provide complementary geometric information beyond reconstruction error, enabling better assessment of tensor decomposition quality, particularly for applications where subspace structure and multilinear interactions matter (e.g., hyperspectral imaging).

title: Understanding Machine Unlearning Through the Lens of Mode Connectivity
summary: Machine Unlearning aims to remove undesired information from trained models without full retraining from scratch. Despite recent progress, the loss landscape and optimization geometry of unlearning are poorly understood. In this paper, we study machine unlearning through the lens of mode connectivity--the phenomenon that independently trained models can often be connected by smooth low-loss paths in parameter space. We introduce {\em mode connectivity in unlearning} (MCU) and evaluate it across a range of settings, including curriculum learning, second-order optimization, and connectivity across different unlearning methods. We find that many unlearned models lie in connected basins with smooth retain/forget behavior, while changes in training dynamics can move solutions into different basins. MCU also reveals that models within the same basin can differ substantially on privacy metrics, and that unlearning progresses nonlinearly from the original model to the unlearned model. In addition, linear connectivity suggests that most approximate unlearning methods are mechanistically distinct from retraining. Finally, MCU-based ensembling can improve generalization and robustness to relearning attacks, and MCU smoothness correlates with unlearning difficulty. To our knowledge, this is the first study of machine unlearning through the lens of mode connectivity.

AI.tldr: This paper studies machine unlearning through mode connectivity, showing that unlearned models often lie in connected basins with smooth retain/forget behavior, but changes in training dynamics can shift solutions to different basins. MCU reveals that models in the same basin differ on privacy metrics, unlearning progresses nonlinearly, approximate methods are mechanistically distinct from retraining, and MCU-based ensembling improves robustness while MCU smoothness correlates with unlearning difficulty.
AI.motivation: The loss landscape and optimization geometry of machine unlearning are poorly understood, motivating the need to study unlearning through mode connectivity to gain deeper insights into how unlearned models behave in parameter space.
AI.method: The authors introduce Mode Connectivity in Unlearning (MCU), evaluating it across curriculum learning, second-order optimization, and connectivity across different unlearning methods, using smooth low-loss paths to analyze relationships between models.
AI.result: Unlearned models lie in connected basins with smooth retain/forget behavior; changes in training dynamics shift solutions to different basins; models in the same basin differ on privacy metrics; unlearning progresses nonlinearly; approximate unlearning methods are mechanistically distinct from retraining; MCU-based ensembling improves generalization and robustness; MCU smoothness correlates with unlearning difficulty.
AI.conclusion: Mode connectivity provides a novel lens for understanding machine unlearning, revealing geometric properties of unlearned models and offering practical benefits like ensembling for improved robustness.

title: Verification-Notebook Learning for Source-Aware Multimodal Misinformation Detection
summary: Multimodal misinformation verification is challenging because misleading signals may come from different parts of a post and require different forms of evidence. LVLMs are well suited to this task, but their verification performance often depends on the inference procedure applied to each instance. Existing methods improve this procedure through stronger prompting, retrieval, or deliberation, but rarely retain the verification patterns learned from previous examples. We propose Verification-Notebook Learning (VNL), a non-parametric framework that learns an external verification procedure for a frozen LVLM before inference. VNL builds a compact notebook of decision principles, evidence cues, and recurring pitfalls from prior verification experience. The notebook remains fixed during inference and guides the verification of new examples. Rather than updating model parameters or storing demonstrations, VNL records learned knowledge in an artifact that can be inspected directly. Experiments show that VNL consistently outperforms a range of competitive baselines. Further analyses show that the Verification Notebook improves fine-grained source attribution while remaining compact and interpretable, providing an effective way to accumulate verification knowledge without model training.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Verification-Notebook Learning (VNL), a non-parametric framework that builds a compact, inspectable notebook of decision principles, evidence cues, and pitfalls from prior verification experience to guide a frozen LVLM in multimodal misinformation verification without model training or parameter updates.
AI.motivation: Multimodal misinformation verification is challenging because misleading signals come from different parts of a post requiring different evidence forms. Existing methods improve verification through stronger prompting, retrieval, or deliberation but rarely retain verification patterns learned from previous examples.
AI.method: VNL is a non-parametric framework that constructs a compact notebook containing decision principles, evidence cues, and recurring pitfalls derived from prior verification examples. This notebook remains fixed during inference and guides a frozen LVLM's verification process without updating model parameters or storing demonstrations.
AI.result: VNL consistently outperforms a range of competitive baselines. The Verification Notebook improves fine-grained source attribution while remaining compact and interpretable.
AI.conclusion: VNL provides an effective way to accumulate verification knowledge without model training, offering an interpretable and compact artifact that retains learned patterns from prior verification experience.

title: AptAvatar: Fast and Vivid Long-Form Audio-Driven Video Generation for Production-Ready Avatars
summary: Production-ready audio-driven avatar generation requires efficient inference without sacrificing fidelity or motion expressiveness. However, existing acceleration methods often compromise quality through restrictive architectural choices, such as causal attention and short temporal horizons, or by reducing model capacity and resolution. Without such compromises, we propose AptAvatar, a 14B-parameter long-form audio-driven avatar generation framework that delivers fast and expressive inference. For efficiency in production-level applications, AptAvatar addresses the extreme two-step generation challenge. To bridge the gap between the multi-step teacher model and the two-step student model, we introduce Endpoint-Anchored Distribution Distillation. It augments vanilla distribution matching with a dedicated Anchor Score Estimator trained on the trajectory-endpoint distribution defined from a frozen pretrained 4-step bridge generator. This provides an attainable endpoint-level anchor for the evolving two-step student. To improve long-horizon consistency, we further introduce Self-Generated History Replay, which reuses cached outputs from earlier generator checkpoints as history conditions during chunk-wise training. This approximates inference-time conditioning on self-generated histories without costly online rollouts, mitigating quality degradation from accumulated history errors. Extensive experiments demonstrate that AptAvatar generates vivid 720p long-form avatar videos with only 2 NFEs, achieving a 60x speedup while preserving visual fidelity and long-horizon identity. Code is available at https://github.com/TaoLiveAIGC/AptAvatar

AI.tldr: AptAvatar is a 14B-parameter audio-driven avatar generation framework achieving 60x speedup (2-step inference) for 720p long-form videos via Endpoint-Anchored Distribution Distillation and Self-Generated History Replay, without sacrificing quality.
AI.motivation: Existing acceleration methods for audio-driven avatars compromise quality through restrictive architectural choices (causal attention, short temporal horizons) or reduced model capacity/resolution. The goal is efficient production-ready inference without fidelity or motion expressiveness loss.
AI.method: (1) Endpoint-Anchored Distribution Distillation: trains a two-step student model by augmenting vanilla distribution matching with an Anchor Score Estimator that operates on the trajectory-endpoint distribution from a frozen 4-step bridge generator.
