(2) Self-Generated History Replay: reuses cached outputs from earlier generator checkpoints as history conditions during chunk-wise training, approximating inference-time conditioning on self-generated histories without costly online rollouts.
AI.result: Generates vivid 720p long-form avatar videos with only 2 NFEs, achieving a 60x speedup while preserving visual fidelity and long-horizon identity.
AI.conclusion: AptAvatar demonstrates that extreme acceleration (2-step) for audio-driven avatar generation is achievable without compromising quality, enabling production-level applications.

title: Adaptive Data Admission and Retention for Streaming Federated Learning
summary: We study streaming federated learning with limited client memory, where newly generated training data incur time-varying sampling costs and must be selectively admitted and retained over time. We consider a joint server-side admission and client-side memory-management framework with the objective of minimizing the cumulative excess population risk under a sampling-cost budget and buffer constraints. We first derive a learning-error bound that explicitly captures the effects of instantaneous training sample size, distinct-sample growth, and reuse imbalance through a characterization of the effective sample size. Through a surrogate penalty obtained from this bound, we develop an Active-Constraint Drift-Plus-Penalty (ACDPP) policy that combines a structured client-side $K$-step retention rule with a server-side online admission rule and a time-varying rectangular admission region. We further present a sequence of comparison arguments, via an auxiliary constant-admission policy, that connects the ACDPP learning bound to a costless oracle benchmark. This yields explicit guarantees in terms of sublinear regret and sampling-cost violation, while the buffer-occupancy violation is controlled through offline selection of the retention horizon. Experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate that the proposed policy remains close to the oracle benchmark while satisfying the sampling-cost and buffer constraints.

AI.tldr: The paper studies streaming federated learning with limited client memory, proposing an Active-Constraint Drift-Plus-Penalty (ACDPP) policy that jointly handles server-side data admission and client-side memory management under sampling-cost and buffer constraints, achieving sublinear regret and cost violation guarantees with experimental validation.
AI.motivation: To address the challenge of streaming federated learning where newly generated training data incurs time-varying sampling costs, and clients have limited memory for data retention, requiring selective admission and retention over time.
AI.method: Derives a learning-error bound capturing effective sample size dynamics (instantaneous sample size, distinct-sample growth, reuse imbalance); develops an ACDPP policy combining client-side K-step retention with server-side online admission and time-varying rectangular admission region; uses comparison arguments via an auxiliary constant-admission policy to connect to a costless oracle benchmark.
AI.result: Achieves explicit sublinear regret and sampling-cost violation guarantees; buffer-occupancy violation controlled via offline retention horizon selection; experiments show performance close to oracle benchmark while satisfying constraints.
AI.conclusion: The proposed ACDPP framework effectively manages the trade-off between learning performance and resource constraints (sampling cost and buffer memory) in streaming federated learning, with theoretical and empirical validation.

title: Are You Still the Agent I Authorized? Earned Authority under a Fixed Ceiling for Evolving Agents
summary:
Long-lived AI agents increasingly evolve after deployment by retaining experience, acquiring skills and tools, revising workflows, delegating work, and moving across task phases. This improves adaptation but creates a distinct authorization problem. Tool-enabled agents can turn model errors and prompt injections into consequential external actions; when evolution occurs under a live grant, the subject exercising that authority or the context in which it acts may no longer match what the user evaluated. Evolution can change both the effects reachable under an old grant and the authority required by the task, which may rise, fall, or become incomparable. Existing tool policies constrain actions but do not determine when a grant survives this change.
  We formulate authorization continuity: when does an existing grant remain valid, how may active authority change, and what boundary must never move? Our state-bound model fixes a transition envelope and an immutable effect ceiling at grant time. The envelope determines whether the grant survives a mutation; below the ceiling, authority may contract freely and expand only under specified evidence conditions. We distinguish requested from realized effects and prove that, under complete mediation, sound effect abstraction, attenuating delegation, and monitor integrity, mutation cannot amplify protected effects beyond the user-issued ceiling. Agent-produced evidence may allocate authority below the ceiling but cannot raise it. Finally, we map six mutation classes to their authorization consequences.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "authorization continuity" for long-lived AI agents that evolve post-deployment, proposing a state-bound model with an immutable effect ceiling to ensure that agent mutations cannot amplify protected effects beyond user-set limits.
AI.motivation: Long-lived AI agents evolve after deployment (retaining experience, acquiring skills/tools, revising workflows, delegating work), which creates a distinct authorization problem: when evolution occurs under a live grant, the subject or context may no longer match what the user evaluated, and existing tool policies do not determine when a grant survives this change.
AI.method: The authors formulate authorization continuity with a state-bound model that fixes a transition envelope and an immutable effect ceiling at grant time. They distinguish requested from realized effects and prove that under complete mediation, sound effect abstraction, attenuating delegation, and monitor integrity, mutation cannot amplify protected effects beyond the user-issued ceiling.
AI.result: Agent-produced evidence may allocate authority below the ceiling but cannot raise it. Six mutation classes are mapped to their authorization consequences.
AI.conclusion: The envelope determines whether a grant survives mutation; below the ceiling, authority may contract freely and expand only under specified evidence conditions. The model ensures mutation cannot amplify protected effects beyond the user-issued ceiling under the specified conditions.

title: DailyBench: A Unified Benchmark for AI-Generated and Manipulated Images from Modern Generative Models
summary: Recent advances in generative models have shifted AI-generated image detection from identifying easily distinguishable, fully synthetic images to identifying highly realistic content generated by both modern generation and manipulation pipelines. However, existing detection benchmarks are often built with outdated generative models and primarily emphasize full-image synthesis, creating a growing mismatch between benchmark data and the images encountered in real-world generation and editing scenarios. To bridge this gap, we introduce DailyBench, a high-quality unified benchmark for evaluating whether AI-generated image detectors can generalize across both modern full-image synthesis and object-level manipulation. DailyBench contains two complementary subsets: FakeBench, which includes high-quality images synthesized by recent open-source and commercial generative models, and ManipulationBench, which introduces challenging object-level edits applied to real images using advanced image-conditional models. This design makes DailyBench a realistic testbed for studying both generator-level generalization and manipulation-aware detection under subtle local edits. Experiments on DailyBench reveal substantial robustness gaps in current detectors: methods reporting 91-96% balanced accuracy on GenImage drop to 60-76% on FakeBench and 54-66% on ManipulationBench. These results show that existing detectors remain poorly generalized to realistic synthesis and manipulation, highlighting DailyBench as a rigorous testbed for developing robust and manipulation-aware AI-generated image detection methods. The project is available at https://dailybench.github.io/

AI.tldr: DailyBench is a unified benchmark for evaluating AI-generated image detectors on modern full-image synthesis and object-level manipulation, revealing substantial robustness gaps where detectors' accuracy drops from 91-96% to 54-76%.
AI.motivation: Existing detection benchmarks use outdated generative models and emphasize full-image synthesis, creating a mismatch with real-world generation and editing scenarios. DailyBench aims to bridge this gap with modern, realistic evaluation.
AI.method: DailyBench includes two complementary subsets: FakeBench (high-quality images from recent open-source and commercial generative models) and ManipulationBench (subtle object-level edits on real images using advanced image-conditional models).
AI.result: Current detectors achieve 91-96% balanced accuracy on GenImage but drop to 60-76% on FakeBench and 54-66% on ManipulationBench, demonstrating poor generalization to realistic synthesis and manipulation.
AI.conclusion: Existing AI-generated image detectors remain poorly generalized to realistic synthesis and manipulation. DailyBench serves as a rigorous testbed for developing robust and manipulation-aware detection methods.

title: When Should Active RAG Retrieve? A Budget-Aware Evaluation of Utility, Calibration, and Cost
comment: Accepted at the ACM SIGKDD KDD 2026 Workshop on Evaluation and Trustworthiness of Agentic AI; 7 pages, 1 figure, and 4 tables
summary: Active RAG systems decide when to retrieve external knowledge during generation, making them a budget-sensitive case of agentic RAG and self-adaptive retrieval. Yet evaluations often leave the operating point underspecified: two systems may both claim a 50% evidence-usage budget while realizing different held-out usage rates, so higher accuracy can reflect a looser budget rather than a better retrieval policy. We study budget-aware evaluation for Active RAG by recasting active retrieval as utility estimation, where retrieval is valuable only through its marginal correctness change over a no-retrieval answer. This view separates three questions that single-point evaluations conflate: whether trigger scores rank useful retrieval decisions, whether thresholds calibrated on past data meet future budgets, and how trigger-side computation changes deployment cost. We operationalize these questions with exact top-k utility frontiers, deployable threshold frontiers, conservative budget frontiers, harm audits, and cost decompositions. Across knowledge-intensive multi-hop QA datasets and open instruction models, retrieval harm is non-negligible, router rankings change across datasets and budgets, nominal thresholds can miss target usage, and simple uncertainty or retrieval-score baselines often rival learned utility routers. Budget-aware Active RAG evaluations should therefore report frontiers, realized usage, threshold-transfer error, harm rates, and cost decompositions alongside accuracy.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that Active RAG evaluations are often budget-unaware, conflating retrieval policy quality with budget looseness. It proposes recasting active retrieval as utility estimation and introduces tools like utility frontiers, harm audits, and cost decompositions for budget-aware evaluation. Experiments show retrieval harm is non-negligible, router rankings shift across datasets/budgets, and simple baselines often match learned routers.
AI.motivation: Current Active RAG evaluations leave the operating point (budget) underspecified, so two systems claiming the same 50% evidence-usage budget may actually use different held-out rates, making accuracy comparisons unfair and conflating retrieval policy quality with budget looseness.
AI.method: Reformulates active retrieval as utility estimation (retrieval is valuable only through marginal correctness change over no-retrieval). Introduces exact top-k utility frontiers, deployable threshold frontiers, conservative budget frontiers, harm audits, and cost decompositions to separate trigger score ranking quality, threshold calibration, and deployment cost.
AI.result: On multi-hop QA datasets and open instruction models: (1) retrieval harm is non-negligible; (2) router rankings change across datasets and budgets; (3) nominal thresholds often miss target usage rates; (4) simple uncertainty or retrieval-score baselines often rival learned utility routers.
AI.conclusion: Budget-aware Active RAG evaluations should report frontiers, realized usage, threshold-transfer error, harm rates, and cost decompositions alongside accuracy, rather than relying on single-point comparisons.

title: Hybrid Advantage Estimation with Unified Critic for VLM Agentic Reinforcement Learning
summary: Large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) now act as agents in interactive environments, where success requires coherent reasoning and decision-making across turns. Although end-to-end training in agentic environments can improve such multi-turn decision-making abilities, current methods mainly rely on either token-wise optimization over concatenated token trajectories or turn-wise optimization with uniform within-turn credit. In this work, we establish theoretical formulations for the two levels of optimization and derive a hybrid advantage that serves both objectives. Furthermore, with an appropriate choice of discount factor and learning target, we prove that a unified critic model can estimate values for both turn-wise and token-wise. As such, we propose HyGAE, an actor-critic framework that jointly optimizes token- and turn-level objectives with the hybrid advantage and unified critic. We conduct extensive evaluations of HyGAE across five multi-turn decision-making environments, where it achieves an average success rate of 91% and a significant improvement of 10% over other methods. Furthermore, we provide an in-depth analysis showing that the exact analytic form of the hybrid advantage and return is crucial for optimization. Project Page: https://wx-zhang.github.io/hygae-web/.

AI.tldr: HyGAE is an actor-critic framework for VLMs that jointly optimizes token-level and turn-level objectives using a hybrid advantage function and unified critic, achieving 91% average success rate and 10% improvement over baselines across five multi-turn decision-making environments.
AI.motivation: Current methods for training VLMs in multi-turn agentic environments rely on either token-wise optimization (over concatenated trajectories) or turn-wise optimization (with uniform within-turn credit), lacking a principled approach to jointly optimize both levels.
AI.method: Establishes theoretical formulations for token- and turn-level optimization, derives a hybrid advantage serving both objectives, proves a unified critic can estimate values for both levels with appropriate discount factor and learning target, and proposes HyGAE actor-critic framework.
AI.result: Achieves 91% average success rate and 10% improvement over other methods across five multi-turn decision-making environments.
AI.conclusion: The exact analytic form of hybrid advantage and return is crucial for optimization; joint token- and turn-level optimization significantly improves multi-turn decision-making in VLMs.

title: Disentangling Semantic Attention from Structural Bias in the Attention Manifold
summary: The empirical success of attention mechanism in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) often obscures its inherent, subtle flaws. Specifically, MLLMs consistently exhibit disproportionate attention toward certain semantically uninformative visual tokens, a phenomenon termed "register" or "Visual Attention Sinks." While existing inference intervention methods attempt to identify these sink tokens and redistribute their attention weights, such approaches typically treat these tokens in isolation and suffer from computational inefficiency. Instead, we reframe this phenomenon as a generalized textual bias exerted over visual features that extends beyond isolated sink tokens. From this perspective, a pervasive structural bias leads to the dilution of the semantic visual signal, precipitating multimodal hallucinations as the model prioritizes linguistic priors over valid visual evidence. To address this limitation, we introduce Saliency-guided Purification and Adaptive Redistribution (SPAR), a training-free, plug-and-play intervention. SPAR mitigates this generalized textual bias by purifying structural noise and subsequently redistributing the reclaimed attention budget to the most informative visual regions. Comprehensive evaluations across a diverse spectrum of hallucination benchmarks demonstrate that SPAR effectively restores authentic visual grounding with negligible computational overhead.

AI.tldr: SPAR is a training-free, plug-and-play method that mitigates multimodal hallucinations in MLLMs by purifying structural noise from visual attention sinks and redistributing attention to informative visual regions, effectively restoring visual grounding with low computational cost.
AI.motivation: Existing MLLMs exhibit "Visual Attention Sinks" where disproportionate attention is paid to semantically uninformative visual tokens, causing multimodal hallucinations. Previous inference intervention methods treat sink tokens in isolation and are computationally inefficient, lacking a holistic understanding of the structural bias.
AI.method: SPAR (Saliency-guided Purification and Adaptive Redistribution) is a training-free, plug-and-play intervention that reframes attention sinks as a generalized textual bias. It purifies structural noise from visual features and adaptively redistributes the reclaimed attention budget to the most informative visual regions.
AI.result: Comprehensive evaluations across diverse hallucination benchmarks demonstrate that SPAR effectively restores authentic visual grounding with negligible computational overhead.
AI.conclusion: Treating attention sinks as a pervasive structural bias rather than isolated tokens, and addressing it through noise purification and adaptive redistribution, offers an efficient solution to reduce multimodal hallucinations in MLLMs.

title: Capacity-Aware Deep Learning for Generalizable Traffic Volume Estimation Across Links and Cities
summary: Network-wide traffic volume estimation typically relies on propagating measurements from fixed sensors, making performance highly dependent on sensor density and limiting deployment in sparsely instrumented networks. We propose a link-level learning framework that estimates hourly traffic volumes from widely available territorial data only, including probe speed profiles, road and topological descriptors, along with weather observations. A supervised local mapping is learned from sparse sensor measurements and evaluated under two generalization settings: intra-network (unseen links within the training network) and inter-network (unseen city). This formulation frames traffic volume estimation as a spatial out-of-distribution generalization problem under sparse supervision. To enhance spatial robustness, we introduce a capacity-aware formulation that models volume as the product of a link-specific structural capacity and an hourly regime-aware utilization ratio, embedding traffic-theoretic constraints directly into the learning process. Extensive experiments in both generalization settings demonstrate that the proposed structural constraints consistently outperform a state-of-the-art baseline under spatial distribution shift.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a link-level learning framework for estimating hourly traffic volumes using only widely available territorial data (probe speeds, road/topological descriptors, weather), without requiring dense fixed sensor networks. It introduces a capacity-aware formulation that models volume as the product of structural capacity and regime-aware utilization, tested under intra-network and inter-network generalization settings.
AI.motivation: Network-wide traffic volume estimation typically depends on fixed sensor measurements, making performance highly dependent on sensor density and limiting deployment in sparsely instrumented networks.
AI.method: A supervised local mapping is learned from sparse sensor measurements using probe speed profiles, road/topological descriptors, and weather observations. The framework introduces a capacity-aware formulation that models volume as the product of link-specific structural capacity and hourly regime-aware utilization ratio, embedding traffic-theoretic constraints into learning. Evaluated under intra-network (unseen links within training network) and inter-network (unseen city) generalization settings.
AI.result: The proposed structural constraints consistently outperform a state-of-the-art baseline under spatial distribution shift in both intra-network and inter-network generalization settings.
AI.conclusion: The capacity-aware formulation with traffic-theoretic constraints enhances spatial robustness for traffic volume estimation, enabling effective generalization to unseen links and unseen cities without relying on dense sensor networks.

title: SpecAHD: Localize to Specialize for Automated Heuristic Design in Large-Scale Routing Problems
comment: 9 pages, 1 figure, and 3 tables. Supplementary material included
summary: LLM-based automated heuristic design (AHD) typically scores executable programs on complete instances or within fixed solver components. In large-scale routing problems, localized reconstruction reduces the size of each optimization task, but repair regions within the same incumbent can exhibit substantially different structures. One construction rule must therefore compromise across them. In this paper, we propose SpecAHD, a coupled bilevel framework for within-instance specialization. An upper-level search learns where to expose bounded repair regions, while a lower-level search evolves a complementary repertoire of executable heuristics for the induced repair tasks. The upper-level program determines the repair tasks seen by the lower level, while checked repair outcomes determine how upper-level programs are evaluated. The lower-level objective favors heuristics that perform well on average or solve tasks that the current repertoire handles poorly. For the repair tasks induced by a fixed upper-level program and a fixed lower-level candidate pool, this objective is monotone submodular, allowing greedy repertoire selection with a (1-1/e) approximation guarantee. Across four routing problems and multiple LLM backbones, SpecAHD reduces held-out objective cost by up to 57.7% against the strongest competing AHD baseline and outperforms the per-instance baseline envelope on most public instances.

AI.tldr: SpecAHD is a coupled bilevel framework for within-instance specialization in automated heuristic design, where an upper-level search learns where to expose bounded repair regions and a lower-level search evolves complementary heuristics, achieving up to 57.7% cost reduction over baselines in large-scale routing problems.
AI.motivation: In large-scale routing problems, localized reconstruction reduces optimization task size, but repair regions within the same incumbent can exhibit substantially different structures, making a single construction rule compromise across them.
AI.method: Proposes SpecAHD, a coupled bilevel framework: an upper-level search learns where to expose bounded repair regions, while a lower-level search evolves a complementary repertoire of executable heuristics for the induced repair tasks. The lower-level objective is monotone submodular, enabling greedy repertoire selection with a (1-1/e) approximation guarantee.
AI.result: Across four routing problems and multiple LLM backbones, SpecAHD reduces held-out objective cost by up to 57.7% against the strongest competing AHD baseline and outperforms the per-instance baseline envelope on most public instances.
AI.conclusion: SpecAHD effectively addresses the structural diversity of repair regions within the same instance via bilevel specialization, significantly outperforming existing AHD baselines.

title: A Unified Stereo Geometry Estimation Framework for Disparity and Surface Normal
summary: Stereo matching and surface normal estimation are fundamental tasks in 3D vision. However, existing feed-forward stereo methods still struggle to produce reliable predictions in challenging regions, mainly due to the lack of strong geometric priors. In this paper, we propose $\textbf{GeoStereo}$, a unified stereo geometry estimation framework that leverages powerful diffusion priors to jointly predict disparity and surface normals. Specifically, GeoStereo couples a feed-forward stereo matching pipeline with a diffusion-based normal estimation branch. To enable effective interaction between the two tasks, we introduce a disparity to normal initialization strategy and construct a warp to left-view condition for the diffusion process. This coupled design allows the diffusion branch to provide strong structural priors that enhance disparity estimation in ill-posed regions, while the feed-forward branch offers reliable geometric guidance for accurate normal prediction. Extensive experiments show that GeoStereo performs reliably in challenging scenarios, including low-light environments, highly reflective surfaces, and transparent objects. Under zero-shot settings, it achieves Rank-1 disparity estimation on multiple benchmarks, including KITTI and NYUv2, and delivers the best normal estimation accuracy on many real indoor benchmarks, such as iBims-1 and ScanNet. Project page: https://qz-wei.github.io/GeoStereo.github.io/

AI.tldr: GeoStereo is a unified framework that couples feed-forward stereo matching with diffusion-based normal estimation to jointly predict disparity and surface normals, achieving state-of-the-art results on multiple benchmarks under zero-shot settings.
AI.motivation: Existing feed-forward stereo methods struggle in challenging regions (low-light, reflective surfaces, transparent objects) due to lack of strong geometric priors.
AI.method: GeoStereo couples a feed-forward stereo matching pipeline with a diffusion-based normal estimation branch, using a disparity-to-normal initialization strategy and warp-to-left-view conditioning to enable bidirectional information flow between the two tasks.
AI.result: Achieves Rank-1 disparity estimation on KITTI and NYUv2, and best normal estimation accuracy on iBims-1 and ScanNet under zero-shot settings.
AI.conclusion: The coupled diffusion-feedforward design effectively leverages strong geometric priors to improve both disparity and surface normal estimation in challenging scenarios.

title: Constrained Reinforcement Learning Using Successor Representations
comment: published in Transactions for Machine Learning Research 2026
summary: Real-world Reinforcement Learning depends on the ability to formulate safety constraints into a policy. A common way to model such constraints is to introduce an additional cost signal in the Markov Decision Process, which notifies the agent of unwanted behavior independently of the reward signal. Unfortunately, current methods are hard to adapt to changes in the cost function introduced by, e.g., domain shift or obstacles moving over time. The lack of adaptability means that policies are too unflexible to deal with complex real-world conditions. We propose the Safe Deep Successor Representation (SafeDSR), a novel method that allows quick retraining of policies towards new cost structures. SafeDSR extends the Deep Successor Representation (Kulkarni et al., 2016) to Constrained Reinforcement Learning by introducing a single learnable weight matrix to decouple the learned value function across dynamics, rewards, and costs. This matrix can be updated in a supervised manner instead of having to adapt the whole network if the cost structure of the environment changes. We demonstrate this ability in a freely configurable two-dimensional navigation environment and show that our method is competitive on a simple navigation task while being considerably more flexible

AI.tldr: SafeDSR extends Deep Successor Representation to Constrained RL by decoupling value functions across dynamics, rewards, and costs via a learnable weight matrix, enabling quick policy retraining when cost structures change.
AI.motivation: Current Constrained RL methods lack adaptability to changes in cost functions caused by domain shifts or moving obstacles, making policies inflexible for real-world conditions.
AI.method: Safe Deep Successor Representation (SafeDSR) introduces a single learnable weight matrix to decouple the learned value function across dynamics, rewards, and costs, allowing supervised updates to the matrix instead of full network retraining when cost structures change.
AI.result: SafeDSR is competitive on simple navigation tasks while being considerably more flexible when cost structures change, demonstrated in a 2D navigation environment.
AI.conclusion: SafeDSR enables quick retraining of policies towards new cost structures, addressing the adaptability limitation of current Constrained RL methods for real-world applications.

title: Focus Is All You Need: Adaptive Goal-aware Attention Orchestration for Multi-Agent Graph Systems
summary: Large language models (LLMs) enable autonomous agents for reasoning, planning, and tool use. Recent systems increasingly organize these agents as graphs of specialized, interconnected nodes. Although graph-based orchestration supports flexible decomposition and coordination, it creates a key challenge: \textbf{attention allocation}. As workflows grow, existing approaches often execute graph components uniformly, wasting resources on irrelevant or low-impact tasks. We introduce \textbf{Attention Orchestration}, a paradigm that extends Transformer-style attention from token representations to workflow-level agent coordination. Our framework, \textbf{Adaptive Goal-aware Attention Orchestration (AGAO)}, dynamically estimates agent importance based on user objectives, graph dependencies, and computational constraints. AGAO combines three components: (1) goal-aware attention, measuring semantic relevance between user goals and agent capabilities; (2) topology-aware attention, modeling structural dependencies in agent graphs; and (3) resource-aware attention, allocating budgets and execution priorities across heterogeneous agents. Together, these mechanisms transform static agent graphs into adaptive systems that focus computation on goal-critical reasoning paths. Experiments across diverse multi-agent workloads show that AGAO improves task effectiveness while reducing unnecessary computation, latency, and token consumption compared with existing graph-based execution strategies. Our work establishes \textbf{Attention Engineering} as a direction for scalable, intelligent multi-agent systems. Code: https://github.com/MingzhouFan97/AGAO.

AI.tldr: AGAO introduces Attention Orchestration, a paradigm extending Transformer-style attention to workflow-level agent coordination, dynamically allocating computational resources based on goal relevance, graph topology, and resource constraints to improve efficiency in multi-agent LLM systems.
AI.motivation: Existing graph-based multi-agent orchestration executes graph components uniformly, wasting resources on irrelevant or low-impact tasks as workflows grow. This creates an attention allocation challenge that current approaches fail to address.
AI.method: AGAO combines three attention mechanisms: (1) goal-aware attention measuring semantic relevance between user goals and agent capabilities; (2) topology-aware attention modeling structural dependencies in agent graphs; and (3) resource-aware attention allocating budgets and execution priorities across heterogeneous agents.
AI.result: AGAO improves task effectiveness while reducing unnecessary computation, latency, and token consumption compared to existing graph-based execution strategies across diverse multi-agent workloads.
AI.conclusion: This work establishes Attention Engineering as a direction for scalable, intelligent multi-agent systems, transforming static agent graphs into adaptive systems that focus computation on goal-critical reasoning paths.

title: Sol-Attn: Accelerating Video Generation Inference via On-the-Fly Attention Sparsification
summary: Diffusion transformers are essential for high-fidelity video generation, but long token sequences make attention a dominant inference bottleneck. Training-free dynamic sparse attention alleviates this bottleneck by computing only selected key-value blocks, yet existing methods struggle to sparsify attention both efficiently and accurately for two reasons: (1) Rigid, unpredictable, and costly routing: selecting a fixed fraction of top-ranked blocks by proxy score imposes fixed budgets, whereas retaining blocks to reach a target cumulative proxy probability mass yields dynamic but potentially imbalanced budgets; both incur non-negligible overhead from computing and materializing proxy scores. (2) Lossy keep-or-drop sparsification: unselected blocks are discarded entirely, degrading accuracy under aggressive sparsity. These limitations motivate cheaper dynamic-budget routing while limiting accuracy degradation. In this paper, we introduce training-free Sol-Attn (Sparsifying online attention), which unifies dynamic routing, sparse computation, and approximation correction in a single online-softmax pass, achieving a better accuracy-efficiency trade-off in sparse attention. The core of Sol-Attn is on-the-fly block thresholding with proxy-score reuse, which selects critical blocks by comparing block proxy scores against a threshold during online softmax. This design enables dynamic yet controllable block budgets without materializing the proxy map, while directly reusing the proxy scores of unselected blocks to approximate their contribution. Experiments across image and video generation tasks show that Sol-Attn advances the quality-efficiency frontier of training-free sparse attention, delivering 2.1 times and 2.3 times end-to-end speedups for video generation and editing, respectively, while preserving visual quality.

AI.tldr: Sol-Attn introduces training-free dynamic sparse attention for diffusion transformers, using on-the-fly block thresholding with proxy-score reuse in a single online-softmax pass to achieve better accuracy-efficiency trade-offs, delivering 2.1× and 2.3× end-to-end speedups for video generation and editing while preserving quality.
AI.motivation: Long token sequences in diffusion transformers make attention a dominant inference bottleneck. Existing training-free dynamic sparse attention methods struggle with (1) rigid, unpredictable, and costly routing with fixed or dynamic budgets, and (2) lossy keep-or-drop sparsification that degrades accuracy under aggressive sparsity.
AI.method: Sol-Attn unifies dynamic routing, sparse computation, and approximation correction in a single online-softmax pass via on-the-fly block thresholding with proxy-score reuse, enabling dynamic yet controllable block budgets without materializing the proxy map and reusing unselected blocks' proxy scores to approximate their contribution.
AI.result: Achieves 2.1× and 2.3× end-to-end speedups for video generation and editing, respectively, while preserving visual quality across image and video generation tasks.
AI.conclusion: Sol-Attn advances the quality-efficiency frontier of training-free sparse attention by jointly addressing routing cost, budget flexibility, and sparsification accuracy in a unified online-softmax framework.

title: ACRL: Adaptive Control of Training-Inference Discrepancy for Stable Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reinforcement Learning (RL) training for Large Language Models (LLMs) often suffers from instability due to the discrepancy between training and inference. This training-inference discrepancy stems from two primary factors: an architectural separation between training and inference engines, and the use of low-precision quantization in inference versus higher-precision computation in training. To address training instability issues caused by high training-inference discrepancy, we present the principles and methods for its adaptive control. We propose Adaptive Control Reinforcement Learning (ACRL), which adaptively maintains the training-inference discrepancy within a reasonable range to ensure stable RL training. Beyond stabilization, ACRL inherently increases policy entropy, thereby enhancing exploration and improving accuracy. The experimental results show that when the inference engine utilizes FP8 quantization, ACRL consistently maintains the training-inference discrepancy within a reasonable range and stabilizes RL training. Furthermore, ACRL not only matches the accuracy of the BF16 baseline but also outperforms importance sampling (IS) fixes.

AI.tldr: ACRL adaptively controls training-inference discrepancy in LLM RL training to stabilize FP8 quantization, improving exploration and matching BF16 accuracy while outperforming importance sampling.
AI.motivation: RL training for LLMs suffers instability due to training-inference discrepancy caused by separate training/inference engines and low-precision quantization (FP8) in inference vs. higher-precision in training.
AI.method: Proposes Adaptive Control Reinforcement Learning (ACRL) which adaptively maintains training-inference discrepancy within a reasonable range to stabilize RL training.
AI.result: ACRL consistently maintains discrepancy within a reasonable range, stabilizes RL training with FP8 quantization, matches BF16 baseline accuracy, and outperforms importance sampling fixes.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive control of training-inference discrepancy is effective for stabilizing RL training under low-precision inference, with additional benefits of increased policy entropy and improved exploration.

title: Compute Globally, Materialize Locally: The Memory Contract of Sparse Event-KV
summary: Long-horizon agents increasingly reuse their KV cache as memory: a serving system keeps a subset of cached entries and drops the rest. Eviction and episodic-memory schemes therefore rest on a premise rarely tested directly, that a retained event is still informative once the observations that produced it are gone. We test it by omitting one earlier observation from what is served, across otherwise identical agent histories. Among items sensitive to that observation, the answer overwhelmingly follows the omitted value, though no served span says which value is correct. We call this semantic materialization: a downstream event's cached rows act as an independently servable view of computation whose inputs are gone. It can also be written on purpose. A deliberately phrased, answer-free event raises donor-aligned recovery from 6% to 51% on Qwen3-8B without ever naming the value, whereas passively harvesting natural mentions from long-term dialog yields no detected advantage. What such a row carries is specific and bounded. Compact state survives, larger payloads decay toward chance, and whether a construction writes at all turns on phrasing rather than on meaning alone, so two phrasings the model comprehends equally well can diverge sharply. The result is a memory contract for sparse event-KV serving: what to write, where it lands, and what survives once the source is gone. For anyone who evicts the corollary is that dropping a source event and observing no accuracy loss does not show the source was unnecessary.

AI.tldr: KV cache reuse in long-horizon agents exhibits "semantic materialization" where downstream cached events can independently recover information from omitted upstream observations. This effect is controllable through deliberate phrasing but not through natural dialog, and is limited in capacity and sensitive to phrasing over meaning.
AI.motivation: To test the unverified assumption underlying KV cache eviction and episodic-memory schemes: that a retained cached event remains informative after the source observations that produced it are removed.
AI.method: Omitted one earlier observation from otherwise identical agent histories and measured downstream answer behavior; compared deliberate phrasing vs. natural mentions for inducing semantic materialization.
AI.result: Downstream answers overwhelmingly follow the omitted value despite no served span containing it. Deliberate phrasing raises donor-aligned recovery from 6% to 51% on Qwen3-8B; natural mentions show no detectable advantage. Effect is capacity-limited and phrasing-dependent rather than meaning-dependent.
AI.conclusion: KV cache entries can function as independently servable views of computation whose inputs are gone. This implies that observing no accuracy loss after evicting a source does not prove the source was unnecessary.

title: PointCHR: Point Cloud Analysis via Curvature-Aware Hyperbolic Rectification
summary: High-curvature regions in 3D point clouds encapsulate critical fine-grained geometric semantics yet exhibit a distinct long-tail sparsity in their spatial distribution. The inherent limitations of polynomial volume growth in Euclidean space frequently render these intricate geometric features challenging to adequately resolve within a uniform-scale feature space. Consequently, these regions are frequently overshadowed by smooth global features dominated by low-curvature regions, thereby limiting the discriminative capacity of the network. To address this issue, we propose PointCHR, a curvature-aware hyperbolic rectification (CHR) for point cloud analysis. Utilising the property of exponential volume expansion in the vicinity of hyperbolic manifolds, CHR presents a learnable curvature-guided radial rectification mechanism. By adaptively projecting high-curvature points towards boundary regions endowed with larger effective embedding capacities, PointCHR effectively mitigates the representation crowding problem inherent in Euclidean settings. Extensive experimentation has demonstrated that PointCHR significantly enhances the ability of backbone to capture fine-grained geometric details, achieving state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks.

AI.tldr: PointCHR introduces a curvature-aware hyperbolic rectification mechanism that leverages hyperbolic geometry's exponential volume expansion to better represent high-curvature regions in 3D point clouds, mitigating representation crowding in Euclidean space and achieving SOTA performance.
AI.motivation: High-curvature regions in 3D point clouds contain critical fine-grained geometric details but suffer from long-tail sparsity and are poorly resolved in uniform Euclidean feature spaces due to polynomial volume growth, causing them to be overshadowed by smooth low-curvature features and limiting network discriminative capacity.
AI.method: PointCHR proposes a learnable curvature-guided radial rectification mechanism that leverages hyperbolic manifolds' exponential volume expansion property to adaptively project high-curvature points toward boundary regions with larger effective embedding capacities, alleviating representation crowding.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show PointCHR significantly improves backbone networks' ability to capture fine-grained geometric details, achieving state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: PointCHR effectively addresses the long-tail sparsity and representation crowding of high-curvature regions in 3D point clouds via hyperbolic rectification, enhancing discriminative power and achieving superior results.

title: Learning Reusable Hybrid Motion Priors for Humanoid Locomotion from Motion Imitation
summary: Reinforcement learning can produce robust humanoid controllers, but each new task is typically trained as a separate policy with its own reward design and training process. Motion imitation provides an alternative source of motor competence by training policies to track retargeted human motions, yet the resulting controllers remain reference trackers and are not directly usable as task policies. We propose a three-stage pipeline that turns motion-imitation skills into a reusable hybrid motion prior (HMP) for humanoid locomotion. First, an expert policy is trained to imitate retargeted human motion-capture clips. Second, the expert is distilled into a frozen architecture composed of a proprioceptive encoder, a residual vector-quantized (RVQ) codebook, and an action decoder. Third, task-level policies are trained to solve locomotion tasks by selecting discrete codebook entries while the HMP remains frozen. We evaluate the method on velocity tracking, point-goal navigation, and fall-recovery velocity tracking in simulation, and deploy the velocity-tracking policy on a real Unitree G1 robot. The distillation process preserves the tracking behavior of the expert, while the resulting HMP can be reused without retraining as the action interface for different downstream locomotion policies. The learned HMP reveals an interpretable codebook structure in which the number of active RVQ stages modulates the available gait patterns. We further show that training the codebook with the rotation trick improves latent organization and reduces downstream falls compared with a standard straight-through estimator.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a three-stage pipeline that distills motion-imitation skills into a reusable, frozen hybrid motion prior (HMP) using a residual vector-quantized (RVQ) codebook, which serves as the action interface for training downstream locomotion policies (velocity tracking, navigation, fall recovery) without retraining, validated in simulation and on a real Unitree G1 robot.
AI.motivation: Current RL-trained humanoid controllers require per-task reward design and separate training, while motion-imitation policies remain reference trackers not directly usable as task policies. The goal is to create a reusable motion prior that bridges imitation skills and downstream task policies.
AI.method: Three-stage pipeline: (1) train an expert policy to imitate retargeted motion-capture clips; (2) distill expert into a frozen architecture with a proprioceptive encoder, residual vector-quantized (RVQ) codebook, and action decoder; (3) train task-level policies that select discrete codebook entries while HMP stays frozen. The codebook uses a rotation trick for better latent organization.
AI.result: The HMP preserves expert tracking behavior, is reusable across velocity tracking, point-goal navigation, and fall-recovery tasks without retraining; deployed on a real Unitree G1 robot. The RVQ codebook is interpretable, with active stages modulating gait patterns. The rotation trick improves latent organization and reduces downstream falls vs. straight-through estimator.
AI.conclusion: Motion-imitation skills can be successfully distilled into a frozen, reusable hybrid motion prior that enables efficient training of diverse downstream locomotion policies with interpretable codebook structure, and the rotation trick enhances codebook quality and task performance.

title: Offline-to-Online Creative Optimization with Generative Models and Adaptive Testing
summary: Ad creative optimization is increasingly constrained by evaluation rather than generation. Generative models can produce many plausible creatives, but reliable evaluation requires online experiments, in which only a limited slate can be tested. We study how to use data from historical A/B tests to generate and select the candidates in that slate. We developed and deployed a performance-driven offline-to-online workflow that guides creative generation with a predictive model as an inference-time critic. In the offline phase, we use a predictive model trained on historical experiments to rank and refine variants created by a generative model. A final test slate is then deployed in an online adaptive experiment. In a 50-arm field experiment, we found that the best creative generated with this method yielded 45.1% higher engagement than the best human-authored creative. Two additional experiments showed the same upper-tail pattern, with lifts of 46.7% and 36.2%. We found that despite the predictive model being too noisy to directly identify the best creative offline, it effectively guides the generative model toward creating strong candidates that can be efficiently evaluated in an adaptive experiment. The results suggest a design principle for creative optimization with generative models: use predictive models to guide generation of a slate to test, judge the slate by whether it contains high-performing candidates at a feasible test size, and use adaptive experiments to select among candidates while limiting traffic lost to weak arms.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an offline-to-online workflow for ad creative optimization where a predictive model trained on historical A/B tests guides a generative model to produce candidate creatives, which are then evaluated in adaptive online experiments. In a 50-arm field experiment, the best AI-generated creative outperformed the best human-authored creative by 45.1% in engagement, with two additional experiments showing lifts of 46.7% and 36.2%.
AI.motivation: Creative optimization is bottlenecked by evaluation, not generation—generative models can produce many plausible creatives, but reliable evaluation requires costly online experiments with limited test capacity. The authors aim to efficiently use historical A/B test data to guide generation and selection of creatives for testing.
AI.method: The authors develop an offline-to-online workflow: (1) offline, a predictive model trained on historical experiments ranks and refines generative model outputs; (2) a test slate is deployed in an online adaptive experiment. The predictive model serves as an inference-time critic during generation. Three field experiments with 50 arms each were conducted.
AI.result: Best AI-generated creative outperformed best human-authored creative by 45.1% in engagement (Experiment 1), with lifts of 46.7% and 36.2% in two replications. Despite the predictive model being too noisy to directly identify the best creative offline, it effectively guided generation toward strong candidates that could be efficiently evaluated online.
AI.conclusion: Design principle for creative optimization: use predictive models to guide generation of a test slate, judge the slate by whether it contains high-performing candidates at a feasible test size, and use adaptive experiments to select among candidates while limiting traffic lost to weak arms.

title: MarineEVT: Advancing Event-Centric Marine Video Understanding via Visual Tool Reasoning
comment: Accepted to The 19th European Conference on Computer Vision (ECCV) 2026
summary: Recent Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have achieved remarkable success in visual understanding, driven by the growing availability of high-quality image-text pairs. However, the performance of VLMs often degrades in the video domain due to the essential need for temporal understanding and the scarcity of large-scale annotated video data. In this work, we focus on marine video understanding, which brings further challenges: first, it requires substantial domain expertise; and video VLMs usually struggle with localizing and interpreting critical information from marine videos, as the informative events are typically sparse, unpredictable, and unevenly distributed. To address these challenges, we carefully curate the first event-centric marine video understanding dataset called MarineEVT, which features 20K multi-task, video-level visual question-answering pairs spanning multiple dimensions of marine understanding and analysis. Meanwhile, based on MarineEVT, we decompose marine video understanding as an Event-centric Visual Tool-integrated Reasoning process EVT-R1 for short, where we leverage powerful visual tools to drive the model to localize and interpret critical information aligned with visual questions and human intent. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we compare EVT-R1 against 11 SOTA VLMs in different settings. EVT-R1 outperforms the top open-source and top commercial models by 5.22 and 11.09, respectively. MarineEVT and EVT-R1 lay the foundation for ecological discovery and marine education, fostering the development of VLMs capable of interpreting marine dynamics, reasoning about ecological interactions, and supporting sustainable ocean video understanding and analysis.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MarineEVT, the first event-centric marine video understanding dataset with 20K multi-task VQA pairs, and proposes EVT-R1, an Event-centric Visual Tool-integrated Reasoning framework. EVT-R1 outperforms 11 SOTA VLMs (including top commercial models) by 5.22-11.09 points, addressing domain expertise needs and sparse event localization challenges in marine video understanding.
AI.motivation: VLMs perform poorly on video understanding, especially in the marine domain, due to: (1) the need for temporal understanding and scarcity of annotated video data; (2) requirement for substantial domain expertise; and (3) difficulty in localizing sparse, unpredictable, and unevenly distributed informative events in marine videos.
AI.method: (1) Curated MarineEVT dataset: 20K multi-task, video-level VQA pairs spanning multiple dimensions of marine understanding; (2) Proposed EVT-R1: Event-centric Visual Tool-integrated Reasoning framework that leverages powerful visual tools to drive the model to localize and interpret critical information aligned with visual questions and human intent.
AI.result: EVT-R1 outperforms the top open-source VLM by 5.22 and the top commercial model by 11.09, demonstrating effectiveness across 11 SOTA VLMs in different settings.
AI.conclusion: MarineEVT and EVT-R1 lay the foundation for ecological discovery and marine education, fostering VLMs capable of interpreting marine dynamics, reasoning about ecological interactions, and supporting sustainable ocean video understanding and analysis.

title: MAPLE: Efficient and Diverse Multi-Alpha Generation for Portfolio Construction
summary: Classical alpha mining achieves strong risk-adjusted returns by combining many low-correlated predictive signals, yet deep learning stock-ranking methods typically produce a single alpha per stock, rely on increasingly complex architectures with diminishing gains, and obtain diversity only through separate models or implicit routing, without explicitly controlling inter-alpha correlation. We introduce MAPLE (Multi-Alpha Position-aware Listwise Ensembling), a backbone-agnostic framework that recovers this diversity principle within a single training pass. MAPLE combines a unified, capacity-scaled prediction head with an extreme-rank weighted listwise ranking loss and a diversity regularizer that explicitly penalizes pairwise correlation across alphas. Across four equity markets spanning the US, China, and Japan, MAPLE achieves the best average Sharpe and Calmar ratios among nine baselines, using up to 55x fewer parameters and 2.5x less training time, and generalizes across five backbone architectures with Sharpe and Calmar Ratio gains of 10-23% and 17-43%, respectively. Behavioral analysis further shows why each component works: the unified head already reduces inter-alpha correlation before any diversity loss is applied, and the extreme-rank loss lets diversity regularization improve rather than erode per-alpha ranking quality as capacity scaling sustains this balance at scale. These results show that principled loss design and capacity allocation, rather than architectural complexity, drive diverse and effective multi-alpha generation.

AI.tldr: MAPLE is a backbone-agnostic framework that recovers the multi-alpha diversity principle in a single training pass using a unified prediction head, extreme-rank weighted listwise loss, and a diversity regularizer, achieving superior Sharpe and Calmar ratios across US, China, and Japan markets with up to 55x fewer parameters and 2.5x less training time than baselines.
AI.motivation: Classical alpha mining achieves strong returns via many low-correlated signals, but deep learning stock-ranking methods produce a single alpha per stock, rely on complex architectures with diminishing gains, and lack explicit control over inter-alpha correlation.
AI.method: MAPLE combines a unified capacity-scaled prediction head, an extreme-rank weighted listwise ranking loss, and a diversity regularizer that explicitly penalizes pairwise inter-alpha correlation.
AI.result: MAPLE achieves best average Sharpe and Calmar ratios across nine baselines in four equity markets (US, China, Japan), with up to 55x fewer parameters and 2.5x less training time, generalizing across five backbone architectures with Sharpe gains of 10-23% and Calmar gains of 17-43%.
AI.conclusion: Principled loss design and capacity allocation, rather than architectural complexity, drive diverse and effective multi-alpha generation.

title: Offline-Online Curriculum RL for Multimodal Reasoning
summary: Multimodal large language models exhibit capabilities on reasoning tasks, yet often produce flawed intermediate steps while yielding correct final answers. This behavior undermines interpretability and reliability, suggesting reliance on spurious shortcuts rather than faithful reasoning. Although efforts have explored step-level supervision, distinguishing decisive steps from redundant ones remains challenging. We propose $O^2$-CritiCuRL, a novel curriculum reinforcement learning framework that introduces critical-step awareness through an iterative offline-online paradigm. In the offline stage, $O^2$-CritiCuRL conducts multi-rollout analysis over step-annotated trajectories to estimate step-level importance, allowing the framework to distill critical reasoning steps and filter out redundant ones. In the online stage, we employ a progressive step-level reinforcement learning strategy, where truncated chains guide the model to infer missing steps and refine its reasoning, thereby sharpening its focus on critical steps and overcoming the limitations of static supervision. Extensive experiments on multimodal reasoning benchmarks show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance while delivering superior training and inference efficiency. Code is available at https://github.com/kk0013/CritiCuRL.

AI.tldr: O2-CritiCuRL is a curriculum reinforcement learning framework that enhances multimodal LLM reasoning by identifying critical reasoning steps via offline multi-rollout analysis and then refining reasoning through progressive step-level online RL with truncated chains, achieving SOTA performance with improved efficiency.
AI.motivation: Multimodal LLMs often produce flawed intermediate steps yet correct final answers, indicating reliance on spurious shortcuts rather than faithful reasoning. Existing step-level supervision struggles to distinguish decisive steps from redundant ones.
AI.method: A curriculum RL framework with two stages: (1) offline multi-rollout analysis over step-annotated trajectories to estimate step-level importance and distill critical reasoning steps; (2) online progressive step-level RL using truncated chains to guide the model to infer missing steps and sharpen focus on critical steps.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on multimodal reasoning benchmarks with superior training and inference efficiency.
AI.conclusion: The proposed critical-step-aware curriculum RL approach effectively addresses the flawed intermediate reasoning problem in multimodal LLMs, outperforming prior methods while being more efficient.

title: When Low CER is Not Enough: An Analysis of Hallucinations in Vision-Language OCR Systems on Historical Uruguayan Documents
summary: Optical Character Recognition (OCR) is a key component in the digitization of historical archives. Recently, Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have emerged as strong alternatives to traditional OCR systems, achieving state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks. However, their suitability for archival transcription remains insufficiently understood. In this work, we benchmark traditional OCR systems and VLM-based approaches on the Berrutti dataset, a challenging collection of Uruguayan dictatorship-era documents derived from microfilm scans. While VLMs consistently outperform traditional methods in terms of Character Error Rate (CER) and Word Error Rate (WER), we show that these improvements hide a more complex picture. Through a detailed qualitative analysis, we uncover systematic failure modes that are invisible to standard metrics, including orthographic normalization, spurious content generation, and semantic substitutions that preserve fluency while altering meaning. Errors affecting named entities are particularly critical, as they can introduce substantial semantic distortions with minimal impact on CER and WER. These findings reveal a critical gap between quantitative OCR performance and transcription fidelity in real-world archival settings, and highlight the need for evaluation frameworks that go beyond character-level accuracy to capture the semantic reliability of generated transcriptions.

AI.tldr: VLMs outperform traditional OCR on the Berrutti dataset but exhibit systematic failure modes (orthographic normalization, spurious content, semantic substitutions) invisible to CER/WER metrics, especially harming named entities; standard metrics fail to capture semantic transcription fidelity.
AI.motivation: Traditional OCR systems are being outperformed by VLMs on benchmarks, but their suitability for real-world archival transcription is insufficiently understood, motivating an investigation into whether standard metrics reflect true transcription fidelity.
AI.method: Benchmarked traditional OCR systems and VLM-based approaches on the Berrutti dataset (Uruguayan dictatorship-era microfilm documents), evaluating via CER/WER and performing detailed qualitative analysis to uncover systematic error patterns.
AI.result: VLMs consistently outperform traditional methods in CER/WER, but qualitative analysis reveals systematic failures including orthographic normalization, spurious content generation, and semantic substitutions. Named entity errors cause significant semantic distortions with minimal impact on CER/WER.
AI.conclusion: There is a critical gap between quantitative OCR performance and transcription fidelity; evaluation frameworks must go beyond character-level accuracy to capture semantic reliability of transcriptions in archival settings.

title: An Empirical Study of Feature Selection Granularity
summary: Feature selection aims to identify the most informative and relevant features for a given dataset, either in terms of capturing the underlying data structure and distribution better, or with respect to the performance on a downstream task. Existing research in this area has largely focused on developing novel algorithms (in both supervised and unsupervised settings), proposing new evaluation metrics and frameworks, or benchmarking the performance of existing methods. In this work, we examine feature selection through an algorithmic design perspective. Conventional feature selection algorithms typically compute feature importance scores globally across the entire feature set and then select the top-ranked features in a single step. However, this approach raises a critical question: Can the presence of less informative (or noisy) features mask or obscure the true importance of other, more relevant features? In other words, would a recursive strategy, where features are removed one by one while re-evaluating importance at each step, yield different and potentially better results than the standard global ranking approach? To answer this question, we conduct an extensive empirical study using five diverse feature selection algorithms. We implement each algorithm under both the conventional global selection design and the greedy recursive elimination design. We then analyze the impact of this algorithmic choice, both individually for each method and collectively across all methods, on a range of standard feature selection evaluation metrics. The empirical evaluation results show that the greedy approach improves the overall feature selection quality almost consistently, albeit on the expense of higher computational cost, supporting our initial expectation that the curse of dimensionality also obscures the ways of mitigating it.

AI.tldr: This study investigates whether recursive feature elimination (removing one feature at a time with re-evaluation) yields better results than conventional global ranking (selecting top features in one step). Experiments with five algorithms show the greedy recursive approach consistently improves feature selection quality at the cost of higher computation.
AI.motivation: The authors question whether less informative or noisy features can mask the true importance of relevant features in conventional global ranking, motivating an exploration of recursive elimination as an alternative design.
AI.method: Five diverse feature selection algorithms were implemented under both conventional global selection and greedy recursive elimination designs, then evaluated on standard feature selection metrics across multiple datasets.
AI.result: The greedy recursive approach consistently improves overall feature selection quality compared to global ranking, albeit with higher computational cost, supporting the hypothesis that dimensionality obscures importance signals.
AI.conclusion: Recursive feature elimination is a more effective algorithmic design choice than global ranking for feature selection, though practitioners must weigh the quality gains against increased computational overhead.

title: E-Bench: Benchmarking Multi-Step Tool-Use Agents in Real-World Product Scenarios
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as agents that interact with stateful environments over multiple steps: gathering hidden information, composing tool calls, and committing state changes. We refer to this capability as multi-step tool use. Existing benchmarks have advanced tool-use agent evaluation, but often focus on isolated API calls, short trajectories, or settings that are difficult to scale or control. We introduce E-Bench, a fully synthetic benchmark with 323 state-changing tasks across three product domains: Honor of Kings, QQ Music, and Tencent Meeting. E-Bench decouples environment synthesis from task synthesis: graph-guided database filling builds reusable, orphan-free product environments, while generator-solver asymmetry creates tasks with both an information gap and a tool gap, requiring agents to discover hidden data and compose multiple tool calls before changing state. Outcomes are graded deterministically by database-state diffs. Since both environments and tasks are synthetic, E-Bench is controllable at the environment level and scalable at the task level. Benchmarking 11 cutting-edge LLMs shows that multi-step tool use remains challenging: Pass^3 stays below 60% for the strongest models, and even with code execution in the E-Bench-Code extension, reliability (Pass^3) remains below 70%.

AI.tldr: E-Bench is a fully synthetic benchmark with 323 state-changing tasks across three product domains, designed to evaluate LLMs' multi-step tool use capabilities. It decouples environment synthesis from task synthesis using graph-guided database filling and generator-solver asymmetry. Results show multi-step tool use remains challenging: Pass^3 stays below 60% for strongest models and below 70% even with code execution.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for tool-use agent evaluation often focus on isolated API calls, short trajectories, or settings that are difficult to scale or control. There is a need for a controllable, scalable benchmark that tests LLMs on multi-step tool use in stateful environments where agents must gather hidden information, compose tool calls, and commit state changes.
AI.method: E-Bench uses a fully synthetic approach with 323 tasks across three product domains. It decouples environment synthesis (graph-guided database filling for reusable, orphan-free environments) from task synthesis (generator-solver asymmetry creating information gaps and tool gaps). Outcomes are graded deterministically via database-state diffs.
AI.result: Benchmarking 11 cutting-edge LLMs shows that multi-step tool use remains challenging. Pass^3 stays below 60% for the strongest models, and even with code execution in the E-Bench-Code extension, reliability (Pass^3) remains below 70%.
AI.conclusion: E-Bench demonstrates that current LLMs struggle with multi-step tool use in stateful environments, highlighting a significant gap in agent capabilities. The synthetic, controllable nature of E-Bench makes it suitable for scalable evaluation of tool-use agents.

title: Cascade Forgery Mining Network for Fingerprint Presentation Attack Detection
summary: Fingerprint Presentation Attack Detection (PAD) is a critical component of fingerprint identification systems, serving as a protective measure against unauthorized access. In this paper, we observe that different regions of a fingerprint image can exhibit varying Artifact Extraction Difficulty (AED), with high-AED regions requiring more sophisticated extraction mechanisms to capture more subtle discriminative evidence. To address this issue, we propose to quantify AED using local Gabor feature certainty and partition fingerprint images into multiple regions based on their respective AED values. We then propose an AED guided Cascade Forgery Mining Network (CFM-Net) that employs an adaptive-depth feature extraction architecture to detect more precise and comprehensive artifact evidence across regions with heterogeneous AED values. Furthermore, we introduce an Orientation Guided Adversarial Training (OGAT) module to filter out identity information from PAD features while preserving the integrity of original artifact evidence. Experimental evaluations on LivDet datasets demonstrate the superior performance of our approach compared to state-of-the-art methods and achieve significant improvement in the classification ability of high AED fingerprints.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes CFM-Net, an AED-guided cascade forgery mining network for fingerprint presentation attack detection, which adaptively extracts artifact evidence across regions with varying difficulty levels, and uses Orientation Guided Adversarial Training to remove identity information while preserving artifact features.
AI.motivation: Different fingerprint image regions exhibit varying Artifact Extraction Difficulty (AED), with high-AED regions requiring more sophisticated mechanisms to capture subtle discriminative evidence, but existing PAD methods do not account for this heterogeneity.
AI.method: Quantifies AED using local Gabor feature certainty; partitions images into regions by AED values; proposes CFM-Net with adaptive-depth feature extraction; introduces OGAT module to filter identity information while preserving artifact evidence.
AI.result: Superior performance over state-of-the-art methods on LivDet datasets, with significant improvement in classification ability for high AED fingerprints.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling region-wise artifact extraction difficulty and adapting feature extraction depth accordingly improves PAD performance, especially for challenging high-AED regions.

title: Calibrated Tree-Neural Fusion for Fine-Grained Vegetation Community Classification
summary: Accurate vegetation-community classification is essential for ecological monitoring, habitat assessment, and evidence-based environmental management in heterogeneous landscapes. Existing studies often rely on standalone tree ensembles or generic neural networks, although fine-grained ecological classes frequently exhibit overlapping spectral, topographic, and structural characteristics. Many frameworks also provide limited protection against stacking leakage, insufficient probability calibration, weak minority-class evaluation, and little evidence of stability across repeated data splits. To address these limitations, this study proposes Calibrated EcoTreeFuseNet-Plus, a tree-neural probability-fusion framework that combines out-of-fold tree probabilities, EcoFuseNet-V2 outputs, validation-selected meta-learning, and post-hoc temperature scaling. Raster values from six LiDAR-derived terrain and canopy variables and two hyperspectral vegetation indices were extracted at coordinate-based reference locations. Quality control removed 26 samples with missing elevation and one sample with non-finite NDWI, producing 1,833 complete records across 29 vegetation and non-vegetation classes. On the held-out test set, the proposed model achieved an accuracy of 0.8000, a macro F1-score of 0.7768, a balanced accuracy of 0.7903, and an MCC of 0.7903. Calibration reduced the expected calibration error from 0.3866 to 0.0651 without changing class predictions. Five-seed evaluation yielded a macro F1-score of 0.7717 +/- 0.0112, indicating stable performance across repeated splits. The results demonstrate a reliable discrimination-calibration trade-off for small-sample, fine-grained ecological classification.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Calibrated EcoTreeFuseNet-Plus, a tree-neural probability-fusion framework combining out-of-fold tree probabilities, EcoFuseNet-V2 outputs, meta-learning, and temperature scaling for fine-grained vegetation classification using LiDAR and hyperspectral data, achieving 0.8000 accuracy and stable performance across 29 classes.
AI.motivation: Existing vegetation classification methods using standalone tree ensembles or generic neural networks struggle with fine-grained ecological classes that exhibit overlapping spectral, topographic, and structural characteristics. Additionally, current frameworks suffer from stacking leakage, poor probability calibration, weak minority-class evaluation, and unstable performance across repeated data splits.
AI.method: The proposed Calibrated EcoTreeFuseNet-Plus integrates (1) out-of-fold tree probabilities, (2) EcoFuseNet-V2 neural network outputs, (3) validation-selected meta-learning, and (4) post-hoc temperature scaling. Input features include six LiDAR-derived terrain/canopy variables and two hyperspectral vegetation indices extracted at coordinate-based reference locations, with quality control yielding 1,833 complete records across 29 classes.
AI.result: On the held-out test set: accuracy=0.8000, macro F1=0.7768, balanced accuracy=0.7903, MCC=0.7903. Calibration reduced ECE from 0.3866 to 0.0651 without altering predictions. Five-seed evaluation: macro F1=0.7717±0.0112, confirming stability.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework achieves a reliable discrimination-calibration trade-off for small-sample, fine-grained ecological classification, demonstrating stable and well-calibrated performance across repeated data splits.

title: Training Language Models to Cooperate with Inference-Time Controllers
summary: Large language model (LLM) performance increasingly depends not only on the base model, but also on the inference-time controller used to organize reasoning. Existing post-training methods, however, typically optimize for a single fixed interaction pattern, despite real deployments relying on diverse controllers such as Chain-of-Thought, self-consistency, debate, planning, and verification pipelines. This creates a training--deployment mismatch and limits transfer to new workflows. We introduce CALM (Controller-Aware Language Models), a post-training framework that explicitly places controllers in the training loop. We formulate controller-aware post-training as multi-task reinforcement learning over controller-induced interaction protocols, where controllers are compositions of reusable local reasoning modules. This structure also induces a module-level decomposition of mixed-controller training under a turn-level GRPO objective, enabling a systematic study of controller and module-aware training strategies. We evaluate CALM on held-out controller compositions and broader controller shifts, showing that controller-aware post-training improves generalization across inference-time workflows beyond single-controller optimization.

AI.tldr: CALM is a post-training framework that incorporates diverse inference-time controllers (CoT, self-consistency, debate, planning, verification) into LLM training via multi-task RL over controller-induced protocols, improving generalization across inference-time workflows beyond single-controller optimization.
AI.motivation: Existing post-training methods optimize for a single fixed interaction pattern, causing a training-deployment mismatch since real deployments use diverse controllers (CoT, self-consistency, debate, planning, verification). This limits transfer to new workflows.
AI.method: CALM formulates controller-aware post-training as multi-task reinforcement learning over controller-induced interaction protocols, where controllers are compositions of reusable local reasoning modules. It uses a turn-level GRPO objective to enable module-level decomposition for mixed-controller training.
AI.result: Controller-aware post-training improves generalization across held-out controller compositions and broader controller shifts compared to single-controller optimization.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly incorporating controller awareness into post-training mitigates the training-deployment mismatch and enables better transfer to diverse and unseen inference-time workflows.

title: ReflexTrack: A Feedback-Driven Agent for Training-Free Referring Video Object Segmentation
summary: Referring video object segmentation (RVOS) requires segmenting a target specified by natural language throughout a video. Recent agentic approaches combine multimodal large language models with promptable segmentation models to perform RVOS without task-specific training. However, most pipelines rely on one-shot spatial grounding followed by mask propagation, leaving both the initial prompts and temporal predictions largely unverified. We introduce ReflexTrack, a training-free, feedback-driven agent that closes this loop at both spatial and temporal levels. Mask-guided Spatial Refinement evaluates the mask induced by the current keyframe prompt and iteratively updates the bounding box together with positive and negative points, yielding a more reliable initialization. Video-level Mask Reflection assesses the complete mask sequence, localizes unreliable intervals, selects complementary repair keyframes, and generates candidate predictions through mask-guided re-propagation. Only candidates that provide a verified improvement are used to update the affected intervals, preserving reliable predictions elsewhere. All components remain frozen during inference. ReflexTrack achieves an overall $\mathcal{Q}$ score of $69.7$ on Ref-VPS and a $\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F}$ score of $67.2$ on ReasonVOS. These results demonstrate that prediction-level feedback substantially improves the reliability of training-free RVOS.
