The authors aim to bridge the gap between historical cognitive architectures and modern language-agent systems by providing a precise, mechanism-level comparison.
AI.method: The authors analyze 10 historical cognitive architectures, 8 language-agent runtime families, and 42 mechanism-focused modern systems. They reconstruct each mechanism across 7 dimensions (state, control, transition, persistence, failure, learning, resource governance) and code them using two scales: evidence relation (E1-E4) and migration depth (D0-D4). They also identify mechanism bundles via closest-baseline screening against GraSP.
AI.result: Modern agents have operationalized adaptive memory, failure recovery, dynamic team selection, workflow search, skill induction, resource scheduling, and uncertainty-conditioned action, but often via independent convergence. Five residual mechanism bundles remain: (1) activation with latency and action utility; (2) typed impasse with isolated substates and resolution compilation; (3) bounded content competition with broadcast and admission learning; (4) persistent intention with reconsideration and live method authority; (5) uncertainty with resource allocation, interruption, and stopping.
AI.conclusion: The paper contributes a distinctive-mechanism catalog, an auditable evidence-depth framework, and a falsifiable agenda for testing the five identified bundles as composable runtime invariants, suggesting that the strongest remaining opportunities lie in couplings among mechanisms rather than isolated features.

title: Face Age Verification Vulnerabilities Under Simple Appearance Manipulations
summary: Online platforms increasingly rely on automated age estimation systems to enforce minimum-age policies. Focusing on vision-based models designed for this task, concerns arise regarding their robustness to simple appearance changes that underage individuals may use to bypass such systems, such as drawing a mustache or applying lipstick. In this work, we present a systematic study of age verification robustness by simulating visual alterations that can be easily achieved by underage individuals. We evaluate seven models, including vision, vision-language, and multimodal large language models, across three datasets and four manipulation types. Interestingly, under drawn beard stubble, up to 61% of True Negatives are flipped into False Positives. Furthermore, we investigate how different demographics are affected by such manipulations, finding that Indians are more affected by beard stubble manipulations, while females are more affected than males across all manipulations. Finally, we explore how these biases can be mitigated using bias mitigation methodologies in lightweight linear probe settings.

AI.tldr: Vision-based age estimation systems are vulnerable to simple appearance manipulations (e.g., drawn mustache, lipstick), with up to 61% of underage true negatives flipped to false positives under beard stubble; Indians and females are disproportionately affected, and bias mitigation methods can reduce these effects.
AI.motivation: Online platforms use automated age estimation to enforce age restrictions, but the robustness of these vision-based models to simple appearance changes that underage users might exploit (e.g., drawing a mustache, applying lipstick) is not well understood.
AI.method: Systematically simulated visual alterations (4 manipulation types) and evaluated 7 models (vision, vision-language, multimodal LLMs) across 3 datasets. Analyzed demographic disparities and tested bias mitigation via lightweight linear probe settings.
AI.result: Under drawn beard stubble, up to 61% of true negatives (underage) flipped to false positives. Indians more affected by beard stubble; females more affected than males across all manipulations.
AI.conclusion: Age verification models are not robust to simple appearance manipulations; demographic biases exist and can be partially mitigated using bias mitigation techniques.

title: Unsupervised Graph Representation Learning with Complementary View Alignment
summary: Unsupervised graph representation learning aims to derive meaningful node embeddings by capturing both structural and attribute information without relying on labeled data. Existing methods, such as GAEs, have demonstrated effectiveness but typically rely on message-passing mechanisms that assume homophily, leading to performance degradation on heterophilous graphs, where connected nodes exhibit dissimilar features. This homophily bias results in the loss of critical high-frequency components that are essential for identifying heterophilous patterns. To address these challenges, we propose \textsc{AlignGAE}, a novel extension of \textit{MaskGAE} that preserves the full frequency spectrum through complementary view alignment. Our framework introduces a dual-encoder architecture that separately processes structural and attribute information, incorporates node positional encoding to approximate Neighborhood Identity Distribution (NID), and employs dual reconstruction tasks for both edges and node attributes. We further propose theoretically grounded NID alignment strategies that ensure semantic consistency across views while preserving their distinct characteristics. Through comprehensive spectral analysis, we demonstrate that \textsc{AlignGAE} achieves optimal representation properties when the alignment loss converges. Extensive experiments across 12 benchmark datasets validate our approach, showing that \textsc{AlignGAE} outperforms state-of-the-art methods by up to 18.7\% on heterophilous graphs in node classification, while maintaining competitive performance on homophilous graphs. Our results establish a new paradigm for frequency-aware graph representation learning.

AI.tldr: AlignGAE is a novel unsupervised graph representation learning framework that extends MaskGAE with a dual-encoder architecture, node positional encoding, and complementary view alignment to preserve the full frequency spectrum. It addresses the homophily bias of existing GAE methods that lose high-frequency components on heterophilous graphs. AlignGAE achieves optimal representation properties when alignment loss converges and outperforms SOTA methods by up to 18.7% on heterophilous graph node classification tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing unsupervised graph representation learning methods like GAEs rely on message-passing mechanisms that assume homophily, causing performance degradation on heterophilous graphs where connected nodes have dissimilar features. This homophily bias leads to the loss of critical high-frequency components needed for identifying heterophilous patterns.
AI.method: AlignGAE introduces: (1) a dual-encoder architecture that separately processes structural and attribute information; (2) node positional encoding to approximate Neighborhood Identity Distribution (NID); (3) dual reconstruction tasks for both edges and node attributes; (4) theoretically grounded NID alignment strategies ensuring semantic consistency across views while preserving distinct characteristics.
AI.result: Through spectral analysis, AlignGAE achieves optimal representation properties when alignment loss converges. Extensive experiments on 12 benchmark datasets show AlignGAE outperforms state-of-the-art methods by up to 18.7% on heterophilous graphs in node classification, while maintaining competitive performance on homophilous graphs.
AI.conclusion: AlignGAE establishes a new paradigm for frequency-aware graph representation learning by preserving the full frequency spectrum through complementary view alignment, effectively addressing the homophily bias limitation of existing methods.

title: DICA: Dual-Indicator Guided Contrastive Alignment in Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: Human visual reasoning typically follows a coarse-to-fine attention process, starting from global scene understanding and gradually focusing on question-relevant regions. However, multimodal large language models may deviate from this pattern due to attention drift and the underutilization of visual evidence, which can lead to hallucinations. To mitigate these issues, this study proposes a Dual-Indicator Guided Contrastive Alignment (DICA), which tracks two information-theoretic indicators during inference: Visual Attention Entropy (VAE), which reflects the concentration of visual attention, and Output Image Correlation (OIC), which measures the dependence of generated outputs on the visual input. An abnormal increase in VAE or a decrease in OIC corresponds to different failure modes, which trigger targeted contrastive alignment to restore visual grounding. Experimental results across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that DICA consistently outperforms existing approaches and substantially reduces hallucinations, highlighting the effectiveness of indicator-driven intervention in improving multimodal inference reliability. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/BGWH123/DICA/.

AI.tldr: DICA uses two information-theoretic indicators (VAE and OIC) to detect and correct attention drift during multimodal inference, reducing hallucinations through targeted contrastive alignment.
AI.motivation: Multimodal large language models suffer from attention drift and underutilization of visual evidence, causing hallucinations that deviate from the coarse-to-fine human visual reasoning pattern.
AI.method: DICA tracks Visual Attention Entropy (VAE) for visual attention concentration and Output Image Correlation (OIC) for output dependence on visual input; abnormal shifts trigger targeted contrastive alignment to restore visual grounding.
AI.result: Consistently outperforms existing approaches across multiple benchmarks and substantially reduces hallucinations.
AI.conclusion: Indicator-driven intervention improves multimodal inference reliability, with open-source code available.

title: Reasoning to Regulate: Chain-of-Thought for Traffic Rule Understanding
summary: Understanding and complying with traffic regulations is a safety-critical requirement for autonomous driving, yet remains challenging due to the diversity and context dependence of traffic signage. Importantly, regulation understanding is not a simple recognition task, but a reasoning problem: whether a rule applies depends on interpreting the sign in relation to the spatial layout of lanes and scene context. To support such reasoning, MapDR provide fine-grained annotations that link each traffic sign's regulatory rules to the specific lanes they govern. Existing methods, however, largely treat this as direct sequence prediction, ignoring the underlying reasoning that connects sign semantics and map structure. To address this limitation, we explicitly incorporate reasoning into this task and propose a framework that equips vision-language models (VLMs) with chain-of-thought (CoT) capabilities. We first design a scalable CoT curation pipeline that bootstraps rationales from a strong LLM through a two-round strategy and employs a VLM-based verifier to filter out incorrect cases, yielding a high-quality set of (CoT, answer) pairs. Building on this foundation, we adopt a two-stage training scheme: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to teach rationale-to-answer generation, followed by GRPO reinforcement learning with answer-grounded, fine-grained rewards to further improve final answer accuracy. Extensive experiments on MapDR show that our approach significantly improves both interpretability and accuracy, establishing the first reasoning-based framework for regulation-aware autonomous driving.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a reasoning-based framework for autonomous driving regulation understanding, using chain-of-thought and reinforcement learning to improve traffic sign interpretation accuracy on the MapDR dataset.
AI.motivation: Traffic regulation understanding requires reasoning about sign semantics in relation to lane layouts and scene context, not just recognition. Existing methods treat it as direct sequence prediction, ignoring the underlying reasoning connecting signs and map structure.
AI.method: Proposes a CoT curation pipeline (two-round bootstrapping from LLM + VLM-based verifier) to create high-quality (CoT, answer) pairs, followed by two-stage training: SFT for rationale-to-answer generation, then GRPO reinforcement learning with answer-grounded fine-grained rewards.
AI.result: The approach significantly improves both interpretability and accuracy on the MapDR benchmark compared to existing methods.
AI.conclusion: This work establishes the first reasoning-based framework for regulation-aware autonomous driving, demonstrating that explicit reasoning through CoT and RL improves regulatory compliance understanding.

title: Beyond Aggregate Risk: Role-Stratified Conformal Risk Control for LLM Tool Calls
summary: Language-model agents act through structured tool calls whose arguments carry different risks. Untrusted content may safely influence an email body but should not determine a recipient, account, command, or credential. Existing statistical methods typically control risk over the entire action, allowing failures in rare, high-risk fields to be obscured by benign arguments. We introduce role-stratified per-field conformal risk control, a calibration layer that wraps any per-field detector and sets separate thresholds and risk budgets for semantic argument roles. For a role with prevalence $p_r$, aggregate-only certification must use an effective budget of $αp_r$ to guarantee role-specific risk $α$, whereas role-stratified calibration certifies each sufficiently sampled role directly with a finite-sample guarantee; rarer roles are handled by pooled certification. Across AgentDojo and InjecAgent with six language models, the empirical utility gap tracks this predicted price of coarseness, and our method achieves the most consistent role-specific budget compliance under model and attack transfer, detector noise, gradual drift, unseen tool suites, and adaptive attacks. It provides formal per-role guarantees under exchangeability or after recalibration, and empirical compliance under frozen distribution shift. These results suggest that structured tool calls should be certified at the semantic-role level, not the whole action.

AI.tldr: Introduces role-stratified per-field conformal risk control, a calibration method that sets separate thresholds and risk budgets for semantic argument roles in LM agent tool calls, providing per-role guarantees instead of aggregate-only certification.
AI.motivation: Existing statistical methods control risk over entire actions, allowing failures in rare, high-risk fields (e.g., recipient, command, credential) to be obscured by benign arguments. Structured tool calls have different risk levels per argument role, requiring role-specific treatment.
AI.method: Role-stratified per-field conformal risk control: a calibration layer that wraps per-field detectors, setting separate thresholds and risk budgets for each semantic argument role. For well-sampled roles, direct certification with finite-sample guarantees; for rare roles, pooled certification handles them.
AI.result: Across AgentDojo and InjecAgent with six LMs, the method achieves the most consistent role-specific budget compliance under model/attack transfer, detector noise, drift, unseen tools, and adaptive attacks. Empirical utility gap matches the predicted "price of coarseness."
AI.conclusion: Structured tool calls should be certified at the semantic-role level, not the whole action. The method provides formal per-role guarantees under exchangeability or after recalibration, with empirical compliance under frozen distribution shift.

title: EviBack: Search-Agent Reinforcement Learning via Evidence-Constrained Teacher Backoff
summary: Reinforcement learning enables Agentic RAG systems to learn multi-turn search from verifiable outcome rewards, but all- zero rollout groups provide no comparative signal and may hide useful search behavior. We present EviBack, an evidence- constrained Teacher backoff that supplies auxiliary super- vision to such groups while preserving verifiable Actor re- wards. It separates evidence assessment from answer refine- ment, preventing reference answers from overriding evidence- insufficiency judgments. A fully automated, end-to-end GPT- 5.5-assisted APE pipeline starts from a manually authored single-prompt dual-task Teacher, automatically partitions and labels rollout data, and performs ablation, task decomposition, evaluation, and selection to produce a gated two-stage Teacher. Compared with the manual design, the resulting Teacher im- proves downstream F1 and valid-answer rate while reduc- ing search, duplicate queries, and forced termination. Across seven open-domain QA benchmarks and three Qwen3 scales, EviBack improves F1 over Search-R1 and raises both single- and multi-hop macro F1. We guarantee that the code will be made publicly available at a later stage.

AI.tldr: EviBack is an evidence-constrained Teacher backoff method that improves Agentic RAG systems by providing auxiliary supervision to zero-reward rollout groups, separating evidence assessment from answer refinement, and using an automated APE pipeline to produce a gated two-stage Teacher that outperforms manual designs across multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement learning for Agentic RAG systems suffers from all-zero rollout groups that lack comparative signal and may hide useful search behavior, motivating the need for auxiliary supervision that preserves verifiable outcome rewards.
AI.method: EviBack introduces evidence-constrained Teacher backoff that separates evidence assessment from answer refinement. A fully automated GPT-5.5-assisted APE pipeline starts from a manually authored single-prompt dual-task Teacher, automatically partitions and labels rollout data, and performs ablation, task decomposition, evaluation, and selection to produce a gated two-stage Teacher.
AI.result: Across seven open-domain QA benchmarks and three Qwen3 scales, EviBack improves F1 over Search-R1, raises both single- and multi-hop macro F1, and improves downstream F1 and valid-answer rate while reducing search, duplicate queries, and forced termination compared to manual design.
AI.conclusion: EviBack effectively addresses the limitation of zero-reward groups in RL-based Agentic RAG by providing targeted supervision without overriding evidence-insufficiency judgments, leading to more efficient and accurate multi-turn search and answer generation.

title: Effect of User-Prompted Priors on Semi-Automated Cancer Lesion Segmentation in Whole-Body Computed Tomography
comment: Accepted at MIUA (Medical Image Understanding and Analysis). To appear in Lecture Notes in Computer Science (LNCS). 12 pages, 2 figures
summary: In clinical oncology studies, metastatic cancer is commonly evaluated using "Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors" (RECIST), in which the diameter of up to five lesions is measured and followed over the course of treatment. However, RECIST shows limited correlation with overall survival. Total tumour volume (TTV) is a stronger predictor but typically relies on manual ground-truth segmentation of all lesions, which is time-consuming and requires expert domain knowledge. Semi-automated approaches leveraging user-prompted priors, such as bounding boxes and single-slice contours, as inputs to automated segmentation methods can facilitate the generation of ground-truth segmentations. This work investigates the impact of different user-prompted priors on semi-automated cancer lesion segmentation performance in whole-body computed tomography. Across 3-fold cross-validation and external testing, more complex spatial priors consistently improved performance, with contour priors from three orthogonal planes (axial, coronal and sagittal) achieving the best results. On the external test (n=3865 lesions), this approach achieved a mean Dice score of 0.882, compared to a mean Dice score of 0.671 for the baseline model with no spatial prior. These findings suggest that the use of multi-plane orthogonal user-prompted priors can improve semi-automated tumour lesion segmentation and support efficient generation of high-quality volumetric ground-truth data.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how different user-prompted spatial priors (bounding boxes, single-slice contours, multi-plane orthogonal contours) affect semi-automated cancer lesion segmentation in whole-body CT, finding that multi-plane orthogonal contour priors achieve the best performance (Dice 0.882 vs 0.671 baseline).
AI.motivation: RECIST-based lesion diameter measurement shows limited correlation with overall survival, while total tumour volume (TTV) is a stronger predictor but requires labor-intensive manual ground-truth segmentation of all lesions, motivating the need for efficient semi-automated segmentation approaches.
AI.method: The authors compared semi-automated lesion segmentation performance using different user-prompted spatial priors (bounding boxes, single-slice contours, and multi-plane orthogonal contours from axial, coronal, and sagittal planes) in whole-body CT, evaluated via 3-fold cross-validation and external testing on 3865 lesions.
AI.result: More complex spatial priors consistently improved segmentation performance. Multi-plane orthogonal contour priors achieved a mean Dice of 0.882 on external test, compared to 0.671 for the baseline model with no spatial prior.
AI.conclusion: Multi-plane orthogonal user-prompted priors can improve semi-automated tumour lesion segmentation and support efficient generation of high-quality volumetric ground-truth data, facilitating better TTV estimation.

title: Perturbative-NeuSA: A Structured Spectral Framework for Time-Dependent PDEs
comment: 16 pages, 5 figures, 14 tables; supplementary material included
summary: Neural spectral PDE solvers often learn an entire unresolved vector field even when an inexpensive approximate model can already capture most of the trajectory. Here we introduce Perturbative-NeuSA, a residual formulation that decomposes the target solution into a low-fidelity background and a high-resolution perturbation, so that only the unresolved dynamics is learned. Starting from the exact perturbation equation, the method combines a fixed spectral operator, a background-dependent correction, the background defect in the target PDE, and an optional neural closure. This construction makes the roles of physical structure and neural closure separately measurable. Across 2D Burgers, Klein-Gordon, and heterogeneous 2D wave equations, the deterministic structured solver outperforms the trained NeuSA baseline while requiring no neural-network training. The largest gains occur on Burgers, where the deterministic correction reduces training and extrapolation errors by factors of 24 and 44, respectively. In addition, a Klein-Gordon sweep over seven background resolutions shows that the effect of the closure is conditional: it improves a poor background by 3.6 times, becomes neutral at intermediate resolutions, and degrades a well-resolved background. For the wave equation, however, the closure provides an additional 18% reduction when the remaining residual is interface-localized. Multi-initial-condition diagnostics further show that the useful closure regime depends on the initial-condition spectrum and can disappear in extrapolation when structured correction already captures the dominant Burgers dynamics. Perturbative-NeuSA therefore reframes neural closure as a conditional, diagnosable correction governed by background fidelity, residual organization, and compatibility with the closure model.

AI.tldr: Perturbative-NeuSA is a residual spectral PDE solver that decomposes target solutions into a low-fidelity background and a high-resolution perturbation, learning only unresolved dynamics. It outperforms trained neural baselines without training on Burgers, Klein-Gordon, and wave equations, and shows neural closure is conditionally beneficial depending on background fidelity, residual structure, and initial-condition spectrum.
AI.motivation: Neural spectral PDE solvers waste capacity by learning the entire vector field even when an inexpensive approximate model already captures most of the trajectory. The goal is to learn only the unresolved dynamics via a residual formulation.
AI.method: The method decomposes the target solution into a low-fidelity background and a high-resolution perturbation. It combines a fixed spectral operator, a background-dependent correction, the background defect in the target PDE, and an optional neural closure, making physical structure and neural closure separately measurable.
AI.result: On 2D Burgers, deterministic structured solver reduces training/extrapolation errors by factors of 24 and 44 vs. trained NeuSA. Closure improves poor background 3.6×, is neutral at intermediate resolutions, degrades well-resolved background. For wave equation, closure gives 18% reduction when residual is interface-localized.
AI.conclusion: Perturbative-NeuSA reframes neural closure as a conditional, diagnosable correction governed by background fidelity, residual organization, and compatibility with the closure model. The useful closure regime depends on initial-condition spectrum and can vanish in extrapolation.

title: Grokking on the Weight-Decay Clock: A Rate Hierarchy from Softly Broken Symmetries
summary: Delayed generalization, or grokking, remains poorly understood despite extensive empirical study. We identify an exactly solvable late-time relaxation mechanism for grokking in linear models trained with full-batch heavy-ball optimization and weight decay, together with a locally quadratic extension to nonlinear neural networks. Our analysis reveals a distinguished population-active component of the empirical null space, which we call the grokking subspace. Along this subspace, the training predictions remain unchanged, leaving weight decay as the sole restoring force and giving rise to a slow dissipative relaxation governed by an exact discrete-time and continuous-time law. We show that only this subspace contributes to the slow asymptotic decay of the population risk and derive explicit iteration-scale predictions for the grokking time, recovering the familiar $(1-β)/(ηλ)$ scaling in the weak-regularization regime. The theory further predicts distinct effects of optimizer choice, distinguishing coupled $L_2$ regularization from decoupled weight decay, and yields causal predictions for interventions that modify the grokking component. We verify all theoretical identities without fitted parameters in a synthetic model where every subspace and relaxation rate is computable in closed form. We further observe genuine delayed generalization in modular addition, where the measured delay follows the predicted scaling and the late-time relaxation agrees closely with the theoretical clock.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies an exactly solvable late-time relaxation mechanism for grokking (delayed generalization) in linear models with heavy-ball optimization and weight decay, extending to nonlinear neural networks. It introduces the concept of a "grokking subspace" where training predictions remain static while weight decay drives slow dissipative relaxation, yielding explicit scaling laws for grokking time and distinct effects of optimizer choices.
AI.motivation: Grokking (delayed generalization) remains poorly understood mechanistically despite extensive empirical study. The authors aim to provide an analytically tractable framework to explain the late-time relaxation dynamics underlying grokking.
AI.method: The authors analyze linear models trained with full-batch heavy-ball optimization and weight decay, identifying a "grokking subspace" (a population-active component of the empirical null space). They derive exact discrete-time and continuous-time relaxation laws, and extend the analysis via a locally quadratic approximation to nonlinear neural networks. Theoretical predictions are validated on a synthetic model with closed-form computable quantities and on modular addition tasks.
AI.result: The theory yields explicit iteration-scale predictions for grokking time, recovering the (1-β)/(ηλ) scaling in the weak-regularization regime. It distinguishes coupled L2 regularization from decoupled weight decay, and produces causal predictions for interventions. All theoretical identities are verified without fitted parameters in a synthetic model, and delayed generalization in modular addition follows the predicted scaling with close agreement to the theoretical clock.
AI.conclusion: The grokking subspace mechanism provides an exactly solvable explanation for delayed generalization in linear models and extends to nonlinear networks. The derived scaling laws and optimizer-specific effects offer a unified theoretical account of grokking dynamics.

title: TreeAdapter: Hierarchical Taxonomy-Guided Adapter Composition for Fine-Grained Species Image Generation
summary: Although general text-to-image models excel in open-domain generation, their performance degrades significantly in specialized downstream domains, particularly when generating images of rare biological species. Hindered by long-tailed distributions, general models struggle to capture subtle fine-grained details, while per-species fine-tuning methods over-isolate individual species and consequently ignore the shared visual features among closely related taxa. To address this, we propose TreeAdapter, a novel framework that explicitly leverages hierarchical taxonomic data. Rather than using a monolithic model or independent per-species modules, TreeAdapter attaches lightweight adapters to every node of the taxonomic tree. Specifically, leaf-node adapters capture species-specific visual traits, while internal-node adapters encapsulate shared semantics among descendant taxa. We introduce a two-stage training paradigm where ancestor adapters are optimized to model only the residual visual features unexplained by their descendants. This model architecture and training paradigm enable the model to fully leverage hierarchical information, ensuring the accurate generation of visual features for each species. Extensive experiments across three large-scale biodiversity benchmarks demonstrate that TreeAdapter achieves state-of-the-art fine-grained generation quality, outperforming both general-purpose and domain-specific baselines.

AI.tldr: TreeAdapter is a framework that leverages hierarchical taxonomic data for fine-grained image generation of rare biological species, using lightweight adapters attached to each node of the taxonomic tree with a two-stage training paradigm that models residual visual features, achieving SOTA on biodiversity benchmarks.
AI.motivation: General text-to-image models fail on rare biological species due to long-tailed distributions, and per-species fine-tuning ignores shared visual features among related taxa. There is a need to leverage hierarchical taxonomic relationships for better generation.
AI.method: TreeAdapter attaches lightweight adapters to each node of the taxonomic tree: leaf-node adapters capture species-specific traits, internal-node adapters capture shared semantics among descendants. A two-stage training paradigm optimizes ancestor adapters to model only residual visual features unexplained by descendants.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art fine-grained generation quality on three large-scale biodiversity benchmarks, outperforming both general-purpose and domain-specific baselines.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling hierarchical taxonomic information with tree-structured adapters and residual learning effectively improves fine-grained generation of rare biological species.

title: MobiWave: Dispatch-Oriented Graph Wavelets and Drift-Guided Selective Optimization for Autonomous Fleet Rebalancing
summary: Autonomous fleets enable mobility platforms to coordinate idle vehicles directly, making fleet-wide rebalancing possible. However, two obstacles limit reliable deployment: overlapping regional and local traffic patterns can hide roads that remain useful for dispatch, and mobility drift can make a trained policy unreliable. Existing spatial aggregation mixes these patterns, while updating all parameters from limited recent data is costly and can damage stable knowledge. We propose \name, a framework that connects a dispatch-oriented multi-scale graph wavelet module with Drift-Guided Layer-Selective Optimization (DGLS). The first module addresses the representation challenge by separating graph-frequency patterns and weighting each scale according to its value for demand prediction and feasible rebalancing. DGLS addresses the adaptation challenge by measuring Dispatch-weighted Spectral Drift, selecting affected layers within a resource budget, and separating short shocks from persistent changes through a drift-aware fast--slow update. Candidate validation further rejects updates that fail to improve held-out dispatch reward without worsening monitored service or safety constraints. Experiments on both real-world datasets and simluated environments demonstrate the effectiveness of \name\ in comparing with state-of-the-art methods. The source code and datasets are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MobiWave-40F8/.

AI.tldr: MobiWave is a framework for autonomous fleet rebalancing that uses a multi-scale graph wavelet module for spatial representation and Drift-Guided Layer-Selective Optimization (DGLS) for adapting to mobility drift, outperforming state-of-the-art methods on real-world and simulated datasets.
AI.motivation: Overlapping regional/local traffic patterns hide useful dispatch roads, and mobility drift makes trained policies unreliable; existing spatial aggregation mixes patterns, and full parameter updates are costly and damage stable knowledge.
AI.method: The framework connects (1) a dispatch-oriented multi-scale graph wavelet module that separates graph-frequency patterns and weights each scale for demand prediction and rebalancing, with (2) Drift-Guided Layer-Selective Optimization (DGLS) that measures Dispatch-weighted Spectral Drift, selects affected layers under a resource budget, separates short shocks from persistent changes via fast-slow update, and rejects invalid updates via candidate validation.
AI.result: Experiments on real-world datasets and simulated environments demonstrate effectiveness compared to state-of-the-art methods.
AI.conclusion: MobiWave effectively addresses both representation and adaptation challenges for reliable autonomous fleet rebalancing deployment.

title: Plato-Bio: verification-first biological novelty screening with temporal rediscovery and structural benchmarks
comment: 16 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables. Companion code and data: https://github.com/Eldergenix/Plato-Scientific-Research-Autonomous-Agent. This fork-specific validation study cites, but does not duplicate, arXiv:2510.26887
summary: Large language model research agents can connect literature retrieval, analysis code, and manuscript preparation, but coherent output does not establish scientific validity. We developed Plato-Bio, a biology-routed extension of the open Plato/Denario architecture that couples explicit workflow states with provenance records, citation checks, claim-to-evidence links, scoped file writes, and publication gates. A source audit identified and repaired three defects that could distort evaluation: loss of task domain in the default factory, omission of declared method signals from scoring, and evidence sidecars that lacked the drafted-claim denominator. On the current clean revision, the full Python suite completed with 931 passes, six skips, and no failures or errors; targeted biology, genomics, evidence/citation, and adversarial-safety suites likewise completed without failure. We evaluated two narrow use cases. In a frozen historical rediscovery task, independent pre-1986 literature bridges ranked the later-studied relation between fish oil and Raynaud phenomenon first; TF-IDF ranked it second and corpus frequency third. This single curated task measures retrospective ranking, not prospective discovery. In a separate comparison of AlphaFold models with experimental structures for 15 human proteins, 11 targets had high-confidence-core C-alpha RMSD below 1 Angstrom (median 0.501 Angstrom). Four targets exceeded 2 Angstrom, and confidence masking reduced the SUMO1 discrepancy from 16.61 to 2.58 Angstrom over 74 residues. The workflow emitted 27 traceable discrepancy regions, all retained as unvalidated hypotheses. Plato-Bio therefore provides reproducible software contracts and auditable screening baselines; broader claims of agent efficacy or biological novelty require preregistered evaluation, independent review, and prospective validation.

AI.tldr: Plato-Bio is a biology-routed research agent built on the Plato/Denario architecture that enforces explicit workflow states, provenance, citation checks, and claim-to-evidence links. After fixing three evaluation defects, the system passed all test suites. In a historical rediscovery task, it ranked the fish oil-Raynaud phenomenon relation first. In an AlphaFold comparison, 11/15 targets had sub-1 Å Cα RMSD, and confidence masking reduced a SUMO1 discrepancy from 16.61 to 2.58 Å. The authors caution that coherent outputs do not imply scientific validity without preregistered evaluation and independent validation.
AI.motivation: Large language model research agents can produce coherent outputs that appear valid but lack scientific rigor. The authors aim to build a system that couples structured workflow states with provenance, citation verification, and claim-to-evidence links to produce auditable, reproducible research outputs rather than merely plausible ones.
AI.method: Plato-Bio extends the Plato/Denario architecture with biology-specific routing, explicit workflow states, provenance records, citation checks, claim-to-evidence links, scoped file writes, and publication gates. A source audit identified and repaired three defects (loss of task domain, omission of declared method signals, and missing drafted-claim denominator in evidence sidecars). Evaluation used a historical rediscovery task (fish oil and Raynaud phenomenon) and a structural biology comparison (AlphaFold vs. experimental structures for 15 human proteins).
AI.result: After fixes, the full Python suite had 931 passes, 6 skips, no failures/errors. In the historical rediscovery task, independent literature bridges ranked fish oil-Raynaud first (TF-IDF second, corpus frequency third). In the AlphaFold comparison, 11/15 targets had high-confidence Cα RMSD <1 Å (median 0.501 Å); 4 targets exceeded 2 Å; confidence masking reduced SUMO1 discrepancy from 16.61 to 2.58 Å over 74 residues; 27 traceable discrepancy regions were emitted as unvalidated hypotheses.
AI.conclusion: Plato-Bio provides reproducible software contracts and auditable screening baselines, but broader claims of agent efficacy or biological novelty require preregistered evaluation, independent review, and prospective validation. The system's structured outputs enable auditing but do not themselves establish scientific validity.

title: MATS: A novel multi-modality multi-task learning framework for 3D perception in autonomous driving
summary: Multi-modality data from different sensors provides rich complementary information for 3D perception, becoming an essential component in reliable autonomous driving systems. Current research typically designs intricate and complex fusion strategies to integrate information from multimodal data on a unified bird's-eye-view (BEV) feature map for the joint learning of multiple perception tasks. However, such a single feature map hardly carries sufficient information to simultaneously meet the requirements of various perception tasks, leading to a very limited perception performance. To mitigate this limitation, this paper proposes MATS, a novel multi-modality multi-task learning approach with modality-adaptive BEV fusion and task-specific Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) for 3D perception. Specifically, a simple modality-adaptive BEV fusion module is designed to adaptively recalibrate the BEV features by modeling the global cross-modality dependencies, generating diverse BEV feature maps for various perception tasks. For joint multi-task learning, this paper proposes a task-specific MoE module to decouple the tasks and enable the network to automatically choose the appropriate BEV feature candidates for each specific task. To validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, we conduct extensive experiments on the large-scale benchmark nuScenes. With the camera- and LiDAR-modality input data, the proposed approach outperforms the state-of-the-art (SOTA) by a significant margin. Furthermore, the experimental results on the single tasks show that the proposed approach significantly outperforms the baselines. The code and trained models will be available upon publication.

AI.tldr: MATS proposes a multi-modality multi-task learning approach using modality-adaptive BEV fusion and task-specific Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) for 3D perception in autonomous driving, outperforming SOTA on nuScenes.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-modality fusion methods produce a single unified BEV feature map that cannot simultaneously satisfy the diverse requirements of various perception tasks, leading to limited perception performance.
AI.method: (1) A modality-adaptive BEV fusion module that adaptively recalibrates BEV features by modeling global cross-modality dependencies to generate diverse BEV feature maps for different tasks. (2) A task-specific MoE module that decouples tasks and automatically selects appropriate BEV feature candidates for each task.
AI.result: Outperforms state-of-the-art methods on the nuScenes benchmark by a significant margin using camera and LiDAR data. Also significantly outperforms baselines on single tasks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed modality-adaptive fusion and task-specific MoE effectively address the limitation of single feature map insufficiency in multi-task 3D perception, achieving superior performance.

title: MXAttention: Data-Free Optimal Scaling and Pre-Normalization Quantization for MXFP4 Attention
summary: The quadratic cost of attention is a major bottleneck in diffusion-based video generation models. MXFP4 attention provides a promising path toward efficient inference, but direct MXFP4 quantization often degrades generation quality due to two numerical issues: the clipping-underflow trade-off from power-of-two scaling and the row-wise normalization error introduced in the softmax loop. We propose MXAttention, a data-free post-training quantization framework for MXFP4 attention. MXAttention introduces two components: Universal Optimal Scaling (UOS), which exploits the periodic structure of power-of-two microscaling to derive a distribution-independent optimal scaling boundary Qmax=7.25 without calibration or search, and Pre-Normalization Quantization (PNQ), which quantizes unnormalized softmax exponentials before row-wise summation to preserve normalization by construction. Experiments on Wan2.2 and HunyuanVideo show that MXAttention closes at least 95% of the VBench Imaging Quality gap between OCP MXFP4 and FP16, substantially improves frame-level similarity, and preserves FP16-level generation quality with less than 0.01 absolute degradation on all reported VBench metrics. MXAttention also achieves performance competitive with strong NVFP4-based baselines with negligible overhead when fused into the attention pipeline. The implementation is publicly available in MindIE-SD.

AI.tldr: MXAttention is a data-free post-training quantization framework for MXFP4 attention in diffusion-based video generation, introducing Universal Optimal Scaling (UOS) and Pre-Normalization Quantization (PNQ) to close at least 95% of the quality gap between MXFP4 and FP16 while maintaining near-lossless performance.
AI.motivation: The quadratic cost of attention in diffusion-based video generation models is a major bottleneck. MXFP4 attention offers efficient inference but suffers from degraded generation quality due to the clipping-underflow trade-off from power-of-two scaling and row-wise normalization error in softmax.
AI.method: Proposes MXAttention, a data-free post-training quantization framework with two components: (1) Universal Optimal Scaling (UOS) that derives a distribution-independent optimal scaling boundary Qmax=7.25 by exploiting the periodic structure of power-of-two microscaling, eliminating the need for calibration or search; (2) Pre-Normalization Quantization (PNQ) that quantizes unnormalized softmax exponentials before row-wise summation to preserve normalization by construction.
AI.result: On Wan2.2 and HunyuanVideo, MXAttention closes at least 95% of the VBench Imaging Quality gap between OCP MXFP4 and FP16, substantially improves frame-level similarity, and preserves FP16-level generation quality with less than 0.01 absolute degradation on all reported VBench metrics. It also achieves competitive performance with NVFP4-based baselines with negligible overhead.
AI.conclusion: MXAttention effectively addresses numerical issues in MXFP4 quantization for diffusion video generation, achieving near-FP16 quality without calibration data or search, and is publicly available in MindIE-SD.

title: Exploring Budgeted Image Classification with Content-Sensitive Resource Allocation
summary: The ever-growing adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) creates the need to deploy Deep Neural Networks in a variety of computational environments. We consider dynamic environments, where computational requirements are subject to change, and we pose the following question: How do we adjust the complexity of an AI classification system, in order to maximize its accuracy, while meeting changing computational constraints? We call this problem Budgeted Image Classification, and we formally formulate it as a resource allocation integer program. Given a computational budget, a batch of images, and a classification system that can make decisions with varying complexity (it has multiple decision points), we explore strategies to allocate images to decision points, in order to maximize accuracy within the available budget. The original integer program is NP-Hard, so, we propose a continuous relaxation, leading to a content-agnostic allocation strategy which assigns images to decision points without considering their particular content. We address this issue by proposing a content-sensitive strategy, that we experimentally show it leads to superior performance. We theoretically study the behavior of our strategies, deriving conditions that must be satisfied by decision points to be suitable for budgeted classification. We analyze fails cases, offering insights for future research directions.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes Budgeted Image Classification as an integer programming problem, proposing both content-agnostic and content-sensitive strategies to allocate images to decision points of varying complexity, maximizing accuracy under changing computational budgets.
AI.motivation: The need to deploy Deep Neural Networks in dynamic environments where computational constraints change, requiring adaptive complexity adjustment for classification systems.
AI.method: Formulates the problem as a resource allocation integer program (NP-Hard), proposes a continuous relaxation leading to a content-agnostic strategy, and then develops a content-sensitive strategy. Theoretical conditions for suitable decision points are derived, and failure cases are analyzed.
AI.result: The content-sensitive strategy experimentally outperforms the content-agnostic one. Theoretical conditions for decision point suitability are identified.
AI.conclusion: Content-sensitive allocation is superior for budgeted classification; failure case analysis provides insights for future research directions.

title: FilmBench: A Film-Grade Benchmark for Cinematic Video Generation
summary: Progress in video generation keeps narrowing the visual gap between AI-generated and professionally produced footage, yet most benchmarks still draw prompts from web sources or LLM templates and score them with untrained, generic multimodal models. More fundamentally, their evaluation taxonomies remain rudimentary (overall visual quality, coarse text alignment and temporal smoothness) rather than the professional Cinematic Language criteria by which films are actually made and judged, so they assess basic video plausibility rather than film-grade craft. We introduce FilmBench, a text-to-video (T2V) and reference-to-video (R2V) benchmark grounded in the professional Cinematic Language of the film- academy tradition and co-developed with directors and faculty from the Beijing Film Academy and the Hujing Digital Media & Entertainment Group film studio. It rests on three choices. First, prompts are reverse-engineered from clips of award-winning films spanning 20 cinematic genres and chosen by professional directors, so every prompt is anchored to a verified live-action reference; the prompts follow real shot lists, and most script multiple shots (1,056 of the 1,169 prompts are multi-shot), unlike prior single-clip benchmarks. Second, evaluation follows a three-level Cinematic taxonomy of 3 axes, 12 components and 35 (T2V) +3 (R2V-only) sub-metrics. Third, we develop an in-house expert-grade automatic evaluation agent and open-source its core suite of Cinematic Language operators (FilmOps). Benchmarking leading video generation models (9 for T2V, 7 for R2V), the evaluator reproduces the human model ranking at model-level Spearman \r{ho} = 0.95 (T2V) and 0.96 (R2V). Scores fall well below prior web-style benchmarks, with two consistent gaps in dynamic aesthetics and a marked single- to multi-shot performance drop that widens for weaker models.

AI.tldr: FilmBench is a new text-to-video and reference-to-video benchmark grounded in professional Cinematic Language, using prompts derived from award-winning film clips and evaluated by an expert-grade automatic agent. It reveals significant gaps in existing video generation models—especially in dynamic aesthetics and multi-shot coherence—that prior benchmarks failed to capture.
AI.motivation: Existing T2V benchmarks rely on web-sourced or LLM-generated prompts, use untrained generic multimodal models for scoring, and employ rudimentary evaluation taxonomies (visual quality, coarse text alignment, temporal smoothness) that assess basic plausibility rather than film-grade cinematic craft. There is a need for a benchmark grounded in professional filmmaking standards.
AI.method: (1) Prompts are reverse-engineered from award-winning film clips spanning 20 cinematic genres, chosen by professional directors, with most being multi-shot (1,056/1,169). (2) A three-level Cinematic taxonomy is used with 3 axes, 12 components, and 35+3 sub-metrics. (3) An in-house expert-grade automatic evaluation agent (FilmOps) is developed and open-sourced.
AI.result: Evaluating 9 T2V and 7 R2V models, the evaluator achieves model-level Spearman ρ = 0.95 (T2V) and 0.96 (R2V) against human ranking. Scores are significantly lower than prior benchmarks, with consistent gaps in dynamic aesthetics and a marked single-to-multi-shot performance drop that widens for weaker models.
AI.conclusion: FilmBench provides a more rigorous, cinematically-grounded evaluation that exposes substantive deficiencies in current video generation models—particularly in dynamic aesthetics and multi-shot coherence—which prior benchmarks failed to identify.

title: K-Survival Means
summary:
In this work, we propose K-SurvMeans, a novel extension of K-Means for clustering survival data. The method explicitly uses the survival outcome in the clustering process to optimize cluster centers, thereby maximizing pairwise survival differences between clusters. The objective function encourages the clusters to be well-separated from the survival perspective. Since the resulting optimization problem is non-differentiable, we employ the Particle Swarm algorithm for the Optimization process.
  To further improve flexibility and mitigate the curse of dimensionality, we extend the framework to operate in a learned low-dimensional latent space obtained via a dimensionality reduction. This allows the method to capture better-separated clusters and enhance optimization efficiency by reducing the search space.
  Experiments on multiple publicly available benchmark survival datasets demonstrate that K-SurvMeans consistently yields clusters with improved separation in survival distributions compared to existing deep learning-based survival clustering methods.

AI.tldr: K-SurvMeans extends K-Means to cluster survival data by explicitly optimizing cluster centers to maximize pairwise survival differences, using Particle Swarm Optimization and dimensionality reduction for improved performance.
AI.motivation: Existing clustering methods for survival data often fail to explicitly incorporate survival outcomes into the clustering process, leading to clusters that are not well-separated from a survival perspective.
AI.method: 1) Extends K-Means by defining an objective function that maximizes pairwise survival differences between clusters. 2) Uses Particle Swarm Optimization to handle the non-differentiable objective. 3) Operates in a low-dimensional latent space via dimensionality reduction to improve flexibility and mitigate the curse of dimensionality.
AI.result: On multiple benchmark survival datasets, K-SurvMeans consistently produces clusters with better separation in survival distributions compared to existing deep learning-based survival clustering methods.
AI.conclusion: K-SurvMeans is an effective and flexible approach for survival clustering that outperforms deep learning baselines, with the latent space extension further enhancing optimization efficiency and cluster quality.

title: Self-Supervised Consistency Enhanced Disentangled Learning for Neural Decoding Generalization in Brain-Machine Interface
summary: Brain-Machine Interfaces (BMIs) provide a direct communication pathway between the brain and external devices, enabling humans to control assistive and robotic technologies, with potential applications in rehabilitation, human motor augmentation, and human-centered robotics. However, due to neural drift, the performance of BMIs decreases over time, posing challenges for long-term viability, particularly for invasive BMIs (iBMIs). Existing solutions suffer from two main drawbacks: (i) difficulty in learning robust neural representations, and (ii) neglecting that neural drift varies across motor parameters (e.g., velocity, direction, and speed). To overcome these limitations, we propose Self-Supervised Consistency enhanced Disentangled Learning (SSCDL), a neural decoding generalization framework built on two key innovations. We first design a backbone model named Consistency enhanced Neural Decoder (CND), using a novel teacher-student consistency constraint with simulated neural signal perturbations to learn robust representations invariant to neural drift. Then, we employ three dedicated CNDs under the Complementary-Disentangled Generalization (CDG) mechanism, which disentangles motor signals into velocity, direction, and speed with inspiration from neural preference theory. This disentangled learning enables SSCDL to capture invariant neural representations from diverse neural preference perspectives, significantly enhancing cross-day generalization. Extensive experimental results show that SSCDL delivers state-of-the-art decoding performance, exhibiting high robustness and cross-day stability. These capabilities underscore its strong potential for long-term interaction in human-centric robotic and fine-grained assistive applications.

AI.tldr: SSCDL is a self-supervised framework for brain-machine interfaces that uses consistency-enhanced disentangled learning to combat neural drift, achieving state-of-the-art cross-day generalization by separately modeling velocity, direction, and speed based on neural preference theory.
AI.motivation: Existing BMIs suffer from performance degradation over time due to neural drift. Current solutions fail to learn robust neural representations and overlook that neural drift affects different motor parameters (velocity, direction, speed) differently.
AI.method: Two innovations: (1) Consistency enhanced Neural Decoder (CND) using teacher-student consistency with simulated neural signal perturbations for robust representations; (2) Complementary-Disentangled Generalization (CDG) mechanism employing three dedicated CNDs to disentangle motor signals into velocity, direction, and speed, inspired by neural preference theory.
AI.result: State-of-the-art decoding performance with high robustness and cross-day stability.
AI.conclusion: SSCDL shows strong potential for long-term interaction in human-centric robotic and fine-grained assistive applications.

title: SILICA: Repurposing Diffusion Priors for Joint Glass Segmentation and Depth Estimation
comment: IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS), 2026
summary: Standard depth sensors systematically fail on transparent surfaces, creating corrupted 3D maps and severe navigation hazards. While specialized hardware sensors can detect glass, they lack modularity and have extensive hardware dependencies. Consequently, learning-based monocular depth estimation has emerged as a compelling alternative. However, domain-specific glass-aware monocular depth estimators struggle with unfamiliar indoor layouts; restricted by the severe scarcity of real-world glass depth annotations, they fail to generalize zero-shot to new settings. This motivates us to explore whether the extensive priors of text-to-image diffusion models can enable generalizable perception of transparent surfaces. We introduce SILICA, a unified pipeline leveraging these priors to jointly predict glass segmentation and glass-aware depth. This mutual information exchange establishes a robust spatial hierarchy, entirely eliminating the need for paired real-world glass depth annotations. Subsequently, we use the predicted segmentation mask to explicitly filter incorrect glass depth points from standard sensors, recovering accurate metric glass depth for downstream 3D mapping and autonomous collision avoidance. Supported by our novel Mirage 18k dataset, extensive experiments demonstrate that SILICA achieves remarkable zero-shot transfer across diverse, unseen environments, outperforming state-of-the-art models by almost 20% and setting a new benchmark for transparent surface perception.

AI.tldr: SILICA is a unified pipeline leveraging text-to-image diffusion priors to jointly predict glass segmentation and glass-aware depth, eliminating the need for real-world glass depth annotations and achieving state-of-the-art zero-shot generalization for transparent surface perception.
AI.motivation: Standard depth sensors fail on transparent surfaces; existing glass-aware monocular depth estimators suffer from scarce real-world annotations and poor zero-shot generalization to unfamiliar environments.
AI.method: SILICA leverages text-to-image diffusion model priors for joint glass segmentation and depth prediction, with mutual information exchange establishing spatial hierarchy, eliminating paired real-world glass depth annotations. Predicted segmentation masks filter incorrect depth points from standard sensors to recover accurate metric depth.
AI.result: SILICA achieves remarkable zero-shot transfer across diverse unseen environments, outperforming state-of-the-art models by almost 20%, supported by the novel Mirage 18k dataset.
AI.conclusion: Diffusion model priors enable generalizable perception of transparent surfaces without real-world glass depth annotations, setting a new benchmark for the task.

title: Context Is King: How In-Context Specification Shapes the Geometry of Concepts
summary: Large language models place structured concepts on geometrically faithful manifolds: weekdays lie on a circle, months on another, usually taken to be a fixed world-model the network stores and looks up. We show that context is king: the structure a model actually uses is set by the in-context specification. A declarative rule fixes not only which relations the geometry encodes but its topology type: the same tokens form a cycle or a branching tree on command, built even on arbitrary, meaning-free tokens with no prior to inherit, which a relabeled stored shape cannot do. When the specification conflicts with a strong pretrained prior, the context-set geometry dominates it in capable models, read from the same activations (representational similarity 0.6--0.9 to the imposed structure versus near-zero to the prior), across the priors we test and both families we study (Gemma, Qwen). Activation patching shows the map is causally used, not a probe correlate: swapping one entity's activation for another's makes the model answer with the other entity's successor under the imposed order. A rough map forms readily, present even in small and base models; what scale gates is using it cleanly: clean dominance and the causal crossover emerge only in the larger models (up to Gemma-31B and Qwen-27B) and weaken or reverse below, so a mechanism present in a large model can be absent in a smaller one of the same family. Whether the model builds this geometry anew or reconfigures a stored one we leave open; operationally, the geometry it uses is the one the context specifies.

AI.tldr: Large language models can dynamically construct geometric structures (cycles, trees) based on in-context specification, overriding pretrained priors, with this ability scaling with model size.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether LLMs' structured conceptual representations are fixed world-models or can be dynamically reconfigured by context.
AI.method: Declarative rules specify topological structures (cycles, branching trees) for tokens; tested across Gemma and Qwen families; used representational similarity analysis and activation patching to verify causal use.
AI.result: Context-specified geometry dominates pretrained priors (similarity 0.6-0.9 to imposed structure, near-zero to prior). Activation patching shows causal usage. Large models (Gemma-31B, Qwen-27B) show clean dominance; smaller models fail to use it cleanly.
AI.conclusion: LLMs dynamically construct geometric structures from context rather than relying solely on stored world-models; this capability scales with model size and is causally employed in reasoning.

title: A Cyclic Adaptation-Generalization Framework with Uncertainty-Guided Self-Paced Learning for Long-Term Brain-Machine Interfaces
summary: Brain-Machine Interfaces (BMIs), which link the brain to external devices, hold great potential in rehabilitation, human performance augmentation, and human-centered robotics. However, invasive BMIs face a critical challenge for long-term deployment due to neural drift, which degrades decoding performance over time and necessitates frequent recalibration. Existing methods designed to mitigate neural drift typically rely on either domain adaptation (DA) or domain generalization (DG) alone and often fail to capture fine-grained distribution shifts across neural subdomains, resulting in limited performance. To overcome these limitations, we propose Uncertainty-guided Self-paced Cycling (UnSPC), a robust framework that synergizes DA and DG for target domain refining under an Uncertainty-guided Self-paced Pseudo-labeling (UnSPL) mechanism. To handle subdomain neural drift across domains, UNSPL is proposed to iteratively mine reliable pseudo-labeled samples with a noise-robust ranking strategy for further fine-tuning. Leveraging these high-quality samples, we introduce a novel Cycling Adaptation and Generalization (CycAG) strategy, which integrates DA and DG within an iterative cycle to progressively mitigate both global and subdomain drift. This cyclic process enables effective alignment to evolving target distributions while preserving robust and transferable representations, thereby mitigating performance degradation under long-term neural drifts. Extensive experiments on multiple neural decoding datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of UnSPC. To our knowledge, our proposed UnSPC is the first to cyclically integrate DA and DG with pseudo-labeling, paving the way toward stable long-term BMI controls.

AI.tldr: UnSPC is a robust framework that synergizes domain adaptation and domain generalization with uncertainty-guided self-paced pseudo-labeling to mitigate neural drift in long-term Brain-Machine Interfaces, achieving superior performance on multiple neural decoding datasets.
AI.motivation: Invasive BMIs suffer from neural drift over long-term deployment, which degrades decoding performance and requires frequent recalibration. Existing DA or DG methods fail to capture fine-grained distribution shifts across neural subdomains.
AI.method: UnSPC proposes Uncertainty-guided Self-paced Pseudo-labeling (UnSPL) to iteratively mine reliable pseudo-labeled samples with noise-robust ranking, and a Cycling Adaptation and Generalization (CycAG) strategy that integrates DA and DG in an iterative cycle to address both global and subdomain neural drift.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on multiple neural decoding datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of UnSPC compared to existing methods.
AI.conclusion: UnSPC is the first framework to cyclically integrate DA and DG with pseudo-labeling, paving the way toward stable long-term BMI controls.

title: Superpixel-Based QUBO for Scalable Quantum-Enhanced Medical Image Segmentation
summary: Quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) has emerged as a powerful framework for medical computing problems. Binary decision variables naturally represent clinical choices, making QUBO formulations well-suited for quantum annealing hardware. However, a fundamental scalability challenge limits practical deployment: problem size grows rapidly with input dimensionality, creating computational bottlenecks that restrict applications to simplified scenarios. This paper addresses this challenge through hierarchical problem reduction, as demonstrated in medical image segmentation, where pixel-level QUBO formulations create over 65,000 variables for a 256x256 image, forcing existing approaches to downsample to 42x42 resolution and discard 97% of pixel information. A superpixel-based QUBO framework is proposed using simple linear iterative clustering (SLIC) to group pixels into perceptually meaningful regions, then formulate segmentation as QUBO over a region adjacency graph (RAG) combining min-cut and smoothness objectives. Validation on INbreast mammography breast cancer images demonstrates a 4.2% improvement in segmentation quality (mean IoU 0.76 vs 0.73) with 33 computational speedup (0.67s vs 21.97s) and a 97.3% reduction in problem size (1764 to 48 variables), all achieved while processing full-resolution images rather than downsampled versions. The reduced problem size also fits well within current quantum annealer connectivity limits, removing the embedding overhead that has historically blocked direct deployment of pixel-level QUBO segmentation on quantum hardware.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a superpixel-based QUBO framework using SLIC clustering and region adjacency graphs to overcome the scalability limitations of pixel-level QUBO formulations for medical image segmentation, achieving 4.2% better IoU, 33× speedup, and 97.3% problem size reduction on INbreast mammography images.
AI.motivation: QUBO formulations for medical image segmentation suffer from fundamental scalability issues—pixel-level formulations create over 65,000 variables for a 256×256 image, forcing downsampling to 42×42 resolution that discards 97% of pixel information and prevents deployment on quantum hardware due to connectivity constraints.
AI.method: The authors propose a hierarchical reduction approach using SLIC (simple linear iterative clustering) to group pixels into perceptually meaningful superpixels, then formulate segmentation as QUBO over a region adjacency graph (RAG) combining min-cut and smoothness objectives.
AI.result: Validation on INbreast mammography breast cancer images shows mean IoU of 0.76 (vs 0.73, +4.2%), computational speed of 0.67s (vs 21.97s, 33× faster), and problem size reduction from 1,764 to 48 variables (97.3% reduction), all while processing full-resolution images.
AI.conclusion: The reduced problem size fits within current quantum annealer connectivity limits, removing the embedding overhead that previously blocked direct deployment of pixel-level QUBO segmentation on quantum hardware, enabling practical quantum-amenable medical image segmentation.

title: DraftExpert: Expansion-Aware Self-Speculative Decoding for End-Device MoE Inference
summary: Large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models are attractive for end-device deployment because only a small subset of experts is active per token, but their routed expert weights often exceed accelerator memory. We target latency-critical single-user settings where routed experts are staged on demand from CPU memory to a GPU or from Flash to a mobile NPU. In this setting, self-speculative decoding faces a new bottleneck: increasing the draft expert set improves accuracy but triggers extra expert loading, while cheap small-footprint drafts have low acceptance; moreover, verifying a multi-token block activates the union of target experts and is no longer close to one target step. We propose DraftExpert, an expansion-aware self-speculative decoding framework for expert-offloaded MoE inference. DraftExpert trains one lightweight accelerator-resident draft expert per layer by self-distilling residual, logit/token, and router-agreement signals from the frozen target MoE. At inference time, it uses a fixed-footprint shared+top-1+draft-expert drafter together with confidence--expansion truncation and target-expert prefetching, while final tokens are still exactly verified by the target model. On DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Moonlight-16B-A3B across CPU-GPU and Flash-NPU offload, DraftExpert improves decode throughput by 1.45x on average, raises draft acceptance to 84~87%, and achieves 86~88% prefetch hit rates.

AI.tldr: DraftExpert is an expansion-aware self-speculative decoding framework for expert-offloaded MoE inference that trains lightweight accelerator-resident draft experts via self-distillation to improve throughput by 1.45x with 84-87% draft acceptance and 86-88% prefetch hit rates on CPU-GPU and Flash-NPU offload settings.
AI.motivation: Large MoE language models are attractive for end-device deployment due to per-token expert sparsity, but routed expert weights often exceed accelerator memory. In latency-critical single-user settings where experts are staged on demand from CPU/Flash, self-speculative decoding faces a new bottleneck: larger draft expert sets improve accuracy but trigger extra expert loading, while small-footprint drafts have low acceptance; multi-token verification activates the union of target experts and is no longer close to one target step.
AI.method: DraftExpert trains one lightweight accelerator-resident draft expert per layer via self-distillation of residual, logit/token, and router-agreement signals from the frozen target MoE. Inference uses a fixed-footprint shared+top-1+draft-expert drafter with confidence-expansion truncation and target-expert prefetching, while final tokens are exactly verified by the target model.
AI.result: On DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Moonlight-16B-A3B across CPU-GPU and Flash-NPU offload, DraftExpert improves decode throughput by 1.45x on average, raises draft acceptance to 84-87%, and achieves 86-88% prefetch hit rates.
AI.conclusion: DraftExpert effectively addresses the expert loading bottleneck in self-speculative decoding for expert-offloaded MoE inference, achieving significant throughput improvements with high draft acceptance and prefetch efficiency.

title: The Half-Lives of Generative-AI Evidence: A 40-Record Audit, a Claim-Currency Framework, and a Reflexive Case of Frontier-Model-Assisted Research
comment: 20 pages, 6 tables, 1 figure, 1 appendix. Ancillary file corpus_coding.csv contains the record-level coding. Data cutoff: 17 July 2026; submission-stage frontier note: 27 July 2026
summary: Generative-AI evaluations can become historical before publication, yet calendar age does not affect every conclusion equally. This paper has two linked purposes. First, it audits a maximum-variation purposive corpus of 40 empirical records appearing between 18 July 2025 and 17 July 2026. The audit coded publication route, execution timing, model identity, age of the newest named generation or immutable snapshot, same-family supersession and refresh behaviour. At appearance, the newest named model was a median 281 days old (middle 50%: 75-478; range: 11-939). Median age was 395 days for 25 journal articles, 56 days for 14 preprints and 49 days for one laboratory report. Thirty-five records included a superseded family, seven supplied a precise dated identifier, three clearly refreshed model evidence, and one added a late sensitivity test. All 40 included an OpenAI system, a feature of this corpus rather than a prevalence estimate. The paper distinguishes model age from claim currency and proposes six reporting practices. Second, it treats its own two-day production process as a reflexive case of frontier-model-assisted research creation. GPT-5.6 Sol Pro in ChatGPT supported candidate discovery, source reconciliation, calculations, drafting and critique; the author checked sources, made all substantive decisions and accepts responsibility. This is a proof-of-practice, not a controlled estimate of productivity or quality. By applying its own Model Facts and model-currency statement, the paper shows how rapid AI-assisted research can be made inspectable without treating model output as independent validation. The title uses half-lives metaphorically; no universal decay rate is estimated.

AI.tldr: This paper audits 40 Gen-AI evaluation papers (July 2025–July 2026), finding the newest named model a median 281 days old at publication. It proposes six reporting practices for model currency and reflexively demonstrates AI-assisted research production (GPT-5.6 Sol Pro) over two days, advocating inspectability without treating model output as independent validation.
AI.motivation: Generative-AI evaluations rapidly become outdated (aging before publication), yet calendar age does not uniformly affect all conclusions. The paper aims to quantify this temporal gap and propose practices to improve transparency regarding model currency.
AI.method: Maximum-variation purposive audit of 40 empirical records (18 July 2025–17 July 2026), coding publication route, execution timing, model identity, age of newest named model/frozen snapshot, supersession, and refresh behavior. Also includes a reflexive case using GPT-5.6 Sol Pro for candidate discovery, source reconciliation, calculations, drafting, and critique over two days.
AI.result: At appearance, newest named model median age = 281 days (middle 50%: 75–478; range 11–939). Journal articles: median 395 days (n=25); preprints: 56 days (n=14); lab report: 49 days (n=1). 35 records had superseded family; 7 gave precise dated identifier; 3 clearly refreshed model evidence; 1 added late sensitivity test. All 40 included an OpenAI system (corpus feature, not prevalence estimate).
AI.conclusion: The paper distinguishes model age from claim currency, proposes six reporting practices, and demonstrates that rapid AI-assisted research can be made inspectable via its own Model Facts and model-currency statement, without treating model output as independent validation.

title: UMI3D: Robust 3D Generation on Unconstrained Multi-Image Inputs via Simultaneous Focus Cross-Attention Routing
summary: Recent 3D foundation models can generate high-quality assets from a single image, but degrade markedly on unconstrained multi-image inputs, often producing distorted geometry, over-smoothed textures, and chaotic colors. We argue that this failure stems not from limited model capacity, but from a mismatch between single-image cross-attention and the multi-image setting: existing models lack a principled way to decide which image each 3D voxel should trust at each denoising step. Revisiting recent single-image 3D foundation models, we show that explicitly routing each voxel to its most informative image is sufficient to unlock strong performance on inconsistent multi-image inputs. Based on this observation, we propose UMI3D, a training-free and plug-and-play framework that restructures cross-attention for unconstrained multi-image 3D generation. Its core, Simultaneous Focus Cross-Attention (SFC-Attn), activates all conditioning images at each denoising step while allowing each voxel to focus on the single image that best explains it. To enable this routing, we derive the Voxel Reference Score (VRS), a model-intrinsic metric for voxel--image affinity that requires no external matching, segmentation, or correspondence models. Extensive experiments show that UMI3D unlocks the multi-image potential of single-image 3D generation frameworks across diverse tasks. Project Page: UMI3D-Project.github.io.

AI.tldr: UMI3D is a training-free, plug-and-play framework that restructures cross-attention to enable single-image 3D foundation models to handle unconstrained multi-image inputs, using Simultaneous Focus Cross-Attention (SFC-Attn) and Voxel Reference Score (VRS) to route each voxel to its most informative image.
AI.motivation: Existing single-image 3D foundation models fail on unconstrained multi-image inputs, producing distorted geometry, over-smoothed textures, and chaotic colors. The authors argue this is due to a mismatch between single-image cross-attention and the multi-image setting — models lack a principled way to decide which image each 3D voxel should trust.
AI.method: Proposes UMI3D, a training-free framework with Simultaneous Focus Cross-Attention (SFC-Attn) that activates all conditioning images at each denoising step while letting each voxel focus on the single best-matching image. Routing is achieved via Voxel Reference Score (VRS), a model-intrinsic voxel-image affinity metric requiring no external models.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show UMI3D unlocks multi-image potential of single-image 3D generation frameworks across diverse tasks, significantly improving quality over unmodified baselines on multi-image inputs.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly routing each voxel to its most informative image is sufficient to enable strong performance on inconsistent multi-image inputs, without requiring training or external correspondence models.

title: What do Reward Models Memorize?
summary: This paper studies what discriminatively trained reward models (RMs) memorize by measuring counterfactual memorization on two human preference datasets. We show that RMs 1) misallocate memorization to easy, high margin preference pairs, 2) memorize dataset-specific shortcuts (e.g., model identity, user sampling strategy), and 3) overgeneralize simple heuristic correlates of human preference (e.g., length, compliance) when confronted with unseen preference pairs.
