Overall, our findings indicate that discriminative training of RMs from human preference data results in biased RMs not yet capable of judging response quality in context-dependent scenarios.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates memorization in discriminatively trained reward models (RMs) for human preference data, finding three key issues: misallocation of memorization to easy preference pairs, memorization of dataset-specific shortcuts (like model identity and sampling strategies), and overgeneralization of simple heuristics (like length and compliance) when encountering unseen preference pairs. These biases prevent RMs from accurately judging response quality in context-dependent scenarios.
AI.motivation: To understand what reward models memorize from human preference datasets and whether this memorization leads to biased judgments of response quality.
AI.method: The authors measure counterfactual memorization on two human preference datasets to analyze what discriminatively trained reward models memorize.
AI.result: RMs misallocate memorization to easy, high-margin preference pairs; memorize dataset-specific shortcuts such as model identity and user sampling strategy; and overgeneralize simple heuristic correlates like length and compliance when faced with unseen preference pairs.
AI.conclusion: Discriminative training of RMs from human preference data results in biased reward models that are not yet capable of judging response quality in context-dependent scenarios.

title: Quantum-Inspired Evolutionary Neighborhood Search for Arrival-Departure Track Utilization Adjustment under Short-Term Disturbances
summary: Short-term disturbances at major passenger railway stations alter train arrival and departure times as well as the release sequence of station resources. Effective recovery therefore requires coordinated adjustment of arrival-departure track allocation, station resource occupation, and train retiming. This study represents the station resources involved in train arrival, track occupancy, and departure operations as zone-level resource-occupation intervals. An arrival-departure track allocation adjustment model is formulated. Resource compatibility is imposed as the feasibility condition, while train delays and resource reassignment costs are jointly considered. A quantum-inspired evolutionary algorithm combined with neighborhood search (QEA-NS) is proposed to solve the model. Perturbation instances are constructed using GTFS timetable data from Frankfurt Hauptbahnhof, Germany. QEA-NS is compared with CP-SAT under the same candidate resource set and feasibility criteria. Both methods generate solutions satisfying the modeled resource compatibility constraints. QEA-NS yields a total delay of 388 min, compared with 519 min for CP-SAT, representing a reduction of 25.2\%. The mean delay of delayed trains decreases from 4.99 to 3.73 min, although QEA-NS requires a longer solution time. Across 10 random perturbation instances, QEA-NS achieves lower total delay in every case. Its mean total delay and standard deviation are 390.5 min and 35.945 min, respectively, compared with 673.8 min and 105.739 min for CP-SAT. The results indicate that, under the adopted resource representation and constraints, QEA-NS improves the delay performance of recovery plans. Its computational efficiency, however, requires further improvement.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a quantum-inspired evolutionary algorithm with neighborhood search (QEA-NS) to coordinate arrival-departure track allocation, station resource occupation, and train retiming at major passenger railway stations after short-term disruptions. Using GTFS data from Frankfurt Hauptbahnhof, QEA-NS reduces total delay by 25.2% compared to CP-SAT (388 min vs 519 min) and achieves lower delays across all 10 random perturbation instances, though with longer computation time.
AI.motivation: Short-term disturbances at major passenger railway stations disrupt train schedules and resource release sequences, requiring coordinated recovery of track allocation and resource occupation. Existing methods lack effective joint optimization of these interdependent decisions.
AI.method: Station resources are modeled as zone-level resource-occupation intervals. An arrival-departure track allocation adjustment model is formulated with resource compatibility constraints and a joint objective of minimizing train delays and resource reassignment costs. A quantum-inspired evolutionary algorithm combined with neighborhood search (QEA-NS) is proposed and compared against CP-SAT using GTFS timetable data from Frankfurt Hauptbahnhof, Germany.
AI.result: QEA-NS yields 388 min total delay vs 519 min for CP-SAT (25.2% reduction). Mean delay of delayed trains drops from 4.99 to 3.73 min. Across 10 random instances, QEA-NS achieves lower total delay in every case (mean 390.5 min, std 35.945 min) vs CP-SAT (mean 673.8 min, std 105.739 min). QEA-NS requires longer solution time.
AI.conclusion: Under the adopted resource representation and constraints, QEA-NS improves delay performance of recovery plans compared to CP-SAT, though its computational efficiency requires further improvement.

title: Multiview Multi-Person Human Mesh Recovery Under Large Scenes with Occlusions
summary: Human mesh recovery (HMR) aims to recover 3D human meshes from images. Most existing HMR benchmarks and methods focus on either multi-person reconstruction from a single view or single-person reconstruction from multiple views, where the number of subjects and the scene scale are relatively limited. Such settings are insufficient for real-world applications with large scenes and severe inter-person occlusions. To address this limitation, we introduce a large-scale synthetic benchmark for multiview multi-person HMR, termed MVMP-HMR. The proposed dataset contains 15 complex scenes with up to 50 camera views and 30 interacting persons, featuring large spatial coverage and severe occlusions, which significantly increases the difficulty of human mesh recovery. Based on this benchmark, we further propose a multiview multi-person whole-body human mesh recovery model, referred to as MVMP-HMR model. The model first fuses multiview features into a scene-level 3D feature volume, and then leverages pelvis joints predicted by a 3D pose estimation network to extract person-specific queries from the 3D feature volume. These human queries are cross-attended with the 3D feature volume and integrated to decode each person's 3D mesh. Moreover, we introduce two novel losses--the orientation loss and the 3D joint density loss--to alleviate orientation and pose ambiguities under severe occlusions. Experiments demonstrate that existing state-of-the-art HMR methods struggle on the proposed MVMP-HMR benchmark, while our method consistently outperforms prior SOTAs in large-scale scenes with severe occlusions.

AI.tldr: MVMP-HMR introduces a large-scale synthetic benchmark for multiview multi-person human mesh recovery with up to 50 cameras and 30 interacting persons, along with a novel model that fuses multiview features into 3D volumes and uses pelvis-guided queries to decode meshes, outperforming prior methods under severe occlusions.
AI.motivation: Existing HMR benchmarks are limited to either multi-person single-view or single-person multi-view settings with small scenes and limited occlusions, insufficient for real-world large-scale applications with heavy inter-person occlusions.
AI.method: The model fuses multiview features into a scene-level 3D feature volume, uses pelvis joints from a 3D pose estimator to extract person-specific queries, cross-attends queries with the 3D volume, and decodes per-person meshes. Two novel losses (orientation loss and 3D joint density loss) are introduced to resolve ambiguities under occlusion.
AI.result: Existing SOTA HMR methods fail on the MVMP-HMR benchmark, while the proposed method consistently outperforms prior SOTAs in large-scale scenes with severe occlusions.
AI.conclusion: Scaling multiview and multi-person settings is crucial for real-world HMR; the proposed benchmark and model advance the field by addressing large-scale occluded scenarios.

title: UNIFUSION: Adapting Autoregressive Language Models into Discrete Diffusion under a Unified Reverse-Rate Objective
summary: Existing methods mainly adapt pretrained autoregressive (AR) language models to masked diffusion, whereas we directly adapt them to uniform-noise diffusion, where every token remains editable during sampling. However, adapting AR checkpoints across corruption kernels remains challenging because existing DLMs use different objectives and prediction parameterizations. We establish connections among SEDD, MDLM/GIDD, M2S, and Neural CTMC by expressing their conditional losses as a single generalized Kullback--Leibler objective over model reverse rates. We further derive conversions from clean-token predictions to concrete-score, posterior-mean, and exit-rate/jump parameterizations, yielding a shared \(x_0\) interface that supports switching between mask and uniform kernels. Building on these connections, we propose \ours{}, a simple continual pre-training approach for directly adapting pretrained GPT2 checkpoints to uniform-noise diffusion. Through systematic evaluation of 124M- and 355M-parameter models, we show that \ours{} steadily improves the trade-off between generative perplexity (GenPPL) and unigram entropy as the sampling budget increases from 16 to 256 steps. At 256 steps, \ours{}-S and \ours{}-M achieve GenPPL/entropy pairs of \(97.783/5.2626\) and \(71.516/5.6669\), respectively; no evaluated model at the same scale simultaneously outperforms \ours{} on both metrics. At both scales, \ours{} also achieves the highest WinoGrande, SIQA, and BBH accuracy among the compared diffusion models.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a method to adapt pretrained autoregressive language models (GPT-2) to uniform-noise diffusion models by establishing theoretical connections between various diffusion loss functions and parameterizations, enabling a shared interface for switching between mask and uniform kernels. Their approach, called Ours, improves the trade-off between generative perplexity and unigram entropy across sampling budgets, and achieves strong performance on downstream benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion language models (DLMs) are adapted from pretrained AR models only to masked diffusion, not uniform-noise diffusion, due to differences in objectives and prediction parameterizations across corruption kernels. The authors aim to enable direct adaptation to uniform-noise diffusion where every token remains editable during sampling.
AI.method: 1) Establishes theoretical connections among SEDD, MDLM/GIDD, M2S, and Neural CTMC by expressing their conditional losses as a single generalized KL objective over model reverse rates. 2) Derives conversions from clean-token predictions to concrete-score, posterior-mean, and exit-rate/jump parameterizations, yielding a shared x₀ interface supporting switching between mask and uniform kernels. 3) Proposes a continual pre-training approach (Ours) to directly adapt pretrained GPT-2 checkpoints to uniform-noise diffusion.
AI.result: At 256 sampling steps, Ours-S and Ours-M achieve GenPPL/entropy pairs of 97.783/5.2626 and 71.516/5.6669 respectively, outperforming all compared models at the same scale on both metrics. The approach also achieves the highest WinoGrande, SIQA, and BBH accuracy among compared diffusion models at both 124M and 355M scales.
AI.conclusion: The proposed continual pre-training approach successfully adapts pretrained AR checkpoints to uniform-noise diffusion, achieving better trade-offs between generative perplexity and sampling diversity, along with stronger downstream task performance compared to existing diffusion language models.

title: Success Is Not Self-Explanatory: Auditing Success Provenance in Agent Evaluation
comment: 17 pages, 3 figures, including supplementary material. Code: https://github.com/luojingkun22/acquabench
summary: A correct answer can conceal why an agent succeeded. Once agents change their information state during evaluation, correctness no longer distinguishes intended reasoning from answer acquisition. Outcome evidence and exposure detection do not establish whether success depended on an acquired target; we call this missing evaluation object success provenance. AcquaBench audits it through matched CLEAN, GOLD, and SHAM value substitution on four standardized surfaces with joint qid-clustered analysis. CLEAN retains benchmark-authorized information. GOLD makes the correct target available. SHAM preserves source structure and exposure opportunity but substitutes a matched incorrect value. GOLD minus CLEAN measures the total score response to correct-target availability; GOLD minus SHAM tests whether that response tracks target correctness beyond matched source exposure. In D0, GOLD exceeds SHAM by 19.1 to 25.9 percentage points, showing that success follows the correct value. In D2, GOLD still exceeds SHAM under distributed sufficiency while coloc no longer transfers as a high-score marker, with AUROC 0.376 and 0.142. Behavioral dependence can thus persist beyond this probe's intended observation unit. In model comparison, a supported 5.0-point CLEAN score gap compresses to a raw GOLD difference of -0.6 points without establishing rank inversion. Agent benchmarks should report success together with whether the evaluated information state supported it.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces AcquaBench, an audit framework that distinguishes genuine reasoning from answer acquisition by measuring whether agent success depends on access to the correct target value (via GOLD, CLEAN, and SHAM substitutions). Results show models often succeed based on correct-target availability rather than intended reasoning, with behavioral dependence persisting even when superficial cues are removed. The paper argues benchmarks should report both correctness and information-state provenance.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation methods fail to distinguish genuine reasoning from answer acquisition because correctness alone does not indicate whether an agent's success depended on acquiring the correct target value. Outcome evidence and exposure detection lack "success provenance" — they cannot establish whether success relied on an acquired target.
AI.method: AcquaBench audits success provenance through matched CLEAN, GOLD, and SHAM value substitutions across four standardized surfaces with joint qid-clustered analysis. CLEAN retains benchmark-authorized information, GOLD makes the correct target available, and SHAM substitutes a matched incorrect value while preserving source structure and exposure. Metrics include GOLD-CLEAN (response to correct-target availability) and GOLD-SHAM (distinguishing target correctness from source exposure).
AI.result: In D0, GOLD exceeds SHAM by 19.1-25.9 percentage points, indicating success follows the correct value. In D2, GOLD still exceeds SHAM under distributed sufficiency while coloc no longer transfers as a high-score marker (AUROC 0.376 and 0.142), showing behavioral dependence persists beyond the probe's intended observation unit. A supported 5.0-point CLEAN score gap compresses to a raw GOLD difference of -0.6 points without rank inversion.
AI.conclusion: Agent benchmarks should report success together with whether the evaluated information state supported it, as behavioral dependence on correct-target availability can persist even when superficial cues are removed.

title: PRISM: Prompt Refinement via Image-grounded Self-rewarding Mechanism for Text-to-Image Generation
summary: Text-to-image generation models can synthesize high-quality images from natural language descriptions, but their performance remains highly sensitive to prompt formulation. Existing prompt optimization methods mainly rely on text-side rewriting, prompt expansion, or external reward signals, offering limited image-grounded diagnosis and weak support for learning reusable optimisation policies. In this paper, we propose PRISM, a Prompt Refinement framework via Image-grounded Self-rewarding Mechanism. PRISM closes the prompt-image-feedback loop by interpreting generated images with structured visual diagnosis and scoring them along semantic consistency, aesthetic quality, and human preference alignment. It first initializes a unified VLM through multi-task supervised fine-tuning, and then improves the prompt policy via self-rewarding optimization with a hybrid ideal-point and Chebyshev reward. Extensive experiments show that PRISM improves holistic image quality and fine-grained semantic alignment, while providing interpretable feedback for targeted prompt refinement. The code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/PRISM-FF81.

AI.tldr: PRISM is a prompt refinement framework for text-to-image generation that uses image-grounded self-rewarding—interpreting generated images via a VLM to score semantic consistency, aesthetics, and human preference—and then optimizes prompts via self-rewarding with hybrid ideal-point/Chebyshev reward, improving image quality and alignment.
AI.motivation: Existing prompt optimization methods rely on text-side rewriting, prompt expansion, or external reward signals, offering limited image-grounded diagnosis and weak support for learning reusable optimization policies.
AI.method: PRISM closes the prompt-image-feedback loop by (1) interpreting generated images with structured visual diagnosis via a VLM fine-tuned with multi-task supervised fine-tuning, (2) scoring along three dimensions (semantic consistency, aesthetic quality, human preference alignment), and (3) improving the prompt policy via self-rewarding optimization using a hybrid ideal-point and Chebyshev reward.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show that PRISM improves holistic image quality and fine-grained semantic alignment, while providing interpretable feedback for targeted prompt refinement.
AI.conclusion: The closed-loop self-rewarding framework effectively bridges prompt and image evaluation, enabling reusable and interpretable prompt optimization for text-to-image generation.

title: Physics Transformer: Tailoring Transformer for General PDE Prediction
summary: Transformer architectures have attracted increasing attention for solving partial differential equations (PDEs), owing to their flexibility in handling irregular discretizations and their ability to capture long-range physical dependencies. However, unlike discrete language tokens or fixed-resolution image patches, observed physical fields are finite samples of underlying infinite-dimensional functions. Consequently, effectively applying Transformers to PDEs requires a tokenizer that respects the functional nature of physical fields and constructs physically expressive tokens from arbitrary discretizations.To this end, we propose \methodname{Physics Transformer}, a function-projection-based Transformer architecture for physical field prediction. Physics Transformer treats a physical field as a continuous function and partitions its discretization into locality-preserving spatial patches. Within each patch, it dynamically learns a set of adaptive local basis functions and projects the sampled field onto these bases to obtain compact physics tokens. The resulting tokens capture diverse latent physical states while preserving fine-scale spatial structures, enabling efficient global interaction through factorized attention across space and physical states. The projected representation further supports efficient decoding at arbitrary query locations. Extensive experiments on diverse benchmarks, ranging from two-dimensional PDE dynamics to industrial-scale three-dimensional CFD simulations, demonstrate that Physics Transformer accurately captures fine-grained physical structures and achieves state-of-the-art predictive performance. These results establish function projection as a practical and effective foundation for designing Transformer architectures for PDE solving.

AI.tldr: Physics Transformer proposes a function-projection-based tokenizer that treats physical fields as continuous functions, learns adaptive local basis functions per spatial patch, and projects sampled fields onto these bases to create compact physics tokens. It achieves SOTA predictive performance on PDE benchmarks from 2D dynamics to industrial 3D CFD simulations.
AI.motivation: Existing Transformer architectures for PDEs struggle because physical fields are finite samples of infinite-dimensional functions, unlike discrete tokens or fixed-resolution images. A tokenizer that respects the functional nature of physical fields and constructs physically expressive tokens from arbitrary discretizations is needed.
AI.method: Treats physical fields as continuous functions, partitions discretization into locality-preserving spatial patches, dynamically learns adaptive local basis functions per patch, projects sampled fields onto these bases to obtain compact physics tokens, then applies factorized attention across space and physical states for efficient global interaction, with decoding at arbitrary query locations.
AI.result: Experiments on 2D PDE dynamics and industrial-scale 3D CFD simulations show Physics Transformer accurately captures fine-grained physical structures and achieves state-of-the-art predictive performance.
AI.conclusion: Function projection is established as a practical and effective foundation for designing Transformer architectures for PDE solving.

title: The Cost of Knowing: A Resource-Aware Protocol for Benchmarking Hallucination Beyond Static Leaderboards
summary: On standard factuality tasks, frontier models now cluster near the top of the scale. The question is therefore shifting from how factual a system is toward how much compute that factuality costs. Static leaderboards score factuality in isolation and treat compute as free, so they cannot tell a genuinely better system apart from one that simply spends more. Consider a ranking reversal. A brute-force Best-of-4 agent posts the higher raw factuality score (H-Score 0.9169 vs 0.9103) and would top a static leaderboard, but once cost is counted it is the worse system, losing on Q-Score (0.5169 vs 0.5217) at roughly four times the tokens and latency, under a reported cost weight whose sensitivity we sweep. So the system that tops a static leaderboard can be the worse one to deploy. To make this trade-off visible, we introduce MAS-HQ (Multi-Agent System Hallucination Quest), a resource-aware evaluation protocol. It wraps any factuality detector and normalizes for cost, and it pits systems against each other rather than scoring them in isolation. The Q-Score measures factuality minus normalized cost under a competitive match. Across summarization and open-domain QA, single-agent baselines drift into resource-heavy over-optimization, while competition elicits more resource-efficient policies. These gains are small but consistent, and stable across 100 trials. The axis stays discriminative for frontier systems (Gemini-2.5-Pro, and GPT-5 in simulated preview) whose raw factuality scores are already bunched near the ceiling. MAS-HQ provides a reproducible way to measure how much a factual answer costs.

AI.tldr: MAS-HQ is a resource-aware evaluation protocol that measures factuality normalized by computational cost, revealing that systems topping static leaderboards (e.g., Best-of-4) can be worse to deploy than cheaper alternatives when cost is factored in via competitive matches and the Q-Score metric.
AI.motivation: Frontier models cluster near the top on standard factuality benchmarks, shifting the question from "how factual" to "at what cost." Static leaderboards ignore compute cost and cannot distinguish genuinely better systems from those that simply spend more resources.
AI.method: MAS-HQ wraps any factuality detector, normalizes for cost, and pits systems against each other in competitive matches. It uses Q-Score (factuality minus normalized cost) and sweeps over a cost-weight sensitivity parameter.
AI.result: A Best-of-4 agent achieves higher raw H-Score (0.9169 vs 0.9103) but loses on Q-Score (0.5169 vs 0.5217) at ~4x tokens and latency. Single-agent baselines over-optimize resources, while competition elicits more efficient policies. Gains are small, consistent across 100 trials, and discriminative even for frontier models (Gemini-2.5-Pro, GPT-5 simulated).
AI.conclusion: MAS-HQ provides a reproducible, resource-aware evaluation paradigm that reveals cost-factuality trade-offs hidden by static leaderboards, and remains discriminative for frontier systems with bunched raw scores.

title: TaoMate: Anchor-Guided Memory Bridging Evolving and Reference States for Real-Time Audio-Video Digital Human Generation
summary: Real-time long-form digital-human generation relies on causal models to extend audio-visual content while preserving subject appearance and audio-video synchronization across successive segments. A bounded cache retains local motion and phonetic context but discards older evidence, whereas attending to the complete generated history is computationally expensive and can propagate accumulated errors. We present \method, an anchor-guided persistent-memory framework for few-step joint audio-video generation. The framework preserves an immutable visual anchor, compresses completed video and audio blocks into fixed-capacity dynamic states, and retrieves those states through modality-specific residual attention without extending the active cache. A reference-aware modulation method additionally conditions video features on dynamic and anchor appearance statistics. Anchor-preserving causal-context distillation varies rollout horizon, prefix provenance, and cache-history reliability while keeping the immutable visual anchor unperturbed. By separating persistent memory from stage-local denoising dependencies, \method further admits stage-parallel execution across blocks, accelerating autoregressive inference without pipeline-specific retraining. We evaluate long-form video continuations with appearance, temporal, synchronization, facial, and speech diagnostics. Results show that \method preserves stable appearance across prompt-conditioned segments and strong audio-visual synchronization under autoregressive generation. Our project page is https://taoliveaigc.github.io/TaoMate.

AI.tldr: TaoMate is an anchor-guided persistent-memory framework for real-time long-form digital-human generation that uses immutable visual anchors, compressed dynamic states, and modality-specific residual attention to achieve stable appearance and audio-visual synchronization across autoregressive segments, while enabling stage-parallel execution for accelerated inference.
AI.motivation: Real-time long-form digital-human generation requires causal models to extend audio-visual content while preserving subject appearance and synchronization. Existing approaches face a dilemma: bounded caches lose older evidence, while attending to the full history is computationally expensive and propagates accumulated errors.
AI.method: The framework (1) preserves an immutable visual anchor, (2) compresses completed video/audio blocks into fixed-capacity dynamic states, (3) retrieves states via modality-specific residual attention without extending the active cache, (4) uses reference-aware modulation to condition video features on dynamic and anchor appearance statistics, (5) employs anchor-preserving causal-context distillation, and (6) separates persistent memory from stage-local denoising to admit stage-parallel execution.
AI.result: The method preserves stable appearance across prompt-conditioned segments and strong audio-visual synchronization under autoregressive generation, as evaluated on long-form video continuations with appearance, temporal, synchronization, facial, and speech diagnostics.
AI.conclusion: TaoMate effectively addresses the memory-efficiency trade-off in long-form digital-human generation by introducing persistent memory with immutable anchors and parallel execution, achieving stable appearance and synchronization without full-history attention costs.

title: Low-Rank Dependence Decomposition via Accelerated Symmetric Non-negative Matrix Factorization
summary: Symmetric non-negative matrix factorization (SymNMF) recovers latent group structure from a dependence matrix, but its dense, quadratic-memory objective has confined prior work to moderate sizes. We present a large-scale GPU study of seven algorithm families (over 30 configurations) on absolute Pearson correlation and tail pairwise dependence matrices from Extreme Value Theory, two proxies for empirical risk-factor estimation on large portfolios. A trace-identity reformulation eliminates all $n \times n$ intermediates, so a single GPU reaches $n \approx 10^5$ and multi-node distribution scales to $n = 10^6$ and beyond. Under a two-phase protocol, eleven methods converge at moderate scale; six remain efficient enough at $n = 10^5$ (five AdaGrad-family plus ADMM), and five AdaGrad-family methods still converge at $n = 10^6$: AdaGrad, RMSprop, and three we introduce (Piecewise AdaGrad, Row-Stochastic SVRG, Block-SVRG AdaptGrow). At $n = 10^6$ the fastest solver tracks the matrix spectrum: Block-SVRG AdaptGrow wins on the flat, ill-conditioned tail-dependence spectrum, where its lower per-iteration cost decides a long factorization, and full-batch AdaGrad wins on the dominant-low-rank correlation spectrum, where the run is short. We also benchmark spherical K-means as a hard-label baseline: cheaper when angular cluster structure is present, yet provably degenerate once the matrix collapses toward a single common factor, where the soft factorization remains necessary.

AI.tldr: This paper scales Symmetric NMF to large matrices (n=10^5–10^6) on GPUs via a trace-identity reformulation that eliminates quadratic memory, evaluating seven algorithm families (30+ configs) on two risk-factor proxies. AdaGrad-family methods dominate at scale, with Block-SVRG AdaptGrow best for ill-conditioned spectra and full-batch AdaGrad best for dominant-low-rank spectra.
AI.motivation: Prior SymNMF work was limited to moderate sizes due to dense, quadratic-memory objective. The authors aim to scale SymNMF to large portfolios (n≈10^5–10^6) for empirical risk-factor estimation.
AI.method: A trace-identity reformulation eliminates all n×n intermediates, enabling single-GPU n≈10^5 and multi-node distribution to n=10^6. Seven algorithm families (over 30 configurations) are evaluated: AdaGrad, RMSprop, Piecewise AdaGrad, Row-Stochastic SVRG, Block-SVRG AdaptGrow, ADMM, and spherical K-means baseline.
AI.result: Eleven methods converge at moderate scale; six remain efficient at n=10^5 (five AdaGrad-family + ADMM); five AdaGrad-family methods converge at n=10^6. Block-SVRG AdaptGrow wins on flat ill-conditioned tail-dependence spectra; full-batch AdaGrad wins on dominant-low-rank correlation spectra. Spherical K-means is cheaper but degenerate under single-factor collapse.
AI.conclusion: SymNMF can be scaled to n=10^6 via memory-efficient reformulation and GPU distribution. Algorithm choice depends on spectral structure: AdaGrad variants for dominant-low-rank, SVRG-style for ill-conditioned. Soft factorization remains necessary when matrix lacks angular cluster structure.

title: MiSS: A Logic-Driven Explanation of Minimal Sufficient Coalitions for Point Cloud Classifiers
summary: We present MiSS, a black-box, query-based framework for explaining 3D point cloud classifiers through perturbation-relative sufficiency reasoning. MiSS treats a superpoint partition as an interpretable abstraction layer and asks whether the original prediction can be certified from a minimal coalition of geometric regions under a specified perturbation distribution. Unlike abductive explainers that require Boolean feature spaces or white-box logical encodings of the predictor, MiSS separates candidate proposal from verification: a weighted MaxSAT procedure proposes coalitions using a heuristic adaptive cardinality floor, certified exact-size fallback, a safely tightened upper bound, blocking clauses, and a surrogate acquisition heuristic learned from previous oracle evaluations, while a blackbox statistical oracle decides sufficiency from prediction queries. The system returns a statistically verified sufficient coalition as a binary attribution, with minimum cardinality guaranteed when certified search completes. Experiments on ModelNet40 and ShapeNet with PointNet and PointMLP classifiers show higher precision and coverage than rule-based baselines in most settings, with lower explanation time than exhaustive search.

AI.tldr: MiSS is a black-box, query-based framework that explains 3D point cloud classifiers by finding minimal sufficient coalitions of superpoint regions via a weighted MaxSAT proposer and a statistical oracle, achieving higher precision and coverage with lower computational cost than baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing explainability methods for 3D point cloud classifiers require white-box access, Boolean feature spaces, or logical encodings of the predictor, which limits their applicability to black-box models. There is a need for a perturbation-robust, query-based explanation framework that can certify sufficiency from geometric regions without internal model access.
AI.method: MiSS uses superpoint partitions as interpretable units, then separates candidate proposal (via weighted MaxSAT with heuristic adaptive cardinality floor, certified exact-size fallback, safely tightened upper bound, blocking clauses, and surrogate acquisition heuristic) from verification (via a black-box statistical oracle that queries the classifier under a specified perturbation distribution).
AI.result: On ModelNet40 and ShapeNet with PointNet and PointMLP classifiers, MiSS achieves higher precision and coverage than rule-based baselines in most settings, with lower explanation time than exhaustive search.
AI.conclusion: MiSS provides a practical black-box approach for certifying sufficient explanations in 3D point cloud classifiers, with statistical guarantees on sufficiency and, when certified search completes, minimum cardinality.

title: HistoGPA: A Context-Conditioned Gene-Prior Attention Framework for Histology-Based Spatial Gene Expression Prediction
summary: Predicting spatial gene expression from routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) images provides a practical complement to experimental spatial transcriptomics. Existing approaches focus on local or multi-scale visual features and often treat pretrained gene representations as fixed priors, although the interpretation of local morphology and the relevance of gene priors depend on tissue context. We propose HistoGPA, a context-conditioned gene-prior attention framework that uses a shared slide-level representation in two parallel pathways: one modulates local morphological features, whereas the other conditions pretrained gene embeddings and retrieves gene-prior information through cross-attention. This design enables each spatial location to retrieve context-adapted gene-prior information using its local morphology, position, and slide context. Across ten cancer types in HEST-1k, HistoGPA achieves the highest macro-averaged gene-wise Pearson correlation coefficient among the compared methods under the same evaluation protocol for both the top-50 and top-1,500 highly variable gene sets. Additional analyses show that HistoGPA better recovers the spatial expression patterns of cancer-associated genes and yields greater agreement between clusters derived independently from predicted and ground-truth expression profiles. Together, these findings motivate a context-dependent view of histology-to-expression prediction, in which local morphological representations and gene priors are jointly adapted to the broader tissue context.

AI.tldr: HistoGPA is a context-conditioned gene-prior attention framework that predicts spatial gene expression from H&E images by jointly adapting local morphological features and pretrained gene embeddings to the slide-level tissue context, achieving state-of-the-art results across ten cancer types in HEST-1k.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches for predicting spatial gene expression from H&E images treat local visual features and pretrained gene representations as fixed priors, ignoring that the interpretation of local morphology and relevance of gene priors depend on broader tissue context.
AI.method: HistoGPA uses a shared slide-level representation in two parallel pathways: one modulates local morphological features, while the other conditions pretrained gene embeddings and retrieves gene-prior information through cross-attention, enabling each spatial location to retrieve context-adapted gene-prior information using its local morphology, position, and slide context.
AI.result: Across ten cancer types in HEST-1k, HistoGPA achieves the highest macro-averaged gene-wise Pearson correlation coefficient among compared methods for both top-50 and top-1,500 highly variable gene sets, better recovers spatial expression patterns of cancer-associated genes, and yields greater agreement between clusters from predicted and ground-truth expression profiles.
AI.conclusion: The findings motivate a context-dependent view of histology-to-expression prediction, where local morphological representations and gene priors are jointly adapted to the broader tissue context rather than treated as fixed.

title: Stress-Testing EEG Foundation Models for Clinical Decoding: Dataset Identity and Targeted Negative Controls
summary: Pretrained EEG foundation models are increasingly proposed for clinical decoding, but their transfer across populations and robustness to negative controls remain unclear. We benchmark six models (LaBraM, EEGMamba, CBraMod, REVE, BENDR, and BIOT) on five clinical tasks across four datasets using frozen linear probes with leave-one-subject-out, subject-grouped, or explicitly identified recording-level splits. Selected REVE findings are tested against random initialisation, random features, label permutation, scrambled-label fine-tuning, and projection sensitivity. On Korean dementia (CAUEEG, three-way), frozen REVE reaches 0.568 AUROC versus 0.769 for classical features; the ordering persists on a patient-disjoint held-out split (0.565 versus 0.768). Dataset identity is readily decoded from frozen embeddings (AUROC 1.000 at PCA-50; 0.9998 after band restriction and per-epoch z-scoring), whereas the same PCA-50 pipeline decodes Korean diagnosis at 0.528. A randomly initialised encoder also outperforms pretrained REVE on this task (0.659 versus 0.570). On Alzheimer's disease, Gaussian random projection and PCA of the same pretrained embeddings perform similarly, and classical features nominally exceed REVE at the subject level. The clearest controlled positive is cross-subject ictal detection on CHB-MIT (n=23), where REVE achieves 0.793 AUROC, 9.2 percentage points above a randomly initialised encoder. These results show that EEG foundation-model conclusions depend strongly on evaluation unit, dataset shift, comparator strength, and targeted controls.

AI.tldr: Benchmarking six EEG foundation models across five clinical tasks reveals that their apparent performance is heavily influenced by evaluation design, with dataset identity decoded nearly perfectly from embeddings, classical features often matching or exceeding pretrained representations, and only cross-subject seizure detection showing clear positive transfer over random initialization.
AI.motivation: To systematically assess whether pretrained EEG foundation models genuinely transfer across populations and clinical conditions, given that their robustness to negative controls and sensitivity to evaluation splits remain poorly understood.
AI.method: Benchmarked six EEG foundation models (LaBraM, EEGMamba, CBraMod, REVE, BENDR, BIOT) on five clinical tasks across four datasets using frozen linear probing with rigorous splitting (leave-one-subject-out, subject-grouped, recording-level). Applied targeted controls: random initialization, random features, label permutation, scrambled-label fine-tuning, and projection sensitivity analysis.
AI.result: REVE reached 0.568 AUROC on Korean dementia vs 0.769 for classical features. Dataset identity decoded at AUROC 1.000 from embeddings but Korean diagnosis only 0.528. Randomly initialized encoder outperformed pretrained REVE (0.659 vs 0.570). Alzheimer's task showed similar performance between random projection and PCA. Only cross-subject seizure detection (CHB-MIT) showed clear benefit: 0.793 AUROC, 9.2 points above random initialization.
AI.conclusion: EEG foundation model conclusions depend strongly on evaluation unit, dataset shift, comparator strength, and targeted controls; many reported gains may reflect dataset confounders rather than genuine clinical transfer.

title: Towards High-Level Semantic Intelligence
summary: Recent advances in AI have substantially expanded its cognitive and reasoning capabilities. From the perspective of semantic complexity, the development of AI reveals a clear trajectory from simple to complex semantic processing. While early AI systems mainly addressed tasks involving direct and literal semantic perception or expression, contemporary systems are increasingly expected to perform more sophisticated cognitive reasoning, enabling the understanding and generation of High-Level Semantics (HLS). A similar trajectory can also be observed in human cognitive development. We define this transition as the shift from Basic-Level Semantic Intelligence (BLSI) to High-Level Semantic Intelligence (HLSI). However, this issue has not yet been systematically and comprehensively examined in prior work. Motivated by this gap, this survey reviews the development of AI semantic intelligence from the perspective of semantic complexity. We systematically survey existing research on HLS tasks, including humor, sarcasm, metaphor, empathy, persuasion, narrative, and other general HLS phenomena, across text, speech, vision, and multimodal scenarios. Specifically, we summarize data construction methods, modeling and optimization strategies, and evaluation methodologies for both understanding and generation. HLS is essential for advancing AI toward genuinely human-like intelligence. By synthesizing existing methods and insights from the perspective of semantic intelligence, this survey aims to support the continued development of AI toward HLSI.

AI.tldr: This survey examines the shift from Basic-Level Semantic Intelligence (BLSI) to High-Level Semantic Intelligence (HLSI) in AI, reviewing tasks like humor, sarcasm, metaphor, empathy, persuasion, and narrative across text, speech, vision, and multimodal domains, covering data construction, modeling, optimization, and evaluation methods.
AI.motivation: The transition from basic to high-level semantic intelligence in AI has not been systematically examined in prior work, despite its importance for achieving human-like intelligence.
AI.method: The authors systematically survey HLS tasks (humor, sarcasm, metaphor, empathy, persuasion, narrative, etc.) across text, speech, vision, and multimodal scenarios, summarizing data construction, modeling/optimization strategies, and evaluation methodologies for both understanding and generation.
AI.result: A comprehensive taxonomy and synthesis of existing approaches to High-Level Semantic Intelligence across modalities, including data construction methods, modeling strategies, and evaluation frameworks.
AI.conclusion: High-Level Semantics is essential for advancing AI toward genuinely human-like intelligence, and this survey aims to support continued development toward HLSI.

title: Ambient pressure compensation and robust position control of oil-filled electric joint systems for underwater manipulators
summary: Electric joint systems are significant elements of an underwater manipulator for its actuation, drive, and control. Working in an underwater environment, the joints suffer huge ambient pressure. To withstand it, the pressure compensation method is usually deployed, whereas the pressurized oil introduces sealing problems as well as parametric uncertainties and unknown disturbances for the dynamic model of the joint. To tackle these issues, this study proposes a design framework for the underwater oil-filled electric joint. The dynamics of the pressure compensation module is analyzed and the structure of the joint is optimized to seal the internal hydraulic oil. An uncertainty dynamic model of the oil-filled joint is established and a robust position controller is designed based on the structured singular value synthesis (mu-synthesis). Experimental results validate the feasibility of the proposed methods.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a design framework for underwater oil-filled electric joints, including structural optimization for sealing, uncertainty dynamic modeling, and a robust mu-synthesis-based position controller to handle pressure compensation issues and parametric uncertainties.
AI.motivation: Underwater manipulator joints face huge ambient pressure; conventional pressure compensation using pressurized oil introduces sealing problems, parametric uncertainties, and unknown disturbances that degrade dynamic model accuracy and control performance.
AI.method: The study analyzes the dynamics of the pressure compensation module, optimizes the joint structure for oil sealing, establishes an uncertainty dynamic model of the oil-filled joint, and designs a robust position controller using structured singular value synthesis (mu-synthesis).
AI.result: Experimental results validate the feasibility of the proposed design framework and control approach for underwater oil-filled electric joints.
AI.conclusion: The proposed design framework effectively addresses sealing and control challenges in underwater oil-filled electric joints, with validated experimental performance.

title: FlowCTS: On-policy Continuous Trajectory Supervision of Flow Models
summary: While on-policy distillation (OPD) effectively addresses sparse rewards and exposure bias in large language model post-training, its extension to flow models remains underexplored. To this end, we propose Flow Continuous Trajectory Supervision (FlowCTS), which matches subsequent student and reference trajectories initialized from the same student-visited state. Using the integral relation between trajectories and velocity fields, we derive a temporally weighted velocity-matching upper bound and discretize it into practical objectives parameterized by the number of supervision steps. Under a multi-reference setup, single-state FlowCTS-OPD outperforms vanilla KL-based OPD with faster convergence. FlowCTS-OPD improves GenEval from 0.90 to 0.93, OCR from 0.90 to 0.92, and PickScore from 22.75 to 23.06, while outperforming a mixed-reward RL baseline across all target metrics. Further analysis reveals a clear temporal supervision mismatch in vanilla KL-based OPD arising from its auxiliary SDE transition kernels. Beyond on-policy setting,FlowCTS also consistently outperforms vanilla SFT , particularly on OCR, while increasing supervision steps exhibit a trade-off between richer trajectory information and greater optimization difficulty.

AI.tldr: FlowCTS extends on-policy distillation to flow models by matching student/reference trajectories from the same student-visited state using temporally weighted velocity-matching, achieving improved GenEval (0.90→0.93), OCR (0.90→0.92), and PickScore (22.75→23.06) over vanilla KL-based OPD.
AI.motivation: On-policy distillation (OPD) effectively addresses sparse rewards and exposure bias in LLM post-training, but its extension to flow models remains unexplored.
AI.method: FlowCTS derives a temporally weighted velocity-matching upper bound from the integral relation between trajectories and velocity fields, discretized into practical objectives. It matches subsequent student/reference trajectories initialized from the same student-visited state under a multi-reference setup.
AI.result: Single-state FlowCTS-OPD outperforms vanilla KL-based OPD with faster convergence: GenEval 0.90→0.93, OCR 0.90→0.92, PickScore 22.75→23.06, and surpasses mixed-reward RL baseline on all metrics.
AI.conclusion: Vanilla KL-based OPD suffers from temporal supervision mismatch due to auxiliary SDE transition kernels. FlowCTS consistently outperforms vanilla SFT, especially on OCR, with a trade-off between richer trajectory information and optimization difficulty as supervision steps increase.

title: MemChain: Learning Interpretable Memory Traces for Memory-Augmented LLM Agents
summary: Memory-augmented LLM agents typically answer queries by retrieving relevant memories and feeding them directly to an answer model. This retrieval-as-evidence paradigm assumes retrieved memories are already suitable for reasoning, leaving the answer model to resolve redundancy, conflicts, and weak relevance while incurring substantial context overhead in long-term memory tasks. We propose MemChain, a trainable post-retrieval memory policy that transforms retrieved candidates into answer-facing active memory, represented as a compact and grounded evidence context. Given a user query and retrieved candidates, MemChain first generates a question-conditioned evidence plan, then constructs an ordered grounded evidence trace that organizes retrieved memories according to their semantic roles and dependencies, and finally executes explicit memory actions to produce a concise evidence context for answer generation. To train the mediator, we introduce a two-stage learning framework. Supervised trace learning first teaches the policy to generate structurally valid plans, traces, actions, and evidence contexts. We then propose Trace-Guided Memory Policy Optimization (TMPO), a reinforcement learning objective that optimizes the memory policy using downstream answer quality while jointly encouraging trace grounding, evidence support, structural validity, and answer stability across multiple rollouts. Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S demonstrate that MemChain consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance across both closed-source and open-weight frozen answer models while substantially reducing the memory context passed to the answer model.

AI.tldr: MemChain is a trainable post-retrieval memory policy that transforms retrieved candidates into compact, grounded evidence contexts for LLM agents, using supervised trace learning and TMPO reinforcement learning to improve answer quality while reducing memory context overhead.
AI.motivation: Current memory-augmented LLM agents use a retrieval-as-evidence paradigm that passes retrieved memories directly to the answer model, causing issues with redundancy, conflicts, weak relevance, and substantial context overhead in long-term memory tasks.
AI.method: MemChain proposes a three-step process: (1) question-conditioned evidence plan generation, (2) ordered grounded evidence trace construction organizing memories by semantic roles/dependencies, (3) explicit memory actions to produce concise evidence context. Training uses two-stage learning: supervised trace learning for structural validity, followed by Trace-Guided Memory Policy Optimization (TMPO) using reinforcement learning to optimize answer quality with grounding, evidence support, structural validity, and stability constraints.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S benchmarks across both closed-source and open-weight frozen answer models, while substantially reducing memory context passed to the answer model.
AI.conclusion: Post-retrieval memory policies can effectively transform retrieved memories into compact, grounded evidence, improving answer quality and reducing context overhead in long-term memory tasks for LLM agents.

title: GenSplatCodec: Feed-Forward Gaussian Splatting Compression via One-Step Diffusion
summary: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables scalable scene reconstruction without per-scene optimization, yet produces dense Gaussians that are costly to store and transmit. Existing feed-forward Gaussian compression methods formulate decoding as deterministic representation recovery, which becomes inadequate at low bitrates when high-frequency textures and view-dependent appearance are discarded. Although generative models offer a promising alternative, using them as standalone post-processing decouples generation from the transmitted scene structure, thereby compromising cross-view consistency. To address these limitations, we propose GenSplatCodec, a unified feed-forward Gaussian codec that reformulates low-bitrate Gaussian compression as geometry-guided generative decoding. We present a detail-aware feed-forward Gaussian coding scheme within a dual-stream formulation, where the resulting compact Gaussian structural stream is complemented by a lightweight reference appearance stream. We further introduce a geometry-guided one-step generative decoding approach that jointly exploits decoded structural and appearance cues through hierarchical geometry control to reconstruct high-fidelity and view-consistent novel views. Finally, we develop a three-stage optimization strategy that stabilizes the learning of the unified codec and adapts the generative decoder to codec-derived structural and appearance cues. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate that GenSplatCodec consistently achieves superior rate-distortion (RD) performance over existing methods.

AI.tldr: GenSplatCodec is a unified feed-forward Gaussian codec that reformulates low-bitrate 3D Gaussian Splatting compression as geometry-guided generative decoding, achieving superior rate-distortion performance via a dual-stream formulation, hierarchical geometry control, and a three-stage optimization strategy.
AI.motivation: Existing feed-forward Gaussian compression methods use deterministic decoding that underperforms at low bitrates, while generative models used as post-processing lack cross-view consistency. The goal is to achieve high-fidelity, view-consistent reconstruction at low bitrates.
AI.method: A dual-stream coding scheme (compact Gaussian structural stream + lightweight reference appearance stream) with geometry-guided one-step generative decoding using hierarchical geometry control, trained via a three-stage optimization strategy.
AI.result: Consistently achieves superior rate-distortion (RD) performance over existing methods across multiple datasets.
AI.conclusion: GenSplatCodec effectively bridges generative modeling and scene structure for low-bitrate 3DGS compression, outperforming prior work in both fidelity and view consistency.

title: From Machine Learning to Large-Scale EO Products: Best Practices for Making Maps
comment: ECCV 2026 TerraBytes II Workshop paper, non-archival
summary: Recent years have seen a rapid expansion in the production of large-scale geospatial maps derived from Earth observation (EO) data, driven largely by advances in machine learning (ML) and large computing infrastructure. Although the barrier to generating such maps has dropped substantially, established best practices have yet to emerge, and design decisions made early in the pipeline can quietly propagate errors into the final product. Producing a technically sound and scientifically credible product remains challenging. Choices made at every stage are tightly coupled: preprocessing decisions shape the training signal, dataset design governs what the model can learn and how reliably its performance can be assessed, and global-scale inference introduces engineering challenges in compute and data access at scale, as well as artifact mitigation. Furthermore, uncertainty quantification and independent map validation each require dedicated methodological attention that is often underestimated. This paper presents a concise, end-to-end account of the recommended practices spanning the pipeline from satellite data to an operational map product. We organize the discussion around six interconnected themes: the EO data infrastructure landscape, data selection and preprocessing, ML dataset construction and model training, uncertainty quantification, map production and distribution, and validation. This paper is a condensed version of a longer guide that provides greater depth across all stages, accessible online at ghjuliasialelli.github.io/MLEO-Maps/.

AI.tldr: This paper provides recommended end-to-end practices for producing large-scale geospatial maps from Earth observation data using machine learning, covering six interconnected themes: EO data infrastructure, data selection/preprocessing, ML dataset construction/training, uncertainty quantification, map production/distribution, and validation.
AI.motivation: Despite advances in ML and computing infrastructure lowering the barrier to generating geospatial maps from EO data, established best practices are lacking. Design decisions made early in the pipeline can propagate errors into final products, and producing scientifically credible maps remains challenging due to tightly coupled choices across preprocessing, dataset design, inference, uncertainty quantification, and validation.
AI.method: The paper presents a concise, end-to-end account of recommended practices organized around six interconnected themes: (1) EO data infrastructure landscape, (2) data selection and preprocessing, (3) ML dataset construction and model training, (4) uncertainty quantification, (5) map production and distribution, and (6) validation. It is a condensed version of a longer online guide.
AI.result: The paper synthesizes recommended best practices across the entire pipeline from satellite data to operational map products, addressing how choices at each stage are coupled and how to mitigate artifacts and errors at global scale.
AI.conclusion: Producing technically sound and credible geospatial maps requires careful consideration of tightly coupled design decisions across the entire pipeline. This work provides a structured framework of recommended practices, with a more detailed version available online.

title: Scaling GUI Agents with Visual State Transitions
summary: We introduce State Transition Pretraining (STP) as a new scaling axis for GUI agents. During the STP stage, we continually pretrain a unified multimodal model on visual state transitions by jointly optimizing inverse dynamics (predicting actions from state changes) and forward dynamics (predicting next states from current states and actions). This optimization equips the model with better action-grounded visual representations and an internal world model of GUI dynamics. When subsequently fine-tuned on trajectories with task instructions, our STP-trained models consistently outperform baselines trained solely via direct trajectory fine-tuning across agent benchmarks in both desktop and mobile GUI scenarios (AgentNetBench, AndroidControl, and GUIOdyssey). Further empirical studies show that joint dynamics optimization yields stable improvements over single-objective training, and downstream performance scales steadily with the volume of transition data.

AI.tldr: State Transition Pretraining (STP) is a new scaling axis for GUI agents that uses joint inverse and forward dynamics optimization on visual state transitions, consistently outperforming baselines in desktop and mobile benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing GUI agents lack action-grounded visual representations and an internal world model of GUI dynamics, limiting their ability to understand state transitions and generalize across environments.
AI.method: STP continually pretrains a unified multimodal model on visual state transitions using joint optimization of inverse dynamics (predicting actions from state changes) and forward dynamics (predicting next states from current states and actions).
AI.result: STP-trained models consistently outperform baselines across AgentNetBench, AndroidControl, and GUIOdyssey in both desktop and mobile scenarios; joint dynamics optimization outperforms single-objective training; downstream performance scales steadily with transition data volume.
AI.conclusion: Joint dynamics optimization during pretraining provides stable improvements, and STP serves as a scalable approach for building better GUI agents through state transition data.

title: Mixture-of-Thought-Tokens: Unifying Perception and Reasoning for Free-form Multimodal Grounding
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models have made great progress in grounding tasks, yet existing methods still struggle to unify precise localization and complex reasoning. For one thing, text-based methods rely on coordinates or index prediction, severely limiting the perceptual capabilities of the model for dense visual objects. Meanwhile, latent token-based methods employ special tokens without inherent spatial references and use a decoding mechanism that lacks thinking steps, weakening high-level reasoning capabilities. Consequently, developing a unified framework that excels in both perception and reasoning remains challenging. To address this, we propose Mixture-of-Thought-Tokens (Motto), a new free-form multimodal grounding method that bridges the perception-reasoning gap, enabling MLLMs to empower diverse, arbitrary grounding queries. Specifically, we introduce Spatially-Grounded Thought Tokenization to explicitly align special tokens with spatial locations for clear spatial correspondence and visual interpretability. We further design a Context-Adaptive Chain-of-Tokens that dynamically switch grounding modes within an interleaved reasoning chain, achieving robust grounding across tasks of varying complexity. In addition, we construct PR-Bench, a new referring expression comprehension benchmark to evaluate the perception-reasoning gap. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Motto achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse free-form grounding tasks.

AI.tldr: Motto introduces Mixture-of-Thought-Tokens, a free-form multimodal grounding method that bridges perception and reasoning gaps in MLLMs via spatially-grounded thought tokenization and context-adaptive chain-of-tokens, achieving SOTA on diverse grounding tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing MLLMs struggle to unify precise localization and complex reasoning. Text-based methods limit visual perception via coordinates/index prediction, while latent token-based methods lack spatial references and reasoning steps, creating a perception-reasoning gap.
AI.method: (1) Spatially-Grounded Thought Tokenization: aligns special tokens with spatial locations for clear correspondence and interpretability. (2) Context-Adaptive Chain-of-Tokens: dynamically switches grounding modes within an interleaved reasoning chain. (3) PR-Bench: a new benchmark for evaluating the perception-reasoning gap.
AI.result: Motto achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse free-form grounding tasks, demonstrating superior perception and reasoning capabilities.
AI.conclusion: Motto effectively bridges the perception-reasoning gap in multimodal grounding via thought tokenization and adaptive reasoning chains, setting a new SOTA for free-form grounding.

title: The K-SCAN Clustering Algorithm
summary: In the Big Data era, the scalability of clustering algorithms constitutes a key challenge. Traditional density-based methods (e.g., DBSCAN) offer robustness to noise and the ability to detect non-linear clusters, yet their quadratic time complexity $O(N^2)$ drastically limits their applicability. Conversely, partitional algorithms (e.g., K-Means), with their linear complexity $O(N)$, impose sphericity on the resulting groups and fail in the presence of outliers. This paper presents K-SCAN -- a novel hybrid algorithm that optimizes this trade-off. The method integrates preliminary vector quantization (stochastic Mini-Batch K-Means) to extract a reduced set of weighted micro-clusters, followed by a subsequent density-based structural analysis. Empirical evaluation on datasets of up to $10^6$ samples confirms the linear computational complexity of the proposed solution. K-SCAN achieves more than a 3-fold speed-up over the hierarchical BIRCH algorithm, avoiding the costly management of tree-based structures. The method precisely identifies non-linear manifolds while maintaining structural stability (Adjusted Rand Index > 0.99), even with noise levels reaching 55\% of the data volume. The main limitation of the proposed algorithm, which could not be fully eliminated in the present study, remains its susceptibility to over-smoothing and its difficulty in separating clusters with highly heterogeneous local density. In complex visual spaces, this can lead to the loss of the finest topological details.

AI.tldr: K-SCAN is a hybrid clustering algorithm combining Mini-Batch K-Means for vector quantization with density-based analysis, achieving linear O(N) complexity and over 3x speedup vs BIRCH while maintaining >0.99 ARI even with 55% noise, though limited by over-smoothing and difficulty with heterogeneous density clusters.
AI.motivation: Traditional clustering methods face a trade-off: density-based methods (DBSCAN) are robust to noise and detect non-linear clusters but have quadratic O(N²) complexity, while partitional methods (K-Means) have linear O(N) complexity but impose spherical cluster shapes and fail with outliers. The paper aims to design a hybrid algorithm that achieves the best of both worlds — linear scalability with density-based structural flexibility.
AI.method: The K-SCAN algorithm operates in two stages: (1) preliminary vector quantization using stochastic Mini-Batch K-Means to extract a reduced set of weighted micro-clusters, followed by (2) density-based structural analysis on these micro-clusters to identify non-linear cluster structures.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on datasets up to 10⁶ samples demonstrates linear computational complexity, over 3-fold speed-up compared to BIRCH, and high structural stability (ARI > 0.99) even with noise levels up to 55%. The method effectively identifies non-linear manifolds.
AI.conclusion: K-SCAN successfully optimizes the scalability-robustness trade-off by combining linear-time vector quantization with density-based analysis. However, it remains susceptible to over-smoothing and struggles to separate clusters with highly heterogeneous local density, potentially losing fine topological details in complex visual spaces.

title: Grading the Narrators: An Isnad-Rijal Framework for Claim-Level Provenance in Multi-Agent Knowledge Systems
comment: 25 pages. Code, data, and analysis: https://github.com/alizahidraja/isnad (v2.0.4). Software archived at doi:10.5281/zenodo.21216873
summary:
Modern multi-agent knowledge systems increasingly accumulate knowledge through chains of autonomous transformations rather than direct retrieval. Existing provenance work records what happened - execution traces, tool calls, evidence links - and source-reliability estimation is long established (truth discovery, reputation systems). What is missing is an operational framework that attaches graded, per-domain transmitter reliability to claim-level transmission chains, with completeness semantics, transformation-typed aggregation, decoupled content criticism, and serve/review/quarantine routing.
  Classical Islamic hadith science confronted a structurally similar problem: deciding whether knowledge transmitted through chains of human narrators should be accepted. Over centuries it developed a rigorous methodology - isnad (a complete transmission chain attached to every claim), rijal (systematic grading of each narrator's integrity and precision), weakest-link chain evaluation, corroboration through independent chains, and matn criticism (content evaluated independently of chain quality). This paper transfers that methodology to AI system design.
  We contribute a formal mapping from hadith-science concepts to multi-agent pipelines, a relational schema implementing claim chains and a graded narrator registry, a decision matrix combining chain grade with content criticism, and an evaluation on 20,000 claims from real physics textbooks. The evaluation validates weakest-link quarantine and independent-chain corroboration; reports a partial failure of the grade-recovery loop, which missed the highest-fault narrator; and reports two analyses as inconclusive, including a matched-coverage comparison the framework could not reach with the reference content critic. The paper is explicit throughout about which claims the evidence does and does not yet support.

AI.tldr: This paper transfers classical Islamic hadith science methodology—isnad (transmission chains), rijal (narrator grading), weakest-link evaluation, corroboration, and matn (content) criticism—to multi-agent AI knowledge systems, providing a formal mapping, relational schema, decision matrix, and evaluation on 20,000 physics textbook claims. Results validate weakest-link quarantine and corroboration but report a partial grade-recovery failure and two inconclusive analyses.
AI.motivation: Existing provenance work records execution traces and source reliability (truth discovery, reputation systems) but lacks an operational framework for graded, per-domain transmitter reliability with completeness semantics, transformation-typed aggregation, decoupled content criticism, and routing (serve/review/quarantine) for claim-level transmission chains in multi-agent knowledge systems.
AI.method: The paper transfers classical Islamic hadith science methodology to AI system design: (1) formal mapping from hadith concepts to multi-agent pipelines; (2) relational schema implementing claim chains and a graded narrator registry; (3) decision matrix combining chain grade with content criticism; (4) evaluation on 20,000 claims from real physics textbooks.
AI.result: Weakest-link quarantine and independent-chain corroboration were validated. A partial failure of the grade-recovery loop occurred (missed the highest-fault narrator). Two analyses were inconclusive, including a matched-coverage comparison the framework could not reach with the reference content critic.
AI.conclusion: The hadith-inspired framework is largely viable for multi-agent knowledge systems, with explicit acknowledgment of which claims the evidence does and does not yet support. However, the grade-recovery loop and certain coverage comparisons require further work.

title: Accuracy potential of visual localization exploiting high-end street-level imagery
summary: Accurate and reliable pose information with respect to a reference frame is increasingly demanded across applications such as autonomous navigation, surveying, robotics, and augmented and mixed reality. Visual localization can serve as a complementary positioning modality to GNSS, whose applicability and accuracy are often limited. Yet, the accuracy potential of visual localization has not been systematically investigated against survey-grade demands. This is mainly due to the lack of publicly available, large-scale outdoor datasets with ground-truth poses in the sub-centimeter range. In this work, we address both gaps. We introduce a scalable visual localization pipeline that employs precisely georeferenced, high-resolution street-level imagery directly as the scene representation. It combines prior-guided reference candidate selection with on-the-fly local Structure-from-Motion reconstruction and PnP-based pose estimation. We further present the FHNW Muttenz dataset, a real-world dataset covering a contiguous 10 km street network mapped in two mobile mapping campaigns approximately 1.5 years apart. It consists of high-resolution reference imagery and query sequences acquired by four different cameras across five representative scenes. All images are precisely co-registered, yielding 6-DoF ground-truth poses in the sub-centimeter range. Using this dataset, we evaluate the accuracy potential of visual localization. Our experiments demonstrate median pose accuracies in the range of 1-5 cm for translation and 0.05-0.1° for rotation, reaching as low as 1 cm and 0.03° under favorable conditions. These results show that visual localization can complement survey-grade GNSS positioning, paving the way for 3D geospatial data acquisition using consumer devices and fully automated georeferencing approaches. The dataset is publicly available at: https://fhnw-muttenz-vl-dataset.github.io/.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a visual localization pipeline achieving sub-centimeter-to-centimeter-level pose accuracy using precisely georeferenced street-level imagery, validated on a new public dataset (FHNW Muttenz) covering 10 km of street networks with survey-grade ground truth, demonstrating that visual localization can complement GNSS for high-precision geospatial applications.
AI.motivation: Despite growing demand for accurate pose information, the accuracy potential of visual localization against survey-grade requirements has not been systematically investigated due to the lack of large-scale outdoor datasets with sub-centimeter ground-truth poses.
AI.method: A scalable visual localization pipeline combining prior-guided reference candidate selection, on-the-fly local Structure-from-Motion (SfM) reconstruction, and PnP-based pose estimation using precisely georeferenced high-resolution street-level imagery as the scene representation. A new dataset (FHNW Muttenz) was created with two mobile mapping campaigns (1.5 years apart) covering 10 km of street networks, featuring four different cameras and sub-centimeter 6-DoF ground-truth poses.
AI.result: Median pose accuracies of 1-5 cm for translation and 0.05-0.1° for rotation, reaching as low as 1 cm and 0.03° under favorable conditions, across five representative scenes using four different cameras.
AI.conclusion: Visual localization can effectively complement survey-grade GNSS positioning, enabling 3D geospatial data acquisition using consumer devices and fully automated georeferencing approaches.

title: EchoBridge: Long-Tail-Aware ECG-Echocardiography Text Alignment for Echocardiography-Derived Cardiac Findings
summary: Standardized echocardiography conclusions provide meaningful supervision for learning ECG representations of echocardiography-derived cardiac findings. Global ECG--text alignment may entangle modality-specific factors, while long-tailed finding distributions provide sparse positive supervision for low-prevalence conditions. We propose EchoBridge with Complementary Shared--Private Projection (CSPP) and Adaptive Prototype Boundary Calibration (APBC). CSPP maps each modality into shared and auxiliary private projections, reduces directional redundancy via within-modality orthogonality, and bidirectionally aligns normalized shared projections. APBC organizes the shared hypersphere with class-specific prototypes, training-frequency-adaptive angular margins, and spherical Riesz repulsion. We evaluate EchoBridge on EchoNext-Mini and independent PKUPH and SHTMU cohorts under four protocols: prompt-based inference without downstream classifier training, in-domain frozen linear probing, target-domain cross-center frozen linear probing, and source-only cross-center transfer, supplemented by finding-specific analyses. EchoBridge improves classifier-free AUROC, AUPRC, and F1 over the strongest baselines by 7.88, 5.61, and 4.54 points, respectively, and achieves the highest point estimates across all in-domain and target-domain probing budgets and both source-only transfer cohorts. Finding-specific analyses show gains for most conditions, including several low-prevalence valvular findings.

AI.tldr: EchoBridge uses Complementary Shared-Private Projection and Adaptive Prototype Boundary Calibration to improve ECG representation learning from echocardiography-derived cardiac findings, outperforming baselines across multiple evaluation protocols, especially for low-prevalence conditions.
AI.motivation: Global ECG-text alignment entangles modality-specific factors and long-tailed finding distributions provide sparse supervision for low-prevalence conditions, limiting the effectiveness of standardized echocardiography conclusions for learning ECG representations.
AI.method: Proposes EchoBridge with two components: (1) Complementary Shared-Private Projection (CSPP) which maps modalities into shared and private projections with within-modality orthogonality and bidirectional alignment of normalized shared projections; (2) Adaptive Prototype Boundary Calibration (APBC) which organizes the shared hypersphere with class-specific prototypes, training-frequency-adaptive angular margins, and spherical Riesz repulsion.
AI.result: EchoBridge improves classifier-free AUROC, AUPRC, and F1 over strongest baselines by 7.88, 5.61, and 4.54 points respectively. Achieves highest point estimates across all in-domain and target-domain probing budgets and source-only transfer cohorts, with gains for most conditions including low-prevalence valvular findings.
AI.conclusion: The proposed architectural innovations (CSPP and APBC) effectively address modality entanglement and long-tail supervision challenges in ECG representation learning, demonstrating robust performance across multiple evaluation protocols and clinical cohorts.

title: A Motion-Aware Vector Quantization Framework with Centroid Reuse for Efficient VLA Inference
summary:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong potential for embodied AI, yet their high inference latency on GPUs limits real-time deployment. Existing accelerators, such as Dadu-Corki, improve efficiency but treat VLA models as full-precision workloads, leaving substantial redundancy in both memory and computation underexploited.
  In this paper, we propose VQVLA, an algorithm-hardware co-design framework that accelerates VLA inference by exploiting weight similarity and execution dynamics. We first introduce MotionVQ, a motion-aware vector quantization scheme that dynamically adjusts quantization precision based on the robot's execution state, reducing memory access while preserving task success rate. We then propose a merged-centroid vectorized GEMM paradigm that operates on the codebook-index representation, eliminating redundant multiplications through spatial aggregation and temporal reuse of centroids. To realize these optimizations, we design an accelerator that efficiently supports dynamic precision selection and centroid-reuse computation. Experimental results show that VQVLA achieves 6.5x, 2.8x, 1.9x, 3.3x, and 4.3x speedup over the A100 GPU, Dadu-Corki, LUT-DLA, CodeGEMM, and ShiftAddLLM, respectively, with negligible accuracy degradation.

AI.tldr: VQVLA is an algorithm-hardware co-design framework that accelerates VLA model inference by exploiting weight similarity and execution dynamics through motion-aware vector quantization (MotionVQ) and merged-centroid vectorized GEMM, achieving 1.9x-6.5x speedup over various baselines with negligible accuracy loss.
AI.motivation: VLA models have high inference latency on GPUs, limiting real-time deployment. Existing accelerators like Dadu-Corki treat VLA models as full-precision workloads, leaving significant redundancy in memory and computation unexploited.
